name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri cannabis regulators recall pre-rolled joints after mold found in testing
description: State cannabis regulators issued a recall Wednesday after random testing found mold in pre-rolled joints sold in the state.  The product, Juicy J’s cherry limeade infused pre-rolls, failed testing for Aspergillus, “a common mold that can be tolerated in small amounts by healthy individuals but may cause adverse health effects in high amounts or in […]
text:
Last year, state cannabis regulators began double checking the work of licensed testing labs to catch potential problems with mold, pesticides and other contaminants (Rebecca Rivas/Missouri Independent).State cannabis regulators issued a recall Wednesday after random testing found mold in pre-rolled joints sold in the state. 
The product, Juicy J’s cherry limeade infused pre-rolls, failed testing for Aspergillus, “a common mold that can be tolerated in small amounts by healthy individuals but may cause adverse health effects in high amounts or in individuals with compromised immune systems,” the recall notice states.
No adverse reactions have been reported, according to the Missouri Division of Cannabis Regulation.
The division said it is working with the Waynesville-based manufacturing facility to address the problem. The Independent did not immediately receive a response from the company.
Last year, regulators began double checking the work of licensed testing labs to catch potential problems with mold, pesticides and other contaminants. 
Mold, in particular, has been a concern raised by cannabis testing experts. 
During an MJ Unpacked cannabis conference panel in 2024, testing experts discussed information obtained through the Missouri Sunshine Law that showed 82% of Missouri’s cannabis testing is conducted at one licensed lab, Greenway Magazine reported. The data showed the laboratory detected mold problems far less frequently than other Missouri labs and laboratories nationwide. 
The lab, identified in the data as “Lab D,” reported an Aspergillus failure rate of just under 0.5% — roughly one-eighth the national average. 
The state’s other labs had a failure rate of 3.3%, compared with the national average of 3.8%. 
The disparity raised questions about whether cannabis products were being adequately screened for mold.  However, Ryan Bernard, the division’s testing and research unit manager, told The Independent last year that those results didn’t raise any alarm for him. 
“Everybody’s being held to the same standards as far as testing is concerned,” Bernard said. 
The manufacturer of the recalled Juicy J’s products is owned by CCMRB Processing LLC, whose owners also lead Michigan-based cannabis company Common Citizen. The group also owns a Fresh Karma dispensary through CCMRB Retail LLC, which was named in a lawsuit against Good Day Farm filed in May.
Wednesday’s action is the second cannabis product recall Missouri regulators have issued this month.
The division also issued a recall earlier this month for several products made at a manufacturing facility in Cuba whose parent company is GF Extraction Lab LLC. The ownership group also owns five Root 66 Dispensary locations.  
According to that recall notice, “The recalled products contain cannabinoids produced through chemical modification, conversion, or synthetic derivation of cannabinoids.” 
In previous recalls in which regulators cited the same issue, the products involved hemp or cannabinoids that did not originate in Missouri.
Asked whether the recalled products were properly entered into Metrc, Missouri’s statewide marijuana tracking system, the division’s spokeswoman Lisa Cox said, “We cannot comment at this time due to it being an ongoing investigation.”
The Independent repeatedly sought comment from the owners of GF Extraction Lab but did not receive a response.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Hattiesburg voters pack hearing to oppose redistricting plans
description: Residents address a joint House and Senate panel on redistricting at a hearing in Hattiesburg on Sept. 17, 2026.
text:
HATTIESBURG — Hattiesburg is one of the most crucial areas in Mississippi’s redistricting fight this year, and dozens of its voters packed a room on Thursday night to say they’re opposed to it. 
Only a handful of the many people who addressed the Joint House and Senate Redistricting Committee said that they support efforts altering congressional and state legislative districts. The vast majority said they’re against it because they believe it would waste taxpayer dollars and diminish Black voting power.
“I ask you don’t disenfranchise the citizens that voted for you,” Deanna Douglas said. “Listen to us and please don’t do this.” 
Thursday’s hearing was the sixth in a slate of eight public hearings the committee is holding across the state.
Hattiesburg will be a crucial area in redistricting and would likely determine whether the Republican Party can achieve a two-thirds supermajority in the Senate. 
Lawmakers redrew legislative boundaries in 2022 to create two majority-white Senate districts in Forrest County, the county where Hattiesburg is located. Sen. Chris Johnson and former Sen. John Polk, two white Republicans, represented that area. 
But a federal three-judge panel determined in 2024 that lawmakers diluted Black voting strength in the Pine Belt area and ordered the Legislature to redraw maps. The Legislature followed the court order and in 2025 made one of the districts majority Black. Sen. Johnny DuPree, a Black Democrat, won the seat in a special election later that year. 
The Callais vs. Louisiana U.S. Supreme Court decision removed protection for majority-minority districts and cleared the way for Republican-controlled state legislatures to redraw political lines in their favor. But Forrest County voter Kennen Walker said on Thursday night that he wanted DuPree to continue representing the area. 
“I’m against mid-decade redistricting because I don’t want to lose representation we just voted for,” Walker said. 
Gov. Tate Reeves is expected to call a special legislative session before the end of the year for lawmakers to redraw legislative districts. Will Spradling said he wants the committee to draw districts that elect more Republicans, so that lawmakers enact more conservative policies. 
“Mississippi should be as conservative as states like California are progressive,” Spradling said. “No matter how these lines are drawn, these citizens will have their vote.”  
A few people, including Petal Alderman Drew Brickson, asked legislators to specifically draw maps in a way that keeps the nearby town of Petal fully intact and not split between legislative districts. 
The committee will conduct two more hearings: One on Sept. 22 at Gulf Coast Community College in Gulfport and another on Oct. 1 at the state Capitol in Jackson. Both will start at 6 p.m.
The public can also submit written comments to the committee by emailing ted.booth@peer.ms.gov.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Poll: Most voters favor tapping CT coffers to ease federal social service cuts
description: The poll found that more than half of respondents would ease CT budget caps to bolster human service programs affected by federal cuts,
text:
More than eight in 10 voters support tapping the state’s flush coffers to bolster human service programs weakened by severe federal cutbacks, according to a new poll commissioned by Connecticut nonprofit social service agencies.
The survey released by the CT Community Nonprofit Alliance also found slightly more than half of voters favor these investments, even if it requires adjusting the state budget caps that have forced unprecedented surpluses since their enactment nine years ago.
“I understand the need to save for the future,” Gian-Carl Casa, president and CEO of the alliance, said this week. “But it doesn’t help somebody hungry to get food.”
The poll, conducted online last month by the Connecticut-based STATS Group, surveyed 602 voters and has a 4% margin of error.
State government uses hundreds of community-based nonprofits to deliver the bulk of publicly-sponsored social services to people with disabilities or mental illness, patients struggling with addiction, children with various needs and people re-entering society following incarceration.
The alliance, which represents most of those agencies, has argued in recent years for a major adjustment in state compensation, insisting payments have lagged inflation for more than a decade, costing the industry more than $300 million annually.
Agencies praised the General Assembly and Gov. Ned Lamont last May for boosting funding by roughly $60 million for the fiscal year that began July 1. But they also fear new and impending cuts in federal programs will create a climate of need and demand for aid that swamps all services.
For example, nearly 63,000 residents have lost federal nutrition benefits since Congress and President Donald Trump tightened eligibility last July — roughly double state officials’ projections, New Haven-based Connecticut Voices for Children reported last month.
An estimated 110,000 low-income adults who receive health insurance through the Medicaid-funded HUSKY D program are at risk of losing coverage this January due to new federal work rules. And hundreds of lawfully present immigrants are expected to lose Medicare eligibility — regardless of work status — at the same time.
State officials project the maximum, federally-funded heating and energy assistance benefits this winter will be down 33% from prepandemic levels for Connecticut residents in need.
The survey found 86% of voters want the state, which has run up unprecedented surpluses averaging more than $1.8 billion or about 8% of the General Fund since 2017, to spend Connecticut dollars to ease this pain.
The state has been using those surpluses chiefly to build reserves and reduce the state’s hefty pension debt, which still exceeds $30 billion.
But critics say Connecticut could shift hundreds of millions of dollars toward social services and still wipe out pension debt by a significant margin each year, especially now that the emergency reserve — commonly known as the rainy day fund — holds nearly $4.5 billion or 18% of annual operating costs, the maximum allowed by law.
The survey found 54% of voters favor adjusting the state’s budget caps to redirect more funds to top social services.
And 56% of those surveyed said they would be more likely to support a gubernatorial candidate who wants to adjust those caps to send more funds to community-based nonprofits.
Gov. Ned Lamont, a fiscally moderate Democrat, largely opposed all efforts to modify budget caps during six of his eight years in office, frustrating many liberals in his party.
But the governor compromised and supported several efforts to work around the caps in recent years, including dedicating $712 million outside of the formal budget system to expand affordable childcare. He also declared fiscal emergencies — the first step in legally exceeding the cap — to allow legislators to order more than $280 million in additional municipal aid this spring.
He also helped legislators create a special $550 million fund, also outside of the formal budget, to begin to mitigate cuts to federal programs. Since last November Lamont has used this fund to help low-to-moderate income households purchase health insurance, bolster food pantries, provide $300 grocery store gift cards to 25,000 residents removed from SNAP,  and to assist legally present immigrants that have been stripped of temporary protected status by President Trump’s administration.
But all of that assistance has been one-time in nature, and many legislators are pressing for Connecticut to establish ongoing, state-funded assistance programs for many of these groups.
The governor has not ruled out providing ongoing assistance in some cases, but has cautioned legislators that state government cannot afford to backfill all federal cuts.
“Governor Lamont shares concerns about federal cuts that affect critical services for our residents,” Chris Collibee, the governor’s budget spokesman, said Wednesday. “The Lamont administration continues working with nonprofit providers and legislative leaders to protect essential services while maintaining the fiscal stability that allows us to be there for residents when they need us most.”
Republican gubernatorial nominee Ryan Fazio does not support modifying the caps. But Fazio, a state senator from Greenwich, also says Lamont and legislators have not done enough to cut wasteful spending, which then could have been redirected toward social services.
Fazio and others have criticized Lamont and Democratic legislators for awarding most unionized state employees annual raises around 4.5% since 2022, compensation Republicans say tops most private sector pay hikes.
The GOP also says Democrats have allowed public colleges and universities to spend far too much on administrative costs and also could save on Medicaid by denying benefits to undocumented immigrant adults and children.
Sen. Cathy Osten of Sprague, who co-chairs the Appropriations Committee, is one of several Democrats who predicts the 2027 session will feature an extensive debate on expanding Connecticut’s role in protecting vulnerable residents.
Osten has called for a state-funded benefit to assist those who’ve lost federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, benefits but still cannot work due to mental illness or disability.
As inflation rises and the average price of regular gasoline tops $4.40 per gallon in Connecticut according to the AAA, “it’s becoming dire for people. Their incomes are not going up anywhere near the level the need. And it’s eating into the middle class,” she said.
Rep. Tammy Nuccio of Tolland, ranking House Republican on the Appropriations Committee, said the GOP is ready to find more dollars to assist Connecticut’s most vulnerable.
But for that to happen, she added, majority Democrats in the General Assembly must be ready to hear ideas on cutting wasteful spending.
That effort “has to be fully bipartisan, and not just bipartisan in name,” she said.

name: Nevada Current
title: Lombardo doubles down on data centers, offers trimmed tax breaks, ‘commitments’ to wary public
description: Gov. Joe Lombardo in a new executive order is making clear his eagerness to welcome more AI data centers into the state, calling them “the means by which Nevada will meet an unprecedented challenge and realize an unprecedented opportunity, one of the most significant for economic growth and fiscal diversification this State has seen in […]
text:
The announcement of the governor's executive order was accompanied by a statement issued through the governor's office from the Data Center Coalition, the self-described "voice of the data center industry” whose members include many of the largest players in data centers and AI, including Google, Microsoft, Meta, Anthropic, and Open AI, as well as Nevada data center giant Switch. (Image of Switch data center in Las Vegas from Switch promotional video)Gov. Joe Lombardo in a new executive order is making clear his eagerness to welcome more AI data centers into the state, calling them “the means by which Nevada will meet an unprecedented challenge and realize an unprecedented opportunity, one of the most significant for economic growth and fiscal diversification this State has seen in a generation.”
The Republican governor on Friday is expected to sign an executive order to establish  data center development standards in Nevada.
The executive order, which was provided to media outlets in advance, reduces the amount of sales and use tax data centers are eligible to have abated. It does not eliminate the tax breaks entirely, as some are calling for.
The executive order also requires data centers seeking tax abatements to sign a “community support commitment” intended to ensure that regular and emergency water and power costs are borne solely by the data centers and not by ratepayers. Standards for those commitments must be set by the Governor’s Office of Economic Development by Nov. 6, three days after Election Day.
Lombardo’s executive order comes just days after Axios reported that a Trump pollster warned GOP candidates that “unqualified support for building more AI data centers is a losing position” and they should avoid using the phrase “build more data centers.”
Attorney General Aaron Ford, the Democrat hoping to make Lombardo a one-term governor, has promised to pause data center tax abatements. Ford has called Lombardo and President Trump “data centers’ biggest cheerleaders” and pointed to the $240 million in data center tax breaks handed out during Lombardo’s time in office so far.
Lombardo’s campaign countered that by pointing out Ford helped champion the 2015 legislation to establish the tax abatements for data centers. A PAC affiliated with the Clark County Education Association, which has endorsed Lombardo, attacks Ford on the same grounds.
The 2015 legislation passed with wide bipartisan support when Republicans controlled both houses of the Legislature, and was signed by Republican Gov. Brian Sandoval. Ford and others have emphasized that the conversation surrounding data centers and their projected future utility needs were markedly different during those conversations more than a decade ago.
Nevada Democratic state Sen. Dina Neal, who like Ford has recently come under attack from the CCEA, has noted that when data center tax abatements were being passed in 2015, CCEA itself did not object.
Communities across Nevada have pushed back against plans for data centers. Boulder City is currently fighting an attempt to build one on nearby federal land. Nye County outright banned the development of them. Several state lawmakers have expressed an openness to ending all tax abatements to the industry.
On the opposite end, CCEA earlier this month called for the state to bargain with data centers. The union said its priority was to end the abatement of the local schools support tax, which is a portion of the state’s sales tax.
That proposal aligns with what Lombardo’s executive order does. Currently, data centers can get most of their sales tax abated and pay a reduced 2% sales tax rate. The executive order exempts the local schools support tax from abatements, effectively making the sales tax rate data centers pay 4.6%.
Sales tax for everyone else in Nevada ranges from 7.1% to 8.375%, depending on the county.
Data centers can also get 75% of their personal property tax abated.
In a statement released through the the governor’s office, the Data Center Coalition thanked the governor “for his leadership on this issue and for his willingness to engage directly with all stakeholders as Nevada works through the complex issues associated with data center development.”
The self-described “voice of the data center industry,” the coalition’s members include most of the largest players in data centers and AI, including Google, Microsoft, Meta, Anthropic, and Open AI, as well as Nevada data center giant Switch.
Lombardo’s executive order removing some of the data center industry’s tax abatements would apply only to new data centers and not the tax breaks at existing facilities which have cost the state nearly $340 million in lost tax revenue over fiscal years 2021-2024.

name: Nevada Current
title: Public Utility Commission approves gas plants to power data centers
description: Nevada regulators on Thursday approved the construction of two private methane gas power plants proposed by a major data center developer, which says its power needs have outpaced NV Energy’s ability to supply electricity for a surge of new developments. During a special meeting in Carson City, the Public Utilities Commission of Nevada (PUNC) approved […]
text:
Public Utilities Commission of Nevada Chair Hayley Williamson. (Legislative/PUCN screengrab)Nevada regulators on Thursday approved the construction of two private methane gas power plants proposed by a major data center developer, which says its power needs have outpaced NV Energy’s ability to supply electricity for a surge of new developments.
During a special meeting in Carson City, the Public Utilities Commission of Nevada (PUNC) approved a request by Tract Capital Management and its subsidiary Fleet Data Centers to build two massive methane gas power plants to power projects at and near the Tahoe Reno Industrial Center (TRIC) in Storey County.
Fleet’s Peru Ridge and South Valley gas power plants are the first methane gas-powered electricity supply approved specifically for data center use in Nevada. Once constructed, the gas power plants will generate more than 360-megawatts of electricity, or enough power to serve the equivalent of 396,000 homes. 
In filings, Fleet said that it expects the gas plants to operate between two and three years, “until NV Energy can deliver permanent utility service to the site.”
Regulators said the approval is conditioned on environmental and local permits, including review by the Nevada Division of Environmental Protection and approvals from Storey County.
“No permit will be issued without proper state agency oversight, and I think that’s important to reiterate,” said PUCN Commissioner Randy Brown.
The vote to approve Fleet’s two massive methane gas power plants came after nearly three hours of heated public comment, where Nevadan’s voiced strong opposition to the gas power plants. Opponents urged the commission to deny the proposals, citing health risks from air pollution, climate impacts, and potential harm to Nevada’s air, water, and quality of life.
Nevadans who spoke during heated public comment after the vote said they felt their concerns were being ignored by public utility commissioners.
“I thought you were supposed to represent the people and the utilities, and it feels like everyone here is trying to tell you that we aren’t being heard,” said Elizabeth Bree Kasper, a frequent participant in PUNC hearings. “My follow-up public comment is trying to ask how we can follow up, and the response from everyone here is that there is no follow-up; that we need to just take it.”
PUCN Chair Hayley Williamson said utility commissioners have statutory constraints on what evidence they can consider when evaluating whether a project will serve the public interest.
PUCN Commissioner Tammy Cordova echoed Williamson’s comments, adding that she did “appreciate the comments of everyone who came out today and has taken an interest in our proceedings.”
“It does show something that the community is very interested in, but I think I would be failing in my responsibility if I somehow held this applicant to a different standard or a different set of laws than all of those other applications that the commission has prosecuted over the years,” Cordova said. 
PUCN general counsel Garrett Weir told the crowd that utility commissioners can’t consider public comments as evidence when determining their vote. Weir advised the public to contact the Nevada Attorney General’s Bureau of Consumer Protections, who he said “have an obligation to advocate for the public interest” when it comes to utility cases of public concern. 
“It is tragic that folks show up with expectations that aren’t realistic about what the public comment can actually achieve,” Weir said. 
“The representation in Nevada before the Public Utilities Commission is generally through intervention by the Bureau of Consumer Protection,” said Weir. “In the case that most of the public comments were made on today, the Bureau of Consumer Protection didn’t participate.”
John Sadler, the communications director for the Nevada Office of the Attorney General, said that while the BCP occasionally intervenes in utility proceedings they were confident that Nevadans for Clean Affordable Reliable Energy (NCARE) —  the only organization that intervened in opposition on the case —  could represent the community’s concerns effectively. 
The PUCN “failed to account for evidence that was placed directly before them. The commissioners’ disregard for that evidence, while issuing a ruling that favored the applicants, represents a genuine failure of their public duty,” Sadler said. 
Western Resource Advocates, representing Nevadans for Clean Affordable Reliable Energy (NCARE), intervened before the Commission in a hearing on July 30 to challenge Fleet’s proposal to build two private methane gas power plants. The organization has the right to appeal the PUCN’s decision as an intervening party.
Private gas plants to power data centers would skirt state’s renewable energy law

“We’re disappointed in today’s outcome and will be exploring next steps,” said George Cavros, senior attorney at WRA. “Western Resource Advocates represented Nevadans for Clean Affordable Reliable Energy in these cases to give everyday Nevadans a voice as a party to these proceedings, and to ensure the Commission applied transparent and meaningful analysis under the Utility Environmental Protection Act.”
The coalition argued approval of Fleet’s proposal would bypass Nevada’s renewable energy portfolio standard, which mandates power providers utilize 50% renewable energy by 2030.
Fleet maintains that its methane gas power plants are not subject to the state’s renewable energy portfolio standard because it is not technically an energy provider like NV Energy.
In PUCN filings, NCARE said the size and capacity of the private gas power plants would nearly rival utility scale methane gas plants across the U.S., where about 80% of gas power plants average about 500 megawatts or less.
An analysis by NCARE found that the new gas-burning plants, if built to specifications, would burn about three times as much methane gas as NV Energy’s entire Northern Nevada residential and commercial customer base in 2025, or enough gas to supply about 652,000 homes.
If the new gas-burning plants were operating in 2025, Nevada’s emissions would have increased by nearly 12%, according to NCARE’s analysis.
Sadler criticized the PUCN for giving “no apparent weight” to NCARE’s testimony when evaluating whether the gas power plants would serve the public interest.
“The PUCN’s current attempt at damage control is disingenuous. Telling today’s public commenters that their concerns weren’t part of the evidentiary record is simply false — NCARE introduced that same evidence, and in fact amplified those very issues during the due process hearing,” Sadler said.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: What will we do when all the newsrooms go dark?
description: Late last week, I woke in the middle of the night with vertigo. The floating ear-crystals kind where the room spins and spins, floor-to-ceiling, and for which the cure is to do something called the Epley maneuver which, for seconds that feel like hours, intensifies the spinning, making you feel like you have slipped gravity […]
text:
The Lexington Herald-Leader recently laid off a majority of its staff. (Julia Shumway/Oregon Capital Chronicle)Late last week, I woke in the middle of the night with vertigo. The floating ear-crystals kind where the room spins and spins, floor-to-ceiling, and for which the cure is to do something called the Epley maneuver which, for seconds that feel like hours, intensifies the spinning, making you feel like you have slipped gravity until the spinning finally, mercifully, slows and stops.
Also late last week, the Lexington Herald-Leader gutted its newsroom.
Veteran reporter John Cheves shared this news on Comment on Kentucky, saying, in part, “It’s popular in some quarters to sort of sneer and then mock newspapers, or to greet with apathy the demise of newspapers, but I can assure you you’re gonna miss us when we’re gone.”
It is popular to sneer and mock. But as someone who already lives in the small-town news desert of Anderson County, KY — where there are, to my knowledge, at least two complex local investigations that need to be done, but no one is here to do them — I already have a too-real sense of what he means.
Last week was also the 25th anniversary of 9/11, and I repeatedly thought of that last part from Cheves — you’re gonna miss us when we’re gone — as I rested my head to keep from triggering the vertigo and listened to dozens of archived news reports from the morning of 9/11 and the months and years that followed. Virtually every story was from 60 Minutes or other accredited news sources, including local newspapers and TV stations that were trusted by everyone from grieving families to fire departments to companies who’d been housed in the World Trade Center trying not only to recover their businesses, but to support families of employees who’d died or were still listed as missing.
You can’t do this without thinking about today’s fractured media landscape.
Consider:  If a 9/11 happened today, would you know the difference between a true or false report? Could you trust an “influencer” — or a hundred “influencers” — over credentialed journalists? How would you know which photos and videos are real, or if someone’s statement had been fairly edited? Who might a vulnerable, grieving family trust with their story? How many scams and false reports would there be due to jackals just trying to get clicks and make a buck?
Considering the preponderance of lies and AI-slop produced daily by the U.S. President himself — on his own social media platform and on video/microphone — how will we know what to believe or what to do in a national emergency?
Because in 2026, that’s where we are.
And here comes AI.
I read and watch a lot of conservative news these days. Not Fox or OANN— that’s not news, that’s junk food — but serious, professionally edited outlets like The Dispatch and the Wall Street Journal. If you’d have told me 10 years ago that my information diet would soon include men like Jonah Goldberg, Kevin D. Williamson, and Robert Kagan, to name a few, I’d have laughed. And yet I am increasingly convinced that, just like the regular physical exercise we abhor, the daily exercise of considering opposing arguments, of talking to each other, of being able to separate straight reporting from thoughtful opinion while being open to both, are the keys to our sanity and our future.
I was talking recently with a local friend who does not agree with me politically. We both miss having a robust, local newspaper. “We have no idea who we are as a community anymore,” they said. 
One of the 9/11 stories I listened to over the weekend, while I kept my head still, was with veteran Associate Press photographer Richard Drew from the 60 Minutes archive. “My job is to record history every day,” he said. And when John Dickerson asked him what happens without the focus on facts and history?  “You’re not a journalist,” Drew said. “Then you’re just a person with a camera.”
What will we do when the newsrooms go dark?
When we are flooded with so many photos and videos and stories from so many sources that we don’t know what’s real?
When there is no one left with the resources, protections, and skills to conduct proper investigations and hold the powerful to account?
When we find ourselves out searching the massive, disorienting swirl of information, how will we find our history?
As with vertigo, the room spins.

name: Nevada Current
title: Incumbent NSHE regent challenged by UNR public health professor
description: Peter Reed, a long-time UNR professor, is challenging Nevada System of Higher Education regent Joseph Arrascada, who is seeking a second term, in the upcoming election for District 10.  Arrascada, who was first elected in 2020, said he wants another term representing Northern Nevada constituents in order to provide continuity and build on the work […]
text:
Joseph Arrascada and Peter Reed (Candidate photos)Peter Reed, a long-time UNR professor, is challenging Nevada System of Higher Education regent Joseph Arrascada, who is seeking a second term, in the upcoming election for District 10. 
Arrascada, who was first elected in 2020, said he wants another term representing Northern Nevada constituents in order to provide continuity and build on the work he has done in his first term. He said that consistent representation would benefit constituents and prevent   
“Right now, the system is flourishing, and it’s doing well with the leadership in place,” Arrascada said. 
Peter Reed, a professor in the school of public health, said he is running because he believes the board, and the future of higher education, would benefit from having insight from a faculty member. 
“I believe that there should be faculty perspectives fully represented in the governing decisions that affect the lives of the people that learn and work within Nevada’s colleges and universities,” Reed said.  
Faculty members and professors for Nevada universities have run, and been elected to serve, as regents in previous years. The question surrounding the ethics was posed in 1996 when UNR professor Howard Rosenberg was elected to serve as regent. The ethics commission ruled in Rosenberg’s favor, allowing him to continue to serve as regent and keep his faculty positions.  
If elected to the Board of Regents, officials serve six-year terms.
In addition to managing a biennium budget of more than $2 billion, NSHE oversees two research universities, four community colleges, a research institute, and a state college that combined has more than 100,000 students.
Arrascada, who previously worked in the homelessness nonprofit sector, earned both undergraduate and graduate degrees from UNR. 
Arrascada has relied on a wheelchair after a spinal injury nearly 40 years ago. He began considering a run for regent after he clashed over 2016 renovations to Mackay Stadium at UNR that excluded the perspectives of those with disabilities. 
“I called them out on it,” he said, adding that originally overlooking disability access ended up costing more money for revisions to ensure the building was in compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act. 
“That really fueled my fire in wanting to make a difference not just with accessibility for people,” he said, but also making sure there were strong diversity and equity protections so that all students could access higher education. 
Reed has worked as a professor at UNR for 13 years and is also the director of the Sanford Center for Aging at the university.
He has chaired the faculty senate at the university and NSHE’s Council of Senate Chairs, positions which have afforded him interaction with the regents.
Those experiences, he said, helped convince him that the board should have the perspective of a faculty member.
“I work with students every day, and so I won’t merely be bringing the voice of faculty into those conversations, but will also be bringing the voice of the learner. I think that’s really important,” he said. 
Tuition increase
Last year the regents approved a measure to increase tuition over the next three years by 12% for universities and upper-division courses at community colleges.
Arrascada, who voted in favor of the increase, said at the time of the vote that the proposed increase posed a choice between “planned investment now or reactive cuts later.”
“It was just an extremely difficult vote,” he said during an interview, adding that he backed the tuition increase at the time “to help Nevada colleges and universities because we had to retain high quality educators and staff.”
He said he opposed other fee increases that he felt were too burdensome. 
Reed said the reason regents raised tuition on students was because it was one of the few options available that regents could use.
“If the state did a better job of investing in higher education at levels that would ensure that we’re able to make it accessible to students,” he said, adding that if elected he would want “to proactively advocate for increased resources for the system.”
Diversity and equity
Since returning to office in 2025, President Donald Trump has attacked diversity, equity, and inclusion programs within higher education systems. 
NSHE considered eliminating its Inclusion, Diversity, Equity and Access (IDEA) Committee this summer, but postponed the vote. 
Arrascada is against efforts to sunset the IDEA committee and argued diversity programs were needed to ensure a competition of ideas on campuses.
“At the core of post-secondary education, it’s the competition of ideas, which I think flourishes on each campus,” he said. 
Reed agreed, looking at it also from a public health perspective. 
“I see health disparities and health inequality as something that we can address by creating resources that enable people to have equal access,” Reed said. “There are people who need support in ways that are different than other people to be able to succeed. I certainly hope to have an opportunity to promote that.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah has 2 new officials helping to steer the state’s response on the Great Salt Lake
description: Utah is bringing on new officials guiding decisionmaking on the saline lake as it dips toward a historic low.
text:
Great Salt Lake Commissioner Hannah Freeze and Department of Natural Resources Commissioner Jamie Barnes are pictured at the Utah Capitol on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026. (Annie Knox/Utah News Dispatch)  


This article is published through the Great Salt Lake Collaborative, a solutions journalism initiative that partners news, education and media organizations to help inform people about the plight of the Great Salt Lake — and what can be done to make a difference before it is too late.


It’s a season of change for state leadership on the drying Great Salt Lake. 
Utah has a new lake commissioner, Hannah Freeze, and a new chief leading the Department of Natural Resources, Jamie Barnes, after the Senate voted this week to confirm them. 
Both are familiar faces. They were promoted from within their agencies and praised by lawmakers and colleagues at the Capitol this week. Come next year, they’ll be joined by a new Senate president, a top decision-maker on policy and funding for the lake and other issues facing the state, after the defeat of Sen. Stuart Adams in the Republican primary. 
The new crop of leadership comes as the lake dips back toward 2022’s historic low due to decades of drought, climate change and redirection of water, most of it for agriculture. The lake reached its lowest level on record four years ago before a season of record snowfall helped replenish some of it, but it has since dropped back down. 
Its decline threatens Utah’s environment and economy. It’s also raised concerns about public health as dust containing heavy metals kicks up from its exposed lake bed.  
Hannah Freeze, who’d been serving as deputy Great Salt Lake commissioner, replaces Brian Steed, who left to take a role as vice president at Utah State University. 
“I couldn’t be happier to get the opportunity to be the quarterback and pull our many interested stakeholders into the Great Salt Lake huddle,” she told members of the Senate Natural Resources, Agriculture, and Environment Confirmation Committee on Tuesday. 
Lee Creek flows through mudflats into the Great Salt Lake near Magna on Tuesday, Aug. 5, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
Freeze, a former program manager in the Utah Department of Agriculture and Food’s water optimization program, noted she and her family run a farm in northern Utah’s Box Elder County. 
“Many often think of the Great Salt Lake and agriculture as being one of the state’s largest collisions, but I see it as an opportunity to find solutions that protect agriculture, while also benefiting the Great Salt Lake,” Freeze told the committee. “The collision doesn’t have to be a negative one.”
She said she’s built trust and relationships with farmers around the state and wants to further develop collaboration with philanthropic groups, in addition to working with federal officials to secure the $1 billion President Donald Trump proposed for the lake.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Both Freeze and Barnes won praise in Tuesday’s hearing from Steed, representatives of the Utah Farm Bureau and the Great Salt Lake Watershed Enhancement Trust, and former Department of Natural Resources commissioner Joel Ferry, who stepped down over the summer and said he plans to consult and lobby. No one at Tuesday’s committee hearing opposed their nominations. 
Freeze has faced criticism for selling hats in 2024 that said “Make alfalfa great again,” as much of the water diverted from the lake flows to irrigate the crop. Her office has said in response that the hats drew attention to the alfalfa’s value as part of the solution to water issues.
Barnes served as Utah’s state forester before the promotion, but also has a background in the department examining policy and issues relating to mineral extraction and to rivers and lakes, including the Great Salt Lake.
“I think what we’re really looking at on Great Salt Lake is, how do we get a really solid, long-term plan in place?” Barnes said after the hearing. She said the focus now is on managing a rock barrier separating the lake’s north and south arms to control salinity, stabilizing the ecosystem and managing dust. And she emphasized a need for long-term thinking.
The shores of the Great Salt Lake are pictured at Great Salt Lake State Park near Magna on Tuesday, Aug. 5, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
“Really overall, it’s conservation and planning, and what does that look like for the state of Utah, and how do we push more water to the lake?” she said. 
Ben Abbott, executive director of conservation group Grow the Flow, said of Freeze and Barnes that Utah “couldn’t have better leadership.” 
And they have their work cut out for them. Abbott noted researchers have estimated it could cost the state hundreds of millions of dollars each year to replenish the lake.
“We either increase water flows to Great Salt Lake,” Abbott said, “or we suffer the consequences of the lake collapse that could come as soon as two or three years from now.” 
Sen. Scott Sandall, who voted to confirm Freeze and Barnes, told Utah News Dispatch he believes the next Senate president will keep a focus on the lake.
“Whoever that president is, I think, will assume the role of knowing that the Great Salt Lake is important not just for Northern Utah but across all of the state, and quite honestly, across the region,” Sandall said.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Northwest rail fans eager for Sept. 30 debut of Amtrak’s Airo fleet
description: A date that Pacific Northwest train riders and advocates have long awaited is finally nigh. Amtrak’s sleek, amenity-packed new trains will debut on the Cascades intercity route on Sept. 30. Amtrak leaders previewed the launch of commercial service of the “Airo” fleet in an event streamed live on YouTube Thursday.   “This is one of the […]
text:
A sleek new Amtrak Cascades train passed through the Willamette Valley in July on a test run. Regular service with this next-generation train model begins in Washington and Oregon on Sept. 30.  (Photo courtesy of Oregon Department of Transportation)A date that Pacific Northwest train riders and advocates have long awaited is finally nigh. Amtrak’s sleek, amenity-packed new trains will debut on the Cascades intercity route on Sept. 30.
Amtrak leaders previewed the launch of commercial service of the “Airo” fleet in an event streamed live on YouTube Thursday.  
“This is one of the most significant modernization efforts in Amtrak’s history. While customers will notice the beautiful new interiors and all of the features, this is really setting up Amtrak for the future of rail,” said Celia Ann Pfleckl, the assistant vice president for the Airo program, during the launch announcement livestream.
Initially, one new Airo train will make one roundtrip each day between Seattle and Vancouver, B.C., and a second new train will operate one roundtrip a day between Seattle and Eugene, Oregon.
Amtrak Cascades will operate with a mixed fleet this fall and winter, gradually switching over  to solely next-generation trains by early 2027, the rail operator said. Each new train added will follow the schedule of the older one it replaces. The modernization will not result in schedule additions regionally for the time being.
The state-supported Amtrak Cascades line serves eighteen cities from Vancouver, Canada, to Eugene, Ore., including Bellingham, Seattle, Tacoma, Olympia and Portland. 
Pfleckl and her colleagues gushed Thursday about amenities that customers can look forward to, including comfy seats with moveable headrests, individual power outlets, improved onboard Wi-Fi, bigger windows, reading lights and digital info displays. The revamped cafe cars have self-service options and mood lighting. The six large restrooms feature touchless controls.
The 300-passenger Airo trainsets offer significantly more seats per departure than the coaches they will replace on the Cascades line, some of which date to the 1970s. That increased seat count is the most important detail, said Charles Hamilton, executive director of the passenger rail advocacy group All Aboard Washington.
“That has been what has kept us from moving forward,” Hamilton said in an interview, noting that the existing trains are regularly sold out, particularly on Fridays and Sundays.
 “This will give us more capacity to have more folks riding,” Hamilton said. “That’s going to be a big deal.”
The Amtrak Cascades line has been operating with reduced passenger capacity since March 2025, when dozens of 1980s-era Horizon rail cars were pulled from service due to corrosion problems. Ridership statistics consequently showed a decrease last year compared to the record high of nearly 1 million riders in 2024.
Amtrak placed a large order for new Siemens-built trains in 2021 as part of a nationwide modernization campaign. In total, eight new trainsets, two new diesel locomotives, and a spare cab car are coming to the Northwest. The Amtrak Cascades service is the first in line to receive next-generation railcars from the national fleet renewal order. 
“These new Amtrak Cascades trains are a game-changer for rail travel in the Pacific Northwest,” said Washington’s Secretary of Transportation Julie Meredith in a news release. “They bring improved reliability, comfort, and amenities to one of the most scenic rail corridors in the country. We’re particularly excited to be the first in the nation to introduce these new trains into service.” 
The Amtrak Cascades route serves 18 stations between Vancouver, Canada, and Eugene, Ore. Shown here is a new Airo train entering the Salem station during testing in July. (Photo courtesy of Oregon Department of Transportation)
Can’t wait’ 
Many in the Pacific Northwest’s sizeable community of rail enthusiasts sound eager to climb on board the new trains at the first opportunity. Over the past few months, trainspotters have closely tracked the arrival of each new Airo train and posted photos on social media and online rail forums of them being tested locally.
The reveal of Sept. 30 as the date for their inaugural service was greeted with  comments such as, “Can’t wait,” “Let’s go,” “My 10yr old son wants to go on the first day,” and “I am so happy!” on Reddit and Facebook.
On the launch date, Amtrak said the new Airo equipment would be assigned to Trains 516/519 on the Seattle-British Columbia route and Trains 503/508 on the Seattle-Eugene segment.
“I wouldn’t be at all surprised to see those first trains totally booked very quickly,” Hamilton said.
Same speed and frequency
The new trains will be more fuel efficient, but they won’t improve travel times. The freight-dominated corridor has an existing top speed limit of 79 mph due to track conditions.
Their arrival also won’t unclog the periodic bottlenecks and congestion on the privately-owned tracks. The subpar on-time performance of Amtrak Cascades, while improving, continues to present a challenge and headache.
The Oregon and Washington state transportation departments are in the early stages of updating the Amtrak Cascades long-range plan to identify what it would take to add additional roundtrips at higher speeds. That could entail a mix of track improvements, siding extensions and signal upgrades. 
An updated Service Development Plan will then set the stage for difficult negotiations with Union Pacific and BNSF to shoehorn more passenger rail trips in between rising freight train traffic. Not to mention, the state and federal governments would need to find tens of millions of dollars to pay for a rail service expansion.
“We expect the current Amtrak Cascades schedule to continue for the foreseeable future,” was how a Washington transportation department spokesperson assessed the outlook this week.
Washington and Oregon co-manage the regional route and contract with Amtrak to operate the service. Passenger fares cover slightly more than half of the annual operating expenses with taxpayers picking up the rest. Unlike with long-distance routes, Amtrak requires states to subsidize the shorter regional services it operates, such as the 467-mile Cascades line.
In conjunction with the arrival of the new trains, construction workers are putting the finishing touches on a new $300 million train maintenance facility just south of downtown Seattle. This federally-funded project was needed to modernize and enlarge the existing Amtrak rail yard, in part because the new Airo train cars can’t be easily decoupled for servicing.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: A forward-thinking Agriculture secretary gifted us a wonder 100 years ago
description: This week marks the 100th anniversary of the policy directive by U.S. Agriculture Secretary William Jardine that 640,000 acres of forests and waters in northern Minnesota be managed as a roadless wilderness area.  “It will be the policy of the Department (of Agriculture) to retain as much as possible of the land which has recreational […]
text:
Night sky in the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness. (Photo by Joe Pohle, courtesy of Save the Boundary Waters)This week marks the 100th anniversary of the policy directive by U.S. Agriculture Secretary William Jardine that 640,000 acres of forests and waters in northern Minnesota be managed as a roadless wilderness area. 
“It will be the policy of the Department (of Agriculture) to retain as much as possible of the land which has recreational opportunities of this nature as wilderness… Not less than 1,000 square miles containing the best of the lakes and waterways will be kept as wilderness recreation areas.” 
Jardine’s directive established three wilderness roadless areas — the Caribou Lake, the Little Indian Sioux, and the Superior — in the heart of our priceless canoe country. Until then, the only federal public lands managed as wilderness was the Gila roadless area in New Mexico.
The designation of these roadless areas was the Department of Agriculture’s response to demands from northeastern Minnesota business boosters that roads be built across the canoe country — from the Fernberg Road to Seagull Lake and from Ely to Buyck (with spur roads to Lac la Croix, Loon Lake, and Trout Lake) — and that a road be built to every lake. 
Long under the thumb of mining and logging companies owned by distant barons — “outsiders” — leaders viewed tourism as their economy, run by locals, that they could control. They thought that the proposed roads would be a major step to provide access to tourists to every corner of the North Woods.
But others took a longer view of canoe country management. The U.S. Forest Service’s first landscape architect, Arthur Carhart, paddled the canoe country many times during the period from 1919 to 1921. He saw the unique value of the canoe country of the Superior National Forest as a recreational wilderness area that excluded automobiles. 
Congress betrayed the Boundary Waters. Time for Minnesota to act.

Carhart’s perspective on a roadless wilderness area was advanced by Paul Riis and the Izaak Walton League. They were supported by Aldo Leopold, a giant of public lands conservation. Leopold articulated his land ethic by urging that wilderness protection preserve unique and representative natural areas, wildlife and scenery. 
He paddled the canoe country for two weeks in 1924, and again for 10 days in 1925. Alarmed by the road building proposals, Leopold transmitted his view of wilderness management to Jardine, the Agriculture secretary. Leopold defined wilderness as a “continuous stretch of country preserved in its natural state, open to lawful hunting and fishing, big enough to absorb a two weeks’ pack trip, and devoid of roads, artificial trails, cottages, or other works of man.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Jardine’s directive was a compromise brokered by Leopold. The three roadless areas were of exceptional value for wilderness canoeing. No roads or any recreational developments would be allowed. The policy conserved lands that provided “a virile and wholesome form of recreation off the beaten paths.” Although the heart of canoe country was kept free of roads, the Echo Trail from Ely to Buyck was completed in 1928. Spur roads to Lac la Croix and Loon and Trout Lakes were banned as was the Fernberg-Gunflint road.
Following Jardine’s directive, the Forest Service planned a development-free canoe area within the Superior National Forest. Portages would be maintained and minimal improvements made to camp sites, but no roads or other recreational developments would be allowed. Jardine also committed to acquire, for the public’s benefit, private inholdings. 
The 1926 policy ushered in a new and fundamental change in forest administration; Jardine’s policy explicitly acknowledged that societal uses of national forests for recreation were as important as timber harvesting.  
But it was also clear that the protection of the canoe country wilderness was a lightning rod. The struggle between conflicting views for managing Minnesota’s wildest country seems endless.  
Reflection and thanksgiving can be very personal. Preservation of the Boundary Waters has given us an utterly priceless wild landscape of woods and water. 
In addition to the 100th anniversary of the Jardine directive, this year also marks the 75th anniversary of my first canoe trip to Knife Lake. 
This summer, at the age of 77, I ventured on two Boundary Waters canoe trips in the company of younger people who fully appreciate the value of this place and who will work to protect it. They and I are eternally grateful for Carhart, Riis, Leopold, Jardine, Ernest Oberholtzer, Sigurd Olson, Bud Heinselman, Bill Magie and countless others who had the vision and the gumption to fight for the canoe country.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi midterms: In traditionally red 3rd District, Guest faces political newcomer farmer from Shubuta
description: Candidates for Mississippi's 3rd District House seat are, from left, Erik Kiehle, Michael Guest and Michael Chiaradio.
text:
Four-term incumbent Republican Rep. Michael Guest faces a challenge from a Democratic farmer from Shubuta and a Libertarian real estate investor from Meridian for the 3rd District congressional seat in central Mississippi.
The challengers are coming at Guest from the left and right with criticism of Guest’s support of, and lack of pushback against, Trump administration policies.
Mississippi’s 3rd Congressional District covers central portions of the state, such as the GOP stronghold of Rankin County, and stretches from the Louisiana border in the west to rural Alabama border towns in the east. 
Democrats are leading in many congressional race polls across the country, and are favored to reclaim a majority in the House. But the 3rd District in Mississippi has been a GOP stronghold. Yet, if Republicans are to stand a chance at retaining their razor-thin majority in the chamber, defending territory in areas like Mississippi’s 3rd District is critical.

Guest, who was first elected in 2018, is running for a fifth term in office after sailing to general election victories three times. In 2024, he survived a primary challenge from the right that went to a runoff but ran unopposed in the general election. He ran unopposed for the Republican nomination this cycle.
The race also features Libertarian candidate Erik Kiehle of Meridian. Kiehle, a businessman in property management and a volunteer firefighter, said he is “a strong believer in America First.” He has criticized incumbent Republicans’ support of “U.S.-Israel military integration” and has called for an end to foreign wars and a halt to spending on wars in Ukraine and Iran along with an end to aid to Israel. He said he would push for a constitutional amendment to require a balanced budget and end deficit spending. He supports mass deportation and a ban on Muslim immigrants.
Guest serves as chair of the House Ethics Committee, and also serves on the Homeland Security and Appropriations committees. In August, NOTUS reported that Guest, whose chairmanship on the Ethics Committee includes enforcing compliance of the Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act, violated the insider trading and transparency law. Guest’s Democratic opponent, Michael Chiaradio, and the Mississippi Democratic Party have highlighted the story in social media posts.
Guest, the outlet said, was more than six months late disclosing three stock sales made by a family trust fund owned by his wife involving shares of the oil giant Chevron, the lodging platform Airbnb and the cosmetics company e.l.f. Beauty. A spokesperson for Guest said he “does not have any decision-making role” in the trust and “was not consulted on these, or any other, transactions made by the trust.”
Otherwise, Guest has run a steady, low-profile campaign, appearing at local events hosted by the Mississippi Federation of Republican Women and with U.S. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, who is also on the ballot this year. He has emphasized his endorsement from President Donald Trump and his work helping enact the administration’s agenda.
“Under President Trump’s leadership and with a conservative Congress we have restored law and order in our country, rebuilt our military and respect around the world, cut taxes, and secured the border,” Guest told Mississippi Today.
Guest also holds a massive financial advantage, outraising Chiaradio by a nearly 5-to-1 margin, as well as maintaining significantly more cash on hand, Federal Election Commission reports show.
Chiaradio, a first-time candidate for Congress originally from New Jersey, is a former baseball player turned farmer living in rural Mississippi. He traveled the country while playing baseball at Eastern Nazarene College, and after playing in the inaugural season of what became the Empire Professional Baseball League, he launched a professional softball league in Satsuma, Alabama.
He also has professional experience working for a government contractor that provides administrative services for health care agencies.
He came to Mississippi in search of a lifestyle that would suit his interest in farming. In 2023, he purchased a house on several acres of land in Shubuta.
A constituent of Guest, Chiaradio said he grew weary of watching the four-term incumbent act as a rubber stamp for Trump and the national Republican agenda. When he saw Guest’s name alone on his 2024 ballot, Chiaradio decided he would supply political competition himself.
“Michael Guest is the only name on my ballot,” he recalled. “My God, I could step up and stand up to this guy. And who the heck is going to do it if not me?”
Chiaradio ran unopposed for the Democratic nomination. He told Mississippi Today he believes a localized message built around economic frustration can unite both disaffected conservatives and a fractured Democratic Party. His policy agenda includes expanding safety net programs to offer universal childcare and food assistance.
Chiaradio launched his campaign with the help of Zee Cohen Sanchez, a strategist who worked on U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders’ surprisingly strong challenge to Hillary Clinton in the 2016 Democratic presidential primary and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s shock upset of a powerful New York Democratic incumbent in 2018.
Sanchez, who is no longer with the campaign, had earlier said she believed a successful challenge to Guest would cost over $1 million. Chiaradio has fallen well short of that sum, raising just under $140,000 in total contributions. 
On the campaign trail, Guest has criticized Chiaradio’s hiring of Sanchez and, by extension, U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, the progressive firebrand from Vermont.
“The far-left ideology promoted by Bernie Sanders and other Democrat radicals is the last thing we need representing the people of Mississippi in Congress,” Guest said.
The general election is on Nov. 3.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Embattled Lancaster County treasurer rejects GOP officer’s call to resign
description: LINCOLN — Lancaster County Treasurer Rachel Garver rejected a call to resign in the wake of a state audit alleging “gross mishandling” of local tax revenues by her office. Jack Riggins, chair of the Lancaster County Republican Party, issued a media release seeking Garver’s immediate resignation, saying the findings released Wednesday by State Auditor Mike Fo[...]
text:
(Courtesy of Getty Images) LINCOLN — Lancaster County Treasurer Rachel Garver rejected a call to resign in the wake of a state audit alleging “gross mishandling” of local tax revenues by her office.
Jack Riggins, chair of the Lancaster County Republican Party, issued a media release seeking Garver’s immediate resignation, saying the findings released Wednesday by State Auditor Mike Foley represented a “serious failure of stewardship of the public’s trust and money.”
Rachel Garver, Lancaster County treasurer (Photo courtesy of Lancaster County)
Riggins also called on Kristen Anderson, who was chief deputy to Garver during part of the period in question, to withdraw from the race for Lancaster County District Court clerk.
Anderson, in a statement, also rejected his call.
Both Anderson and Garver, who is running for reelection, are Democrats. The general election is Nov. 3.
“I have no intention of resigning,” Garver told the Examiner. “I have a responsibility to the citizens of the county to take care of things. I fixed what needed to be fixed. … I have a couple of more things to work out. We’re working on new procedures.”
State auditor finds big ‘blunders’ by Lancaster County treasurer, who takes ‘blanket’ responsibility

Foley, a Republican running for reelection as state auditor, said the bulk of nearly $1 billion in accounting “blunders” uncovered by his team amounted to accounting mistakes and “incompetence” — not embezzlement. Garver, who was elected treasurer in 2018, said the biggest failure had to do with a financial report that she said had been done incorrectly apparently since 2013.
Garver acknowledged that the scenario “doesn’t look good.” She said corrections have been made or are underway. 
A $1.27 million underpayment to the state, for example, was “hand-delivered” in a check about a month ago, Garver said. Foley said the treasurer had improperly distributed state property tax credit money, resulting in that amount being overpaid to local taxing authorities between 2023 and 2025. That money was supposed to be available for property tax relief, he said.
“We expect higher standards from those entrusted with our county’s finances and records,” said Riggins.
Kristen Anderson, former chief deputy Lancaster County treasurer. (Photo courtesy of Anderson campaign)
Until about a year ago, Anderson served six years as chief deputy in the Lancaster County Treasurer’s Office. Her statement said she was proud of her work.
“While the audit period overlaps with part of my tenure, the financial functions identified in the report were not among my responsibilities. My primary areas of oversight included human resources, workplace culture, contracts and office operations. The treasurer and the office accountant handled financial reporting, investments and distributions.” 
Garver said the office accountant resigned amid “medical issues” a couple of weeks ago. She said she anticipates improving the treasurer operation.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Shellfish farmers warn overregulation could drive NJ aquaculture to ‘extinction’
description: Shellfish farmers pleaded with New Jersey legislators to ease restrictions on aquaculture. An Assembly panel approved four measures Thursday.
text:
Shellfish farmers pleaded with New Jersey legislators to ease restrictions on aquaculture. An Assembly panel approved four measures Thursday. (Photo courtesy of New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection)Legislators advanced a package of bills Thursday intended to help New Jersey’s aquaculture industry, with shellfish farmers complaining that state regulations stifle expansion and have driven some to move out of state.
The Assembly’s agriculture and natural resources committee listened to an hour of testimony during an afternoon hearing at the Statehouse, where shellfish farmers blasted a common boogeyman: the Department of Environmental Protection.
Oyster farmer Matt Gregg, co-founder and operator of the Barnegat Oyster Collective and president of the New Jersey Aquaculture Association, likened the department to a villain from a Scooby-Doo cartoon. Like Scooby’s gang of teenage detectives, shellfish farmers have had to band together to fight foes like the pandemic, marine predators, and extreme weather, Gregg said.
“But more often than not, the foe is the New Jersey DEP,” Gregg said. “If we don’t do something, we will die a death of a thousand cuts. We will regulate everyone into extinction.”
Larry Hajna, a department spokesman, declined to comment.
One of the industry’s biggest challenges, farmers testified, has been the state’s longtime narrow definition of aquaculture, which specifically bars “construction of facilities and appurtenant structures” from the definition. That has set aquaculture farmers up for zoning and permitting hurdles that land-based farmers don’t face and also discouraged commercial investors from investing, Gregg and other shellfish farmers testified.
“It’s like telling a farmer that the barn that he’s built and owns isn’t part of his farm,” said Scot Mackey, executive director of the Garden State Seafood Association.
So one bill the Assembly panel considered would expand the state’s definition of aquaculture beyond in-water operations to include land-based hatcheries, processing facilities, storage sheds, and other structures that support the industry. It passed unanimously.
Bill sponsor Assemblyman Alex Sauickie (R-Ocean) called it “a minor change but it is a game-changer.”
“These folks are treated like second-class farmers right now, from my point of view,” he said.
The panel also passed a bill that would get more industry voices on the Aquaculture Advisory Council in the state Department of Agriculture. Shellfish farmers complained that public officials now pack the council, which has had longstanding vacancies and sometimes flouts its statutory mandate of meeting four times a year.
“It’s hard to advise anyone on aquaculture matters if the aquaculturists aren’t involved in the discussion,” said Matthew Williams, who owns the Cape May County-based South Bay Shellfish Company. “In recent years, about half of the current industry-related seats have been vacant, and there’s been little industry attendance at the meetings. I think many members of our industry have been disenfranchised because of how things work at the council. Meetings get canceled. Members of the industry have literally been shushed, and the most recent aqua-development plan was six years late.”
The bill would expand the council’s membership from 13 to 18 members, at least eight of whom would have to be residents experienced in the aquaculture industry.
Committee members also passed a bill that would task the council, the agriculture and health departments, and other agencies with developing guidance on aquaculture agritourism. And they approved a resolution to recognize the work of Rutgers University’s Haskin Shellfish Research Laboratory. Scientists there have developed disease-resistant, hardier, and faster-growing oyster strains, the legislation notes.
Assemblywoman Andrea Katz (D-Burlington), the committee’s chair, said the bill package arose out of a visit she and other legislators made earlier this summer to see shellfish farmers in action in Barnegat Bay.
“What became pretty clear quickly is that our laws hadn’t quite caught up with what these farmers are actually doing,” she said.
Most of the aquaculture in New Jersey is shellfish production, with more than 50 mollusk farms in coastal bays here that primarily harvest hard clams and Eastern oysters, according to Rutgers. Farmers here also harvest trout, baitfish, koi, and aquatic plants, according to Sauickie.
One clam farmer said he hopes the legislative package passed Thursday is just the start.
William Mayer of Brigantine-based Clam Daddy’s told committee members clam farming is the backbone of New Jersey’s aquaculture industry but remains “microscopic” compared to its competitors down South because of “the red tape and the government restrictions.”
He urged lawmakers to consider giving aquafarmers financial assistance to offset skyrocketing labor and utility costs and persuading state environmental officials to expand the coastal acreage where they’re permitted to work.
“We have difficulty accessing commercial working waterfronts, never-ending electrical rate hikes, and labor costs that never seem to stop rising,” Mayer said. “The cost of doing business is a boatload of clams. As the marine commercial waterfront is erased by mega mansions, clam farmers are stuck with nowhere to go.”
