name: Virginia Mercury
title: Early voting begins in Virginia, as Trump mail-ballot restrictions remain blocked
description: Early voting begins Friday across Virginia, kicking off more than six weeks of voting for the Nov. 3 midterms just days after the U.S. Supreme Court blocked new mail-ballot restrictions sought by President Donald Trump’s administration.  Voters will choose a U.S. senator and representatives in all 11 of Virginia’s congressional districts, and approve or reje[...]
text:
Early voting for the Nov. 3 midterm elections begins Friday, with a U.S. Senate race, all 11 congressional seats, three proposed constitutional amendments and numerous local referendums on ballots across the commonwealth. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)Early voting begins Friday across Virginia, kicking off more than six weeks of voting for the Nov. 3 midterms just days after the U.S. Supreme Court blocked new mail-ballot restrictions sought by President Donald Trump’s administration. 
Voters will choose a U.S. senator and representatives in all 11 of Virginia’s congressional districts, and approve or reject three proposed amendments to the state constitution. Depending on where they live, some voters will also see local races, referendums and special elections. 
The election comes with control of Congress at stake after months of uncertainty over Trump’s attempt to require the U.S. Postal Service to change how it handles mail-in ballots nationwide. 
For Virginia voters, however, the procedures will remain unchanged after the Supreme Court on Monday left in place an injunction blocking the Postal Service rule. 
“Virginia election officials have had to continuously adapt to changing election landscapes, and their ability to do so quickly showcases their significant experience and dedication to running accurate and secure elections,” Deputy Commissioner of Elections Ashley Coles said during Tuesday’s State Board of Elections meeting in Richmond. 
Early in-person voting will continue through Saturday, Oct. 31. Although Virginia’s official 45-day early voting window technically begins Saturday, state officials said registrar offices that will be closed that day must begin offering early voting Friday. 
Voters can cast a ballot at an early voting location in the locality where they are registered. Locations and hours vary, and the Virginia Department of Elections recommends voters check with their local registrar before heading out. 
There are more weekend options this year compared to previous years. Local registrars will be required to offer voting on the second and third Sundays before Election Day, a new requirement for 2026. Weekend voting will be available Oct. 18, Oct. 24, Oct. 25 and Oct. 31. 
Stephen Farnsworth, professor emeritus of political science at the University of Mary Washington, said the fight over mail voting and concerns about Election Day could persuade more people to cast their ballots early. 
“President Trump’s continuing efforts to make voting harder, and the possibility of mayhem on Election Day, should really energize early voting in Virginia and around the country this fall,” Farnsworth said. “Virginians have already demonstrated a great willingness to vote early and this year may see even more interest.”
 What voters will decide and how to cast a ballot

At the top of the statewide ballot, Democratic U.S. Sen. Mark Warner is seeking a fourth — and what he said would be his final — term against Republican Bert Mizusawa. 
All of Virginia’s 11 congressional seats are also on the ballot, including several of the state’s most contentious races. 
In the 1st District, Republican U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman of Westmoreland faces Henrico County Commonwealth’s Attorney Shannon Taylor, the Democratic nominee. 
U.S. Rep. Jen Kiggans, R-Virginia Beach, is running against former Democratic U.S. Rep. Elaine Luria in a 2nd District rematch of their 2022 contest, when Kiggans unseated Luria. 
Republican U.S. Rep. John McGuire of Goochland faces former Democratic U.S. Rep. Tom Perriello and independent Cooke Harvey in the 5th District. 
In the 7th, Democratic U.S. Rep. Eugene Vindman of Woodbridge is running against Douglas Ollivant, the GOP nominee. 
Democratic U.S. Rep. Don Beyer of Alexandria faces Republican Tony Sabio, Libertarian Shelly Arnoldi and independent Tim Sharman in the 8th District. 
Of the three proposed constitutional amendments, one deals with reproductive healthcare decisions, including access to abortion, fertility care, birth control and miscarriage care. Another would remove Virginia’s constitutional ban of same-sex marriage and require legally valid marriages to be treated equally regardless of sex, gender or race. 
The third would automatically restore voting rights to people convicted of felonies after their release from incarceration.
In addition, voters in Richmond, Chesterfield County and dozens of other localities will consider whether to authorize a sales-tax increase of up to 1% to pay for school construction and major renovations. 
Any registered Virginia voter may request an absentee ballot without providing a reason. The deadline to request one by mail or online is Oct. 23. 
Mail ballots must be postmarked by Election Day and and received by the voter’s general registrar by noon on Nov. 6. Because a ballot arriving after Election Day cannot be counted without a postmark, election officials recommend taking the envelope inside a post office and asking that it be hand-stamped.
“For individuals who have requested an absentee ballot by mail, we want to make sure you complete your ballot, fill out the required information on your envelope, and return it without delay,” Coles said. 
Voters can also take mail ballots directly to their registrar’s office or designated drop-off locations during early voting, or return them at polling places on Election Day. 
Anyone who requested an absentee ballot but decides to vote in person instead should bring the ballot to an early-voting site or polling place. An election officer can exchange it for an in-person ballot. 
Tram Nguyen, executive director of New Virginia Majority, said voters should remain confident that voting by mail remains available. Nguyen is one of about 400,000 Virginians on the state’s permanent absentee-voter list and said she plans to return her ballot through a drop box. 
“All Virginians should be able to trust that our election systems are safe, that they can safely cast their ballots, that their votes will be counted, and any action by any entity to interfere with that right should be fiercely rejected,” Nguyen said. 
Oct. 23 is also the deadline to register and cast a regular ballot. Same-day registration begins Oct. 24, but voters who register after the deadline must cast a provisional ballot. 
 Federal effort forced local officials to prepare for changes

Trump issued an executive order March 31 directing the Postal Service to adopt regulations that would bar it from transmitting mail ballots to voters who were not included on a list controlled by the agency. 
The Postal Service followed on Aug. 21 with a rule requiring states to register every voter eligible to vote by mail with the agency, which would then compile state-by-state voter lists. 
States also would have faced new requirements for ballot envelopes, including submitting designs to the Postal Service for approval. Ballots could have been withheld from voters whose names were missing from the agency’s lists, while envelopes that failed to meet the new standards would have gone undelivered. 
Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones joined a multistate lawsuit Aug. 26 seeking to block the rule. Two days later, a federal court granted the states’ request for a temporary restraining order, finding that compliance before the November election was “practically impossible” and carried a significant risk of disenfranchising voters. 
The Supreme Court’s action Monday means those requirements will not take effect for the November election. 
“Voters may have heard about possible changes to procedures for mailed absentee ballots for the upcoming election related to a new rule by USPS,” Coles told the elections board. “The most important thing for Virginia voters to know is that the requirements of this rule will not be in effect for the 2026 General Election.”
For local election officials, the decision removed one uncertainty as they tested equipment, hired staff, trained poll workers and prepared ballots. 
Richmond Elections Director and General Registrar David Levine said his office expects substantial interest because city voters have congressional races, constitutional amendments, a local referendum and a special school board election on their ballots. 
Preparations have also included confirming voting sites are available and accessible and updating the city’s election security plan. Richmond also added staff to help with registration, absentee voting, technology and training, Levine said.
The city purchased additional ballot printers as well. The machines allow election officers to print the correct ballot for each voter as needed, which Levine said could speed up voting and reduce the numbers of preprinted ballots the city has to purchase and later recycle.  
“We’re focused right now on making sure everything is in place for voters when they walk through the door,” Levine said. 
Joan Porter of the League of Women Voters of Virginia said the proposed federal changes had already caused confusion among voters. 
“There’s nothing wrong with mail and voting. There is no fraud that was proven many times in 2020,” Porter said. “The big problem is creating chaos and uncertainty, and people were already asking about ‘what do I do if this is in effect,’ and there’s just no reason for this type of distraction and disenfranchisement.”
Jones, a Democrat, sharply criticized Trump after the Supreme Court declined to allow the new rules to take effect this fall.
“The commonwealth of Virginia runs free, fair, and secure elections,” Jones said in a statement. “Contrary to the lies he peddles, the greatest threat to confidence in our elections is not Virginia’s voters, election officials, or our election system — it is Donald Trump.”
Jones urged Virginians to vote by mail, use a drop box or vote early, saying his office was working with the Department of Elections to protect access to the ballot. 
Polling places will be open from 6 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Election Day.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia confronts $1.7 billion shortfall in highway maintenance funding
description: Virginia faces a funding gap of at least $1.7 billion for highway maintenance work, with roads falling into disrepair creating an economic and safety liability that could affect future construction projects across the commonwealth, state transportation department staff reported this week.  Over the past 20 years, Virginia’s bridge inventory has grown by 400,[...]
text:
Construction work along the Dulles Connector in Northern Virginia, with roadwork equipment and activity visible along the roadway. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)Virginia faces a funding gap of at least $1.7 billion for highway maintenance work, with roads falling into disrepair creating an economic and safety liability that could affect future construction projects across the commonwealth, state transportation department staff reported this week. 
Over the past 20 years, Virginia’s bridge inventory has grown by 400, with a current total of 21,200 bridges. Pavement has increased by 2,000 miles, to 59,700 miles, while pavement lane miles have increased by 5,000 to 130,400 lane miles. All of them require millions annually for maintenance and repair.  
Virginia’s Appropriation Act makes maintaining transportation assets the priority for budgeting, allocation, and spending. State law also requires the Commonwealth Transportation Board to set aside adequate maintenance money before funding construction. 
However, the board learned from Virginia Department of Transportation staff during a work session on Tuesday that funding all the necessary projects will not be easy to address. 
Solutions like reducing construction funding would be complicated by a prior 2025 action that reduced road maintenance funding for most of the years covered by the current fiscal year plan.
“There is no mitigation strategy that makes this not painful,” said Secretary of Transportation Nick Donohue on Tuesday. “This is going to be painful no matter what we do moving forward.”
Laura Schewel, deputy secretary of transportation, said that one method to address the deficit is to use crossover funds — money shifted from the construction program to maintenance — which would create a sizable shortfall in construction program dollars.
Beginning in fiscal year 2028, she proposed increasing maintenance to roughly $290 million per year, over the next six years. That would significantly reduce construction funding, including the state’s Smart Scale program, unless it adopts mitigations.
The agency is also watching whether the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act and the Federal Surface Transportation Act will be reauthorized, which have infused bridge repair and maintenance funding. Virginia receives about $115 million per year from the IIJA to help cover its bridges, VDOT representatives reported. 
Next month, the secretary will provide the board with mitigation options to reduce the construction-program hit while still meeting maintenance targets. The options include phasing, timing adjustments, or balancing strategies across funding rounds.
Funding for transportation projects through the Smart Scale program could drop temporarily by around 51%. Severe weather events and a decline in federal funding could also increase maintenance needs.
Crews put down asphalt on Prince William Parkway. (Photo courtesy of the Virginia Department of Transportation)
 How the deficit was created

Increasing highway construction costs and prior budget assumptions are key factors driving the projected deficit.
Beginning in 2022, the agency learned that pavement investments had begun to exceed the increased costs. As a result, the CTB made a series of one-time infusions by moving money from the annual construction budget to crossover funding to cover the gap, but those infusions were not sustained.
The discrepancy stems from previous budgetary decisions made under Gov. Glenn Youngkin’s administration. The board instead allocated funds for pavement maintenance through 2031 to Round 6 of Smart Scale.
On Jan. 14, 2025, then-Secretary of Transportation Shep Miller, appointed by Youngkin, led a conversation with the board about the agency deliberately striking a balance between maintaining infrastructure at acceptable condition levels and preserving funding for construction and other transportation priorities, rather than maximizing maintenance spending at all costs.
Then, in June 2025, the previous administration introduced a Six-Year Improvement Program (SYIP) to the board that did not assume the continued level of crossover funding. Instead, it assumed about $200 million less in crossover funds and allocated those funds to construction programs. 
In addition, the SYIP included an approximately $40 million reduction in crossover funds for local maintenance programs.
Last November, the board also approved a plan to use unallocated funds from the Priority Transportation Fund and Grant Anticipation Revenue Vehicle (GARVEE) Bonds, along with $103.5 million in revenue collections, to advance several priority projects worth $715 million. That money could have given the transportation program more flexibility.
The much larger current deficit is mainly due to a structural mismatch between maintenance costs and the funding planned for fiscal year 2027 and beyond.
At Tuesday’s meeting, board member Marianne Moffat Radcliff, appointed by Gov. Abigail Spanberger, questioned whether prior decisions included any analysis on what would happen to pavement conditions if higher funding levels weren’t maintained.
Donohue said he was not serving as secretary when the decisions were made.
However, he said this was the first year the agency could analyze what had been done and share it publicly, most recently during the board’s July meetings.
“There were discussions in January 2025 when the decision was made to go from about $300 million extra a year in funding down to $100 million, but this year’s work is the first clear, public analysis of the longer-term impacts,” he said.
The board members who voted to advance the reduced funding didn’t comment on their decision.
Virginia’s 2019 and Current Pavements Inventory. (Photo courtesy of the Virginia Department of Transportation)
 Deficit faces criticism

The deficit invited criticism from advocacy groups, including the Coalition for Smarter Growth (CSG), which promotes walkable, bikeable, inclusive, and transit-oriented growth in the Washington, D.C. region.
“This deficit highlights the importance of a fix-it-first approach to our transportation network, spending our limited funds wisely by making efficient use of existing infrastructure and ensuring more compact and efficient land use,” Stewart Schwartz, CSG executive director, said in a statement.
Schwartz said Virginia should enable more housing near jobs, services, and transit, helping families shorten commutes and spend less on gas and vehicles. Doing so could “help the state achieve better transportation and quality of life outcomes without breaking the bank,” he said.
Bill Pugh, CSG’s transportation and climate director, emphasized that the think tank Transportation for America’s recent Repair Priorities report rated Virginia’s road maintenance in the bottom category of states, putting it in the category of “Bad Spending; Bad Repair Conditions.” 
Pugh said highway expansion spending has outpaced maintenance. From 2018 to 2024, the state spent just 58 cents on maintenance for every dollar spent on expansion. The think tank’s analysis shows the proposed SYIP would continue that trend, with 35% of VDOT funds going to construction and 23% to maintenance.
The report notes that Virginia has improved bridge conditions from 2018 to 2024. Pugh said he believes that this was based upon the policy decision last decade to direct more funding to keeping special structures in a state of good repair. 
Pugh said, “Virginia should similarly better prioritize funding maintenance of state-owned roads, including their ancillary facilities like streetlights, and walking and biking facilities.”
 What’s next

The board is expected to take a final vote at its Dec. 9 business meeting, where it will decide on the maintenance strategy and the exact crossover amount. That decision will directly determine the available construction funds.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont funded lawyers for tenants facing eviction. The program is out of money.
description:
Lawyers stepped in to prevent 73 evictions over two years through a pilot program that is now shutting down. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont funded lawyers for tenants facing eviction. The program is out of money. .
text:
Vermont Legal Aid’s offices in Burlington on Sept. 17, 2026. Photo by Carly Berlin/Vermont Public and VTDigger 
Carly Berlin covers housing and infrastructure for Vermont Public, in partnership with VTDigger.
Last year, Steve Koren slept on a friend’s sofa for nearly six months while searching for an apartment he could afford on his Social Security disability payments and gig work. When the 54-year-old with lupus landed a studio apartment at a subsidized building in downtown Brattleboro this January, he was filled with relief.
But a few months ago, a law enforcement officer arrived at Koren’s door with eviction paperwork, Koren said. His landlord, the nonprofit Windham and Windsor Housing Trust, claimed he owed $200 in past-due rent, according to court records. 
Koren was shocked. He’d had an issue with the auto-rent payments from his bank account soon after moving in, but at the time of the eviction summons, he had believed he’d paid off the balance, he said. (Kim Chewning, director of property and asset management at the housing trust, said the organization cannot comment on the specifics of individual cases but that “unresolved rent balances can grow quickly if we are unable to make contact or address the underlying issue,” and in those instances, “we may move forward with legal action as part of our standard process.”)
Koren found a program run by Vermont Legal Aid that offered free representation for tenants facing eviction. He quickly connected with an attorney, who helped get the case dismissed this July. In the end, Koren only needed to pay a fraction of the court costs demanded by his landlord – and he got to stay in his apartment.
Without the legal assistance, Koren thinks he could have ended up homeless.
“I would have been forced to pay the money that I don’t have, and in that, I would’ve lost the apartment,” he said.
The Vermont Legal Aid program that helped prevent Koren’s eviction is now shutting down. The Tenant Representation Pilot Project began in November 2024 and is ending this fall after running out of state funding. 
Nationwide, landlords are much more likely than tenants to have legal representation in eviction cases. The Vermont program was part of a crop of publicly-funded tenant right-to-counsel initiatives launched in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, when eviction moratoriums were lifted and courts reopened – leading to a rise in eviction cases. 
In Vermont, there’s generally no right to an attorney in civil court cases, the way there is when someone is accused of a crime. 
Everything is different when a tenant has a lawyer beside them in the courtroom, said Sara Kagle, the project director of the Tenant Representation Pilot Project. Tenant representation helps ensure fairness, and also keeps the court process moving efficiently, she said. 
She likens tenants entering court without legal counsel to a patient being asked to take over in the operating room.
“You’re going in for surgery, and the surgeon hands you the scalpel and says, ‘I’ll talk you through it,’’” she said. “If the tenant only has us on the telephone before the hearing, and they don’t actually have an attorney with them in court, they are really at a disadvantage. There is so much at stake for them – because it’s literally a roof over their head.” 
Vermont’s two-year pilot program, funded with just over $1 million during the 2024 legislative session, focused on Lamoille and Windsor counties in its first year and then expanded to Rutland and Windham counties in its second year.
In those areas, Legal Aid sent out letters about its services to tenants facing eviction. Sheriff’s departments brought along flyers when they served eviction paperwork, Kagle said. 
Out of 207 cases that Legal Aid resolved through August, attorneys were able to prevent eviction in 73 cases – over a third. In other instances when tenants did move out, attorneys helped negotiate down debts related to past maintenance issues, for example. 
The program did not have strict income requirements, which meant attorneys could help any tenant who sought their services. After the state grant ends on Oct. 31, Legal Aid will still be able to take on tenant cases through other programs, but on a much more limited basis. 
Democratic Rep. Marc Mihaly, chair of the General and Housing committee in the Vermont House, said he wants to direct more state resources toward eviction prevention to stem homelessness. This past session, his committee supported continued funding for a program that helps tenants pay back-rent. 
But the committee did not advocate for continued funding for the tenant representation program, and lawmakers ultimately did not include it in the state budget. Mihaly struggled to recall the exact reasons, but said the issue stemmed from the timing of when lawmakers received the funding request during the budget-writing cycle.
To Koren in Brattleboro, that’s a loss for future tenants who will lack the opportunity for free eviction defense.
“That’s just a real, real crying shame that there’s a possibility that that will not be there for the next person that has a misunderstanding, a misstep, or something they’re unable to navigate themselves with a landlord,” he said.

title: Hoosiers using diesel receive no relief from tax suspensions
description: Our daughter called last week, and she was absolutely beside herself. She had just topped off her diesel-powered VW Jetta. It cost $42 for not even half a tank. As a young woman working and living independently, her rising fuel costs have her in panic mode. Diesel has surpassed $6 a gallon for the first […]
text:
Gas and diesel prices in Indiana on Sept. 17, 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chroncile)Our daughter called last week, and she was absolutely beside herself. She had just topped off her diesel-powered VW Jetta. It cost $42 for not even half a tank.
As a young woman working and living independently, her rising fuel costs have her in panic mode. Diesel has surpassed $6 a gallon for the first time in U.S. history. And yet Gov. Mike Braun has left her and other diesel owners out of state relief.
(For those wondering, our daughter’s car gets much better mileage than mine and likely yours.)
The governor’s continual gas tax suspensions don’t apply to diesel purchases, which means she hasn’t saved a cent from what could end up being $1.1 billion in savings for motorists over eight months.
She isn’t the only one asking why, so I checked in with Braun.
“Diesel is normally used by businesses. So, businesses versus households. That was the reason it wasn’t included,” he said, noting the diesel price spike was only recent.


Hoosiers have not paid Indiana’s gasoline use tax — a 7% sales tax calculated each month — since Gov. Mike Braun declared an energy emergency at the start of the Iran war in April.
Braun suspended the state’s 37-cent excise tax when he renewed the emergency order the following month. Both taxes have been suspended since May.


“Diesel’s a valid issue. It’d be something else that we could do. That’ll probably have to wait though until we see how long it sticks there. My prediction is once we get through the midterms, there’ll be a lot of dynamics that change,” Braun said.
But this answer falls short for me. First off, Indiana has the fourth-highest diesel tax in the nation, according to the Tax Foundation. You heard that right. It’s 64 cents per gallon. Comparatively, Indiana’s gas tax is 37 cents a gallon.
Add federal and sales taxes on top of that, of course.
Braun intimates that suspending the diesel tax doesn’t help real people. But Indiana’s Vehicle Fuel Dashboard shows 227,500 diesel vehicles were registered in the state during 2025. It’s a small percentage of the overall number of vehicles, about 4%. But that doesn’t mean those people shouldn’t count.
The percentage of diesel vehicles is actually growing while gasoline powered is decreasing over time.
In addition to my daughter, who drives her Jetta every day, my husband also has a diesel pickup truck. So do many farmers in Indiana. Luckily for us, the truck isn’t his daily vehicle.
Ignoring thousands of taxpaying citizens is a flawed choice.
And it’s not just about my family: here are a few comments I have received from readers.
– “Nothing for the guy with a diesel pickup truck though. $5.60 + a gallon.”
– “Wonder why not — truckers are taking a big hit rn.”
I would argue we are all paying for higher diesel in the price of goods, which are shipped all over the nation and to our homes.
Gas and diesel prices in Indiana on Sept. 17, 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chroncile)
Our trash service has a fuel surcharge because many of the trucks run on diesel. Guess what? That surcharge has gone up $1 in the last year, or about 30%. And it’s applied to every bill.
I know that businesses don’t have to pass on the savings to customers, which is a concern, but you could say the same about many policy discussions including those involving healthcare.
I’ve been vocal that I think Braun is pushing the limits of the law that allows the gas tax suspension. But he has used that lever, and his choices are not treating Hoosiers equally.
Gasoline was hovering around $4.44 per gallon nationally as of Thursday, according to AAA. A year ago, that was $3.20, a 38% increase. Meanwhile diesel has reached an all-time high of $6.40 a gallon – up 72% from a year ago when it was at $3.71.
We are all paying for this diesel surge, but especially my daughter. Which is why I just sent her about half my savings from the gas tax suspension. She can fill up her tank once.

name: National
title: Tribes hit hard by wildfires face health effects, cultural losses
description: Neighbors across the Colville Tribes communities in Washington state knew Matilda Bob’s log home as the “rainbow house,” for its brightly painted exterior. Now it’s gone. Sparked by a lightning strike in mid-July, the Kaiser Canyon Fire destroyed Bob’s home and 42 other houses on the Colville Reservation, along with 100 outbuildings such as sheds […]
text:
The Columbia Princess Ferry stays on the Gifford side of the Columbia River as the Modrite Fire exhibits extreme fire behavior just south of Inchelium, Washington. Fires in the state hit tribes particularly hard this year. (Photo courtesy of Colville Tribal Broadcasts, News and Information)Neighbors across the Colville Tribes communities in Washington state knew Matilda Bob’s log home as the “rainbow house,” for its brightly painted exterior.
Now it’s gone.
Sparked by a lightning strike in mid-July, the Kaiser Canyon Fire destroyed Bob’s home and 42 other houses on the Colville Reservation, along with 100 outbuildings such as sheds and barns, tribal leaders said.
“I couldn’t believe that it had happened,” said Bob. “It went so fast.”
Tribal leaders across Washington and Oregon told Stateline that this year’s record-breaking wildfires burned timber that they rely on for income, threatened food sources and waterways, and harmed the health of their communities. Power outages left families without food they’ve hunted or gathered and frozen.
Hotter, drier conditions driven by climate change already have made wildfires nationwide more frequent and intense, a trend that is expected to accelerate. Substandard housing and higher rates of acute and chronic underlying health conditions, including respiratory illnesses, make tribal communities more vulnerable during and after the fires. 
“What typically used to be like a two-month fire season for us when I first started fighting fire about 25 years ago — now that’s at least three months and sometimes longer, depending on the year,” said Cody Desautel, executive director of the Colville Tribes, who is also a forester and wildland fire expert.
An especially warm winter also left Washington state with about half its usual snowpack, raising drought concerns and wildfire risks.
Nighttime view of the Kaiser Canyon Fire during firing operations on Whitmore Mountain. (Photo courtesy of Colville Tribal Broadcasts, News and Information)
This year saw particularly devastating fires in eastern Washington, including arson-instigated fires that destroyed over 700 homes in Spokane. The conditions prompted Washington state Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson to declare a statewide state of emergency on Aug. 1, citing an “unprecedented” red flag alert of extreme fire danger from the National Weather Service. 
The Colville Reservation includes the southern portion of Ferry County, which has the second-lowest median household income of all counties in the state. The tribe lost a significant amount of timber, a main source of income, during the fires.
Many residents didn’t have home insurance because the housing didn’t qualify or they couldn’t afford it, said Cindy Marchand, chairwoman of the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation, adding that about half of homes destroyed in the fires weren’t insured. Other residents couldn’t afford to upgrade to more fire-resistant material, she said.
“The rates are just astronomical in the sense that a lot of people in our area are not able to afford this,” Marchand said. “We have elders living on a single income, they’re on a fixed income, and so they’re having a hard time making it as it is.”
By mid-September, the total acres burned across the state reached roughly 900,000 acres, the worst since 2015. 
Since July, about 200,000 acres burned across the Colville Reservation alone, with the Kaiser Canyon Fire scorching over 138,000 acres and the Modrite fire burning more than 57,000 acres.
In Oregon, over 60,000 acres burned across the reservation of the Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs, where at least six homes were destroyed.
The Wrights Spring Fire in Oregon burned through 55,000 acres across Klamath County, national forest and tribal lands.
Health effects
Faith Zacherle-Tonasket has seen how the wildfires have affected perinatal health. Founder of xa?xa? Indigenous Birth Justice, which offers perinatal and doula support across the Colville Reservation, Zacherle-Tonasket said three of her clients went into early labor during this year’s fires. She and her team believe stress amid displacement due to evacuations contributed to the early labor. Emerging research is also showing how wildfire smoke is a primary pollutant affecting pregnancy.
Wildfire smoke is now the primary pollutant affecting pregnancy, study shows

Zacherle-Tonasket also helps lead the River Warrior Society, a nonprofit offering wildfire relief for tribal and non-tribal members. The group has been coordinating shelter placements for elders, donations and food assistance.
“This is one of the biggest fires our reservation has had,” she said. “The biggest need we have on our reservation is air purifiers.”
Respiratory health has been a major concern post-wildfires amid smoke and poor air quality. American Indian and Alaska Native people disproportionately have chronic respiratory health conditions exacerbated by wildfire smoke, including asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Matilda Bob’s father, a veteran who is now displaced with her, has COPD.
Along with respiratory distress, there’s been “tremendous stress, anxiety, grief, trauma — and we expect and know that those behavioral health needs are going to continue beyond this current emergency. Post-fire recovery creates additional health concerns,” said Dayna Seymour, the Colville Tribes’ health and human services chair. “Our members are going in now to clean up the ash and debris, and aren’t really always sure what’s in that ash and debris, whether there’s hazardous materials, heavy metals, asbestos or other contaminants.”
Seymour added that community members helped deliver medications to their displaced neighbors and helped each other dig fire lines.
Research shows disproportionate smoke exposure among tribes in California, noted University of Kansas Assistant Professor Melinda Adams, a cultural fire practitioner and scholar who teaches in the Department of Earth, Energy, and Environment.
This Washington town is burning. That’s the plan.

“Because wildfire is increasing in frequency and intensity,” said Adams, a member of the N’dee San Carlos Apache Tribe of Arizona, “we must look at cumulative effects and identify patterns in human and environmental health while investing in climate and wildfire mitigation strategies that include Indigenous knowledge.”
Prescribed burns, carefully controlled fires to reduce brush that could fuel megablazes, are crucial tools in preventing dangerous wildfires and preserving ecosystem health. But regulatory barriers have made implementing traditional Indigenous burn practices difficult, Desautel and Adams said.
This week, the U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee advanced legislation that would streamline approval of prescribed burns, while the EPA issued guidance last year. 
Funding and staffing limitations are also a barrier, Desautel added. The Indian Forest Management Assessment Team found that Indian trust forest lands are funded at about a third per acre of comparable federal forests. 
Waterway pollution, cultural art lost
Seymour added that traditional foods including huckleberries and herbs and roots, such as bitterroot and camas, that the tribes rely on were scorched across the land.
“Those are things that we utilize to help us in ceremony, that we utilize to eat for subsistence. So that was a huge loss for our people,” Seymour said.
In Oregon, while no homes were lost on the Klamath Tribes’ lands, leaders still have concerns and uncertainty around environmental aftereffects, particularly on traditional food systems the tribes were finally in the process of regenerating.
The tribes had just started restoring their ancestral salmon after removal of four dams two years ago. Last year, the tribes documented the first adult Chinook salmon in the Williamson River, and earlier this year detected the first salmon hatch in over a century in the tributaries of the Upper Klamath Lake.
“The biggest (wildfire) impact is the effects on hunting and gathering that may be felt in the future. …With this high-intensity, high-severity wildfire, there’s likelihood of sedimentation into the streams that could serve as spawning grounds for that blue salmon,” said Tim Sexton, Wildland Fire Program Manager at the Klamath Tribes. Research is showing how wildfires affect fish habitats.
Deer stand near firing operations on the western perimeter of the Kaiser Canyon Fire, near Omak Lake Road and Coyote Creek Road area on July 25, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Colville Tribal Broadcasts, News and Information)
Klamath Tribes Chairman William Ray Jr., a former firefighter of 40 years, said he’s been advocating for tribal control of the waterways amid pollution that already existed before this year’s wildfires.
“We have ecological collapse going on. Our water quality in our lake and rivers isn’t very good,” he said.
At the Colville Reservation, Zacherle-Tonasket said many of her community members are holding off on traditional hunting and instead her nonprofit has gotten discounts from local butchers to help families.
“We don’t want to hunt this year,” she told Stateline. “It’s just ethically not right to hunt when our own animals are suffering the way we are.”
Bob said that many cultural heirlooms burned — her own traditional beadwork, a 100-year-old berry basket passed down from her great grandmother, and her nephew’s handmade attire worn during special dances at powwows. 
But her family will continue to dance as they do “for the people who can’t,” she said, on their ancestral land.
“Every time your foot hits the floor’s a prayer,” she said. “We were raised to respect the land. … We’re still standing in the fact that we’re all OK, that we all made it, that we didn’t lose anybody.”
Stateline reporter Nada Hassanein can be reached at nhassanein@stateline.org.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana prepares to pay more to its remaining private Medicaid plans
description: The Louisiana Department of Health has proposed new, larger contract extensions for the four health insurance companies that will remain a part of the Medicaid program. The deals were shared with state lawmakers Thursday and will follow the exit of two private companies that are leaving the state — and up to 580,000 enrollees — by the end of the year.
text:
Four companies who provide Louisiana Medicaid plans will receive $16.1 billion from state in 2027 if lawmakers sign off on their contracts next month. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)The Louisiana Department of Health has proposed new, larger contract extensions for the four health insurance companies that will remain a part of the Medicaid program. The deals were shared with state lawmakers Thursday and will follow the exit of two private companies that are leaving the state — and up to 580,000 enrollees — by the end of the year.  
Health officials provided details of the proposed contracts to the Joint Legislative Committee on the Budget. The remaining plans include Aetna Better Health, AmeriHealth Caritas, Humana Health Horizons and Louisiana Healthcare Connections. 

The four companies will collectively receive $16.1 billion from Louisiana in 2027, assuming state lawmakers sign off on the agreements next month. The individual contracts are the largest in state government, ranging from $3.2 billion to $5.8 billion per year each, according to information the health department provided.
Medicaid provides publicly funded health insurance to lower-income families, pregnant people and those with disabilities. In Louisiana, the program covers 1.3 million people overall, about 1.2 million of whom have a Medicaid plan through one of the private insurers.

Louisiana started 2026 with two additional private Medicaid plans, UnitedHealthcare and Healthy Blue, that covered 278,000 and 292,000 people, respectively. But UnitedHealthcare abruptly left Louisiana’s Medicaid program at the end of March following a legal dispute with Attorney General Liz Murrill over its affiliated pharmacy benefits manager. The health department then announced Sept. 1 that Healthy Blue, offered by Elevance Health and Blue Cross Blue Shield of Louisiana, would shut down at the end of the year. 

Blue Cross Blue Shield representatives have not responded to questions about why the company is shuttering Healthy Blue, but Elevance Health announced on a quarterly earnings call in July it would end several of its state Medicaid plans because of financial difficulties, according to Fierce Healthcare. 
The drop to four privately-run Medicaid programs should ultimately be beneficial for Louisiana, Health Department Secretary Bruce Greenstein said Thursday. Hospitals, doctors and other healthcare providers will now deal with less administrative work when it comes to treating Medicaid patients because there will be fewer insurance companies, he said. 

“I would say I feel more confident today than I’ve ever felt … in the history of the Medicaid managed care program,” Greenstein told lawmakers. 
Jeff Reynolds, executive director of the Rural Hospital Coalition of Louisiana, agreed with Greenstein and said he expects his members to be pleased with the change. Fewer privately run Medicaid plans should make it easier for rural hospitals to submit insurance claims, he said. 
Greenstein doesn’t expect any of the four remaining private Medicaid plans to pull out of Louisiana.

“I’ve spoken to the senior leadership in each of these plans in their national office and have great assurance that none of them plan to leave,” he told lawmakers. 
Having fewer Medicaid insurance options is not expected to save the state a significant amount of money, however. The remaining companies are being paid more to absorb participants from UnitedHealthcare and Healthy Blue. 

The cost of Medicaid programs for Louisiana will go down, from $16.7 billion in 2026 to $16.1 billion next year, due to lower overall Medicaid enrollment over the past year, state Medicaid director Seth Gold said. 
Louisiana’s overall Medicaid enrollment has fallen by 176,000 people so far this year. It went from approximately 1.5 million in December to 1.3 million people at the beginning of this month, according to the health department. 
Current Healthy Blue enrollees will have a window from Oct. 15 to Nov. 15 to choose a new Medicaid plan for 2027, according to the health department. Those who do not pick a plan will be assigned to one of the four remaining programs using an algorithm. It will prioritize assigning family members to the same plan and picking plans that are accepted by their existing medical providers. 
Medicaid plans with better performance evaluations will also receive preferential treatment, in some cases, and could receive more enrollees who are existing Healthy Blue participants, according to the health department. 

Regardless of where the Healthy Blue enrollees end up, their new plan will be required to cover all medical services previously authorized under Healthy Blue, including prescription medications, for the first 60 days of 2027, Gold said.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Trump administration looks to tap childcare funds to pay stay-at-home parents
description: Earlier this month, The New York Times reported that the Trump administration is drafting a plan to pay stay-at-home parents using funds currently aimed at helping working parents with childcare costs. While the rule change has not been proposed yet, New Hampshire childcare providers and family advocates worry about its impact.  The proposal would change […]
text:
A teacher plays with baby at Rochester Child Care Center on July 14, 2026. The Trump administration is working on a proposal to redirect childcare funding to married, stay-at-home parents. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)Earlier this month, The New York Times reported that the Trump administration is drafting a plan to pay stay-at-home parents using funds currently aimed at helping working parents with childcare costs. While the rule change has not been proposed yet, New Hampshire childcare providers and family advocates worry about its impact. 
The proposal would change rules for the Child Care and Development Fund, or CCDF, the primary funding source for childcare subsidies in most states. It includes dollars from both the federal and state governments, and in New Hampshire, the fund pays for the Child Care Scholarship Program, childcare quality initiatives, administrative services, and more. 
JD Vance, shown here during an August 2025 event in Peachtree City, Ga., is proposing a rule change to the Child Care and Development Fund. (Photo by Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder)
The proposal would change CCDF rules and allow married couples with a stay-at-home spouse to collect money from the subsidy program, the first of its kind. The Times reported it was a “top priority” for Vice President J.D. Vance and a formal change to the fund could happen without congressional approval. 
The majority of CCDF dollars in New Hampshire go to the scholarship program, which around 70-80% of New Hampshire’s childcare programs participate in. The scholarship program assists families by paying a portion of their childcare tuition directly to programs. More than 5,800 children were enrolled in the program as of July 2026.
The program has strict income and work eligibility requirements and does not extend to stay-at-home parents. To qualify, parents must be working, looking for work, or in school or a training program and making less than 85% of the state median income. Earlier this year, the state Legislature adjusted eligibility to extend to retirees who needed help paying for childcare for children in their custody. 
Trina Ingelfinger, early care and education policy director at New Futures, said the proposal is “out of touch” with what Granite State families want. 
“It would be devastating to our fragile childcare sector, which really is a backbone of support for the workforce and for the broader economy,” she said. “The stated purpose of helping stay-at-home parents for this policy is really at odds with other federal policy developments that the administration is supporting.”  
She said that if the federal government wanted to support stay-at-home parents, there would be universal paid parental leave and not new work requirements for Medicaid and SNAP. She also said the proposal is an issue of “fairness.”
“I don’t think the federal government has ever implemented a subsidy program that is accessible to only married people,” Ingelfinger said. “And I think there are people who are concerned that the policy is built on stereotypes about gender roles and raising concerns about that as well.”
MacKenzie Nicholson, senior director of Moms Rising, an advocacy group for women and families, said that while caregivers should be valued for their work, the proposal is a “non-solution.” 
“Taking limited (CCDF) resources away from moms who are in the labor force who need it created a new problem instead of that solution they’re looking for,” she said. “No matter whether you’re a stay-at-home mom, whether it’s done by paid professionals, all of that is real work and should be paid in our economy and that does need to be recognized. But this thing, where we pit moms against each other, has got to stop.” 
The potential rule change could also have widespread fiscal implications on the scholarship program. By taking funds away from working families, some are worried that it will hurt an already-struggling funding system. 
A new report from the New Hampshire Fiscal Policy Institute found that state investment in the childcare scholarship program has decreased, resulting in higher reliance on extra federal funds to prevent a waitlist for the program as enrollment has increased. 
Under current eligibility requirements and spending trends, the N.H. Department of Health and Human Services has said there is a “potential need” in the future to increase funding to avoid a waitlist for the program. By expanding eligibility to include non-working parents, the risk of a waitlist due to lack of funding for the program would increase. 
“We already need stronger state support for the existing program, and if funds are siphoned away from childcare, that is going to put enormous pressure on our state to try to backfill that need and address that need,” Ingelfinger said. 
Additionally, the Times reported that national experts are worried that redirecting away from working families and childcare providers could cause increased tuition rates and more program closures. 
According to the Fiscal Policy Institute, the average cost for having both an infant and toddler in center-based childcare in New Hampshire in 2025 was over $31,000. For married couples, it can account for up to 25% of a married couple earning the median income if they have two children under age 5. 
The draft rule proposal changes come as, across the nation, there is a broader conservative effort to push for more traditional family roles and more women out of the workforce. In New Hampshire, that might not be feasible for most families due to the high cost of living and the need for dual incomes. 
Shannon McGinley is the executive director of Cornerstone Action, a conservative Christian advocacy group based in New Hampshire. She said she wants government policy that supports “the enormous value of the care a mother or father provides at home” and does not financially disadvantage parents. 
“We welcome efforts to give parents greater freedom to choose the arrangement that is best for their children, including making it more financially possible for a parent to stay home,” McGinley said. “As the details of this proposal develop, we would want to ensure that it strengthens families without unnecessarily pitting one group of parents against another.”
Nicholson shared a similar sentiment. 
“Finding a way to help stay-at-home moms become economically safe themselves, so they have real choice, is definitely a part of the solution, and not one that comes at risk of every other part of the childcare problem,” she said. “But they are choosing to do it this way because they want to define who are the haves and have nots, and so we can have both. They just choose not to.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Mosquitos seem less active this year, but state still urges caution to avoid illness
description: There’s a word that might seem apt for describing how the 2026 New Hampshire mosquito season has played out thus far, but you won’t hear it from Manchester Deputy Public Health Director Phil Alexakos. “I’m not going to use the word that starts with a ‘Q,’ because we don’t do that in public health,” he […]
text:
Culiseta melanura mosquitos, found from Quebec to Florida, are one of the species of mosquito capable of carrying the potentially fatal disease Eastern equine encephalitis. However, they do not typically bite humans, preferring to feed on birds — like this specimen, shown preparing to bite a blue jay. (Photo courtesy CDC/Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station)There’s a word that might seem apt for describing how the 2026 New Hampshire mosquito season has played out thus far, but you won’t hear it from Manchester Deputy Public Health Director Phil Alexakos.
“I’m not going to use the word that starts with a ‘Q,’ because we don’t do that in public health,” he joked in a phone call on Tuesday. “But it’s been a less-than-active season.” (The taboo word? “Quiet.”) 
As of Sept. 10, there had been no detections this year of Eastern equine encephalitis virus, or EEE, in New Hampshire mosquitos, according to the New Hampshire Department of Health and Human Services. Detections of West Nile virus and Jamestown Canyon virus were lower than they had been in the past five years, a department spokesperson said.
The three pathogens are the major viruses of concern to humans that are known to circulate in New Hampshire’s mosquito population. In people, these pathogens can cause a range of symptoms, including potentially serious inflammation of the brain. One in three people who contract EEE dies.
Though rates have been lower than in recent years, this year’s detections of West Nile virus and Jamestown Canyon virus still call for precautions, officials said. 
Twenty-nine towns in New Hampshire, largely concentrated in the Seacoast and southeastern New Hampshire, have town-sponsored mosquito testing programs, according to DHHS. 
To surveil them for viruses, researchers use outdoor traps baited with alluring things like dry ice, which releases carbon dioxide gas like a breathing, blood-meal-bearing animal would; or a slurry of manure, hay, and water, which egg-bearing female mosquitos tend to love, Alexakos said.
The mosquitos are then removed from the traps, sorted by species, and sent for virus testing in clusters called “batches.” More than 5,000 batches have been tested so far this year in New Hampshire, according to the department.
Of those, seven batches had tested positive for Jamestown Canyon virus as of Sept. 10, according to DHHS. The insects came from traps in Exeter, Salem, Fremont, Kingston, Hampton, and Derry. Four batches had tested positive for West Nile virus, coming from Nashua, Kingston, and Rye.
No humans had tested positive for mosquito-borne illnesses in New Hampshire as of Sept. 10.
Similarly, no human cases have been reported so far this year in Vermont or Maine, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Massachusetts has reported eight human cases of West Nile virus, according to the CDC. 
A “great reset” will come with cooler weather, with the first hard frost subduing mosquitos for the year, according to Alexakos and DHHS. 
But for now, the risk remains — and according to DHHS, mid-September is often the peak of mosquito-borne illness activity.
The department urged residents to continue taking precautions against mosquito bites throughout the fall — such as wearing long sleeves and pants outdoors; using EPA-registered mosquito repellents; and staying indoors in evenings and early mornings, when mosquitos are most active, according to the department. Eliminating standing water can also reduce opportunities for mosquitos to breed.
Environmental shifts linked to climate change, such as rising temperatures, milder winters, and increasing rainfall, are linked to the expansion of diseases transmitted by vectors such as mosquitos and ticks.
New Hampshire has seen 20 reported cases of EEE in humans since 2003; 10 cases of West Nile Virus since 1999; and 23 cases of Jamestown Canyon Virus since 2011, according to the CDC.
It’s not clear why virus detection in New Hampshire mosquitos has been lower this season than in recent years, Alexakos said. If anything, he added, he anticipated this summer would have seen higher risk of West Nile virus, which is carried by mosquitos that thrive in warm and dry conditions. But a season could also theoretically be too dry, with less standing water for the bugs to breed, he said. 
Alexakos sees this year’s reports from New Hampshire municipalities as the tip of a larger iceberg. Manchester has run a surveillance program for mosquito-borne illnesses since 2000, shortly after a crow found dead in a city cemetery tested positive for West Nile virus in what was the first confirmed detection of the pathogen in New Hampshire. 
After that, for more than 25 years, city employees collected mosquitoes from traps across the city three to four times a week throughout the summer season. The program was reduced this year to one sample per week and handed off to a contractor, a move that Alexakos attributed to staff turnover and the labor-intensive nature of the project. 
But the data is still used for the same purpose, Alexakos said: Informing decisions about public safety, like deciding whether to initiate pesticide application when threat levels reach a certain benchmark (something Manchester has done on about six occasions over the years, according to Alexakos).
But even when the city was testing their three trapping locations multiple times weekly, the data was only a “snapshot,” he said. On a statewide scale, he pointed to the geographically limited spread of municipally run mosquito surveillance programs.
“If we have detections, I think that definitely gives information that we have more activity than we’re finding,” he said. “… If we don’t find things, that doesn’t mean we’re free and clear.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana Supreme Court hears Duke Energy case that could reshape your legal representation
description: A dispute over Duke Energy Indiana's natural gas plant now threatens the concept of associational standing in Indiana.
text:
A substation. (Courtesy Duke Energy Indiana)Indiana Supreme Court justices on Thursday sketched out a “middle ground” in a power plant dispute that could upend legal precedent allowing groups to sue on behalf of their members.
Attorneys for Duke Energy Indiana, ratepayer watchdog Citizens Action Coalition and others met for oral arguments in a case that has united dozens of disparate groups for coal, clean energy, gun rights, retirees, rural education and beyond in favor of the concept of associational standing.
Indiana’s high court accepted jurisdiction on an emergency basis, despite concerns.
“Looking at this case, I mean, for some reason, we think this is an emergency,” said Justice Christopher Goff, who voted against the emergency transfer. “This has been a legal proposition that’s been accepted, at least, by the lower courts — and, certainly, prior iterations of this court — for some time.” 	


Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US




“That’s the concern that I have, is that this has been rushed through by people who have really powerful interests … at a time when people who have to organize — it’s really important for them to have a voice, for the long-term legitimacy of the process,” Goff said. “We took this on an emergency. It does have constitutional implications, and I’m concerned … when we decide something of such high importance in that way.”
Peter Rusthoven, a Barnes & Thornburg attorney representing Duke Energy Indiana, assured Goff that not only was the case “fully briefed,” but that it would have reached the court regardless.
“This issue is going to come up to this Supreme Court if you put it through the Court of Appeals first,” Rusthoven said. “… I don’t think it’s being rushed in terms of this argument. It’s an important issue.”
Case’s origin
The legal battle began as a case before the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission.
Duke sought permission to build two natural gas-fired units at the existing Cayuga Generating Station in western Indiana’s Vermillion County. The utility maintains that a pay-as-you-build approach for the $3.3 billion project will save customers nearly $560 million in additional financing costs, according to the IURC’s 2025 approval.
The Cayuga Generating Station. (Courtesy Duke Energy Indiana)
The Citizens Action Coalition and another organization, Vote Solar, opposed Duke’s use of the construction-work-in-progress financing mechanism, arguing it would force customers to pay higher prices before the natural gas units go online and produce any electricity.
When the two groups appealed the IURC’s decision to the Indiana Court of Appeals, Duke asked the high court to take over the case. The utility challenged their standing to sue.
A split Indiana Supreme Court in April granted the emergency petition to transfer. Goff was joined by Chief Justice Loretta Rush in voting to deny, with the rest of the five-person panel voting in favor.
Arguments made
Duke maintains that Citizens Action Coalition doesn’t have standing — enough of a connection to sue — because the organization itself isn’t a Duke customer and no customers are individually listed as plaintiffs in the lawsuit.
“Unless we have an actual injured party before us, we cannot proceed,” Rusthoven told the court.
“These associations aren’t injured in any of those ways. But you do have people who can claim to be: in this case, Duke ratepayers who don’t want this (construction-work-in-progress), they’re free to sue,” he said later. “They’re free to come in, and this association and others can throw all their power behind them.”
Rusthoven argued that associations could also participate in lawsuits through other means, like by writing friend-of-the-court briefs, and take part in regulatory and legislative proceedings. 
Peter Rusthoven, a Barnes & Thornburg attorney representing Duke Energy Indiana. (Screenshot of livestream)
A coalition of more than a dozen states has aligned with Duke, pointing out downsides to explicitly recognizing associational standing in Indiana.
The organizations fighting Duke, however, argued that it’s a key way for regular people to access courts.
Earthjustice attorney Kirti Datla, representing Citizens Action Coalition and Vote Solar, said the dozens of friend-of-the-court briefs filed by other associations “justify why people would come together in a group for the protection that groups offer, (so) you aren’t standing out in the crowd in your own name.”
A brief filed by a coalition of nonprofits — led by the American Civil Liberties Union of Indiana and prominent conservative lawyer Jim Bopp — argued associational standing allows legal violations to be fixed even when would-be plaintiffs can’t sue themselves. The document offers reasons like privacy, fear of retaliation, disability, immigration status, cost and more.
Another coalition of builders, real estate agents, restaurants and others wrote that associational standing litigation benefits large groups of stakeholders and that explicitly allowing it wouldn’t open the floodgates to interest-group litigation.
“Requiring a member to sue as a plaintiff on behalf of all other members of the association would not make their dispute any more concrete,” Datla said.
Earthjustice attorney Kirti Datla, representing Citizens Action Coalition and Vote Solar. (Screenshot of livestream)
Datla and Rusthoven disagreed on whether Indiana’s Office of Utility Consumer Counselor, which represents ratepayers in IURC cases, would still be able to sue without associational standing.
Goff and others separately asked both sides about a possible middle route: having an association list an affected individual as a “nominal” plaintiff while maintaining control of the lawsuit itself.
Datla said that would probably work like a class-action lawsuit.
“If the individual is going to control all this, and the association can support it, why does there have to be something called associational standing?” Rusthoven said.
If associational standing were kept in some form, he said the court should require proof that an association is actually working with affected members on the lawsuit, and limit what disputes are relevant to a group’s purpose.
“If I declare my interest as good governance, well, then, my association has associational standing to challenge everything that we disagree with, because we are in favor of good governance,” Rusthoven said.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: How did China get wrapped up in the competitive race for Wisconsin’s 17th state Senate District?
description: Both the Democratic and Republican leaders of the Wisconsin Senate have said of their efforts to win control of the chamber that their candidates are staying focused on issues close to home. However, this week the focus of the race for the 17th Senate District turned to a country 6,000 miles away: China. The race […]
text:
Rep. Jenna Jacobson ran a campaign ad claiming Sen. Howard Marklein "invested thousands of dollars in Chinese corporations."   (Photo of Jacobson courtesy of campaign. Photo of Marklein by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner) Both the Democratic and Republican leaders of the Wisconsin Senate have said of their efforts to win control of the chamber that their candidates are staying focused on issues close to home. However, this week the focus of the race for the 17th Senate District turned to a country 6,000 miles away: China.
The race in Wisconsin’s 17th Senate District, a key district that will help determine control of the body, pits Sen. Howard Marklein (R-Spring Green), the incumbent in the race, against Rep. Jenna Jacobson (D-Oregon), a two-term state representative. Marklein was first elected to the seat in 2014 after serving two terms in the Assembly and has served for the last two sessions as the co-chair of the powerful Joint Finance Committee, which drafts the state budget.
The subject of China entered the race when the Jacobson campaign began running an ad last week that claimed Marklein had “invested thousands of dollars in Chinese corporations” while voting against a “measure that would have made Wisconsin buy more American made products.” The ad displays an image of Marklein’s face beside the Chinese flag. 
“While Marklein was making money off of his Chinese investments, he was stealing money from American workers like me,” a man dressed as a construction worker says in the ad. “Someone who sold us out like that should never be in the state Senate.” 
The ad led to Sen. Patrick Testin (R-Stevens Point), head of the Committee to Elect a Republican Senate, to call a press conference to defend Marklein Tuesday. Testin called the ad “deceptive” and a “sick smear campaign.”
Barry Burden, director of the University of Wisconsin-Madison Elections Research Center, told the Wisconsin Examiner in an email that it’s “quite unusual for China or another other foreign country to be much of an issue in a campaign for a state legislative seat.” 
Burden said the “focus on China in the 17th district is a kind of proxy for other issues,” including concerns about politicians “enriching themselves unethically because of investments” as well as worries about the construction of new data centers that some Wisconsinites see as drain on resources and harmful to the environment in addition to being related to U.S. AI developers’ competition with China. 
The ad, however, is seeking to tie some of Marklein’s prior reported investments to his lack of support for a Democratic bill in 2013 that would have required state and local contracts to give preference to materials manufactured in the United States.
Wisconsin public officials and candidates are required to file a Statement of Economic Interests under state law to disclose financial relationships and prevent conflicts of interest. 
According to his 2022 statement of economic interest, Marklein had over $50,000 in a WisdomTree Emerging Markets Fund as well as between $5,000 and $50,000 in investments in the JPMorgan Emerging Markets Fund. According to Sofi, investing in emerging market funds means owning shares in companies from India, Brazil, South Africa and China with the latter representing a large portion of many emerging market index funds.
Marklein’s most recent statement of economic interest included no emerging market funds.
In his press conference defending Marklein, Testin appeared to think the ad was related to investments made through the Wisconsin Retirement System, saying Jacobson, and every state employee, has similar investments. (The Wisconsin Retirement System is not prohibited from making investments in businesses in China, though Republicans have proposed barring the State of Wisconsin Investment Board from doing so in the past.)
Testin said Jacobson was “trying to be tough on foreign adversaries now that it might be politically beneficial for her.” 
“The truth is that Jacobson could have spent months standing up to our nation’s adversaries like China, but when she had the opportunity to support meaningful legislation that would protect Wisconsin from foreign influence, she voted no,” Testin said, referring to bills that would have restricted business with China. 
Testin proposed and Marklein co-authored a bill that would have barred Wisconsin agencies from contracting with certain foreign businesses, including China. Two other bills would have prohibited China from buying Wisconsin land and prohibited the University of Wisconsin system from providing study abroad and research there.
“Jacobson has no backbone, only a slick eye for political gain. She’s quick to point a finger at people like Sen. Marklein when it benefits her, but when she has the chance to help Wisconsin, she’s only interested when there could be gains for her,” Testin said. 
Jacobson voted against the two bills that passed the Assembly. Both were vetoed by Gov. Tony Evers. The issue has also come up in the race for governor, with Republican candidate Tom Tiffany saying he would have signed at least one of those bills as governor.
Burden said connecting politicians to China could “tarnish” their reputations. According to a Nov. 2025 Marquette Law School Poll, 65% of Americans held an unfavorable view of China and its leader, President Xi Jinping, while 19% said they had a favorable view of China. 
Burden said of Jacobson’s ad that “a connection to Marklein’s potential support for Chinese businesses and government is a way for her to point out to voters without a strong partisan preference why he should be defeated.”
Will Karcz, a spokesperson for the state Senate Democratic Campaign Committee, said in a statement to the Examiner that the ad was meant to provide voters in the 17th with “the truth of Howard Marklein’s personal foreign investment history.”
“Howard has repeatedly voted against protecting Wisconsin manufacturing while cashing in on tens of thousands of dollars he invested in Chinese-owned corporations,” Karcz said. “He got rich on the backs of Wisconsin workers. Jenna Jacobson is running to make Wisconsin stronger while Howard has spent the last 10 years putting his bottom line ahead of his constituents.” 
Whether the message resonates with voters is unclear. 
Todd Allbaugh, a former Republican who grew up in Richland Center and formerly worked for Sen. Dale Schulz, told the Examiner in an interview that he was confused when he saw the ad about a week ago. He lives in Madison, but still has family in the district. 
“I’ve seen this ad now probably somewhere around 20-ish times. It was baffling,” Allbaugh said. He said he didn’t understand what it was trying to get at until he looked it up using Claude, the AI assistant developed by Anthropic. “If you have to go to Claude to figure it out, it probably isn’t a really effective ad.”
Allbaugh acknowledged that Marklein has some advantages in the race given his status as an incumbent. Marklein won his 2022 race with 60% of the vote, though the district has changed considerably under the new maps. It now represents Iowa, Lafayette, Green, Crawford and Grant counties as well as parts of Dane County. 
“I know the 17th Senate District pretty much like the back of my hand because it’s home,” Allbaugh said. “With the newly drawn maps it’s certainly become more competitive for Democrats, probably the most competitive in a very long time.” 
Allbaugh said that he thinks Marklein is “scared for his political life,” as he is suddenly running in a competitive district and that can be seen in his campaign. One of Marklein’s recent ads positioned him as a bipartisan “bridge builder” and as “your man in the middle” and highlighted tax cuts that have been made while he’s been in office as well as some investments that have been made into local EMS and into the Lone Rock Bridge, which opened this year after two years of construction. 
In Allbaugh’s opinion, Jacobson’s campaign should focus on local issues that Marklein has had some say over. He noted the closure of the UW-Platteville Richland Center campus and the UW-Platteville Baraboo Sauk County campus that have happened while Marklein has chaired the Joint Finance Committee as well as the struggle that public schools in the district have had. 
“I think she’s a super strong candidate. She’s affable. She is enormously more likable and connects to people better than Howard Marklein, and I would if I were advising them, which I’m not, I would lean into that,” Allbaugh said. “Be authentic instead of listening to consultants with boilerplate things that they’re using in the other races. It doesn’t seem like a smart use of money when there are so many more easily understood issues that are particular to the 17th Senate District.”
Jacobson’s economic statement of interest from 2022 and 2024 does not list any emerging market funds.
Her 2024 statement lists an investment in the American Funds The New Economy Fund. According to the Capital Group website, it is mainly invested in the U.S. though it has a mix of investments abroad. About 15% of the fund is in Asia, including China.
