name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: MassHealth lowers estimate of members facing new work rules
authors: Ella Adams | State House News Service
description: Roughly 50,000 fewer MassHealth members are predicted to be impacted by Medicaid work and education requirements.
text:
MASSHEALTH HAS ITS EYES on January 2027, when it now anticipates that closer to 310,000 members in Massachusetts will be subject to new federal work and education requirements. 
MassHealth Chief Operating Officer Elizabeth LaMontagne’s new figure is lower than the prediction she made at a 2026 Medicaid summit in June, when she said about 360,000 members would be impacted by the overarching Medicaid work and education requirements in President Donald Trump’s July 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
LaMontagne on Wednesday pointed to ways the law will also shorten retroactive coverage and require renewals more often for some groups. But she told the Permanent Commission on the Status of Persons with Disabilities that “most individuals with disabilities are likely not going to be subject to work and education requirements because they often don’t fall into the impacted population.” 
“If you do have a federal or state disability, not only will you be automatically exempt from work and education requirements, assuming you were subject to them, but you also will not be impacted by the six-month renewal,” LaMontagne said. She said across MassHealth’s roughly 1.9 million-resident caseload, 250,000 members have a disability. 
MassHealth sent initial notices to members who may be impacted by the new requirements in August, and will be following up with emails, texts, and robocalls through the fall. Work and education requirements will be applied at a person’s regular renewal, she explained, at which point MassHealth will do a data check to try to automatically exempt them. 
MassHealth is “actively exploring new data sources” to try to exempt as many people as possible, LaMontagne said.
For those with disabilities or who are dependents under 14 years of age, the agency will use its eligibility system and Social Security Administration data. MassHealth is newly planning to use claims data to exempt those who are pregnant or postpartum, along with people who have a complex medical condition or are considered to have a “medical frailty.” 
“We also are working with the federal government to ingest Veterans Affairs data, which will allow us to automatically exempt veterans with a total or 100 percent disability rating,” LaMontagne said. “We are setting up a data exchange with the Department of Transitional Assistance, which will allow us to exempt people who are compliant already with [Transitional Aid to Families with Dependent Children] work requirements or who are subject to SNAP work requirements.” 
“If we’re not able to exempt people, then it falls to step two: do we have data that can show that people are already meeting work requirements?” she continued. “So for income, we already have access to federal and state data sources like Department of Revenue data, IRS data, and we’re newly integrating with Equifax, which will allow us to have more real-time data in terms of hours worked.” 
The agency is working through “technical hurdles” to integrate data from the National Student Clearinghouse, which LaMontagne said would allow it to pull in data on people enrolled in higher education. MassHealth is also working with a small group of nonprofits to support people who will want to comply with the requirements through volunteering. 
If the state can’t automatically prove a member is exempt from work and education requirements, the individual will have to answer new questions on their application or renewal, and if they’re considered “medically frail,” they will have to reply to a “request for information” with more details.
There are 47 community-based organizations that will be providing outreach and enrollment assistance as part of a statewide campaign to address federal changes, according to Hannah Frigand, senior director of the HelpLine and public programs at Health Care For All. LaMontagne said MassHealth is also working to connect people with volunteer and educational opportunities, as well as providing resources to help them fill out paperwork. 
MassHealth applicants in 2027 will have to show they’re meeting work and education requirements in the month before they apply, while existing members will have to show they’re meeting the requirements in any one month between renewals. While people won’t have to provide additional documentation proving they’re compliant in 2027, that won’t be the case in 2028 when self-attestation methods change, LaMontagne said. 
LaMontagne also told the Commission on Persons with Disabilities on Wednesday that MassHealth is also preparing for this October, when it anticipates about 7,300 individuals in Massachusetts will see their coverage impacted by new federal limits to coverage for certain noncitizens.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Gov. Stein: Trump ‘flat out wrong’ about NC crime
description: A day after President Donald Trump delivered a grim campaign speech in Gastonia, Gov. Josh Stein described Trump’s categorization of North Carolina as “political nonsense.” In his stump speech for Republican U.S. Senate candidate Michael Whatley, Trump portrayed the state as one of the most violent in the nation. He referred to North Carolina as […]
text:
Governor Josh Stein said President Trump's portral of a crime-ridden North Carolina is political nonsense.  Stein said his administration has been working on a bipartisan basis with the legislature to improve public safety. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)
A day after President Donald Trump delivered a grim campaign speech in Gastonia, Gov. Josh Stein described Trump’s categorization of North Carolina as “political nonsense.”
In his stump speech for Republican U.S. Senate candidate Michael Whatley, Trump portrayed the state as one of the most violent in the nation. He referred to North Carolina as “criminally dangerous,” and described its cities as “blood-soaked killing fields.”
“North Carolina, it was beautiful, it was apple pie, right? And now it’s one of the most violent and one of the worst in the whole nation,” Trump claimed.
Stein said the remarks were intended to generate fear and turn out voters in Whatley’s closely watched race against Democratic former governor Roy Cooper.
“Statistically, he’s just flat out wrong. There are 20 states that have a more violent crime than we do,” said Stein on Thursday. “We want to make sure that people are safe and feel safe in this community.”
Stein said his administration has been working on a bipartisan basis with the legislature to improve public safety.
The $34 billion state budget signed by Stein in July included double-digit salary increases for law enforcement. Last October, Stein signed a Republican-led bill aimed at addressing violent crime in North Carolina. The bill, “Iryna’s Law,” is named for Irina Zarutska, a  Ukrainian woman  who was killed on public transit in Charlotte in August 2025.
‘I am still with that guy’: Whatley doubles down on Trump at North Carolina event

Trump also wrongfully said Wednesday that Cooper released DeCarlos Brown Jr., the suspect in Zarutska’s death. That claim has been debunked.
Stein said Trump’s misleading claims do not advance the debate about how best to keep citizens safe.
Prior to Trump’s arrival, the White House issued a release that also seemed to contradict the president’s messaging. The press advisory stated that overall crime in Charlotte fell 9% in 2025 with violent crime falling 21%. And for the first half of this year, violent crime in North Carolina is down 5.8%.
Trump ties Whatley win to Helene relief
Stein also took exception to Trump’s off-the-cuff remark that if Whatley did not win the Senate seat in November, North Carolina might not see additional FEMA funding for Helene recovery.
“You know, you’re waiting for some additional funding,” Trump joked with the crowd at the Gastonia Municipal Airport. “If Michael loses, I’m not sending it.”
In the wake of Helene, Trump named Whatley his “recovery czar” for western N.C. But local officials have said Whatley has been largely absent from the area during the recovery, and federal funding has been unprecedentedly slow to arrive.
The governor said while politicians often say silly things, this was no way to respond to a tragic disaster.
“What he said that very much troubled me was to in any way connect recovery from an actual disaster to a political outcome,” said Stein.
Stein said western North Carolina has been working tirelessly for two years to recover from Hurricane Helene and needs more federal funding to flow to the region. The storm is estimated to have caused nearly $60 billion in damage. An estimated $9.8 billion in federal funds has been awarded since 2024. but the governor has requested more than $10 billion in additional funding from Congress.
“We’re doing everything we can to get whatever funding we’ve got out the door as quickly as we can,” Stein said. “To have any illusion that that funding is somehow tied to how people vote is absolutely offensive.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: New Louisiana security council puts foreign researchers under microscope
description: Faculty at Louisiana universities from certain countries will soon have to seek state permission to do their research under a new, far-reaching law that dramatically increases surveillance of researchers.  Act 505 by Sen. Adam Bass, R-Shreveport, created the Higher Education Research Security Council, which met for the first time this week.  Bass sold the le[...]
text:
Sen. Adam Bass stands at the podium in the Senate Chamber. (Photo by Allison Allsop / Louisiana Illuminator) 


Key points: 

A new state-created council has the power the approve or reject partnerships at Louisiana universities involving schools and researchers from China, Cuba, Iran and Russia
The council’s approval is needed even if a researcher is employed at a Louisiana university 
There are now new reporting and monitoring requirements for research and cultural partnerships at state colleges and universities.

The Illuminator’s staff writes key points for our stories, not AI. 



Faculty at Louisiana universities from certain countries will soon have to seek state permission to do their research under a new, far-reaching law that dramatically increases surveillance of researchers. 
Act 505 by Sen. Adam Bass, R-Shreveport, created the Higher Education Research Security Council, which met for the first time this week. 
Bass sold the legislation as an extra layer of security to prevent Chinese spies from stealing research conducted at Louisiana universities. But the law goes much further, creating a new framework that subjects research faculty from China, Cuba, Iran and Russia to an unprecedented level of scrutiny. American faculty will also be subject to review when they want to work with researchers from those countries. 
Bass’ legislation was crafted with the help of the nonprofit policy group State Armor, which  founder Michael Lucci said works with state and local governments “to defend and develop resilience against the Chinese Communist Party” when he appeared before a state Senate committee in March.
Texas and Louisiana so far are the only states that have set up research security councils, though the proposal has been made in other states. 
Critics of State Armor have said its tactics amount to modern-day McCarthyism. 
The increased scrutiny has raised concerns from faculty, who consider foreign collaborators vital to the research conducted at Louisiana universities, particularly in the sciences. 
“As you can expect, it is not difficult to think of a scenario where this bill will add delays or directly limit the collaborations we can do with foreign scientists,” said Rodrigo Diaz, who leads LSU’s Center for Research Excellence for the Study of Invasive Species. 
“We have collaborated with Chinese colleagues working on invasive species and biological control,” Diaz added. “This work is important because those natural enemies will help with management of invasive species in the USA.” 
The new security council must meet quarterly, though it might meet more frequently, said Commissioner of Higher Education Kim Hunter, who chairs the council. Its members include appointees of the lieutenant governor, attorney general and chairs of the legislature’s two homeland security committees — all offices that Republicans currently hold. 
The Louisiana State Police superintendent and the lead agent for the FBI’s New Orleans office also have representatives on the security council, as does the state’s chief information officer. Three university researchers, four research security officers and five representatives from the state’s private universities are also included.
The law allows the attorney general to investigate any violations of the research security law and offers a monetary reward to any whistleblower who identifies related violations. 
The security council has the power to approve or reject, for any reason, any research partnership between a Louisiana university and a university from one of the foreign adversary nations, which are designated under federal law. The council must also sanction any partnerships involving Louisiana researchers who are citizens of those nations. 
The legislation also requires university employees to report any interaction, communication or meeting they have with someone from the listed nations within 30 days, even if the security council gives its approval to a collaboration. It means the Louisiana faculty member has to submit every email and text message and log all phone calls with their foreign collaborator for review by the state. 
The definition of a research partnership is extensive, encompassing any work that involves more than one institution. Who counts as a researcher is also broad, including everyone from full-time faculty to graduate and undergraduate students. 
That means the council will have to give their approval to numerous projects. They range from an agricultural research collaboration between the LSU AgCenter and a Chinese university to an archival research project a student from China at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette is doing with the help of a Louisiana Tech librarian. 
Given the hundreds of faculty and students at Louisiana universities from the listed countries — and the hundreds of co-authors from those countries who work with Louisiana researchers — the security council is likely to review a long list of projects at each meeting. 
This new reporting system is on top of existing research security protocol that universities follow to monitor for undue foreign influence as well as state and federal laws with a similar purpose. 
“To protect our institution and our researchers LSU not only has a formal policy addressing research security, we also conduct rigorous annual trainings to ensure compliance with the most up to date federal guidance,” LSU spokeswoman Meg Sunstrom said.  
“The best practice for research institutions like ours is to embrace collaborative science while providing appropriate guardrails to protect our intellectual property and our people,” Sunstrom added. 
The new law also gives the governor, the Louisiana Senate president, House speaker and legislative auditor authority to request an audit of any research partnership, contract or grant involving foreign adversary nations or researchers from those countries. 
It prohibits partnerships with institutions or researchers from those nations if the project is funded partially or totally by the federal defense, health or energy departments. 
Jason Li, a graduate research associate with LSU’s Department of Physics and Astronomy, told state lawmakers at a March hearing on the Bass bill that these collaborations with federal grant backing constitute a considerable portion of higher education research.
“They are the vast majority of research projects,” Li said. “…This bill in its current form will impact virtually all the research projects, especially those at Tulane, LSU Health Sciences Center and Pennington (Biomedical Research Center) that rely heavily on (U.S. Health Department) funds.”     
Additionally, the law requires the Louisiana Board of Regents, which oversees higher education in the state, to maintain a public online database disclosing proposed gifts, contracts and partnerships submitted to the council for approval, along with the council’s decision. Reed said it has not yet been determined if the database will post faculty member names publicly. 
Other provisions of the law include: 

requiring the Board of Regents to develop policy that prioritizes research and partnerships with Israel and Taiwan. Any cultural exchange programs involving foreign adversaries must also receive security council approval. 
a research security review of the state done by the council and submitted to the governor, attorney general and legislature every even-numbered year. 
research security policy for Louisiana’s colleges and universities and development of an annual training program for research security officers at each school. 

The law in place now is a narrower version of Bass’ original proposal, which required students and employees from China to sign a pledge certifying they were not members of the Chinese Communist Party, the People’s Liberation Army or any Chinese intelligence agency, affiliate or subsidiary. The provision was removed over constitutional concerns. 
The security council will next meet in November and start reviewing research projects in January.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Faith leaders gather at Capitol to announce protection of free, fair election
description: Minnesota faith leaders gathered Thursday at the State Capitol pledging to protect the right to vote and to have votes properly counted.  Early voting begins Friday.  “We don’t get to just vote as normal because, unfortunately, this is not a normal election. We have already witnessed the numerous attacks on our democracy,” said JaNaé Bates […]
text:
JaNaé Bates Imari, the co-executive director of ISAIAH, a progressive ecumenical religious group, speaks to a gathering of faith leaders at the Minnesota State Capitol in St. Paul, Minnesota on Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026. (Photo by Izzy Wagener/Minnesota Reformer)Minnesota faith leaders gathered Thursday at the State Capitol pledging to protect the right to vote and to have votes properly counted. 
Early voting begins Friday. 
“We don’t get to just vote as normal because, unfortunately, this is not a normal election. We have already witnessed the numerous attacks on our democracy,” said JaNaé Bates Imari, the co-executive director of ISAIAH, a progressive ecumenical religious group. “We protect our elections, and we make sure that we are clear that we’re going to act free in order to stay free in this state.”  
The phrase “act free to stay free” has become a rallying cry among Minnesota democracy defenders this year. It serves as the title of a memo written by Doran Schrantz — former ISIAIAH executive director — that lays out the ongoing threats to a free and fair election and calls for specific steps to ensure votes are counted and winners seated. 
President Donald Trump’s administration has repeatedly sought to intervene in the voting and tabulation process, despite the U.S. Constitution’s clarity that this is a state, not a federal role.  Trump has continuously claimed that election fraud by non-citizens is rampant, even though it is extremely rare. The U.S. Supreme Court blocked Trump’s attempt to restrict mail-in voting on Monday, though the administration recently ordered more than two dozen states, including Minnesota, to maintain records from the 2024 election as it seeks to gain access to voter registration information. 
At the Capitol, faith leaders said they would use lessons from Operation Metro Surge to defend Minnesota’s election integrity. Last winter, churches, mosques and synagogues and their clergy played a key role in protecting, feeding and housing immigrants. Many religious leaders participated in several protest actions, including a demonstration at the Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport that led to the arrest of about 100 clergy members. 
Imam Abdulahi Farah, co-chair of the Somali American Leadership Table, said Trump’s immigration policies were a deliberate attempt to disenfranchise immigrants.

“We had a president who decided to call my community garbage, and also attack us and say that he will deport all of us. We knew those were his spectacles of cruelty. That was a strategy to make sure a community that shows up to vote are in fear and don’t show up to vote,” Farah said. 
Trump has not said that he would send ICE agents to polling locations. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said ICE agents would only be deployed if there were potential threats at the polls or the agents were serving a warrant. 
The blueprint for fighting Trump’s attempt to sabotage the election, drawn up in Minnesota

“We have heard threats and discussions about sending federal agents, including ICE agents, to polling places. As we’ve heard this morning, as Minnesotans, we do not have to imagine the presence of ICE and what it can mean for a community. The fear and the harm caused by immigration enforcement is still fresh in our very bodies, not to mention our minds,” Pastor Quinlan Koch of First Lutheran Church said. “So our response cannot simply be to watch this happen.” 
The faith leaders said they will train congregations on how to build rapid response networks in their communities and hold election night vigils. After the remarks, those gathered walked to nearby Christ on Capitol Hill, a Lutheran church, to eat lunch and attend trainings. As they walked, they sang the refrain, “Put one foot in front of the other, and lead with love.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Advocates call on Clearfield County commissioners to vote ‘no’ on ICE contract extension
description: The GEO Group operates Moshannon Valley under an agreement with Clearfield County, in which the local government serves as a pass-through for more than $5 million a month to skirt a ban on federal agencies contracting with private prison operators.
text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement headquarters in Washington, D.C., pictured in Feb. 3, 2026. (Photo by Heather Diehl/Getty Images)Immigration rights advocates say there’s evidence the federal government plans to buy a privately owned and operated detention center in Clearfield County and are calling on Pennsylvania elected leaders to act.
The Moshannon Valley Processing Center in Decatur Township is owned by The GEO Group, a for-profit prison company that operates nearly two-dozen immigration detention centers around the country. 
It has beds for about 1,800 people and has been the subject of scrutiny by members of Congress amid detainee deaths and complaints about physical and psychological abuse, a lack of adequate access to health care, and retaliation for standing up against mistreatment.
The GEO Group operates Moshannon Valley under an agreement with Clearfield County, in which the local government serves as a pass-through for more than $5 million a month to skirt a ban on federal agencies contracting with private prison operators.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE 
Jasmine Rivera, executive director of the Pennsylvania Immigration Coalition, called on the Clearfield County board of commissioners Thursday to reject a request from ICE to extend its current contract, which expires Sept. 28. The board is expected to consider the request Tuesday.
“We need Clearfield to stand up for justice and to vote no,” Rivera said in a video call with reporters. “They should not be making it easier for The Geo Group and the Department of Homeland Security to continue on with these plans.”
Commissioners Tim Winters, John Sobel and Dave Glass did not respond to a message Thursday.
Tim Smith, who lives in Osceola Mills and sued the county in 2021 to stop the center from opening, said the county has a remarkable history of standing up for the oppressed and marginalized. Smith noted his hometown was named for an indigenous chief by the eastern European immigrants who settled it.
“That spirit of standing up for human dignity is woven into the foundation and DNA of this community,” he said, adding that the county has a choice about its future in its decision about the contract.
“We do not have to choose an economic future that depends on the confinement of human beings,” Smith said. 
During the news conference, speakers also told the stories of detainees at Moshannon from Azerbaijan, Mexico, and Haiti who have been held at the center for months, experiencing isolation, chronic illness and mental health struggles. 
Rivera noted the request to extend the contract comes as the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is seeking proposals for turnkey detention sites including one in its “Philadelphia Area of Responsibility. According to ICE, that includes all of Pennsylvania, Delaware and West Virginia.
In a request for proposals issued last month, DHS said it intends to award 10-year contracts for “the provision of comprehensive detention facility services, transportation services, food services, operations and maintenance services” for ICE detainees in the custody of its Enforcement and Removal Operations branch.
“The RFP is the next step in building a massive, intractable detention system, a detention system that includes Moshannon here in Pennsylvania, but many other turnkey facilities across the country,” Rivera said.
Moshannon Valley opened as a privately run federal prison in 2006 and closed in March 2021 after President Joe Biden signed an executive order barring new contracts with private prison companies. It reopened later that year as an ICE facility operated under contract by The GEO Group.
ICE did not respond to an email seeking comment on its plans for Moshannon Valley.
The move toward buying its own facilities comes shortly after DHS abandoned plans to convert vacant warehouses in Pennsylvania and elsewhere into detention centers. 
Rivera noted that DHS has already bought several private detention facilities from Tennessee-based CoreCivic, including two in California, one in Kansas and one in Minnesota, according to the company.
The GEO Group’s CEO George C. Zoley said in an earnings call in August that the company is in “an active process” for the sale of several of its facilities subject to an agreement on price and the company’s continued management of the facilities under long-term contracts.

“We believe we have two types of assets: the buildings and the businesses of providing support services,” Zoley said. “We are pursuing a potential sale of the buildings, but we want to retain the business.”
Rivera noted any sale would include both the facility buildings and land, which includes several undeveloped acres that could be used to build additional housing for the facility. She said advocates believe the contract extension is needed to allow The GEO Group and DHS to complete their due diligence before a sale. 
“This cements private ICE detention in Pennsylvania for another decade, with the only decision makers, the only oversight coming from this federal government,” she said.
Federal ownership of Moshannon Valley would also limit efforts by Pennsylvania to regulate the facility as some other states have taken steps to inspect immigration detention centers. And because of the type of contract DHS is offering, the amount it pays The GEO Group could grow.
“DHS will be able to add more services to the contract without going through any additional contract steps,” Rivera said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT child advocate report shows mixed trends on youth fatalities
description: The report showed a drop in "non-natural" child fatalities in CT, but a concerning increase in the percentage of suicides by kids under 15.
text:
A report released Thursday by the Office of the Child Advocate showed a slight decline in “non-natural child fatalities” in 2025 in Connecticut, although the office noted a concerning increase in the percentage of children under 15 who had died by suicide.
The report showed a total of 67 child deaths in 2025, compared to 83 the previous year. The decline marked a 15% when compared to the previous five-year average.
According to the report, 62% of children that died by suicide were under the age of 15 in 2025, compared for 34% in the four previous years.
“The fact that we have more children at younger ages who die by suicide is deeply concerning and we want to make sure that parents know the resources available to them,” Child Advocate Christina Ghio said, such as urgent crisis centers and the 988 mental health and suicide hotline.
Ghio said that while the number of children who died was concerning, so too is the number of children who visit Connecticut emergency departments daily with self-harm or suicidal ideation: 16. 
“This is a report on the deaths but I think it’s important to remember that there are many, many many more children also experiencing the same feelings,” she said.
Earlier this month, state officials and providers announced the state’s Transforming Children’s Behavioral Health Policy and Planning Committee are launching a marketing campaign to promote mental health services available to children in the state.
Connecticut has urgent crisis centers, which operate as walk-in clinics for children needing mental health services in Hartford, New Haven, Waterbury and New London. The state also has a mobile crisis intervention program available by calling United Way at 211. 
The report also found that 15 babies died in 2025 due to unsafe sleep conditions, and in all of those cases their environments did not comply with recommendations from the American Academy of Pediatrics for safe sleep.  That number is down from 23 babies in 2024, but Ghio said it’s a troubling figure in light of efforts that have been made to raise awareness. 
“The state has made an ongoing effort to reduce those numbers but there is sort of a persistent significant number over time that continues, so we really want to get the word out to parents and caretakers to ensure children are placed in safe sleep environments at all times,” she said. 
Parents should always place a baby on its back, Ghio said. The AAP recommends that babies sleep in a space such as a crib or bassinet with no other people, with a firm mattress, a fitted sheet and no loose blankets, pillows or soft toys around them.
The report also noted an increase in the number of children who died in moped or motorcycle accidents in 2025, up to four children from two in 2024. The trend concerned Ghio because of the increased prevalence of e-bikes and related injuries among children.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Common Cause launches nationwide election protection effort for 2026
description: National voting rights group Common Cause is training thousands of volunteers to assist voters during the 2026 midterm elections. The nonpartisan advocacy group announced the effort Thursday during a virtual news conference. It said it has recruited thousands of volunteers so far and is seeking more than 10,000 nationwide. Volunteers will monitor polling pla[...]
text:
Voters fill out their ballots at a Sioux Falls polling place during the South Dakota primary election on June 2, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)National voting rights group Common Cause is training thousands of volunteers to assist voters during the 2026 midterm elections.
The nonpartisan advocacy group announced the effort Thursday during a virtual news conference. It said it has recruited thousands of volunteers so far and is seeking more than 10,000 nationwide.
Volunteers will monitor polling places, staff voter-assistance hotlines and work with legal teams on issues that could interfere with voting, the group said. The Trump administration has said armed federal agents could be deployed at voting sites.
“We take direct legal action, we combat voter intimidation, and we provide millions of voters with the trusted real-time support they need to cast their ballots both safely and confidently,” said Virginia Kase Solomón, president and CEO of Common Cause.
In North Carolina, Common Cause plans to have a presence in all 100 counties during the election, said Brooks Fuller, policy director of Common Cause North Carolina. The organization is working with grassroots groups to recruit poll monitors. 
“We will be across the state from the beginning of early voting through certification, working with communities of voters to make sure that their ballots are counted,” Fuller said.
Bishop William Barber, NC faith leaders call for ‘conspicuous courage’ to combat voter confusion

Common Cause North Carolina also has a state-specific voter hotline, 888-OUR-VOTE, staffed by lawyers, paralegals and law students trained and supervised by voting rights attorneys, Fuller said.
Common Cause Vice President Suzanne Almeida noted the group recruited over 15,000 election protection volunteers in 2024.
Volunteers receive 60 to 90 minutes of training on state voting laws, poll monitoring and how to report issues. Some specialized roles require longer, in-person training.
“We are training volunteers on how to show up well at a polling location in your state,” Almeida said. “What are the rules about where you can stand, who you can talk to, what kind of support you can give to voters.”
Common Cause has also filed lawsuits over the potential presence of federal law enforcement at polling places and challenged federal attempts to collect voter data.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Blumenthal touts passage of Russia sanctions bill as CT Dems split
description: CT's delegation supports Ukraine. But its House members voted against sanctioning Russia because of the authority it gives President Trump.
text:
After a years-long effort to exert pressure on Russia for its war in Ukraine, Congress took the final step in passing a sanctions bill before lawmakers departed for campaign season.
But the effort faced resistance from some House Democrats, including those in Connecticut, who fear it gives more latitude to President Donald Trump. The party needed to weigh its support for Ukraine while considering giving such authority to Trump, who’s been sympathetic to Russia and its leader Vladimir Putin and has exercised an aggressive tariff agenda since taking office.
The bill ultimately overcame that opposition in a Wednesday night vote, with several dozen House Democrats backing the bill alongside most Republicans. Notably, all five of Connecticut’s Democratic members opposed it, with those concerns in mind.
For U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who played a major role in crafting the bill, he’s still in a bit of euphoric disbelief a day later.
“I still have to pinch myself, quite honestly, when I think we’ve done it because there were so many moments when it seemed impossible, with this White House and all the complexities of sanctions and tariffs and international relations,” Blumenthal said on his way to votes on Thursday. “There are very few major bills that get through the United States Congress these days, especially dealing with an issue as challenging and controversial as this one.”
Passage of the legislation was the culmination of years of work on a bill alongside the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, the South Carolina Republican who died in July as he finished negotiations on it. Blumenthal has made nearly a dozen visits to Ukraine since Russia invaded in early 2022 and visited as recently as a couple of weeks ago.
The reception the Connecticut Democrat got from his colleagues at the U.S. Capitol on Thursday underscored the gravity of the moment: getting a bipartisan bill across the finish line in the current political climate right before a pivotal election.
Following House passage, Blumenthal and members who played a role in its passage celebrated the legislative victory, which they said was a testament to Graham’s work on the legislation up until his death.
The legislation named for Graham will impose tariffs up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil or gas, including China and India. It will also place sanctions on Russia’s energy sector, its financial institutions and officials as well as the country’s “shadow fleet” of oil tankers that seek to circumvent sanctions. It will also extend sanctions to Iran.
“On this day of joy and pride, I want to try to channel my inner Lindsey Graham: This is a big freaking deal,” Blumenthal said to laughs from his colleagues Wednesday night. “He used a different word, and there is no way of my imitating or replicating Lindsey Graham.”
Blumenthal noted the challenges they encountered along the way: holding together a majority in the Senate and then doing the same in an “obstacle-ridden” House. There were also hurdles to getting the White House on board, but when Graham met with Trump at the beginning of the year, the senator said the president “green lit” the bill. 
But support for a vote didn’t come to fruition until the summer.
The bill got significant momentum and attention after Graham’s death. The Senate passed it a few weeks after in early August and just before its month-long recess. Connecticut’s other U.S. senator, Chris Murphy, also voted for the bill.
Congress fully returned to D.C. this week, but the House has already wrapped up its work and won’t come back into session until after the midterms. But the Russia sanctions bill was one of the House’s final acts on Wednesday evening, sending the measure to Trump for his signature.
In a joint statement penned by U.S. Reps. John Larson, Joe Courtney, Rosa DeLauro, Jim Himes and Jahana Hayes, the delegation explained the reasoning behind their vote while pledging their support for Ukraine and commending Blumenthal’s work on it.
The Democrats pointed to a different bill that passed the House in June that would provide military assistance to Ukraine along with enforcement language on sanctions. They noted the bill that ultimately passed leaves sanctions to the discretion of Trump “who has repeatedly demonstrated bias towards Russia’s war goals of seizing the eastern Donbas” and could “enable the President’s penchant for imposing reckless tariffs at the expense of the American consumer” without more military aid.
“Our delegation has staunchly support Ukraine and are determined to provide tangible assistance as well as enforceable sanctions against Putin’s war machine. We recognize the Senate’s hard work and applaud Senator Blumenthal and his colleagues for their efforts,” the joint statement reads. “Due to our concerns, we could not vote for this bill in its current form and remain committed to continuing to stand unwaveringly with the Ukrainian people and enacting tough sanctions that hold the Putin regime accountable.”
Other members of the delegation have visited Ukraine in recent months. Himes visited with Blumenthal in May to meet with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and DeLauro, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, traveled there in August.
Connecticut’s entire congressional delegation has continued to push for additional aid to Ukraine and a continued commitment to the country amid four years of war.
But Democrats were largely wary of the tariff authority it grants to Trump, who has aggressively sought to implement sweeping tariffs and is currently engaged in a trade war with Canada. The result has led to an increase in prices for U.S. consumers.
Blumenthal said he shares those concerns with his Democratic colleagues and had spoken with the Connecticut delegation. At Wednesday’s press conference, he urged Trump to “aggressively and effectively” implement the bill.
He said he doesn’t know the timing of when it’ll move over to Trump’s desk. The president supports the bill and is expected to sign it into law.
“I was sympathetic to the concerns about the bill. Obviously, with a different president and a different majority in Congress, there would be a different bill,” Blumenthal said in an interview on Thursday. “But I sensed all the way along, talking to President Zelenskyy and Ukrainians on my trips there, that this bill really mattered. And they are the best judge of what matters to them in their fight. And I think it will matter.”
“This bill is far from perfect, but we couldn’t let the perfect be the enemy of the good. And I hope those concerns are unfounded, and if Trump misuses his existing authority or any of the new authority, I will be all over it with very blunt criticism,” he continued, noting that the courts have already struck down the “misuse” of his current authority. He now believes there will now be bipartisan support in Congress to address it.
While he sees it as a major step forward, Blumenthal said more needs to be done for Ukraine, including additional aid. But a full Congress won’t be able to move legislation until after the Nov. 3 elections. And when they return, lawmakers will only have a short window in the lame duck session before the end of the year as they contend with other priorities and government funding.
Still, he hopes the momentum of enacting this new law will bode well for future action.
“But alone, it’s not enough. We are far from done,” Blumenthal said. “The momentum that we have as a result of this bill should enable us to fight for the military aid, the economic support, the political and moral bolstering that Ukraine needs and deserves.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Regents approve state university funding requests as efficiency work continues
description: The Iowa Board of Regents has entered into a new phase of revenue enhancement and cost efficiency work at state universities as the institutions ask for increased state government support to help with rising expenses in essential areas. The board at its Thursday meeting approved fiscal year 2028 state appropriations requests from the University of […]
text:
The Iowa Board of Regents approved increases to state appropriations requests from Iowa's public universities, whose leaders said they hoped to avoid passing inflationary expenses on to students. (Photo by Catherine McQueen/Getty Images)The Iowa Board of Regents has entered into a new phase of revenue enhancement and cost efficiency work at state universities as the institutions ask for increased state government support to help with rising expenses in essential areas.
The board at its Thursday meeting approved fiscal year 2028 state appropriations requests from the University of Iowa, Iowa State University and the University of Northern Iowa — each asking for a $2 million increase in general education funding.
Kent Farver, chief business officer for the board, said during the meeting that the total funding request from the universities, including additional $2 million requests from the UI and ISU for special programming in rural health and artificial intelligence, represents a 1.6% increase from fiscal year 2027 appropriations.
“We’re asking for $2 million to be able to help offset some of the inflationary costs that we expect, and to be able to continue to innovate and create new programs to serve the needs of the state of Iowa,” UNI President Mark Nook said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Both UI President Barbara Wilson and ISU President David Cook agreed with Nook’s comments, saying the main drivers behind the general education funding increases are to help with rising expenses due to inflation and to not have to place that burden on students through tuition or fee increases.
While UNI isn’t requesting any other increases to its state-supported funding streams, Cook said ISU is seeking $2 million for its AI-Ready Workforce and Innovation Initiative in order to place the university in its best position to lead the state in AI education, research and innovation.
In his travels around the state, Cook said, AI was one of the topics most brought up, with questions of its impact, appropriate education of young people, and how it’s changing both the job market and ISU. The Ames university is already diving into these topics through its Translational AI Center and other efforts, he said.
“This is a moment in time to get out to lead, to lean into something that I think is distinct for Iowa State, and where we have a great history in being excellent in these areas,” Cook said. “And so that’s what informed this ask, of really trying to build Iowa’s next generation economy, embracing the ethical use of AI, which is critical.”
Funding requests from the UI fall into three “buckets,” Wilson said, split between the $2 million ask for its general education funding, $2 million on a recurring basis for a rural physician pipeline to bolster healthcare in rural areas and a capital project request of $25.5 million to develop a nursing simulation and training center.
Wilson said the UI will match every dollar of state support for the training center with its own funds that are being put aside for this purpose and there will be support from donors as well. The new facilities would house simulation suites and debriefing areas for student training, she said, and the UI estimates it would expand enrollment by around 58 students annually.
“This is a really important investment, I think, in the healthcare and well-being of the state, in addition to the rural pipeline program I just mentioned,” Wilson said. “We’re very hopeful, and we’re as committed as we can be, and the matching dollars, I hope, underscores that.”
REAPS reaches second phase
As universities work to save money in their own budgets and seek support from the state, board members and staff involved with the board’s Revenue Enhancement and Productivity Study (REAPS) reported Wednesday that they are getting closer to forming practical recommendations for the board to discuss.
Board Chief Efficiency Officer Jacob Nicholson said Wednesday the REAPS initiative, launched in December 2025, is “progressing on time and on target” to bring forward “specific, actionable and validated recommendations not only on efficiency and productivity gains but also on revenue enhancement opportunities” to the board at its February 2027 meeting.
“Importantly, the board will not receive a list of theoretical possibilities,” Nicholson said. “The end product will be a practical roadmap that outlines implementation considerations, timelines, milestones, and performance measures … so that outcomes can be monitored and validated over time.”
Phase one of the initiative, which Nicholson said is now complete, included contracting with Huron Consulting Services to aid in the study, establishing guiding principles and solidified the study’s methodology and what to prioritize. During this period, the universities provided more than 70 datasets and reports for analysis and leadership completed 56 interviews.
Phase two — the longest and most intense of the three-phase initiative — focuses on that analysis, Nicholson said, as well as benchmarking against other universities and “rigorous validation of opportunities.”
Nine focus areas were identified by the REAPS committee for analysis, including alternative revenue; research, innovation and commercialization; institutional capabilities as a service; workforce, professional and lifelong learning; real estate optimization and development; service enhancement; facilities and space management; cost rationalization and procurement and spend efficiency.
“Over the coming months, Huron and the REAPS committee will conduct deeper evaluation within these areas, quantify potential benefits, validate findings with institutional leaders, and refine recommendations for consideration by the board,” Nicholson said.
Work in this phase is expected to last through the end of the year, with Nicholson set to provide another update in November.
United Faculty leader calls for further state support
Chris Martin, UNI faculty member and president of faculty union United Faculty, took to the microphone during public comment Wednesday to call out the “dismal” funding of public universities by the state.
UNI has been flat-funded five of the past six years, with the exception of fiscal year 2023, Martin said, and during that same period the “compound cost of living in the Midwest region” has increased by around 13.5% based on data from the Consumer Price Index.
“At the same time, some leaders in the Iowa Legislature believe that there are greater and greater efficiencies to be wrung out by continually flat funding the regents universities,” Martin said. “The problem with this view is that instead of efficiencies, we have experienced years of deficiencies.”
Where a decade ago UNI’s average faculty salaries sat in the middle of its peer universities, Martin said now the university is dead last, and fewer faculty members are receiving “competitive funding” in the form of professional development assignments.
Despite not keeping up with funding needs, Martin said the Iowa Legislature is exerting more control over daily university operations through “unfunded mandates” like the new rules for civic education requirements at state universities included in House File 2800.
“These are the people who are the center of the university, and if we don’t reduce the current trajectory of rock-bottom salaries for faculty, the lack of professional investment in faculty, and unfunded mandates, then we lose the very thing that makes UNI an outstanding community,” Martin said. “I would like to think that you don’t want that, and that the good people of Iowa who started investing in UNI 150 years ago don’t want that either.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lamont, Fazio present dueling visions for CT economy
description: In separate remarks to CBIA, the candidates shared concerns about affordability, but offered vastly different plans for how to address it.
text:
Speaking before more than 400 members of Connecticut’s business community on Thursday morning, the state’s candidates for governor mapped out plans for the economy that shared common roots but veered in very different directions, highlighting key policy distinctions in the weeks leading up to their first debate. 
The incumbent Democrat Gov. Ned Lamont and his Republican challenger, Greenwich Sen. Ryan Fazio both spoke at an event organized by the Connecticut Business and Industry Association, the state’s largest business group. The candidates did not share the stage and were interviewed separately by CBIA leader Chris DiPentima. 
The competition loomed over the candidates’ remarks, with both seeking to frame their economic plans as the best for Connecticut, a state that has seen a fair share of ups and downs in recent months with rising unemployment alongside GDP growth. The discussion comes less than two months before Election Day and as new polling shows Lamont with a double-digit lead in the race, even as prospective voters express a desire for change.
While both candidates agreed that affordability, cost of living, and jobs remain top concerns, they differed on the specifics, with Fazio arguing the state needs to turn its economy around. Fazio pledged to pursue tax reforms, cut several regulations for businesses and reduce red tape around occupational licensing and expand apprenticeships.
“Connecticut really does have all the fundamental attributes to succeed, like no other state economy in the entire country, and yet people are pessimistic,” Fazio said. “People are struggling to pay their bills. I know that this state and the state economy can grow and succeed like no other place, but it’s going to take a change in direction and policy from the top in order to accomplish that.” 
Lamont, meanwhile, countered that his work over the past eight years has improved the state’s financial situation and that with four more years he could further deliver on recent progress. He called attention to his plans for healthcare in the state, increasing housing supply, improving workforce pathways, and continuing to support the state’s efforts in innovation and the life sciences. 
“We’ve had eight balanced budgets in a row, and are becoming increasingly a place of economic opportunity,” he said, adding the state has “gone from one of the slowest growing states in the country to, I think, it’s the 12th fastest.”
The visions presented highlight that the differences between the candidates largely rest on a question of change versus maintaining momentum, and how state government should provide relief amid national economic changes. Those questions will likely weigh heavily in the minds of the state’s business community, which argues that lawmakers and state officials need to be doing more to address Connecticut’s uneven economic picture, particularly the workforce and affordability issues that continue to affect both employers and employees. 
The Fazio Plan
The 36-year-old state senator was up first, with Fazio using his time to call attention to various proposals that would make a variety of cuts, from cuts to the income tax to reductions in electricity bill costs.  
The Republican candidate also discussed his proposal to reduce healthcare costs by supporting more competition in the marketplace. That includes through association health plans, a proposal that would allow small businesses to form a group and purchase insurance for employees. 
Several of these points have been raised by the Republican politician before, with Fazio regularly arguing that the state’s economy has been failed by Lamont’s vision. The senator continued that argument on Thursday, challenging the Lamont administration’s figures when it comes to economic growth and arguing that cutting spending would put the state on the path to economic success.  
Republican gubernatorial candidate Ryan Fazio answers a question from CBIA president Chris DiPentima during CBIA’s The Connecticut Economy conference Thursday, Sept. 17, at the Hartford Marriott. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
“We could limit spending, find savings to the tune of $2 billion per year or more in a state budget over 20 billion dollars, and use that to reduce taxes on middle-class families, make our state affordable, and help our economy grow,” he said.  
Throughout the conversation, Fazio argued that the state’s regulations often stifle economic growth, making it harder for businesses to operate. 
“This state can flourish like no other place in the entire country, but we need change in policy, leadership, affordability and relief,” he said.  “Then we can create jobs and opportunity.” 
The Lamont Plan
The two-term incumbent was up next, framing his time in office as an improvement for the state finances while adding that a third term would enable him to take things further. 
During his remarks, Lamont  sought to strike a middle-ground at an event where many in the room, including DiPentima, have often criticized the economic policies enacted under his administration. 
“Going back 10, 20, years, the business community and the state government have a pretty lousy relationship, and there was a lot of back and forth. It was not very helpful,” he said. 
But in recent years, Lamont argues, that has changed. “ We’ve had a good opportunity to work together,” he said. 
He said that a third term would largely focus on healthcare, a growing area of concern for residents that has only intensified in the wake of federal cuts to benefits. 
The governor also called attention to the need to increase housing supply, build out pathways from education to the workforce, and continue to promote and support both Connecticut’s innovation-based economic development efforts, as well as the state’s small businesses.
Gov. Ned Lamont answers a question from CBIA president Chris DiPentima during CBIA’s The Connecticut Economy conference Thursday, Sept. 17, at the Hartford Marriott. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
But the governor took a sharper tone when speaking to reporters after his appearance, noting that as the incumbent, he faces different expectations than his challenger. 
“I made some promises eight years ago. I was going to get our fiscal house in order, balance the budget, and cut taxes for the middle class. Eight years later we’ve delivered on that,” he said. “I can get out promised in a campaign, but nobody’s going to outdeliver what we’ve been able to accomplish.”  
The state’s business community continues to grapple with  affordability, economic issues
The candidates remarks came at end of event marked by several calls for Connecticut officials to address the economy, from job openings to a lack of affordability in the hopes of both boosting the state’s quality of life and economic competitiveness.  
The organization’s recent publications have called attention to this with a  recent CBIA consumer survey finding that half of Connecticut residents feel worse off than they were a year ago. In two additional releases on Thursday morning, the state’s latest annual survey of Connecticut businesses and new data on CT’s economic competitiveness both find that even as the state sees improvements in some economic figures, it is also struggling with high costs and affordability issues that are straining both companies and the people working for them.
The candidates say that as the race unfolds, they both have the solution that could help the state. Voters will soon decide which of the candidate’s visions they prefer.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana approved for mass SNAP replacement
description: The Indiana Family and Social Services Administration will begin issuing additional Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefit replacements to Hoosiers in 19 counties whose food perished in power outages on Aug. 11. The U.S. Department of Agriculture approved the agency’s request Thursday to replace SNAP benefits for affected households in all or part[...]
text:
Gov. Mike Braun, right, and Indiana Department of Homeland Security Director Jonathan Whitham update reporters on state and federal disaster response. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The Indiana Family and Social Services Administration will begin issuing additional Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefit replacements to Hoosiers in 19 counties whose food perished in power outages on Aug. 11.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture approved the agency’s request Thursday to replace SNAP benefits for affected households in all or parts of Carroll, Dearborn, Decatur, Delaware, Fayette, Franklin, Hancock, Henry, Lake, LaPorte, Madison, Marion, Porter, Pulaski, Randolph, Rush, Tipton, Union and Wayne counties.
Families lost weeks of food they couldn’t afford to replace. Then their SNAP claims were denied.

Gov. Mike Braun directed FSSA to apply for the federal waiver, which allows the agency to automatically replace anywhere from 15% to 60% of a family’s monthly SNAP allotment to alleviate the financial toll on families whose food spoiled in power outages.
The benefits will be loaded directly to each household’s electronic benefits transfer card on or around Sept. 26 — no paperwork or interview is required.
Earlier waivers permitted the agency to replace benefits for some Hoosiers, but were more restrictive in which households qualified and came with strict application deadlines, prompting the Braun administration to pursue a simpler process.
Amounts will vary based on when each household received their benefits.
Hoosiers whose benefits came through between Aug. 5 and Aug. 9 will see the highest replacement at 60% of their monthly allotment, according to a news release from the governor’s office.
The agency will replace 30% of monthly SNAP benefits for Hoosiers whose allotments were received July 19 through July 23, while benefits distributed between July 11 and July 17 will be replaced at a rate of 15%.
Households that already received replacement benefits will not see an additional allotment.
The state anticipates 36,533 households will qualify for the federal support, estimated to be worth up to $10 million.
Eligible zip codes include:

All of Lake and Porter counties
Carroll (46932, 47926)
Dearborn (47032, 47060)
Decatur (46156, 47240)
Delaware (47320, 47334)
Fayette (47024, 47352)
Franklin (47003, 47024, 47240)
Hancock (46117)
Henry (46117, 47334, 47352, 47360)
LaPorte (46340, 46345, 46346, 46348, 46350, 46360, 46365, 46371, 46382, 46390, 46391, 46532, 46552, 46574)
Madison (46016)
Marion (46107)
Pulaski (46366)
Randolph (47320, 47360)
Rush (46156, 46182, 47240, 47352)
Tipton (46979)
Union (47003)
Wayne (47339, 47345, 47360).

Braun also told reporters Thursday the Federal Emergency Management Agency has distributed $89 million in disaster relief to Hoosiers. Total aid distributed by federal, state and local governments for temporary housing, food, clothing and other assistance has surpassed $100 million, he said.
The Indiana Housing and Community Development Authority will renew hotel vouchers for Hoosiers displaced by last month’s severe storms for another 30 days.
“What we didn’t want were families and households that have been in these hotels since the disaster to be out on the street again in the coming days,” said Jonathan Whitham, executive director of the Indiana Department of Homeland Security.
At peak, some 360 households relied on vouchers for temporary shelter following severe flooding in August.
Whitham said roughly 260 households remain in hotels ahead of the initial 30-day deadline, which has been extended.
“We’re not to that point in the recovery phase where we’ve got that long-term option for some of these families,” he said. “So we want to extend it. We want everybody to know that if you’ve got a roof over your head right now, you’re going to have that as that expiration comes up on that first 30 days.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Arbitrator finds TF Green officials lacked cause to fire union leader, awards 2 years back pay
description: An arbitrator has ruled that the head of the union representing police and firefighters at Rhode Island T.F. Green International Airport can return to work nearly two years after he was fired from the airport’s fire department. But the outcome still depends on the resolution of a lawsuit filed last year in Providence Superior Court. […]
text:
The Airport Fire Department on Cedar Swamp Road in Warwick. Local 2873 of RI Council 94 President Steven Parent was ordered reinstated after an arbitrator found he was fired without just cause by the Rhode Island Airport Corporation October in 2024. (Photo by Christopher Shea)An arbitrator has ruled that the head of the union representing police and firefighters at Rhode Island T.F. Green International Airport can return to work nearly two years after he was fired from the airport’s fire department. But the outcome still depends on the resolution of a lawsuit filed last year in Providence Superior Court.
In a 67-page decision published Tuesday, arbitrator Sheila Mayberry found officials at the Rhode Island Airport Corporation (RIAC) failed to prove its misconduct allegations against Steven Parent and had effectively decided to terminate him before giving him a chance to respond at a hearing.
“In terminating the grievant, RIAC disregarded almost every principle of just cause,” Mayberry wrote.
Parent, who had worked as a firefighter at T.F. Green for more than a decade before his firing, expressed relief in an interview after learning the arbitrator agreed with his case that he had been terminated without cause. Parent has been president of Local 2873 of RI Council 94 for the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees (AFSCME) since 2019.
“Two years, nine arbitration hearings, and they didn’t have it,” Parent said in an interview.
Mayberry ordered the airport corporation to reinstate Parent and make him whole for lost wages and benefits, less any interim earnings, unemployment compensation or other applicable offsets. Parent estimated the back pay and lost benefits could total as much as $350,000.
Mayberry also directed airport officials to remove references to Parent’s termination from his personnel file and to treat his service as continuous for purposes of seniority and other contractual benefits.
The Rhode Island Airport Corporation moved to terminate Parent in October 2024, claiming he “knowingly and willfully engaged in efforts to sabotage airport operations” by discouraging applicants from working at T.F. Green. Airport officials also accused him of benefiting from overtime pay caused by ongoing vacancies.
Parent was officially fired after a closed-door meeting with airport officials Oct. 28. Two days later, Council 94 filed an unfair labor practice claim with the Rhode Island State Labor Relations Board.
The dispute was part of a broader deterioration in relations between airport management and the union who were in the midst of negotiating a new three-year contract for airport workers, which was eventually ratified in March 2025. 
The same month Parent was fired, airport executives hired Providence-based DeSisto Law to investigate anonymous letters alleging a toxic workplace, including one sent to airlines and the Federal Aviation Administration claiming the airport would close Aug. 13, 2024, because of an employee walkout. No walkout ever happened.
Mayberry found officials never told Parent during the termination process that they believed he was discouraging applicants to keep the department understaffed and generate more overtime for himself. Representatives from the airport corporation raised that allegation for the first time during arbitration, according to the reinstatement decision.
There were examples of alleged discouragement dating to 2022, including one firefighter’s report that Parent said he did not know why anyone would want to work at T.F. Green. But airport officials never questioned Parent about the comment at the time, nor did the firefighter who made the claim testify during arbitration.
No evidence of overtime review
As for allegations Parent benefited from overtime, Mayberry wrote proving such a scheme would have required airport officials to review overtime records, examine its union contract and interview firefighters. She found no evidence they did any of that. 
Parent acknowledged he worked substantial overtime, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic. But any extra work was a result of the department’s staffing requirements, which called for four firefighters per shift while allowing two to be out on paid time off at any given time.
“You don’t have to be a mathematician to figure out that if your minimum staffing is four and two are out at any given time, that’s going to cost overtime,” Parent said. 
Mayberry noted that his performance evaluations praised him for taking on so much overtime, with one captain stating Parent was “instrumental in coordinating the manpower void.”
Bill Fisher, a spokesperson for the Rhode Island Airport Corporation, said the arbitrator’s decision was unsurprising. He also maintained that the ruling does not resolve whether Parent can actually return to his job.
A final determination would come from a lawsuit airport officials filed last year in Providence County Superior Court seeking a ruling that the corporation could not be compelled to reinstate Parent.
The complaint alleges Parent trespassed by entering T.F. Green’s fire station without an escort on Nov. 1, 2024 — four days after he was fired. Airport officials said Parent took work materials without authorization after his firing. 
Parent previously said he went to retrieve a copy of the union’s contract. The lawsuit was stayed by Judge Brian Stern in January pending the outcome of the arbitration.
“Regardless of what the arbitrator has decided concerning contractual issues related to just cause, the fundamental security issues remain unchanged and must now be resolved in the proper forum, which is the court,” Fisher said in an emailed statement.
Even if Parent were to secure a final legal victory, there’s a big question on whether he wants to continue working at the Warwick airport.
“Do I want to go back and be a RIAC firefighter? Absolutely,” he said. “Do I want to go back and work for the Rhode Island Airport Corporation? I’m not so sure.”
But Parent is 60 this year and said he does not expect to find another job as a firefighter. And despite his reservations about his most recent workplace, he said he wants to see the airport succeed.
“Nobody wants the airport not to do well,” Parent said.
