text:
Deep Fission, which is building a nuclear reactor in Parsons, Kansas,  fabricated and tested a prototype reactor canister. The testing determined the canister met requirements for structural integrity and leak tightness, the company said on its website. (Photo by Deep Fission)TOPEKA — The company building a nuclear reactor one mile underground in Parsons made its federally approved safety report available to the public Monday. 
The U.S. Department of Energy approved Deep Fission Inc.’s safety design for its Gravity nuclear reactor in July. The company publicly shared the report, with only a few small redactions that relate to security, a news release said.
“We’re publishing our full (Nuclear Safety Design Agreement) because we think the public deserves to see the actual safety case behind this reactor, not just our word that DOE reviewed one,” said Liz Muller, CEO and co-founder, in a news release. “A project with this kind of ambition should be built in the open, and we hope more of the industry joins us in doing that.”
The reactor, which is a pilot project revolving around placing a small nuclear reactor in a one-mile deep bore hole, will be located at the Parsons Great Plains Industrial Park. Area residents have objected to the innovative and untested design, raising concerns about its safety.
Marjorie Reynolds founded Prairie Dog Alliance, a local advocacy group asking for transparency and regulations around the site’s development. She said their concerns extend to plans throughout the life of the reactor, such as understanding what will be done with spent nuclear material.
“At some point in time, they’re going to have to store nuclear material above ground because we do not have a national repository for nuclear waste,” Reynolds said.
She pointed to Burlington’s Wolf Creek nuclear generating station, which stores spent nuclear material on site. The Kansas Department of Health and Environment runs an environmental radiation surveillance program that checks Wolf Creek storage “to ensure there are no radioactive materials in excess of technical specifications released to the environment,” a state website said.
The 81-page agreement for the Gravity reactor creates a safety and regulatory framework with the U.S. Department of Energy, encompassing design requirements, safety analysis approach, regulatory process and key safety decisions, said Deep Fission spokesman Michael Padovano in an email to Kansas Reflector. 
The Energy Department’s approval was an early regulatory milestone for the project, he said.
“It means DOE has accepted the framework Deep Fission will use to advance the reactor’s design and safety analysis through the next stages of the Reactor Pilot Program,” Padovano said. “It does not authorize operation of the reactor, which will require additional safety reviews and approvals.”
Deep Fission worked with the Energy Department in a review process to develop the agreement, and Energy Department input was integrated through revisions, he said.
“The reactor design is not final, and Deep Fission will continue refining it as the project moves through preliminary and final design,” Padovano said.
The Parsons project is moving through design stages, safety analysis and regulatory review, he said. Further Energy Department approval will be needed.
The Deep Fission project is part of the Energy Department’s Reactor Pilot Program, which created a new pathway to advance nuclear reactors through commercial licensing.
“The program aims to leverage a DOE’s authority to expedite the research and development of advanced nuclear reactor technologies with the larger goal of reaching criticality for at least three advanced nuclear reactor concepts located outside of the national laboratories by July 4, 2026,” said an Energy Department page about the program.

title: Hagley Car Show, Chadds Ford Days, Milford Riverwalk Festival Lead a Packed Delaware Weekend
description: Our “Gotta Love the Weekend” Report: More than 500 classic vehicles headline a weekend filled with college football, festivals, living history, theater, outdoor programs, and fall family activities. WILMINGTON, Del. — From classic automobiles and college football to fireworks, German food and Revolutionary War history, Delaware and the surrounding region off[...]
text:
Caption: Nobody should be bored this weekend… there is a festival, events, outing, sale or musical for everyone! Enjoy Delaware!
Our “Gotta Love the Weekend” Report: More than 500 classic vehicles headline a weekend filled with college football, festivals, living history, theater, outdoor programs, and fall family activities.
WILMINGTON, Del. — From classic automobiles and college football to fireworks, German food and Revolutionary War history, Delaware and the surrounding region offer a full schedule of activities this weekend.
Hagley Car Show
More than 500 antique and restored vehicles from the early 1900s through the early 2000s will fill the grounds of Hagley Museum and Library during the annual Hagley Car Show from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. Sunday, Sept. 20.
This year’s special feature, “American Independent Automakers,” celebrates companies that competed outside Detroit’s traditional Big Three. Three feature fields will highlight vehicles connected to those manufacturers.
The rain-or-shine show also includes a vehicle parade, motoring music, food trucks and access to “Du Ponts Down the Road,” an exhibition of vehicles once owned and used by members of the du Pont family. Featured pieces include a horse-drawn carriage, an early electric car, a 1918 Cadillac, a 1928 DuPont Motors Model G Phaeton and a World War II-era Indian motorcycle.
Advance admission is required and sold by the carload for up to eight people. Passes cost $30 for the general public and $25 for Hagley members. Dogs are not permitted. Passes will be sold until 11:59 p.m. Saturday or until the event sells out. Details are available on the Hagley Car Show website.
Blue Hens Host Coastal Carolina
The University of Delaware football team returns to Delaware Stadium at 11:30 a.m. Saturday to face Coastal Carolina in a nationally televised game on CBS Sports Network.
The Blue Hens enter the game with a 1-1 record after opening the season with a 42-7 victory over Merrimack and losing 35-26 at Vanderbilt. Saturday’s game is also Band Day at Delaware Stadium.
The game gives families and football fans an early Saturday option before visiting one of the afternoon or evening festivals. Tickets and game-day information are available from University of Delaware Athletics.
Riverwalk Freedom Festival
Downtown Milford will host the 26th annual Riverwalk Freedom Festival from 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. Saturday along the Mispillion Riverwalk and throughout the downtown area.
The free event will feature more than 150 vendors, food trucks, live music, a car show, children’s games, a pet park and a brew garden. The Mispillion River Duck Dash begins at 3:30 p.m., with numbered ducks available for $5 and cash prizes of $500, $250 and $100.
The festival concludes with Milford’s only public fireworks display of the season at 8:30 p.m. Families should arrive early and bring blankets or folding chairs. Popular viewing locations include the Riverwalk and Memorial Park.
More information is available from the Chamber of Commerce for Greater Milford.
Battle at Chadds Ford
The Chadds Ford Historical Society will bring the American Revolution to life Saturday during the Battle at Chadds Ford and Historic Chadds Ford Days.
The daytime program runs from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. and features Revolutionary War skirmishes, military encampments, artillery demonstrations, colonial trades, music, food and family activities. Visitors can watch blacksmithing, woodworking, candle making and other demonstrations showing what life was like during the Revolutionary era.
Tavern Night in the Grove follows from 6 to 10 p.m., offering period music, costumed entertainment, traditional food and beverages, cannon fire and fireworks. The event takes place at the historical society’s Barn Visitors Center, 1736 Creek Road in Chadds Ford, Pennsylvania.
Tickets and the complete schedule are available from the Chadds Ford Historical Society.
Oktoberfest Returns to Newark
The Delaware Sängerbund Oktoberfest brings German food, music, dancing and family entertainment to 49 Salem Church Road near Newark from Friday through Sunday.
The long-running festival recreates the atmosphere of a traditional Bavarian celebration with live bands, German beer, folk dancing and foods prepared by Sängerbund members. The menu typically includes bratwurst, potato pancakes, schnitzel, sauerkraut, potato salad and German desserts.
Amusement rides are available for children, while the large festival tent offers music and dancing throughout the weekend. Admission is $10, with children 16 and younger admitted free when accompanied by an adult. Visit the Delaware Sängerbund for hours, parking and event details.
“Fiddler on the Roof” Opens at Candlelight
The Candlelight Theatre opens “Fiddler on the Roof” on Friday at its historic dinner theater at 2208 Millers Road in Wilmington.
The Tony Award-winning musical follows Tevye, a Jewish dairyman struggling to preserve his family’s traditions amid cultural and political upheaval in early 20th-century Russia. Its familiar score includes “Tradition,” “If I Were a Rich Man,” “Matchmaker” and “Sunrise, Sunset.”
The production runs through Oct. 25. Candlelight tickets include a meal served before the performance, and a full-service cash bar is available. Performance times vary. Tickets and show information are available from The Candlelight Theatre.
Delaware Nature Society Native Plant Sale at Coverdale Farm
The Delaware Nature Society is offering several outdoor programs for people interested in native plants, birds, wildlife and hiking.
Saturday’s activities include the Fall Native Plant Sale at Coverdale Farm Preserve in Greenville and Hawk Watch at Ashland Nature Center in Hockessin. Other programs include farm activities, nature art, marsh exploration and monarch butterfly programs at locations around the state.
Sunday opportunities include guided bird walks, another day of Hawk Watch and a hike through Flint Woods Preserve, which is not ordinarily open to the public. Times, fees and registration requirements vary by program. The complete schedule is available through the Delaware Nature Society events calendar.
More Weekend Options
The Delaware Seafood Festival will bring crabs, oysters, shrimp, lobster, crab cakes, live music and cooking demonstrations to Schellville near Rehoboth Beach on Saturday. Ticket and scheduling information is available through Visit Delaware.
Fifer Orchards near Wyoming is also opening its fall festival season with a corn maze, outdoor play areas, seasonal food and apple picking when available. Festival information and tickets are available from Fifer Orchards.
Meals on Wheels Delaware will hold its Hats & Heels fundraiser Saturday evening at Bally’s Dover Casino Resort. The event features food, music, fashion and contests while raising money to support homebound older Delawareans. Information is available from Meals on Wheels Delaware.
To Go Box

What: Major weekend events across Delaware and the Brandywine Valley
When: Friday through Sunday, Sept. 18-20
Top attraction: Hagley Car Show, 10 a.m.-3 p.m. Sunday
Sports: Delaware vs. Coastal Carolina, 11:30 a.m. Saturday
Free event: Riverwalk Freedom Festival, 9 a.m.-10 p.m. Saturday
Family options: Oktoberfest, Fifer’s Fall Festival, Chadds Ford Days and Delaware Nature Society programs
Evening options: “Fiddler on the Roof,” Tavern Night, Hats & Heels and Milford fireworks
Planning: Check individual event websites for tickets, registration, parking requirements and weather updates.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Mike Rogers gets big boost from business community with new slate of endorsements
description: Michigan’s business leaders are going all in on support for the U.S. Senate bid of Republican nominee Mike Rogers. On Thursday, both the Detroit Regional Chamber and the National Federation of Independent Business announced that they would be backing Rogers in the fall against Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed. The Detroit Regional Chamber PAC nod, in […]
text:
Former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers (R-White Lake) after he filed signatures in Lansing in his bid for the Republican nomination for U.S. Senate. April 17, 2026 | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan AdvanceMichigan’s business leaders are going all in on support for the U.S. Senate bid of Republican nominee Mike Rogers.
On Thursday, both the Detroit Regional Chamber and the National Federation of Independent Business announced that they would be backing Rogers in the fall against Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed.
The Detroit Regional Chamber PAC nod, in particular, is a big pickup for Rogers, but it was not a necessarily unexpected endorsement. As the premier business group in Detroit, the chamber also organizes the state’s annual Mackinac Policy Conference, of which El-Sayed has been hypercritical of during his current bid and also during his 2018 gubernatorial run. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In its endorsement of Rogers, the chamber noted that El-Sayed did not respond to an invitation for an endorsement interview. In May, when El-Sayed attended the chamber’s policy conference for its Democratic primary debate, the candidate told Michigan Advance that the policy conference represented everything that was wrong with Michigan’s political culture.
U.S. Senate debate at Mackinac Policy Conference exposes deeper debate over who gets heard

“Mike Rogers is a proven public servant with a deep background in federal policy who will represent Michigan well in the U.S. Senate as our state and nation faces major economic headwinds,” said Sandy Baruah, president and CEO of the Detroit Regional Chamber, in a statement. “Over the years, he’s been willing to defend our state’s industrial base while drawing on tremendous foreign policy experience to understand the global forces challenging our top industries.”
Rogers said he was grateful for the Detroit Regional Chamber’s support.
“The Detroit Regional Chamber is right: The house is on fire. And we can’t sit back as it rages on,” Rogers said in a statement, referring to the Chamber’s main theme of the 2026 Mackinac Policy Conference. “We need leaders who build our state back, not ones who continue to manage its decline — and I’ll work with anyone to get it done. We will get kids reading at grade level again. I have released plans to make housing and healthcare more affordable. And we’re going to re-attract good-paying jobs in the skilled trades.”
Rogers’ communications team also noted that this was the first time in more than 30 years that the Detroit Regional Chamber has endorsed a Republican nominee for the U.S. Senate. The last Republican candidate to earn that distinction was former U.S. Sen. Spencer Abraham, who served in the U.S. Senate from 1995 to 2001.
A message seeking comment from El-Sayed was not returned at the time of publication. A comment will be added to this story once one is received.
The chamber’s PAC said that it did have concerns about Rogers’ previous comments on election integrity, the federal Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act, which calls for documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to vote. The chamber also pointed to what it called a major “misalignment with the candidate on tariffs.”
That said, the chamber noted that it “welcomed many of Rogers’ other views on how to make housing more affordable, grow the economy and empower employers to create good-paying jobs in Michigan.”
“No candidate is perfect, and we won’t agree on every issue,” Baruah added. “But Mike Rogers impressively shared his vision for a stronger Michigan. We believe he will put the needs of Michigan and Michiganders above partisan politics and political rhetoric as he did in his previous service in Congress.”
NFIB similarly chose Rogers for his commitment to the business community in the race.
“Michigan small business owners are resilient, often having to navigate harmful policies at the state level,” said Amanda Fisher, NFIB Michigan State Director. “Having a pro-small business delegation in Washington is necessary for Main Street to be able to thrive in our state. The candidates we have endorsed for Congress have a proven record of backing legislation that benefits small firms and supports economic growth. We are eager to work with these leaders to ensure that Michigan owners are able to successfully operate their businesses.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC elections director disputes judge’s claim that GOP-led agency is politically biased
description: N.C. Board of Elections Director Sam Hayes said the board will serve all voters regardless of party. His statement came after a state appellate judge wrote a blistering assessment of election administration after it shifted to Republican control.  This week, the state Appeals Court in a 2-1 decision okayed a 2024 law that stripped Democratic […]
text:
North Carolina State Board of Elections Executive Director Sam Hayes speaks to members of the media on Wednesday, March 18, 2026. (Photo: Brandon Kingdollar/NC Newsline)N.C. Board of Elections Director Sam Hayes said the board will serve all voters regardless of party.
His statement came after a state appellate judge wrote a blistering assessment of election administration after it shifted to Republican control. 
This week, the state Appeals Court in a 2-1 decision okayed a 2024 law that stripped Democratic Gov.-elect Josh Stein of appointments to the state Board of Elections and gave that power to incoming Republican state Auditor Dave Boliek. Afterward, the state board and county boards shifted from Democratic to Republican majorities, with Boliek appointing all state board members and all county elections board chairs. 
“Today’s ruling affirms the constitutional authority of the General Assembly to allocate responsibilities among the Council of State agencies that make up the Executive Branch,” Hayes said. However, regardless of where the independent State Board of Elections is administratively housed, our mission remains the same—to serve all voters of this state regardless of party.”  
Stein said in a statement Wednesday that he will appeal the decision.
Two Republican judges on the panel decided the case for legislators and Boliek. 
Appeals Court Judge John Arrowood, a Democrat, dissented and disagreed with the majority that the board is apolitical.
NC Appeals Court OKs auditor appointing elections board members

He noted that the state board replaced its director with Hayes, who was chief counsel to Republican House Speaker Destin Hall. Boliek hired a former state Republican Party executive director to work as a liaison with county boards of election.
Other board decisions, including eliminating Sunday voting hours in some counties, eliminating polling places at some college campuses and moving to make it easier to reject absentee ballots, “appear to be designed to make it more difficult for citizens, who have historically voted in favor of candidates not favored by the majority of the members or the Legislature or the Auditor, to vote,” Arrowood wrote. 
In his statement, Hayes took issue with Arrowood’s characterization.
“The dissent not only mischaracterizes recent decisions of the current Board, but it also perpetuates the fiction that my predecessors were non-partisan actors. Despite these distractions, our focus remains on successfully administering elections in North Carolina.”
Hayes continued: “Regardless of my political affiliation, as Executive Director of the State Board of Elections, I have always endeavored to follow the letter and the spirit of the law with every decision, and I intend to do so going forward. Faithful adherence to the law, not meaningless platitudes, is what inspires confidence in elections.”

name: VTDigger
title: I’m a former second-home owner. We should tax second homes higher.
description:
A high tax on second homes could push more properties back into the hands of year-round residents.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  I’m a former second-home owner. We should tax second homes higher. .
text:
This commentary is by Alden Wicker, a homeowner, journalist and author who lives in Windham.
In 2014, I bought an income-restricted co-op in Brooklyn for $250,000. The market price for that apartment would have been around $650,000, but it was under New York City’s Housing Development Fund Corporation, a low-income housing cooperative with rules to prevent these units from becoming investments instead of homes. If your income is below the neighborhood’s median and it will be your primary home, you qualify. When you sell, you pay 30% of your profits back to the building in a flip tax so it can make capital improvements. You can only rent it out for a few months at a time. That affordable housing, with all its rules and regulations, allowed me to be a journalist who pursued poorly paid but important stories while also putting money away.
When the pandemic hit, my husband and I made a now-cliché decision to purchase a second home in Vermont. Look, I’m not saying buying a big old farmhouse in desperate need of repair ended our marriage, but it certainly didn’t help. The renovation took much longer and cost much more than it needed to because of Vermont’s severe construction labor shortage. My marriage suffered, then ended. But I stayed.
I knew that I was part of the problem. I heard the conversations at the grocery store and the hardware store about the lack of employees and housing for those employees. But I justified it: This house used to be a vacation house anyway! It’s too big for me to live there alone! I donate to the volunteer fire department! I patronize local businesses! 
I was kidding myself. It’s been shown everywhere from Jackson Hole, Wyoming, to Portugal that when people who earn their money elsewhere move in, they push the cost of living and home prices so high that it far outpaces the economic input they provide. They just don’t buy enough lattes or pay enough to the cleaning crews to create meaningful attendant wage increases for locals. It’s just consumption, not a true contribution to what makes Vermont so special. 
We need more than just tourism money. We need a high tax on second homes. 
The argument that second-home owners don’t use the schools or healthcare is shortsighted. They complain about the lack of good restaurants, the limited business hours, how they can’t find a good handyman, contractor, house cleaner or babysitter, and how the local plumber won’t even call them back. Believe me, I know. I was one of them. But to have a thriving economy with diverse businesses, you need young folks who live here full time. To have young folks, you need good schools, accessible healthcare and affordable housing. 
Just as I was struggling to pay for the final round of renovations on the house, I came across a dream job in Vermont. But there was only one problem: I couldn’t be paid a salary in Vermont and keep the Brooklyn apartment. So I had to choose: Vermont full time, or New York City full time. 
I had fallen in love with the summer drives, stopping at yard sales and pay-what-you-can cookie stands. It was deeply satisfying to build a fire in the stove after two hours snowshoeing through the silent woods. I found it soothing to listen to Vermont Public and hear how the Republican governor and Democratic Legislature have been respectfully debating how to unravel the Gordian knot of healthcare, housing and education. So one day I drove down to Brooklyn, packed up the rest of my belongings and staged the apartment for sale. I wept as I took one final look at the sunset view, then left. That era was over. 
I could have been mad at New York for limiting me. Instead, I respected the system for doing its job: giving middle-class people an opportunity to live and work in the city. It was time for someone else to pursue their dreams with the support of a small one-bedroom they could call their own. 
Many city folk who have bought second homes in Vermont don’t make that choice. They finish their renovations and decide that they actually don’t like living here. Or their jobs call them back to the city. In any case, instead of putting that house on the market or renting it to a young couple, they just decide to turn it into a short-term rental. 

READ MORE

A higher second-home tax wouldn’t solve all our problems. We also need to reduce the ability for a few strong-willed people to reject apartments and smaller homes, and we need to fund sewage infrastructure updates. Lifting restrictions on building in dense downtowns with Act 181 is also a great step in the right direction. 
But financial incentives need to change. I could imagine a tiered system where unwinterized family camps and cabins are left alone, mid-value second homes owned by Vermonters and rented long-term are in the middle, and high-end rentals owned by out-of-state corporations are taxed the highest.
Some second-home owners could absorb the higher costs and thus contribute more to making Vermont a supportive state for families and young people. For some, this would change the economics, and they would put their house on the market or switch to long-term rentals. 
As I finished the house renovation, my contractor shared that in his nearby neighborhood, he was one of the only full-time residents left. Just him plowing the snow in front of a half-dozen vacant houses.
So imagine my delight a year later when I pulled up to a house right across the street from him. Some friends and I had come together to help a young couple in their long project to turn a vacation home into a home-home. While the very pregnant wife passed out watermelon and fresh-baked cookies with help from her enthusiastic toddler, our group of friends worked with the husband to put in a fence, tape and mud the drywall, paint the interior window trim and put in plants in the front. 
It was one of my favorite days I’ve had so far in Vermont. Being grounded here in community, feeding and helping each other, is what Vermont life is made of. I wish that more people could have the privilege of experiencing a cozy home, good neighbors, pulling together and putting down roots.
But as long as we reward people who treat houses as investments instead of homes, that life will remain out of reach for too many.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  I’m a former second-home owner. We should tax second homes higher. .

name: VTDigger
title: Stop taxing Vermonters out of their own homes
description:
Abolishing property taxes on homesteads and shifting the burden to luxury vacation properties would ease the housing crisis.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Stop taxing Vermonters out of their own homes.
text:
Dear Editor,
A real solution to the property tax problem is to abolish property taxes on homestead property. Tax sales of homestead property should also be banned. The lost revenue could be made up in other ways that are less impactful on most residents. State income tax could make up a large share of the revenue, with a bigger increase for high earners. Nonhomestead property would need to be classed under some new categories.
Property with structures on it should be divided into suitable for habitation and unsuitable for habitation. In other words, a hunting camp not built for year-round use would be taxed at a lower rate than nonhomestead homes built for year-round use. A luxury slopeside condo or house being used for limited periods as a vacation home by the wealthy should be taxed at a higher rate. 

READ MORE

When working-class Vermonters compete with those with deep pockets looking for a vacation home, the Vermonters usually lose. This contributes to our current housing crisis. Therefore, the tax burden should fall more on those who contribute to the problem than on residents.
Casey JenningsLunenburg, Vt.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Stop taxing Vermonters out of their own homes.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Federal court weighs whether it’s too late to revive Missouri’s gerrymandered map
description: The last legal battle over Missouri’s 2025 redistricting plan played out Thursday, with a panel of federal appeals court judges hearing from Republicans that they should reinstate the map designed to help the GOP flip a Democratic-held congressional seat. The hearing via videoconference before the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals featured sharp exchanges ov[...]
text:
Marc Ellinger, attorney for the U.S. Rep. Bob Onder and state Sen. Rick Brattin, argued Thursday to the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals that it should order Missouri to use the gerrymandered 2025 plan for the Nov. 3 election. Ellinger is shown speaking Sept. 2 during a Missouri Supreme Court hearing (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).The last legal battle over Missouri’s 2025 redistricting plan played out Thursday, with a panel of federal appeals court judges hearing from Republicans that they should reinstate the map designed to help the GOP flip a Democratic-held congressional seat.
The hearing via videoconference before the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals featured sharp exchanges over the meaning of a recent U.S. Supreme Court order, which parties were legally allowed to argue the case and whether it is too late to change Missouri’s congressional districts before the Nov. 3 election.
The hour-long hearing took place just a day before local election authorities are scheduled to mail ballots to overseas voters and five days before absentee ballots are supposed to be ready for people who can’t make it to the polls on Election Day.
As Thursday’s hearing began, Judge James Loken, the panel’s presiding judge, said the case needs a final resolution and he expected to hear arguments that time to change the map again has already passed.
“Can we do that?” he said. “Can we come to a disposition in time for there to be an election?”
It is the court’s duty, he said, to try.
“Whether it’s impossible or not, we have to do our best to follow the Supreme Court’s instructions and get it to a place where there is an order that they consider final order from their perspective, so they can decide these issues that are worthy of their review,” he said.
Missouri GOP still see path for gerrymandered congressional map. Legal experts see little hope.

The judges on the panel were all appointed by Republican presidents. Loken was appointed to the court by President George H.W. Bush in 1990. Judges David Stras and Justin Smith were appointed by President Donald Trump, Stras in 2017 and Smith earlier this year.
If the judges order a change in the district map, it would be the fourth time since Sept. 3 courts have altered which districts Missouri is supposed to use in November.. And it could change a fifth time, if the U.S. Supreme Court reversed the decision.
All the questions before court stem from the referendum petition filed by the political action committee People Not Politicians to have a statewide vote on the redistricting plan Republicans passed during a special legislative session in 2025. Prior cases have resolved the power of the General Assembly and the governor to revise district lines in a special session and the power of the secretary of state to set the pace of reviewing signatures.

Secretary of State Denny Hoskins waited until the day of the primary to reject the referendum, declaring it unconstitutional even though his attorneys acknowledged in court that it had met the signature threshold. The Missouri Supreme Court ordered Hoskins to use the map created in 2022 for the Nov. 3 election when it found the referendum was legal and the Missouri Constitution means what it says when it prevents a legislative act subject to a vote from being enforced until after it is approved.
That was the first change and it put the referendum on the ballot as Proposition A. A “yes” vote will approve the map and it would be used in 2028. A “no” vote will reject it and the map drawn in 2022 will continue to be used.
The second change came as a result of a temporary restraining order from Chief U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark that directed Hoskins not to use any congressional district map except the one passed by lawmakers in 2025.
Clark issued the order in a case filed by U.S. Rep. Bob Onder, a Lake St. Louis Republican, state Sen. Rick Brattin, a Republican from Harrisonville, and two voters. Onder represents the 3rd District. Brattin is the Republican nominee in the 5th District and the voters are people who will have voted in the 5th District in the primary but will vote in the 3rd District if the map used in 2022 and 2024 is used this fall.
Two days after Clark’s order came the third change. The U.S. Supreme Court stayed Clark’s order, putting the 2022 districts back in place while the federal appeal proceeds.
The Supreme Court said Clark’s order would remain blocked “pending the disposition of the appeal in the” 8th Circuit “and disposition of a petition for a writ of certiorari in this court, if such a writ is timely sought.”
Loken and Chuck Hatfield, attorney for People Not Politicians, clashed over what that language allows the appeals court to do.. Loken said the Supreme Court meant the 8th Circuit could issue a final ruling. Hatfield argued that the Supreme Court’s stay prevents the 2025 map from taking effect while that process plays out. 
And, Hatfield said, the case has never been fully argued. Hatfield urged the court to send the case back to Clark and allow a full trial.
“We haven’t been given an opportunity to do any of that,” Hatfield said.
Loken, however, said that would mean it was certain no decision would be reached before it was too late to change anything.
“You’re not going to get a remand so you can write more briefs until the election passes,” Loken said. “You’re not going to, at least, maybe you will, but over my dissent.”
Judge David Stras focused much of his questioning on whether People Not Politicians has standing to pursue the appeal. 
Onder and Brattin sued Hoskins, and People Not Politicians intervened when the filings from Hoskins did not defend the Missouri Supreme Court’s decision.
Marc Ellinger, representing Onder and Brattin, said the only interest of People Not Politicians in the case was whether the referendum occurred. It will, he said, and he did not ask the court to stop it.
“Their sole interest was to put a referendum together and all their filings indicate that,” Ellinger said. “The intervenors in this case have gotten all the relief they get.”
Lou Capozzi, Missouri’s solicitor general, submitted filings in the case supporting Onder and Brattin and asking the court to tell the state to use the map created in 2025. But he disagreed on the question of whether People Not Politicians had a right to argue the case.
“That argument was before the U.S. Supreme Court, and they proceeded,” Capozzi said. “And so the state operates from the position that we have to sort of take the U.S. Supreme Court hints and abide by them.”
Hatfield argued People Not Politicians was an essential party to the case because Capozzi was not defending the Missouri Supreme Court’s interpretation of state law. 
“They cannot object to our intervention because without my client, no one is willing to defend the unanimous decision of the Missouri Supreme Court under state law,” Hatfield said.
Richard von Glahn, director of People Not Politicians, is also an intervenor. Stras asked Hatfield if von Glahn changed districts under the 2025 map, like the voter plaintiffs. 
He has, Hatfield said. 
“We have the same allegations as the plaintiffs,” he said.
In other arguments, Ellinger tried to convince the judges that there was still time to order Missouri to conduct the election under the 2025 map. Capozzi backed that argument and added that it was wrong to allow the Missouri Constitution to direct that a law not take effect because of a petition.
“There’s an opportunity to prevent this catastrophe from recurring every time Missouri does redistricting,” Capozzi said.
The discussion between Hatfield and the judges over legal questions raised in the suit went beyond the 20 minutes allotted for his argument. After about five minutes debating points of law at the end, Loken was ready to end it.
“We could go all day,” he said, “and the voters would just have more confusion and upset.”

title: State to allocate $855.4K in Rural Health funds to West Virginia Health Information Network
description: The state of West Virginia will distribute $855,400 of its federal Rural Health Transformation funds to the West Virginia Health Information Network to strengthen “health data infrastructure and improve the secure exchange of health information” across the state, Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced Thursday.
text:
Gov. Patrick Morrisey speaks to an audience in Bluefield, West Virginia, about the Rural Health Transformation Program in November 2025. (Photo courtesy of the West Virginia Office of Gov. Patrick Morrisey)The state of West Virginia will distribute $855,400 of its federal Rural Health Transformation funds to the West Virginia Health Information Network to strengthen “health data infrastructure and improve the secure exchange of health information” across the state, Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced Thursday. 
“Doctors and healthcare professionals need the right information at the right time to provide the best care for their patients,” Morrisey said in a news release. “This investment will better connect providers across West Virginia so patients can receive more coordinated care closer to home. When we improve care and healthcare outcomes, we help more West Virginians get healthy, stay healthy, and get back to work.”
The network serves as the state’s Health Information Exchange, connecting healthcare providers and organizations through secure data sharing, Morrisey said. 
“A stronger healthcare system requires strong data infrastructure,” said Secretary of Health Dr. Arvin Singh. “This investment will help providers access more timely and actionable information to support better care coordination, more informed decision-making, and improved health outcomes for West Virginians.”
The money will support the Connected Care Grid, which is one of seven initiatives the governor has planned for the Rural Health Transformation funds. The funds will expand participation in the statewide health information exchange, Morrisey said, and increase the number of healthcare organizations capable of exchanging information across systems.
West Virginia was awarded $199 million this year from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services for the Rural Health Transformation Program. The program aims to “empower states to transform the existing rural health care infrastructure and build sustainable health care systems that expand access, enhance quality of care, and improve outcomes for patients.”  
Morrisey also recently announced that $2.4 million in Rural Health Transformation funds will expand worksite and employer-based health services, and $2.4 million will go to the Ascend program to recruit healthcare professionals to the state. 
The Rural Health Transformation Program is part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which made historic cuts to healthcare and food assistance.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: How the EPA rollback of carbon emission rules could play out in Georgia’s coal-fired power plants
description: The federal Environmental Protection Agency has rolled back rules restricting climate warming emissions at electrical power plants, including those in Georgia. The rules the EPA ended this week date from the Biden administration and would have required coal and natural gas-fired power plants to restrict carbon emissions starting in 2030. That was about the s[...]
text:
The coal yard of Georgia Power's Plant Scherer is seen Sept. 3, 2025.
Credit: Grant Blankenship/GPB NewsThe federal Environmental Protection Agency has rolled back rules restricting climate warming emissions at electrical power plants, including those in Georgia.
The rules the EPA ended this week date from the Biden administration and would have required coal and natural gas-fired power plants to restrict carbon emissions starting in 2030.
That was about the same time Georgia Power had planned to shutter its two largest coal plants — Plant Bowen, which is north of Atlanta, and Plant Scherer, just north of Macon. But now with the data center boom, Georgia Power is keeping the plants running. With the help of a third coal plant over the border in Alabama, Georgia Power hopes to meet fully 70% of the data center demand.
Plant Scherer is on the Ocmulgee River, in the Altamaha River watershed. Altamaha Riverkeeper Fletcher Sams said the decision is a greenlight for unchecked pollution.
“This rollback is going to allow Georgia Power to run these aging antique coal plants indefinitely,” he said.
Plant Bowen’s units all came online in the 1970s. Plant Scherer’s went online in the ’80s. The Trump administration is fighting to keep even older coal plants up and running.
Last year, the two Georgia plants produced about 22 million tons of carbon dioxide, putting them near the top for greenhouse gas pollution among over 1,000 U.S. power plants and accounting for just under half of the carbon emissions of Georgia Power’s entire generation fleet.
Sams points to other pollutants in coal plant emissions as things Georgians will still be living with once the looser carbon rules keep the coal plants online rather than replacing them with cleaner combined cycle natural gas turbines.
“It’s hard to run a coal plant clean,” he said. “You have the mercury emissions and heavy metal emissions coming out of the stack that wouldn’t be coming out with the combined cycle turbines.”
Sams says much of that pollution will still end up in the state’s streams and rivers. Other things, such as particulate emissions, will continue to contribute to ground-level ozone and health conditions that come with it, such as asthma.
A 2023 study by a host of universities which included Georgia Tech suggested those emissions contributed to 500,000 excess deaths over 20 years. Plant Bowen was found to be the second most deadly power plant in the study. Bowen was thought to be responsible for deaths as far away as New York.
Meanwhile, the EPA in its announcement of the rule change said it now expects coal use to increase by a factor of 10. The EPA also set its intention to repeal any remaining carbon emissions rules, too. That would include any new natural gas power plants, such as the 1,500 megawatt power plant proposed for rural Mitchell County, south of Albany. Resident Lauren Dorminey has been organizing political opposition for months to the project pursued by Florida based NextEra Energy.
“I cannot trust energy industries who benefit by the millions from regulatory rollbacks,” Dorminey said. “Air, along with water, are two of our major concerns. So of course this is alarming.”
Maggie Shober, research director with the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy, also blasted the rollback.
“Through this action, the administration once again prioritizes short-term gains for wealthy donors over the lives and livelihoods of the American people,” Shober said. “Coal and gas are fossils, and the dinosaurs are in charge.”
Shober pointed to the effects of Hurricane Helene as a piece of the fallout from continued greenhouse emissions.
Gudrun Thompson, Energy Program Leader for the Southern Environmental Law Center, called the rule rollback a “gift to polluters.”
“In the South, climate pollution is harming our neighbors and the places we love,” Thompson said. “With power plants spewing over a quarter of the carbon pollution in the U.S., this rollback not only violates the law, it defies common sense.”
In an emailed comment, a Georgia Power representative said the company is reviewing the EPA’s actions on greenhouse gas emissions under the Clean Air Act and will “continue to constructively engage with our state public service commissions and environmental regulators to serve customers with clean, safe, reliable, and affordable energy.”
The EPA rule change will almost certainly face court challenges.


This story comes to the Georgia Recorder through a reporting partnership with GPB News, a non-profit newsroom covering the state of Georgia.

title: Bipartisan push to set rules for college athletes’ pay continues to advance in US Senate
text: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Senate on Thursday took another step forward on a sweeping bipartisan bill to overhaul the college sports world. The measure, clearing its second procedural hurdle on a 77-22 vote, would set national standards for college athletes’ compensation, provide certain antitrust protections to the NCAA, establish a five-year eligibility timeline for athletes and bar professional athletes from competing in college athletics.GOP Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas and Democratic Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington state championed the bill, with Republican Sen. Eric Schmitt of Missouri and Democratic Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware as original cosponsors.  Senators will now move ahead with debating and possibly amending and conducting a final vote on the measure.‘Reason to the craziness’Cantwell took to the Senate floor to push for her colleagues’ support ahead of Thursday’s procedural vote, saying the bill attempts to “bring some reason to the craziness that has basically been plaguing the most important aspects of college sports.” She noted that the “historic” measure would put into law “more than a dozen ... important provisions that help athletes and protect them for the future.” But critics argue the measure, which is notably neutral on the classification of athletes as employees, would undermine the labor rights of college players. One of the most vocal opponents, Sen. Chris Murphy, told MS NOW on Thursday that the bill “seeks to preserve the exploitative model of college sports.” The Connecticut Democrat also criticized the priorities of Congress in taking up the college sports issue amid the war in Iran and its impact on gas prices. “We have a war that is out of control in the Middle East, we have gas prices that are soon going to be $6 a gallon,” Murphy said. “This seems to be the last issue that Congress should be dealing with, and I think it shows how out of touch Republicans are.” As of mid-afternoon Thursday, the procedural vote on the college sports bill and a procedural vote on a federal judge, to be followed by a confirmation vote if successful, were the only items on the Senate majority whip’s notice for floor action.NCAA guidelines falloutThe bill marks a major attempt to combat many of the problems facing the college sports landscape, which continues to wrestle with the fallout of the NCAA’s guidelines in 2021 allowing athletes to profit from their name, image and likeness. College sports leaders also are grappling with a patchwork of state NIL laws, gender inequity in compensation deals and the NCAA’s controversial transfer portal, among other key issues.Adding fuel to the fire, a federal judge last year approved the terms of a nearly $2.8 billion antitrust settlement, which paved the way for schools to directly pay athletes. Meanwhile, if the Senate ultimately passes the bill in the coming days, the House would not take up the measure until the lame-duck session beginning after the midterm elections.  The lower chamber left town Wednesday for a seven-week campaign break ahead of the midterms in November.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Morrisey administration reveals more details on child deaths but key CPS information still missing
description: After the lack of details on child welfare deaths drew sharp criticism from lawmakers, the Morrisey administration released more information about how children are dying in West Virginia. At least one of the children was in the state’s custody through the foster care system.  The latest version of the report still lacks some details lawmakers […]
text:
The gold dome of the West Virginia state Capitol in fall 2021. (West Virginia Legislative Photography)After the lack of details on child welfare deaths drew sharp criticism from lawmakers, the Morrisey administration released more information about how children are dying in West Virginia. At least one of the children was in the state’s custody through the foster care system. 
The latest version of the report still lacks some details lawmakers wanted to review, including if Child Protective Services was aware of the children prior to death.
West Virginia screens in CPS referrals at the highest rate in the country, more than double the national average. A 2025 federal audit said West Virginia’s CPS failed to properly investigate a bulk of child abuse and neglect referrals.
Del. Adam Burkhammer, R-Lewis (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
“I appreciate the thoughtful details of the Department of Human Services and the updated report … One of the main details that needs to be included is the prior involvement of CPS in each of these cases,” said Del. Adam Burkhammer, R-Lewis, who has spearheaded child welfare reform as the Legislature grapples with the state’s troubled foster care system. Burkhammer is a foster parent.
“I think when we look to improve CPS policy and culture, we have to know if CPS was involved in any of these fatalities or near fatalities prior to the incident,” he said. 
A 2025 state law mandated the creation of the Critical Incident Review Team as lawmakers hoped to get more timely information about child deaths, particularly children in the foster care system or in active Child Protective Services cases.
The legislation came in the wake of the 2024 death of 14-year-old Kyneddi Miller, who starved to death on the floor of her Boone County home. State officials maintained that CPS didn’t know about Miller prior to her death, despite reporters obtaining documents showing that a CPS referral had been made about her. 
The Critical Incident Review Team released their first required report in July after they reviewed 29 incidents where a child died. However, it was light on information about individual child deaths and whether CPS had been involved with the child’s parents or caregivers ahead of the death.
“Twenty-nine kids died and we got three bullet points to send out,” Burkhammer said last month in a meeting where lawmakers strongly criticized the state Bureau for Social Services about the short report. 
The second quarterly report, released this week, was more expansive and included specifics about several child deaths. 
“This report continues to show us that we’ve got a lot of work to do in protecting vulnerable kids, and I look forward to working with CPS to make that happen in the future,” Burkhammer said on Thursday. The Critical Incident Review Team reviewed 20 cases between May and July, including 16 fatalities. 
Of those 16 fatalities, four children were involved in open CPS cases or assessments. 
Twelve referrals were accepted for assessment, and five were determined to be the result of abuse.
In one case, a male infant died from exposure to fentanyl while in the custody of kinship/relative placement after CPS removed the baby from the parents. Despite the infant’s removal from the parents, the kinship caregiver allowed the biological mother to care for the infant. Three adults have been arrested as a result of the infant’s death.
In another case reviewed by the team, a male infant died while cosleeping with an adult. The report notes that “the home was reportedly in deplorable condition,” and the parents were charged criminally. The report doesn’t say whether CPS was aware of the child prior to his death; a CPS investigation is ongoing.
Lawmakers tasked the Critical Incident Review Team with making recommendations to decrease preventable child fatalities and near fatalities in the state’s child welfare system.   
The team recommended that the Bureau of Social Services establish and require refresher training for child welfare staff on substance use investigations and drug-affected infant referrals. 
The Bureau of Social Services also needs to, according to the report, develop additional procedures for field investigations as it relates to substance use in homes where children under the age of three reside, “given the correlation between early childhood and substance use-related critical incidents.”
The Critical Incident Review Team’s report said that a female infant survived after receiving naloxone because she was showing signs of overdosing. “ The family has had two prior CPS referrals, according to the report. “The parents were referred to informal services,” the report said.
“We’ll continue to work with CPS and the Department of Human Services to make sure all the information is getting shared properly, as well as all of the corrective measures are being implemented,” Burkhammer said.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota Supreme Court upholds ban on transgender healthcare for minors
description: The North Dakota Supreme Court on Thursday unanimously found the state’s ban on gender-affirming care for minors constitutional, upholding a lower court’s ruling from last year.  The 2023 law makes it a crime to prescribe puberty blockers and other treatments to adolescents. The high court’s reasoning for its decision mirrored that of South Central Judicial[...]
text:
A crowd listens to oral arguments during a Supreme Court hearing at the North Dakota State Capitol on Tuesday, June 30, 2026. (Photo by Tanner Ecker/Bismarck Tribune)The North Dakota Supreme Court on Thursday unanimously found the state’s ban on gender-affirming care for minors constitutional, upholding a lower court’s ruling from last year. 
The 2023 law makes it a crime to prescribe puberty blockers and other treatments to adolescents.
The high court’s reasoning for its decision mirrored that of South Central Judicial District Judge Jackson Lofgren, who in October 2025 rejected a North Dakota pediatric endocrinologist’s claims that the law forces him to withhold necessary medical care from his patients. 
The Supreme Court found that the North Dakota Legislature hadn’t abused its power in enacting the ban, and that it isn’t the court’s place to interfere with how lawmakers want to regulate the medical field.
Judge rules in favor of North Dakota’s ban on transgender care for minors

“The forum for Dr. Casas’s factual arguments regarding the safety and effectiveness of gender-affirming treatment is the Legislature, not this court,” the justices said in an opinion authored by Justice Douglas Bahr.
The North Dakota Supreme Court also agreed with Lofgren’s conclusion that transgender people do not qualify for special legal protections, and that the gender-affirming care ban does not discriminate on the basis of sex.
Bahr noted in the opinion that other state and federal appellate courts have arrived at the same conclusion about similar laws restricting access to gender-affirming care.
Unless judges find that a law affects a protected group or restricts an important right, they usually are deferential to the Legislature, experts told the North Dakota Monitor previously.
Pediatric endocrinologist Luis Casas and his attorneys announced in February they would appeal Lofgren’s decision to the Supreme Court. 
The North Dakota Supreme Court heard oral arguments on the appeal in late June. Northeast Judicial District Judge Michael Hurly sat in for Justice Mark Friese, who recused. 
Attorneys for Casas claimed the law discriminates on the basis of sex because it bars minors with gender dysphoria from obtaining medical treatments that are otherwise available to kids to treat other medical conditions. They argued that because Lofgren did not make this finding, he used the incorrect framework to analyze the law. They asked the high court to send the case back to Lofgren for further review.
Casas’s attorneys also claimed the law interferes with North Dakotans’ right to make their own healthcare decisions.
One of the attorneys representing Casas, Tanya Pellegrini, during oral arguments called it “completely unprecedented” for North Dakota lawmakers “to single out a population from being able to receive medical care, categorically ban their medical treatment, and override parental consent.”
Defending the law, North Dakota Solicitor General Phil Axt during arguments before the court characterized gender dysphoria as a mental health condition, and said that North Dakota courts have not found that North Dakotans have a right to obtain care for mental health purposes. He said that the safety of gender-affirming care is still being debated and that the state has an interest in regulating access to the treatment to protect minors. Axt also said that the law does not discriminate based on sex.
The lawsuit was originally brought against the state of North Dakota in 2023 by three families with transgender children, in addition to Casas. Lofgren later dismissed the families and children from the suit, finding they did not have standing to participate. That left Casas as the sole plaintiff.
Lofgren presided over a seven-day court trial in early 2025 that included testimony from doctors, as well as two transgender teens and their parents who were initially plaintiffs in the case.
Attorneys for Casas during the trial noted that the majority of leading medical associations in the U.S. have found gender-affirming care to be a safe and effective treatment for adolescents with gender dysphoria.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Election 2026: Constitutional Amendments 1-3
description: New Mexico voters on Nov 3, 2026, will have four constitutional amendments to consider. The first three address the governor's vetoes; school elections; and regent appointments.
text:
Voters cast ballots at Holly Plaza Election Center in Albuquerque during the June 2, 2026, primary election. (Danielle Prokop/Source NM)Several amendments to the New Mexico Constitution will appear on the Nov. 3 general election ballot which, if approved, would require governors to explain their vetoes, eliminate the requirement to hold school elections on odd-numbered years and pare back the governor’s authority to nominate regents at public universities.
To place a constitutional amendment on the ballot, state lawmakers must first sponsor them as joint resolutions during a legislative session.
Source NM reviewed these three constitutional amendments, as well as the Legislative Council Service’s arguments for and against each of them. Source NM also spoke with state lawmakers who sponsored or co-sponsored each one.
A fourth amendment, which seeks to give state lawmakers paid salaries for the first time, will also appear on the ballot, and will be detailed in a separate news story.
Constitutional Amendment 1: pocket vetoes
When the Legislature passes a bill, the governor must sign it before it becomes a law. New Mexico law requires that the governor sign or veto bills, with a written message indicating why she or he approved or disapproved of the bill, by a specific date after the legislative session.
If the governor does neither, it becomes a “pocket veto,” meaning the bill does not become a law but the governor does not have to explain why.
The proposed amendment would require the governor to provide written messages explaining vetoes. If the governor does not act on a bill, it would become law under the proposed amendment.
State Rep. Matthew McQueen (D-Galisteo) co-sponsored a resolution in the 2025 legislative session to get Constitutional Amendment 1 on the ballot, and told Source NM he believes the measure supports “transparency and good government.”
“I’ve been in the Legislature for 12 years and it’s really hard to pass legislation,” he said. “When you have legislation that just passed, sometimes with a large majority, it goes up to the governor’s desk and the governor doesn’t sign it and doesn’t tell you why, what are you supposed to do?”
The Legislative Council Service’s guide to constitutional amendments provides two arguments for and against Constitutional Amendment 1.
Supportive arguments include providing more transparency to the public and the Legislature, and potentially bringing more balance to the three branches of state government. Opposing arguments include a concern that the amendment is superfluous and could be burdensome, and that it doesn’t adequately define its requirement for the governor to provide a “substantive explanation” with a veto.
Constitutional Amendment 2: school elections
Currently, New Mexico school districts can only hold statewide elections in odd-numbered years, when many local governments hold elections for city council seats.
Supporters of Constitutional Amendment 2, which would eliminate that requirement if approved, say that the current model imposes too much of a burden on schools. If a school district needs to put a bond question on the ballot to get funding for big projects, they would rather do that during a bigger general election when voter turnout is higher, Sen. Linda Trujillo (D-Santa Fe), who co-sponsored the resolution to get this on the ballot, told Source NM.
“This is really to streamline” a district’s process to put bond questions before voters, she said.
Putting school elections on a November general election ballot would require the state, rather than individual school districts, to foot the bill for the election and would put important local issues before voters during what are typically elections with the highest levels of turnout.
Trujillo said she’s encountered a common misconception that moving school elections to a general election ballot, which often includes mid-term or presidential races, would suddenly allow school board candidates to run in partisan elections. That is not the case, she said.
She added that the requirement prohibiting local school races and bond questions from appearing on a general election ballot is “kind of the last little semblance of women not being allowed to vote in anything but school elections.”
The Legislative Council Service published five arguments in favor of the constitutional amendment and four in opposition.
The arguments in favor are: School districts won’t have to pay for expensive mail-in elections; higher levels of participation in school elections; it could increase the number of school districts that participate in the state capital outlay system and result in new construction; districts could still choose to hold special elections; it would dilute the “outsized influence” of advocacy groups in influencing school elections.
The arguments against the proposal are: Adding to a general election ballot could increase voter fatigue and increase election costs; it could lead to politicizing school elections; it could reduce the voting power of teachers and school staff by increasing the size of the electorate; and it could diminish the attention paid to school elections if they’re on a crowded ballot.
Constitutional Amendment 3: nominating university regents
Constitutional Amendment 3, which would require that the governor appoint university regents from a pool selected by a nominating committee, has been in the works for so many years that “I’ve lost count,” Sen. Jeff Steinborn (D-Las Cruces) told Source NM.
He said he’s taken issue with the regent selection process since he was first elected, initially to the state House of Representatives, 20 years ago.
In New Mexico, the governor appoints regents, whom the state Senate must confirm, to oversee the state’s public universities. Current law also requires that boards of regents contain a roughly equal number of people from different political parties.
Steinborn said that system has allowed governors in several administrations to appoint friends or political allies to the posts.
If approved, Constitutional Amendment 3 would task the Legislature with creating a regent nominating committee. The governor would have to choose regents from a pool of people selected by the nominating committee. It would also prevent someone from serving as a regent if they changed their political affiliation in the year prior to their appointment. 
“It’s been abused and we’ve had too many appointments that had no higher education experience and nothing to offer our state,” Steinborn said of the current model.
He co-sponsored a resolution to get this placed on the ballot during this year’s legislative session. He said it was the “perfect moment — between governors, when no one was protecting their power,” to finally get this done.
The Legislative Council Service published two arguments for and against the proposal.
In support, it wrote that a nominating committee could comprehensively vet candidates to ensure they have the necessary experience to oversee a university, and a nominating committee could remove the influence of politics from the process.
In opposition, it wrote that the amendment would alter the checks and balances that currently exist between the Legislature and the governor’s office, and that it could weaken the accountability for the governor and the Senate in the appointment and confirmation processes.

title: White House yanks nominee to lead Immigration and Customs Enforcement
text:
WASHINGTON — The White House Thursday withdrew the nomination of Richard “Lance” Schroyer to lead the agency the president tasked with carrying out his mass deportation campaign, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.Schroyer, a former Oklahoma state trooper, had yet to have his confirmation hearing before the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs. The chair of the committee, GOP Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky, had no objections to Schroyer’s nomination, his office said in an email to States Newsroom. 

 






Richard "Lance" Schroyer (Photo courtesy Department of Homeland Security)

The White House did not immediately respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment. The withdrawal was announced in a brief statement on the White House website along with those of several other nominees.The Trump administration nominated Schroyer on June 27. He worked to establish Oklahoma's law enforcement partnership with the federal government to assist with immigration enforcement in the 287g program, and is a close ally of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who previously served as Oklahoma’s U.S. senator. Schroyer also worked in law enforcement for nearly 30 years.The current acting director of ICE is David Venturella, a longtime federal immigration official and former vice president of the private prison company GEO that rakes in billions through federal contracts by detaining immigrants at its facilities across the country. He took over in May after former acting ICE director Todd Lyons stepped down, following the shooting of two U.S. citizens by immigration officials in Minneapolis earlier this year.The White House has not announced a replacement for Schroyer. The last time the Senate confirmed someone to lead ICE was 11 years ago.

The 2026 Nebraska candidates running for Congress (top row); governor and lieutenant governor (second row); attorney general, secretary of state, state treasurer, auditor of public accounts and Public Service Commission (third row); Legislature (rows four through seven, arranged by legislative district); and State Board of Education and University of Nebraska Board of Regents (bottom row, from left, arranged by district). (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The Nebraska Examiner has officially launched its November 2026 voter guide for all candidates for federal and state office, statewide ballot measures and judges facing an up-or-down vote to remain in office.
The 2026 General Election Voter Guide combines answers from candidates ahead of the May primary and a handful of new, policy-specific questions. Of the 92 candidates on the ballot for federal and state-level races — Congress, state constitutional officers, Nebraska Legislature, State Board of Education and University of Nebraska Board of Regents — more than 90% participated. Gubernatorial candidates select a lieutenant governor running mate.
Among office-specific policy topics included in the voter guide: the economy and affordability, federal and state budgeting, international relations, medical cannabis, property taxes, public safety, consumer protections, election oversight, natural resources and data centers, debate procedure and filibusters, NU tuition/fees, local control and classroom/library content.
Questions were provided to candidates in mid-July. Responses were due in early September.


2026 General Voter Guide
Check out the full voter guide here.


The guide also includes information on key election dates, how Nebraskans can check their voter registration or ballot status and other general election details.
New to the general election guide is context for three voter-proposed statewide ballot measures: two related to online sports betting and one related to sex-based constitutional restrictions for K-12 and collegiate sports.
Voters will also see one constitutional amendment that state lawmakers placed on the ballot to ask whether they should be allowed to serve more consecutive terms than current voter-set limits.
48 Nebraska judges face an up-or-down vote to stay in office after 2026

This fall, all voters will see a handful of judges on their ballot, at least two and as many as 15. More information on the 48 judges who filed for retention — an up-or-down vote on whether they should remain in office for six more years — is available online here.
The voter guide is part of the Examiner’s continued coverage of the 2026 election. Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen certified the ballot Sept. 11. The first certified ballots must be sent to military and overseas voters by Sept. 18.
Additional race- and campaign-specific previews will be published ahead of the election.
Questions about the voter guide can be directed to info@nebraskaexaminer.com or zwendling@nebraskaexaminer.com. Media partners can republish parts of the voter guide, including portions of candidate answers, free of charge with attribution.

title: Wisconsin Supreme Court votes not to suspend law license of former Judge Hannah Dugan
description: The Wisconsin Supreme Court ruled this week that it would not suspend the legal license of former Milwaukee County Judge Hannah Dugan, who was convicted earlier this year of obstructing federal agents trying to make an immigration arrest in the county courthouse.  In an order released Wednesday, the Court overruled the request of the state […]
text:
Milwaukee County Circuit Judge Hannah Dugan leaves the Milwaukee Federal Courthouse on May 15, 2025. Judge Dugan appeared in federal court to answer charges that she helped Eduardo Flores-Ruiz, an undocumented immigrant, elude federal arrest while he was making an appearance in her courtroom on April 18. (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)The Wisconsin Supreme Court ruled this week that it would not suspend the legal license of former Milwaukee County Judge Hannah Dugan, who was convicted earlier this year of obstructing federal agents trying to make an immigration arrest in the county courthouse. 
In an order released Wednesday, the Court overruled the request of the state Office of Lawyer Regulation to suspend her license on the grounds that she was convicted of a “serious crime.” Wisconsin’s court rules state attorneys found guilty of a serious crime can have their licenses suspended until their disciplinary proceedings are complete. 
Dugan was convicted of one felony count of endeavoring to obstruct a pending proceeding after helping an undocumented man appearing in her court briefly evade federal agents. The case drew national attention and in July she was sentenced to pay a $5,000 fine. 
The Supreme Court suspended Dugan from her position as a circuit court judge in April 2025, shortly after she was arrested. 
In its Wednesday order, the Court found that “in its exercise of its discretion … a summary suspension of Attorney Dugan’s license to practice law is not warranted under the facts of the matter.” 
The two conservatives on the Court, Brian Hagedorn and Annette Ziegler, dissented from the order. 
Ziegler wrote that the standard practice of the Court has historically been to suspend attorneys convicted of crimes to expedite the investigation of the Office of Lawyer Regulation. She also questioned why the majority wouldn’t act to discipline Dugan for her actions. 
“These charges concerned then-Judge Dugan, in her capacity as a circuit court judge, wearing a judicial robe, at the courthouse, obstructing federal agents,” Ziegler wrote. “I am confounded by our court’s inaction.”

text:
Walks in southern Delaware and Wilmington will raise money for Alzheimer’s care, support and research
WILMINGTON, Del. — Delaware residents are being invited to join the fight against Alzheimer’s disease during two Walk to End Alzheimer’s events this fall.
The Alzheimer’s Association Delaware Chapter will hold its Southern Delaware walk Saturday, Sept. 26, followed by the Wilmington walk Saturday, Oct. 31.
“Alzheimer’s is a growing crisis in Delaware. As our population ages, more individuals and families are confronting this devastating disease,” said Glen Gray, chair of the Alzheimer’s Association Delaware Chapter. “Early detection and decades of research have improved outcomes for heart disease and many cancers, including breast cancer. But no one survives Alzheimer’s. That is why this walk — and the research, care and support it funds — is so important to our community.”
The annual walks bring together people living with Alzheimer’s, caregivers, families and supporters while raising money for research and the association’s care and support programs.
A central part of each event will be the Promise Garden ceremony, during which participants carry flowers representing their personal connections to Alzheimer’s disease and other forms of dementia.
Each flower color has a different meaning. Participants may walk in honor of someone living with Alzheimer’s, in memory of someone who died from the disease, as a caregiver or as a supporter of the association’s goal of ending Alzheimer’s.
More than 7 million Americans are living with Alzheimer’s disease, one of the leading causes of death in the United States. Nearly 13 million relatives and friends provide care for people living with Alzheimer’s and other dementias.
In Delaware, more than 22,300 people are living with Alzheimer’s, and more than 37,000 people serve as caregivers, according to the association.
The Walk to End Alzheimer’s is described by the Alzheimer’s Association as the world’s largest event dedicated to raising awareness and funding for Alzheimer’s care, support and research. Its roots date to 1989, when the organization began holding Memory Walk events across the country.
Participation is open to individuals, families, businesses and community organizations. Walkers may register individually or create or join a team.
Funds raised support the Alzheimer’s Association’s work to accelerate research, encourage early detection and risk reduction, and provide care and support services for families affected by dementia.

Registration: Participants may register, form a team, join an existing team or donate at alz.org/walk.

Learn more: Visit alz.org or call the Alzheimer’s Association’s 24-hour helpline at 800-272-3900.

title: Uzbekistan delegation learns from Mississippi emergency responders
description: An Uzbekistan delegation member captures video with his cellphone as firefighters perform a specialized airport rescue training exercise at the Mississippi State Fire Academy in Pearl on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026.
text:
PEARL — Members of the Uzbekistan Ministry of Defense and National Guard are taking part in a weeklong tactical exchange through the Mississippi National Guard’s State Partnership Program.
The program is a National Guard Bureau effort that pairs individual state National Guards with foreign countries. Mississippi has partnered with Bolivia since 1999 and Uzbekistan since 2012.
Lt. Col. Amanda Villaret, Mississippi National Guard state partnership director, said the group toured the Mississippi State Fire Academy in Pearl on Wednesday to learn how the state structures and administers its fire academy as Uzbekistan develops its own.
The Mississippi State Fire Academy says it trains about 15,000 students each year and offers more than 90 courses. Fire academy instructor chief Marcus Collier said the group observed airport firefighter refresher training, trench rescue training and basic firefighter recruits conducting three-dimensional flammable liquid fire training during their visit.
The visitors also observed other state emergency-response operations, including building-collapse search and rescue training in Philadelphia and backcountry rescue training. They will also observe high-rise rescue and public safety and order training during the week.
