name: WyoFile
title: Devastated by DOGE, Wyoming food nonprofit navigates new funding landscape
description:
Feeding Laramie Valley lost grants, shed positions and discontinued programs in the last two years. As the program focuses on survival, Wyoming food insecurity grows. 
The post Devastated by DOGE, Wyoming food nonprofit navigates new funding landscape appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
LARAMIE—The headquarters of Feeding Laramie Valley, a sprawling historic building at the edge of LaBonte Park, was quiet on an early September afternoon. The empty commercial kitchen gleamed, the main room was deserted and staff desks in a large office sat unoccupied.
The only soul in the nonprofit’s building other than Gayle Woodsum was her dog, Ethete, who lay under her desk snoozing. 
Woodsum, who founded the organization 17 years ago and helped build it through food share initiatives, community gardens and a community composting program, is growing used to the quiet. 
Trump administration efforts since 2025, including Department of Government Efficiency-related cuts and cancelled grants, have hobbled Feeding Laramie Valley, forcing the organization to shed employees, shelve programs and navigate a new world of rules and regulations. 
Today, the nonprofit’s mobile pantry is parked indefinitely, the composting program has been put on ice and a commercial kitchen project remains unfinished. Grants have been pulled, reinstated and in some cases pulled again — a dizzying cycle of disruption and dashed hopes, Woodsum said. 
Feeding Laramie Valley founder Gayle Woodsum at her desk in the organization’s Laramie headquarters on Sept. 2, 2026. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
“It’s been an insanely difficult year,” Woodsum said, one filled with quixotic efforts to communicate with federal partners, deep funding losses and panicked emergency grant requests. Many of her friends think she’s crazy for clinging to the mission that has fueled her work for nearly two decades. 
But, she said, “I just can’t stop.”
That attitude doesn’t surprise Woodsum’s acquaintances. She has never been one to back down, said Lina Dunning, a former Feeding Laramie Valley employee who has known Woodsum for decades. 
“She is a force of nature,” Dunning said. “I don’t know if anybody else would have had the strength of character” to keep the nonprofit operating. “She certainly has sacrificed a lot.”
One thing that keeps Woodsum going is framing the situation not as a tragedy but a provocation.
“I’ve come to feel the hugeness of the disaster as motivation,” she said. “This is a major battle, and people like me and this program and programs like this all across the state are on the front lines of it. We have to have that attitude in terms of determination and hanging in there. But it’s not easy.”
There have been 20-hour days, she said, along with hours of agonizing about what to cut. But, she said, there is also a new sense of camaraderie, a feeling of supporters being in the trenches together. 
The nonprofit’s gritty approach could offer inspiration for other Wyoming organizations learning to survive on less funding. In a time when food insecurity in the state is on the rise, Feeding Laramie Valley is managing to get fresh, healthy produce in the hands of those in need on a weekly basis. 
A card table and an idea
Woodsum, who has roots in Maine, has been a community organizer for more than 40 years. She founded her first organization, a support provider for families of terminally ill children, in the 1980s after her son developed a rare and fatal medical condition. She went on to, among other things, launch a nonprofit for survivors of childhood sexual assault, raise llamas at a ranch in Colorado and work with victims of crimes in Albany County. 
In the 2000s, she began thinking about food systems. She had been working with elders in Laramie and noticed that food insecurity was a key issue for them, she said. 
Instead of just collecting and distributing food to those in need, Woodsum was interested in addressing the root of the problem, the systems-based causes of food insecurity, she said. 
It struck her that people in need were expected to be grateful for standard food pantry fare like canned peas or Hamburger Helper. Woodsum, a lifelong gardener, hatched a vision for getting them fresh fruits and vegetables instead, and for helping them become more empowered in food production. 
Feeding Laramie Valley founder Gayle Woodsum looks at an apple tree on Sept. 2, 2026, that she helped plant 12 years ago. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
In the late 2000s, she took a card table to the Laramie Farmers Market, which back then was the end of the line for produce, she said, and asked farmers if they could spare any leftovers. The produce she collected became the origins of Feeding Laramie Valley, which she launched under her nonprofit Action Resources International.  
Woodsum split the goods between the Laramie Soup Kitchen chef, the Interfaith Good-Samaritan food pantry and a share program she set up for residents of an independent senior housing center. Not long after, she secured community garden space. 
In 2011, a stroke of luck came for the nascent organization when it was selected as one of five national sites for the Food Dignity Project. The USDA-grant-funded collaboration between community organizations and three universities set out to identify effective strategies for sustainable community food systems. For Feeding Laramie Valley, it provided access to a network of innovative trouble-makers who were trying to get to the roots of system changes, Woodsum said. 
Feeding Laramie Valley grew steadily through the 2010s. It found its current home near LaBonte Park — in a building that is reportedly Laramie’s oldest. It launched a summer lunch program for kids, planted more gardens, established a food hub and started a mobile market to get produce to further flung communities. As an AmeriCorps VISTA intermediary, Feeding Laramie Valley placed VISTA volunteers all over the state, and also worked with the AmeriCorps NCCC program. 
Vegetable gardens, a fairy garden and a sensory garden surround Feeding Laramie Valley’s headquarters, which sit on one edge of LaBonte Park. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
By late 2024, the headquarters was bustling, with a staff of 14 that would grow with seasonals to about 30 in the summer. Its annual budget reached over $2 million. It had a plan to wean off federal grant support through programs that could ultimately make money such as the budding composting program. 
Sign of the times
The first sign of trouble arrived in January 2025, Woodsum said. She received an email about anticipated changes to AmeriCorps funding that noted words that were becoming off-limits in grant or program language. 
Thus began a period of disruption in which funding was cancelled or thrown into doubt with little or no notice, Woodsum said. Federal partners became unresponsive, and alarming emails forewarned cuts. The organization lost its summer AmeriCorps volunteers after it had already made commitments for housing and placements. It lost a $116,915 grant for a commercial kitchen project on the eve of the construction work. Even with some grants reinstated, Woodsum said, by fall 2025 the organization was down an estimated $600,000. 
As funding dwindled, the pool of applicants for remaining grants multiplied, which created more competition. Starting at the beginning of 2026, the organization had to make hard decisions, Woodsum said, shutting down programs that weren’t as essential to the mission and laying off staff.
“It was just shocking, and all done so poorly and maliciously, in my opinion,” Dunning, who worked as Feeding Laramie Valley’s VISTA program coordinator, said about the federal government’s approach. Dunning and other employees initially faced salary cuts, she said, and eventually lost their jobs. 
“I’ve come to feel the hugeness of the disaster as motivation.”Gayle Woodsum
At the beginning of this summer, a fundraising push raised $13,000, enough to pay for the Kids Out to Lunch summer program and 10 weeks of summer shares.
With the summer programs over, Feeding Laramie Valley is still offering regular weekly shares, but the operation is bare bones. Year-round staff has dwindled to zero. (As founder, Woodsum has never been a paid staffer). As for the annual budget, once over $2 million, Woodsum said, “now there’s like nothing on the table.” 
The Laramie community has been extremely supportive of Feeding Laramie Valley, she said. But patching together small emergency grant funding isn’t a sustainable strategy, and she would like to secure a larger investment in the organization’s future. 
She doesn’t want the account of the last year and a half to sound like an obituary, but said she is struggling to now formulate a message. 
When programs were growing and accolades and funding were flowing, she said, “that was really easy to articulate … Then we get flattened, and I start to lose my own words.” 
Picking up pieces
Increasing numbers of Wyoming residents are food insecure, according to Feeding America’s Map the Meal Gap report. More than 94,000 residents, or 16%, lacked consistent access to food in 2024 — an increase of about 4,000 from a year earlier.
While a whole constellation of food-related charities exist across the state and country, Feeding Laramie Valley is unique, said Monica Hargraves, who was a Cornell University partnership evaluator during the Food Dignity Project. Even though the project has long ended and Hargraves lives in New York, she has stayed involved with Feeding Laramie Valley, which she said is distinct in its authentic and innovative approach to responding to community needs. 
Cosmos and sunflowers grow next to a sign at Feeding Laramie Valley’s headquarters, which sit in an old building on one edge of LaBonte Park. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
“What stands out to me about Feeding Laramie Valley and the way they approach everything is this: It is truly community connected, community driven, not just in a drop-in kind of way,” she said. “It just feels different. Every human being is being celebrated and welcomed, and there’s much respect. I find it just astonishing.”
Even with the “horrific” DOGE cuts, Hargraves said, the organization is built on a sturdy set of values and has gained its community’s trust.
Though Feeding Laramie Valley had long wanted to become independent of federal grants, this isn’t at all how it planned to do that, Woodsum said. But the lifelong activist believes her community stands a better chance of preparing for future challenges “if we build on what we’ve brought together and successfully advanced in many directions, than if we erase it when the going gets tough.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: As Idaho extends slim budgets and feds shift stance, disability care may face cuts, advocates worry
description: In January, as Idaho state lawmakers prepared for budget cuts, the state’s governor laid out a list of options for Medicaid decreases. One of them called to cut a set of programs that help people with disabilities live in their homes. In the end, lawmakers only adopted a more narrow cut to disability care.  But […]
text:
Members of the Idaho Legislature's Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee and their staff tour Southwest Idaho Treatment Center, or SWITC, in Nampa on Nov. 20, 2024. (Photo by Clark Corbin/Idaho Capital Sun)In January, as Idaho state lawmakers prepared for budget cuts, the state’s governor laid out a list of options for Medicaid decreases.
One of them called to cut a set of programs that help people with disabilities live in their homes. In the end, lawmakers only adopted a more narrow cut to disability care. 
As federal protections fade, Americans with disabilities fear a return to institutions

But as Idaho’s tight budget years dwell — and the federal government softens its stance on prioritizing keeping people with disabilities in their homes instead of in institutions — disability advocates are growing worried that home care might face cuts.
Expanded decades ago, home and community-based services have become a staple for state Medicaid programs. But as the Trump administration seeks to reinterpret a U.S. Supreme Court decision that serves as a foundation for expanded rights of people with disabilities to receive care in their homes, disability advocates worry that home and community-based services could be threatened. Advocates maintain that the underlying laws requiring home care options remain.
The federal government’s stance — detailed in a recent memo by the U.S. Justice Department — comes before states will see the impact of massive federal Medicaid cuts enacted in President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
“When (states’) federal funding shrinks, they’re going to be reluctant to replace it with state funding, and so they will be tempted to try to reduce funding for home community-based services,” retired Idaho disability rights attorney Jim Baugh said. “But, I presume without a plan for what to do with the people who lose those services, or who have their services reduced, because we don’t have any alternative. So I just see this leaving people in the lurch. I see this being a dangerous possibility.”
Several advocates also worry that there aren’t enough institutional settings to care for people with disabilities, if home and community-based services faced cuts. 
Earlier this year, Idaho officials estimated home and community-based services cost the state more than $176 million in state general funds, and were used by more than 16,000 Idahoans at least once a year. 
Most Idahoans who use home and community-based services are aging seniors who paid off their homes and want to remain there but need support, said Disability Rights Idaho Executive Director Amy Cunningham.
“That’s consistent with Idaho values — that people buy homes and they live in their homes for as long as they can,” she said. “And home and community-based services allows that to happen. And it would be very sad if Idaho decided to move toward institutionalization versus allowing people to stay in their homes, in their communities, participate in community activities, participate in their community churches, be close to their families.”

 Feds’ letter ignores that not providing home care will be costly, disability advocates say 

The concerns stem from a June memo from the U.S. Justice Department that sought to reinterpret the Supreme Court ruling issued in Olmstead  v. L.C., along with several other related disability rights laws.
In the memo, the Justice Department wrote that neither the Americans with Disabilities Act or the Rehabilitation Act “imposed an integration mandate on states in their treatment of mentally disabled individuals.” And pushing back against the Supreme Court ruling, the Justice Department added that the court didn’t interpret either of those laws to “require states to treat mentally disabled patients in the most integrated setting appropriate to their needs.”
Essentially, disability advocate Tara Rowe recently wrote that the federal government is saying that the Supreme Court incorrectly interpreted the laws “that have preserved the rights of people with disabilities to live in their homes and communities for nearly three decades,” and that “the federal government no longer needs to abide by the previous flawed interpretation.”
Christine Pisani, executive director of the Idaho Council on Developmental Disabilities, walks away from the lectern after testifying at a Senate Health and Welfare Committee meeting on March 10, 2025, at the Idaho Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
In a joint statement, several disability advocates from Idaho and surrounding states said the Justice Department’s memo doesn’t mention many of the risks of shifting people with disabilities to institutions.
“It is silent on the fact that institutional placements are the most expensive placements,” the joint statement said. “It is silent on the fact that those costs will be passed on to Idaho taxpayers. It is silent on the cost to Idaho taxpayers to defend Idaho actions based on the memo should it be sued for not following current law and US Supreme Court decision.”
The Justice Department could not be immediately reached for comment. 
To Christine Pisani, the executive director of the Idaho Council on Developmental Disabilities, the memo reads like the Justice Department “will no longer enforce or do investigations when integration is being challenged for people with disabilities.” But she said that doesn’t mean people with disabilities can’t raise those challenges. 
In Idaho recently, the feds investigated the alleged over-institutionalization of people with disabilities. More than a year ago, in the final days of the Biden administration, the Justice Department warned Idaho officials that the state was violating the Americans with Disabilities Act by unnecessarily institutionalizing people with physical disabilities. 
 Advocates worry Idaho doesn’t have enough institutions to care for people with disabilities. The state agreed. 

To some, like Baugh, the letter appears to open the door for states to consider cutting home and community-based services when tight budget years hit. But he said there isn’t an infrastructure big enough to support a big shift toward institutional care. 
He called experiences in institutions “horrific.”
“Things that we would all now call abuse and neglect were literally the standard,” Baugh said. “It’s just — it’s how institutions were operated.”
“What I’m afraid of is that people who don’t understand why community services first has become the rule might do something that would cause a tremendous amount of suffering because they don’t understand how the system has evolved,” he said. 
That’s one area the state might agree on. 
Idaho lawmakers dodged Medicaid expansion repeal. But what did they do with Medicaid?

In an internal budget memo earlier this year, obtained through a public records request, state officials with the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare wrote that if the state cut home and community-based services, the state agency “anticipates need for additional institutional providers as current capacity would not be sufficient to transition all Idahoans with disabilities who are served in the community today.”
Building those institutions would be “an astronomical cost,” Pisani said. Cunningham said her nonprofit, Disability Rights Idaho, spends a lot of time monitoring facilities, and it regularly finds abuse and neglect occurring.
During this year’s legislative session, lawmakers decided not to eliminate home and community-based services more broadly, but they did target one service under its umbrella for cuts. The Legislature passed, and Gov. Brad Little approved, $22 million in cuts to how much the state pays providers of residential habilitation, a service that helps people with disabilities with day-to-day living tasks. 
As lawmakers prepare for next year’s legislative session, the governor’s budget chief instructed state agencies to prepare for continuing to operate state agencies and public programs with less funding, instead of trying to restore past budget cuts.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming is the ideal state for tech facilities
description:
Built the ‘Wyoming Way,’ data centers could bolster economic development and help support our state’s existing energy industries, writes the Wyoming Driven Innovation advisory board.
The post Wyoming is the ideal state for tech facilities appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming is a leader in energy and energy technology. For decades, we have powered the nation and answered the call when America needed reliable, essential resources.

Opinion

For generations, the people of this state have mined minerals, produced energy, worked the land and built the infrastructure that has helped fuel the nation. We did it across long distances, through harsh winters and in places where success demanded ingenuity, resilience and neighbors being willing to work together. Wyoming developed its own approach to progress — practical, independent and grounded in respect for the land, private property and local communities. Wyoming isn’t just a place to build. It’s where we work, raise our families, know our neighbors and plan to be for generations.
Today, America once again needs Wyoming to answer the call as our economy and national security become increasingly dependent on technology and growing energy needs. Data centers are becoming essential infrastructure, powering communications, commerce, scientific research, critical services and national defense. Where these facilities are built and how they are powered matter to America’s economic strength and national security.
Wyoming’s abundant energy resources, available land, skilled workforce and experience with major industrial development make us ideal for tech facilities. Data centers require reliable power, creating opportunities for new generation, transmission, storage and energy innovation. They generate market expansions for Wyoming coal, natural gas, uranium, wind and critical minerals while bringing traditional industries and emerging technologies together.
But Wyoming’s experience has also taught us that how we build matters just as much as what we build.
Wyoming Driven Innovation supports data centers designed and built the “Wyoming Way,” with clear expectations, responsible investment, honest communication and lasting benefits for the people who live here and have a stake in Wyoming’s future. We know how to build things that last, while caring for our natural resources and ensuring that neighbors are heard.
We stand for development done the “Wyoming Way,” investing in infrastructure, stewarding our natural resources, respecting private property rights and working with local communities. Wyoming families and existing utility customers should not be left holding the bill for costs created by new data centers.
Our natural resources are critical to our way of life. We defend and fight for our water. We know the value of every drop. Data center developers must pursue efficient, responsible solutions that make growth possible while respecting the state’s water resources, local conditions and existing users.
Wyoming was built by people who value independence and understand the responsibilities that come with it. Property owners should retain the right to make decisions about their land while working to be good neighbors and respecting surrounding properties. Private property rights aren’t an afterthought here. They are part of who we are.
Decisions made in Cheyenne or in a boardroom hundreds of miles away cannot replace local knowledge. Data center developers should show up here and answer questions. They should engage with communities through robust local and state processes. Local voices must be part of shaping local development.
This is also an opportunity to create long-term value that endures long after construction ends. That means commitments tailored to specific communities, quality jobs, tax revenue, workforce training, opportunities for Wyoming businesses and new reasons for our young people to build their futures here.
This is the opportunity before us, to connect Wyoming’s energy heritage with America’s digital future. Done the “Wyoming Way,” data centers can strengthen the industries that have sustained our state, expand opportunities for our communities and help protect the infrastructure on which our nation increasingly depends.
For generations, Wyoming has powered America. With Wyoming values leading the way, we’re ready to power what comes next.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee Democrat to propose bill to ban corporations from political spending
description: A Tennessee Democrat is set to push for new restrictions on corporate campaign spending, following the seminal steps of a movement to limit dark money in politics. State Sen. Charlane Oliver, a Nashville Democrat, said she plans to introduce a bill in January mirroring a move by Hawaii to ban corporations, unions and dark money […]
text:
State Sen. Charlane Oliver, a Nashville Democrat, plans to propose a bill to ban corporate money in politics. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)A Tennessee Democrat is set to push for new restrictions on corporate campaign spending, following the seminal steps of a movement to limit dark money in politics.
State Sen. Charlane Oliver, a Nashville Democrat, said she plans to introduce a bill in January mirroring a move by Hawaii to ban corporations, unions and dark money organizations from spending money in state politics as a condition of receiving a state business license. 
Montana voters will have the chance to adopt a similar bill as part of a November ballot measure.
“Right now, we have money being tossed around, and the corporate interests get everything they want and the Tennessee taxpayers get stuck with the bill,” Oliver said. 
The legislation, called the Corporate Power Reset Act in other states, would ban any group that must form as a business in Tennessee from donating money to political campaigns as a condition of receiving its operating license.
The legislation comes from the Center for American Progress, a progressive think tank that, among other issues, has been urging lawmakers across the country to address the influx of corporate money into politics.
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in the Citizens United case in 2010 that a ban or limits on independent spending was unconstitutional. This effect was corporations, unions or other organizations like dark money groups sometimes called 501(c)4s, could spend unlimited amounts in elections as long as it was spent independently.
Michael Beckel, the Money in Politics Reform Director at One Issue, said the proposed law is about rethinking corporate power.
“The way that we now think about artificial persons, i.e., corporations having all of the same powers and privileges as natural persons, doesn’t need to be that way,” said Beckel. “The foundation of this legal theory is that artificial persons should be treated differently than natural persons.”
One Issue is a nonprofit founded to reduce the influence of money in politics through bipartisan reform and supports states passing the Corporate Reset Act. 
Tennessee and the federal government limit how much candidates can raise from corporations and dark money groups. But because of Citizens United, these dark money groups can raise unlimited sums of money, never disclose their donors and spend the money in elections without limits. 
Oliver said one of the most prominent examples of money’s “corroding influence” in Tennessee politics was the passage of a universal private-school voucher program.
Pro-school voucher groups spending tops $4.5 million in Tennessee Republican primaries

In 2024, Tennessee lawmakers failed to pass the universal statewide voucher plan. But that election year, the School Freedom Fund spent more than $3 million to ensure pro-private-school voucher candidates were elected to the Tennessee General Assembly. 
The School Freedom Fund is affiliated with Club For Growth, which has raised millions of dollars from New York finance billionaire Jeff Yass. 
The School Freedom Fund flooded specific state House and Senate districts during the Republican primary with advertisements supporting pro-voucher candidates and tearing down voucher opponents with a smear campaign. 
 Lawmakers revisited a statewide private-school voucher plan in January 2025 and narrowly passed it. 
“It’s a shame billionaires can wield millions of dollars and get vouchers passed,” Oliver said.

title: Alabama inmate who stopped nitrogen execution scheduled to die by lethal injection
description: The state of Alabama Thursday plans to execute a death row inmate amid clemency efforts by death penalty opponents, who cite a jury’s initial recommendation that he be sentenced to life without parole, a recommendation later overruled by a judge. Jeffery Lee, 49, was convicted of the murders of Jimmy Ellis and Elaine Thompson during […]
text:
Jeffrey Lee, 49, who was convicted of the murders of Jimmy Ellis and Elaine Thompson during a pawn shop robbery in 1998, is scheduled to be executed on Thursday. Death penalty opponents are seeking clemency for Lee, who was sentenced to death after a Dallas County judge overrode a jury's recommendation of life without parole. (Alabama Department of Corrections)The state of Alabama Thursday plans to execute a death row inmate amid clemency efforts by death penalty opponents, who cite a jury’s initial recommendation that he be sentenced to life without parole, a recommendation later overruled by a judge.
Jeffery Lee, 49, was convicted of the murders of Jimmy Ellis and Elaine Thompson during the robbery of a pawn shop in Orrville in 1998. A jury voted 7-5 to recommend Lee be sentenced to life without parole; Lee’s attorneys at the time cited his youth and the fact that he had two children. They also argued that Lee had an intellectual disability.
Dallas County Circuit Judge Jack Meigs ultimately overruled the jury and imposed a death sentence, writing that Lee “mercilessly” took Ellis and Thompson’s lives.
Lee is scheduled to be executed by lethal injection. He was originally scheduled to be executed by nitrogen gas, but a federal court in June imposed an injunction on the state’s protocol for the execution method following a lawsuit from Lee and a trial. Federal judges cited the potential for unconstitutional levels of pain and Lee’s argument that he could be executed by firing squad, an argument the state has rejected. The U.S. Supreme Court allowed the ruling to stand on June 12.
“To be able to walk out of that death cell on June 12, it felt like I was in Lala Land,” Lee said in a recording made by his legal team at the end of August. “It felt like I didn’t actually walk out of there, it is kind of hard to explain that feeling of being alive, just simply being alive.”
The Alabama Attorney General’s Office filed a motion to execute Lee by lethal injection hours after the U.S. Supreme Court issued its ruling.
“That day I found out, ‘Oh, they are going to seek another date for you,’ I came up with a phrase, ‘I was going to enjoy the victory, but I wasn’t going to enjoy the spoils,’” Lee said in the recording.
Death penalty opponents hosted a film screening and delivered a petition signed by more than 8,000 people to the Gov. Kay Ivey’s office on Tuesday to plead that she suspend the execution she set for Jeffery Lee.
“Governor Ivey is a woman of faith,” said Abe Bonowitz, executive director of Death Penalty Action, one of the organizations that delivered the petition to the Governor’s Office. “I think I heard it somewhere that ‘Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy.’”
Ivey, who has presided over 26 executions as governor, has only commuted two death sentences to life in prison: Rocky Myers in 2025 and Charles “Sonny” Burton earlier this year. Ivey cited doubts about the evidence presented in Myers’ trial and concerns about disparate sentencing in Burton’s case.
Lee’s supporters said he does not disregard his role in the incident, only that the judge should not be allowed to override the will of a jury that recommended his life be spared.
Organizers cited the jury’s original recommendation of life in prison. For decades, Alabama allowed judges to override jury recommendations of life and impose death sentences. It was the last state to give judges that power until the Alabama Legislature passed a law in 2017 that prohibited the practice.
However, lawmakers did not make it retroactive, so people who had been sentenced to death because of judicial override prior to the bill getting enacted into law remain on death row.
“I find it strange that the same governor who would sign that legislation, and outlaw judicial override, would allow someone who was sentenced in that way, to be executed,” said Rep. Chris England, D-Tuscaloosa, the sponsor of the 2017 law, in an interview Wednesday. “Under any circumstances, if this trial occurred today and the jury came back with life without parole, he would not be on death row and scheduled to die tomorrow.”
Gina Maiola, a spokeswoman for Ivey, said in a statement Wednesday that the law “made very clear that it would not apply retroactively.”
“It preserved all existing death sentences, ensuring promises are kept to victims’ loved ones,” the statement said. “So this argument is moot on its own, as we saw when Governor Ivey and the Alabama Department of Corrections carried out the execution of murderer-for-hire Kenneth Eugene Smith in 2024.”
Lee’s attorneys have fought the state’s attempt to conduct the execution through lethal injection, arguing that Alabama forfeited its right to use the method after he and the state agreed in 2018 to dismiss a 2016 lawsuit brought by Lee against lethal injection. Lee at the time agreed to be executed by nitrogen gas. U.S. District Judge Emily Marks ruled against Lee and said that the facts of the case changed the agreement made in 2018.
“I feel like they owe me their word because they came into agreement in 2018, that they wouldn’t do what they are trying to do now,” Lee said in the recording. “In a way, it is kind of hard to rely on their word being kept.”
Lee filed an appeal with the U.S. Supreme Court on Sept. 11, seeking to stop the execution after the federal district court denied his request to expand the injunction to include lethal injection. Alabama state courts rejected his request for a stay.
The execution would be the second conducted by Alabama this year. Jeremy Williams, who was convicted of the rape and murder of a five-year-old child in Russell County in 2021, was executed on Aug. 13.

text:
The number of Tennesseans living below the 2025 federal poverty level increased, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. (Photograph by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee’s poverty rate rose from 10.1% to 10.7% last year, according to newly released U.S. Census Bureau data. 
Overall, the Census estimated last year 762,000 Tennesseans made less than the $33,000 federal poverty threshold for a family of four. In 2024, the number was 716,000. 
The numbers are within the margin of error for the Census’ Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement, meaning the year-over-year difference is marginal. 
Tennessee’s poverty trend is the opposite of the United States’, where the number of people in poverty nationwide and the overall rate fell last year compared with 2024, Census Bureau data shows.
But a September report from The Sycamore Institute, a nonpartisan think tank, found more than 40% of Tennessee households struggled to afford basic needs in 2024. Those basic needs, like housing, childcare and food, have been increasing faster than inflation since 2019. 
Tennessee families must earn 85%-164% more than federal poverty limit to get by, new study finds

 
Mandy Spears, Sycamore’s executive vice president, said the census’ poverty threshold is “not reflective” of current spending patterns and often underestimates economic struggles.
The report found in Tennessee’s lowest cost-of-living counties, families needed a minimum yearly income of $50,000 to avoid living paycheck to paycheck. 
Sycamore relied on United Way’s “ALICE” method, an alternative to the federal poverty level statistic that accounts for a broader range of family expenses.
“The Census poverty measure was created in 1960 based on spending patterns then,” Spears said. “It’s outdated.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: West Virginia lawmaker raises concerns over Rural Health grant recipient
description: As West Virginia continues to announce recipients of its federal Rural Health Transformation program funding, a state lawmaker this week raised concerns about one organization set to receive a grant of more than $1 million.
text:
Del. Gary Howell, R-Mineral, watches a presentation during the Joint Committee on Finance meeting at the Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia, on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026. Howell raised concerns about one recipient of Rural Health Transformation program funds. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)As West Virginia continues to announce recipients of its federal Rural Health Transformation program funding, a state lawmaker this week raised concerns about one organization set to receive a grant of more than $1 million.
The state Department of Health awarded the Spotted Owl Health Organization in Kanawha County $1.17 million in Rural Health Transformation funds to fund employer-based work sites, Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced earlier this month. 
Del. Gary Howell, R-Mineral, asked questions about the grant award to state Health Secretary Arvin Singh Tuesday as Singh provided an update on the Rural Health Transformation Program to the Legislature’s Joint Standing Committee on Finance. 
Howell said Tuesday that after looking into the organization, he has concerns it does not have experience doing employer health care programming. 
“The requirements (for the Rural Health Transformation program) were specifically looking for experience with multi-employer worksite healthcare, and the ability to launch quickly,” Howell told West Virginia Watch. “When I went through the public record, Spotted Owl, you know, they were doing wellness programs.”
Howell also raised concerns with Spotted Owl’s prior grant experience. He said $50,000 is the biggest grant the organization has received, according to the records Howell could find. The $1.17 million from the state is 23 times that amount, he said. 
“It just seems really odd,” Howell said. “They’ve never been in this field before. Obviously, the other (grant recipients) have. And then when I seen what the grant was, it’s like 23 times the biggest grant (they’ve had). They’ve never administered anything over $50,000. Now we’re asking to do almost $1.2 million.”
According to its website, the Spotted Owl Health Organization, based in Dunbar, operates the “Healthy Kids, Healthy Adults program,” which provides “a holistic wellness offering that will reduce the number of obese kids, adults, families, and communities in WV and thus Kanawha County.” The organization addresses “chronic diseases associated with obesity by introducing education on nutrition and fitness classes.” 
Besides the $1.17 million to Spotted Owl, the state also announced Sept. 4 it would give $612,000 to Charleston Area Medical Center/Vandalia Health and $612,000 to the Cabell Huntington Hospital Foundation to fund worksite clinics and employer-based healthcare services.
Singh told Howell Tuesday he was not part of the decision to award Spotted Owl funding but said that every decision the state makes to award Rural Health Transformation funding is based on merit. 
“They went up against a bunch of other competitors and demonstrated true merit,” Singh said. “I don’t have the score in front of me but they offer employee-based prevention, occupational health support, recovery focused work force retention and in their proposal they’re planning three anchor employer sites active by year one.”
Singh said the state has performance and payment based milestones for grant recipients. If programs are not meeting expectations, the state has the ability to claw back the federal dollars, he said. 
West Virginia received $199 million in Rural Health Transformation program funding for 2026 from the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. The five-year Rural Health Transformation program is designed to “empower states to transform the existing rural health care infrastructure and build sustainable health care systems that expand access, enhance quality of care, and improve outcomes for patients.” The program is part of the One Big Beautiful Bill, which made historical cuts to healthcare and food assistance. 
Singh told Howell he would get back to him about Howell’s question about what metrics Spotted Owl was graded on, and what makes Singh confident they’ll be able to do the work the funding is for. 
Orlando Craighead, executive director of Spotted Owl Health Organization, said he was not available Wednesday for a phone interview. In a written response to West Virginia Watch, he said the $1.17 million from the state for its program Work Well WV is the single largest grant the organization has received. Craighead said he does not dismiss the concerns Howell raised about its capacity but will address them. 
“We are addressing them through dedicated program management, grant administration, financial oversight, data evaluation, defined performance measures and formal partnerships with healthcare and community organizations,” Craighead wrote. “Grant funds will be restricted to the approved program budget and subject to the state’s reporting, documentation, and monitoring requirements.”
He called Spotted Owl “a community-based public health organization focused on prevention, education, navigation, wellness, partnerships, and population health.” 
Work Well WV will work with small and midsized employers to “provide voluntary wellness assessments, health education, screenings through qualified partners, care navigation, referrals, and follow-up support,”  Craighead said. The initiative will also “help connect individuals recovering from substance use disorder with employment-support resources and appropriate health and social services.”
Work Well WV isn’t an employer-sponsored health insurance program, he said, and the Spotted Owl will not replace physicians, hospitals or licensed healthcare providers. 
Chesapeake Health Center is the first hub and partner that Spotted Owl has established, Craighead said. The organization has plans to establish three more hubs across Kanawha County, he said. 
“(Spotted Owl Health Organization’s) role is to coordinate the initiative, engage employers and residents, provide prevention and navigation services, manage closed-loop referrals, track outcomes, and report results to the state. Clinical services will be provided by appropriately qualified healthcare partners,” Craighead wrote.
“We welcome appropriate oversight and the opportunity to demonstrate that a smaller community-based organization can responsibly manage a significant investment when it has clear controls, qualified personnel, strong partnerships, and measurable expectations,” he said.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado has a new, voluntary program to conserve Colorado River water. Farmers are wary.
description: As the clock winds down on a historically dry year in the Colorado River Basin, Colorado water officials Wednesday said they’re willing to launch a new state-run conservation program that would chip in to address system-wide shortages — but not without more certainty from the federal government, and possibly the state Legislature, about how the […]
text:
Hay bales lie in pastures near Stagecoach Reservoir in Routt County on Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)As the clock winds down on a historically dry year in the Colorado River Basin, Colorado water officials Wednesday said they’re willing to launch a new state-run conservation program that would chip in to address system-wide shortages — but not without more certainty from the federal government, and possibly the state Legislature, about how the program would work.
Members of the Colorado Water Conservation Board, the state’s lead water agency, voted 9-0 to conditionally approve a “near-term contribution program” to fulfill the voluntary conservation efforts requested by federal officials this year, as the seven states that rely on the Colorado River continued to fall short of a long-term agreement on how to share its shrinking water supplies.
The program aims to reduce water use during the 2027 “water year,” which will officially begin Oct. 1. Funding provided by the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation would pay for fallowing, deficit irrigation, crop-switching and other conservation projects that would be approved by the CWCB and the federal government before the spring runoff begins next year.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“None of us want to be in this situation, where we are dealing with these kinds of impacts from climate-change-driven drought,” CWCB member Taylor Hawes said during the board’s monthly meeting, held at the Copper Mountain ski resort. “We’re not doing this for fun. We’re doing this because our situation requires it.”
In nearly a century of record-keeping, the Colorado River’s cumulative streamflow at Cameo, just upstream of Palisade and Grand Junction, has never been lower than it has been in water year 2026. Downstream, Lakes Powell and Mead fell to record lows, forcing the Bureau of Reclamation to make deep cuts to water allotments for the Lower Basin states of California, Nevada and Arizona. The unprecedented drought conditions are part of a long-term warming and drying trend fueled by human-caused climate change.



Quotation







We understand that climate change is wreaking havoc on the system, and all of us need to figure out ways to contribute.


– Andy Mueller, Colorado River District's general manager


Colorado officials have faced mounting criticism and threats of litigation over the state’s refusal to agree to mandatory cuts like the ones the Lower Basin states are facing. But the CWCB’s rollout of the near-term contribution plan put a spotlight on the internal political pressures and legal obstacles that stand in the way of more substantial conservation commitments in the Colorado River’s headwaters state.
“There’s better ways that we can put this money to use than to put farmers on welfare,” Troy Waters, a fifth-generation farmer in Fruita, told the board during public comment.
“There needs to be statewide participation, not just West Slope ag,” said Wendell Koontz, a Delta County commissioner and chair of the CWCB’s Gunnison Basin Roundtable. “West Slope ag always feels like it’s got a bullseye, and often a knife, in the middle of our back.”
Water levels in the Wolford Mountain Reservoir in Grand County, which dams a tributary of the Colorado River, have dropped by more than 30 feet during extreme drought conditions in 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)
The scale of the reductions targeted by CWCB officials in the near-term contributions program is relatively modest — 50,000 acre-feet in water year 2027, only a fraction of the 1.25 million acre-feet of cuts that will be forced on water users across the three Lower Basin states next year. But even that has been a tough pill for Colorado water users to swallow in the wake of the program’s announcement in July.
“This program is only going to be run on a voluntary basis. We’re not going to force anyone to participate. It’s going to be compensated by federal funds, as we’ve discussed, and temporary, which is especially important for agricultural projects,” said Amy Ostdiek, chief of the CWCB’s Interstate, Federal, and Water Information Section. “We’re not contemplating permanent reductions in our state’s water use.”
Legal framework
In an 18-page letter sent to the CWCB on Aug. 26, the Colorado River District, a water manager serving 15 Western Slope counties, outlined a long list of concerns with the proposed program, including its potential to “inadvertently create regional sacrifice zones on Colorado’s West Slope.” The district requested changes to the criteria the agency will use to select conservation projects and more guardrails to ensure impacts to agriculture are temporary.
Agriculture accounts for about 90% of all Colorado water use. Under the project criteria adopted by the board Wednesday, the CWCB will prioritize “participation statewide and across water sectors” — meaning municipal users, not just farmers and ranchers.
What climate science tells us about the causes of the Colorado River crisis

“We’re very much in agreement that this program, unfortunately, is — we look at it as kind of a necessary evil,” Andy Mueller, the Colorado River District’s general manager, told CWCB members. “We understand that climate change is wreaking havoc on the system, and all of us need to figure out ways to contribute.”
Mueller thanked agency staff for the outreach work they’d conducted since July, but said the proposed project criteria were still too vague. He and other Western Slope water managers are especially concerned that the state lacks clear legal authority to “shepherd” conserved water downstream — that is, to track and verify the amount of conserved water flowing to Lake Powell, and ensure Colorado is properly credited for it.
The CWCB outlined the existing legal authorities it says it will use for the conservation plan, including its instream flow program, a legal mechanism the agency uses to preserve natural streamflows for environmental purposes. But the Colorado River District, in its letter, urged the board to let the state Legislature to establish a clearer legal framework when it reconvenes next year, ensuring “adequate legal protections and intentional criteria” are “clearly articulated in statute.”
“Frankly, it could result — if not done correctly — in huge disruptions to our agricultural industry, to the communities that rely on it,” Mueller said of the CWCB’s administration of the program. “Just thinking about all the thriving communities within my district that may suffer losses of main street businesses, and other consequences — school districts without funding, you can go down the list.”
Mike Camblin, the CWCB’s vice chair, agreed that the state’s shepherding authority was “fuzzy.” After extensive discussion, the board adopted the program criteria “subject to and conditioned on agreement or assurance” from the Bureau of Reclamation that the Upper Basin states will be credited for the conserved water.
Ostdiek also said the state “still need(s) additional clarity on what projects” the feds will allow the available funding to be spent on. Many agricultural users urge the state to prioritize long-term infrastructure upgrades over temporary fallowing, or “buy and dry” schemes.
Becky Mitchell, who leads the state’s Colorado River negotiations as its commissioner to the Upper Colorado River Commission, said she “heard loud and clear” that water users on the Western Slope want to avoid large-scale fallowing.
“I heard a lot of comments from the public today, a lot of comments from the board today,” Mitchell said. “It is my responsibility to take that back to the Bureau of Reclamation and the Department of Interior and say, these are the kinds of things that we can do in Colorado — and fallowing is not the only answer, and the impacts of that may be too great.”

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Doug Jones, Phillip Ensler propose overhaul of Alabama lieutenant governor’s role
description: The Alabama lieutenant governor has a dwindling number of powers. The Democratic nominees on the top of November’s ballot want to change that. Former U.S. Sen. Doug Jones, the party’s nominee for governor, announced Wednesday that he plans to work with the Legislature to introduce a constitutional amendment to reorganize the state government, if elected, […]
text:
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones speaks at a press conference on the steps of the Alabama State Capitol on Sept. 16, 2026 in Montgomery Alabama as  Rep. Phillip Ensler, the party's nominee for lieutenant governor, looks on. The pair on Wednesday announced a plan to propose a constitutional amendment to make the offices jointly elected. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)The Alabama lieutenant governor has a dwindling number of powers. The Democratic nominees on the top of November’s ballot want to change that.
Former U.S. Sen. Doug Jones, the party’s nominee for governor, announced Wednesday that he plans to work with the Legislature to introduce a constitutional amendment to reorganize the state government, if elected, hearkening back to efforts made over two decades ago to redefine the office.
“It’s almost like the lieutenant governor is a figurehead in the Legislature that just sits with a gavel,” Jones said. “The lieutenant governor, in my view, always should be a part of the executive branch, a partner with the governor to help implement the administration’s policies.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The governor and lieutenant governor are elected separately. Jones said he would support a constitutional amendment that would have the governor and lieutenant governor elected as a ticket, like the president and vice president of the United States. According to the National Lieutenant Governor’s Association, 27 states jointly elect the two positions together. 
Rep. Phillip Ensler, D-Montgomery, the party’s nominee for lieutenant governor, joined Jones on Wednesday and touted his bipartisan record in the Legislature. 
“There is so much that I can do because of the relationships I have, as Doug said, across the aisle, and to be able to help carry out a vision, help fight for the people of Alabama,” Ensler said. 
Jones wants to treat the lieutenant governor – regardless of November’s results – as a team member. 
“I want him to have a seat at the table, whether as officially as a member of the government’s cabinet or at least as a member of the government’s cabinet in an advisory role, we’re going to talk during a transition about what portfolio he might want to work on,” Jones said of Ensler on Wednesday. 
Messages seeking comment were left Wednesday afternoon with Tommy Tuberville and John Wahl, the Republican nominees for governor and lieutenant governor. 
Section 280 of Alabama’s Constitution prohibits an individual from financially benefiting from two public offices – like a lieutenant governor and a cabinet position or staff member. 
“When you elect Doug Jones and Phil Ensler, you’re electing a team to help implement the same strategies, the same efficiencies in government, the same programs that we’re talking about on the campaign trail,” Jones said. “So he’ll have a seat at the table, and more importantly, a voice at the table. It will not be double dipping, so to speak, at all.”
First attempt in two decades
State lawmakers filed similar legislation to redefine the lieutenant governor’s role more than 20 years ago, but no proposal received a floor vote in its house of origin. Sen. Bobby Denton, D-Tuscumbia, filed a proposal in 1999; Rep. Mary Sue McClurkin, R-Pelham, filed a proposal in 2004; and then-Rep. Cam Ward, R-Alabaster, filed proposals in 2005 and 2006.
Jones and Ensler said they plan to work with legislators in both chambers to get their proposal passed. Jones said he had “cleared it” with Senate Minority Leader Bobby Singleton of Greensboro and House Minority Leader Anthony Daniels of Huntsville. 
A message seeking comment was left with Singleton. Daniels confirmed his support for the proposal in a phone interview Wednesday afternoon.
“The lieutenant governor is someone that’s elected statewide, so their duties should exceed just presiding over the Senate,” Daniels said. “I do think that they can be extremely valuable in the government.” 
Currently, the lieutenant governor becomes governor should the occupant of that office die, resign or be removed. The office once had powers comparable to those of the Speaker of the House, with powers to control legislation and assign senators to committees. 
But the office was stripped of its power in 1999 after a lengthy standoff between then-Lt. Gov. Steve Windom, a Republican, and the Democratic-controlled Senate, which transferred most of Windom’s powers to the Senate President Pro Tem.  
The role had its powers further decreased by the Senate this spring through Senate Resolution 108, sponsored by Sen. Arthur Orr, R-Decatur. It allows Senate President Pro Tem to preside over the Senate if the lieutenant governor has not taken their seat five minutes after a meeting time. 
The resolution also removes the lieutenant governor from a committee that assigns committee chairs, removes their power to appoint members to conference committees, gives the Pro Tem the power to recommit bills to committees and gives the Pro Tem and to direct the lieutenant governor to call up legislation carried over to the call of the chair.
Republicans have held the office since 2010.
Jones hopes to get the amendment through the Legislature in time for the 2028 election to be considered by voters. Amendments need two-thirds support in each chamber, and a simple majority on the ballot. Republicans hold a supermajority in both chambers, and there are not enough contested races in November to challenge that hold.  
Daniels said there could still be support from his colleagues across the aisle.
“I think that it’s something that has probably been thought about by both sides, but never been acted upon,” Daniels said. “Someone has to start the conversation.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: As police increasingly embrace AI, some wait for regulations and proof it works
description: New Jersey has no statewide guardrails on police use of artificial intelligence, but that hasn't stopped cops from using it.
text:
New Jersey has no statewide guardrails on police use of artificial intelligence, but that hasn't stopped cops from using it. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)In Cape May County, police stumped by the decades-old mystery of a missing 11-year-old boy turned to artificial intelligence to hunt for clues human detectives might have missed. In Trenton, an expanding web of AI-powered surveillance cameras tracks pedestrians and motorists as they navigate the capital city. And in towns from Mount Holly to Eastampton, officers now rely on AI to draft incident reports.
New Jersey has no statewide strategy or regulations on police use of AI, even as law enforcement officers across the state are increasingly deploying AI-equipped technological tools to do everything from routine paperwork to complex sleuthing.
The trend comes as unease grows nationally over recent whistleblower warnings of the potentially dire consequences of unrestrained AI, as well as the costs and environmental impacts of data centers, which power the technology.
Critics warn that the multi-billion-dollar industry evolves so fast that police departments have become expensive testing grounds for unproven technology, with taxpayers left holding the bill.
“These are not cheap tools,” said Dillon Reisman, a staff attorney with the American Civil Liberties Union of New Jersey who focuses on the intersection of technology and civil rights. “Law enforcement officers are dipping their toes into a really expensive pool and becoming reliant on AI when no one has actually proven that it reduces crime and solves more investigations.”
Supporters counter that AI can expand what law enforcement can do and save time and money through administrative efficiencies. They downplay concerns that AI tools can trample privacy and civil rights, with Trenton Mayor Reed Gusciora crediting his city’s surveillance system with cutting murders fivefold since 2020.
“I have a bigger fear of getting shot,” Gusciora said. “We’ve done a remarkable job of bringing down crime, and I’ll take my chances with the cameras.”
Paterson police used an AI tool to review body camera footage to determine if officers acted professionally. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
 No statewide guardrails
New Jersey officials have tiptoed around regulating law enforcement use of AI.
The state Attorney General’s office solicited public comments on facial recognition technology in 2022 but then issued no guidance. Legislators have introduced a bill twice since May 2025 to study AI in policing, but it has not advanced. They introduced two more bills just this week to restrict government use (and prohibit private use) of automated license plate readers and limit their data retention.
Yet policymakers have not adopted any statewide directives or guardrails for police mulling new AI tech tools — although that could soon change.
Attorney General Jen Davenport’s office “is actively pursuing statewide governance to ensure ethical, constitutional, and fair evaluation and implementation of AI by New Jersey law enforcement,” Davenport spokesman Rob Rowan told the New Jersey Monitor. Rowan declined to offer a timeline or details on what such governance would look like.
The inaction from policymakers has discouraged some law enforcement officials from leaning into the AI trend.
“If you sign a two-year contract with a company, and then you’re six months in and the attorney general says you can’t use that? We’re still obligated to pay that contract,” said Middle Township Police Chief Tracey Super.
Super thinks AI will shape the future of law enforcement. But beyond budgetary concerns, he has been hesitant to adopt AI tools because of uncertainties about “how the public’s information is protected.” He also shares Reisman’s reservations about whether AI works the wonders its developers promise.
In 2023, his department partnered with the AI company Terawe to try to crack the cold case of Mark Himebaugh, who was 11 when he vanished in November 1991 after walking down his street to watch firefighters tackle a brush fire.
“It really didn’t do what we were hoping,” Super said. “It was more like a search engine with a database, which was helpful, but nothing that we were able to actually solve Mark’s disappearance.”
Under the partnership, the department got a free yearlong trial of the service. When that ended, investigators could have continued using it for $30,000 a month, a considerable cost for a 55-officer police force in a community of about 20,000 residents, Super said.
“We’re a medium-sized agency. Our budget isn’t big enough. We still want to find Mark, but we can’t devote one tenth of our budget to it,” he said.
Super said many of his fellow chiefs have been similarly cautious about AI adoption, especially those that head smaller departments with stretched budgets.
A researcher with the New Jersey State Policy Lab agreed such caution is common among public safety officials. Policymakers want proof AI tools work well given their costs and operational risks, and they fear AI could undermine community trust and replicate existing biases and injustices because they often rely on historical data, researcher Canyu Gao found in April.
Yet others have forged ahead.
Police in Camden County and Newark have deployed drones to bolster surveillance systems. Detectives around the state have used facial recognition technology, which compares facial images captured by security cameras against databases of known faces, to identify suspects.
Agencies from the Mount Holly Police Department to the Morris County Sheriff’s Office have employed AI software developed by Code Four that analyzes footage from police body cameras to draft incident reports.
In Paterson, the police department used an AI tool by Truleo to review body camera footage to determine if officers acted professionally. In Pennsauken, police used a robotic dog Wednesday to enter a home where two people were found dead in a suspected murder-suicide.
And the Mercer County Prosecutor’s Office rolled out a surveillance program in 2022 that now relies on more than 500 cameras (many of which include automated license plate readers) that primarily target crime hotspots, violence-prone locations, community events, and critical infrastructure, spokeswoman Casey DeBlasio said. The system, which uses technology from Lyndhurst-based Packetalk, will be expanded, she added.
Those efforts haven’t always gone smoothly.
The mass surveillance capabilities created by Packetalk, Flock, and companies peddling similar products have spawned protests and petitions demanding safeguards both in New Jersey and nationally. And in 2023, federal authorities indicted Packetalk’s owner on charges that he sold equipment from Chinese companies banned under the National Defense Authorization Act. The feds later dropped the charges without explanation, but the episode prompted Passaic County to scramble to recover $13 million it had paid Packetalk for its tech tools. Packetalk staff referred questions to owner Tamer Zakhary, who did not respond to a request for comment.
Facial recognition technology has resulted in enough wrongful arrests that the state Office of the Public Defender took one case to the state Supreme Court in a bid to expose the technology’s deficiencies and expand transparency. In that 2023 case and another that led to a decision issued in June, the state’s top court sided with defense attorneys in ruling that police and prosecutors must more fully disclose how the technology works and how authorities use it.
Such problems seem inevitable when solving crimes can be “a messy human endeavor,” Reisman said.
“It’s extremely concerning that public agencies, including ones as sensitive and important as law enforcement agencies, could adopt tools with no guardrails,” Reisman said. “What we really need now is radical transparency about what happens when a law enforcement agency anywhere in the state or the state itself adopts technology based on large language models.”



Quotation







I think we’re going to be litigating a lot of conclusions that were drawn through AI.


– Jennifer Sellitti, the state public defender


 AI in the courts
As police and prosecutors increasingly use AI, defense attorneys and judges are more frequently facing the consequences in court.
Many AI tools pose thorny civil rights and privacy questions, said Tamar Lerer, who heads the state public defender’s forensic science unit. The surveillance systems that span the state can store people’s personal data for a long time and be searched at will for any reason, she said. In other states, police have used them to track women who sought abortions or stalk romantic interests.
“The automatic license plate readers don’t just see license plates. They also see bumper stickers, so we’re talking about expressive information now, not just license plate numbers. They can often capture who’s in a car, or at least part of them. They’re also capturing where someone is, whether you’re at home with your lawn signs or you’re at the strip club or at the abortion clinic,” Lerer said. “We have to be very clear about what this all means.”
She added: “For other kinds of privacy invasions, there are rules: You need a warrant to search someone’s house. You don’t need a warrant to track someone’s face down the streets for days, for weeks, for months.”
Jennifer Sellitti, the state public defender, echoed those concerns.
She pointed to unexpected ways AI has cropped up in court, including a fire marshal who revealed in January that he used ChatGPT to prepare his court testimony in a deadly arson in Monmouth County and a dead man who delivered his own victim impact statement via an AI avatar last year in an Arizona courtroom.
“I think we’re going to be litigating a lot of conclusions that were drawn through AI,” she said.
AI software that uses body camera footage to draft incident reports has been touted as a tool that frees up officers from writing their own reports, but Sellitti sees problems there too.
“When a witness testifies in court, they have to testify on personal knowledge, things that they actually observed,” Sellitti said.
Using AI to write incident reports flouts that legal doctrine, she added.
“With human beings, certain things are important in a moment because our brain can’t handle everything at once. So we decide that certain things are important, and that is critical to understanding an officer’s intent, the reason they stopped someone, the reason they found something suspicious,” Sellitti said. “The AI can look at everything all at once and analyze it, and then write a report that creates reasonable suspicion that that officer didn’t actually have in her mind at the time she pulled the car over, which is the relevant test under constitutional law.”
AI-drafted legal filings have proven so problematic in courts around the country that judicial officials in New Jersey issued guidance in March urging attorneys and jurists to “trust but verify” any AI tools, cautioning they could fabricate case citations and quotes, overstate legal principles, and misstate holdings. Lawyers remain responsible for what they file, the courts warned. The guidance came three years after New Jersey court officials established an AI committee that issued broader guidelines in 2024 that still stand today.
Chief Justice Stuart Rabner, during his annual address in May to the state bar association, lamented that AI has made judges’ jobs more complex.
“Years ago, for example, a self-represented litigant might have filed a 2-count complaint with the court,” Rabner said. “Today, with help from AI, the same complaint may well have 15 counts prepared in minutes with the press of a button. Multiply that by thousands to appreciate how much more time and attention judges must devote to resolve those cases each calendar year.”
Despite these concerns, Sellitti and Rabner both see a place for AI in and out of courtrooms.
In July, Sellitti’s office launched a new AI-powered database developed by Princeton University that allows public defenders to access years of briefs, motions, legal research, training materials, and institutional expertise through one unified, searchable system — materials that otherwise existed across various offices, servers, and databases.
“It used to take hours to do that. Now it literally takes seconds,” Sellitti said.
Judiciary officials developed a similar tool, called NJ Courts AI Access, that state court judges, court executives, and law clerks can use to summarize, search, analyze, and review legal documents, courts spokesman Peter McAleer said.
Court officials also have provided ongoing training since 2023 — required of all incoming law clerks — on AI literacy, ethics, confidentiality, accuracy, and human oversight, while a dedicated AI specialist provides individualized support to judges and staff, McAleer said.
Sellitti has tasked an AI-interested group of “super users” in her office with trying new AI tools to determine if wider use is warranted. Any staff who gets training also now must consider how AI might assist whatever they’re getting trained on, she added.
“The right strategy is to make sure that the AI is not doing the job that the witness or the lawyer should be doing and to make clear that AI is a tool that should be used by people to save time, to make us more efficient. But it doesn’t replace the work product of an attorney or the observations of a police officer or lay witness or forensic scientist,” Sellitti said.
Every technology is “a blessing and a curse” that will present new challenges for police, prosecutors, public defenders, and judges, especially given the speed with which some have raced to adopt it, she said.
“But I also think you’ve got to get ahead of it, so that we’re the ones using it to our advantage in courtrooms,” she added. “And we’ve been trying to do that.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Talking points from data center supporters don’t stand up to the facts in West Virginia
description: There was a lot of talk this summer about data centers in artificial intelligence West Virginia. Let’s get to it. The governor outlined his Responsible Data Center Development Plan, which is full of a lot of “musts” but mostly empty promises. A data center developer in Mason County started buying out homes, then residents learned […]
text:
An anti-data center bumper sticker hangs on the door of the Stumptown Ales brewery in downtown Davis, West Virginia on Nov. 1, 2025. (Photo by Caity Coyne/West Virginia Watch)There was a lot of talk this summer about data centers in artificial intelligence West Virginia. Let’s get to it. The governor outlined his Responsible Data Center Development Plan, which is full of a lot of “musts” but mostly empty promises. A data center developer in Mason County started buying out homes, then residents learned that they now have to deal with a second data center, after the governor announced a surprise approval at a conference in August. Zooming out, AI CEOs and employees are saying that we need guardrails and that this technology could lead to civilizational collapse by 2030. Sweet. 
Typically in opinion pieces you want to use more words to flesh out your own arguments and give less airtime to your opponents’ points. But sometimes you’re just mad, just like the 70% of Americans who oppose data center construction in their communities, or the two-thirds of Americans who want AI guardrails. 
So I want to use this space to look at just a few talking points from data center-loving Republicans in West Virginia and beyond. 
“We should put data centers only in communities that want them”
This has been a common refrain across the country. Even the White House said as much in a statement to Politico this month. They said President Donald Trump “has been clear that he only wants data centers to be built in local communities that want them and “all of the significant benefits they bring.”
In some states in the country, maybe that’s true. Maybe other communities have the right to say no, they don’t want a certain development. 
But not here in West Virginia. 
Thanks to Gov. Patrick Morrisey and the West Virginia Legislature’s House Bill 2014, passed in April 2025, communities in West Virginia have almost zero input when it comes to large, dirty data centers. With HB 2014, the governor and Legislature concentrated the decision-making when it comes to big data centers to state bureaucrats. Ask the residents in Tucker, Mason, Putnam, Mingo, and Berkeley counties if they want the data centers that have been proposed for them. 
(These localities still have the authority to say no to comparatively small data centers, but those don’t seem to be breaking down the door to come to West Virginia.)
“We’ve had data centers for a long time”
Data center lovers say this when they want to trivialize people’s worries about data centers, along with some version of “the people are using technology and data centers to complain about data centers.” Congratulations, you’ve revived the “yet you participate in society” meme. 
Saying we’ve had data centers for a long time is akin to saying that Hitler was a rightfully appointed Chancellor. Both are true, but there’s a lot more to the story. Yes, we’ve had data centers for years, but what is being shoved down peoples’ throats now are hyperscale data centers intended to train and grow AI use. These data centers are being proposed with huge gas plants and dozens of diesel fuel generators connected to them. Loudoun County, Virginia, which is often invoked by data center supporters, did not see what is being proposed in West Virginia, which is onsite gas plants for several of the data centers under consideration. Gas plants and diesel generators emit toxic pollutants that can make people sick. Even data centers that are grid connected are going to lead to increased power production elsewhere. 
“Only leftists, tree-huggers and people who want China to win are against data centers”
At the end of August, Trump said the following: “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor… [if] we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame.” He’s not the only Republican or corporate lobbyist making this kind of talk. 
This one’s simple. It hurts to see the president say something like that to people I’ve gotten to know. I saw Fox News at the gym earlier this week and the guest was saying that raising the alarm about AI and data centers is just a leftist tactic to take power, which made my eyes roll as I thought about how culpable Fox has been in ginning up anger about immigrants and trans issues. 
I encourage anyone who is unsure about sentiments on data centers to look at polling, or talk to a single person who lives next to, or even close to, a proposed data center. 
Which takes me to the final point I’ll discuss today.
“I want one in my own neighborhood so it will lower my property taxes”  
Spoiler, no. These people don’t actually want a data center next to them. No one wants to live next to noxious diesel and gas emissions, put their children at higher risk of asthma and other health conditions, or live in fear of some sort of disaster. If anything, maybe they’d move near one if it existed. But who wants to own a home and then learn “by the way, we’re going to build a mega-complex in your line of sight?” 
It’s easy to pop off on social media about wanting data centers in your backyard when you’re wealthy and know that no one’s going to build a data center and a big natural gas plant in South Hills, Charleston or another rich neighborhood in West Virginia. 
The same people who say this are ones who lobby on behalf of the wealthy families, polluting corporations, or other elite. 
My friends and others I know who work on issues like this don’t represent those people. They talk to real people, who are affected by what happens in Charleston, Silicon Valley and Washington, D.C. They see people as people, not just numbers in a spreadsheet or as obstacles to remove. 
They don’t look at people who own homes near proposed data centers and say “maybe you should accept a buyout and move?”
How wonderful it is to be a millennial, where you’re scolded for not owning homes or starting families, meanwhile people in power are making everything more expensive, polluting your air and water, and then saying, “OK, just move” if you do finally get a house and don’t want to have your property next to a data center or seized for a transmission line.
At the beginning I mentioned Morrisey’s Responsible Data Center Plan. He released that plan after reading the room, seeing that people are mad. That West Virginians don’t want corporations to trample on their communities without any right to push back. They don’t want a free pass to pollute water and air getting handed out. They don’t want their utility bills and other expenses to go up for reasons beyond their control. 
But reading the room now is not the same as being in the room the whole time, talking to real West Virginians, as long as community and environmental advocates have been. We’ve been raising the alarm about concerns regarding data centers since HB 2014 was being debated. 
What West Virginians need to do is seriously consider whether their state and local representatives truly have their best interests at heart. In other states, leaders seem to be listening to their residents’ concerns. But politicians are doubling down here in West Virginia in many cases. The 2026 election is going to be the first of many data center and AI referendums to come. West Virginia voters should choose the correct side.
