name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Families of Arkansas children with disabilities say more action needed on waitlist
description: Families of Arkansas children with disabilities packed the Old Supreme Court room at the state Capitol on Wednesday and urged Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders to take further action toward clearing a waiting list for supportive services. More than 2,400 Arkansas families are waiting for a Medicaid waiver that will help them meet their children’s complex […]
text:
From left: Disability advocate Paige McCammon addresses a rally at the Arkansas Capitol urging Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders to clear the waitlist for supportive living services while Arkansas Support Network CEO Syard Evans, Libertarian gubernatorial candidate Colt Shelby and disability advocate Blake Landers listen on Sept. 16, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)Families of Arkansas children with disabilities packed the Old Supreme Court room at the state Capitol on Wednesday and urged Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders to take further action toward clearing a waiting list for supportive services.
More than 2,400 Arkansas families are waiting for a Medicaid waiver that will help them meet their children’s complex medical and non-medical needs. A maximum of 8,233 Arkansans can receive supportive services from the waiver, and many families spend years on the waitlist.
Sanders announced Tuesday that the Department of Human Services will work to provide supportive living services to families on the waitlist starting in January.
Paige McCammon said at Wednesday’s rally that she appreciated Sanders’ effort, which came after weeks of social media posts from her and other parents sharing stories of their children’s needs.
“This was the moment Arkansas said, ‘Enough.’ This was the moment that a small group changed history, and Governor Sanders, you have a huge opportunity to help us change that,” said McCammon, whose son Turner has severe epilepsy and a neurodegenerative condition.
Sanders, a Republican, was not present at the rally. Her two opponents for reelection, Democratic state Sen. Fred Love and Libertarian Colt Shelby, were both present and among the speakers.

Democratic state Sen. Fred Love of Mabelvale, who is challenging Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders in November’s election, and Little Rock Democratic Rep. Denise Ennett, whose son receives supportive living services for his disabilities via a Medicaid waiver, attend a rally at the Arkansas Capitol urging Sanders to clear the waitlist for the waiver on Sept. 16, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)

McCammon and other parents continued to ask Sanders to convene a special legislative session to address the waitlist. Tamerah Cooper, whose son Maceo has a neurodegenerative disorder, called the waiting families’ needs “an unbiased issue.”
“I speak for the children deteriorating while they wait,” Cooper said. “I speak for the caregivers who are not paid for the work they do, but they do it out of love. I speak for the parents who have to go to work worrying if their child’s needs will be met.”
Families on the waitlist can receive most of the services available to people on the waiver, but one of the few exceptions and the one most requested is supportive living services, or affordable in-home care for people with disabilities.
Sanders said Tuesday that it should cost about $17 million for the state’s managed-care Medicaid program to provide supportive living services to more families by January.
Sanders “will continue to look at options to improve services across the state,” her spokesperson Sam Dubke said Wednesday.
Her immediate predecessor, fellow Republican Gov. Asa Hutchinson, directed $37.6 million toward disability support services in an effort to clear the waitlist in 2021. More than 3,000 people were waiting at the time, and all received services by 2025.
Syard Evans, CEO of the disability advocacy group Arkansas Support Network, noted that caregivers are being paid the same rates they were in 2018 when the managed care program for Arkansans with disabilities began. A Department of Human Services study last year showed that supportive living services cost 23% more than what the insurers reimburse.

Waitlist, policy changes stir worries among families of Arkansans with disabilities


The law mandating the study also required the state to increase reimbursement rates, and Evans said those rates are expected to go into effect Jan. 1.
“My fear is that it’s too late for many providers and people,” Evans said. “We have seen colleagues close their waiver programs and stop providing supported living services.”
Dr. Hannah Lewis, a pediatric neurologist whose patients include Turner McCammon, said her patients often struggle to implement their treatment plans because they don’t have enough equipment, respite or insurance coverage.
“I have seen parents lose jobs, go without sleep, and lose their financial security to pay for bills or stable housing,” Lewis said. “I have seen the strain this places on marriages and on siblings, and despite all of these challenges, their goal remains simple: to keep their child at home, where they are known, loved, and cared for by their family.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Entergy Arkansas drops lawsuit over newspaper’s publication of data center agreement details
description: Entergy Arkansas is dropping the lawsuit it filed over a newspaper publishing details about a West Memphis data center agreement that came from documents the utility said were released in error by state regulators. The utility on Wednesday filed a notice of dismissal of its lawsuit against the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette, the Arkansas Times and central […]
text:
Exterior of the Richard Sheppard Arnold Federal Courthouse in downtown Little Rock. (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)Entergy Arkansas is dropping the lawsuit it filed over a newspaper publishing details about a West Memphis data center agreement that came from documents the utility said were released in error by state regulators.
The utility on Wednesday filed a notice of dismissal of its lawsuit against the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette, the Arkansas Times and central Arkansas resident Jessica Kivell. 
A federal judge earlier this month denied Entergy’s request for a temporary restraining order that would have prohibited the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette and Arkansas Times from disclosing details about Entergy’s agreements with Altitude Capital LLC, a Google subsidiary being used to set up the data center. 
The Democrat-Gazette published a story based on non-public and confidential documents that were released through a Freedom of Information Act request. Kivell, who made the FOIA request, provided the documents to the newspaper. Entergy said those documents were released in error and were trade secrets. 
The day after the ruling, Entergy said it would not pursue a preliminary injunction blocking publication. But the utility’s lawsuit had left open the possibility it could seek damages against the newspaper and Kivell.
The lawsuit and Entergy’s attempt to block further publication about the agreement alarmed press advocates who said the move undermined the First Amendment and went against decades of court rulings against prior restraint.
An Entergy spokesperson did not immediately respond to an email requesting comment late Wednesday afternoon. Democrat-Gazette Executive Editor Lee Wolverton declined to comment on the filing.
The Arkansas Times was named as a defendant in the case, though the outlet said it did not have the documents.
“We’re obviously so pleased Entergy called off their legal threats against the journalists and the good citizen who did nothing wrong and were simply trying to answer a question so many people have been asking,” Times Editor Austin Gelder said. “This was a heartening reminder that running to the courts won’t save anyone from the truth.”
The co-chairman of the Legislature’s Joint Energy Committee on Tuesday criticized Entergy over the lawsuit during a hearing on data centers. 
The legal fight occurred as several Arkansas communities have enacted measures blocking data centers or imposing new restrictions. The centers have sparked bipartisan pushback across the country over concerns about energy use and the lack of transparency surrounding such projects.

title: With McConnell back, Senate ag committee advances farm bill on party lines
description: Republican members of the Senate Agriculture Committee voted Wednesday to advance a farm bill, though Democrats on the committee voted against the package due to continued disagreements on a nutrition section of the bill.  The committee marked up the bill in August, then recessed after a failed vote as Democrats held out over their proposal […]
text:
A farmer harvests soybeans Oct. 7, 2025 near Dike, Iowa. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Republican members of the Senate Agriculture Committee voted Wednesday to advance a farm bill, though Democrats on the committee voted against the package due to continued disagreements on a nutrition section of the bill. 
The committee marked up the bill in August, then recessed after a failed vote as Democrats held out over their proposal for an extension of when some states will have to begin paying for a share of federal nutrition benefits. Republican leadership amended the bill before the August hearing to offer a one-year extension, but Democrats continued to argue for a two-year extension. 
While Republicans hold the majority in the committee, Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell’s more than 90-day public hiatus due to a health issue meant the body didn’t have enough votes to pass the farm bill from the committee in August. 
McConnell returned to the Capitol earlier in the week, allowing Republicans in the agriculture committee to advance the bill along party lines. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, said in each of the five farm bills he has worked on, the opposing parties “always seem to come together at the end” to get the bill done.
“Honestly, that’s what ought to be happening here, folks,” Thune said. 
Thune said he didn’t understand why Democrats were choosing to “block vote” against a bipartisan bill that is “principally about production agriculture.” 
The farm bill is typically reauthorized every five years, but the many programs under the bill have operated on various extensions of the 2018 farm bill for the past several years. 
Democratic Sen. John Fetterman from Pennsylvania said the ag sector is “begging” for a new farm bill. 
“We’ve got to find a way to pass this thing because people are coming all the way from my state saying, ‘We can’t keep waiting for this,’” Fetterman said. “We have to deliver for our farmers.” 
The error rate issue
Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act included language that requires states to lower their Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program payment error rates, which measures a state’s accuracy in determining who is eligible for SNAP and how much they receive. 
The latest SNAP payment error rates show only nine states are below the 6% error rate threshold that allows their SNAP programs to continue to be 100% funded by the federal government. As the law currently stands, all other states will have to pay 5%, 10% or 15% of SNAP benefits costs in their state starting Oct. 2027. 
States with an error rate above 13.34%, however, are eligible for a two-year extension. Democrats sought to extend this extension to all states, especially as some states are seemingly raising their current error rates so they can benefit from the extension. 
In August, Republicans on the Senate agriculture committee adjusted the farm bill proposal to include a one-year extension, but Democrats would not vote in favor of the bill.
Farm bill proposal fails in US Senate ag committee over SNAP error rate issue

Ranking member Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota said it was her goal to “get this farm bill done, and to get it done by the end of the year,” and noted difficulties facing farmers and ranchers – like global trade disruptions, input costs and “headwinds” from tariffs. 
The Democrat said she was appreciative of Chairman John Boozman’s one-year delay, but said it would still allow certain states to get off “scot-free” while other states need tens of millions of dollars, according to estimates from the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, to pay for their nutrition programs. 
“We don’t want to have a situation where high-error-rate states get off scot-free while the rest of us pay,” Klobuchar said. “And we have shown our commitment and will continue to do that to improving this bill to get us to a bipartisan product that can be successful on the Senate floor.”
If the version of the bill that advanced Wednesday is passed and signed into law, states would have until October 2028 to lower their error rates before they are required to shoulder part of the costs. 
Thune argued Democrats should be supportive of the bill, because if it doesn’t pass, current law will remain in effect and states will have to start paying for their error rates in 2027.
Thune also noted that the bill included a number of Democrat-led amendments, and bipartisan issues like allowing year-round, nationwide access to E15, a fuel blend with 15% ethanol. 
Several senators sported buttons at the hearing that read “E15 now” and agricultural groups, including National Corn Growers Association, National Farmers Union and the Renewable Fuel Association, thanked the committee for advancing the measure. 
Iowa senators try for amendments to bill
At the August markup of the bill, senators went through the massive piece of legislation title by title with amendments and objections, before voting, unsuccessfully, on the bill as a whole. Boozman did not open the bill up again for amendments Wednesday, though Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa, attempted to talk over the roll call vote to argue her amendment should be heard. 
Ernst argued she had filed her amendment prior to the August deadline and held that the final title of the bill was not closed prior to the committee’s recess in August. 
Ernst said her amendment presented a “balanced middle ground approach” to address Proposition 12 – a California law stipulating that certain products, including pork products and bacon, must come from animals who were raised under certain conditions. 
Senate farm bill draft focuses on farm economy, keeps ‘Big Beautiful’ SNAP cuts

Congressional efforts to undo Proposition 12 have been championed by Iowa Republicans and supported by agricultural groups including the National Pork Producers Council and American Farm Bureau Federation. Animal rights, environmental groups and some producer groups, have pushed back against these efforts and celebrated that such language was not included in the Senate’s farm bill. 
Ernst said her amendment would have preserved Prop 12 and other existing laws, while preventing “future mandates from creating an unaffordable patchwork of 50 different production standards for farmers across this country.” 
“This is a serious attempt to find common ground and give our producers certainty going forward,” Ernst said. “Yet, after following the recommended process, again given by your staff, and doing the bipartisan work, we are not even being given an opportunity to bring the solution before the committee for a vote.” 
Boozman said he did not block the amendment from being brought forward during the bill markup in August. 
Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-New Mexico, said that while he might not vote with Ernst, “procedure” in the committee is supposed to “protect the voices of colleagues to raise issues that matter to us in our states.” 
“Because the senator from Iowa was recognized, and then just run over, that does not sound like the rights of those of us that sit on the committee were protected,” Luján said to Boozman. 
Sen. Chuck Grassley supported his Iowa colleague and said he was “hoping” the committee would “get a chance to vote on an amendment very important to Iowa” as the top pork producing state in the nation.
“It’s just stupid that we don’t have a chance to bring Iowa’s interest to this debate on the first farm bill that we’ve had in discussion for now the third year,” Grassley said. 
Grassley said he had also hoped to discuss his own bipartisan amendment, drafted with Democratic Sens. Cory Booker of New Jersey and Adam Schiff of California to “finalize” certain rules in the Packers and Stockyards Act. 
Grassley has previously criticized U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins for delaying the implementation of rules, which he said were “put in place to protect” meat producers in the U.S., in particular poultry producers who have invested in infrastructure costs while corporations haven’t “honored fully” their commitments with family farmers. 
“I just want to express my irritation about the whole thing, and just hope that somewhere along the line, at least the Secretary of Agriculture will wake up and draw back her delays of these rules,” Grassley said. 
Rollins said in June the rule was a “Biden-era” regulation and that USDA needed additional time to review the rule. 
Boozman said if he opened the bill up for Ernst or Grassley’s amendments, he would have to restart the markup, and “we’re not prepared to do that.”
Sen. John Hoeven, R-North Dakota, reminded his colleagues that there would still be room for amendments to the bill on the Senate floor. 
“Let’s go to the floor, offer up amendments, have robust debate, and get this done for our farmers and ranchers,” Hoeven said. 
Before the House left town Wednesday, members of the House Agriculture Committee heard testimony from producers across the country about increasing demand for “homegrown products” by advancing things like stronger antitrust laws, country of origin labeling and expanded biomanufacturing opportunities. 
In his opening comments, Chairman Glenn Thompson, R-Pennsylvania, noted that the House had already passed its version of the farm bill, and he looked forward to “the Senate upholding its end of the bargain soon.”
In a statement Wednesday evening, Boozman said advancing the bill from the Senate committee was a “critical step” toward getting results to a “hurting” farm country. 
“While this is clearly welcome progress, we need more of our colleagues’ votes to reflect the urgency of supporting farmers, ranchers, forest landowners and rural communities,” Boozman said.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah declares September a month for suicide prevention and awareness
description: Utah officials joined suicide prevention advocates in emphasizing the 988 hotline is available for anyone who needs to talk.
text:
Matt and Lindsay Albrecht are pictured during a news conference on suicide prevention at the Utah Capitol on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026. (Courtesy of the Utah Department of Health and Human Services) 

 Suicide prevention resources

If you or someone you know is experiencing suicidal thoughts or is in distress, call or text 988 to speak to crisis counselors 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year. 
More information and ways to connect are available at 988.utah.gov and 988lifeline.org. There is no wrong reason to call.



Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson joined suicide prevention advocates and other state officials on Wednesday in reminding Utahns to keep a close eye on loved ones and emphasizing the 988 hotline is available for anyone who needs to talk.
Henderson read a proclamation declaring September a month of awareness for suicide prevention and said “a significant act of bravery is not only speaking up when we need help, but noticing and then acting when we see things in others.”
A total of 709 Utahns took their own lives in 2025, Henderson said, noting barriers to getting help include a lack of resources. But she said bystanders can intervene and help by staying alert for warning signs and knowing where to turn for help. 
Lindsay and Matt Albrecht fought emotion at the Capitol as they spoke about her brother Quinn, of Holden, who took his own life in 2024. A fixture in Utah’s rodeo community, he was a doting father and husband and a talented roper, she said. 
Matt Albrecht spoke of his own experience with lifelong depression and suicidal ideation, but didn’t realize Quinn was in crisis at the time of his death. Looking back, he remembers his brother-in-law saying about a month earlier that he was feeling so poorly, he almost came to Albrecht’s house.
In hindsight, he sees the conversation as Quinn reaching out for help. 
State officials, advocates and others wrote messages of encouragement and posted them to a display raising awareness for suicide prevention at the Utah Capitol on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026. (Courtesy of the Utah Department of Health and Human Services)
“I didn’t say, ‘you’re welcome any time,’” Albrecht recalled, pausing to compose himself. Going forward, he said, “I will notice the signs and speak up and make myself available to prevent suicide.”
Rep. Steve Eliason, R-Sandy, said the national 988 “lifeline” has a Utah genesis. More than a decade ago, he and former Utah Sen. Daniel Thatcher made several attempts to bring about a three-digit mental health crisis line, he recalled, but they were unsuccessful.
So they took their idea to members of Utah’s congressional delegation, urging former Utah Rep. Chris Stewart and the late Sen. Orrin Hatch to take on the cause. The Federal Communications Commission and Congress established 988 as the national crisis line in 2020, and the resource  launched nationwide in 2022.
At the news conference on Wednesday, he joined other officials and advocates in writing messages of encouragement and support on blue sticky notes. They posted them to two panels forming a corner of a partial, makeshift room in the Capitol rotunda, saying the display seeks to emphasize to Utahns that “we’re in your corner.”  
Eliason noted a study published in the Journal of the American Medical Association in April recorded nearly 4,400 fewer suicides among young adults and teenagers than had been predicted in the hotline’s first two-and-a-half years. 
Utah’s rate has declined in the last decade, he said, adding, “let’s keep this momentum going.”

title: ‘Go stop them now,’ Burlington man says a voice told him before shooting three Palestinian students, recording reveals in trial
description:
A defense expert testified Wednesday on the third day of Jason Eaton’s trial that he was legally insane at the time of the incident.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘Go stop them now,’ Burlington man says a voice told him before shooting three Palestinian students, recording reveals in trial.
text:
Jason Eaton appears during his trial in Chittenden Superior criminal court in Burlington on Monday, September 14, 2026. Eaton is accused of shooting three Palestinian students in November of 2023. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
BURLINGTON – Jurors heard from Jason Eaton saying that he was acting under the direction of  voices he was hearing through his FM radio from CIA and government intelligence agencies before authorities allege he opened fire and injured three Palestinian students.
Parts of a recording of Eaton talking to his attorneys was played in court Wednesday on the third day of his trial where he faces three counts of attempted second-degree murder in the shooting that took place Nov. 25, 2023, in Burlington. 
Also Wednesday, Eaton’s sister, Amy Rubright, told jurors of her brother’s longstanding difficulties with finding and keeping a job, housing and relationships. 
Dr. Fabian Saleh, a forensic psychiatrist with The Johns Hopkins Hospital in Maryland, testified Wednesday for the defense that he relied heavily on the recording as well as other medical and court records and his own interviews with Eaton in reaching his conclusion that Eaton was legally insane at the time of the shooting. 
At one point in the recording taken five days after the shooting, Eaton disputed that it was a hate crime. “I think it’s a love crime,” he told his attorneys. 
At the start of the conversation Eaton sounded reluctant in the recording to even talk to his attorneys. 
“Do you have security clearance?” he asked his lawyers. “I may have gotten myself mixed up with some intelligence agencies.” 
He agreed to talk to them after receiving reassurance that they were trying to help him. 
Eaton describes in the recording that prior to the shooting he had been hearing voices through his portable FM radio tuned to public radio from government agencies, the CIA and the Israeli Mossad. 
Eaton added in the recording that he had been keeping watch from his apartment on North Prospect Street in Burlington on a residence across the street where a Jewish family lived, and he viewed it his job to protect them.

READ MORE

The voices he said he was hearing through the radio in the beginning validated and praised him, he said in the recording. They then began to direct him, he said, including on the evening of Nov. 25, 2023, when they told him to shoot people.
On that evening, Eaton added in the recording, he saw three men on the street near the house he was watching walking on the street wearing keffiyehs, a traditional scarf that is a symbol of Palestinian identity.
“I’ve been sitting for six months and I’ve never seen them,” Eaton said in the recording, adding that he got a “very strong” message from a voice in his ear bud through bluetooth that he had been hearing. “Go stop them now,” he said of the voice directing him, as the men appeared to be near the house he saw as his duty to protect.
During the recording played in court, Eaton could also be heard talking about the conflict in Gaza, hostages, armageddon and praying before the shooting. 
He said he also heard the voice of his grandfather. 
“If you don’t do it, I will,” he said his grandfather’s voice told him, with the voice adding, “This is your chance to make the right choice and join us in heaven.” 
Saleh, on the witness stand Wednesday, said he diagnosed Eaton with a psychotic disorder that includes delusions and hallucinations.
“As a result of that mental disease he lacked the ability to appreciate the criminality of his conduct,” Saleh told jurors under questioning from Joshua O’Hara, Eaton’s attorney.
Saleh described delusions as fixed, false beliefs and Eaton was experiencing them at the time of the shooting and leading up to it. 
Saleh said he didn’t believe Eaton was faking the condition or that his actions may have been induced from marijuana use or alcohol.
Under cross-examination from Chittenden County State’s Attorney Sarah George, Saleh continued to push back on the suggestion that at the time of the shootings Eaton may have been acting under the influence of marijuana or alcohol.
Saleh said that after the shooting, Eaton reported carrying on as normal, taking a shower, sleeping, and waiting in his apartment for authorities.
George also pressed Saleh on medical records from the state Department of Corrections. Eaton has been held in custody since his arrest a day after the shooting. Medical personnel there, George said, had diagnosed Eaton with narcissistic personality disorder. 
Saleh said that may be because those medical providers had not seen the recording he did, and also might never have asked Eaton about delusions. In addition, Saleh said, Eaton was told by his attorneys not to discuss details of the case against him with corrections staff. 
Eaton, 51, is charged with three counts of attempted second-degree murder for allegedly shooting  Hisham Awartani, Kinnan Abdalhamid and Tahseen Aliahmad on the evening of Nov. 25, 2023, as the three U.S college students walked on North Prospect Street in Burlington. 
The men were treated for their injuries and one remains paralyzed. 
The prosecution closed its case Tuesday, presenting forensic evidence they say ties Eaton to the shootings, including a handgun seized from his apartment that matched casings recovered from the scene.
The trial is expected to continue through the week. An expert for the state is expected to testify that Eaton was not insane at the time of the shootings.

Amy Rubright at the trial of Jason Eaton in Chittenden Superior criminal court in Burlington on Wednesday, September 16, 2026. Pool photo by Paul Heintz/Boston Globe

Rubright, Eaton’s sister, told jurors Wednesday of her brother, “He’s always had struggles.”
She said Eaton had moved around a lot, having lived in Vermont, New York and “out west.” 
Rubright said while she has had limited contact with Eaton in recent years she recalled an odd phone call she received from him in December 2021 when he was living out of his truck in Syracuse, New York. 
In that call, Rubright said, he spoke to her about hearing messages and him being a “lightbearer” and how lightbearers needed to join together to save the world, and demons did not appear to be a threat to lightbearers.
She said Eaton said since he had his own struggles that he made a good lightbearer to help others because he would understand other peoples’ hardships.
Rubright said she knew that her brother smoked marijuana. She also testified that she never noticed any major changes in his behavior from smoking marijuana.
Also, Rubright said, at times Eaton would refer to himself as a “whistleblower,” voicing problems at places where he worked. 
Sally Adams, Chittenden County chief deputy state’s attorney, asked Rubright if that might be the reason Eaton has had difficulty holding down a job.
“Yes,” Rubright responded.

title: Cold shoulder: Brattleboro won’t be welcoming ICE
description:
Brattleboro’s police chief said he wants community members to call his department if they hear that officers from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement are in town.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Cold shoulder: Brattleboro won’t be welcoming ICE.
text:
A couple hundred people march from Plaza Park to the Wells Fountain in Brattleboro during a locally organized No Kings march on Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026. Photo by Kristopher Radder/Brattleboro Reformer

This story by Chris Mays was first published in the Brattleboro Reformer on Sept. 15, 2026.
BRATTLEBORO — Local police aren’t planning to work with federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers if they come to town. 
At a special selectboard meeting Monday, Brattleboro Police Chief Jeremy Evans said he would like community members to give his department a call if they hear ICE is in town. 
“Because you’ll probably be the first call we get,” he said. “They don’t call us. There’s no collaboration there. They saw that in South Burlington. They’ve seen it elsewhere. That is a common thread where ICE doesn’t tell law enforcement that they’re showing up.”
Evans said his department collaborates “with federal partners on a lot of investigations on a regular basis, not related to immigration, and that continues to this day.” If ICE asked to stage at the police station, he said, “the answer would be no.”
“And if they showed up at our facility, we would go out and find out who was there because I’m assuming we’d see a group of people that looked like cops but weren’t dressed like cops in our parking lot,” Evans said. “We’d say, ‘What are you doing?’ And they would say who they were, and we would ask them to leave because we’re not going to be a part of that. If they were elsewhere in town, I’m sure the town would ask us to do the same thing in that format.”
Janice Stockman, of Brattleboro, read a statement signed by 175 Brattleboro residents, 81 people from other towns, and 16 organizations, institutions and businesses, calling for the town to ensure that its police force abides by the Fair and Impartial Policing Policy and consider adding new language supported by Migrant Justice to the local policy. They also urged the police not to enter into any partnership agreements with federal ICE or border protection agents; honor and enforce state law prohibiting detentions in protected spaces; create policies or consider creating an ordinance that prohibits federal immigration enforcement agents from using town property in any manner; decline any material support to federal agents; and intervene if an officer is seen using excessive force.
Stockman thanked the town for hosting a meeting to “express our concerns and expectations proactively before we are thrust into the kinds of situations that happened in South Burlington, Londonderry and Keene.” 
Select Board Chair Oscar Heller described the town’s existing Fair and Impartial Policing Policy as “a fairly sturdy, strongly worded document.” The revision suggested by Migrant Justice “might be something the board takes a look at in the future,” he said. 
Robin Morgan, of Brattleboro, said the goal of the proposed revision is to try to “close loopholes and strengthen the language that’s in there, so that it doesn’t leave folks in a situation where there’s ambiguity about how police are supposed to conduct themselves with regard to this, and that’s really the position that we don’t want to put our police force in.”
“We want to make sure that there’s clear boundaries around how they should be participating and what their responsibilities are when there is any immigration enforcement that’s happening in our town,” she said. 
A subgroup of Brattleboro Indivisible is asking the selectboard to approve a resolution “dedicated to committing to protect and support Brattleboro’s immigrant community,” said Nick Biddle, of Brattleboro. 
Regarding the high-tension South Burlington raid and standoff that included confrontations between citizens and ICE,  Evans said the footage he has seen in Vermont Public’s “No Exit” documentary and the news made him uncomfortable.  
“We’re more focused on what might happen here,” he said when asked to weigh in on the incident. “I did take some time to meet with administrators from up in that area and say, ‘Talk to me about what happened. Talk to me about what went down at your department. Talk to me about mistakes, problems, issues, concerns that you had,’ so that I could bring that information back to us and hopefully mitigate those things happening here.” 
The Brattleboro Police Department “won’t be entering into any agreements with federal government with regards” to ICE, Evans said.
“We’re not planning it,” he said. “We’re not interested in it. We have plenty of work to do of our own and don’t want to do anyone else’s.”
Officers are trained on how to handle incidents involving excessive force by law enforcement at the Vermont Police Academy, Evans said. 
Ivan Hennessy, of Brattleboro, called the chief’s comments “very encouraging, especially in light of the habitual violence that ICE brings.” 
Evans said he serves on a committee that maintains the Fair and Impartial Policing Policy and helps with the training of officers annually throughout the state. A meeting is held virtually every month. 
Currently, the committee is in the process of creating the module for next year’s training on the policy. Any input “would be extraordinary,” Evans said.
Hank Poitras, creator of the “Planet Hank” YouTube channel, who shoots and posts video of law enforcement making arrests, said the proposed policy revisions would “help activists interfere with law enforcement.”
“I don’t really think that’s a good idea,” he said. “If they provoke a confrontation and somebody gets hurt, these activists will evaporate and disappear and move on, and Brattleboro will be left with tragedy, lawsuits and the bill.”
Anne Beekman, of Putney, chair of the Windham Southeast Supervisory Union Board, said she wants “ICE to be kept away from our children, all of our children, our immigrant children, our citizen children.”
Heller said a bill passed by Vermont lawmakers in the last legislative session “greatly expanded the role of protected spaces, which used to just be courthouses.”
“But this is a protected space,” he said of the library, where the meeting was held. “You cannot be arrested on a civil immigration warrant. That list was expanded from courthouses to places of worship, libraries, social service agencies like food shelves or domestic violence shelters, hospitals.”
Another new law “essentially created a right for Vermont residents to sue federal agents for violations of their constitutional rights,” Heller said. 
After the meeting, Heller told the Reformer he’s “proud of how the community tackled such a difficult subject.”
“The meeting was emotional, informative and at times challenging, but in the ways that make us all stronger and closer-knit,” he said. “This was community engagement at its best.”
Heller described being “appreciative for everyone who attended and spoke, and for those who spoke for others who couldn’t attend in safety in person.”
“The police department, represented by Chief Jeremy Evans and Assistant Chief Adam Petlock, continued to demonstrate their dedication to the principles of justice and community safety for everyone in town,” Heller said. “There’s always more to be done, but we all showed up very well for each other, and I’m grateful.”

title: Pardon request 25 years after sex offense sparks discussion on purpose of clemency in South Dakota
description: SIOUX FALLS — A request for clemency from a man convicted of a sex offense 25 years ago spurred a discussion on the purpose of a pardon Wednesday at a meeting of the South Dakota board empowered to make recommendations to the governor. The 57-year-old who applied for the pardon hasn’t been charged with a […]
text:
Pardons in South Dakota are granted by the governor, who may consider recommendations by the Board of Pardons and Paroles. (Illustration by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)SIOUX FALLS — A request for clemency from a man convicted of a sex offense 25 years ago spurred a discussion on the purpose of a pardon Wednesday at a meeting of the South Dakota board empowered to make recommendations to the governor.
The 57-year-old who applied for the pardon hasn’t been charged with a crime since he was convicted of sexual contact with a minor. 
He wants to have the 2001 offense cleared from his record, he said in his application, because he felt his actions since the crime show that he’s paid his debt to society. He also said he’d recently lost a job he’d held for years in the logging industry, and felt the conviction would make it difficult to find employment again.
More inmates denied early release as more parolees return through crackdown

His application included recommendations from family members, and a letter from the victim, who was 13 years old at the time and now says she has forgiven him. 
The victim wrote that the man now requesting a pardon had “gone above and beyond to make things right with her,” Shelli Gust, administrator for the South Dakota Board of Pardons and Paroles, told board members on Wednesday.
The man, whose name and picture are listed in the South Dakota Sex Offender Registry, is a father of three who’s married to the same woman he was at the time of his conviction, Gust said. He served four years in the Marines, Gust said, and had the support of “a very large family.” He was never incarcerated for the crime, but was sentenced to 10 years on probation.
Two members of the parole board had recommended denying a pardon recommendation during an initial review process on Tuesday. The full board reviewed the request on Wednesday.
Nature of offense sparks questions 
Most criminal arrests and convictions in South Dakota are part of a person’s permanent record. Unlike some states, there are no provisions of state law that automatically remove old crimes after a period of good behavior.
The legal avenues to clear a crime from the public record in South Dakota are spare. 
Those convicted of a crime can ask a judge for a suspended imposition of sentence. In such situations, the crime is removed from the person’s record after a period of good behavior and meeting any other conditions imposed by a judge.
A person who’s arrested, but for whom no formal charges are filed, can ask a judge to remove an arrest from their record.
A pardon from the governor is the only other way to get a crime removed, and the pathway to a pardon typically begins with the parole board. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Aaron Pilcher, an attorney from Huron whom Rhoden appointed to the board in February, said on Wednesday that the 57-year-old’s situation didn’t stand out as deserving of a pardon recommendation.
Having a felony, Pilcher said, “isn’t convenient,” but that inconvenience alone shouldn’t be enough to qualify a person who’s behaved since their felony conviction.
He noted that the applicant had lost a job and wants a new one, but didn’t list a specific job or explain why his offense would prevent him from getting one. 
“What about this guy’s offense raises it above the level of an inconvenience?” Pilcher said.
Kirsten Aasen, a defense lawyer who serves as vice chair of the board, said that Pilcher’s comments “triggered” her. 
Plenty of states offer easier ways to clear a record, Aasen said, because felony convictions make it harder to get and hold down a job or find a place to live. Several states, including California and Michigan, have laws that automatically clear some convictions from a person’s record after periods of good behavior.
For people with decades of good behavior in South Dakota, Aasen said she operates on a “presumption” that a pardon is appropriate.
A felony “is more than just an embarrassing social stigma,” she said. “It’s financially debilitating.”
Kurt Hall, one of the two board members to recommend denial of the man’s pardon on Tuesday, said he understands why a person with a sex offense on their record would like to see it removed. Rau was the other member to recommend denial Tuesday.
But Hall, the Faulk County sheriff, also said the recent case of Mark Milk has made him cautious. In 2023, the board recommended a commutation for Milk, who’d been serving a life sentence for manslaughter. Former Gov. Kristi Noem granted the commutation; the board later paroled Milk.
Milk is in custody again, facing federal drug distribution charges in Iowa after police alleged he provided his teenage niece with the cocaine that killed her.
Given the scrutiny that high-profile case has placed on the board, “it’s a perfect storm to go against” a convicted sex offender’s request for clemency, Hall said.
Pilcher, in response to Aasen’s comments, said he’s also concerned about the way the applicant described the offense.
“It looks more severe or deliberate in the actual report than in how he describes what happened,” Pilcher said 
Governor will decide
Board member Peter Lieberman moved to recommend a pardon. Lieberman, a former judge, said he agrees with Aasen about what qualifies a person for a pardon. Lieberman pointed to the applicant’s service in the Marines as a major factor weighing in his favor. 
“I’m as tough on sex offenders as anyone, but I don’t want to see someone who served in the Corps and has stayed out of trouble for 25 years to be saddled with” the stigma of being a sex offender, Lieberman said.
The board voted 5-4 to recommend a pardon to Gov. Rhoden. Hall ultimately voted yes with Lieberman, as did Aasen, board members John Brown and Patricia Meyers. Pilcher and members Myron Rau, Vaughn Beck and Jan Steele voted against the recommendation.
Rhoden will review the man’s application. As of May, Rhoden had issued 90 pardons and two commutations since he became governor in January 2025. He’d denied four pardon requests and one commutation request by that time. 
State lacks strict rules for pardon eligibility
The parole board can release inmates on parole or pull them back into prison for parole violations, but only acts as a screening panel for pardons. Under the state constitution, the governor has the exclusive authority to issue or deny pardons.
State law does not have binding rules to define who does or does not qualify for a pardon.
Sioux Falls man on parole for manslaughter is charged with providing drugs that killed his niece

The board’s administrative rules on executive clemency list seven factors that “may” be considered at a hearing on a person’s application for a pardon. Among them are the applicant’s age and medical status, a demonstration of “remarkable rehabilitation,” a showing that their sentence was excessive or “a miscarriage of justice,” or that they’re seeking “a professional career from which society can benefit, but a conviction prevents it.”
The board may also consider “the applicant’s attitude, character, capabilities, and habits; the nature and circumstances of the offense or offenses,” as well as “the effect the applicant’s clemency will have on the victims of the crime and the community.”
The administrative rules offer guidance, but are ultimately suggestions that leave room for interpretation, according to Rau, the board’s chair.
If the board recommends a pardon, the governor gets any materials offered in the person’s application, background information on a case, and audio and video of any board discussion on the person’s situation.
Gov. Larry Rhoden, in an interview with South Dakota Searchlight in 2025, said he bases his pardon decisions on his own feelings and personal judgment. When he’s denied clemency to someone for whom the board had recommended it, Rhoden said, it was mainly because he felt that not enough time had passed since a crime occurred.
A pardon clears an old crime completely from the public record, though a copy of the pardon showing the pardoned crime or crimes remains on file at the South Dakota Secretary of State’s Office. After a period of five years, the pardon document is sealed. 
The governor can also grant another form of clemency called a commutation. That reduces the sentence for current inmates, typically making them eligible for parole earlier than they’d otherwise be. The board typically must vote to authorize parole after a commutation is granted — as its members did with Milk in 2024 — though a governor has the authority to issue a commutation that results in an inmate’s immediate release.

name: VTDigger
title: Barre schools eye cuts to sports and other activities after budget fails on third attempt
description:
Voters in Barre Town and the city of Barre shot down the district's proposed $57.1 million budget at the polls Tuesday.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Barre schools eye cuts to sports and other activities after budget fails on third attempt.
text:
Signs advocating for and against the Barre school district’s budget stand outside the Barre Town Middle and Elementary School on Sept. 15, 2026. Photo by Charlotte Oliver/VTDigger

BARRE — Board members in the Barre Unified Union School District will look at making cuts to winter sports, school transportation and extracurricular activities after voters rejected the district’s annual budget for the third time Tuesday. 
“It’s definitely a heartbreaking result because ultimately all cuts are going to affect students,” said Garrett Grant, chair of the school board.
For the second time in three years Barre remains the last district in Vermont without a voter-approved budget, even as it ranks among the lowest-spending districts in the state. This year’s budget saga resembles the district’s struggle in 2024, when it took four attempts to break the deadlock. The recent rejection splits the merged district along municipal lines, with Barre Town casting most of the no votes. 
The rejection is likely costly for the district. It expects to spend up to $22,000 in monthly interest payments as it has to take out a line of credit to keep schools running. 
Up for vote was a $57.1 million annual spending plan, which was the lowest budget figure the district’s voters have seen on the ballot so far this year. Voters rejected a $57.8 million budget in March and a $57.5 million budget in May.
The latest proposal was rejected by 52.6% of voters in the district, while 47.3% approved, according to clerks in the district’s municipalities. 
In the district that spans both Barre Town and the city of Barre, the majority of voters who said no to the budget — about 65% — came from Barre Town. 

READ MORE

Michael Carr, who showed up to vote at the Barre Municipal Auditorium, said he voted “hard no” on the district’s budget — and he didn’t mince words explaining why. 
“Taxes are ridiculous,” said Carr, who anticipates his taxes will rise this year. 
Carr, who doesn’t have kids enrolled in the district, said he thinks taxes have gotten out of control. He worries that high costs will remain the norm if voters approve the school budget. He said he thinks administrators and board members need to get more serious about cutting costs. 
Carr’s vote was in the minority in the city of Barre. The majority of voters there were in favor of the budget, 628-526, according to the city clerk. 
Julie Swift, who went to vote at Barre Town Middle and Elementary School, said she approved the district’s budget proposal Tuesday. 
“I just feel that going back to the drawing board and cutting more isn’t what’s best for our kids,” Swift said. 
Swift said she suspects her property taxes will go up. Still, she said she wanted to support the students in the school system, which her kids used to attend. 
Swift was also in the minority of voters in her community. Most voters in Barre Town opposed the budget proposal, 993-773, according to the town clerk. 
Barre is already among the lowest-spending districts in the state, according to Grant, and has historically been a low spender. The budget that voters rejected Tuesday proposed spending 2.1% more than in the previous school year, a rate lower than inflation. 
Gov. Phil Scott said at a press conference earlier this month that he was hopeful Barre would pass its budget. Grant previously told VTDigger late last month that Scott, a proponent of cutting school spending statewide, has strong influence over voters in his hometown. 
As for Carr’s concerns, Grant said he’s heard similar comments before. He said there’s a common misconception that board members haven’t gone line by line through the district’s budget, which is already $700,000 less than the first version that voters rejected in March. 
Grant also said he thinks that disagreement over the district’s budget is fueled by how complicated the state’s education funding model is. People in Barre can’t agree on the same set of facts, Grant said, because the state’s funding model is so convoluted that people often end up comparing apples to oranges and making incorrect claims about the school board. 
As long as the district lacks a voter-approved budget, it has to take out a line of credit to keep its doors open, Superintendent Emilie Knisley previously told VTDigger. Districts without an approved spending plan are allowed to spend up to 87% of their previous year’s budget, but the district also has to open a line of credit with a local bank, meaning it has to make interest payments, Knisley said.
Grant said the district’s school board will meet next week to discuss when it might hold a fourth budget vote. In the meantime, he said, he’s trying to educate people in town to combat rumors and misinformation. 
“I’ve joked before that it’s kind of like playing whack-a-mole. You debunk one thing and another comes back up.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Regents give initial approval for Center for Intellectual Freedom organizational plan
description: The Iowa Board of Regents Wednesday received an update from its new Center for Intellectual Freedom Committee on its search for a permanent director as the center carves out the details of its own independence from the University of Iowa. Regent Christine Hensley, chair of the regents committee overseeing the Center for Intellectual Freedom at […]
text:
Iowa Board of Regents Executive Director Mark Braun, left, and Regent Christine Hensley attend a board meeting on Sept. 16, 2026. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The Iowa Board of Regents Wednesday received an update from its new Center for Intellectual Freedom Committee on its search for a permanent director as the center carves out the details of its own independence from the University of Iowa.
Regent Christine Hensley, chair of the regents committee overseeing the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa, said the center advisory council’s executive committee has narrowed the pool of 62 center director applicants to 11 candidates. Board Executive Director Mark Braun also clarified during the meeting that no less than three, but no more than four, finalists can be brought to the full board of regents for consideration.
Advisory council executive committee members in a Sept. 1 meeting went through the applicants for the center’s executive director role and discussed the center’s interactions with the UI.
“I know, to be perfectly honest, that there will be some members of the executive committee that are not pleased with us moving forward,” Hensley said. “But it’s critical that we keep the process going. We want to notify all applicants today what their status is, whether they’re in that pool, and or whether or not they’re not going to be invited for an interview.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Hensley said the executive committee members will meet again next week to decide whether they want to eliminate a few more of the current candidates before setting up Zoom calls in the last week of September and in-depth interviews the week of Oct. 5. Discussions of campus visits and the finalist list will take place in mid-October, she said, with the possibility of calling a special board of regents session at the end of the month to select the center’s permanent director.
Board President Robert Cramer, who also sits on the center committee alongside Regent Steve Lacy, called this work “the beginning of a reset” and said he believes the center is moving in the right direction.
Members of the center’s advisory council have said how necessary the relationship is between the center for intellectual freedom and the UI, and have expressed concerns about trying to create an academic framework and curriculum when the details of that relationship — and leadership of the center — have not been solidified.
The organizational plan released by the board of regents for the center is focused on “back of the house” operations, Hensley said, including infrastructure and assigned responsibilities. It states the chair of the center for intellectual freedom committee — Hensley — has authority to sign off on purchases and contracts totaling $25,000 or more, according to the plan, and will act as the director’s “supervisor of record in University of Iowa systems and hold approval authority in those systems on behalf of the Board.”
Whoever becomes the center director will have signature authority on purchases less than $25,000, the plan stated. They will have “sole and exclusive authority” over recruitment, hiring and firing of center staff and will supervise all personnel, including approving time off and work situations outside of the norm, like a hybrid format.
Hensley in her role as committee chair will also initiate annual budget reviews and submit them to the board of regents, serve as the board’s administrative contact for human resources transactions, and work with university HR and other departments for special payments. She will also approve the director’s “time and attendance,” as well as trip requests, and serve as the director’s supervisor for administrative processes in university systems.
Advisory council members pushed back against restrictions on director travel at the Sept. 1 meeting, after interim director Luciano de Castro said the board committee didn’t allow him to travel to different conferences.
“I’ll be real honest with you right now; they’re not satisfied with the document, but they are an advisory committee, and the board of regents has final authority to approve that,” Hensley said.
She added that the executive committee members were given “the opportunity to provide additional comments” after the meeting, but none were provided.
A memorandum of understanding is also in the process of being developed, Hensley said, but those involved have decided that it needs input from whoever the permanent center director will be before it is finalized. The memorandum will outline the academic side of interactions between the university and center.
According to the organizational plan, the center director will be in charge of negotiating and implementing the memorandum when it comes to information technology services, as well as facilities-use agreements.
“The university will still be playing a role because we will be utilizing the systems and IT at the university,” Hensley said. “I mean, we can’t have; they can’t be completely independent … we’ve got to rely on the university providing that support.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota farmers increasingly rely on foreign labor
description: As demand for agricultural labor grows, North Dakota farmers are looking abroad to fill their vacant positions. There were just under 500 unfilled agricultural jobs across North Dakota in August, according to Job Service North Dakota. Most of those positions were in the northeastern and south-central parts of the state. So far this year, 478 […]
text:
Mark Martens, center, vice president of Agri Placements International, discusses agricultural labor trends and growing demand for H-2A visa workers during a panel at the Big Iron Farm and Construction Show in West Fargo on Sept. 16, 2026. Also pictured are moderator Korrie Wenzel, left, and Caleb Zook. (Photo by Ceilidh Kern/For the North Dakota Monitor)
As demand for agricultural labor grows, North Dakota farmers are looking abroad to fill their vacant positions.
There were just under 500 unfilled agricultural jobs across North Dakota in August, according to Job Service North Dakota. Most of those positions were in the northeastern and south-central parts of the state.
So far this year, 478 employers in North Dakota were approved to hire seasonal foreign workers through the H-2A visa program, according to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. The program connects agricultural employers with workers when they’re unable to fill their positions with Americans.
Those employers have hired nearly 5,000 foreign workers this year, up from just over 1,000 in 2025. 
“It has grown substantially, the need for these workers, because there aren’t enough folks here in the state to go up and do that work,” said Dustin Hillebrand, a workforce center manager for Job Services North Dakota, during a Wednesday panel on agricultural labor during the Big Iron Farm and Construction Show in Fargo.
Record diesel prices hit North Dakota farmers at the wrong time

Farmers are hiring fewer North Dakotans to fill open positions in part because the state has very low unemployment and high workforce participation, meaning that most of the state’s residents already have jobs, according to Hillebrand.
Another reason, he said, is that North Dakota’s average wages aren’t competitive with other states in the region. At the end of May 2025, the average wage for North Dakota farm workers was $28,000 to $33,000, while Montana, Wyoming, Colorado, South Dakota and Nebraska saw wages ranging from $40,000 to $51,000, Hillebrand said.
Between wages, hard working conditions, the seasonal nature of farm work and competition from better-paying industries like oil and gas, many farmers in North Dakota and across the country are struggling to find American workers, said Mark Martens, vice president of Agri Placements International, a company that helps employers apply for H-2A visas.
The H-2A visa helps farmers fill this gap so they don’t have to downsize their operations, Martens said.
“It’s (also) a win for workers because they’re coming over here and earning a lot higher wages than they get in their own country,” added Caleb Zook, director of business development at Agri Placements. 
How the visa process works
In order to hire H-2A visa workers, employers must first post their open positions locally and prove that they aren’t receiving applications from any qualified Americans.
Before they apply, they must also have worker housing coordinated so it can be inspected as part of the application process. That presents a challenge for many North Dakota farmers as the state reckons with a rural housing shortage, Hillebrand said.
“There isn’t enough housing in small-town North Dakota. You’re fighting against the people who want to live in those communities that aren’t in the farming (industry),” he said. “It’s a battle between the two of them, because there’s not enough housing.”
North Dakotan overseeing federal farm programs out to cut red tape, modernize 

During the panel, Hillebrand mentioned the Spark Building Initiative, an effort in northeastern North Dakota to build more housing and spur growth. He told the Monitor he hopes that effort can help small-town residents move out of their rental units and open up their apartments for farm workers.
But in the meantime, many farmers who can’t find homes for their workers are providing transportation from neighboring communities, building homes or installing mobile homes on their own properties, Hillebrand said.
While the cost of hiring visa workers can vary depending on the size and type of agricultural operation, as well as other factors, Zook said an employer could expect to spend $5,000 to $10,000 per worker for application and other fees, approvals and transportation from the worker’s country to the farm.
“That’s basically just getting the worker to your farm,” he said, adding that housing, workers’ compensation and wages will increase costs further.
H-2A visa workers’ wages are set by the federal government and can vary based on location, type of work and other factors. This year, H-2A workers in North Dakota have been paid anywhere from $9.99 and under to $30 and more per hour, according to USCIS.
