title: KY Court of Appeals frees former Gov. Matt Bevin from jail sentence while it considers appeal
description: Former Gov. Matt Bevin will be immediately released from a 60-day jail sentence while the Kentucky Court of Appeals decides whether his incarceration was the proper punishment for his contempt of court charges, the Appeals Court ruled late Wednesday. Bevin, 59, was arrested Sept. 3 and lodged in the Jefferson County jail to serve a 60-day sentence […]
text:
Former Kentucky Gov. Matt Bevin smiles at his arraignment in Jefferson County Court. Judge Angela Johnson sentenced him to 60 days in jail for contempt of court. (Pool photo by Matt Stone of the Louisville Courier-Journal)Former Gov. Matt Bevin will be immediately released from a 60-day jail sentence while the Kentucky Court of Appeals decides whether his incarceration was the proper punishment for his contempt of court charges, the Appeals Court ruled late Wednesday.
Bevin, 59, was arrested Sept. 3 and lodged in the Jefferson County jail to serve a 60-day sentence for contempt for failing to produce financial documents a judge had ordered him to provide in an ongoing legal battle with his estranged, adopted son, Jonah Bevin.
His lawyers appealed the decision.
Jefferson Family Court Judge Angela Johnson had sentenced him for contempt after finding he failed to release all documents she had ordered he produce as part of his divorce case with his ex-wife, Glenna, in which Jonah is seeking support.
Bevin also skipped a July 28 hearing the judge had ordered him to attend in person over the matter. The one-term Republican governor was arrested Thursday while working as an extra on a Christmas movie being filmed at a Bourbon County horse farm.
In the appeal, Bevin’s lawyers argued that he had already has produced over 1,000 pages of financial documents and, because the case involving his son’s claims for support has been submitted to the judge for a decision there is nothing further he can do to meet requirements of the court, it said.
His continued incarceration, it said, “amounts to nothing more than punishment for his past conduct.”
The court agreed.
“This conclusion neither excuses Matthew’s prior noncompliance nor determines the merits of his petition,” Jones wrote in the ruling. “It recognizes only that Matthew has made a colorable showing that his present incarceration may be unlawful and that, because the injury is the ongoing loss of his physical liberty, relief granted only after final disposition of this original action could come too late to provide a meaningful remedy.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: Will a new federal education tax credit be available in Washington?
description: Gov. Bob Ferguson has yet to decide whether Washington will join 31 other states that have opted into a new federal tax program aimed at driving more private dollars into the education of K-12 students.   Beginning in January, taxpayers in participating states will be able to donate up to $1,700 to an  approved nonprofit organization. […]
text:
Gov. Bob Ferguson has not publicly stated whether or not Washington will opt into a new federal tax credit program. (Photo by Aspen Ford/Washington State Standard)Gov. Bob Ferguson has yet to decide whether Washington will join 31 other states that have opted into a new federal tax program aimed at driving more private dollars into the education of K-12 students.  
Beginning in January, taxpayers in participating states will be able to donate up to $1,700 to an  approved nonprofit organization. Those groups will provide “scholarships” to students to defray expenses, which will vary depending on whether the person attends a private or public school. Contributors will receive a dollar-for-dollar credit on their federal tax liability.
The Education Freedom Tax Credit program is open to any state whose governor opts in.  Participating states must submit a list of scholarship granting organizations to the federal government by Jan. 1.
Advocates say participating should be a no-brainer for Washington as it potentially could bring in hundreds of millions of additional dollars for students. Critics consider the tax credit a voucher program with a different name and worry it will divert funding to private institutions. 
Arne Duncan, who served as the U.S. Secretary of Education under Democrat President Barack Obama, called it “not just an educational opportunity,” but a “moral obligation,” during a panel on Tuesday hosted by the Washington Policy Center, a conservative think tank. 
“I just desperately hope we choose the right thing for kids and the right thing for our country,” Duncan said. “It doesn’t replace a single dollar. It’s additional. It’s additive.”
The program is gaining momentum in some Democrat-held states including Colorado, Virginia, and more recently New York. Others – Oregon, New Mexico, Hawaii — have publicly declined participating.  
“This program has the potential to convert ordinary Americans, ordinary taxpayers, and to create millions of new philanthropists,” said Jorge Elorza, CEO of Democrats for Education Reform, during the panel. Elorza’s organization estimated donations could net over $700 million in added spending on students in Washington. 
Scholarship eligibility is limited to students from families with household incomes 300% or less than the area median income, according to the Congressional Research Service. In King County where the median income is nearly $125,000, the limit is around $374,000. 
But critics warn it won’t remove the threat of budget cuts for public schools. 
During the past legislative session, state lawmakers cut the Transition to Kindergarten program, reduced access to college courses for high schoolers and did not make planned increases to a program that supports rural school districts. 
For private school students in Washington, a scholarship could pay for their tuition, room and board, and other fees.
For public school students, the money cannot be used to pay for their basic education. They could use it to offset costs of certain special needs services, tutoring sessions, computer equipment and other activities not paid for by the school district or state. 
“It’s especially problematic if those services come through this program instead of what’s already constitutionally mandated in the state of Washington,” which requires ample funding for basic education, said David Knight, an associate professor of education finance at the University of Washington, who recently authored an op-ed opposing the program. 
The largest public school teachers’ union in the state is wholly opposed to the program, calling it a federal voucher scheme that diverts public money into private hands. 
“With public schools, we have very transparent accountability standards that ensure high quality instruction,” said Toni Lindquist, vice president of the Washington Education Association. Private schools aren’t held to the same standards, she added. 
Waiting on the governor
For weeks, state Rep. Michael Keaton, R-Puyallup, has been trying to speak with Ferguson. He said his office has been in contact with different staff members, but he is hoping to meet with the governor by the end of the month. 
Keaton, the assistant ranking member in the House Education committee, says opting into the program “is an easy decision.”
“It’s not a voucher, it’s free federal dollars for our state’s education,” Keaton said. “Is the governor gonna let people know [this program] exists?”
Earlier this year, Keaton and state Rep. Jim Walsh, R-Aberdeen, urged Ferguson to opt in. 
The governor hasn’t spoken publicly on the issue and his office did not respond for comment. 
Brionna Aho, communications director for the governor, previously told the Standard that Ferguson was waiting until the program’s rules were final to make a decision. 
They still aren’t, but they are expected to be in the coming weeks.
Superintendent of Public Instruction Chris Reykdal has said the program “needs a substantial rewrite” as it “pulls future opportunities away from young people to primarily enrich existing private providers” in a February letter to Washington’s congressional delegation. 
“Marketing of the tax credit program make it clear that the program is not intended to support public schools at scale as a substitute for state funding,” said Katy Payne, chief strategy officer for the superintendent’s office.  
Even if Washington doesn’t opt in, taxpayers can still contribute to scholarship granting organizations in other states. 
“If I have a choice of sending money to Washington, D.C. … versus keeping that money in my state and funding kids who are struggling, I can’t think of an easier choice to make,” said Duncan, former U.S. Secretary of Education.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Allegheny County officials tell Pa. lawmakers that building alone won’t fix housing shortage
description: Panelists told lawmakers that addressing Pennsylvania's housing shortage must be focused on affordability and preserving existing homes in addition to building new structures.
text:
Panelists told lawmakers that addressing Pennsylvania's housing shortage must be focused on affordability and preserving existing homes in addition to building new structures.  (Photo by Robbie Sequeira/Stateline)Government employees and community advocates warned state lawmakers Wednesday that the commonwealth can’t build itself out of the housing shortage, but needed to also focus on preserving existing homes and keeping homes affordable for low-income Pennsylvanians.
“We can build all we want, but if we continue to lose units, we will still wind up in a negative situation,” said Sara Innamorato, the county executive of Allegheny County and a former state representative. 
Though the lack of homes impacted people across the economic spectrum, those with limited means — specifically seniors — struggled to afford their homes, she continued. 
Sara Innamorato, Allegheny County Executive (Photo from Allegheny County)
The county lost more than 44,000 apartments between 2019 and 2024 where the monthly rent was less than $1,000. During that period, it gained 13,000 units where it cost more than $2,000 to live in each month, according to Innamorato. 
Over the next decade, the pace of Pennsylvania’s homebuilding is projected to fall short by 185,000 homes. The southwest corner of the state, including Allegheny and eight other counties, will need more than 66,000 homes to keep up with the demand, according to the state Housing Action Plan. 
Jen Schuchart, the director of meeting basic needs with the United Way of Southwestern Pennsylvania, said requests for housing assistance were up at the community organization. According to her, just over one-third of the region’s households don’t earn enough to make ends meet and are considered to be Asset Limited, Income Constrained and Employed, or ALICE.
Many ALICE households also spend more than 30% of their income on housing or utilities, cutting into their budgets for other, everyday needs, she continued. 
“As the committee discusses the need for increasing our housing supply, we encourage you to keep the full ALICE population, which includes both our most vulnerable neighbors and our working families, at the forefront of your thoughts to create pathways to affordable housing for all Pennsylvania residents,” Schuchart said. 
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
David Dean, the president of the Pennsylvania Association of Realtors, cautioned that  affordability couldn’t be addressed until the state increases its inventory. 
“We do a disservice when we convince ourselves and others that … any single bill or idea will magically end our affordability woes,” said Dean. “This problem is much bigger and requires a wide range of changes in policy.”
 Still a need to speed up permitting

Pennsylvania lawmakers have held several hearings in recent months on the housing shortage and affordability, with many emphasizing the need to reform permitting processes on the state and local levels. 
Developers have said that delayed approvals add to the bottom line at a time when other expenses are increasing. On top of other industry woes, the federal crackdown on immigration is driving up labor costs and tariffs add to the price of materials. 
To make the process faster and more predictable, Pittsburgh’s newest mayoral administration is overhauling its approach, according to Matt Singer, the deputy chief of staff for Pittsburgh Mayor Corey O’Connor. 
Bipartisan coalition of state lawmakers looks to incentivize ‘pro-housing’ communities 

“Our permitting system has not kept pace with Pittsburgh’s needs. It was not built for today’s necessary pace of investment,” said Singer. “As a whole, cities must make it easier to build, convert, permit and repair new and existing housing units.”
This includes smaller scale projects for things like accessibility modifications, he added, which the city is trying to speed through with a fast-track pilot program and virtual inspections. 
Jon Knudsen, who works on housing projects with Commonwealth Development Partners, said he was “extremely optimistic” about the future despite the challenges, giving the city credit for the improvements. 
“Development is difficult everywhere right now. Construction costs are high, interest rates and financing costs remain challenging,” said Knudsen. 
His firm is redeveloping the 37-story Grant Building in downtown Pittsburgh. The 1929 structure was the first high-rise in the city and is a recognizable part of the skyline, but transforming some of its floors from empty offices to apartments has been challenging. 
Jon Knudsen, the director for development with Commonwealth Development Partners, called the struggles to redevelop Pittsburgh Grant Building from offices to housing a “useful case study.” (Screenshot from livestream)
“There is no shortage of buildings that need a new purpose post-COVID … the problem is getting from where they are today to a point where someone can actually invest the tens of millions of dollars necessary to give them that second life,” he added. 
He recommended more cities creating “a single point of contact,” pointing to an experience he had in Chicago. One city staffer guided his firm through permitting and coordinated the process across various agencies. 
“It was still a lengthy process … but we knew exactly what and where we were going,” he said. 
Minority Chair Rep. Rich Irvin (R-Huntingdon) weighed the compromise between increasing the supply of houses at the potential cost of local autonomy, such as proposals requiring municipalities to consider accessory dwelling units or reform their zoning to be friendlier to multi-family homes.
“Something that I have struggled with is how to not be heavy-handed to local governments, but to try to encourage local governments to actually do exactly what you’re trying to do here,” he said. 
Innamorato recommended using incentives, rather than penalties. For a local fund, the county prioritizes applications with pro-housing policies that span multiple municipalities. 
“It doesn’t mean you’re eliminated from being able to access these funds, it just means that your likelihood of getting this money for your community increases if you’ve adopted some of these best practices,” she added. 
 A focus on affordability

But Maura Jacob, the policy and community impact officer of The Pittsburgh Foundation, warned that expanding the housing supply without also planning for the poorest Pennsylvanians would be unwise, citing an analysis from the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. 
“While expanding housing supply can reduce average rents, it isn’t enough by itself to help people with the lowest incomes afford housing,” read the post. “Supply-only strategies — even those designed to create affordable housing — won’t create housing options affordable enough for them.”
The paper argues in favor of expanding rental assistance programs, noting that existing rental efforts don’t reach the majority of qualifying households. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“In 2024, the median extremely low-income renter household could afford about $308 a month in rent. The median national rent was close to five times that,” said Jacob. “No amount of construction closes a gap that wide without sustained, targeted support.”
Jacob supported efforts to expand tenant protection, prevent evictions and preserve affordable housing — the last of which was the goal of the short-lived Whole Homes Repair Program. 
Using one-time federal funds designed to offset economic losses from COVID-19, Pennsylvania devoted $125 million for homeowner grants, workforce development and more. The popular program has repeatedly failed to get enough support from legislators for state funding, however, though a national version inspired by Pennsylvania’s model is in development. 



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



“The impact of the program was incredible,” Lena Andrews, the CEO of ACTION-Housing Inc., told lawmakers. Her organization oversaw Allegheny County’s portion of the funds and was able to meet just 3% of the application demand.
Sometimes aging properties can be more expensive to fix than building something new “because they’re in such bad shape,” Andrews shared, noting that Pittsburgh has some of the oldest housing stock in the nation. 
“Often, when we look at doing renovations, the cost per square foot is more than new construction. Which seems crazy, but it is true,” she continued. 
“We’re trying to fundraise for continuing that work and we’re piecing together local sources of funds, but the state investment in that program was just hugely important,” she continued. 
State lawmakers are set to reconvene in Harrisburg at the end of the month.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming billionaire Joe Ricketts alleges he was defrauded out of $34 million in failed federal land swap
description:
New lawsuit contends that TD Ameritrade founder’s former agent and a Star Valley developer conspired to run up costs, rig appraisals and falsely suggest that the U.S. Forest Service was interested in a land trade. 
The post Wyoming billionaire Joe Ricketts alleges he was defrauded out of $34 million in failed federal land swap appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Billionaire and Sublette County financier Joe Ricketts filed a civil lawsuit this week alleging he was defrauded out of tens of millions of dollars in real estate dealings that were pursued during efforts to trade for federal land that would connect his private holdings along the Hoback River.
Filed Monday in the U.S. District Court of Wyoming, the lawsuit claims that two men, former business agent Morgan Fischer and Star Valley developer Dan Schwab, conspired to defraud Ricketts out of $33.6 million by getting him to pay $55.6 million for real estate that was only worth $22 million. 
“The scheme paired two financially desperate men, each burdened by substantial debt and each seeking to financially exploit Ricketts for his own personal gain,” attorneys for Ricketts wrote. 
“Defendant Schwab, who previously served a federal sentence for fraud and against whom a bank was then pursuing a legal judgment for $1.2 million, controlled multiple stagnant properties encumbered by major debt and co-owned with increasingly disgruntled business partners,” the introduction to the lawsuit states. “Defendant Fischer controlled something even more valuable: Ricketts’s trust and confidence.” 
Fennemore law firm attorneys January Allen, Daniel Reilly, John McHugh and Amy Jones are representing Ricketts, the founder of TD Ameritrade who’s worth an estimated $9.8 billion. His family also owns the Chicago Cubs.
Fischer, formerly Ricketts’ agent during his efforts to develop a Bondurant resort, did not respond to an interview request. 
Schwab deferred to his attorney, Frank Chapman, who said he’ll be defending his client “vigorously” against what he called a “slap suit.” (Frank Chapman is not the same person who just ran for Congress, although both are Jackson Hole residents.) 
“This is apparently typical business for Mr. Ricketts, to try to bully people with his money,” Chapman told WyoFile on Wednesday. “Much of what they’ve alleged here is just materially untrue. He soured on the deal, apparently, because he couldn’t get his way with the Forest [Service], and now he’s trying to slap back.” 
Ricketts declined an interview for this story. He “respects the legal process and will not comment on this matter while proceedings are ongoing,” a spokesperson said in a statement.






Click to enlarge: The Renegade subdivision along the Greys River in Lincoln County, where Joe Ricketts owns 19 parcels of the private fly-in community roughly 25 miles from Alpine. (Ryan Dorgan)






Click to enlarge: Seven parcels owned by Joe Ricketts’ Riparian Lands, LLC, sit atop a brush-covered bench at the confluence of the Snake and Greys rivers near Alpine. The 5.69-acre property is surrounded by Bureau of Reclamation-managed land and is inaccesible except by boat or air. (Ryan Dorgan/WyoFile)


The 60-page complaint includes an elaborate narrative that argues Ricketts was misled and overpaid for two primary properties. One is the luxury fly-in community once marketed as “Renegade, Wyoming,” which is surrounded by Bridger-Teton National Forest land up the Greys River. Formerly, the development was known as the Blindbull Meadows subdivision, a development that caused a stir in Star Valley when Schwab, a part owner, sought to develop it in 2013. The second acquisition was for inaccessible riparian land dubbed “The Point” that’s located near the Snake and Greys river confluence outside of Alpine. 
Ricketts purchased the properties for $55.6 million with the intent of exchanging them with the Forest Service for Bridger-Teton land that connects two ranches he owns in Bondurant. Along Upper Hoback River Road, the billionaire possesses the Jackson Fork and the Dead Shot ranches, which he tried and failed to conjoin under a conditional-use permit.  
The lawsuit states that “for decades” Ricketts wanted to restore the Hoback River where it flows through his ranch.
A flattened hillside overlooking Upper Hoback River Road was going to host a luxury resort, but it was canceled mid-construction in 2024 by billionaire Joe Ricketts. This photograph was taken from adjacent Bridger-Teton National Forest land. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
“To achieve that goal, Ricketts would first have to secure adjacent lands belonging to the Forest Service,” the lawsuit states.  
According to the lawsuit, Ricketts tasked his former agent Fischer with developing a strategy for the federal land exchange. Unbeknownst to the billionaire, his representative “was experiencing significant financial pressures.”
“ …Defendant Fischer determined that the land he was tasked with acquiring for the potential federal land swap could serve as the basis to defraud Ricketts,” the complaint states. “In his desperation to relieve his financial strain, he found a willing partner in Dan Schwab.”
The lawsuit includes photographs and meeting notes and it quotes correspondence to make the case that Ricketts was misled. Fischer allegedly told Ricketts that a real estate agent told him the Forest Service “would do back flips” to acquire the The Point and Renegade properties, and were “salivating” about them. 

Joe Ricketts’ agent Morgan Fischer addresses Sublette County commissioners in March 2023. Sublette County planner Dennis Fornstrom is on his left. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)

Ricketts “recently” learned in a meeting with Forest Service officials that the Bridger-Teton was “not interested” in a land exchange for the properties, calling it a “non-starter,” according to the complaint. 
The lawsuit also contends that Ricketts also overpaid as a result of “rigged appraisals, concealed insider pricing, and captive intermediaries.” An independent appraisal of the Point valued it at $171,000, just 6% of the $2.9 million he paid. And Ricketts forked over $52.75 million for the Renegade properties, nearly two and a half times the $21.9 million appraised value. 
The lawsuit adds another twist to Ricketts’ Wyoming saga. The bison rancher is a divisive figure in Sublette County. 
After purchasing Bondurant ranchland cut by the Hoback River in the late 1990s, he earned accolades for a $1.75 million donation that helped seal the deal on a buyout that kept gas wells out of the Noble Basin and Cliff Creek areas. The 85-year-old businessman also donated $1 million that helped open the doors on Sublette County’s first hospital, and he purchased Pinedale’s often-struggling White Pine Ski Area. Just recently, he earned some flattering publicity for his investments in a new nonprofit, Saving Yellowstone, that aims to conserve the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem. 
But his land dealings have also drawn significant scrutiny. A 2020 effort to develop an all-inclusive luxury Bondurant resort was initially rebuffed, then approved despite heavy opposition in the small Bondurant community. After a failed effort to get county commissioners to waive seasonal wildlife stipulations, he canceled the resort in 2024, citing high costs. Around the same time, Ricketts purchased the 33-acre Safari Club International property along Granite Creek north of Bondurant, which he plans to expand and open as a guest ranch, dubbed The Hawken.
Ricketts’ lawsuit includes allegations of violations of interstate land sales, a breach of fiduciary duty, fraudulent inducement, fraudulent misrepresentation, civil conspiracy and a “Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations” claim. 
His attorneys’ request for relief include a payment of $33.6 million, various fees and reimbursements and “all other relief available … as the Court may deem appropriate.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Here’s what Reps. Nunn and Miller-Meeks said about their war powers vote
description: Two Iowa Republicans, U.S. Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn, broke party lines to vote in favor of a resolution to curb President Donald Trump’s military powers in Iran. Miller-Meeks, who represents Iowa’s 1st Congressional District, and Nunn in the 3rd District are expected to face tough reelection campaigns in 2026, with races rated as […]
text:
U.S. Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, incumbent Republicans, voted in favor of curbing President Donald Trump's war powers in Iran in a Sep. 15, 2026 vote as they defend their seats against Democratic challengers in the 2026 general election. (Photos by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch; photo illustration via Canva)Two Iowa Republicans, U.S. Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn, broke party lines to vote in favor of a resolution to curb President Donald Trump’s military powers in Iran.
Miller-Meeks, who represents Iowa’s 1st Congressional District, and Nunn in the 3rd District are expected to face tough reelection campaigns in 2026, with races rated as “toss ups” by political forecasters heading into the midterms. The two GOP incumbents were among seven Republicans who broke party ranks to vote in favor of the Iran War Powers Resolution, a measure sponsored by Rep. Seth Moulton, a Massachusetts Democrat.
The resolution, which passed 220-204 Tuesday, would require congressional approval for Trump to continue his war in Iran.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The most recent resolution was the third time since June that the House has voted to pass a measure to restrict Trump’s ability to continue the war with Iran, which began in late February. In previous votes, Nunn and Miller-Meeks voted against the war powers resolutions — but the two Iowa Republicans, alongside Rep. Nancy Mace of South Carolina, joined four other Republicans and all Democrats in the Tuesday vote in favor of reining in the administration’s military actions.
Both Nunn and Miller-Meeks are military veterans, and both cited their military experience when explaining their decision to vote in favor of the resolution.
Nunn said “having deployed multiple times and flown over 700 combat hours in the Middle East, I will not support another open-ended war.” He argued the resolution would still preserve the president’s authority to defend from imminent attacks while providing more oversight.
“Iran must be held accountable for killing Americans, supporting terrorism, threatening the Strait of Hormuz, and pursuing nuclear weapons. Iowa has already paid a devastating price, including two service members killed by an Iranian drone in Kuwait,” Nunn said in a statement. “Congress owes them, their families, and every American in uniform clear objectives and constitutional oversight. With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization. … We can defend Americans, pressure Iran, and pursue peace while ensuring Congress fulfills its constitutional responsibility.”
Miller-Meeks brought up her 24 years of service in the Army in a statement explaining her vote.
“I said it in March: the mission had to stay focused and limited, because Americans do not want another forever war,” Miller-Meeks said. “I will not vote to keep our soldiers in an open-ended war, with Iowans paying too much at the pump. The Iranian regime and its nuclear ambitions have been defanged. The President needs to present a plan to Congress and the American people for how this ends so we can focus on bringing our soldiers home and lowering prices.”
But Iowa Democrats criticized the two representatives for voting against previous measures introduced in the U.S. House to curb Trump’s power in the Iran conflict. State Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott, the Democratic nominee in the 3rd District, said Nunn voted five times in favor of continuing the war, citing both previous war resolutions votes as well as a Pentagon funding bill vote.
“I’ve always been against this war, while Zach Nunn has cheered this war on from day one and voted five times to keep it going,” Trone Garriott said in a statement. “Because of Zach Nunn’s votes, Iowans have paid more for gas, diesel, fertilizer and groceries. He called the cost worth it and told us to grow a stronger spine. If you want this war to continue, vote for Zach Nunn, if you want this war to end, I’m asking for your vote this election.”
Democrat Christina Bohannan, who is facing Miller-Meeks in the upcoming election, similarly criticized her opponent for previous votes.
“Rep. Miller–Meeks voted 5 times for the Iran War, continuing it for over six months, as gas, diesel, and fertilizer prices have skyrocketed for Iowans,” Bohannan said in a statement. “The fact that it took her until weeks before an election to realize how angry the people she represents are, shows just how out of touch she is in her Washington bubble.”
The two other members of Iowa’s all-GOP delegation in the U.S. House, Reps. Ashley Hinson and Randy Feenstra, voted against the most recent measure, as well as the previous Iran war resolutions.
Hinson, currently representing Iowa’s 2nd District, is running for U.S. Senate in 2026. In a statement, she said she supports ending the war, but called for the U.S. to pursue a “decisive and immediate victory.”
“Like all Americans I want this war to end — I believe President Trump should immediately bring this war to a successful end in a way that keeps Americans safe from the threat of a nuclear armed Iran,” Hinson said. “And I support the full court press economic sanctions to bring the Iranian terrorist regime to its knees. We owe it to our troops, their families, and every American being squeezed by high prices to deliver a decisive and immediate victory in this war.”
State Rep. Josh Turek, the Democrat running for Iowa’s U.S. Senate seat, released a plan Wednesday to provide relief for rising fuel costs stemming from the Iran conflict and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a major petroleum trade route. His proposals which include pausing diesel exports and temporarily suspending the federal gas tax.
In a statement, Turek positioned his plan in contrast to Hinson’s votes on the Iran conflict.
“Ashley Hinson is failing Iowans,” Turek said in a statement. “She should be in Washington doing whatever she can to lower the skyhigh fuel prices she caused by voting seven times to continue this war. Instead, she’s taking yet another extended vacation, leaving Iowans struggling to fill up their gas tanks and harvest their fields while her Big Oil donors continue to rake in record profits.”
The U.S. House was expected to recess after its Wednesday session until after the November elections.

name: Nevada Current
title: NV senators voted against it, but Trump’s flagrant self-enrichment is what killed the crypto bill
description: Nevada Sens. Catherine Cortez Masto and Jacky Rosen joined the rest of their Democratic Senate colleagues Tuesday, along with a handful of Republicans, in killing a cryptocurrency bill the industry really, really wanted. The industry believed that if the Clarity Act, which the House passed last year, was enacted into law, the legislation would bestow […]
text:
"The cryptocurrency industry’s top legislative priority was torpedoed by the wildly pro-crypto president’s very own cryptocurrency corruption." (Official White House Photo by Molly Riley)Nevada Sens. Catherine Cortez Masto and Jacky Rosen joined the rest of their Democratic Senate colleagues Tuesday, along with a handful of Republicans, in killing a cryptocurrency bill the industry really, really wanted.
The industry believed that if the Clarity Act, which the House passed last year, was enacted into law, the legislation would bestow upon cryptocurrency something it is not widely identified with — intrinsic value and purpose; the product would be legitimized, its “use cases” stamped for approval by none other than the United States government. 
That, so the industry’s thinking went, would allow crypto to creep into all sorts of corners of the U.S. financial system — including your moderate-risk plain-vanilla indexed retirement fund. Whether you like it or not.
Or as the folks at the American Federation of State, County & Municipal Employees (AFSCME) put it Tuesday following the Senate’s rejection of the bill: “This is a major victory for retirees and all working people who want to retire with dignity. The so-called CLARITY Act would have allowed Wall Street to gamble with workers’ pensions and 401(k)s by making it easier to invest their retirement savings in cryptocurrency. Working people do not want to see their hard-earned money put into an unregulated, unpredictable crypto casino.”
Though loyally pro-casino as a rule, Cortez Masto voted against the measure in May when it advanced out of the Senate Banking Committee.
But at that same hearing she indicated she really, really wanted to vote for the bill eventually.
“It’s clear we need to pass market structure legislation, and I’ve worked for months with colleagues on both sides of the aisle to negotiate a bill that provides clear rules of the road for a growing industry,” Cortez Masto said at that committee hearing. 
“I’m committed to finding solutions that allow us to take on bad actors – the criminals, not the everyday coders – while giving the millions of U.S. crypto users the certainty they need,” she said. 
For most Senate Democrats, a more pressing issue was not your everyday run-of-the-mill crypto criminal, but the one in the White House. 
Trump monetized the presidency to the tune of $1.4 billion in cryptocurrency revenue in 2025 alone — most of which would have never ended up in his pocket if people and interests the world over weren’t trying to curry favor with The Transaction President. 
“Ethics” language in the bill sent to the floor by Republicans would not have stopped Trump from continuing to engage in and profit from cryptocurrency transactions while still president.
“All President Trump wants is for the Senate to give him time to crime,” Arizona Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego said in a statement following Tuesday’s vote.
“I won’t support any piece of legislation that enables him,” added Gallego, who unlike Cortez Masto, voted to advance the Clarity Act out of the Banking Committee in May.
Alas, Trump made it clear to Senate Republicans that if they supported a bill that cracked down on or – gasp! – halted the rampant crypto corruption of the sort that’s been serially perpetrated by Trump and his friends and family, Trump would banish them to the cornfield or whatever. 
So Senate Republicans refrained from displeasing the Tantrum Thrower in Chief, and wrote a crypto bill that allowed him to keep raking in digital assets from people … interests … monarchies … who want something from him.
And the Clarity Act lost votes from Cortez Masto, Gallego, and a handful of other Senate Democrats the cryptocurrency industry has spent years lobbying to get its bill passed.
In other words, the cryptocurrency industry’s top legislative priority was torpedoed by the wildly pro-crypto president’s very own cryptocurrency corruption.
The cryptocurrency industry is bummed now. It knows there’s no way the next Congress is going to pass legislation designed to prop up and perpetuate respectability and worth of a product that at best just annoys/bores average people, and at worst poses yet another dire threat to society in the form of a government-blessed Ponzi scheme, and all while increasing the demand for data centers.
Cryptocurrency political action committees raised more campaign money than PACs connected to any other industry in the 2024 campaign cycle (this year they’re merely second, behind AI, with which there is some crossover). Apart from some primaries, the crypto campaign cash has been sort of cooling its heels this cycle. Now we’ll see it the industry will try to exact punishment by uniting with a preponderance of billionaires spending millions against Democratic Senate and House candidates in competitive races.
None of Nevada’s three House Democrats — Dina Titus, Steven Horsford, and Susie Lee — are viewed as particularly vulnerable as they seek reelection this year. And, perhaps with a fearful eye on the industry’s warchest, each of them, like Cortez Masto and Rosen, have previously voted to support some portion or other of the Trump-cryptocurrency agenda. And neither Nevada senator is on a ballot this year. 
So Nevada might be spared the crypto industry’s typical attack ads against Democrats, i.e., ads that might mention anything and everything — except cryptocurrency.
Besides, thanks in large part — perhaps almost entirely — to Trump’s refusal to stop enriching himself through crypto deals while he’s president, the crypto industry’s political arm looks a little limp right now anyway. 
Portions of this column were originally published in the Daily Current newsletters, which is free and which you can subscribe to here.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama Public Television board to survey residents on APT, PBS programming
description: Members of the Alabama Educational Television Foundation Authority Wednesday voted to fund a survey conducted by a Republican-leaning polling group amid disputes over its purpose and funding. The survey, coming after an attempt by some authority members to disaffiliate Alabama Public Television from the Public Broadcasting Service, will be conducted by Cygna[...]
text:
Alabama Educational Television Foundation Authority Chairman William Green (left) and authority member Dick Brewbaker, a former Republican state senator, listen during an AETFA meeting on September 16, 2026. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)Members of the Alabama Educational Television Foundation Authority Wednesday voted to fund a survey conducted by a Republican-leaning polling group amid disputes over its purpose and funding.
The survey, coming after an attempt by some authority members to disaffiliate Alabama Public Television from the Public Broadcasting Service, will be conducted by Cygnal, a polling firm that mainly works with Republican candidates, including U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville’s gubernatorial campaign.
After the meeting, Ferris Stephens, a member of the AETFA, said Cygnal was chosen because it’s a “very reputable company” and the questions provided by the company “speak for themselves.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Alabama Daily News reported Tuesday that a draft script of the survey included questions about APT’s political ideology and the potential for APT to end its relationship with PBS.
According to a resolution Stephens read aloud at the beginning of the meeting, the survey will poll 600 people across the state and cost $39,500. Funds for the poll will come from APT’s rainy day fund.
The members passed the resolution on a 5-2 vote. Commissioners Pete Conroy and Tijuanna Adetunj voted against the survey.
Messages seeking comment were left with Cygnal Wednesday afternoon.
Two APT commissioners in October suggested dropping PBS after the Trump administration cut funding to the Center for Public Broadcasting. But the following month, members of the Alabama Educational Television Commission voted to maintain PBS programming amid a public backlash and after Gov. Kay Ivey recommended a survey before proceeding.
In April, the AETC voted to survey Alabamians on how they feel about the station’s programming. The survey was to be conducted by McLaughlin & Associates, a national survey company that has worked with several Republican candidates, including former Attorney General Jeff Sessions and U.S. Rep. Robert Aderholt, R-Haleyville. 
The contract with McLaughlin fell through in late August. Conroy said during the meeting the cancellation was because “negative public opinion and news coverage concerning APT have reached an unprecedented level in Alabama.”
Prior to the vote, Conroy said he sent an email to all of the board members urging them to reconsider doing the poll. Conroy said he was met with negativity from some board members.
“I will share the one thing you (AETFA Chairman William Green) said in that email, and that was you asked me what was I afraid of, insinuating that somehow or another I was afraid of the answers to the questions that were being posed by this survey,” Conroy said. “I’m afraid that we’re losing public trust. I’m afraid that this whole process, Tijuanna, has been rushed. I don’t understand that. That’s never been explained.”
Members of the public also shared their concerns with the survey.
“Why endanger one of Alabama’s most cost-effective agencies with a no-bid political survey some of us fear the objectivity of?” said Jim Vickery, a former president of the University of Montevallo. “That’s why this process matters. It plays right into the perceptions that we already have that you’re doing this for political reasons, and that’s another reason why it’s outrageous.”
Elaine Whitt, an APT donor and freelancer from Birmingham, raised concerns about using the rainy day fund for the survey.
“The money in the rainy day fund is that money that we donated. That’s where they came from. It’s not budgeted. It’s not from the governor. It’s not from the legislature,” Whitt said.
Whitt also criticized the board for voting to spend nearly $40,000 on the survey, saying the foundation has done surveys in the past for less.
“You have the chairman of the commission picking out the survey company instead of your professional staff, which has been surveying Alabama’s for $6,000 instead of $40,000 a year— and he’s sitting over there shaking his head,” she said.
Alabama Public Television last conducted a survey in 2023 through Troy University, Samford University and the University of Alabama which cost less than $10,000.
Conroy said after the meeting he thinks doing the survey is “headed in a direction of polarizing public media.”
“I don’t think we need to politicize our public media,” Conroy said. “We need to stay in the middle as best we can and just report the facts as they are. Allow PBS to do what PBS does best, and that’s educate kids.”

title: New Mexico Tourism agency reports rise in international travel, bucking national trend
description: The number of international travelers visiting New Mexico increased in 2025, deviating from the national trend, the New Mexico Tourism Department said in a news release Wednesday. An estimated 760,000 international travelers visited the state last year, an approximate 1.1% increase over the prior year, according to a report published by travel research firm[...]
text:
The New Mexico Department of Tourism on Sept. 16, 2026, announced a new report showing the state had a rise in international tourism in 2025, bucking national trends. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)The number of international travelers visiting New Mexico increased in 2025, deviating from the national trend, the New Mexico Tourism Department said in a news release Wednesday.
An estimated 760,000 international travelers visited the state last year, an approximate 1.1% increase over the prior year, according to a report published by travel research firm Tourism Economics. During the same time, international travellers visiting the United States dropped 5.5%, nationally, the report said. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“The country as a whole faced a number of challenges to tourism growth in 2025, but New Mexico was able to defy the national trend thanks to informed marketing strategy and dynamic partnerships,” Acting Tourism Secretary Lancing Adams said in a statement on Wednesday.
One of those challenges, Democrats on the U.S. Congress Joint Economic Committee argued in a May report, is the Trump administration’s tariffs on foreign imports. In a particular example reported by Stateline, tourism hubs that rely on visitors from one of Trump’s tariff targets — Canada — saw a decline of Canadian visitors and economic loss, which business owners interviewed attributed to tariffs and aggressive immigration policies. The United States Travel Association also notes that international travel has not yet returned to pre-pandemic levels, while “policy barriers and declining perceptions of the U.S. are creating new headwinds.”
In total, 42 million visitors to New Mexico brought in $8.8 billion in spending, according to the Tourism Economics report. This number increases to roughly $12 billion when revenues from supply chain and incomes spent by New Mexico tourist sector employees are included, the report noted. A total of $835 million was made by state and local taxes while tourist activity directly supported 72,810 jobs, the report said.
“We will continue to position New Mexico as a welcoming and worthy destination for leisure travel, which is what travelers across the globe are seeking in 2026,” Adams concluded in the statement.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Study warns of electricity shortages unless supply keeps pace with data center growth
description: Even if new power plants are built over the next 15 years, as data center projects come online, the regional electricity grid would fall short of demands six times per decade, on average, according to the report.
text:
Constellation Energy's Limerick Generating Station, branded as the Limerick Clean Energy Center, in Montgomery County, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Peter Hall/Capital-Star)Rolling blackouts would happen more than 13 days a year in a “worst case future” scenario, where data center growth is unrestrained and electricity supplies remain tight, according to a report commissioned by Pennsylvania utility regulators. 
Even if new power plants are built over the next 15 years, as data center projects come online, the regional electricity grid would fall short of demands six times per decade, on average, according to the report. 
“That means we’re running the grid at the red line,” Abe Silverman, a researcher at the Ralph O’Connor Sustainable Energy Institute at Johns Hopkins University, said.
The report also examines a third scenario in which no new data centers get built after 2026; it’s the only scenario in which PJM is able to achieve its reliability goal.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE 
It delivers a blunt message, energy experts and policy makers said, that the electricity grid Pennsylvania shares with a dozen other states and Washington, D.C. needs more power quickly.
The Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission (PUC) released the report Monday. It examines whether sufficient electricity resources will be available to ensure the system is reliable as demand increases and older power plants retire.
“Pennsylvania is at an energy crossroads,” PUC Chairman Steve DeFrank said. “Data center development brings significant opportunities, but that growth cannot come at the expense of the families and businesses that already depend on reliable and affordable electric service.”
DeFrank added that the need to protect consumers and electric reliability is bigger than the commission.
“Pennsylvania’s energy system is changing dramatically, and our energy policies need to evolve with it,” he said, calling on policymakers, regulators, utilities, generators, consumer advocates and other stakeholders to work together toward solutions.
Power lines cross the Susquehanna River near the Hummel Station power plant in Snyder County, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Peter Hall/Capital-Star)
State lawmakers in the divided General Assembly called for swift action, but also were critical of political opponents for past decisions. 
“A failure to address this growing reliability crisis will cost lives, put vulnerable Pennsylvanians at risk and cause enormous economic damage. We need to take this warning seriously and address it now,” a spokesperson for House Majority Leader Matt Bradford (D-Montgomery) said.
Spokesperson Elizabeth Rementer added the Democratic-led House passed a range of bills to speed new generation, improve efficiency and resiliency of the grid and protect consumers from additional costs.
“Unfortunately, Senate Republicans have neither considered any of these proposals nor sent meaningful legislation to the House,” she said. “We urge them to take up our legislation now to help address this impending crisis.”
Senate Majority Leader Joe Pittman (R-Indiana) meanwhile placed blame for the reliability crunch on former Democratic Gov. Tom Wolf’s decision to join a regional carbon trading program, which Pittman said resulted in years of uncertainty for the power industry. 
“As we look ahead, we have been clear that all sources of power should be embraced to strengthen Pennsylvania’s power grid, and I am encouraged the PUC Chairman has expressed agreement on this front and wants to ‘put as many watts on the grid as we possibly can,’” he said.
Data center regulation and electric reliability has also become an issue in the governor’s race in November. Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro is seeking reelection, facing Republican state Treasurer Stacy Garrity, who is critical of Shapiro’s early embrace of the industry. 
Shapiro’s campaign, meanwhile, has hammered Garrity in TV ads over her calls for Pennsylvania to be more competitive in attracting data centers. Garrity now says she supports a pause on development and a requirement for data centers to bring their own power. 
The Shapiro administration points to efforts to drive reform in PJM through public pressure, litigation, a settlement capping energy auction prices and an accord with the Trump administration on market reforms. 
Muncy Township, Lycoming County, is the site of a proposed data center. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
“Governor Shapiro is an all-of-the-above energy Governor, and he is laser focused on bringing more power to the grid while keeping costs down for the good people of Pennsylvania, who are among the 67 million consumers served by PJM,” spokesperson Rosie Lapowsky said.
Consulting firm Synapse Energy Economics found, based on grid manager PJM Interconnection’s forecast demand growth under the two scenarios, the system’s reliability would be between six and 100 times worse than PJM’s planning standard of one “loss of load” event per decade by 2030.
“PJM is lagging far behind all other U.S. grid operators in bringing on-line lower cost, quickly deployed clean energy and distributed resources that could be operational before 2030,” said Jon Gordon, senior policy director for the renewable energy industry group Advanced Energy United. 
But PJM remains hamstrung by slow processes and long timelines for permitting and construction of new power plants and facilities, he said. And PJM’s “fast track” initiatives to bring new generation online quickly have focused on natural gas power plants, which face long lead times for crucial components such as turbines and transformers, he said.
“Time continues to tick away — It’s a race against the clock to try and get supply proposed, financed, permitted, and constructed, and the timelines just don’t add up right now,” Gordon said.
The report also raises the possibility that Pennsylvania could lose its status as a net exporter of electricity as more resources are retired here and new generating plants are built in other states.
Montgomery County-based PJM manages the grid spanning from New Jersey to Illinois and from the New York border to North Carolina. It is responsible for balancing supply and demand, ensuring the grid can supply the most affordable electricity available in a given location at any time. It also holds auctions for power plant owners to bid on contracts to keep power plants standing by to run when needed to meet spikes in demand.
In the last several years, it has come under criticism for allowing a backlog of electricity generation and transmission projects to pile up in its queue to connect to the grid. 
At the same time, PJM forecasts its net energy load will increase 5.3% per year over the next 10 years, growing by nearly 66 gigawatts by 2036. That’s attributable partly to increases in electric vehicle use and greater electrification in industry but mainly to data center growth.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
More than 80 hyperscale data centers planned to power artificial intelligence applications are planned in Pennsylvania, with about five under construction and another five with approvals. While data centers have existed for decades, housing computers that serve e-commerce, streaming and other online services, hyperscale data centers are larger, with energy and water demands that rival those of small cities. 
PJM spokesman Jeff Shields told the Capital-Star the issues raised by the report have been on the organization’s radar since 2023 and that it is continuing to work with states to increase electricity supply. 
Shields said PJM agrees with the PUC’s assessment that electricity demand is growing faster than the ability to build new generation and the grid’s reliability could be compromised over the next five years as electricity prices also increase. He added that the organization agrees the solution will take action at the state and federal levels and across the industry.
PJM has already embraced principles of the Trump administration’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge, in which it called on hyperscale data center developers to “build, bring, or buy all of the energy” they need and pay the full cost of additional infrastructure. 
Pennsylvania has been an effective partner, Shields said, in efforts to streamline permitting and remove barriers for new power resources. Gov. Josh Shapiro’s administration also led litigation to establish a price cap and floor for capacity auctions; and Shapiro was among 13 state governors to join in a statement of principles in accord with PJM’s reform proposals to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC).
“PJM believes these combined, focused efforts can preserve reliable electrical service in the near and long term without unfairly burdening regular ratepayers,” Shields said.
FERC is expected to rule this month on PJM’s proposal to hold a “reliability backstop auction,” in which data center operators and other large load users would be matched with investors willing to build new power plants with guaranteed buyers for their energy, Silverman said.
The commission is also expected to decide in October, Silverman added, on PJM’s proposal for a framework to connect new data centers to the grid when they have secured an energy supply in accordance with the Ratepayer Protection Pledge. Under PJM’s proposal, data centers that don;t have their own power supplies would be cut off first if demand exceeds supply.
“If the grid is stressed, data centers are subject to curtailment unless you bring your own capacity,” Silverman said. “We’re not going to cut off grandma if the grid gets stressed, we’re going to cut off you.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: DOJ orders Amore to preserve 2024 election records in ongoing voter data fight
description: Rhode Island Secretary of State Gregg Amore is facing another demand from the Trump administration to provide the state’s voter data, this time to preserve all documents related to the 2024 election. In a Sept. 4 letter, the U.S. Department of Justice directed Amore not to destroy records from the 2024 election because he is […]
text:
Rhode Island Secretary of State Gregg Amore addresses graduates of the state Election Training and Certification Program in a ceremony at the Rhode Island Board of Elections offices on Thursday, June 18, 2026. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)Rhode Island Secretary of State Gregg Amore is facing another demand from the Trump administration to provide the state’s voter data, this time to preserve all documents related to the 2024 election.
In a Sept. 4 letter, the U.S. Department of Justice directed Amore not to destroy records from the 2024 election because he is “under investigation and ongoing litigation” over his compliance with federal election laws. 
“Your failure to preserve relevant data may constitute spoliation of evidence, which may subject you to civil and criminal sanctions,” Eric Neff, acting chief of the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division’s Voting Section, warned. “We trust that you will preserve for the duration of our investigation and any subsequent litigation all relevant documents.”
Amore has not responded to the DOJ’s letter as of Wednesday, Secretary of State office spokesperson Faith Chybowski confirmed to Rhode Island Current. She declined to comment further, citing the pending litigation. 
The DOJ’s request did not specify what Amore is under investigation for. Similar requests have gone out to 28 other states and the District of Columbia, the Associated Press reported Sept. 10.
Amore was sued by the Justice Department last December after he declined to give the Trump administration access to sensitive information in Rhode Island voter rolls. U.S. District Court Judge Mary S. McElroy dismissed the case in April, but the DOJ appealed on June 4. The complaint remains pending before the 1st U.S. Circuit Court in Boston.
Kiersten Pels, a spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Justice, said in an email Wednesday evening that the letter is “a standard litigation-hold notice” directly related to the ongoing voter roll lawsuit against the state. 
“It is not a new investigation,” she said. 
John Marion, executive director of Common Cause Rhode Island, said the DOJ’s preservation demand goes far beyond the subject of last year’s lawsuit.
“This letter suddenly is about the 2024 documents related to the 2024 election, which is not part of that litigation in any way,” Marion said in an interview.
He said he suspects the DOJ sent the letter because the deadline for keeping the 2024 records was approaching, even though there had been no indication that state officials  planned to destroy them.
Federal law requires election officials to keep election records for 22 months after an election. That period was set to expire this month for November 2024 election records.
“The DOJ was smart with their timing,” Marion said.
Marion also characterized the letter as another example of a broader effort by the Trump administration to pressure election officials with repeated demands and threats.
Amore in July received a letter from the DOJ warning he could face criminal charges if the state fails to prevent noncitizens from voting in the upcoming midterm elections.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Constitution Day reminder: Our democracy is not for sale to the highest bidder
description: The best way to mark Constitution Day, this Thursday, is to fight the influence of money and foreign influence in our politics through active active civic participation, writes Mike Pellittiere, who particularly calls on fellow veterans to step up.
text:
The National Archives on Constitution Avenue in Washington, D.C., in s 2023 photo. The National Archives house the U.S. Constitution. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)As a veteran, the oath I took to support and defend the Constitution against all enemies, foreign and domestic, did not come with an expiration date. National security is not solely the responsibility of the military or even law enforcement. It begins with ensuring a government of, by, and for the people cannot be bought by the ultra-wealthy or left vulnerable to foreign influence.
A nation whose elected officials are propped up by foreign countries and shadow entities is not a sovereign nation, but a puppet. It is time to cut the strings.
As we mark Constitution Day this Sept. 17, I ask my fellow veterans to put that oath into practice through active civic participation. Take action to stand up for a country that is not run by the highest bidder.
Our nation’s Founders anticipated this exact vulnerability. George Washington called foreign influence “one of the most baneful foes of republican government,” while Thomas Jefferson warned that preserving liberty required constant vigilance against corruption and outside interference.
Unchecked dark money and foreign-backed interests are pouring into our elections, bending public policy toward priorities that do not serve the American public. Veterans, working families, and everyday citizens are being drowned out by massive financial influence from masked donors we cannot match.




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




Here in Maryland, State Board of Elections filings reflect the same reality we see nationwide: Out-of-state funding and deep-pocketed donors dominate campaign finance, sidelining Marylanders. But this is not just a Maryland problem, and it is not one that we can solve alone. We need a national response.
According to an Ipsos Poll, Americans across the political spectrum agree that campaign spending is not speech that should be unregulated. Voters overwhelmingly agree that citizens and their elected representatives should be the ones setting the limits, without the Supreme Court sweeping away those protections. In 1976, in Buckley v. Valeo, the Supreme Court determined that spending unlimited money on political campaigns is protected as free speech. In 2010, Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission extended that “right” to corporations.
If money in politics is free speech, then most everyday Americans have no voice at all. Billionaires and corporate entities can spend sums in a single cycle that the vast majority of us will never see in a lifetime.
Americans of all political persuasions are uniting behind a clear objective: passing a constitutional amendment that restores the power to regulate election money to Congress and the states. The movement is real, and the moment has arrived.
The For Our Freedom Amendment, championed by American Promise, achieves exactly that by authorizing state and federal oversight of “contributions and spending in campaigns, elections, or ballot measures.” It has been introduced in Congress and needs active support to reach the floor for a vote.
Why is an amendment necessary? There are only two ways to overturn the Supreme Court: Wait for the court to reverse its own precedent, which is not happening here, or use the mechanism we learned about in high school civics, a constitutional amendment. The ultimate check and balance.
This Constitution Day cannot pass without notice. Having pledged our lives to defend this Republic, veterans hold both the standing and the moral obligation to demand a higher standard. We did not serve this country only to watch foreign wealth and billionaire mega-donors choose our leaders for us.
Fellow veterans, we no longer wear the uniform, but our duty is not finished. Our time standing in formations may be over, but our oath to the Constitution never expires. While we served, many of us were unable to be engaged in politics. That time has passed; we are home, and we are still serving, and we cannot do this alone.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa universities propose new programs for academic and workforce demand
description: The Iowa Board of Regents Wednesday provided initial approval for a slate of new programs and university initiatives, focusing on health and data sciences and centers to provide increased collaboration and projects across campus. Iowa State University was the only institution to bring programs to the board for closure — its master of science and […]
text:
The Iowa Board of Regents meets at the University of Northern Iowa on Sept. 16, 2026. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The Iowa Board of Regents Wednesday provided initial approval for a slate of new programs and university initiatives, focusing on health and data sciences and centers to provide increased collaboration and projects across campus.
Iowa State University
Iowa State University was the only institution to bring programs to the board for closure — its master of science and arts degrees in interdisciplinary graduate studies, the Research Institute for Studies in Education and the Midwest Transportation Center.
Housed in ISU’s Institute for Transportation, funding for the Midwest Transportation Center ended in 2018 and currently there are no financial or project ties to the center, according to board documents.
The interdisciplinary programs have very low enrollment, board documents stated, and the research institute will instead become a subunit of the university’s School of Education. ISU Provost Jason Keith said these programs are the first of those identified through the university’s program vitality review to come to the board for closure.
Only three degrees have been conferred in the graduate programs since 2021, Keith said, and any students in the programs now will be able to finish their studies through teach-out plans.
The Ames university also requested approval to create a new machine learning master’s degree and an international program in partnership with a Greek institution. ISU has worked with the American Farm School University of Science and Technology in Thessaloniki, Greece, for more than 30 years, board documents stated, and ISU programs that would be offered in Greece through the new partnership include bachelor’s and master’s degrees in agricultural business and economics, biochemistry, food science and horticulture.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Ann Marie VanDerZanden, ISU’s associate provost for academic programs, said during the meeting that throughout the two institutions’ relationship, they’ve exchanged more than 300 students, 40 faculty members and multiple academic leaders.
“We know that Iowa State already has a strong international presence and appeal, and we think that we’ll be able to continue to grow on that once we have this new entity in place,” VanDerZanden said.
If approved, the program could see as many as 320 enrolled undergraduate students and 40 enrolled graduate students in its fourth year, according to the document. ISU will establish the degree requirements, provide curricular maps and syllabi, oversee assessment standards and send out transcripts and degree conferrals, while the American Farm School will provide instruction and student supports and handle recruitment and admissions.
She said the program would launch in fall 2027 if approved by the board. A portion of tuition revenue will go to ISU, projected to reach $360,000 in the academic year beginning in 2030.
The new master of science in machine learning and data engineering, set to be provided in a hybrid format if approved by the full board Sept. 17, will train students in forming data-driven solutions to engineering problems and the use of different software tools. According to board documents, enrollment by year five is predicted to reach 40 students, alongside 30 “non-major” students.
Keith said the program would be of interest for computer engineering, computer science and data science students.
“There is a need for engineers who can work with, create, and extract value from large sets of data across nearly every industry, but especially including energy distribution, transportation, agricultural systems, and artificial intelligence,” Keith said.
University of Iowa
The University of Iowa is requesting to form a new center focused on cancer drug development. UI Executive Vice President and Provost Kevin Kregel said Wednesday the Institute for Cancer Drug Discovery and Development, or CANDID, would bring together separate research streams and provide needed education and training for workforce needs.
CANDID would create a formal partnership between the UI’s Holden Comprehensive Cancer Center and College of Pharmacy, as well as coordinate with other university centers and units, board documents stated, to create a cancer drug development pipeline that can more readily respond to medical and pharmaceutical needs in Iowa.
The institute would employ an institute director, other “core directors” and administrative staff, and complete a “strategic cluster hire” of faculty hailing from areas like artificial intelligence-enabled drug discovery, drug delivery and clinical pharmacology.
Funding for the center would come from the cancer center and college of pharmacy, donations, funding reallocations from other departments and “institutional strategic resources,” board documents stated. The UI would also work to secure external funding from federal sources, external partnerships and opportunities for commercialization. According to board documents, the first year will require $1.5 million, then $1 million each year after.
Kregel said many of the pieces are already in Iowa City, with strengths in pharmaceutical sciences, clinical trials and biomanufacturing, and the center will “bring these capabilities together around a common purpose.” The center is also needed as Iowa continues to struggle with high cancer rates, he said.
“This could be a distinctive capability for the University of Iowa and for the state, as CANDID has a specific focus on moving cancer discoveries all the way toward early clinical translation, and that would set us apart nationally,” Kregel said.
The UI also brought forward three new academic programs for board approval, including a master of science in engineering management, doctor of medical science and bachelor of science in health administration.
Tanya Uden-Holman, associate provost for undergraduate education and university college dean, said students enrolled in the health administration program will complete coursework in both public health and health economics, as well as some business classes. She said a market assessment showed “sustained employment demands” in a range of healthcare careers, from hospitals to outpatient clinics and insurance.
Seventy students are expected to be enrolled in the program by its fifth year, Uden-Holman said. The UI will need to hire one “50% instructional faculty,” she said, an expense of more than $59,000 annually, and the program should break even in its second year of operation and reach close to $296,000 in net revenue by year five.
“Exploration of the program was initiated in response to feedback from the UI Office of Admissions, which identified strong interest in a health administration major among prospective students,” Uden-Holman said.
Those who have already earned a master’s-level degree in physician assistance are the target group for the post-professional doctor of medical science program, according to board documents. The program will take place completely online and will have full- or part-time options for students working as well as learning, and with board approval would start in January.
Saba Ali, UI associate provost for graduate and professional education and graduate college dean, said the program will “leverage advanced standing from the University of Iowa Master of Physician Assistant Studies clinical phase,” totaling 48 semester hours, with an additional requirement of 24 semester hours of doctoral coursework delivered over the course of eight weeks.
Enrollment in the online program is expected to reach 60 students in its third year, drawing from UI alumni and other groups through recruitment efforts. Three-quarters of the UI students and alumni who responded to a needs assessment for the program said they were interested, Ali said.
The program is expected to break even in its first year and have $284,000 in net revenue by its fifth year. Total expenses come to $148,000, Ali said, paid for by university reallocations and tuition revenue.
“This focus strengthens the university’s capacity to prepare advanced healthcare leaders rather than expanding clinical instruction,” Ali said.
Students who will enroll in the master’s program in engineering management, if it is approved, will also complete their education entirely online, according to board documents. Ali said the program involves both the engineering and business colleges, with each area developing curriculum for students.
Annual expenses are expected to total $130,000, Ali said, with the program set to break even in year two and have $216,000 in net revenue in its fifth year. The UI predicted that the program would see 75 enrolled students in year five.
“The program will provide education and training in system level engineering and technology leadership and management for individuals seeking roles such as project manager, technical manager, product manager, or engineering director,” Ali said.
University of Northern Iowa
The University of Northern Iowa is working to develop a center that will serve as a repository for important political documents and act as a campuswide resource for civic education, public engagement, leadership development and historical learning.
U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley and his wife, Barbara, committed to providing important documents from Grassley’s political career to the University of Northern Iowa in January 2024, which will add to a collection of papers already donated by the lawmaker.
UNI proposed to the board of regents Wednesday the creation of the Chuck and Barbara Grassley Center, which board documents stated would allow the university to provide the public some access to its archived materials. The center would also operate the Grassley Scholars Program for scholarship and leadership development and facilitate events and discussions for campus and the public.
Funding for the center will come from the university and its endowment earnings, as well as donations, grants, foundation support, corporate partnerships and event revenue. Board documents stated the center will start with an executive director, program coordinator and administrative assistant, with further hiring needs a possibility in the future.
The board of regents will discuss approval of the center at its Sept. 17 meeting.
