name: Georgia Recorder
title: Former Georgia regulator who helped set policy for data centers now works for company building them
description: Tricia Pridemore, who until recently served as an elected utility regulator in Georgia, is now working for a corporation that builds data centers primarily in the southeast.  Pridemore, who is a Republican, will serve as the executive vice president of energy, regulatory and policy for DC BLOX, where she will represent the company in policy […]
text:
Tricia Pridemore is resigning from the Public Service Commission ahead of November's election. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderTricia Pridemore, who until recently served as an elected utility regulator in Georgia, is now working for a corporation that builds data centers primarily in the southeast. 
Pridemore, who is a Republican, will serve as the executive vice president of energy, regulatory and policy for DC BLOX, where she will represent the company in policy discussions with lawmakers, regulatory bodies and utility providers. 
Pridemore resigned from the state Public Service Commission on Sept. 4, leaving her post a few months early. 
Pridemore said in an interview Wednesday that she’ll be “leveraging [her] experienced understanding of the energy space, as well as Georgia policy and law, and being able to do that to support one of the largest customers in the state.”
“The world of energy and utilities is very detailed. It is likely one of the most … detailed policy and regulatory spaces that exist in states, and so I am intimately familiar with rate structures, tariffs, the Georgia Territorial Act, the entire section of the OCGA that regulates energy and energy deployment across the state,” Pridemore said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Pridemore was appointed to the commission in 2018 by former Gov. Nathan Deal despite not having previous energy or regulatory experience. She ran for the seat that November and won with just over 50% of the vote. She has not faced an election since then because the 2024 commission elections were postponed.
While the commission does not directly control the growth of data centers in Georgia, it regulates electric utilities and contracts they sign with data centers, as well as the energy infrastructure that power these facilities. During her tenure, the commission passed a rule aimed at helping ensure data centers pay for the energy infrastructure they need, but critics raised concerns that the rule did not do enough to protect residential ratepayers from paying for some of those costs. Lawmakers attempted to pass legislation that would have codified the rule into law, as well as numerous other bills dealing with data center regulations, but all failed to become law.
Instead of running for the seat she held on the commission, she opted to run for Georgia’s 11th Congressional District seat, but she ended up coming in third in the Republican primary earlier this year.
When asked why step down from the position before her term concluded, Pridemore said that there are federal projects that are moving quickly and “DC BLOX needed [her] to be involved in those in the beginning stages of those projects.” She mentioned particularly that the U.S. Department of Energy tapped DC BLOX to help build a data center at the Savannah River Site in South Carolina.
“This is a project that really gained my interest because it is new not only to what the feds are doing, but it’s great to have it right here in the southeast with such close South Carolina and Georgia ties,” she said.
But her appointment has raised questions about whether it could give DC BLOX an unfair advantage in navigating the regulatory environment in Georgia. DC BLOX already has one data center in Rockdale County, and another in Douglas County, and the company has plans for another one near where Sara Kennedy, a Rockdale resident of 20 years, lives. Kennedy, who has been pushing back against the DC BLOX’s second data center in Rockdale since she found out about the plans in May, called it a “system failure” that the law allows a formerly elected official to go to work for an industry they were charged with regulating.
“When you have someone in place like this person who knows the ins and outs, the way the system is supposed to work, the way that it’s actually working, and they’re moving on to the side of corporate profit over tax-paying residents, it’s terrifying,” Kennedy said.
Brionté McCorkle, the executive director of Georgia Conservation Voters, a political advocacy organization focused on the environment, raised concerns regarding Georgia’s revolving-door policy. Georgia law prohibits public officials from registering as a lobbyist or engaging in lobbying for one year after leaving such office.
“That matters because DC BLOX is actively expanding data centers in Georgia, including a Conyers campus with 216 megawatts of power committed by Georgia Power. During Pridemore’s time on the commission, she voted on major expansions of Georgia Power’s system driven substantially by data-center demand,” McCorkle said.
But Pridemore said her duties at DC BLOX during the first year will be outside of Georgia in neighboring states and at the federal level. While she will continue to live in Georgia, she said her “roles and responsibilities for the first year will be centered around other projects.”
“You won’t see me appearing before the commission, or doing commission-type business, but the years of experience that I’ve gained – they’re all in my head, and it’s the same work that I’ve taken and represented Georgia and the great things that we’ve done in energy and utility regulation and management all across the country,” Pridemore said.
Even so, Edward Queen, the director of Emory University’s Center for Ethics, said in an interview that when a public official moves to the private sector, they run the risk of undermining people’s trust in the system. Even if the rules are followed, he said that there can still be the public perception that corporations have unfair access to insider information.
“Public policies or the acceptance of public policy fundamentally rests on people’s trust in the system, and when there are activities that at least on a kind of facial appearance would lead a reasonable person to lose that trust, there’s a fundamental problem,” Queen said.
Queen said perhaps having a longer waiting period before a public official joins the private sector could help address those concerns, but even that may not be enough to tamp down concerns.
“People that are going to kind of willfully suspect what’s going on are going to do it no matter what happens,” Queen said.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana lawmaker looks to strengthen privacy laws surrounding license plate recognition, camera use
description: Within a few hours of a social media post showing a license plate recognition camera installation in the parking lot of a big box store in Kalispell, hundreds of people had commented in the local community group. Many comments expressed concern or outrage at the camera installation, with many suggesting vandalism might be the solution […]
text:
An Flock Safety automated license plate reader camera in a Kalispell parking lot as seen on Sept. 16, 2026. (Micah Drew, Daily Montanan)Within a few hours of a social media post showing a license plate recognition camera installation in the parking lot of a big box store in Kalispell, hundreds of people had commented in the local community group. Many comments expressed concern or outrage at the camera installation, with many suggesting vandalism might be the solution — a method previously employed. 
License plate readers can be found in private parking lots in many of Montana’s main cities from Great Falls to Missoula. In addition, some municipalities like Billings and Butte use them to monitor parking violations. 
Across the country, privacy concerns over the use of automated license plate reader technology keeps climbing. At least one bill has been introduced into Congress addressing federal access to camera data, and last week Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe signed an executive order establishing strict safeguards on the use of the technology. 
But Montana has some of the strongest privacy protections in place in the country surrounding the use of license plate recognition camera use in public places and by law enforcement. 
In 2017, the Legislature passed a law prohibiting state agencies from using license plate readers on public highways, which has helped keep the cameras largely out of Montana during the last decade. 
“We put some massive restrictions in place,” said state Sen. Daniel Zolnikov, a Billings Republican, who sponsored the privacy legislation in 2017. “There’s limitations on how long data can be held, how they are used, when you need a warrant to access data.”
The largest company behind this technology is Flock Safety which has deployed more than 120,000 cameras across the country. 
A map provided by deflock.org showing the locations of automated license plate readers across the country.
The Washington Post reported that surveillance systems like Flock cameras had broad support as recently as last year, but a recent YouGov survey showed 46% Americans opposed the use of the technology compared to 38% that support it. 
Now, with the daily debate ranging from Facebook posts to the White House, Zolnikov said he’s planning to readdress the issue in the upcoming Legislative session if he’s reelected to office. 
“Back then, it wasn’t a big issue,” Zolnikov said. “It didn’t have the weight of society behind it, so people weren’t really paying attention.”
Zolnikov said there is a trio of bills he plans to introduce that will strengthen the state’s privacy laws and close some loopholes in existing law.
One bill would require local jurisdictions to have public hearings if they plan on utilizing license plate readers, or “LPRs,” on public property. 
Recently, the city of Kalispell stripped out a budget item funding LPRs to monitor parking violations in the city’s downtown corridor after public pushback during a city council discussion over the budget. 
Rather than having public comment on a budget line item, Zolnikov said his bill would require hearings about implementation and installation of the technology, making their use more transparent. 
He also wants to tighten up the state’s current law including changing how long data can be held, how it’s collected, and how it is shared when operated by public entities. 
The last area he wants to address is regulating private surveillance, specifically by limiting how and when data can be shared with the government and law enforcement. The private regulation is more difficult to address, but Zolnikov said it’s clear the public wants lawmakers to consider the issue. 
“I think people just don’t want any more of these,” he told the Daily Montanan. “Let’s put that in legislation.”
Looking further to the future, Zolnikov said he hopes to pass a bill to form an interim committee that will inventory all of Montana’s privacy laws and “figure out where we have gaps.”
“It would really paint a picture of how Montana has the best anti-surveillance laws in the country,” he said. “Montanans, whether they’re left, right, or center, have a libertarian streak against surveillance.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: When this small Alaska town was given $1 million, child care was the top priority
description: This story about child care solutions was produced by The Hechinger Report, a nonprofit, nonpartisan news outlet focused on education. SEWARD, Alaska — It was 2018 when Casie Warner first realized there was a major problem in this popular cruise port, nestled on an inlet about a two-hour drive south of Anchorage. At the time, […]
text:
Josie McClain fixes a swing at her home-based child care program. McClain says support from a local nonprofit has helped her expand and improve her facilities. (Jackie Mader/The Hechinger Report)This story about child care solutions was produced by The Hechinger Report, a nonprofit, nonpartisan news outlet focused on education.
SEWARD, Alaska — It was 2018 when Casie Warner first realized there was a major problem in this popular cruise port, nestled on an inlet about a two-hour drive south of Anchorage. At the time, Warner worked as a home visitor, providing advice, support and resources to low-income parents with young children.
Time and time again, Warner would hear the same story from parents: “‘I wasn’t able to make my medical appointments. I didn’t have child care,’” said Warner. “‘I couldn’t pick up an extra shift at work because of child care.’”
Warner set out to find a solution. But Seward, like many rural communities across the country, is considered a child care desert, where options are scarce and there are no quick fixes.
Then, some unexpected help arrived. In 2021, Norwegian Cruise Lines donated $1 million to Seward to help with post-pandemic economic recovery. The city council voted to spend the money on the two issues deemed to be the most relevant for residents of the town of 2,800: housing and child care.
Five years later, licensed child care slots are up by 150 percent.
In rural communities, the availability of affordable child care is a key component of economic success. At a time when child care shortages are pronounced, especially in rural areas, Seward’s approach of prioritizing child care and investing in new programs and providers offers a potential road map for other communities looking to strengthen their child care industry, support the local economy and eventually retain or attract new residents.
“The hope is that if we can address child care, that perhaps it will have a bigger ripple effect,” said Courtney Bringhurst, a Seward city planner. “We’re hoping that it will help more families be willing to relocate to Seward and stay,” she added. “If we can get more families to stay, that will help strengthen our schools, which will give more opportunities and interest for other businesses to come to Seward.”
The town of Seward, Alaska, is a major cruise port that sees its population nearly double in summer months. (Credit: Jackie Mader/The Hechinger Report)

Although Seward’s success so far in expanding child care slots shows what’s possible with more money, experts caution that in most places, public dollars, not private donations alone, will need to fill the gap.
“It’s impossible math otherwise for these programs to continue operating, particularly in rural communities,” said Hailey Gibbs, associate director of early childhood policy at the left-leaning Center for American Progress.
About 1 in 7 people in the U.S. live in a rural community, and though they need and use child care as much as their urban counterparts, they face many more problems getting it. In sparsely populated areas, families are likely to live far from the few providers that exist. The most used child care option for rural families is a provider that operates from their home, but those small businesses are squeezed by low profit margins and high costs.
According to the Center for American Progress, almost all — 96 percent — of Alaska’s children live in a child care desert, defined by the think tank as an area where there are three or more children for every licensed child care slot. The problem is even more acute in rural areas that are also low income: In those parts of the country, there are nine babies for every one licensed child care slot, CAP says.
Alaska’s economy pays a penalty for the lack of child care — according to a 2023 report from the U.S. Chamber of Commerce Foundation, the state lost $165 million because parents couldn’t access child care to go to work or school.
But the economic effects are only part of the story. Rural families are more likely to experience food insecurity and to be on public assistance, and rural children under 5 have one of the nation’s highest poverty rates. Poverty and food insecurity are linked to poor school performance, which high quality child care could alleviate — but that care is not an option for many.
“We know that fewer than half of children from low-income families are ready for school at age 5, and the gaps are just so much larger in rural communities,” said Karen Harrison, lead adviser for workforce development at the global nonprofit Save the Children, which runs several rural child care initiatives in the United States. “Many families in rural communities are left without options.”
In Seward, Ella Wright said she and her husband spent the first five years of their daughter’s life working part time in nursing and mental health jobs respectively, due to the lack of child care. Until her daughter got a spot at a part-time preschool at age 3, “we had no breaks,” Wright said.
In 2023, about half of Alaskan parents who were surveyed said that, like Wright, they could not fully participate in the labor force because of child care access and affordability.
The picturesque town of Seward, framed by snow-capped peaks on the Kenai Peninsula, cannot afford to lose workers due to a lack of child care. Summers in Seward are lively. On days when cruise ships are in port, tourists meander up and down the main street, stocking up on souvenirs and taking pictures in front of Resurrection Bay’s ice-blue water. During these months, seasonal workers flood the town to work at restaurants and shops.

Some residents of Seward, Alaska, want tourism tax from visiting cruise ships to help fund the town’s infrastructure needs, including child care. (Credit: Jackie Mader/The Hechinger Report)
But the town’s year-round employers, including a state maximum-security prison and a medical facility, face ongoing worker shortages. The shortages have been so pronounced that in 2023 the town had to temporarily close its small local jail, diverting people in custody to state-run facilities, until it could hire more employees.
“It’s very difficult to maintain a strong, year-round economy, because we can’t maintain families year-round in Seward,” said Bringhurst, the city planner. “People just can’t maintain a job if they don’t have reliable child care.”
The donation from Norwegian couldn’t have come at a better time for the town. In 2019, a child care program closed unexpectedly just three years after it opened, eliminating 20 child care spots from the community. (Qutekcak Native Tribe, a Seward-based social services agency that ran the program, did not respond to a request for comment.)
Then in 2021, a preschool program funded by federal Title I money closed after the local elementary school no longer enrolled enough children from low-income families to qualify for the funding. That left two licensed programs and 20 slots for more than 80 children who needed care.
Norwegian’s donation was part of $10 million in support to Alaska port communities that were affected by Covid-related tourism drops. Warner had transitioned from her role as a home visitor to running a child-focused nonprofit, Happy Youth Programs and Educational Resources, or HYPER, which was chosen to lead the town’s new child care strategy.
Using half of the $1 million donation, HYPER trained providers so they could meet requirements for state licensing and offered start-up funds to help cover the high costs associated with launching or expanding home-based child care businesses. The organization also developed a retention bonus program to boost salaries for providers, paid for early educators to attend trainings and established a year-long subsidy program to help families pay for child care.
Seven miles north of downtown Seward, off the only road into town, Josie McClain’s home-based child care program is tucked away in a clearing down a long gravel driveway. The town’s investment has made an immense difference for McClain, who has a degree in elementary education and launched her program in late 2019 after years of running the local teen and youth center for the city.

Josie McClain talks to children at her home-based child care program. McClain is one of two programs in Seward, Alaska, that offers 24/7 care. (Credit: Jackie Mader/ The Hechinger Report)
On a recent morning, a dozen children roamed around a playground fenced off in front of McClain’s house. McClain and her assistant watched, sometimes stepping in to comfort crying toddlers, fix broken sandals and navigate arguments over the swings.
A little girl shuffled over to McClain, her rainbow-colored sandals on the wrong feet, and pointed through the playground fence, across the yard, to a sea of yellow dandelions.
“I see a lot of flowers!” exclaimed the little girl.
“Should we make dandelion jelly this week?” McClain asked. The little girl nodded eagerly.
“I’ll look up a recipe,” McClain promised. She kissed the girl on her head and sent her off to play.
The weight of her role in the community isn’t lost on McClain. The children in McClain’s care have a deep attachment to her. Several call her “grandma” and, during the day, wander over to cuddle on her lap or give her a hug.
Many of the parents McClain serves wouldn’t be able to work if it weren’t for her. Several work in critical industries, like the local bank, the school system and the hospital. As McClain looked around the playground, she pointed out children whose parents would have left Seward if she hadn’t had room for them. Hers is one of two 24-hour programs in Seward, offering reliable care for parents who work nights, as well as backup and emergency care when parents have unforeseen needs.
“There isn’t any place for them to go,” McClain said. “There isn’t an alternative.”
Running her program has involved sacrifice. On weeks when she can’t make the more than two-hour drive to Anchorage to load up on more affordable food and supplies, she must pay more at the stores in Seward. Recently, a federal food program for child care lowered their reimbursement rates, meaning she gets less money for the healthy food she serves children five times a day. To save money, she’s teaching herself how to can food for the winter. She hasn’t taken a vacation in years.
HYPER’s support and recent efforts from the state have helped ease the load a bit. In 2023, McClain was able to expand her child care program thanks to money from the organization. She used $10,000 from the nonprofit to help pay for a new screened-in porch to give children more room to play, including outside in cold and rainy weather.
“It made my small house one thousand times better,” McClain said. She also got licensed as a group child care program, allowing her to take in four more children for a total of 12.
For the first time in years, McClain has been able to stop living paycheck to paycheck and save money. She receives an annual bonus of several thousand dollars from HYPER each year. For the year that HYPER subsidized parent tuition, McClain could count on a reliable payment each month instead of having to “hunt down money” from families.
Recently, Alaska invested more in child care, from which McClain has also benefited. In 2025, the state allocated about $6 million more to expand eligibility for child care assistance, and this year, added close to another $6 million for annual grants to help child care programs operate. More is needed though, experts say. Earlier this year, lawmakers approved $6.4 million to help retain early educators, but Gov. Mike Dunleavy later vetoed those funds, along with $3.7 million that would have gone to Head Start, the federal and state-funded preschool program for low-income children.
While the cruise company’s donation funding boosted child care in Seward, and state initiatives have provided additional support, the town’s child care crisis is far from solved. Early childhood jobs, with their low pay and lack of benefits, are hard to fill, Warner said. McClain fears she will have to drop four children from her program if she can’t find someone to replace her assistant, who is leaving soon.
And although two new providers have opened with HYPER’s support in the last year, there is still a shortage of infant and toddler spots.
“I don’t think that the people who want more child care know how many hoops there are to jump through,” said Katie Shepard, who co-runs the newest program in town, Timberline Learning Center. “Anybody else who is not just dying to work with the kids is not going to go through all that.”

Katie Shepard, who co-runs the newest child care program in town, Timberline Learning Center, helps a child with a bug-themed activity. Shepard was able to open this program with the help of nonprofit funding. (Credit:Jackie Mader/ The Hechinger Report)
When Shepard wanted to open a part-time preschool program, the cost seemed insurmountable. HYPER provided a $30,000 grant to cover start-up costs, program supplies and business licenses. “Unless we had that kind of money to put into something like this, I don’t think it would have been possible,” Shepard said.
On one summer morning, 10 children scampered around the community room of a Methodist church downtown.
“Who wants to play the bug game?” asked one boy, who was sitting in the middle of the room with bug-themed bingo boards. Several children crowded around him.
At the back of the room, Shepard sat by a large poster where students could write their names and stick them by a picture of their favorite bug.
“I LOVE butterflies!” exclaimed a little girl as she ran up to Shepard. With her teacher’s encouragement, she carefully glued her name on the paper. “Glue is so sticky,” she said.

Children at Timberline Learning Center play a bug-themed game on a summer morning. Parents say they have cut work hours due to the lack of child care in town. (Credit: Jackie Mader/ The Hechinger Report)
Nearby, Wright’s daughter sat at a table carefully placing pictures of bugs onto a clear piece of sticky paper. Wright has seen how her daughter, now 4, has thrived at preschool.
“Language-wise she’s grown, she’s task-oriented. She’s an only child, so that socialization is key for her,” Wright said. Last year, the family received a subsidy from HYPER to help pay tuition. “That was huge,” she said, adding that the family was able to save more money. She will be able to take on more hours at work once her daughter enters kindergarten full time in the fall.
Looking forward, Warner is trying to find a permanent source of funding for child care to help more families. Ideally, she says, that funding will come from a tourism tax. Recently, a new cruise ship dock opened, which will allow larger ships — and more people — to dock in Seward. If key infrastructure needs like child care aren’t addressed, Warner fears people won’t be able to live there.
“We have to support our year-round economy,” because, unlike the tourists, “We also love to live here when it’s quiet and cold.”
This story was produced with support from the Education Writers Association Reporting Fellowship program.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Wisconsin Supreme Court hears challenges to congressional maps
description: The Wisconsin Supreme Court on Wednesday heard oral arguments in two cases challenging the constitutionality of the state’s congressional maps. One challenge is based on the claim that the maps unfairly benefit Republicans and the other is on the grounds that the maps are intentionally anti-competitive to protect incumbents.  Both cases were previously dismi[...]
text:
The Wisconsin Supreme Court chambers. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)
The Wisconsin Supreme Court on Wednesday heard oral arguments in two cases challenging the constitutionality of the state’s congressional maps. One challenge is based on the claim that the maps unfairly benefit Republicans and the other is on the grounds that the maps are intentionally anti-competitive to protect incumbents. 
Both cases were previously dismissed by panels of three circuit court judges. In both, the Court is not deciding the merits of the arguments but determining if the circuit panels were correct to dismiss the cases. If the Court determines that the dismissals were incorrect, the cases will be sent back to the circuit court level for discovery and trials on the merits of the argument. 
Because of that process, neither case will change Wisconsin’s maps ahead of this year’s midterm elections, but could install new maps ahead of the 2028 elections. 
Wisconsin’s congressional maps were instituted by the Court in 2022 after Gov. Tony Evers and the Republican-controlled Legislature were unable to reach a compromise on new maps. In that case, the Court installed a “least change” principle in which the newly proposed maps had to match as closely as possible to the maps instituted in 2011 — which were widely considered to be the most gerrymandered in the country. 
The maps selected by the Court in 2022 were drawn by Evers, but followed the least change standard. Democrats and fair maps proponents have argued the least change standard poisoned the maps while Republicans have said the argument falls flat because a Democratic governor created them. 
Wisconsin’s congressional maps have repeatedly been challenged since the initial 2011 gerrymander and since the 2022 update. 
In the first part of the day, the Court heard the arguments of the partisan gerrymandering challenge, in which attorney Abha Khanna said that the Wisconsin Constitution’s equal protection clauses give voters in the state protection against maps designed to benefit one party. 
“Was partisan vote dilution the predominant purpose? Was that in fact the effect of the map, and is there any legislative justification outside of sheer partisan dominance that would justify the configuration of these districts?” Khanna said. 
A trio of attorneys argued in favor of the existing congressional maps, saying that the lawsuit was brought so late in the decade it can’t be litigated in the courts anymore, that if the Court wants to rule that partisan gerrymandering isn’t allowed then this case isn’t the right one and that the lawsuit doesn’t give a good enough standard for assessing what counts as an extreme partisan gerrymander. 
During the first arguments, the two conservative justices on the panel expressed skepticism with the claim that the state Constitution protects against partisan gerrymandering. 
“I actually don’t care what happens in other states. I don’t care at all. I care about our Constitution and our laws and what our law says,” Justice Brian Hagedorn said. 
“I know that some states have explicit prohibitions against partisan gerrymandering, however that’s defined. I don’t know what that means,” he added. “But you’re asking for us to just invent a new right that has never been recognized, that even though our founders were well aware of it, as even your own brief recognizes, from the time of our founding, but have never addressed. And you’re appealing to just democratic self-governance, not our actual Constitution, your just sense of what democracy ought to protect.”
The Court’s liberal majority appeared to give some deference to the argument that the lawsuit didn’t properly set up how to assess the extent of a partisan gerrymandering claim, but often got into extended back and forths over the harm that partisan gerrymandering represents. 
Luke Berg, one of the attorneys arguing to protect the existing maps, said in an exchange with Justice Chris Taylor that partisan gerrymandering “doesn’t implicate the right to vote.” 
“How can you say that there is no remedy if it’s demonstrated that partisanship has led to the dilution of the disfavored group’s vote?” Taylor said. “It makes no sense to me, if our whole government is derived from the people, and the power that they give is through the vote, that’s how the people give the power to the government. And so if their right to vote is diluted because of partisanship, I just don’t understand why you’re saying we have no ability as a state court to remedy that.” 
Khanna said Republicans, including some of the attorneys arguing the case in Madison on Wednesday, have made the exact opposite arguments in other states and that they’ve argued map opponents aren’t following the proper process no matter which process is followed. 
“What we’ve seen from just the last couple of years, and frankly, from this argument, where intervenors have said, ‘Oh no, you can’t do this. Oh, you can’t reopen Johnson. Oh wait, you can’t hear this original action. Oh wait, you can’t appoint a three-judge panel. And now that you have appointed a three-judge panel, you can’t hear this appeal,’” she said. “These are just part and parcel of their strategy, which has been to draw this out, and now they say, ‘you know what? The decade’s almost over. There’s really nothing more that this court can do.’”
In the second part of the day, attorney Nicholas Stephanopoulos argued that the congressional maps are illegally anti-competitive. 
“Our position here is a straightforward one,” he said. “Wisconsin’s Constitution does not tolerate officeholders entrenching themselves in power and cutting out the people by suppressing electoral competition.”
But liberal and conservative members of the Court appeared confused by the distinction between a map that is anti-competitive and a map that is gerrymandered to benefit one party. 
“Because it seems to me that what’s underlying that is that the district lines are drawn in such a way to have it be a foregone conclusion that a particular party will win that district, and so I don’t see a whole lot of airspace between this claim and the partisan gerrymandering claim,” Justice Susan Crawford said. 
Stephanopoulos said the difference is that a map drawn to be anti-competitive isn’t concerned with which party wins. 
“It’s relevant what the odds of re-election would be for a candidate, but the anti-competitive theory is uninterested in which party actually,” he said. 
But opponents argued that designing maps to be as competitive as possible comes with trade-offs that might not be ideal. 
“There is a fundamental tension when you maximize for competitiveness or you increase for competitiveness, you are taking away other legitimate values such as representation, such as incumbency protection, such as bipartisan agreement,” Misha Tseytlin, an attorney for Wisconsin’s Republican members of Congress, said. “If you make a map more competitive, then you make it less likely that their incumbents will retain their seats. You also make it more likely that a larger number of the constituents of a particular district are going to be unhappy with the result. There is a legitimate policy dispute as to whether more competitiveness or more representation, incumbency protection is better. Nothing in the Constitution’s text, history, or discourse precedent settles that question as a matter of text.”

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont Conversation: Filmmaker Bess O’Brien on connection, resilience and joy after tragedy
description:
The inspiration for O’Brien’s new film was seeing what happened after the floods in 2023 and 2024 that ravaged some Vermont communities.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Conversation: Filmmaker Bess O’Brien on connection, resilience and joy after tragedy.
text:
The Vermont Conversation with David Goodman is a VTDigger podcast that features in-depth interviews on local and national issues. Listen and subscribe for free on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube or wherever you get podcasts.
Filmmaker Bess O’Brien. Courtesy photo
Bess O’Brien is best known for making award-winning documentary films that take deep dives into difficult issues like addiction, hunger and homelessness. 
With her latest film, she is taking a different approach: She is inviting audiences on a feel-good journey about resilience and joy.
“Every Day: Big and Small” is about the unsung ways that Vermonters show up for each other in good times and bad to create change. O’Brien introduces us to a writers group for people in recovery from substance use, a boisterous drag show at the Elks club in Rutland, a group of men talking about domestic violence, a horse farm for people with PTSD, a couple recovering from a recent flood, a military museum run by a 13-year-old boy, and girls who want to go into farming. These are among a series of cinematic vignettes that tell a larger story of how people cross divides and lift each other up.
“A lot of times we are told things about how people are acting or feeling that actually aren’t true,” O’Brien told me. People “are actually more generous and more open-hearted than we often assume.”
The inspiration for O’Brien’s new film was seeing what happened after the floods in 2023 and 2024 that ravaged some Vermont communities. “We all recognize that our neighbors came together to help each other. However, this happens every day, and we don’t even know it, and we don’t acknowledge it all the time,” she said. 
O’Brien’s previous documentary films have raised awareness about vulnerable people and social justice. Her 2013 documentary, “The Hungry Heart,” about the prescription drug crisis in Vermont, sparked a statewide conversation about opioids. 
O’Brien’s 2016 documentary, “All of Me,” focused on the lives of people with eating disorders, and in 2018 she directed “Coming Home,” about five people returning to their Vermont communities from prison. Her 2024 film, “Just Getting By,” was about Vermonters struggling with food and housing insecurity.
As she does with most of her films, O’Brien is embarking on a statewide tour with “Every Day: Big and Small.” Her goal is to spark a statewide conversation about the issues in the film. 
Chronicling recovery and resilience has been a throughline in O’Brien’s work. In 2014 she co-founded Writers for Recovery to help people who are struggling with addiction. She is now expanding what recovery means. 
Recovery is “what we do 55 times a day, just as human beings, because we’re depressed, or we’re bummed, or we’re angry at our kid, or we’re frustrated, or we can’t get our Google to work,” she said. 
“It’s the old Vermont thing: You get stuck in the mud and somebody comes and pulls you out. That is recovery. That is somebody coming and helping you. So this film is really about all those small little things that human beings do every day that get us through life. Because if we didn’t have that, we’d be fricking in big trouble.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Former RI Commerce Secretary Liz Tanner takes interim VP role at CCRI
description: Former Rhode Island Commerce Secretary Liz Tanner has joined the Community College of Rhode Island (CCRI)’s leadership team after working a part-time summer gig at the community college. Tanner will serve as the school’s interim vice president for workforce and institutional advancement. She told Rhode Island Current on Wednesday that her new role gives her[...]
text:
Former Rhode Island Commerce Secretary Liz Tanner, who has joined the Community College of Rhode Island as interim vice president for workforce and institutional advancement. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)Former Rhode Island Commerce Secretary Liz Tanner has joined the Community College of Rhode Island (CCRI)’s leadership team after working a part-time summer gig at the community college. 
Tanner will serve as the school’s interim vice president for workforce and institutional advancement. She told Rhode Island Current on Wednesday that her new role gives her a chance to address the concern she heard most frequently from businesses during her three years leading the state’s commerce department.
“The number one concern that I heard from RI businesses when I was Secretary of Commerce was for trained and skilled employees,” Tanner said Wednesday via email. “Leading Workforce Partnerships for CCRI will give me the opportunity to fulfill that need.”
The appointment was announced internally in an email shared with the faculty and staff Tuesday by CCRI President Rosemary Costigan. 
Tanner takes over for Barbara Nauman, who is returning to her previous role as associate vice president of academic affairs, a role she had stepped away from to lead the school’s workforce and institutional advancement wing. 
Nauman is filling the role vacated by Dr. Marianne Raimondo — former-Gov. Gina Raimondo’s sister who came on to lead CCRI’s academic affairs in February — to go work in the state’s Office of the Postsecondary Commissioner, according to Costigan’s email. 
Tanner’s salary, official start date, and the length of her appointment were not immediately available Wednesday. The specifics of Tanner’s new job, meanwhile, involve connecting CCRI with employers, developing short-term credential programs and overseeing and formulating new and established ways to help students enter the workforce.
Whatever her time in the role, Tanner said, “My priority is building a great team that can work at the speed of business and have as many Rhode Islanders get skilled training that will allow them to have good jobs that will support their families.”
The new role marks a return to a state paycheck for Tanner, who served as commerce secretary under Gov. Dan McKee from 2022 to 2025 before departing to lead Rhode Island’s preparations for the 2026 FIFA World Cup with the nonprofit Ocean State 2026. Costigan’s announcement noted Tanner’s plentiful experience with “executive leadership across state government, economic development, and business,” including the oversight of and responsibility for six state and quasi-state agencies plus a $40 million budget in her time as commerce secretary. 

Previously, Tanner served as executive vice president of client services from 2015 to 2017 at the Rhode Island Commerce Corporation, followed by five years leading the Department of Business Regulation before McKee enlisted her to head Commerce in 2022. 
Tanner’s bachelor’s degree in political science is from the University of Rhode Island, and her law degree is from Western New England University School of Law. She also has an executive education certificate in strategic management of regulatory and enforcement agencies from Harvard University’s Kennedy School of Government. 
Applications for the permanent position opened for submissions Tuesday and will close on Sept. 29. According to the job posting, the permanent position has an annual salary range of between $200,000 and $219,000.
When asked if she would be interested in being considered for the permanent position, Tanner did not directly say whether she would like to apply, instead offering, “I would be honored to be able to work with President Costigan on the Workforce Innovation Center — and see that dream become a reality.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Benson, James pitch tariff remedies, business boosts & data center limits at Detroit Economic Club
description: DETROIT — The respective Republican and Democratic nominees for Michigan governor on Wednesday each proposed new solutions to the economic tariffs levied by the administration of President Donald Trump, especially those being used against Canada.  Addressing the Detroit Economic Club on Wednesday afternoon in separate speaking events were Republican U.S. Rep[...]
text:
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson speaks to the Detroit Economic Club about her plans on taxes, economic development and affordability. Sept. 16, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.)DETROIT — The respective Republican and Democratic nominees for Michigan governor on Wednesday each proposed new solutions to the economic tariffs levied by the administration of President Donald Trump, especially those being used against Canada. 

Addressing the Detroit Economic Club on Wednesday afternoon in separate speaking events were Republican U.S. Rep. John James and Democrat Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson. Benson appeared in person while James appeared via video conferencing from Washington, D.C.
Benson said that she plans to negotiate subnational agreements with Canada directly to mitigate the impacts of federal policy — and said that if Trump tried to undercut those efforts, she feels strongly that the law would be on Michigan’s side. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“I’ll partner with other governors from neighboring states like Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Minnesota, who perhaps have similar needs, but of course Michigan’s economic interests come first and are pivotal in this moment,” Benson said. “I’ve already begun having conversations with folks in Canada about how we can carve out a subnational agreement to protect our jobs, protect our costs, and if this escalates further, protect our electricity, which we also need to recognize as a unique partnership with Canada.”
James, meanwhile, told the crowd that he has a bill in the U.S. Congress that “will be dropping in the next few days” to use tariff revenue to reduce the costs that have come from Trump’s go-to economic tool.
“I have told the administration directly that in these negotiations, Michigan will not be a pawn. Michigan will not be collateral damage in these negotiations. But we also have to recognize the truth that you need two parties to negotiate,” he said. “I’m doing my part in Congress to make sure that we have a clear path so that we can insulate our workers and our businesses from any strains that may occur from attempting to bring our jobs back, and have a mutually beneficial and reciprocal trade relationship with our friend and partner in Canada.”
Beyond tariffs, Trump’s policies influenced the forum. 
Benson, who said that “the decisions we will make in this election will define the future of our economy and our democracy,” repeatedly emphasized her ability and desire to stand up to the federal government. 
“In contrast to my opponent, who has supported every failed economic policy that the current president has promoted and has denied election results, as I’ve defended them, we need a leader in this moment who will speak the truth, bring people together, and get stuff done,” she said. “I know everything we do in these next eight years will determine whether or not my son and our loved ones all across the state choose Michigan as their home for my kid and for all of our kids, for our future of this state. I want Michigan to be the best place to be a kid, to raise a kid, and call home.”
Republican gubernatorial nominee U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township) speaks to the Detroit Economic Club about his plans on taxes, economic development and affordability. James spoke virtually due to scheduled votes in the U.S. House. Sept. 16, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.)
James, however, seemed skeptical of Benson tying problems in Michigan to Trump, saying, “I’ll point out to you that I’m the only one you talked to today that hasn’t blamed the other party, because I think that in leadership we need to use our thumbs more than we use our fingers.”
“There’s plenty of blame to go around, and I’m more focused on fixing a problem than fixing the blame. Michigan’s on fire. We are 42nd out of 50 in infrastructure. We’re 43rd out of 50 in the economy,” James said. “We’re 45th out of 50 in education. We’re 46th overall out of 50, and we all have the same president.”
While the visions on how to achieve economic improvement in Michigan — including lowering healthcare costs, improving educational outcomes and boosting the automotive industry — differed between Benson and James, their platforms on some issues seemed nearly identical.
On data centers, for example, both James and Benson emphasized the importance of local control, as well as establishing guardrails to address concerns about privacy and environmental harms of data centers and artificial intelligence.
Both candidates emphasized the need to support business growth in Michigan to match neighboring states like Ohio and Indiana,  which Benson said “are eating our lunch here.” Benson said that the Michigan Economic Development Corporation is at the “top of my list” of agencies to overhaul at the state level.
James similarly remarked, “You talk about competing with Mexico and China. We can barely compete with the Southeast and with our neighboring states,” in regard to economic development and the MEDC’s role in the state. 
As for how to achieve those goals, James leaned into slimming state government in order to free up money for his initiatives, like lowering income taxes. 
“I talk a lot about cutting taxes, but we can’t just cut our way to success,” James said. “We need to make sure that we get our spending under control and that we grow, attracting talent, young talent here from all over the state and from all over the country to be able to grow and keep the talent that we have. We need a change in culture that’s customer service obsessed, more focused on support than enforcement, and actually treats business leaders like yourselves like revenue generators rather than a piggy bank for Lansing’s operations.”
James also emphasized his own past business experience as an important background to be the “CEO of a state” as governor.
Benson said that she wants to “do a wholesale review of how we’re bringing revenue into the state,” also relying on her own background as Secretary of State.
But she also proposed new spending, for example, on improving salaries for public educators and establishing tax credits for childcare and long-term familial care. Benson discussed both during her speech in Detroit and in a roundtable discussion at a Ferndale grocery store, focusing on the need to fix stagnated wages.
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson speaks with Sal Fournia, owner of Ferndale Foods, about affordability and small business ownership in Michigan. Sept. 16, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.)
Asked how state policy can work to actually increase wages, Benson noted that “it’s about boosting our workforce so that we have a talented workforce, investing in apprenticeship programs and other skills training so that we have the talent here, recruiting more employers to come to Michigan so that we are with high-paying jobs.”
James did not speak at the event in-person as initially planned, citing a change in the U.S. House of Representatives voting schedule that required him to be in Washington. 
“My father always taught us that in order to get the job you want, you have to do the job you have well,” James said via Zoom in his speech. “Right now, my job is in Congress, and also to answer your question, I’m not going to wait until I become governor to begin to represent, advocate, and putting my state first.”
Benson, however, criticized James’ absence at an event held later in the afternoon at a grocery store in Ferndale. Benson told reporters that“it’s not lost on me the day when I choose to be here in Michigan, talking not just to the Detroit Economic Club but to residents here, that my opponent chooses Trump, chooses to go to D.C. chooses to vote for a war that is driving up these costs, and that is the choice in this race.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Wildfire near Camden industrial park 65% contained, Arkansas authorities say
description: A wildfire that has burned thousands of acres near a Camden industrial park where several defense contractors are located is 65% contained, Arkansas and local authorities said Wednesday. The Calhoun County Sheriff’s Office said that crews are continuing to battle hot spots in the fire that broke out Monday near the Highland Industrial Park. No […]
text:
An Arkansas National Guard Black Hawk helicopter responds to a wildfire in Camden, Arkansas on Tuesday, September 15, 2026. (Courtesy Arkansas National Guard)A wildfire that has burned thousands of acres near a Camden industrial park where several defense contractors are located is 65% contained, Arkansas and local authorities said Wednesday.
The Calhoun County Sheriff’s Office said that crews are continuing to battle hot spots in the fire that broke out Monday near the Highland Industrial Park.
No injuries or damages have been reported from the fire, which prompted evacuations from nearby residents and workers. Residents were allowed to return to their homes Tuesday.
Highland Industrial Park is home to several defense contractors, including Lockheed Martin and Raytheon. 
Two Arkansas National Guard Black Hawk helicopters have dropped more than 48,000 gallons of water on the wildfire, the guard said in a news release Wednesday. 
Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders mobilized the helicopters and two bulldozers Tuesday to assist in response to the fire.
The Federal Emergency Management Agency approved a grant to assist in the firefighting efforts, the state Division of Emergency Management said in a Facebook post.
The Calhoun County fire has burned more than 2,800 acres, according to the state’s online wildfire dashboard. The cause of the fire is unknown. 
All of Arkansas’ 75 counties are at high risk of wildfires, according to a state Department of Agriculture map. There are burn bans in 67 counties.

name: VTDigger
title: Training doctors is worth every dollar
description:
Cutting medical education to save money misunderstands what builds a healthcare workforce in the first place.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Training doctors is worth every dollar.
text:
Dear Editor,
In defense of my profession, I wish to clarify what lies at the core of medicine: using a distinct skill set to care for people. Have you ever seen a skilled obstetrician deliver twins? Or an orthopedic or emergency medicine provider set a broken humerus? A primary care doctor identifying and treating depression, truly a life-saving clinical skill?
The practice of medicine begins with hands-on education and training, just like nursing, dental and social work professions. This is similar to learning a trade such as plumbing, teaching or carpentry. We must not account for the critical investment in our future workforce by accounting for every dollar spent relative to empowering the next generation of professionals.  
A recent VTDigger article and two commentaries discuss retention of physicians trained in Vermont and the cost to train physicians being borne largely by commercial payers. In 2026, commercial payers are shouldering a growing share of that cost, as the federal government sends fewer Medicaid dollars to Vermont and cuts funding for public health and substance use programs.

READ MORE

Vermont’s retention of residency graduates is slightly lower than the national average and could worsen. This relates to the challenging healthcare climate in our state. Perhaps it also relates to sluggish political will. Vermont has leaned on federal grants and matching funds to get the Maple Mountain Family Medicine Residency program off the ground, rather than committing state dollars of its own.
Vermont’s healthcare ecosystem is under constant scrutiny due to high costs and intense regulation, but the answer is not to cut education and training. The Hippocratic Oath involves four core principles, and one is “duty to teach.” Let’s sustain this joyful, selfless and critical exercise that doctors like me practice every day. 
Elizabeth Hunt
Charlotte, Vt.

title: 6th District race gets heated as Edmonds, Miguez lob residency accusation at each other
description: Two Republican state senators competing for a Baton Rouge-based congressional seat lobbed hefty allegations at one another Wednesday involving their residency and one candidate’s unpaid taxes.  Sen. text:
State Sens. Blake Miguez, left, and Rick Edmonds are clashing over their respective residences in their campaign for the 6th Congressional District seat. (Louisiana Illuminator photos)Two Republican state senators competing for a Baton Rouge-based congressional seat lobbed hefty allegations at one another Wednesday involving their residency and one candidate’s unpaid taxes. 
Sen. Rick Edmonds of Baton Rouge said a New Iberia resident has filed a complaint with Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill that claims Sen. Blake Miguez does not live in his state Senate district that covers portions of Iberia, Lafayette and St. Martin parishes. 
Members of the U.S. House of Representatives are not required to live in their district, but there is a residency requirement for Louisiana state lawmakers. If they move out of their district, their seat becomes vacated according to provisions of Article III of the state constitution. 
That could happen to Miguez if the complaint is found to be accurate, Edmonds said at a news conference where he publicized the complaint. 
“Blake has been caught in a lie regardless of the outcome,” Edmonds said. “Blake Miguez has repeatedly claimed that he lived in Baton Rouge since 1999. … Either his statements that he’s made to the Congressional District 6 voters in this district are misleading, or there are serious questions about where he has satisfied the requirements for representing State Senate District 22.” 
The complaint was filed by David Levy, according to a copy of the document the Illuminator received through a public records request. Levy is a former Democratic candidate for the Louisiana House of Representatives. 
“Senator Blake Miguez cannot have it both ways,” Levy wrote. “The Louisiana Constitution does not allow it. His domicile is either in New Iberia or in Baton Rouge.” 
“This isn’t about party,” Levy said in a statement to the Illuminator. “It’s about whether the people of District 22 have a senator who actually lives among them. Every district in this state is entitled to that.” 
Though Miguez maintains he lives in New Iberia, he has confirmed he has kept a house in Baton Rouge. Miguez lived in Baton Rouge when he attended LSU and earned his law degree at Southern University. 
According to Miguez’s team, it’s Edmonds’ residency that should be questioned. 
Miguez has previously alleged Edmonds lives in Mississippi, where he is the senior pastor of First Baptist Church of McComb. Edmonds has asserted that he lives in Baton Rouge and commutes to the Mississippi church on Sundays to preach. 
“We haven’t seen the complaint, but if Mississippi Pastor Rick Edmonds wants to pick us up a copy the next time he heads home to Mississippi, we’d be happy to take a look,” Miguez spokesman Chris Pack said in a statement. “While he’s home, maybe he can check to see if he has any more Mississippi tax liens to pay off from unpaid income taxes.” 
Edmonds does have an unpaid tax lien in the state of Mississippi, according to the Mississippi Department of Revenue’s website, though the lien has a Baton Rouge address on it. The lien, totaling $5,243.25, is related to income from his job at the McComb church. 
Edmonds spokeswoman Delia Taylor said Edmonds will address the lien, which is dated June 22. A lien notice was sent to Edmonds’ previous address in Baton Rouge, which is why he was unaware of it, Taylor said. 
Taylor said that while Edmonds has lived in Baton Rouge for many years, his wife Cindy is a real estate agent and home “flipper” who briefly owned a house in McComb that she renovated and sold. Taylor said the couple never lived in the house.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT announces AI regulations for state employee health plans
description: Amid a national debate about the dangers of AI, CT unveiled regulations governing the use of the technology by health insurance companies.
text:
Amid a surge in the national debate about the dangers of artificial intelligence, Comptroller Sean Scanlon on Wednesday announced regulations governing the use of AI technology by health insurance companies that administer benefits for the state employee health plan — rules he wants lawmakers to extend more broadly in 2027.
The new rules will apply to the more than 270,000 enrollees in the state employee health plan and the Connecticut Partnership Plan for municipal and other public-sector employees outside state government.
The five policies put in place include a ban on the exclusive use of AI for activities like down-coding claims or reducing payments, as well as a guarantee that plan member data will not be used to train other AI models. The regulations will go into effect Jan. 1, 2027. 
“Our world is changing rapidly and government needs to change with it at the same speed in order to protect people,” Scanlon said at a press conference on Wednesday morning. “That’s what this policy is all about.”
Negotiations between the comptroller’s office and insurance companies have been underway for about a month — even before a former Anthropic researcher set off a national conversation about the potentially disastrous outcomes if AI development forges ahead at breakneck speed.
Connecticut’s state employee health plan works with multiple providers, Scanlon said, and they’ve all agreed to the policies. Anthem administers medical benefits for active employees, Cigna administers dental coverage and Aetna administers the Medicare Advantage plan for retirees. Caremark is the state plan’s pharmacy benefits manager.
Scanlon said he believes the same protections should extend beyond enrollees in the state plans. In January, he will recommend lawmakers require all state-regulated plans to adhere to the same policies.
“There is a national reckoning happening on this right now, and I think there will be an expectation of the legislators that are there next year that they do something about this from their constituents,” Scanlon said. “I’m going to try to work with them to make sure that we do.”
States are limited when it comes to which insurance plans they can regulate. Only what are known as “fully insured” plans fall under their jurisdiction. “Self-funded” plans, which are the type most commonly used by large employers, are regulated by the federal government.
In Connecticut, about 220,000 people — or 6% of residents — get health coverage through state-regulated plans. 
As more insurers use AI to determine if medical care should be covered, patient advocacy and physician groups have warned of the potential harms to access. Three companies — Humana, UnitedHealth and Cigna — are all facing lawsuits over AI and algorithm-based denials of care. 
Despite the legal actions, insurers aren’t slowing down. In recent months, UnitedHealth announced a $1.5 billion investment in AI across more than 1,000 potential use cases, including claims processing and prior authorization.
Tom Swan, executive director of the Connecticut Citizen Action Group, called the state employee health plan regulations “a really great step,” adding that lawmakers and the governor need to pass legislation in 2027 to bring similar safeguards to the state more broadly.
“Without meaningful oversight, this is really dangerous,” Swan said. “Patients and providers need protections.”

name: WyoFile
title: Two neighboring Wyoming cities diverge over controversial automated license plate readers
description:
Douglas debates allowing automated surveillance system plus agreement to share data with state law enforcement. Nearby Glenrock pushes pause on Flock Contract renewal while Flock cameras are vandalized in Jackson.
The post Two neighboring Wyoming cities diverge over controversial automated license plate readers  appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
In Converse County, the city of Douglas is looking into installing controversial license plate readers as a crime-fighting tool while just 30 miles west along I-25, Glenrock is pushing pause on renewing a contract for similar surveillance technology after the cameras sparked an uproar.
The systems that read and track license plates on moving vehicles have raised civil liberty complaints, led to lawsuits over misuse by authorities and are now under fire in numerous states nationwide, including in Wyoming. The Jackson Hole News&Guide reported that on Monday five out of 28 of the controversial Flock Safety-brand license plate reader cameras placed around the northwestern Wyoming tourist destination had their lenses covered with silver spray paint or duct tape. Jackson police told the News&Guide that the extent of the damage remained unclear.
Two Flock Safety cameras that were spray painted silver sit along Snow King Avenue in Jackson. Five out of 28 Flock cameras around town had been tampered with as of Monday, the Jackson Hole News&Guide reported Wednesday. (Rebecca Huntington/WyoFile) 
In Douglas, the Motorola cameras being installed in police department patrol vehicles have the technology to be used as automatic license plate readers — cameras that can search a license plate without an officer pressing the button. The cameras have the hardware to read license plates but need to be manually activated to function. Motorola has offered a free, one-year trial of the system, with the option to renew after the year for $13,470. The contract allows the agreement to be terminated quickly, Douglas City Attorney Mike Armstrong explained Monday to the Douglas City Council.
During Monday’s meeting, the council also discussed a proposed memorandum of understanding to share surveillance data with the Wyoming Division of Criminal Investigation. No decisions were made, but the issue will likely come up in a future council meeting.
The draft MOU between DCI and the Douglas Police Department would allow immediate data sharing between credentialed personnel with access to their respective accounts. It includes a “without cause” termination clause. 
“The purpose of this MOU is to outline conditions under which DCI and DPD will share and use License Plate Recognition (LPR) data (scanned plates) and/or ‘hotlist’ information,” the draft MOU states. “The Motorola Solutions system provides for simple point-and-click data sharing between credentialed DCI and DPD managers with data sharing privileges enabled by their respective agencies.”
While the document states that DCI would share its Motorola data with Douglas, DCI Commander Ryan Cox told the Douglas Budget on Tuesday that the state agency  does not have a license plate reader system in place.
“DCI and DPD each authorize access to its LPR detection data and/or hotlist information residing in its Motorola Solutions account to each other as permitted by applicable state law,” the MOU reads.
The Douglas Police Department is still in the process of developing usage policies for the proposed system, a first for the city. The proposed system would be operational once the Motorola cameras are fully installed in Douglas police cars. Without the license plate reading system activated, the devices function as a more traditional in-car camera, and without city council approval, the department would not activate the automated function. Additionally, the department does not plan to participate in the national data-sharing network, similar to Flock’s. 
“Our agency’s priority remains on serving our community with safety as our top priority. If for any reason the Douglas City Council decides not to move forward with this technology, our efforts on this matter will cease entirely,” the Douglas Police Department said in a statement. The Douglas City Council appeared to favor the approach, although Councilmember Perry Hershberger had reservations.
“And the poor guy in Colorado that has been pulled over every other day for the last six months because a Flock camera, or a license plate reader, has said that license plate (has) got a warrant on it, and they keep pulling him over, and he doesn’t have a warrant,” Hershberger said during the discussion. Hershberger was referring to Kyle Dausman, a resident of Cherry Hills Village, Colorado, who despite not having a warrant has been pulled over repeatedly by his local police after his plate was incorrectly entered into Flock’s hotlist. The story, first reported by 9NEWS in Denver, has made national headlines.
Mayor Kim Pexton and Councilmember Ron McNare were also aware of the concerns.
Councilmember Joel Weeks, a former Converse County undersheriff, touted the potential public safety advantages of such a  system. He cited the case of Stephanie Crane, a 9-year-old who disappeared in 1993 in Idaho while he was stationed there. A late-model yellow pickup was reported in the area, and Weeks believes the system could have helped find the missing girl.
“But (when) we have something like this, this little girl, a situation like that, you can go back and you can say, ‘Okay, look, nobody can get out of town without us knowing… So let’s look.’ and, you know, well, we saw there was a yellow pickup in the area. Well, there’s a yellow pickup and it went out East Antelope Road,” Weeks hypothesized. “At least we have an idea. I think it’s a great idea. 100% support.”
Interim Douglas Police Chief Avery Cowardin said the data collected by the cameras would be subject to the same data retention schedule the city already has in place: a seven-day period before deletion. Cowardin also said their policy has an “officer verification” element to prevent any mistakes potentially made by the system.
“I just didn’t want to feel rushed.”  Glenrock Attorney Amy Iberlin
Glenrock hits pause 
Across the county, Glenrock has put a contract renewal with Flock, a different type of automated license plate reader system, on hold until Oct. 16. That gives town officials time to work out contract terms to their liking. If the terms still aren’t in place by Oct. 16, the town will request another extension, according to Glenrock Police Chief Colter Felton. He said he would make the new contract available to the public after the proposed changes are in place. The cameras are still operating while contract changes are being made.
“I just didn’t want to feel rushed” to renew the contract, Town Attorney Amy Iberlin said in an earlier interview. “(But) if I have questions about the clear language, supposedly clear language of the contract, I want those questions answered from the legal side. “And given the council’s feeling on these issues and given the questions that have been related to this — and after the special meeting where folks are identifying real issues that I think are really important and potentially issues that we need to address in this contract — I just don’t want to feel like we need to make this immediate decision, or else we’re under this automatic renewal for another few years.” 
Felton is considering additional oversight, including potentially having a member of the Glenrock and Rolling Hills town councils perform regular audits with him.
The cameras, which first garnered public attention in early July, have caused an uproar among concerned citizens across Converse County. Residents were outspoken at an Aug. 25 public meeting where they brought up Fourth Amendment due process concerns, privacy and the way the cameras were originally approved. The cameras received a green light during a budget session, which some residents saw as a sleight-of-hand maneuver to get them installed quietly. There are four stationary cameras on the outskirts of Glenrock and one in nearby Rolling Hills.
Jack Street, an outspoken critic of Glenrock’s Flock system and a member of Wy4Privacy.org (which had its first meeting Sept. 10) sees this as a good starting point.
“I appreciate the respectful dialogue and the willingness to hit pause,” Street said. “There’s still work to do, but progress like this gives me hope that we can rebuild trust through openness and accountability.”

name: VTDigger
title: Homeless in Vermont? The path to housing is harder than it should be
description:
Vermont has already paid for the affordable housing. Getting into it is another story.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Homeless in Vermont? The path to housing is harder than it should be.
text:
This commentary is by Maryellen Griffin, a staff attorney at Vermont Legal Aid.
Homelessness is complicated, but for each person the solution is the same: a home. Vermont needs a clear, coordinated path connecting people experiencing homelessness with the affordable housing the public has already funded.
Vermont recently reduced the number of motel rooms available for emergency housing during most of the year from 1,100 to 700. For the roughly 4,000 Vermonters experiencing homelessness, including more than 600 children, fewer emergency shelter rooms means more people sleeping outside, in cars or in other unsafe places while they search for permanent housing. At Vermont Legal Aid, we recently heard from a family asking where they could legally sleep outside with their children. No parent should have to ask that question.
Leaving people without shelter does not save the public money. It shifts costs to hospitals, emergency responders, schools, communities and other public services without solving our crisis of homelessness. Stable housing is both the humane response and the fiscally responsible one.
Vermont invests public money in subsidized housing because thousands of Vermonters cannot afford market-rate rents. But making a home affordable does not mean that the people who need it can access it.
First, a person must find a subsidized apartment in a location and size that work for them, determine whether they qualify, complete the application process, respond to notices from multiple properties for months or years just to stay on the waiting list and then get through a strict screening process. Although Vermont has a statewide directory of subsidized properties and a common rental application, it lacks a coordinated system for getting a subsidized apartment. Applicants must still apply to properties one by one. Then, after waiting months or years, they can be denied because of a prior eviction, unpaid rent or poor credit.
The strict screening criteria create a cruel catch-22: People are evicted into homelessness because they cannot afford the rent, then denied affordable housing because of the eviction.
Subsidized housing cannot fulfill its purpose if it screens out the people who need it most. But reducing screening barriers is only part of the solution. Landlords also need reliable access to responsive case management, conflict resolution, flexible funds for repairs or unit modifications and early intervention when a tenancy is at risk. Vermont should fully fund those supports so that people can both obtain housing and remain housed.
Great River Terrace in Brattleboro shows what happens when those supports are underfunded. The publicly funded development was designed as permanent supportive housing to reduce barriers for people who had experienced homelessness. Earlier this year, its operators ended that model altogether, citing the absence of a comprehensive funding model for the continuum of care many residents needed, and the property is converting to general occupancy. Vermont cannot use its affordable housing system to end homelessness unless it reduces barriers to securing housing and funds the supports people need to remain housed.
Vermont should take two concrete steps.
First, we should create a statewide housing access system that shows current vacancies, open waiting lists, eligibility and screening requirements, accessibility features and application instructions. Applicants should be able to provide core information once, identify properties for which they may qualify, apply to multiple open waiting lists and manage all pending applications in one place, including updating their contact information and confirming their place on each waiting list. Housing Navigator Massachusetts offers one model for this, including the ability to identify units available for immediate occupancy.

READ MORE

Second, Vermont should require aggregate reporting from publicly funded housing providers. That reporting should include vacancies and turnover times, applications and denial reasons, placements from homelessness, eviction filings, successful eviction prevention efforts and exits to homelessness. The goal should not be to shame or rank providers. It should be to identify where the system gets stuck and what resources would help.
Act 143 provides a starting point. The law creating Vermont’s new homelessness program requires the state to report how often households return to homelessness after leaving the program. That requirement matters, but a count alone cannot tell us why people lose housing or what might have prevented it. A recent state auditor’s report found that no state agency systematically examines why so many people return to homelessness or which interventions are most effective at helping them remain housed. The Legislature should build on Act 143 by requiring the state to collect and analyze the information needed to answer those questions and use the findings to improve housing stability.
Public investment makes subsidized apartments affordable. Vermont now needs the infrastructure and support to make those homes findable, accessible and sustainable for the people who need them most.
