name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Penguins, cats and tortoises: SCETV to release series teaching about zoo animals
description: The videos are meant to get children interested in conservation, biology and animal care, the state agency said.
text:
A decorative cake honors Riverbanks Zoo and Gardens' 50-year anniversary Friday, April 26, 2024. The zoo opened to the public on April 25, 1974. (Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — Anyone who’s longed for a closer look at a zoo animal and its habitat will get that chance with a series of videos created through the state’s public broadcasting network.
Starting Friday, SCETV will release educational and immersive videos featuring animals and habitats at Columbia’s Riverbanks Zoo and Gardens. The goal of the series, titled “Zoo Minutes,” is to find a new way to get children interested in conservation, according to the state-funded broadcaster.
“This collaboration is a powerful opportunity to inspire the next generation through dynamic and immersive storytelling,” Riverbanks President Tommy Stringfellow said in a statement.
Education center, new exhibits in store as SC zoo celebrates 50-year anniversary

Each installment will include a short video about the animal, a 360-degree video allowing people to explore a habitat, an interactive video with information to click on and discover, and quizzes to test what people learned. SCETV will also release behind-the-scenes videos showing how teams filmed footage of habitats and creatures.
The first two installments will focus on the zoo’s penguins, fishing cat and radiated tortoises, according to a news release. Later episodes will include poison dart frogs, jellyfish and squirrel monkeys.
“Education is at the heart of ‘Zoo Minutes,’ and the series is designed to give students and educators multiple ways to engage with the same story,” said Salandra Bowman, chief learning officer for SCETV.
Bowman’s educational team designed the videos and quizzes for students in pre-kindergarten through sixth grade, but anyone can access them. Zoo employees in the videos talk about conservation, biology and animal care, including veterinary care, according to the agency.
The broadcasting agency, which also runs the state’s public radio station, has similar educational programming available for teachers.
Other shows include “Corine & Celestine,” which tells the story of the fight for civil rights through the experiences of two Black women, and “Echoes and Insights,” which pulls from SCETV’s archives to teach about history.
“’Zoo Minutes’ builds on SCETV’s legacy of connecting South Carolinians with the animals and their caretakers across the state while using today’s technology to create new ways for audiences to explore and learn,” SCETV president Adrienne Farewell said in a statement.
Riverbanks, which bills itself as the state’s largest gated tourist attraction, receives regular funding in the state budget. This year, legislators split $2 million between the zoos in Columbia and Greenville as part of a supplemental spending bill.
The work with SCETV can help broaden the zoo’s message of conservation and give people who might not get to visit the zoo essentially a virtual field trip, said Greg Peccie, vice president of animal care.
“My hope is that this window into the world of animal care will inspire interest in wildlife for learners of all ages — and maybe even future zookeepers,” Peccie said.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho state revenue exceeds forecast for July and August
description: Idaho revenue exceeded the state’s forecast for the month of August by $37.5 million, marking the second consecutive month in the new fiscal year where revenue beat projections, according to a new state report.  Through the first two months of fiscal year 2027, which began July 1, Idaho’s revenue collections have come in $51.2 million […]
text:
The Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee, the Idaho Legislature's powerful budget committee, meets daily during the legislative session. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Idaho revenue exceeded the state’s forecast for the month of August by $37.5 million, marking the second consecutive month in the new fiscal year where revenue beat projections, according to a new state report. 
Through the first two months of fiscal year 2027, which began July 1, Idaho’s revenue collections have come in $51.2 million ahead of projections, according to the August edition of the fIscal year 2027 General Fund Budget Monitor. 
For the month of August, strong individual income tax collections that exceeded the monthly projection by $40.8 million helped push overall revenue collections ahead of forecast. 
Although it is still very early in the fiscal year, Idaho is projected to end the fiscal year June 30 with a positive ending balance of $657 million if state revenue collections come in as forecasted for the remainder of the fiscal year. 
That would leave the state with a surplus of more than $500 million compared to the budget state legislators set.
Sen. Scott Grow, R-Eagle, makes a comment during the Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee meeting on Jan. 14, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
“My reaction was its very promising report, and I’m glad to see the individual income tax is up,” said Sen. Scott Grow, a Republican from Eagle who serves as co-chairman of the Idaho Legislature’s Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee. 
So far, the state budget picture in fiscal year 2027 looks different than a year ago, when Gov. Brad Little and the Idaho Legislature implemented a series of near-across-the-board, permanent budget cuts to pay for a series of federal and state tax cuts and ensure a balanced budget, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. 
Grow said the increased revenue, so far, in fiscal year 2027 is good news, but he isn’t in a rush to spend any additional revenue. 
Grow said the Idaho Legislature may have additional, unexpected expenses and bills this year related to Medicaid, wildfire suppression, health insurance costs for state employees and the state’s corrections system that may need to be addressed.
Idaho’s prisons are full. Corrections agency will request $45.3 million to open 3 new facilities.

“The challenge is we always have to project a year and a half out when we are working on budgets during the legislative session, so it’s hard to know what is going to happen, which is why we try to be as conservative as we can,” Grow said. 
If there is still a surplus at the end of the year, Grow said he would like to discuss restoring some of last year’s transportation budget cuts.
“With transportation, we had to cut that (budget) pretty skinny last year,” Grow said. “But with all (population) growth we continue to have in Idaho, hopefully we can get some money for transportation to help with the state highways  – not just the maintenance, but to actually help with additional highways we need and expansion.”
The Idaho Legislature is not in session, but the 2027 regular legislative session begins Jan. 11 at the Idaho State Capitol in Boise.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Record diesel prices hit North Dakota farmers at the wrong time
description: Farmers hoping the cost of diesel fuel would go down before fall harvest hits high gear are instead facing the highest prices ever seen.  Diesel is topping $6 per gallon in North Dakota as wars in the Middle East and Russia drive up prices.  Chris McDonald of Leonard in southeast North Dakota said he expects […]
text:
Diesel prices were more than $6 per gallon on Sept. 15, 2026, at Casselton, North Dakota. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)Farmers hoping the cost of diesel fuel would go down before fall harvest hits high gear are instead facing the highest prices ever seen. 
Diesel is topping $6 per gallon in North Dakota as wars in the Middle East and Russia drive up prices. 
Chris McDonald of Leonard in southeast North Dakota said he expects to start harvesting soybeans next week and corn in a month, but diesel costs about are double what he paid last fall. 
“That can erase your profit,” he said Tuesday at the Big Iron farm show in West Fargo. 
Chris McDonald, president of the North Dakota Soybean Growers Association, visits with people at the Big Iron farm show in West Fargo, North Dakota, on Sept. 15, 2026. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)
McDonald, president of the North Dakota Soybean Growers Association, said ideally farmers have a contracted price in place for diesel fuel before the high-demand times of planting and harvest, but many farmers were waiting for prices to go down over the summer after a spring spike tied to the U.S. war with Iran. 
“I think a lot of people expected that maybe the war would wrap up, and the prices would go down some, and they never really did drop very much,” McDonald said. “Then it just skyrocketed.”
Diesel prices reached a record high of $6.31 per gallon in the United States, and gas was at an average of nearly $4.37 a gallon Wednesday, according to AAA.  
Allison Thompson is a market analyst with The Money Farm in Ada, Minnesota. During a panel discussion at the farm show, she called the fuel market “a headline-driven trade.” 
The recent headlines have included the war with Iran heating up again. The war that began in late February has limited oil shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf. 
Dave Ripplinger, a bio energy economist and associate professor with North Dakota State University, said in an interview that an attack on a Saudi Arabian pipeline was what really jolted the energy markets this week. 
“To me, the thing that’s impacted more barrels this week is the pipeline,” Ripplinger said. 
Bryan Dean farms near Velva, North Dakota. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)
Bryan Dean said he filled up the fuel tanks on his farm at Velva in north-central North Dakota as soon as the war broke out. But after spring planting, fertilizing, applying herbicides and pesticides, and harvesting early crops such as wheat, those tanks are empty. 
He said about 70% of his land is planted with soybeans and corn, and harvest is around the corner. He will be buying diesel only as needed until at least the November election. 
The Russia-Ukraine war also is back in the headlines with attacks on energy facilities. Russia on Wednesday announced it would continue to ban diesel exports. 
Ripplinger said the uncharted price territory will be hard for farmers to navigate. 
“We’re kind of outside the norm where you don’t know exactly how high they’re going to go,” he said. 
Some of North Dakota’s soybeans go to a refinery near Dickinson for use in renewable diesel. McDonald says he uses diesel with a 5% renewable blend, but the price is basically at par with traditional diesel. That differs from gasoline blended with corn-based ethanol, which sells for a discount at the pump. 
Tractors, combines and semitrucks use diesel instead of gasoline because it provides more power at low speeds and when pulling heavy loads. 
On his drive from Velva to West Fargo for Big Iron this week, he said he saw diesel as high as $6.53 per gallon.
Dean, a member of the North Dakota Corn Growers Association board, said diesel used to be cheaper than gasoline, too. 
“A few years back, it switched over and went higher,” Dean said. “So I quit buying diesel engine pickups, went back to gas. Plus, the ethanol helps.” 
Reach North Dakota Monitor deputy editor Jeff Beach at jbeach@northdakotamonitor.com.

title: From immigration to voting to education, the pointed politics of the deep freeze
description: This week, NHPR published an analysis by reporter Lau Guzmán focused on the role local police have played in the recent surge in immigration enforcement in New Hampshire. From May through July, 198 people were detained in the state and nearly half of those arrests came as part of the 287(g) Program, which delegates “state […]
text:
Protesters gather in front of the State House in Concord in October 2025. (Photo by Dana Wormald/New Hampshire Bulletin)This week, NHPR published an analysis by reporter Lau Guzmán focused on the role local police have played in the recent surge in immigration enforcement in New Hampshire. From May through July, 198 people were detained in the state and nearly half of those arrests came as part of the 287(g) Program, which delegates “state and local law enforcement officers the authority to perform specified immigration officer functions.”
“There is a clear demographic profile of arrests in New Hampshire,” Guzmán writes of the overall enforcement effort in New Hampshire. “Latino men in their 20s and 30s made up 58% of those arrested in the second Trump administration. Seven minors were also arrested and detained in New Hampshire, including a 4-year old from Ecuador arrested in Manchester in July.”
The analysis also found that of the 198 detained from May through July, just 28 had previous criminal convictions. So much for the Trump administration and its state partners going after “the worst of the worst.”
While immigration hardliners no doubt celebrate New Hampshire law enforcement’s support for the administration’s mass deportation campaign — “We’re a nation of laws,” they and their go-alongs argue — a story from Stateline’s Nada Hassanein this week points to the growing collateral damage. “Four in 10 pediatricians reported kids in immigrant families are avoiding coming in for healthcare out of concerns around immigration status, according to a new survey published Tuesday,” Hassanein writes.
But I’ve misused the phrase “collateral damage.” There is nothing accidental or incidental about the freezing out of immigrant populations.
In fact, across policy areas the “freezing” of populations is not only a prong but the point.
To listen to proponents of ever-broader voter restrictions talk, for example, you would be forgiven for believing the United States was suffering from an epidemic of voter fraud. It’s not. But through an election-meddling partnership with their conservative comrades in the White House, Congress, and the U.S. Supreme Court, New Hampshire Republicans keep challenging or changing state laws — including on voter ID, proof of domicile, and proof of citizenship.
I don’t expect it to stop anytime soon.
Just as claiming “we’re a nation of laws” aims to legitimize inhumane and unjust acts against immigrants, “election integrity” is a marketing slogan that hides a much darker intent: to suppress turnout in favor of a preferred electoral outcome. The idea is not to address fraud but to inject so much confusion in the voting process that people stay home just to avoid the hassles and harassment. So college students stay home, immigrants stay home.
Again, the freeze on selected populations isn’t “collateral.” It’s the point.
Another example. Even before “critical race theory” entered the political lexicon, lawmakers on the right were obsessed with a self-conjured fear of liberal indoctrination in American public schools. They often frame their panic as concern not only about specific thinkers or theories (which are often too niche even for 400-level college classes), but the overall decline in civics education. But they aren’t so much pushing for a “citizenry that understands, values, and practices democracy” — as outlined by the Center for Civic Education — as much as a specific ideological curriculum that elevates unquestioning patriotism and rigid originalism over intellectual rigor.
The demand seems to be that students view colonialism, slavery, and countless other forms of state-sanctioned violence and subjugation only as products of unique historical moments rather than foundational elements of the national system itself. They want students to arrive at prescribed conclusions without ever having to show their work or defend their thesis. It is better in their eyes, it seems, to be a blindly faithful American than a thoughtful one. 
That drive for intellectual control is precisely how New Hampshire, in recent years, has found itself embroiled in perennial debates over “divisive concepts” and its various offshoots, including the broader parental rights movement.
Whether the laws actually stop teachers from challenging students to expand their worldviews, or prevent a troubled student from confiding in a trusted teacher, is almost beside the point. The laws are designed to freeze teachers and students alike, to make what is allowed and not allowed so convoluted that they seek safety in silence.
These assaults on immigrants, voting rights, and education are not disparate endeavours. They are a unified mechanism to assure that one narrow worldview holds sway and power, indefinitely.
The price of that effort is steep, and it is unfolding.
At its heart, the debate over immigration is not about political ideology but suffering. And so if your perception of certain immigrants is that as violators of U.S. immigration laws their suffering is warranted, that position is revelatory. It means you view humanity in terms of a hierarchy, and that is less a political conclusion than a social one.
If you argue for new and broader voter restrictions in the name of “election integrity,” you should be able to do so without relying on false claims of widespread voter fraud or stolen elections. Conservatives cannot simultaneously claim the mantle of protectors of liberty while disenfranchising voters solely to manipulate the makeup of the electorate and, in concert with gerrymanderers, create a closed loop of power.
If your primary concern about public school curriculum is leftist indoctrination, I invite you to search online for the ideas or thinkers that unnerve you the most (or, conversely, that you cherish). It’s all there — usually without context, comparison, or criticism — and it will stay on Google, YouTube, Facebook, X, or Bluesky no matter how many books are banned or how many syllabuses are ripped up by right-wing school boards. What a child is taught matters far less than how they learn to critically interpret and process what they are told by their political leaders, the media, online posters, their parents, or their teachers. That’s your real civics crisis.
And that’s the American crisis, too.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Roxbury warehouse again at center of ICE detention fight
description: Immigrant advocates claim the U.S. Department of Homeland Security is using a Roxbury warehouse for migrant detention purposes in violation of a court order.
text:
Immigrant advocates claim the U.S. Department of Homeland Security is using a Roxbury warehouse for migrant detention purposes in violation of a court order. (Photo by Benjamin Leynse/New Jersey Monitor)A Morris County warehouse is again the focus of an immigration detention fight, with immigrant advocates saying the Trump administration is using it to house migrant detainees in violation of a court order.
Sandra Wittner, a councilwoman in Dover, told the New Jersey Monitor she spoke to the daughter of a man detained during a Sept. 4 immigration raid in Morris County, and Wittner said she believes the man was taken to the warehouse in Roxbury by immigration agents before being detained elsewhere.
“It’s very concerning, extremely concerning, honestly,” she said. “This warehouse is really well situated for ICE’s purposes. It’s very close to a lot of heavily immigrant communities — Dover, Morristown, places like Hackettstown — and I think it makes their objective that much easier.”
Activists across North Jersey have been keeping tabs on the 470,000-square-foot warehouse since plans to convert it into an immigrant processing center were revived in July. They say they’ve been carefully tracking vehicles entering and leaving the property, which is tucked away off Route 46 in this small Morris County town.
“We don’t want a detention facility in our town. We don’t want ICE officers bringing people to detention facilities. And here they are, doing the exact thing they said they wouldn’t be doing,” said David Broderick of Project Ninja (No ICE in North Jersey Alliance).
The warehouse has been a flashpoint since the U.S. Department of Homeland Security first signaled plans to convert it into the state’s third immigration detention facility in late 2025, and then purchased it in February for $129 million. The state and Roxbury officials sued to block the federal government from using it as a detention center, arguing it never completed environmental reviews or consulted local officials. A May consent order bars Homeland Security officials from using the property for detention until it completes the environmental assessment and returns to court. Federal officials this summer said they planned to abandon the warehouse conversion, then reversed course a week later.
In a Tuesday legal filing, state officials told the judge overseeing the warehouse dispute that they have heard reports the warehouse is being used in connection with immigration enforcement. Attorney General Jen Davenport said in the filing that the state would seek relief from the court if it’s found that federal officials are violating the consent order.
“If ICE tries to convert the Roxbury warehouse site into a detention facility, it would violate a court order. We are carefully reviewing reports of ICE activity at the warehouse and will take all necessary steps to address any non-compliance with a court order,” said Mike Symons, spokesman for the Attorney General’s Office.
The Department of Homeland Security declined to comment, citing the pending litigation.
Wittner, a Democrat, believes seven people were arrested during the Sept. 4 raid in Dover, and that they were detained in nearby Roxbury before being transported to Elizabeth Detention Center. She said the daughter of one of the men taken into custody said he was being held in a “jail” west of Dover. He was later processed at the Elizabeth facility that day, and is currently held in Delaney Hall in Newark.
People near the Roxbury warehouse that morning, including Wittner, said they saw ICE vehicles with black tinted windows, matching those used in the Dover operation. Wittner said there was unusual activity outside the warehouse that day, and that ICE agents recorded advocates who were watching nearby.
Broderick said state officials should urge the court to ask ICE whether it’s true that people are being taken to Roxbury illegally.
“If it is true, hopefully they apologize and say, ‘Sorry, your honor, we didn’t realize there were rogue agents doing this, and we’ll stop.’ But with this administration, who knows?” he said. “The ball is in the AG’s court to decide what to do with this information.”
Wittner said it’s hard to know what more the state can do since immigration detention is a federal issue, but hopes that residents stay alert as raids continue.
“It’s heartbreaking. It’s frustrating,” she said. “But it’s a good reminder that people need to know their rights, need to be vigilant, need to look out for their neighbors. We all have a duty, no matter who we are, to stand up for what’s right.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas Constitution Day program goes global with online mock trial for third graders
description: TOPEKA — Twelve years ago, 90 third-grade students walked into District Judge Robert Wonnell’s courtroom on Constitution Day to watch a hearing about whether Goldilocks was guilty of trespassing.  Wonnell put the last-minute mock trial together to teach Olathe’s Forest View Elementary School students about how the court system works. Because he loves teachin[...]
text:
Judge Robert Wonnell presides over a 2025 mock trial held on Constitution Day to teach third graders across the country about the court system. (Photo by Kansas Courts) TOPEKA — Twelve years ago, 90 third-grade students walked into District Judge Robert Wonnell’s courtroom on Constitution Day to watch a hearing about whether Goldilocks was guilty of trespassing. 
Wonnell put the last-minute mock trial together to teach Olathe’s Forest View Elementary School students about how the court system works. Because he loves teaching, he researched how such an event could be conducted every year. 
Wonnell’s research led him to an even stronger commitment when he found that it is written in U.S. law, specifically 36 US Code 106, that government officials should offer educational opportunities to the public on Constitution and Citizenship days. The country celebrates Constitution Day on Sept. 17, in honor of the day the Constitution was signed. 
“I’m someone who very much enjoys following the law, and I thought, ‘Well OK, this is great,’” Wonnell said, laughing. “For the next four years, we had some individuals — court reporters, interpreters, attorneys — we would go to a couple of different elementary schools, and we would put on a little mock trial after we talked about the three branches of government for third graders, and each of the kids would play a role.”
Educators reached out to say how well received the program was and how engaged the kids were. Wonnell said he’s sure it’s because the students actually participate in the mock trial, which usually puts a fourth-grade student on trial for running in the school hall. 
“We really think that we have created something and put something out there that they can come back to, that they can engage with,” he said. “When we announce the verdict, every single kid thinks ‘I was part of that.’” 
Wonnell and others working on the event realized their ability to expand was limited because of physically going to the schools. Then the COVID pandemic hit and classes were conducted online, so the Constitution Day mock trial went online as well, he said. 
Forest View Elementary staff were still involved and they helped put a remote program together in 2020, Wonnell said. It was a “little rough” that first year because everyone was still learning Zoom. 
Online, the children in the classroom become the jury, Wonnell said. 
“We thought the interaction would be entertaining, we thought people would like it, but we just wanted the kids to feel like they were involved,” he said. “We realized that if they’re the jury, they’re listening to the evidence, they’re deliberating, and they will vote and they will come to a verdict.”
The program expanded throughout the school district, and Julie Fishburn, K-12 social studies and science coordinator for Olathe schools, brought a team together to create curriculum teachers can use ahead of time, including presentations and games for students to play. 
In 2024, Wonnell and other coordinators opened enrollment statewide, and about 10,000 students joined in. Gov. Laura Kelly spoke virtually about the executive branch, Kansas Chief Justice Marla Luckert about the judicial branch, and Sen. Jerry Moran about the legislative branch, Wonnell said. 
The next natural step was to open it for national enrollment, he said. 
The result was video presentations by Delaware Gov. Matt Meyer and Supreme Court Justice Neil Gorsuch. Fourteen states joined in and involved about 17,000 third-graders, Wonnell said. 
They decided to go national a little late in the year, Wonnell said, so participation was lower. This year gave them more time to prepare. On Thursday, more than 45,000 third-graders from 47 states will participate, Wonnell said. 
This year’s video presentations will be from Meyer and Supreme Court Justice Amy Coney Barrett, he said. 
As word spread, Wonnell said the federal government reached out to ask if classes at military bases could be included, so more than 70 third-grade classes on military bases from four continents will participate. 
Wonnell never thought his Goldilocks trial would evolve into the current version of a Constitution Day educational activity. But he has a passion for teaching and thinks it is important for youth to learn about their country. 
“I think there’s a real value in learning how our system works, and in the promotion of civil discourse, and I talk about that briefly at a third-grade level,” he said. “When everyone got together to talk about this document, they did not all agree, and there was a lot of listening to someone else disagreeing. But ultimately, they came together and created one of the most important documents in the history of the world.”
While he doesn’t speak deeply about civil dialogue because of student’s ages, Wonnell said it is an important concept. 
“This can lay a foundation for understanding the importance of civil discourse, and just realizing that there are some amazing people who have a different perspective than you do,” he said.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: UNC Board of Governors warned about financial sustainability of university athletics
description: It’s been 15 months since the landmark House v. NCAA settlement received final court approval, paving the way for Division I schools to compensate student-athletes directly. The revenue-sharing framework of that deal set a $20.5 million cap per school for university athletics in 2025-26. That figure is only expected to grow in the coming years. […]
text:
North Carolina Tar Heels players run out with flags before the first half of the game against East Tennessee State Buccaneers at Kenan Stadium on September 12, 2026 in Chapel Hill, North Carolina. (Photo by Jaylynn Nash/Getty Images)It’s been 15 months since the landmark House v. NCAA settlement received final court approval, paving the way for Division I schools to compensate student-athletes directly. The revenue-sharing framework of that deal set a $20.5 million cap per school for university athletics in 2025-26. That figure is only expected to grow in the coming years.
UNC System President Peter Hans (Photo: UNC Board of Governors video stream)
Members of the UNC Board of Governors finance committee worried Wednesday that athletics spending is growing faster than the revenues the programs generate, and schools will have to cover the balance.
UNC System President Peter Hans said while athletics often represent the “front porch” of a university, the changing national landscape around athletics may be financially unsustainable.
“There’s a key paradox here, because most people would agree the college athletics model has never been more broken. And yet, it has never been more popular,” Hans told board members.
Hans said every university president and chancellor across the country that he has spoken with is feeling this new pressure.
“You don’t have to be an economist to figure out that those who spend the most will generally win the most games,” said Hans. “That’s why I’m hoping this will be the start of a conversation amongst the board members about how we can remain competitive in athletics, but not at the expense of the academic mission.”
Sustaining what matters
Kirk Bradley, who chairs the board’s committee on budget and finance, said before talking about cost, he wanted to be sure everyone was clear about the value athletic programs deliver.
“A few years ago, we documented how athletics generated more than $1.1 billion a year in estimated economic impact across North Carolina. That figure is likely closer to $1.5 billion today,” said Bradley.
He said athletics anchor alumni identity, open doors for philanthropy, and attract future students to UNC campuses.
Athletic expenses by university. (Source: UNC System)
“The question this board will wrestle with is never whether athletics matter,” said Bradley. “It is how we sustain what matters on a sound financial footing.”
Bradley said collectively, university athletics generated $412 million in the 2024 fiscal year for the UNC system through ticket sales, media and private giving, but they come with obligations and risks.
“We should be cautious about assuming that athletic success will produce sustained enrollment growth,” Bradley said. “Winning may increase visibility, but sustained enrollment gains are not guaranteed.”
Bradley said as financial pressures grow, universities may need to consider new fees, ticket surcharges, private equity, or separately organized entities.
Josh Lassiter, the UNC System’s vice president for financial health and strategy, said nationally, athlete compensation is projected to exceed $4.5 billion this year.
“Outside the power conferences, generated revenue did not keep pace with spending growth,” Lassiter warned. “That leaves institutions having to strategically decide how important a priority athletics is, and what other sources they’re going to fund it from.”
Jennifer Haygood, the UNC System’s senior vice president for finance and chief financial officer, said all 15 schools’ programs rely on subsidies from their schools. She said not a single North Carolina university fully covers its athletic expenses with generated revenue. NC State University and UNC-Chapel Hill come closest to paying their own way.
At the same time, those two schools have rapidly increased their spending. At Chapel Hill, total athletic expenses rose from $139 million in FY 2023 to $188 million in FY 2025. At NC State, total expenses rose from $119 million in FY 2023 to $134.5 million in FY 2025.
UNC-Chapel Hill hires Bill Belichick as head football coach in $50M deal

Haygood said the Board of Governors isn’t being asked to vote on any policy changes now, but members need to grasp the amount of money that is being spent.
Board member Philip Byer urged his colleagues on the finance committee not to be too quick to try to dial back the spending.
Byer said college athletics have been critically important to helping the mountains recover after Hurricane Helene in 2024.
“If you go to Western Carolina, they’re going to have 13,000 students every [football] game and bring in $5 million to the impact of that community, and App State will bring in $10 million, six times a year,” said Byer.
Harry Brown, a former state senator and current member of the board, said it’s clear that chancellors want to compete at the highest level, but the revenue sources that they can reliably generate on their own make it challenging.
“The NCAA has just botched the whole thing,” said Brown. “I do think it’s going to take some type of legislation to start to rein this thing in.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Challenge to required Oklahoma Bar Association membership heads to federal appeals court
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — A federal appeals court is set to hear a case that could affect how the Oklahoma Bar Association conducts business and collects dues.  The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit is scheduled to hear arguments Thursday about whether Tulsa attorney Mark Schell should be required to pay dues to the […]
text:
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit is scheduled to hear arguments Thursday in a case that could affect the Oklahoma Bar Association. (Getty Images)OKLAHOMA CITY — A federal appeals court is set to hear a case that could affect how the Oklahoma Bar Association conducts business and collects dues. 
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit is scheduled to hear arguments Thursday about whether Tulsa attorney Mark Schell should be required to pay dues to the Oklahoma Bar Association in order to practice law in the state. 
In his federal lawsuit against the state bar and the Oklahoma Supreme Court, Schell argues his First Amendment rights are being violated by being required to associate or pay dues to the Oklahoma Bar Association. Schell disagrees with some of the bar association’s political speech, according to the lawsuit. 
Tulsa attorney Mark Schell is pictured. (Photo provided)
The Oklahoma Bar Association, which predates statehood, acts as “an arm of the Oklahoma Supreme Court,” and is funded through membership dues and other self-generated revenue. It investigates and prosecutes attorneys “who have committed ethical violations.” 
The justices of the Oklahoma Supreme Court are named as a defendant in the 2019 lawsuit only because they ultimately enforce the regulations that require membership to the association.
A spokesperson for the Oklahoma Bar Association declined to comment Wednesday.
Scott Day Freeman, senior attorney with the Phoenix-based Goldwater Institute, which is representing Schell, said Wednesday they are not trying to challenge the regulatory responsibilities of the Oklahoma Bar Association, but want to establish boundaries and guidelines for its conduct unrelated to regulation. 
“I think (Schell) would like to not be required to be a member of the bar,” Freeman said. “He, I think, would acknowledge that he could be required to pay dues to fund sort of the regulatory apparatus of the bar, which is really all it should be doing.”
The Oklahoma Bar Association regularly publishes articles that advocate for specific public policy ideas which is “impermissible,” he said. Its members are by default associated with these views and their dues contribute to this activity, he said. 
Freeman said the Oklahoma Bar Association’s role should be narrowly focused on its regulatory purpose. 
There are many states, like New York, that do not have mandatory bar associations, Freeman said. In New York, attorneys are still regulated through the state Supreme Court and have required fees to fund this, Freeman said. 
Other states have seen challenges to their own bar associations, Freeman said, including Oregon, Louisiana, Texas, Utah and Wisconsin. 
He said two other federal circuit courts have weighed in on similar issues. 
“They’re not all uniform in what they’re saying,” Freeman said. “So ultimately, we may need to get the U.S. Supreme Court to step in and resolve this question.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Quinnipiac poll has Lamont with double digit lead over Fazio
description: Gov. Ned Lamont and Sen. Ryan Fazio will face off in two televised debates. Neither would happen before early voting begins on Oct. 19.
text:
The first Quinnipiac University poll of Connecticut’s race for governor found Gov. Ned Lamont with a 17 percentage point lead over Ryan Fazio, a Republican trying to become the first candidate to unseat a governor in the state since 1954.
Lamont led Fazio 55% to 38%, a comfortable lead attributed to the continuing gender gap in which women favor Democratic candidates: Lamont led 64% to 30% among women, while Fazio was narrowly favored by men, 47% to 44%. 
The poll was released Wednesday, the same day Fazio challenged the Democratic governor to accept invitations to six debates, not the two televised events signed off by the governor’s campaign. Neither would take place before early voting begins on Oct. 19.
Fazio, 36, a state senator from Greenwich elected five years ago, badly trails Lamont, 72, a two-term governor, in name recognition, making him eager for more head-to-head events with the incumbent.
“For the governor not to want to debate more than two times, but also not to want to debate before early voting starts — and tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands of Connecticut voters have already made their decision — it’s a disservice to the public,” Fazio said.
Lamont and Fazio are scheduled to debate Oct. 22 on WFSB and Oct. 27 on WTNH, both at 7 p.m.
“Gov. Lamont has already agreed to 10 public events [with Fazio], including eight forums and two debates,” said Lauren Gray, a spokeswoman for Lamont’s campaign. “The Fazio campaign doesn’t want to debate more, they want to create more noise.”
Forty-five percent of voters told Quinnipiac they didn’t know enough about Fazio to say whether they had a favorable or unfavorable opinion. For Lamont, the number was 11%. Of those with an opinion, the favorable/unfavorable split was 28% to 25% for Fazio; 50% to 36% for Lamont.
A recent Sacred Heart University poll also had Lamont with a double-digit lead that slightly shrunk since its first poll on the race in July.
One of the discouraging findings for Lamont in the Quinnipiac poll is a relative lack of enthusiasm about his candidacy for a third term. Only 27% of voters backing the Democrat described themselves as “very enthusiastic” about their choice, compared to 39% of Fazio supporters.
Fifty-three percent of Lamont voters described themselves as “somewhat enthusiastic,” 10% “not so enthusiastic,” and 4% “not enthusiastic at all.” Fazio’s split: 51%, “somewhat enthusiastic;” 6% not so enthusiastic; and 3% “not enthusiastic at all.”
Voters were split on the degree to which they are satisfied with how things are going in Connecticut: More than half were very satisfied (8%) or somewhat satisfied (44%), compared to 25% somewhat dissatisfied and 22% very dissatisfied.
Slightly more than half of voters had a less than satisfactory view of the Connecticut economy, with 34% calling it “not so good” and 19% rating it “poor.” Two percent called it excellent; 43% said good.
President Donald J. Trump’s approval rating was nearly 40 points under water: only 28% approve of how he is handling his job and 67% disapprove.
The poll was based on live telephone interviews of 1,288 likely voters reached by random digit calling to landlines and cell phones from Sept. 8 to 14. It has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points.

title: Iowa Developmental Disabilities Council presents award to Iowa Capital Dispatch
description: AMES — The Iowa Developmental Disabilities Council presented its first-ever Media Impact award Wednesday to Iowa Capital Dispatch for “producing impactful reporting that amplifies the voices of Iowans with disabilities.” The award, presented during the council’s annual conference in Ames, recognizes the online news organization’s reporting about the “abuse,[...]
text:
Iowa Capital Dispatch Editor-in-chief Kathie Obradovich, left, accepts the Media Impact Award from the Iowa Developmental Disabilities Council, represented by Chairman George Thompson, back row, left, his daughter Stella Thompson, front row, Council Executive Director Brooke Lovelace, and Council Public Policy Manager Carlyn Crowe. (Photo courtesy of Dave Price)AMES — The Iowa Developmental Disabilities Council presented its first-ever Media Impact award Wednesday to Iowa Capital Dispatch for “producing impactful reporting that amplifies the voices of Iowans with disabilities.”
The award, presented during the council’s annual conference in Ames, recognizes the online news organization’s reporting about the “abuse, neglect and mistreatment in Iowa’s long-term care facilities,” Council Chairman George Thompson said.
“They’ve been doing it consistently and reporting on information we can’t find ourselves without a lot of work and dedication,” Thompson said. “… The stories they have uncovered are the hard stories we don’t want to hear, but we need to, and so does everybody else. The stories that give us pause to think about how can we fix this situation.”
He said news covered by Iowa Capital Dispatch of deaths that have occurred in long-term care facilities, minimal fines for abuse and neglect and heartbroken families “has all made us more informed, more concerned and more committed to making a difference.”
Iowa Capital Dispatch Editor-in-chief Kathie Obradovich accepted the award and credited Deputy Editor Clark Kauffman for his reporting on long-term care facilities: “It takes a lot of time. He has to dig through a lot of records. He gets pushback sometimes from state officials and agencies, and he just persists.”
The Iowa Developmental Disabilities Council is a federally funded group that advocates for  Iowans with disabilities. It is made up of volunteers appointed by the governor and includes people with disabilities, family members, state government leaders and other groups that advocate for people with disabilities, according to the council’s website.
Iowa Capital Dispatch, which launched in January 2020, is part of States Newsroom, the nation’s largest not-for-profit news organization dedicated to coverage of state government.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Four rural CT hospitals receive $46 million in federal health grants
description: Charlotte Hungerford, Day Kimball, Sharon and Windham Hospitals were awarded the funds through U.S. Rural Health Transformation Program.
text:
Four rural Connecticut hospitals are getting millions in federal grant dollars that will be used to expand and upgrade imaging, telehealth and transport services, among other initiatives.
The Connecticut hospitals — Charlotte Hungerford, Day Kimball, Sharon and Windham — each received a share of $46 million, officials announced Wednesday. An additional $4 million is going to Mathematica, a computing software system used to provide technical assistance for the four rural hospitals, officials said.
The money comes from the Rural Health Transformation Program, a $50 billion federal effort aimed at improving healthcare in the rural U.S. In total, Connecticut received $154 million through the program.
“We were awarded $54 million above the base of $100 million because of the work that we’ve done,” DSS Commissioner Andrea Barton Reeves said at a press conference at Day Kimball Hospital on Wednesday. “We’ve demonstrated that substantial work has happened here, and substantial work can continue to happen to transform rural communities in the state of Connecticut.”
The remaining $104 million not going directly to hospitals or hospital technology assistance will be used for a range of projects across the state, from healthcare workforce development in rural areas to maternity and postpartum services, mobile health services and the expansion of a multiuse trail to encourage outdoor fitness.
Day Kimball Hospital in Putnam, which has faced serious financial difficulties, is receiving $20.2 million — the largest share of funding for any one hospital.
Currently, some of the hospital’s MRI services are situated in a trailer outside the building. Kyle Kramer, CEO of Day Kimball, said the “first” of the upgrades will be to replace the trailer with a fixed facility for advanced imaging.
“[This] will allow us to keep patients here as opposed to their having to go elsewhere for advanced imaging services,” Kramer said. “That’s exciting, and it’s transformative.”
Kramer also said the funds will be used to expand patient transport services, remote patient monitoring and virtual care initiatives. He said all these upgrades are important to improve access, equity and affordability of care.
Two Hartford Healthcare hospitals — Charlotte Hungerford in Torrington and Windham Hospital in Willimantic — are getting $12.6 million collectively. 
Charlotte Hungerford plans to use the funds to establish the state’s first mobile stroke unit to serve the northwestern corner of the state. This unit is essentially an ambulance equipped with CAT scan and ultrasound equipment, as well as telehealth capabilities to communicate with doctors across the state. The Hartford Healthcare hospital’s will also expand telehealth and in-patient monitoring services.
Sharon Hospital, like the other three recipients, will use the funds to expand virtual care and rehabilitation services as well as introduce a healthy aging program. 
The additional $104 million in statewide funds is going toward more than 100 contracts across 30 projects. These projects are overseen by 10 state agencies, including the Department of Public Health, the Office of Early Childhood, the Department of Education and the Department of Energy and Environmental Protection.
Daniel Sinclair, statewide project director for Connecticut’s program, said the federal Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services is closely monitoring the deployment of funds. Every year, the state will be required to submit annual reports that track progress on the initiative in order to determine the next year’s funding levels. The first report was submitted Aug. 31.
“They’ve set up a pretty rigorous program,” Sinclair said.
Gov. Ned Lamont thanked the members of the state’s leadership team for the Rural Health Transformation Program as well as hospital leaders for their support. He said he hopes the funds will improve care in Connecticut.
“We can get you into a specialized center with a really good doc there, but you have remote access to the very top specialists at, say, UConn Health help with that particular thing,” Lamont said. 
He added that the result is “saving people transportation, providing more accessible, more affordable, faster service than we had before.”
CT Mirror reporter Katy Golvala contributed to this story.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico State Ethics Commission says Oracle’s $3.4M Project Jupiter ads sought to sway permitting
description: The New Mexico State Ethics Commission on Wednesday said that the tech giant Oracle spent more than $3.4 million in recent months on advertisements meant to influence the New Mexico Environment Department’s air quality permitting process for the Project Jupiter data center. The commission said it was “likely the largest lobbying advertising campaign ever dis[...]
text:
The New Mexico State Ethics Commission announced on Sept. 16, 2026, that tech giant Oracle had complied with state lobbying laws and disclosed a $3.4 million lobbying and advertising campaign to influence the air quality permitting process for its Project Jupiter data center. (Screenshot)The New Mexico State Ethics Commission on Wednesday said that the tech giant Oracle spent more than $3.4 million in recent months on advertisements meant to influence the New Mexico Environment Department’s air quality permitting process for the Project Jupiter data center.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In a statement, the commission said it was “likely the largest lobbying advertising campaign ever disclosed in New Mexico,” and noted that it reached a voluntary agreement with Oracle to disclose its advertising expenditures before taking further legal action against the company.
Specifically, the commission said Oracle sought to influence New Mexico Environment Department officials who have the power to approve or deny the data center’s proposed energy source, a natural-gas powered fuel cell system. Projections filed with the state show that, if approved, the system would emit as many greenhouse gases annually as New Mexico’s largest cities combined.
The ethics commission noted that Oracle created the projectjupitertogether.com website that includes a form letter visitors can sign to ask NMED officials to approve the pending air quality permit application. It also cited a statewide effort in which paid canvassers solicited favorable public comments for the permit application and paid sponsored content that appeared on the social media profiles of New Mexico-based social media influencers.
The New Mexico State Ethics Commission on Sept. 16, 2026, announced Oracle filed a report disclosing its lobbying and advertising efforts for Project Jupiter, including an online form letter asking state environment officials to approve the data center’s air quality permit application. (Screenshot)
Oracle’s advertising campaign report shows the company spent $3.4 million between January and April on media production, polling and consulting. The NMED air quality permit hearing was initially scheduled to begin Monday, but is on hold while an environmental group’s challenge is pending before the New Mexico Supreme Court.
The company exclusively paid the national consulting firm Brabender Cox for these services, according to the report. The firm’s website lists locations in Washington, D.C., Dallas, South Carolina, Pittsburgh, New York and Indianapolis.
Its founder, John Brabender, has worked as a consultant and adviser to Republican political campaigns, including those for President Donald Trump and Rick Santorum. His firm has also done work for former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani and former Vice President Mike Pence, according to an archived copy of its website.
Neither Oracle nor Brabender Cox immediately responded to requests for comment.
Wednesday’s announcement comes after Source NM revealed that residents and state lawmakers reported seeing their names wrongfully signed to public comments in support of Project Jupiter. Source NM also revealed that a marketing firm approached local social media influencers about promoting the data center and helping to “increase positive comments” on its website. Oracle in July denied any involvement with such efforts, and said the company supported the state’s investigation.
Canvassers soliciting public comments for Oracle’s Project Jupiter data center under construction in southern New Mexico carried door-hangers containing the company’s messaging regarding water use and local financial investments. (Joshua Bowling/Source NM)
In addition, the State Ethics Commission recently settled a lawsuit it brought against a separate company over an unrelated pro-Project Jupiter advertising campaign.
In March, Source NM identified a Virginia-based company named Elevate New Mexico as the anonymous author of pro-Project Jupiter mailers and digital ads that appeared in New Mexicans’ mailboxes and social media feeds.
The State Ethics Commission sued the group in April and accused it of violating the state Lobbyist Regulation Act. It settled the case in August.
Expenditure filings in that case showed that one of Project Jupiter’s developers had paid the Virginia-based Elevate New Mexico nearly $3.7 million.
“Project Jupiter has attracted widespread public attention because of its potential economic, environmental and energy impacts for New Mexico,” State Ethics Commission Deputy Director Amelia Bierle said in a statement at the time. “These disclosures reveal the significant financial resources devoted to influencing both the public and, indirectly, the NMED officials considering the permits required for Project Jupiter.”

name: VTDigger
title: Fall foliage varies from year to year, for leaf-peepers and trees
description:
A punishing drought muted Vermont’s colors last fall. This year, foresters say, the show is back.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Fall foliage varies from year to year, for leaf-peepers and trees.
text:
Leaves show their fall colors in Jericho in September 2020. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Josh Halman flew over Vermont’s woods late last summer and saw something that surprised him.
Swaths of trees had already gone brown, scorched by an extreme drought that affected more than 64,000 acres. 
This year, from the same vantage, things are looking up.
“We haven’t seen anything even close to the level of damage we were seeing in the foliage last year,” said Halman, who leads a long-running tree-monitoring project at Vermont Forest Parks and Recreation.
The rebound is good news for the leaf-peepers who pour into Vermont each fall. But for the foresters who study those same trees, the annual turning of the leaves is more than a spectacle. It’s a record. It shows, in real time, how a warming climate is quietly rewriting the rules by which Vermont’s forests live.
After last year’s damage, experts say this season is largely back on track, though a few of the hardest-hit spots are turning early. And the reason the leaves turn at all is a process more precise, and more sensitive to weather, than most roadside admirers realize.
“It is showing right in our backyard in Vermont that climate has an influence on how long trees, or sugar maples specifically, are able to be growing in a given year,” Halman said.
His team has tracked individual sugar maples at two moments each year — when leaves emerge in spring, and when they turn in fall — since 1991. The stretch between those two dates is the tree’s growing season, and over three decades of data it has grown steadily longer. Last year, he said it ran 21 days longer than when the project began.
A physical science course refresher
That annual autumn process has a name. Senescence is the orderly shutdown that deciduous trees — the broad-leaved maples, oaks and birches that drop their leaves each year — go through every fall.
Leaves are costly for a tree to grow, but they’re also how they turn sunlight into energy through photosynthesis. Chlorophyll in the leaves’ cells captures the light, and that chlorophyll is what makes summer leaves green.
As days shorten and temperatures drop, the tree begins pulling its investment back inside. It draws nutrients — calcium, magnesium, potassium, nitrogen — out of the leaves and stores them in the roots and wood for next spring. As the green chlorophyll drains away, the oranges and yellows underneath are revealed. 
They were there all along, just hidden.
When the timing slips
That much has held true for as long as there have been maples. What’s changing is the timing.
A longer growing season might sound like a gift. But it comes with a catch, said Ali Kosiba, an assistant professor with the University of Vermont Extension Forestry Program. She studies how climate change is altering fall foliage.
The amount of daylight, she said, declines on the same schedule every year, no matter the weather. Temperatures, on the other hand, are staying warmer later into the fall. 
That mismatch makes for a difficult tradeoff. If they drop their leaves on schedule with the fading light, they could miss out on weeks of mild weather they could have spent making food. Hang on to them too long, and a sudden cold snap or violent storm can strip them before the tree has reclaimed those valuable nutrients.

The Irasburg United Church framed by maple foliage in September 2020. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

But, Kosiba said, trees are generally pretty good at making those tradeoffs.
“Trees are really programmed to take advantage of conditions that benefit the amount of photosynthesis they can do and how much growth they can do in a year,” Kosiba said. “We are seeing that trees are responding to warmer fall conditions.”
Fall foliage, she noted, is one of the less-studied corners of forest ecology, and researchers are still untangling what governs it. But the long-term drift is clear. 
Weather also plays a part in the year-to-year variation. A drought one season can shape the colors the next. This year, Kosiba said, foliage might actually run a day or two early despite the broader slide toward later autumns. 
Local conditions matter too. Trees in nutrient-poor wetlands are among the first to turn, which is why some are already showing color now. Even neighboring trees can turn at different times, depending on their genes, their soil and the storms they happen to weather.
Halman, for his part, says he hasn’t seen the longer growing seasons harm the health of the forest. A healthy tree, he noted, can usually recover from a bad year. This year’s browning was minimal. What the foresters saw last year was not just senescence, but drought killing leaves outright, before they had the chance to turn.
For anyone hoping to catch the show, Kosiba’s advice is to chase it. Vermont’s coldest regions, mapped by the state’s plant hardiness zones, which rank areas by how cold they get, peak first in late September. Each zone to the south follows about a week later, so the color rolls down the state over several weeks.
“Travel around,” she said, “looking for different views.”

title: Fewer South Dakota middle-schoolers trying nicotine, but more using it regularly
description: Fewer South Dakota middle-schoolers are trying nicotine than they were two years ago, but slightly more of them are using it every day. Nicotine use rates for Native American kids in grades six through eight are higher than they are for non-Natives, meanwhile, and South Dakota kids overall are slightly more likely on average than […]
text:
The cover of a South Dakota QuitLine guide to quitting tobacco use. (Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)Fewer South Dakota middle-schoolers are trying nicotine than they were two years ago, but slightly more of them are using it every day.
Nicotine use rates for Native American kids in grades six through eight are higher than they are for non-Natives, meanwhile, and South Dakota kids overall are slightly more likely on average than their peers elsewhere in the U.S. to use cigarettes.
The findings from 2025 come from the recently released Youth Tobacco Survey from the South Dakota Department of Health. The state’s conducted the survey for middle-school kids every two years since 2003. Smoking and nicotine use rates for high schoolers are compiled as part of a wider Youth Risk Behavior Survey. The results of that 2025 survey haven’t been released.
For middle-schoolers in the new survey, 9.6% had tried any form of nicotine at some point in their lives — fewer than the 12.7% of kids nationwide who’d tried nicotine. South Dakota’s figure was 10.7% in 2023. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
E-cigarettes were the most prevalent choice in the 2025 survey for kids who’d tried nicotine at some point in their lives, at 6.6%, followed by cigarettes at 4.3% and smokeless tobacco at 1.5%. Eighty percent of e-cigarette users reported using flavors outside of traditional tobacco, such as fruit or candy.
The e-cigarette rate for all kids has dropped in South Dakota since peaking in 2019, when 16% had tried them and 6.7% of them were current users. In 2025, 3.1% reported current e-cigarette use.
The survey found that 4.7% of middle-schoolers counted themselves as current users of any kind of nicotine, up from 4.5% in 2023. 
For Native American kids, 19.4% had tried any nicotine as of 2025, with 14.8% of kids saying they’d tried e-cigarettes and 9.9% saying they currently vaped nicotine. 
South Dakota’s nicotine use figures trail the national numbers in most areas, but not all. For cigarettes, 4.3% of the state’s middle-schoolers reported trying them and 1.4% reported being regular smokers. For the U.S., the figures were 3.6% and 1.1%, respectively.
The report says kids who’d tried nicotine “were significantly more likely” to come from a household where at least one family member uses nicotine.

name: VTDigger
title: State restricts new superintendent hires to one year
description:
Secretary of Education Zoie Saunders said she adopted this policy, which applies across the state, in light of the Montpelier-mandated school district merger discussions. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  State restricts new superintendent hires to one year.
text:
Zoie Saunders, interim secretary of education, listens during Gov. Phil Scott’s weekly press conference held at the Central Vermont Technical Center in Barre in June 2024. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

This story by Sophia Keshmiri was first published in the Addison Independent on Sept. 11, 2026.
VERGENNES — As the Addison Northwest School District gets the search for a new superintendent underway, the secretary of education confirmed to its board on Friday that going forward she will exclusively approve interim hires with one-year contracts, though those could be annually renewable.
District board Chair Mark Koenig said in a Friday interview with the Independent that the board would take the policy under advisement and figure out its next steps.
Secretary of Education Zoie Saunders adopted this policy, which applies across the state, in light of the Montpelier-mandated merger discussions, she said in a Friday email to Koenig.
“Following the passage of Act 170, I communicated to (Vermont Superintendents Association) and (Vermont School Boards Association) leadership that I would only approve an interim superintendent under a one-year contract, which could be renewed annually thereafter,” she wrote.
“I have provided that consistent message to Board Chairs seeking permission to conduct superintendent searches. There is precedent with how the Secretary’s recommendation for the superintendent approval has been applied historically in Vermont, particularly during a similar period of contemplated mergers. Most recently, Secretary (Rebecca) Holcombe limited new superintendent contracts to one year following the passage of Act 46 as the state contemplated voluntary and required mergers (between 2015 to 2019).”
The Addison Northwest board broached the possibility that it may have to hire with these restrictions in mind previously when the search for a new leader was on the agenda. Since the current superintendent, Sheila Soule, announced in May that the 2026-2027 school year would be her last at the helm, the district has hired a superintendent search firm to help with the process.
After selecting McPherson & Jacobson as the consultant in August, the board met with them to form the beginnings of a job posting. Koenig said it will be finalized after a Sept. 23 visit from the consultant, at which time they will meet with various focus groups, including students, administrators and parents. That night the consultant will host a meeting open to the public to gather additional insights and bring her findings back to the school board so they can include the public’s sentiments in the job posting.
Koenig said school board members won’t be present for any of the Sept. 23 discussions.
Also this summer, school districts began meeting among “cooperative educational service area” peers. Addison Northwest is part of the Champlain Valley South CESA, along with Addison Central, Mount Abraham, Champlain Valley and Mount Mansfield, to identify common services that could be consolidated and shared among them.
Additionally, school districts are required to explore voluntary mergers. Locally, Addison Northwest, Addison Central, Mount Abraham, Lincoln School District and the Patricia A. Hannaford Career Center were grouped together by the state for the purpose of that separate discussion.
In her email to Koenig, Saunders further explained her reasoning behind the one-year, interim hire policy as it relates to Act 170.
“I am also concerned that because a newly formed district assumes the contracts that the forming districts hold, the new district would be put into the position of being obligated to pay out one or more years of superintendent salary upon separation. I decided that the best time to begin this approach is this year, rather than waiting for various contract terms of 2, 3, or more years to expire,” she wrote.
“I recommend approaching recruitment with the broader context of Vermont’s education transformation clearly in mind. As a state, we are working to reshape the delivery of public education to advance consistent educational quality, equity, and long-term sustainability.
“Achieving greater scale is an explicit part of that work. This creates a distinct leadership context for districts and should inform both the candidates you seek and how the opportunity is positioned. I encourage you to recruit an interim superintendent who understands the direction of the transformation, is comfortable navigating uncertainty, and is prepared not only to lead the district as it exists today, but to help inform system-level change.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Unionized hospital workers had high hopes after Roger Williams, Fatima sale. Not anymore.
description: Five months ago, Lynn Blais stood shoulder to shoulder with suit-clad executives at a Friday afternoon press conference in March, smiling and clapping as they celebrated The Centurion Foundation’s long-awaited purchase of Roger Williams Medical Center and Our Lady of Fatima Hospital. On Wednesday, as Blais, president of the United Nurses and Allied Professio[...]
text:
United Nurses & Allied Professionals workers picket outside Our Lady of Fatima Hospital in North Providence on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)Five months ago, Lynn Blais stood shoulder to shoulder with suit-clad executives at a Friday afternoon press conference in March, smiling and clapping as they celebrated The Centurion Foundation’s long-awaited purchase of Roger Williams Medical Center and Our Lady of Fatima Hospital.
On Wednesday, as Blais, president of the United Nurses and Allied Professionals, sat across the table from several Centurion lawyers and human resources representatives, the celebratory mood was over. The 1,200 hospital union workers — half the hospitals’ combined workforce — still have no contracts, and no sign of progress reaching any new ones. 
“They made promises and commitments to the community, to the employees, that they were going to come in and do the right thing, so we helped them to get the money they needed,” Blais, a nurse at Fatima, said in an interview. “They’re now turning their back on the hardworking employees of these hospitals.”
The sticking point: what happens to the nearly 40-year-old home health program, which paired discharged hospital patients with nurses, therapists and home aides for care. 
Former owner Prospect Medical Holdings laid off the couple dozen remaining nurses, therapists and aides in January amid bankruptcy proceedings, referring discharged hospital patients to other home health agencies. 
But the layoff letter suggested it wasn’t permanent, said Lorrie Miller, an occupational therapist among the dozen remaining home health workers who lost their jobs in January.
Miller transferred to a new position with Fatima’s acute rehabilitation facility, but she still clung to the plan to return to home health.
“I loved the patients, I loved my colleagues, we had a great community and network, and at one point, a great reputation,” Miller said. “It’s really frustrating to be displaced and not really have a lot of support. And now you’re saying I can’t go back?”
Miller joined an information picket outside Fatima hospital Tuesday afternoon where union workers in purple T-shirts carried signs reading,“We care!” 
She does not think her new employer feels the same way.
“I firmly believe that healthcare should be a human service, not a business,” she said. 
Lynn Blais, right, president of the United Nurses and Allied Professionals, speaks at a press conference on March 6, 2026, to celebrate the closing of the sale of Roger Williams Medical Center and Our Lady of Fatima Hospital. From left are Governor Dan McKee, Senate President Valarie Lawson, and then-House Speaker K. Joseph Shekarchi. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)
From skeptic to supporter 
Initially critical of The Centurion Foundation’s offer to buy the pair of cash-strapped urban hospitals, Blais and other union healthcare workers rallied behind the Atlanta nonprofit after Prospect filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in January 2025, later threatening to close the hospitals.
Union officials held press conferences, made statements, and spent many late nights at the State House, pressing lawmakers to approve Centurion’s eleventh-hour request for state funding to help close the sale. 
An $18 million reserve made it into the fiscal 2026 budget, the private investors finally lined up, and by March 6, the $101 million bond-financed deal had closed. Just beginning was a new chapter for the facilities, which represent 500 beds between them, accounting for 50,000 annual emergency room visits and providing critical behavioral health and cancer treatment programs.
“The verbal commitment I got from Ben Mingle at the State House was to get to the bargaining table, get the contracts done fairly and quickly,” she said, referring to Centurion’s CEO and president. “It’s not fairly, and it’s not quickly.”



Quotation







They made promises and commitments to the community, to the employees, that they were going to come in and do the right thing, so we helped them to get the money they needed. They’re now turning their back on the hardworking employees of these hospitals. 


– Lynn Blais, president of the United Nurses and Allied Professionals 


Otis Brown, a spokesperson for CharterCARE Health of Rhode Island, Centurion’s subsidiary, did not comment on negotiations but said the union picket was “not an effective means of resolving the current bargaining process.”
Brown also said the home health program was already shut down by the time the sale closed in March.
“Our prior owner, Prospect Medical Holdings, made the decision to close it in late 2025 based on declining volume, significant monthly losses, and the availability of more than 60 competing home care agencies in RI,” he said in an email on Monday. 
Chris Callaci, general counsel for UNAP, claims hospital executives kept union workers in the dark about plans to close the home health program until after the sale was finalized.
“They dodged us, and quite frankly, the public,” he said of the surprise announcement. “Now it’s like, in our view, ‘OK, here we go.’”
Nearly three years earlier, Centurion pledged to invest $100,000 in “home health changes,” in its November 2023 application to state regulators.
“With respect to home health, the New CharterCARE System has planned significant outreach to the community in its first year to promote access to home health services,” Centurion stated
Maintaining essential services — including homecare and hospice — was also one of the 85 conditions imposed by the Rhode Island Attorney General’s Office and Department of Health in its June 2024 approval of the hospital sale.
Union workers picket outside Our Lady of Fatima Hospital in North Providence Tuesday afternoon. The union representing approximately 1,200 workers at Fatima and Roger Williams Medical Center in Providence are entering their fifth month of contract negotiations with hospital owners. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)
Breaking the rules?
Callaci suggests Centurion has broken the legally binding requirements.
Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha’s office, which took an active role in the sale and federal bankruptcy proceedings, concurred with Brown.
Home health was already “nonoperational” when the sale closed, Tim Rondeau, a spokesperson for Neronha’s office, said in an email. 
Brown, of CharterCARE, said the health department and AG’s office were aware of the home health program’s status — meaning, closed — when the sale closed in March,
“The union’s allegation that we have violated any regulatory condition is not true,” Brown said.
Callaci acknowledges that no one has been getting paid or seeing patients through the home health program for months, evidenced by the HR notice sent to union workers in January.
“After careful consideration of business, patient safety and operational factors, we have made the decision to indefinitely suspend all operations of this division,” John Tavares, HR partner for Prospect’s local subsidiary, wrote in a Jan. 7 letter to one home care staff member, and shared with Rhode Island Current. “In connection with this development, all employees working in operations are being indefinitely laid off. Your last day of employment will be January 27, 2026.”
The key word for Callaci is “suspend” — which he said indicates the layoffs are not permanent. 
The federal bankruptcy court-appointed patient care ombudsman also alluded to a reopening plan in court documents. 
“The goal is for the Rhode Island hospitals to maintain the home care license and reopen the service line if the sale transaction closes,” Suzanne Koenig wrote in her Jan. 27 report to the federal judge. “The Ombudsman hopes that home health will be offered again, as it is a vital service to the Rhode Island hospitals’ communities (which include an older, less mobile patient population), but believes that the service line is being closed safely.”
Prospect still has an active license with the state health department for its home healthcare operations, Joseph Wendelken, department spokesperson, confirmed via email. There is no new license for home health under the new CharterCARE owners, though.
Healthcare facilities must renew their licenses by the end of each calendar year, or else they expire. Prospect filed its 2026 renewal on Dec. 18, 2025, weeks before it declared bankruptcy. No renewal applications for 2027 had been submitted as of Wednesday.
“We are going to fight this with them at the bargaining table, in our own process, where we control our own destiny,” Callaci said.
For now, hospital workers, already at their mental limit and physical workload capacity, remain frustrated, Blais said. Staffing shortages remain a problem at both hospitals, with pricey travel nurses and overtime helping to maintain a bare minimum of operations, she added.
“Until you have a stable workplace and a contract in place, you have a hard time hiring people,” she said. “It’s all just been painfully long, unprepared, unorganized on the employer’s side. People are frustrated.”
