name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: NDA secrecy for major projects hovers over Louisiana’s congressional elections
description: Congresswoman Julia Letlow, the Republican U.S. Senate candidate, doesn’t want to answer questions about the nondisclosure agreement she signed with a Meta company about Richland Parish’s $50 billion dollar data center project, said Jamie Davis, the Democratic candidate.
text:
Congresswoman Julia Letlow, R-Baton Rouge, signed an nondisclosure agreement about the Meta data center project in Richland Parish in 2024. Her opponent in the U.S. Senate race, Democrat Jamie Davis, is trying to make her NDA into a campaign issue for voters. (Photo by Piper Hutchinson/Louisiana Illuminator)Jamie Davis believes there’s one specific reason Congresswoman Julia Letlow hasn’t agreed to appear in person with him for debates or any other events during their U.S. Senate race. 
Letlow, the Republican candidate, doesn’t want to answer questions about the nondisclosure agreement she signed with a Meta company about Richland Parish’s $50 billion dollar data center project, he said. 
“Any other questions I want to ask about Meta, she won’t be able to answer because she might break her NDA,” said Davis, the Democratic candidate. 
Letlow not only signed the NDA but also began buying stock Meta and Nvidia, a company that makes computer equipment for data centers, in the months that followed, according to reporting from Gulf States Newsroom. The congresswoman didn’t disclose the stock purchases publicly until more than a year after the federal deadline to do so. 
By signing the NDA, Letlow might have had access to information about Meta’s business operations and finances not available to the public. 
Letlow’s campaign spokesperson did not respond to multiple requests  this week for comment about the NDA. But in August, her congressional staff told Gulf States Newsroom she was unaware the Meta and Nvidia trades were happening on her behalf at the time. 
As Louisiana undergoes an industrial megaproject boom, the extent to which public officials are trading away public transparency for economic investment through NDAs has become controversial. 
Dozens of local and state elected officials signed NDAs related to economic development projects such as the SpaceX complex in Vermilion Parish, the Hyundai steel plant in Ascension Parish and data centers in other parts of the state. 

More than 100 employees in Gov. Jeff Landry’s office also signed blanket NDAs prohibiting them from talking about what they learn working for the governor. 

Landry and his administration have said the NDAs are necessary to attract global brands. But the agreements raise questions about whether government officials are free to share information about the projects’ impacts on resources such as water and the electrical grid.  
LSU political science professor Robert Hogan said backlash over NDAs is part of a broader “general distrust that people have of government” right now. 
“I do believe this could be a very effective issue at sowing seeds of doubt in the minds of voters about people who signed these,” Hogan said in an interview this week.

As the underdog in the Senate race, Davis is trying to make Letlow’s Meta NDA into a campaign issue and brought it up during a speaking engagement at LSU this week. 
Davis said he never signed an NDA when he was an elected member of the Tensas Parish Police Jury and wouldn’t sign one if he was elected to the Senate. 
NDAs could creep into competitive US House races
In addition to the Senate race, the NDA issue could come up in the U.S. House  races, including open races for the 5th and 6th congressional districts, where many of the closely guarded industrial projects will take shape. 

Four state legislators and the chair of the Board of Regents, which oversees state higher education, are among the nine candidates running to replace Letlow in the 5th District. 

Of the five major candidates, two said they signed NDAs as elected officials in order to receive information about economic development projects. 

State Sen. Stewart Cathey, R-Monroe, confirmed he signed an NDA to learn basic details about the Meta data center coming to Richland Parish from state Economic Development Secretary Susan Bourgeois before the project was publicly announced. 
Even after he signed the agreement, Cathey said Bourgeois would only tell him it was a data center project and not the name of the company behind the site. He’s not sure if he would sign an NDA again if elected to Congress. 

“The only legislators who have not signed NDAs are people who weren’t asked,” Cathey said. 
State Rep. Gabe Firment, R-Pollock, said he signed an NDA required to attend a meeting about a data center under construction in Rapides Parish, but the information shared at the meeting didn’t turn out to be particularly confidential. 
“I would not sign one again,” Firment said. “A lot of people I represent and I may represent in the future are not comfortable with that.” 

State Rep. Mike Echols, R-Monroe is one of the three 5th District contenders who has not signed an NDA as an elected official. He said he also wouldn’t sign one as a member of Congress. 
“I want to be as transparent as possible. I don’t see value for me,” Echols said. 

State Rep. Pat Moore of Monroe, the Democratic Party-endorsed candidate, said she has not signed an NDA as a legislator and could not recall signing one while a member on the Ouachita Parish Policy Jury. 

Misti Cordell, a Republican from West Monroe who leads the Board of Regents, said she hadn’t signed an NDA while in her current public position.

But Moore and Cordell wouldn’t rule out signing NDAs if elected to Congress. 

Cordell said she would make sure any agreement she signed didn’t require her to shield information about what might hurt the public. 
Moore said she wouldn’t personally benefit from any information she received through an NDA. 
“If there was confidential information that I could not disclose, I would not do anything to profit off of it,” Moore said. 
Two legislators are also among the 10 candidates running to replace U.S. Rep. Cleo Fields, D-Baton Rouge, in the 6th District. Fields decided against running again after state lawmakers redrew the district’s lines to make it harder for a Democrat to win. 

State Sen. Rick Edmonds, R-Baton Rouge, said he has signed one NDA with the Louisiana Economic Development agency. He said he couldn’t say whether he would sign any if elected to Congress because he doesn’t know entirely what the position would entail yet. 

State Sen. Blake Miguez, R-New Iberia, did not return phone calls seeking comment on his policy regarding NDAs. It’s not clear whether he has signed one as an elected official. 

Two Democrats in the race, Pat Forbes and Lindsay Garcia, have not held elected positions previously and said they would not sign NDAs if elected to Congress. 
“I don’t think NDAs have any place in government,” said Forbes, who led disaster relief efforts as the head of the state Office of Community Development for several years.

“There is a distinct irony in you serving the interest of the public while keeping the public in the dark,” said Garcia, a community organizer and former teacher who graduated from Southern University Law Center last year.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Remembering veterans on Agent Orange Awareness Day and beyond
description: Agent Orange Awareness Day, though not an official federal holiday, is observed in the Beehive State and the rest of the country each year on August 10. That specific date was not arbitrarily chosen. According to the Blinded Veterans Association, the U.S. began spraying Agent Orange in Vietnam on August 10, 1961. Although its use […]
text:
Vietnam veterans affected by Agent Orange chemical exposure pose for a photo with the Rivetin' Rosie's Project at the Utah Capitol on Feb. 12, 2026, the day they were recognized by the Utah Legislature. Hannah Turk, a Utah Agent Orange Veterans Foundation board member, is at the far left. (Photo courtesy of Hannah Turk)Agent Orange Awareness Day, though not an official federal holiday, is observed in the Beehive State and the rest of the country each year on August 10.
That specific date was not arbitrarily chosen. According to the Blinded Veterans Association, the U.S. began spraying Agent Orange in Vietnam on August 10, 1961.
Although its use was intended to save American lives, the herbicide turned out to be extremely harmful to humans and the environment. That was because Agent Orange contained the toxic chemical dioxin.
Dioxin was a consequence of Agent Orange production. According to the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, dioxin was an unwelcome byproduct of the chemical’s manufacturing process. 
As a result of exposure to Agent Orange and similar toxic herbicides, hundreds of thousands of Vietnam veterans have died from one or more illnesses associated with those chemicals. 
In Sunset Veterans Park, the Utah Agent Orange Veterans Foundation has been increasing public awareness of the tragic cost of using toxic chemicals during the war in Southeast Asia. 
Since last November, the foundation has been actively engaged in building one of the largest Agent Orange memorials in the United States. 
A number of organizations have been helping support the foundation throughout its ambitious mission. Among them is the Rivetin’ Rosie’s Project. 
In observance of Agent Orange Awareness Day, the organization shared a message on its Facebook page paying homage to victims of Agent Orange exposure and reminding that its effects continue today. 
The group also supported the Utah Agent Orange Veterans Foundation earlier this year. On Feb. 12, patriotic members showed up at the Capitol in Salt Lake City for a ceremony honoring Vietnam veterans exposed to Agent Orange and similar toxic herbicides.
They were in attendance to support Hannah Turk, a Utah Agent Orange Veterans Foundation board member, who helped facilitate the event. Hannah is also a co-founder and vice president of the Rivetin’ Rosie’s Project. 
The veterans at the ceremony and all Utah veterans exposed to Agent Orange were recognized with an official citation, which was read aloud by Rep. Tyler Clancy on the floor of the House of Representatives.
The presence of members of the Rivetin’ Rosie’s Project made the event even more memorable by evoking a nostalgic glimpse of a bygone era — a time when millions of American women symbolized by Rosie the Riveter helped the U.S. win WWII. 
As a Utah veteran, it is heartening to know that organizations like the Rivetin’ Rosie’s Project are striving to make a positive difference in the lives of veterans on special occasions like Agent Orange Awareness Day and other important times throughout the year.
One of those times is right around the corner, as October marks Agent Orange Awareness Month. It was established because a one-day observance did not seem like an adequate amount of time to increase awareness of the toxic chemical, and the month includes events that recognize veterans harmed by exposure to Agent Orange and similar toxic herbicides.
October also seems like an appropriate time for Utah lawmakers to consider joining the growing number of legislators in more than a dozen states who have officially recognized the Orange Heart Medal. 
While the medal is not yet an official federal award, it is nevertheless an extremely meaningful and well-deserved tribute to veterans who sustained internal injuries from exposure to Agent Orange.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Former Indiana utility regulator calls firing a ‘fishing expedition,’ denies spending allegations
description: Andy Zay rejected allegations he misspent campaign money — and said he settled because he didn't have the time or money to continued the lawsuit.
text:
Former utility regulator Andy Zay speaks with the Indiana Capital Chronicle on Tuesday, Sept. 16, 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Despite agreeing to settle his contentious lawsuit against the state, fired Indiana utility regulator Andy Zay maintains that his dismissal was manufactured to change the outcome in a now-pending review of a $71 million electricity rate increase for AES Indiana.
In an interview with the Capital Chronicle, Zay rejected the Braun administration’s allegations he misspent campaign money from his previous role as a state senator — but said he agreed to the $625,000 settlement because he didn’t have the time or money to see the lawsuit through.
“I never would have done anything to embarrass the administration, the (Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission), the work that we were doing,” he said Tuesday. “… They were on a big fishing expedition to move myself on, to get somebody in that would vote for the appeal, and I think that played out very publicly.”
Griffin Reid, a spokesperson for Gov. Mike Braun, slammed Zay’s remarks.
“Hoosier ratepayers should rest easy knowing they no longer have to guard their wallets from Andy Zay’s terrible judgment,” Reid said, in response to a request for comment from the Capital Chronicle. “This latest unhinged rant is just another sad chapter in his failed career in public service.”
The five-member IURC plays a key role in determining how much Hoosiers pay for electricity, natural gas, water and more.
Zay was one of three commissioners who voted in June to approve a $71 million base rate increase on AES Indiana customers.
AES Indiana’s downtown Indianapolis headquarters are pictured Sept. 15, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Braun — who previously appointed Zay to the commission as chairman — denounced the rate decision, demoted Zay and called for a redo. Indiana Utility Consumer Counselor Abby Gray filed a petition asking regulators to reconsider or rehear the case.
“Honestly, there wasn’t much new,” Zay said of the petition. “It was a lot of the stuff in the main case carried forward and repeated.”
“The problem, at that point, was if we don’t set the guardrails, if we don’t protect the IURC, we’re going to be looking over our shoulder on every decision we make,” he said. “And our intent at that point was just to stand by the order.”
A denial was finalized for consideration at an upcoming meeting.
“On Monday we (published) the agenda, the governor found out about noon, and I was fired at 3:35,” Zay said.
“I feel it’s greatly compromised now,” he said of the commission. “I think they are beyond the … mission of the IURC, they’re beyond statute with the political influence.”
Campaign finance allegations disputed
Zay filed a lawsuit alleging the firing was illegal — commissioners can only be dismissed “for cause” under Indiana law — and motivated by the Braun administration’s desire for control over the AES rate case.
Braun’s legal team fired back with allegations that Zay improperly used about $3,000 in campaign funds to give utility-themed ties and scarves emblazoned with his initials to commission staffers after he’d left the Indiana Senate.
Zay, a Republican from Huntington, resigned on Jan. 8 from the Senate seat he’d held since 2016 and began work at the IURC on Jan. 12.
Braun names 3 new utility commissioners, creating Senate GOP vacancy

But Zay said he made the purchase before switching jobs, even though the credit card statement didn’t come until Feb. 1. He provided the Capital Chronicle with a credit card statement showing the spending went through before he started at the IURC.
“I already had somebody announced to run against me in that seat in the primary, so I had some money,” he told the Capital Chronicle. “… And once (the appointment) was announced, I knew that hard deadline.”
He has been designing custom ties and scarves for about seven years and has cycled through a variety of symbols over that time, like the state flower. Zay said he considered an education theme when he began designing his latest order in November or December, but chose energy after hitting five years on the Senate utilities committee.
“I had a lot of campaign stuff left over, and I worked with my general counsel,” Zay said. “She said, ‘No, don’t hand them out, but have them there as surplus. And if people want to grab them, offer that to them. And that’s exactly how they were done.”
Fifty scarves and 50 ties, worth about $30 each, went up for grabs.
Zay shuffled through papers during this week’s interview, looking through other transactions made just before his departure from the Statehouse: tenderloins at Loughmiller’s Pub for Senate commerce committee members to celebrate the chamber’s passage of his state sandwich bill, a farewell dinner with his Senate staffers at St. Elmo Steak House.
There was another, too: a $15,000 donation to a Braun-aligned campaign fund.
“To show I was a team player, and knowing I couldn’t access my campaign money, I made a pretty good donation to the governor at that time, and that check didn’t clear (until after the job switch) either,” he said. “But, you know, it was kind of interesting that that didn’t come up in the conversation.”
‘Fighting the bank’
Despite his denial of the campaign finance and other claims, Zay agreed to settle with the state.
He received $485,000 in pay and benefits through the end of his expected four-year term on the utility commission, plus $140,000 in legal expenses.
“I’m fighting the bank, so to speak, and going against the house,” Zay said. “And, you know, I didn’t know what to do at that point. And I think there were a lot of wrongs, which has been pretty clearly delineated in litigation, but to take it all the way would have been very difficult.”
Zay plans to lay a low during his statutory yearlong “cooling-off” period from any lobbying work involving the Statehouse and the commission. He said he is watching his son’s football season at the University of Toledo and expecting a fifth grandchild while thinking about what’s next.
The IURC is scheduled to meet Thursday afternoon for a prehearing conference and preliminary hearing in the AES Indiana case.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: After gas companies’ appeal, PURA again orders rate cuts
description: The Public Utilities Regulatory Authority ordered rate decreases for customers of two CT gas companies, following a lengthy legal battle.
text:
The Public Utilities Regulatory Authority ordered rate decreases for customers of two Connecticut gas companies on Wednesday, following a lengthy legal battle in which regulators admitted making procedural errors under former PURA chief Marissa Gillett.
Those errors forced a judge to toss the authority’s original 2024 decision cutting rates for the two companies, Southern Connecticut Gas and Connecticut Natural Gas, by a combined $35 million.
On remand, however, PURA ordered even larger cuts totaling $37 million, or about 4.2% of current revenues. Much of the reduction was due to regulators’ determination that the two companies must return $120 million in past overcollections to customers by Nov. 30, 2027. PURA also approved a return on equity of 9.20% for both companies.
“PURA was right from the start to slash these rates,” Attorney General William Tong said in a statement Wednesday. “Connecticut families cannot afford to bankroll padded profits and unsupported and unnecessary expenses.” 
Tong added, “CNG was over-collecting millions of dollars from Connecticut families before they had the gall to ask for more. PURA got this one right.”
Both SGC and CNG are subsidiaries of Avangrid, which also owns the United Illuminating electric company based in Orange. 
Angela Baccaro, an Avangrid spokeswoman, said in a statement on Wednesday that the decision to cut the companies’ revenues would play a “significant role” in their ability to make future investments in the state’s gas infrastructure.
“We are reviewing PURA’s decision and are disappointed that it does not meaningfully resolve the concerns raised by the Superior Court, which found clear evidence of prejudice and bias against CNG and SCG and concluded the companies had not received the fair legal process required by law,” Baccaro said. “This final outcome remains largely unchanged from the original decision and leaves critical issues unresolved, despite their significant operational, financial, and customer impacts.”
Neither PURA nor Avangrid immediately released a bill impact assessment on either decision Wednesday. 
Both of the remanded rate cases were approved by a 3-0 vote of the authority on Wednesday morning. PURA Chairman Thomas Wiehl, who worked on the previous applications of SCG and CNG while serving as an attorney for the state Office of Consumer Counsel, recused from both decisions.
Vice Chair David Arconti, who previously worked as a lobbyist for United Illuminating, also signaled his intention to recuse from both dockets, Wiehl said. Arconti did not participate in Wednesday’s meeting. 
One of the commissioners who supported the decisions, Janice Beecher, defended the authority’s handling of the remanded cases. Each of the commissioners involved, she said, took a fresh look at cases before issuing their final decision.
“The new findings are not tweaks, they reflect our judgement of the facts and issues of this case,” Beecher said.  
Gillett, the former chair, stepped down in October after facing growing scrutiny from lawmakers and utility officials over her leadership of PURA. Within weeks of her departure, attorneys representing the authority in the appeal of SCG and CNG’s rate cases conceded that Gillett had violated the law by appointing herself “presiding officer” over matters before PURA, without a vote of her fellow commissioners.
Gillett also faced allegations that she deleted text messages with lawmakers to hide her involvement in drafting an op-ed that was harshly critical of the state’s utility companies, including Avangrid and Eversource. Gillett denied the allegations.  
The judge overseeing Avangrid’s appeal of the original SCG/CNG cases, Matthew Budzik of the New Britain Superior Court, also referred two attorneys representing PURA to the Statewide Grievance Committee to determine whether they misled the court during the effort to uncover Gillett’s personal phone records.
An attorney for the Grievance Committee, which reviews ethics complaints against lawyers, said in an email Wednesday that there was no public resolution to either referral.

title: Hunters, anglers and nearly everyone else supports the roadless rule
description: The roadless rule is the single most important regulation that benefits hunting and fishing in America. The rule has been in place for 25 years, a habitat-enhancing force of nature since I started hunting elk some 20 years ago, with nearly universal popularity from the start. As Trout Unlimited President and CEO Chris Wood explained, […]
text:
A view of Oak Flat Trail in Black Canyon of the Gunnison National Park, Montrose County, Colorado, in 2012. (Photo courtesy of NPS)The roadless rule is the single most important regulation that benefits hunting and fishing in America. The rule has been in place for 25 years, a habitat-enhancing force of nature since I started hunting elk some 20 years ago, with nearly universal popularity from the start.
As Trout Unlimited President and CEO Chris Wood explained, “1.6 million comments with 93% in favor came when the Roadless Rule was originally established in 2001.”
The roadless rule is a U.S. Forest Service policy that protects 58.2 million acres of roadless areas in national forests and grasslands from being sold for timber, roadbuilding, mining, or oil-and-gas drilling. The rule itself doesn’t prohibit hunting, fishing, motorized recreation, or other public uses — it regulates land management options in these areas. It places limits on industrial logging and mining, and the associated road-building those activities require.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
While serving as chief of the U.S. Forest Service, Mike Dombeck was struck by the Roadless Area Conservation Rule (i.e., “roadless rule”) support.
“We are hard-pressed to think of many other policies carried on through six presidents — three Republican and three Democratic,” Dombeck and Chris Wood said in a September 2025 Seattle Times opinion piece. “The roadless rule’s staying power reflects its popularity.”
Unfortunately, last summer the Trump administration announced its intention to rescind the rule. The move is wildly unpopular among hunters, anglers, and nearly everyone else. During the 2025 public comment period, out of 625,930 comments received 99% opposed repealing the roadless rule. As hunters know from boots on the ground experience, roadless areas protect some of the best elk, mule deer and black bear habitat in Colorado and the country.
However, two states — Colorado and Idaho — have their own roadless rules, which are not currently being considered for rescission. A recent analysis by onX Hunt Maps looked at hunting and other recreational opportunities in roadless areas. Here’s a snapshot: 58% of roadless rule areas overlap elk habitat; 78% overlap black bear habitat. In Wyoming, 99% of roadless rule areas serve as elk habitat; in New Hampshire, 97% protect black bear habitat; and in Arizona, 96% serve as mule deer habitat.
In addition, the nation’s 370,000 miles of existing national forest roads (the Earth’s circumference is only 24,000 miles) have a $10-billion-plus maintenance backlog. We don’t need more roads. Also, roadless areas include 17,715 miles of hiking and biking trails, 7,201 miles of full-size motorized trails and roads, nearly 1,500 miles of mapped backcountry ski routes, and 3,000 climbing areas. From the sounds of it, there’s something for everyone in roadless areas.
The onX analysis also shows that a mere 3% of the country’s historical wildfire ignition points over the past 50 years occurred within roadless areas. The rule explicitly allows for wildfire suppression and fuel reduction, including road construction in emergency situations. Studies have also shown that 90% of all wildfires start within a half mile of a road, likely due to increased human interaction.
In addition, these lands were never roaded for a reason. They’re often steep, rocky and have marginal timber values. There’s simply no way to build more roads and make timber sales pencil out for the American taxpayer. That’s why Taxpayers for Common Sense is one of the biggest supporters of the roadless rule. “Repealing the 2001 Roadless Rule risks billions in new taxpayer liabilities from subsidized road construction and money-losing timber sales,” the organization says.
“Roadless areas pay for themselves through hunting, fishing and recreation dollars flowing into gateway communities every year,” said Devin O’Dea, Western conservation and policy manager for Backcountry Hunters & Anglers. “This isn’t fixing a broken system — it’s bulldozing one that already works, putting productive fish and wildlife habitat at risk while undermining the outdoor recreation economies they support.”
“Roads fragment habitat, disperse wildlife, and push elk and deer onto private land, out of reach for the average hunter,” BHA explained in a Sep. 6 Instagram post. “This isn’t a bureaucratic footnote — it’s wholesale elimination of protections for the backcountry habitat hunters, anglers, wildlife, and rural communities depend on,” said Ryan Callaghan, BHA president and CEO. In 2025, we fought like heck to keep our public lands from being sold off, but the war continues.
“There is a war being waged against public lands on a scale we haven’t seen in ages, where … the idea of shared ownership by all (is) replaced by profit and privilege for a few,” New Mexico BHA board member Kyle Klain wrote in the Winter 2026 Backcountry Journal. “BHA is one of the few groups willing to meet those pressures head-on, without apology.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Seven rural community colleges receive $5.93 million for healthcare training
description: Seven community colleges in what the Virginia Community College Association dubs the state’s “rural horseshoe” have received $5.93 million to train more healthcare workers.  Virginia has so far disbursed $122 million of its $198 million in Rural Health Transformation Fund money to organizations around the state. Associations, foundations and the state Health[...]
text:
A healthcare worker training mannequin rests in a bed in a classroom at Eastern Shore Community College. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)Seven community colleges in what the Virginia Community College Association dubs the state’s “rural horseshoe” have received $5.93 million to train more healthcare workers. 
Virginia has so far disbursed $122 million of its $198 million in Rural Health Transformation Fund money to organizations around the state. Associations, foundations and the state Health Department have been fielding applications from interested parties. 
Virginia’s blueprint for using the funding is divided into several goals, including addressing healthcare workforce challenges, investing in telehealth, mobile clinics and upgraded healthcare technologies, and supporting chronic disease management and “food as medicine” programs. 
Because community colleges can serve as an entry point for aspiring medical professionals, the RHTF funding for rural colleges is intended to help grow the healthcare workforce in areas of the state that have experienced shortages. 
For Patrick & Henry Community College, the funding means it can add a part-time Licensed Practical Nurse program and a program designed to help LPNs become registered nurses. 
The college already had a full-time LPN program but identified a need among  working parents seeking to enter the field.
“Nursing school is no joke to begin with,” Patrick & Henry President Greg Hodges said. “When you couple that with trying to work and raise a family, that’s very, very challenging. So those students who want to continue to work full time and go to school part time now have that opportunity here.”
The college already partners with Sovah Health Martinsville to provide  students with the clinical hours required as part of their curriculum. But Hodges noted the rural nature of surrounding areas and said students who don’t remain  nearby after earning their degrees can fill positions at other rural hospitals. 


Awardees:

Germanna Community College
Laurel Ridge Community College
Mountain Gateway Community College
Patrick & Henry Community College
Paul D. Camp Community College
Rappahannock Community College
Virginia Highlands Community College



Just as healthcare access more broadly has been a challenge in rural areas, Virginia officials have also noted behavioral health hurdles in those regions. 
Mountain Gateway Community College will be using its RHTF award to expand instruction for future behavioral health workers, said Ben Worth, the college’s vice president of academic affairs. 
“Primarily, we’re talking about bachelor’s-level and master’s-level degrees,” he said of many mental health professions. But the state’s Transfer Virginia program ensures that community college students’ credits can count toward those degrees when they transfer to other institutions. 
That is why Worth said the RHTF can help the college prepare future psychologists and social workers in the region. The funding will support hiring instructors and launching a dual-enrollment program for high school students seeking a head start on earning the degrees they need to enter the workforce. 
“Partly, it’s awareness — making sure (high school students) are aware that there are huge careers out there,” he said. 
Worth added that the college will also focus on existing healthcare workers who lack a bachelor’s degree “so they can do that coursework while they’re still employed, and then earn degrees that can allow them to move up the ladder.”
He said the college’s focus on bolstering the behavioral health workforce also stems from conversations with regional community service boards and hospitals that expressed a need. 
“When we think of healthcare, we don’t always immediately think of mental health needs and behavioral health needs,” Worth said. “So I’m really glad to see that it was included in the list of eligible programs that can be funded through the rural health initiative.”
With the next phase of funding to be announced by the end of next month, the selected community colleges can begin putting their share to work. 
Virginia health leaders, lawmakers share enhanced healthcare resources for rural communities

There are 18 community colleges within the rural horseshoe, which stretches from Virginia’s Eastern Shore in a crescent through Southwest and Southside Virginia and into the mountain region near Winchester. 
Ten colleges applied during the first wave of funding, and seven received awards.
With applications for the second phase of funding having closed on Sep. 14, the Virginia Community Colleges Association anticipates that the next wave of grants will continue to focus on nursing, behavioral health and physical therapy assistants programs. It will also focus on expanding or establishing radiologic technology, sonography and dental hygiene programs. 
As RHTF money continues to roll out around Virginia, patients and providers are bracing for additional strains stemming from other federal actions. 
When Congress created RHTF last summer it also passed H.R. 1, a reconciliation bill that will remove 5,800 lawful immigrants from Medicaid next month and put about 300,000 Virginians at risk of potentially losing coverage by next year. 
Changes to hospital funding mechanisms also stand to strain hospitals as free clinics and other safety-net providers prepare to take on patients who cannot always afford to pay for care. 
The law can also shift more of the cost of funding the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program to states. So far, more than 100,000 Virginians have lost SNAP benefits, which help low-income people and people with disabilities who cannot work stretch their food budgets.  
Virginia Secretary of Health and Human Resources Marvin Figueroa has emphasized that while the RHTF can help alleviate longstanding rural healthcare challenges, it may not be enough to counter certain ripple effects from the reconciliation bill. 
Worth noted that some Mountain Gateway students come from low-income backgrounds, so “SNAP benefits are really important for them.” 
“Food insecurity, housing insecurity, access to transportation, access to childcare,” he said. “Those are all significant needs for some of the students that we serve, and so anything we can do to try to help address that is important.”
Hodges noted “concerns down the road” about the potential impact of H.R. 1 on healthcare. 
For now, he said, the RHTF “gives us a prime opportunity to innovate, to maximize our technology base, and really come out of this.”

title: Fed raises interest rates for first time in 3 years, battling persistent inflation
text: WASHINGTON — The Federal Reserve raised interest rates Wednesday for the first time in three years as inflation continues to dog the economy, largely driven by soaring gas and fuel oil prices while the war in Iran drags on.The central bank’s Federal Open Market Committee voted 12-0 to increase its benchmark interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point, reaching the new range from 3.75% to 4% and making the cost of borrowing more expensive for Americans.The committee released an upbeat statement touting economic growth at “a solid pace.”“While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little,” according to the statement released Wednesday afternoon.“Inflation remains elevated. Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability,” the statement continued.Trump campaign for lower ratesPresident Donald Trump publicly pressured and name-called Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s predecessor Jerome Powell for months for not lowering interest rates. The public attacks escalated into a federal probe of Powell and the Fed for costly renovations at the Fed’s headquarters in Washington. The administration eventually dropped the investigation.The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.The interest hike comes less than a week after the government’s latest consumer price index revealed the cost of food, energy, housing and other goods and services rose 0.4% from July to August. The cost of all items over the past year has risen 3.4%.Soaring gas pricesSpiking energy prices caused by the war in Iran were the main driver behind higher costs. Gasoline alone rose 3.9% over the month of August. As of Wednesday, Americans were paying an average of nearly $4.37 a gallon at the pump, according to AAA. Diesel prices reached a record high of $6.31.The price of a barrel of oil surged above $100 in recent days, including Wednesday afternoon, when it reached $105, as fighting flared in the Middle East. The United States and Iran continue launching rockets in the Strait of Hormuz, where one-fifth of the world’s petroleum traveled prior to the war. U.S. Central Command claimed Sept. 8 that it “destroyed” five Iranian crude oil carriers as part of its naval blockade aimed at damaging Iran’s economy.The conflict spilled over in July into another key waterway for Saudi Arabian oil exports. Iran-backed Houthi rebels restarted an assault on commercial vessels in the Red Sea for the first time since 2024, and are fighting for control of the Bab al-Mandab strait. The group also directly struck targets in Saudi Arabia, a U.S. ally, beginning in July, and is threatening more strikes, according to Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree. The United Nations Security Council is warning of the likelihood of a humanitarian crisis.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC Supreme Court denies death row inmate’s appeal of incompetence
description: Steven Bixby, 59, received a pause in receiving a death warrant to hear claims of delusions and bizarre beliefs.
text:
The state Supreme Court turned down a last-ditch appeal from inmate Steven Bixby, pictured in a Greenville courtroom on Friday, Aug. 22, 2025. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — The state’s highest court turned down a last-ditch effort Wednesday for a death row inmate to avoid execution.
The one-line order could open the door for Steven Bixby to receive a death warrant as soon as Friday. The last execution the state carried out took place in November 2025.
Death row inmate convicted of killing 2 cops is competent for execution, SC judge says

Bixby’s attorneys could attempt to appeal the decision at the federal level. Whether they will do so is unclear. Bixby’s lead attorney did not immediately respond to a call requesting comment.
Bixby, who was convicted in 2007 of gunning down two police officers during a 13-hour standoff in his parents’ Abbeville house, ran out of normal appeals before the state resumed executions in September 2024.
Initially among five inmates slated for back-to-back executions, Bixby’s attorneys asked for a pause in his case, arguing he wasn’t competent to face the death chamber.
Bixby, 59, maintained during a two-day hearing in August 2025 that he did nothing wrong and a judge might still overturn his death sentence. He also told his attorneys he saw an angel at the crime scene, found special significance in numbers and believes most laws are unconstitutional, according to court filings.
Inmates must have a grasp on reality and the ability to communicate with lawyers to face the death chamber, the state Supreme Court has previously ruled.
Bixby met those benchmarks, even though his beliefs were sometimes atypical, making him competent for execution, a circuit court judge ruled last year.
Delusions or political opinions? SC judge to decide if inmate is competent for execution

Bixby’s attorneys then asked the state Supreme Court to weigh in, arguing the judge put too much belief in the state’s experts and didn’t address the full incompetence claim.
The court denied the appeal Wednesday.
If he received a death warrant, Bixby would be the eighth man executed since the state resumed the process in September 2024, following an unintended 13-year hiatus.
He’s one of 21 people on South Carolina’s death row. One inmate who received a death warrant in South Carolina is housed in California for crimes committed there.
One other inmate, Gary Terry, is also awaiting a decision from the court as to whether he is competent for execution.

name: Mississippi Today
title: A data center in the tiny town of Walls? Officials eye rezoning 1K acres
description: Site of the state's mega center, which includes the Amazon data center currently under construction in Canton, Saturday,  Oct. 4, 2025.
text:
An application to rezone over 1,000 acres from agricultural to light-industrial use is facing intense public scrutiny in the small town of Walls. 
While there appears to be no project at this stage, some believe that the town wants to attract a data center. But residents say the larger question is why a rezoning this large is needed.
Rep. Dan Eubanks, a Republican from Walls, wrote on social media that the town is “wanting to put another massive data center right in our back yard.” 
Eubanks said that he’s for more economic development in the area but cautioned that it should not be done “at the expense of the residents.” 
In a letter to the town’s planning director, a representative for the land owner wrote that the rezoning would help attract economic development to the property which will in turn bring jobs and contribute tax dollars to the city. 
The rezoning has attracted so much attention in the majority-Black town of 1,400 that a planning commission meeting scheduled for Sept. 22 was moved to a larger venue, Walls Elementary School, in anticipation of a crowd. Some residents have expressed concern about how a data center or other industrial development would fundamentally change the small town’s character.
Walls resident Emily Harris said she was devastated when she learned of the rezoning, which is about a mile from her home. She and her family moved to Walls for the opportunity to own land in a rural, quiet community. 
“We are not against progress,” Harris said, “Growth is a wonderful thing if we do it smart.”
She and other residents have said they want more information about a potential project.
Residents questioned why the rezoning is coming so quickly after the town approved its comprehensive zoning plan earlier this year and if there has been sufficient change in the past few months to warrant rezoning.
The specter of Elon Musk’s SpacexAI looms large in Walls, which is near the company’s growing data-center operations in Southaven and Memphis. Harris has been to Southaven and has heard the noise that residents of Southaven have been living with for over a year. 
Members of the Walls Board of Aldermen did not respond to requests for comment, but on social media the town wrote that the rezoning was “to create a potential path to economic development” and encouraged residents to attend the meeting to gather facts, ask questions and express concerns.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lamont administration signals universal free school lunch is still on the menu
description: Lt. Gov. Susan Bysiewicz told CT superintendents the Lamont administration wants free breakfasts and lunches for all public school students.
text:
Lt. Gov. Susan Bysiewicz told Connecticut superintendents on Tuesday the Lamont administration wants free breakfasts and lunches for all public school students by next year. 
Legislators in the General Assembly called for exactly that during the 2026 legislative session, but the proposal didn’t make it into the final budget. What did was a narrower $12 million proposal from Gov. Ned Lamont: free breakfasts for all, and free lunches for students currently paying a reduced price.
“The governor and I are looking forward next year to add universal lunch, as well,” Bysiewicz told school leaders, drawing applause. “Because our students can’t learn without food in their stomachs.”
Schools have long offered free meals to students who qualify, but proponents of universal programs argue the restrictions on eligibility create problems. Some students from low-income families avoid taking free meals out of shame; if everyone eats for free, proponents say, that stigma goes away. Other students come from families that don’t qualify but are still struggling financially; with universal free meal programs, that’s no longer an issue.
Further complicating matters is the erosion of SNAP benefits since the passage of 2025’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Enrollment in SNAP is one way families qualify for free school meals, and losing SNAP eligibility can bump families off the free meal list. A July report found nearly 18,900 Connecticut children have lost SNAP benefits since the bill was signed into law.
Bysiewicz told The Connecticut Mirror that concerns about affordability are a factor in the universal lunch conversation.
“It’s a major priority for the governor and I to lower costs for families, and if families don’t have to worry about providing breakfast and lunch for their kids, that’s a big thing,” Bysiewicz said.
The state’s free breakfast program is now in effect, though just weeks into the school year, it’s too early to say what kind of impact it’s having or how well that $12 million allocation is covering the cost. Bysiewicz said the administration still has to work out what adding universal free lunch would cost the state, too, before announcing a concrete proposal.
The Republican challenger in this year’s gubernatorial election, Sen. Ryan Fazio, expressed surprise that the Lamont administration is signaling a desire to pursue universal free lunches.
“I guess I would ask what his rationale is,” Fazio said. 
He expressed a degree of skepticism toward the idea, though he said he’s open to proposals.
“I’m for free and reduced [price] meals for … low and middle-income students. I don’t want middle-class taxpayers paying to subsidize the meals of millionaires’ kids,” Fazio said.
Bysiewicz said she hopes this year’s successful passage of the universal breakfast program will make it easier to get a lunch program over the finish line in 2027.
“Sometimes it takes good ideas a little while to happen, and sometimes good ideas happen in phases,” she said.

name: Delaware
title: Katz, Arminio Give Delaware GOP Two Distinct Federal Campaigns
description: Senate nominee emphasizes affordability and unity; House nominee centers campaign on restoring economic growth and ending overseas wars DOVER, Del. — Delaware Republicans selected two candidates with unconventional political backgrounds Tuesday, hoping Dr. Mike Katz and Dr. Joe Arminio can expand the party’s reach and make the state’s federal races more comp[...]
text:
Photo: Delaware LIVE photo take a Katz Headquarters on 9/15. Dr. Mike Katz is pictured with his wife moments after announcing his victory.
Senate nominee emphasizes affordability and unity; House nominee centers campaign on restoring economic growth and ending overseas wars
DOVER, Del. — Delaware Republicans selected two candidates with unconventional political backgrounds Tuesday, hoping Dr. Mike Katz and Dr. Joe Arminio can expand the party’s reach and make the state’s federal races more competitive in November.
Katz, a physician, business owner and former Democratic state senator, captured about 77% of the Republican vote for U.S. Senate, according to unofficial election returns. Arminio, a political scientist, author and educator, won approximately 48% in the three-way Republican primary for Delaware’s lone U.S. House seat.
Katz will face Democratic U.S. Sen. Chris Coons, while Arminio will challenge Democratic U.S. Rep. Sarah McBride. Both Democratic incumbents begin the general election with Delaware’s recent voting history on their side, but the Republican nominees bring approaches that differ from those of traditional GOP candidates.
Katz wins with coalition message
Katz’s decisive victory over John Shulli affirmed the Delaware Republican Party’s decision to endorse a candidate who has belonged to three political parties.
Katz represented northern New Castle County in the Delaware Senate as a Democrat from 2009 to 2013. He later became an independent and ran for U.S. Senate in 2024 before joining the Republican Party for the 2026 campaign.
Instead of avoiding that history, Katz incorporated it into a campaign centered on “people over party.” His campaign argues that Republicans cannot win statewide in Delaware without attracting independents and some Democrats who are dissatisfied with the cost of living, government performance and the direction of the state.
In his primary victory speech, Katz said he heard similar concerns while speaking with voters across the political spectrum.
“Delaware families are facing an affordability crisis,” Katz said. “The cost of housing, food, health care, energy and simply raising a family has become too high.”
Katz presented himself as a physician and business operator who would bring a problem-solving approach to Washington. His platform emphasizes reducing federal spending, cutting regulations, lowering energy and housing costs, expanding health care access and protecting Delaware employers.
“Leadership is not about talking about problems,” Katz said. “Leadership is about solving them.”
Katz said his medical and business experience taught him to examine evidence, bring people together, make difficult decisions and accept responsibility for the results. He argued that government should operate with the same accountability.
“Public office is not about power or titles, and it should never be about the person holding the office,” Katz said. “Those entrusted with public office — our public servants — work for you.”
His platform also includes traditional Republican positions on border enforcement, public safety, gun rights, election laws and women’s sports. Katz said those principles would not prevent him from working with people outside his party.
“We can stand firmly on our principles and still work with people who disagree with us,” Katz said. “I will work with anyone who is willing to work with me to solve problems for the people of Delaware.”
Coons, meanwhile, is seeking a third full term and won about 78% of the Democratic primary vote against three challengers. He enters the general election with the advantages of incumbency, a substantial campaign organization and more than a decade in the Senate.
Arminio campaigns on two sweeping ideas
The House primary produced a different message.
Arminio defeated attorney John Whalen III and Earl Cooper, the candidate endorsed by the Delaware Republican Party at its state convention. Unofficial returns showed Arminio with about 48%, Whalen with 32% and Cooper with 20%.
The result demonstrated that the party endorsement was not decisive for Republican voters in the congressional contest.
Arminio is a Wilmington native who holds a doctorate in political science from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. He has taught at American University and Lincoln University and has worked on national defense and public policy issues.
He built his campaign around two sweeping ideas: stopping what he calls America’s “endless wars” and returning the country to economic growth comparable to the 1950s.
Arminio argues that the two issues are connected. He says stronger domestic growth and a less interventionist foreign policy would allow the country to direct more attention and resources toward American families, communities and businesses.
His foreign policy proposal, which he calls “The Grand Bargain,” would reduce American involvement in overseas conflicts and pursue negotiated settlements in Europe and the Middle East. Arminio argues that the United States should avoid prolonged foreign entanglements while maintaining enough military and economic strength to deter adversaries.
Arminio has presented voters with detailed explanations of both proposals through campaign materials, policy documents and public appearances. Whether those plans would produce the results he promises — and how they would affect economic growth, national security and America’s alliances — will likely become central questions in the general election campaign.
Following his primary victory, Arminio said Republican voters had endorsed a campaign focused on developing substantial solutions rather than relying on slogans.
“I am grateful Republican voters endorsed a campaign committed to doing the hard work required to solve the issues facing our communities,” Arminio told Delaware LIVE. “I thank my two opponents for stepping forward and offering their ideas. I echo Delaware Republican Party Chairman Gene Truono’s call for unity. Now is the time for Delawareans who want change to come together and work to defeat U.S. Rep. Sarah McBride in November.”
McBride, who was unopposed in the Democratic primary, is seeking a second term in the House.
Can Republicans make Delaware competitive?
The nominations give the Delaware GOP two candidates who can argue that they are offering something different from standard party politics.
Katz is campaigning as a coalition-builder with experience in medicine, business and more than one political party. Arminio is offering detailed but unconventional plans intended to reshape American economic and foreign policy.
Those differences could help Republicans generate attention and focus the general election on affordability, government spending, energy costs, health care, economic growth and America’s involvement in overseas conflicts.
However, making Delaware competitive will require more than distinctive biographies and policy proposals.
Democrats have held Delaware’s U.S. House seat since 2010. McBride won the 2024 election with 57.9% of the vote, compared with 42.1% for Whalen. Republicans have not won a Delaware U.S. Senate election since William Roth’s reelection in 1994. Coons won his most recent election in 2020 with 59.4% of the vote.
The last Republican elected to federal office from Delaware was former U.S. Rep. Mike Castle, who won his final House election in 2008 and served until 2011. Castle was known as a fiscal conservative and social moderate who regularly attracted voters outside his party.
Katz used his victory speech to make a similar appeal beyond the Republican base.
“Ultimately, there are no Republican families, Democratic families or independent families,” Katz said. “There are Delaware families. We are neighbors. We are one community. We share a future and a responsibility.”
Katz and Arminio will now have to demonstrate that their messages can reach voters beyond the Republican primary. The November campaigns will test whether Delaware voters see their unconventional backgrounds and policy plans as credible alternatives or continue the state’s long pattern of supporting Democratic candidates for federal office.

name: Michigan Advance
title: ‘Facts first, conclusions second’: House committee begins review of ballot measure procedures
description: Michigan Rep. Mike Harris (R-Waterford Township) introduced a new House Select Committee, established to examine the rules and procedures of the Board of State Canvassers and the Bureau of Elections, specifically the sampling process used to verify signatures for ballot initiatives, at a first hearing of the committee on Tuesday afternoon. Harris’ approach,[...]
text:
Rep. Mike Harris (R-Waterford Township) introduces the purpose of a new House select committee, which he is chairing, to examine the sampling procedures used by the Board of State Canvassers and Bureau of Elections to determine the qualifications of ballot initiatives. Sept. 15, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.)Michigan Rep. Mike Harris (R-Waterford Township) introduced a new House Select Committee, established to examine the rules and procedures of the Board of State Canvassers and the Bureau of Elections, specifically the sampling process used to verify signatures for ballot initiatives, at a first hearing of the committee on Tuesday afternoon.
Harris’ approach, he said in an introductory statement, is “facts first, conclusions second.”
“That standard will apply to everyone,” he continued. “It applies to the petition proponents. It applies to the Bureau of Elections. It applies to the Board of State Canvassers. It applies to outside organizations, and I hope the members sitting on this committee take that standard to heart.” SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The committee was established after the Board of State Canvassers deadlocked on a vote to approve a ballot petition that would have established strict voter ID laws in the state. Because the canvassers could not come to a majority vote, that means the measure will not be on the November ballot. 
The decision was made on the margin of just a handful of signatures. In a sample of 1,000 votes, the petition was just three valid signatures shy of the needed margin. 
“We are not here to decide whether we agree with the proposed amendment,” Harris said. “We are not here to relitigate a political campaign, and we are not beginning this investigation with a conclusion about whether anyone did anything wrong. We are here because the Michigan House of Representatives determined that the rules, procedures, and practices used in this process deserve serious thought and oversight.”
Citizens-only voting petition sponsors look to 2028 after initiative fails before state canvassers

Earlier this year, a different ballot proposal, Michiganders for Money Out of Politics, did meet the threshold of valid signatures, though also by a small margin in the 1,000-vote sample. 
Some Republicans, including House Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Township), have alleged that conservative-leaning ballot measures have been treated unfairly in the signature verification process, but Harris said that he is going into his role as chair of the new committee as “very open-minded and unbiased.”
“I think that’s part of why I’m chairing this committee, that and my investigative background,” he said. “That is truly the role that I’m going to take, despite anybody else’s comments. My focus here is to get to the facts and understand the process.”
Harris said that the committee has invited representatives of both ballot measures to appear before the committee, though he noted that the scope of the committee would not be limited to those two petitions and would also include previous ballot measures.
New House committee to examine signature verification sampling process for ballot initiatives

Rep. Denise Mentzer (D-Mount Clemens), the minority vice chair of the committee, said that she did not personally have any concerns about what she saw with the state’s recent ballot measures, both this year or in past election cycles, but added that she believes it is good for government to regularly check itself and to make sure that the processes are functioning correctly. 
“I’m looking at the process. Is the process that was followed correct? Is the process the same as what’s been followed in other instances of constitutional ballot questions?” she said. “If the process is correct, as Chair Harris said, we’ve got no issue, right? If the process needs tweaking, we will figure that out as we review things. My goal isn’t to say whether the ballot initiative was correct or fair or whatever. I don’t care about the ballot initiative. I am here to look at, was the process followed appropriately and properly? That’s it.”
Following the hearing, Harris told reporters that he does not have any “predetermined outcomes on what we’re thinking for policy yet,” and that the outcome of the committee will be determined by what it finds.
“My goal by the end of this year is to make sure that we have a report that we submit to the body that has recommendations and findings on what we saw,” Harris said. “If everything’s working great, that’s what the report will show. If there’s what we think are inadequacies or things that are failing the citizens of the state of Michigan, we’ll report that as well, and there may be policy recommendations that come with that.”
Mentzer said that, if Democrats retake control of the state House in 2027, she would enthusiastically take over leadership of the committee to continue its work.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: State Treasury flagged $1.4B in improper payments; lawmakers say greater oversight needed
description: A pair of state lawmakers want to expand efforts to track improper payments by state agencies by requiring them to review and assess programs that fall outside of federal oversight of wasteful spending.
text:
State Treasurer Stacy Garrity announced Wednesday details on her office’s efforts to curb waste as it processes payments for more than 70 state agencies. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Captial-Star)Pennsylvania’s fiscal watchdog halted about 20,000 improper state government payments worth $1.4 billion last fiscal year.
State Treasurer Stacy Garrity announced Wednesday details about her office’s efforts to curb waste as it processes payments for more than 70 state agencies.
“During the last fiscal year, Treasury processed more than 21 million payments totaling $145 billion,” she said, noting that’s a payment ever three seconds.”As demonstrated by the results of the Payment Production and Improper Payments report, Treasury does not provide an automatic rubber stamp when payments are requested.”
A pair of state lawmakers want to expand efforts to track improper payments by state agencies by requiring them to review and assess programs that fall outside of federal oversight of wasteful spending.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“At a minimum, we must hold state government to the same level of responsibility which we hold ourselves to in our own personal finances,” state Sen. Kristen Phillips-Hill (R-York) said.
She noted the lawmakers spend a lot of time debating the budget, often facing disagreements within their own parties.
“But one thing that we should all agree on is … every single cent that we send out should be done properly. It should be transparent, and we must be accountable to the people,” Phillips-Hill said.
Phillips-Hill and Sen. Chris Gebhart (R-Lebanon) said they plan to introduce legislation that would require agencies to perform a review and assessment of each program that is not already subject to the federal Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019 to determine which programs are vulnerable to improper payments.
Additionally, each agency would be required to perform the assessment every two years and post it to a publicly accessible website with detailed information on each agency’s improper payment assessment.
Garrity, who is also the Republican nominee for governor, noted her office released the first ever public report on payment production and improper payments for the 2024-2025 fiscal year.
This year’s edition, for the 2025-2026 fiscal year, shows the Treasurer’s Office saved taxpayers $75 million by preventing payments that were directed to ineligible recipients, addressed incorrectly, duplicates, not supported by a contract or had other procedural and technical errors.
Garrity noted that while the value of the flagged payments was $1.4 billion, the savings were less because the majority went through after the errors were corrected.
Over the last five years, she said, the Treasurer’s Office has stopped nearly 120,000 improper payments totaling $5.5 billion with a savings of more than $325 million.
According to the report, the departments with the largest share of flawed payments are Revenue, at 49.9%; the Liquor Control Board, at 19.8%; Human Services, at 7.3%; the Pennsylvania State Employees Retirement System, at 5.9%; and Transportation at 4%.
While the process usually goes largely unnoticed, this year her office determined that it could not authorize more than $1 million in payments for security upgrades at Gov. Josh Shapiro’s private Montgomery County home. 
The security measures were installed at Shapiro’s Abington residence after state police recommended them following the April 2025 arson attack on the official Governor’s Residence in Harrisburg.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“My team and I did our due diligence and made our decisions as required by state law,” Garrity said. “After extensive back and forth with Pennsylvania State Police, as a result of Treasury’s inability to legally make this payment, the Attorney General issued a settlement agreement, and that was to save taxpayers’ costly litigation.”
Gebhard said Pennsylvania has a mixed track record of preventing improper payments. In 2019, the federal government found Pennsylvania had an error rate of 14% in Medicaid payments. That improved in subsequent years, he noted.
And he noted the commonwealth was cited in a 2024 report by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General for improperly claiming $551 million in Medicaid funds for its school-based health programs.
Commonwealth agencies are required to report improper payments only when they involve federal funds. Gebhard said the legislation he and Phillips-Hill are proposing would address that limitation.
In addition to biennial reporting, each program would be designated as having low, moderate or high risks for improper payments. For high-risk programs, agencies would be required to identify flawed payments and error rates and create a corrective action plan, Gebhard said.

title: FDA acknowledges estrogen patch shortage, says it’s working to increase supply
description: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration says it’s helping manufacturers increase the supply of estrogen-based hormonal patches and acknowledged a current nationwide shortage as more women seek hormonal therapies for symptoms related to menopause. In a release earlier this month, the FDA said it is expediting actions to increase supply, and said all six manufac[...]
text:
Women take photos at a Women’s History Month event in the East Room of the White House in March 2025. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration this month acknowledged a nationwide shortage of estrogen-based hormonal patches, which are prescribed for women experiencing symptoms related to menopause. (Photo by Win McNamee/Getty Images)The U.S. Food and Drug Administration says it’s helping manufacturers increase the supply of estrogen-based hormonal patches and acknowledged a current nationwide shortage as more women seek hormonal therapies for symptoms related to menopause.
In a release earlier this month, the FDA said it is expediting actions to increase supply, and said all six manufacturers are working to expand capacity and prioritize production of the patches.
Shifting attitudes on menopause drive lawmakers to push for new protections

“The FDA views increased interest in menopause treatment as an important development for women’s health and is working closely with manufacturers to help ensure that the supply of estradiol patches keeps pace with demand,” the release said.
Menopause typically occurs between the ages of 45 and 55, according to the National Institute on Aging, when a woman stops having menstrual periods. That hormonal change can cause symptoms such as hot flashes, night sweats, bone density loss, insomnia and more. Estradiol transdermal patches worn on the skin can replace estrogen lost through menopause and reduce those symptoms for some women.
Stateline reported in May that more awareness of menopause and its effects was leading to more states introducing legislation around the topic to mandate more insurance coverage for treatment and to create more workplace accommodations. At that time, the FDA did not list the patches in its list of shortages — this month marks the first time the agency has acknowledged a shortage. The American Society of Health-System Pharmacists first noted a shortage in January, two months after the FDA removed the treatment from its longtime “black box” warning status.
As of May, the National Menopause Foundation said more than 60 pieces of legislation related to menopause had been introduced nationwide this year. Twenty-six, and 26 states have enacted menopause-related laws since 2019, and more bills are expected to be introduced in the upcoming 2027 legislative sessions.
Stateline reporter Kelcie Moseley-Morris can be reached at kmoseley@stateline.org.
