title: Three Brothers Turn a Family Tradition into Hugs for Delaware’s Heroes
description: Hugs for Our Heroes is a story about how remembrance can grow. What began with three grandsons honoring their grandfather has become an effort to recognize many of Delaware’s military veterans. By John Riddle A simple family tradition inspired by love and remembrance has grown into a philanthropic mission dedicated to honoring Delaware veterans. Hugs for Our[...]
text:
Hugs for Our Heroes is a story about how remembrance can grow. What began with three grandsons honoring their grandfather has become an effort to recognize many of Delaware’s military veterans.
By John Riddle
A simple family tradition inspired by love and remembrance has grown into a philanthropic mission dedicated to honoring Delaware veterans.
Hugs for Our Heroes was founded by brothers Lucas, Jonas and Blake Karpinski in tribute to their grandfather, a Korean War veteran. Each Christmas, the family places a wreath on his grave, a meaningful gesture that keeps his memory and military service alive.
The brothers now want to extend that same recognition to other veterans throughout Delaware.
“Our commitment is to continue this wreath-laying tradition for Delaware veterans to honor their military service,” the organization explains on its website.
That commitment is at the heart of Hugs for Our Heroes, which focuses on community engagement, service and the creation of meaningful experiences that bring people together. Although its inspiration began with one veteran and one family, its mission reflects a much larger belief: Every person who served deserves to be remembered and appreciated.
For the Karpinski brothers, supporting veterans is also a way to strengthen the community. The organization emphasizes the importance of connection, collaboration and compassion, particularly when creating opportunities to recognize those who served in the military.
“We believe that strong communities are built through connection, collaboration and care,” the Hugs for Our Heroes website states.
Those qualities can be especially important when it comes to veterans. Military service often requires long separations from family, personal sacrifices and a willingness to face difficult and dangerous circumstances. While national observances such as Veterans Day and Memorial Day provide opportunities for widespread recognition, local programs can help ensure that veterans are remembered throughout the year.
Community-based efforts also allow residents to participate personally. Placing a wreath, attending an event, volunteering or making a donation may seem like a small gesture, but each action sends a message that military service has not been forgotten.
Hugs for Our Heroes seeks to create engaging experiences through thoughtful planning and what it describes as a people-first approach. Its activities are designed to unite participants while keeping veterans and their contributions at the center of the organization’s work.
The organization’s website currently promotes a golf-related event and invites supporters who cannot participate on the course to contribute through donations. The event offers another way for community members to gather around the group’s mission while helping its veteran-support initiatives.
Local businesses are also helping Hugs for Our Heroes expand its reach. Birdie’s Links and Drinks, located at 320 Auto Park Drive, is listed as a gold sponsor. The Middletown-area entertainment and dining venue offers food, drinks and indoor golf in a casual setting.
Business sponsorships can play an important role in community organizations by helping cover program and event expenses, attracting new supporters and introducing the mission to a wider audience. They also demonstrate that honoring veterans is a shared responsibility that can involve families, nonprofit groups, residents and businesses.
At its core, Hugs for Our Heroes is a story about how remembrance can grow. What began with three grandsons honoring their grandfather has become an effort to recognize many of Delaware’s military veterans.
The Christmas wreath placed on one Korean War veteran’s grave represents more than a seasonal family custom. It symbolizes gratitude, continuity and the promise that service will be remembered.
Through Hugs for Our Heroes, Lucas, Jonas and Blake Karpinski are carrying their grandfather’s legacy forward, one veteran, one wreath and one caring community at a time.
Additional information about the organization, its events and ways to help is available at HugsForOurHeroes.com.

name: National
title: Trump admin aims to shift homelessness grants toward addiction treatment, enforcement
description: In its latest effort to overhaul federal homelessness funding, the Trump administration is proposing to provide more money to localities that prioritize treatment-first policies such as sober living, more cooperation with law enforcement and more temporary and transitional housing.  It’s a reversal from a decade-long federal approach known as Housing First t[...]
text:
A campsite is seen in Anchorage, Alaska, last year. The Trump administration has proposed a major shift in homelessness grants. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)In its latest effort to overhaul federal homelessness funding, the Trump administration is proposing to provide more money to localities that prioritize treatment-first policies such as sober living, more cooperation with law enforcement and more temporary and transitional housing. 
It’s a reversal from a decade-long federal approach known as Housing First that sought to permanently house people experiencing homelessness without requiring sobriety or participation in treatment programs as a condition.
The Trump administration has been attempting to overhaul federal funding for homelessness programs in this direction over the past two years but had suffered defeats in court that stalled its efforts to do so in 2025 and 2026.
In a notice posted in the Federal Register on Sept. 11, the Department of Housing and Urban Development argued that current policies aren’t working and said some states and localities have already shifted toward a treatment-based approach to homelessness. The agency will take public comments through Oct. 13.
Under the proposal, the department would change the bonuses it gives to state and local areas that participate in the Continuum of Care program, a federal grant initiative to fight homelessness. The department would incentivize efforts to provide transitional housing with services “concentrating on improving employment income and meeting behavioral healthcare needs.” It would also incentivize addiction treatment and recovery services, sober housing and partnerships with law enforcement.
With homelessness rising, new federal rules could benefit states that take tougher approaches

HUD pointed to policies in Anchorage, Alaska; Houston; Portland, Oregon; and San Francisco as evidence that states and cities are already shifting their homelessness responses toward public camping restrictions with emphasis on treatment and recovery as a condition to housing support.
That shift was made possible by the U.S. Supreme Court’s City of Grants Pass v. Johnson decision in 2024, which allowed local governments to enforce public camping bans. Since then, more than 350 cities and 14 states have adopted laws or measures to crack down on street homelessness. 
HUD had tried twice previously to change the application process for grants along similar lines, but a federal court ruled against the attempts, saying they violated required procedures. 
One lawsuit against HUD’s efforts was brought by a coalition of 22 states and the District of Columbia, while another was filed by local governments and homelessness organizations, including the National Alliance to End Homelessness and the National Low Income Housing Coalition. 
State officials joining the lawsuit were from Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Kentucky, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington and Wisconsin, plus the District of Columbia. 
The Obama administration made Housing First initiatives the predominant federal homelessness policy. The Trump administration argues that it hasn’t worked and that chronic homelessness has increased since 2013. 
But housing advocacy groups say that Housing First initiatives are a proven, bipartisan strategy that can lead to better outcomes and reduce taxpayer spending on emergency services and the criminal legal system.
The National Low Income Housing Coalition pointed to a 2020 review of 26 studies that found Housing First programs decreased homelessness by 88% and improved housing stability by 41% compared with Treatment First programs.

text:
El pastor demócrata Adam Hamilton y el senador republicano Roger Marshall debaten el 12 de septiembre de 2026 en la Feria Estatal de Kansas en Hutchinson. (Foto por Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)Traducido por Claudia Amaro.
HUTCHINSON — El senador republicano titular Roger Marshall y el reverendo Adam Hamilton, demócrata, se enfrentaron el sábado ante una multitud bulliciosa que defendía sus posturas sobre aranceles, la guerra en Irán y la política partidista.
Los dos candidatos de los principales partidos que se postulan al Senado de los Estados Unidos aparecieron juntos en su primer debate tras las primarias, ante cientos de personas que llenaron las gradas de la Feria Estatal de Kansas.
La balanza de la asistencia a veces se inclinaba a favor de Hamilton, ya que la gente abucheaba las respuestas de Marshall.
Marshall defendió su historial en la agricultura y se vio obligado a confrontar su lealtad al presidente Donald Trump, aunque dijo que no estaba de acuerdo con la promesa de Trump de ofrecer $5,000 a cada adulto estadounidense si los republicanos ganaban las elecciones intermedias.
“No es la primera vez que no estoy de acuerdo con el presidente Trump, y probablemente no será —” dijo Marshall antes de ser interrumpido por los gritos de la multitud. “Sabes, en cambio, me voy a enfocar en los empleos en Kansas. Me voy a enfocar en proteger la agricultura y la industria ganadera de Kansas.”
Hamilton dijo: “Esto es exactamente lo que está mal en Washington, D.C., en este momento.”
El debate fue conducido por WIBW 580 Radio y contó con preguntas de un panel de tres periodistas, entre ellos el reportero senior de Kansas Reflector, Tim Carpenter. Ausente del escenario estaba David Graham, un candidato libertario al Senado de los Estados Unidos por Overland Park, quien no fue invitado a participar.
Marshall está terminando su primer periodo en el Senado de los Estados Unidos, habiendo servido previamente dos periodos en la Cámara de Representantes y trabajado como ginecólogo obstetra en Great Bend antes de eso. Hamilton es el fundador de una de las iglesias metodistas unidas más grandes del país, Church of the Resurrection, que es una operación multicampus con sede en Leawood.
Adam Hamilton, un demócrata que compite para el Senado de los Estados Unidos, el 12 de septiembre de 2026 en el escenario del debate de la Feria Estatal de Kansas en Hutchinson. (Foto por Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
Hamilton superó a otros nueve candidatos demócratas en la primaria de agosto y recaudó más fondos que Marshall.
Marshall intentó presentar a Hamilton como antiagricultura, en contra de la industria ganadera y del petróleo y el gas.
“Si fuera por él, iría a ponerles una bolsa de plástico a la boca de estas vacas lecheras aquí atrás”, dijo Marshall, señalando el edificio de ganado en el recinto ferial estatal.
Hamilton criticó duramente el historial de Marshall en el Senado de Estados Unidos, por su apoyo a los aranceles de Trump, su inacción ante la guerra en Irán y los recortes en la atención médica y la asistencia alimentaria.
Dijo que la reciente decisión de la administración Trump de importar carne de res de México fue “una bofetada” para los productores de ganado de Kansas y “llegó exactamente en el momento equivocado.”
Dijo que Marshall fue elegido para ser un campeón de los habitantes de Kansas, no “un portavoz de la Casa Blanca.”
El senador estadounidense republicano Roger Marshall aparece el 12 de septiembre de 2026 en un debate en la Feria Estatal de Kansas, en Hutchinson. (Foto por Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
Marshall dijo que la decisión se debió a la sequía, al “rebaño de ganado más pequeño de mi vida” y a la “sobrerregulación gubernamental.” El partido Demócrata ha “estrangulado la industria agrícola”, dijo.
“Mi oponente es demasiado despierto, demasiado débil y no representa nada”, dijo Marshall.
Pero Hamilton mantenía firme la creencia de que el país iba en la dirección equivocada.
“Debes tener valor”, dijo Hamilton, “y el valor es cuando te enfrentas a tu presidente y a tu partido y dices: ‘Esto está lastimando a la gente en casa’. Y lo dices, aunque tu presidente te vaya a acosar, molestarte e insultarte. Aun así, dices: ‘Esto no está bien.’”
Graham, el libertario que aparecerá en la boleta electoral de noviembre como opción para el Senado de Estados Unidos, observó el debate desde las gradas del pabellón.
Dijo que es una mejor opción para los votantes que Marshall o Hamilton porque no estaría atado al liderazgo ni del Partido Republicano ni del Partido Demócrata. Eso le permitiría hacer lo mejor por los habitantes de Kansas, dijo.
Graham, quien señaló que no es dueño de una casa fuera de Kansas, dijo que, si hubiera podido subir al escenario, su declaración inicial habría sido sobre la necesidad de menos gobierno y más libertad.
“Cuando hagamos eso, tendremos una empresa libre que se encargue de muchos de estos problemas por sí misma”, dijo Graham. “Problemas relacionados con la inflación, derivados de la sobrerregulación. Problemas relacionados con el costo de la atención médica. Nunca hemos intentado realmente el sistema de libre empresa, así que esa sería mi declaración inicial. Creo en la transparencia en el gobierno y en que deberíamos tener una reforma seria de la justicia penal.”
Hamilton y Marshall también respondieron preguntas sobre sus múltiples hogares — la propiedad de vacaciones de Marshall en Florida y la casa de vacaciones de Hamilton en los Ozarks de Missouri—, así como sobre las controversias que han surgido durante sus campañas, la atención médica, el mercado laboral, la inmigración y la deuda nacional.
Sherman Smith contribuyó a este informe.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Political Notebook: Teachers vs. Smith & Wesson
description: The state's largest teachers union is now the single biggest financial backer of keeping a 2024 gun control law on the books.
text:
PUBLIC SECTOR UNIONS in particular are key players on the state’s political landscape, so it’s no surprise to see a burst of activity by organized labor heading into the November election. And this year, along with backing labor-friendly candidates, unions are deploying significant energy and resources on the thicket of ballot questions.
Unions have been some of the loudest critics of a proposal to place a tighter limit on state tax collections, wary that any changes to Beacon Hill’s spending approach could spell cuts for their membership. Another question is itself a labor matter, seeking to allow staff at the state’s public defender agency to unionize. Yet a couple of unions have taken an even broader approach to the issues facing voters in November.
The Massachusetts Teachers Association this summer gave $500,000 to Yes for a Safe Massachusetts, the campaign urging voters to keep a 2024 gun reform law on the books in the face of an attempted repeal. That makes the state’s largest teacher union by far the effort’s biggest financial backer, far outpacing contributions from groups like the Everytown For Gun Safety Action Fund and the Alliance For Gun Responsibility.
MTA delegates supported the spending at their annual meeting in May. The union “has consistently taken stances to support the safety of educators and students through gun controls,” it wrote in a summary of the votes.
It’s not the only educator group to back the tighter gun law. On Tuesday, the Boston Teachers Union endorsed keeping the gun measure on the books.
“Along with other frontline workers, educators and students are impacted by gun violence every day, whether that is navigating the trauma of violence in the community, participating in active shooter drills, or experiencing the fear created by school shootings elsewhere in the country,” Ruth Zakarin, chair of the Yes on 9 campaign, said in a statement.
On the other side of the issue, the biggest single donor to the campaign pushing the repeal question remains firearms manufacturer Smith & Wesson. The former Massachusetts company – Smith & Wesson decamped from its longtime Springfield headquarters for Tennessee in 2023 – contributed $50,000 two years ago, when the effort launched. (A reminder that Question 9 is a bit quirky: Unlike all other questions, proponents here want “no” votes, which will erase the law Gov. Maura Healey signed. A “yes” vote will keep the law on the books.)
Fresh off its victory two years ago on a question eliminating the use of MCAS exams as a high school graduation requirement, MTA has spread out its money this cycle.
At the same time that it steers member dues toward fighting a tax cap reform measure unpopular on Beacon Hill, the union has also dropped cash backing another proposal causing agita among top Democrats: It donated $30,000 toward the campaign to subject the governor’s office and Legislature to the public records law. The National Association of Government Employees, or NAGE, also backed Question 1 with a $25,000 contribution.
No, Question 1 has not actually generated the most spending so far
If you took a passing glance at the official state campaign finance tracker for ballot questions, you might reasonably come away with the impression that supporters of wrenching open access to gubernatorial and legislative records have already spent more than $5 million, the most among any of the nine measures on the ballot.
That would be, to some, a shocking revelation. As much as top House and Senate Democrats have griped about the proposal, there’s no formal opposition campaign, which always puts a damper on how much cash supporters are willing to burn. Plus, two years ago, Auditor Diana DiZoglio and her supporters spent less than half a million dollars on a ballot question voters overwhelmingly approved that allowsher to probe the Legislature, so a tenfold jump for that proposal’s spiritual successor wouldn’t make much sense.
As it turns out, the eye-catching total is simply the result of a record-keeping quirk.
The Coalition for Healthy Democracy campaign committee, which drafted the records proposal (Question 1) before handing it off to DiZoglio last year, supports both that question and a separate measure seeking to replace the state’s partisan primary elections with a single, all-party primary (Question 3). It’s already spent more than $4.7 million altogether, and OCPF’s public-facing dashboard counts that amount twice: once under Question 1, and a second time under Question 3.
There is a small disclaimer at the top of the page, but the effect is that two separate questions look like they’ve each received the entirety of a pot of money that was in fact split between them.
It’s especially odd given that, if a committee supports or opposes more than one proposal, OCPF allows it to delineate which dollars have been spent for which question when filing reports. Those answers are not made public, though an OCPF spokesperson said the agency’s IT department is working on it.
Jesse Littlewood, the campaign manager for the Coalition for Healthy Democracy, told CommonWealth Beacon that a “majority” of the group’s spending in 2025 and 2026 went toward supporting the all-party primary question.
“We’re still active and spending a portion of our resources on [Question 1],” he said, but with DiZoglio and her allies leading the charge there, “our focus is on Question 3.”
Curious about rent control finances? Wait ‘til next year
Real estate industry groups and landlords did not like the prospect of rent control coming back from the dead in the form of a strict statewide cap, so much so that they vowed to spend up to $30 million to defeat the measure at the ballot box.
As for how close they actually got to that promise before the Supreme Judicial Court rendered the issue moot by tossing the question from the ballot in June, you’ll have to wait a few months longer to find out.
Neither the campaign finance committee organized to oppose the ballot question nor the one that backed it has filed any report with state campaign finance regulators since January 2026, and they won’t be required to do so until January 2027.
OCPF has a series of deadlines in the weeks before and after the election that force more insight into initiative petition finances, but those only apply to measures that are actually on the ballot. Campaigns working on questions that were once in the running but will no longer go before voters — including rent control as well as a proposed legislative stipend reform — only need to file year-end reports, which will cover the entirety of 2026.
Spending for and against ballot questions is heavily backloaded to the days and weeks just before Election Day, so don’t expect any bombshells when we finally learn what was spent on the issue before the SJC booted the question from the ballot. But it seems a safe bet to assume that real estate power players and rent control activists each splashed some cash in the first six months of the year.

title: Alaska plans to limit advance reservations for public cabins, update system
description: If you use Alaska’s public cabins, get ready for a change.  On Oct. 1, the Alaska Department of Natural Resources will begin limiting how far in advance reservations can be made to three months, down from six months.  The only exceptions to the three-month reservation window will include the Wood-Tikchik Region and cabins on Afognak […]
text:
Camping Cove Cabin at Point Bridget State Park near Juneau is seen on July 18, 2020. (James Brooks photo/Alaska Beacon)If you use Alaska’s public cabins, get ready for a change. 
On Oct. 1, the Alaska Department of Natural Resources will begin limiting how far in advance reservations can be made to three months, down from six months. 
The only exceptions to the three-month reservation window will include the Wood-Tikchik Region and cabins on Afognak and Shuyak Islands in the Kodiak region, which will continue to allow reservations up to six months in advance.
The change is part of a shift to a new online booking system and website that also opens Oct. 1. Cabin-seeking Alaskans will be unable to change, modify or cancel their existing reservations from Sept. 28 through Sept. 30 as part of the transition.
Beginning Oct. 1, reservations for all facilities can be made for Jan. 1, 2027 and the 3-month rolling window will begin.
Wendy Sailors, community engagement manager for Alaska State Parks, said by email that the new shorter reservation window is the result of feedback from Alaskans who said “that it is difficult to plan that far out, often people forget that they had the reservation and have to cancel last minute or just don’t use it, etc. So in addition to the three-month rolling reservation window, we are incorporating a few new features like an email reminder 7 days out.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Will Massachusetts go deep in the health care affordability playoffs?
description: Like the Red Sox season, the health care picture in the state this year has been marked by big ups and downs.
text:
THE PROSPECTS FOR meaningful reforms addressing health care affordability in the state feel bit a bit like the chances the Red Sox have in the postseason: The local nine are a near-lock to make the playoffs, but whether they can advance even past the first round is harder to count on.  
There have been some promising initial moves on health care policy, but whether state leaders can translate that momentum into tangible wins when it comes to greater health care affordability now hangs in the balance.  Key actions by the Legislature and several state agencies will determine whether we look back on this year as a success or failure for state health policy actions—especially in starting to tackle commercial health care affordability, arguably our biggest challenge right now. 
Like the Red Sox season, the health care picture in the state this year has been marked by big ups and downs.  
The downs have been significant: double-digit premium increases for families and businesses; some legal immigrants excluded from subsidized Connector coverage; and middle-class residents priced out of Connector plans altogether after Congress failed to renew the expanded COVID-era federal subsidies.  
Add to that the loss of bedside caregivers as TPS protections lapsed for Haitian and other immigrant groups. And the CVS-Mass General Brigham MinuteClinic deal, moving forward without pricing or revenue-flow constraints, will surely add to the bottom lines of those two corporate entities, while it is much less clear that it will do much to address the state’s primary care shortage. 
The ups include the limited rollback by the Department of Insurance of prior-authorization burdens facing patients. Beyond that, the positive developments remain works in progress. On Beacon Hill, the Senate and House have each passed a primary care bill responding to the recommendation of a state Primary Care Task Force. And members of the governor’s Health Care Affordability Working Group held private discussions that produced arguably quite tame initial recommendations in early August. She has promised more by later in the year. 
Whether either the primary care or health care affordability efforts land on the positive side of the ledger depends entirely on what happens between now and year’s end.  
The primary care bills  
The primary care bills passed by each branch of the Legislature now sits with a joint House and Senate conference committee, which must reconcile the two versions. Both have real merit. They each increase the flow of dollars to primary care clinicians (on slightly different required schedules), mandate higher payments to community health centers, and seek to expand the primary care workforce pipeline. Importantly, they also attempt to move primary care payment away from fee-for-service. The Senate does so through a Health Policy Commission-monitored capitation model, while the House looks to the Department of Insurance to oversee a value-based payment approach. 
Unfortunately, both bills share a major weakness: Neither requires primary care dollars to actually be redistributed away from hospitals and specialists while stopping overall health care spending from growing beyond the annual growth benchmark set by the state. 
The Senate’s approach is to establish a distinct primary care spending target. And if providers or insurers do not hit the target, they could get placed on a performance improvement plan to try to get them there. But the language of the Senate bill calls for escalating civil penalties only if the improvement plan is totally ignored or given only minimal effort; the penalties are not tied to simply failing to meet the spending target. 
The House version is even weaker—as it left financial penalties out of the scheme entirely—even for failing to make a good faith effort on a performance improvement plan.  
I would much rather see a firmer requirement that is backed by actual penalties for failing to redistribute spending towards primary care—especially in a year when the overall state spending growth target is breached. Maybe the legislative conference committee can find a solution that will get us there. Otherwise, the primary care spending target risks becoming another well-intentioned benchmark that does little to change where health care dollars actually go. 
The Health Care Affordability Working Group 
The governor’s Health Care Affordability Working Group recommendations look more like a placeholder list than a serious affordability strategy. Much of the early-August wish list amounts to telling various groups to keep talking, with the hope that they will eventually land on strategies for innovative care delivery, moving stuck patients out of inpatient beds, workforce investments, lowering drug costs, and using AI to cut costs. In short: it looked like a working group recommending more working groups. 
Most notably absent is any real acknowledgment of what is actually driving Massachusetts health care spending: high provider prices and the market power of a handful of large, prestigious systems. 
I had hoped for a recommendation along the lines of a fixed total annual revenue budget covering all Massachusetts commercial and Medicaid hospital patients. As a new concept for our state, it might make most sense to start with the most financially challenged hospitals. That does not appear to be in the cards yet, but the idea may not be too far down the road. Pairing this hospital payment model with a common fund for primary care could help our system deliver better care while capturing real administrative savings—and demonstrate to Washington that both concepts could work for Medicare as well. 
But two recommendations from the working group give me some hope. 
The first directs the Division of Insurance to set default out-of-network payment rates by regulation, covering areas the federal surprise-billing law enacted in 2020 left untouched. In Massachusetts, surprise bills have traditionally come mostly from physicians, but the biggest offender today is ground ambulance services, whose out-of-network pricing badly needs reining in. And though Massachusetts hospitals are almost always in-network, some believe the DOI’s effort here could also help providers and insurers negotiate in an environment that may be more likely to achieve fairer and more reasonable hospital prices. 
The second promising recommendation asks the Group Insurance Commission, which oversees coverage for public employees, albeit without much detail, to develop a system of “fair hospital prices” for its enormous book of commercial business—covering state employees and a substantial number of municipal employees. 
The GIC has options: price caps tied to a multiple of Medicare rates; reference pricing tied to the market median, putting pressure on high-priced providers to lower their prices or lose market share; or refusing to pay for low-value care while holding beneficiaries harmless. 
Success in implementing one or more of these pricing constraints for GIC beneficiaries could have effects well beyond those public employees and their families. It could demonstrate that insurers and self-insured employers have practical tools for reining in hospital prices and, in turn, putting pressure on the broader commercial market to follow. 
But there is an important caveat: GIC savings cannot come at the expense of everyone else. If hospitals respond by simply shifting higher prices onto the rest of the commercial market, the policy will have moved costs around rather than controlled them. If that becomes the game, there may be little choice but to move toward a fixed annual revenue model for hospitals across the entire market. 
If the Legislature can get a primary care bill across the finish line that includes an effective total-cost-of-care limit tied to meaningful redistribution toward primary care—and if the Division of Insurance and Group Insurance Commission can actually follow through on the most promising affordability recommendations that they have been charged to carry out—there could be real progress on health care affordability before year’s end. 
That would feel a lot like not just making playoffs, but getting at least past the first round. 
Paul Hattis is a senior fellow at the Lown Institute and co-host of the “Health or Consequences” episodes of The Codcast.

name: VTDigger
title: Step by step, Stacy Emerson is achieving her dream of becoming a registered nurse
description:
After nearly twenty years working as an LNA, Stacy decided it was time for a change. Now a nursing student at Vermont State, she’s won a prestigious DAISY Award and is on track to complete her associate degree this spring—with plans to become a Registered Nurse, close to home.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Step by step, Stacy Emerson is achieving her dr[...]
text:
Stacy Emerson at graduation with her instructor and mentor, Nancy Noble.
Stacy Emerson describes herself as “a bit of a mother hen.” She’s on the older end of her classmates in her nursing cohort at Vermont State University (Vermont State), and she’s always looking out for her friends and coworkers. The friendships she’s formed among her nursing peers are so strong that, with their encouragement, she’s continuing on to complete her associate degree and plans to attain licensure as a Registered Nurse after graduation this spring. 
“They said, ‘we all have to stick together,’ and even though I wasn’t sure I would be able to continue on after my Practical Nursing Certificate, they encouraged me and convinced me we could all do it together,” Stacy says. 
Stacy takes her classes at Vermont State Lyndon and does her clinical rotations in Newport, near her home in Derby. She just finished the first year in Vermont State’s stackable nursing program and received her Practical Nursing Certificate. Now, she’s enrolled again and hopes to complete her associate degree this spring. 
From LNA to RN, advancing in nursing was always the goal
For close to twenty years, Stacy worked as an LNA in long-term care facilities in Newport, and then in Barton. She’s continued to work at Maple Lane Nursing Home in Barton part-time while attending school full-time. In 2019, she got certified through North Country Career Center as a Medication Nursing Assistant (MNA). 
“Nursing school has been a long-term goal of mine,” she said. “I worked for years on the prerequisites, taking a couple of classes here and there at Community College of Vermont and always balancing the time I had with my daughter. A few years ago, I decided I just needed to do it. I’m getting older and LNA work is really hard on your body. I needed to make a change.” 
She first applied to Vermont State University in 2019 but wasn’t accepted into the nursing program. She tried again a few years later, and was able to start classes last year. 
“I thought that ship sailed in high school” 
Stacy is an adult learner and she wasn’t sure what her options would be for financial aid. That’s where Marti Kingsley, an outreach counselor with VSAC’s Educational Opportunity Center (EOC), came in. The EOC provides guidance to adults who are interested in college or training. “When I applied, I didn’t even know you could get scholarships as an adult,” Stacy shared. “I thought that ship sailed in high school.” 
The ship had not sailed. Marti helped Stacy identify financial aid, including scholarships and grants, that would help her cover her tuition and other expenses. Last school year, Stacy received workforce development funding through VSAC’s Vermont Trades program, and a Curtis Fund scholarship. She was surprised and delighted to learn that the Vermont Trades funding would cover her full tuition. 
This year, she was awarded the Vermont Rural Health Transformation Tuition Benefit, which provides financing for students to pursue education in eligible health related fields who are committed to serving rural Vermont communities following degree completion. “I grew up in Newport and went to North Country Union High School,” Stacy noted. “I’m planning to stay and live and work in this area. To achieve my goal and to have the support to do it means a lot to me.”
Step by step, Stacy moved forward
Stacy says that she’s working on her confidence. She struggled with school as a teen and overcame a lot of obstacles in her younger years to get where she is today. Her daughter was born just two days after she turned 19, and she notes that she worked hard to make her life better and figure out how to support herself and her child. “I was on my own and I knew resources were limited,” she said “So I knew I had to find something to make a living and a long-term career.” 
That something was becoming a LNA, then working toward her MNA, and eventually admission to nursing school. When she studied for her MNA, her instructor at North Country Career Center was Nancy Noble. Nancy, also a clinical instructor in Vermont State’s nursing program, made a big impression on Stacy. 
The student DAISY Award and support from her friends and family boosted Stacy’s confidence
“Nancy is a great mentor and I’m lucky I was able to have her at North Country and at Vermont State,” Stacy said. Stacy graduated with honors with her Practical Nursing certificate in June, which was a huge confidence boost. Another came when Nancy nominated Stacy for the prestigious student DAISY Award, which Stacy won. “I have no idea how,” she added. “But I’m so proud of myself and impressed with myself!” The award was announced at her Practical Nursing pinning ceremony, and again at Stacy’s graduation. And Stacy’s daughter—now in her early 20s—is proud of her mom’s hard work. 
With those achievements and the encouragement of classmates and family, Stacy is continuing on to complete her associate degree this year. She says her husband is incredibly supportive, doing everything he can to help her out—even bringing her plates of food when she’s holed up in her room studying. Stacy’s parents help wherever they can with bills, and her best friend Trish, a nurse herself, helps Stacy study and answers her questions wherever she can. 
“I have a great support system,” Stacy shared. “Even with that, it’s hard work. But if you believe in yourself and work hard, you can do it.”
Stacy is knee-deep in her fall semester right now and is looking forward to finishing up in the spring. It will be a big moment when she walks across the stage with her degree—and one she’s been looking forward to for a long time. 
“Just because you’re a little older than your peers doesn’t mean that you can’t succeed,” she added.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Records show Kansas election officials refused call to police gender markers on voter files
description: TOPEKA — A Kansas Republican Party officer called the Secretary of State’s Office in July to ask why a new state law that regulates gender markers wasn’t being applied to the voter registration of a transgender Democrat running for a Kansas House seat. Senior election officials disagreed with his interpretation of Senate Bill 244, the […]
text:
Clay Barker, general counsel for the Secretary of State's Office, appears at a Jan. 27, 2026, meeting of the House Elections Committee. Barker authored an internal legal analysis that says election officials have no duty to enforce a new state law that requires gender markers on government records to align with an individual's sex assigned at birth. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — A Kansas Republican Party officer called the Secretary of State’s Office in July to ask why a new state law that regulates gender markers wasn’t being applied to the voter registration of a transgender Democrat running for a Kansas House seat.
Senior election officials disagreed with his interpretation of Senate Bill 244, the new law that requires bathroom use and gender markers on government documents to align with an individual’s sex assigned at birth.
Clay Barker, general counsel for the Secretary of State’s Office, concluded that while the law requires voter registrations to reflect an individual’s sex assigned at birth, election officers are not responsible for enforcement. He inadvertently revealed his legal analysis in records obtained by American Oversight, a nonprofit government watchdog group based in Washington, D.C., which shared the records with Kansas Reflector.
State officials say gender designations are a nonfactor for voter registration and candidate filings, but the records point to the far-reaching and uncertain implications of legislation passed in haste earlier this year without public input.
“Every Kansan deserves a government that treats them with dignity and provides clear, public information about how its laws affect their rights,” said Chioma Chukwu, executive director of American Oversight. “Protecting against the quiet erosion of the fundamental right to vote is central to our mission and why we sought these records.”
Under SB 244, individuals who use a bathroom that aligns with their gender but not their sex assigned at birth can face fines, jail time and — under a bounty provision — civil lawsuits from “aggrieved” individuals. The law also invalidated hundreds of driver’s licenses for those who had changed their gender markers.
American Oversight sent requests to the Kansas Department of Revenue, Kansas Department of Health and Environment, and the Secretary of State’s Office for records regarding the implementation of SB 244. Only the Secretary of State’s Office has complied with the requests.
Barker responded with emails that include an exchange between him and Bryan Caskey, the state elections director. They show Roger Lomshek, a Pittsburg resident who serves as treasurer for the Kansas Republican Party, called the office about Avery Rowland, a Democrat from Girard.
“Roger Lomshek is alleging that SB 244 applies to voter registration and is questioning why a county is not following this law,” Caskey wrote in a July 6 email. “I do not agree with his interpretation.”
Barker attempted to redact his answer to Caskey by placing a black box over it in the PDF file he provided to American Oversight. The file allows the black box to be deleted, revealing his legal analysis.
Clay Barker, general counsel for the Secretary of State’s Office, attempted to redact his legal analysis, but sent a file that allows the black box to be selected and removed. (Document obtained by American Oversight)
Barker wrote that the law “mandates the use of biological sex at birth anywhere” that terms like “gender” are used.
“So gender on voter registration form or declaration of intent for precinct committee person — the voter or candidate must use biological sex at birth,” Barker wrote. “The duty is on the voter or candidate.”
“The statute does not place a duty on the county election officer to verify information on the voter registration,” he added.
The analysis was silent on whether anyone else would have the authority to invalidate a voter registration by enforcing the law. In response to questions for this story, Whitney Tempel, a spokeswoman for the Secretary of State’s Office, said “gender discrepancies can never be a basis for denying anyone the right to vote.”
“What the records show is concerning: the Secretary of State’s own office privately analyzed how this law’s requirements could impact voters, while publicly maintaining that the law had nothing to do with the office’s responsibilities,” Chukwu said. “The Secretary of State’s vague assurance that gender discrepancies will not be used to deny anyone the right to vote is no substitute for clear, written guidance. Kansans should not have to rely on informal assurances when their right to vote is at stake.”
Danedri Herbert, a spokeswoman for the Attorney General’s Office, offered a similar assessment.
“An individual’s sex is entirely irrelevant to being able to vote or to file to run for the Legislature,” she said.
Rob Fillion, executive director of the Kansas GOP, didn’t respond to an email sent Thursday or a phone call and text Tuesday asking to speak with Lomshek about his interest in Rowland’s voter registration.
Rowland said Lomshek’s interest in her was “all news to me” but that she “kind of knew this might become an issue.” She said she knows who Lomshek is from the Crawford County political scene but that they have had no personal interactions.
Rowland last updated her voter registration in 2023, she said, after she changed her name. She said her file would reflect that the gender listed on her driver’s license at the time was “male.” That would mean she is complying with the new law.
She is running against Dan Muter, of Pittsburg, who defeated incumbent Rep. Ken Collins, of Mulberry, in the GOP primary.
“There are much bigger issues in the world,” Rowland said. “Transgender folks are not the 1% of the world screwing everything up. I feel sorry for these people that their world is so small that I am the biggest thing in it. I’m more concerned about education and highways and economic opportunities than what’s on my driver’s license. I want everybody to succeed.”

A research program at University of Iowa is seeking information on arsenic levels in Iowa private wells. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)A University of Iowa research project is attempting to develop a better understanding of arsenic in private drinking wells in Iowa and offering landowners, in certain counties, free testing for their wells. 
Arsenic is a naturally occurring element found in soil and rock that has been linked to health risks, including cancer, from long-term exposure, even at small levels. Because private wells are not regulated, the chemical could be present in the well water at unsafe levels without property owners being aware of it.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to information from the university’s Integrated Network for Science, Information, and Geospatial Health Tracking, or INSIGHT program, some Iowa counties have limited private well testing data for arsenic, even though those counties border other areas with documented, unsafe levels of the chemical element. 
A news release about the new testing program said areas of north central Iowa have some of the highest rates of private wells with arsenic levels exceeding U.S. Environmental Protection Agency drinking water limits. 
“Where you live has a big impact on your exposure to arsenic in drinking water,” said David Cwiertny, the lead of Iowa INSIGHT. “Expanding arsenic testing in at-risk counties can support prevention strategies to improve public health outcomes.”
Private well owners in Mitchell, Floyd, Cedar, Benton, Plymouth and Jones counties can request the free kits from the INSIGHT website.
According to data from Iowa INSIGHT, 0% or 1% of private wells in these counties have been tested for arsenic. 
A map shows the percentage of private wells that have been tested for arsenic per county. The lighter the color, the greater percentage of wells have been tested. (Map courtesy of University of Iowa)
The research project website notes that the absence of testing should “not be interpreted as evidence of low risk.” 
The EPA limit for arsenic is 10 micrograms per liter. The agency holds that exposure to arsenic can lead to skin damage, circulatory issues and potentially “increased risk of getting cancer.”

A microgram, abbreviated as µg, is one thousandth of a milligram. 

The Iowa Private Well Grants program enabled the testing of more than 22,000 wells in Iowa between 2014 and 2024 and found that 11% of tested wells exceeded EPA’s maximum contaminant level and an additional 8.4% of tested wells had levels between 5–10 µg/L. 
The Iowa Department of Natural Resources estimates that 5.5% of the population relies on private wells for their drinking water. Private wells, unlike public drinking water systems, are not subject to regulations — meaning testing is up to the private well owners. 
Reverse osmosis water filtration systems, but not common pitcher filtration or whole-house carbon filtration systems, are effective at removing arsenic from drinking water. 
In addition to calling for private well owners to test their drinking water, Iowa INSIGHT recommends increased funding for the Private Well Grants program, which is run by DNR and offers free private well testing on a schedule. 
Other policy solutions proposed by Iowa INSIGHT include financial incentives for in-home water filtration systems, and local educational initiatives to bring greater awareness of arsenic levels in private wells.

name: Nevada Current
title: Voter ID ballot question returns to Nevadans for final approval
description: When they show up to polling places this fall, Nevadans will not be required to show a photo ID in order to cast their ballots. But it could be the last time that’s the case. Nevadans appear poised to embrace voter ID requirements. They overwhelmingly supported the idea two years ago, with 73% voting in […]
text:
(Photo: Jeniffer Solis/Nevada Current)When they show up to polling places this fall, Nevadans will not be required to show a photo ID in order to cast their ballots.
But it could be the last time that’s the case.
Nevadans appear poised to embrace voter ID requirements. They overwhelmingly supported the idea two years ago, with 73% voting in favor. But they need to pass it a second time for the requirement to go into effect.
Question 7 proposes amending the state constitution to include a requirement that Nevadans present government-issued photo identification before voting in-person. Question 7 would also require that voters using a mail ballot list the last four digits of their Nevada driver’s license number, the last four digits of their Social Security number, or a number provided to them by their county clerk when they registered to vote.
The ballot question has garnered relatively little coverage this election cycle, with no political action committees spending significant amounts of money in support or opposition.
Voter ID ballot questions typically pass when put before voters.
Supporters describe the proposal as a common sense election reform that may help restore people’s faith in the democratic process. Those opposed see it as a solution in search of a problem and say it will disenfranchise people who don’t have an acceptable form of ID.
According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, 36 states have laws requesting or requiring voters to show some form of identification at the polls. Strictness on the forms of ID accepted vary by state, but 21 states require photo identification and 15 states accept non-photo forms of identification, such as utility bills or bank statements that include a person’s name and address.
Nevada is among the 14 states that currently do not require any documentation. Signatures are used to verify identification.
Question 7 lists eight approved forms of government-approved IDs, including driver’s licenses, passports and tribal photo IDs. It also allows the Nevada State Legislature to approve other acceptable IDs, though they must still be government issued. The IDs must be current or not expired for more than four years, unless the voter is over 70, in which case the ID can be expired for any length of time.
Question 7 comes amid broader attacks from the Trump administration on state election systems, including a push to restrict who receives mail ballots and when they can be counted. Those efforts have largely been thwarted by litigation brought by Democratic states.
Full arguments in favor and in opposition of Question 7 will be available in voting materials sent by counties. A coalition that includes Good Trouble Vegas, League of Women Voters Nevada, Nevada NOW, and PLAN Action, Population Connection Action Fund, and Read Freely Nevada will also be hosting an event focused on Question 7 and Question 6 (the abortion rights initiative) at 2:30 p.m. on Sept. 19 at the Spring Valley Library

text:
The Ohio burgee. (Getty images file photo.)Every morning in the Ohio Capital Journal’s free newsletter, The Eye-Opener, we round up the news and commentary from across Ohio and around the country and world that is catching our attention. We call this feature Catching Our Eye, republished here.
Please subscribe to our free daily newsletter to get all the Ohio news you need to know right to your inbox every weekday morning.
If you already subscribe, please share with your family and friends so they know about the Ohio Capital Journal too: https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/subscribe/
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Catching Our Eye

• Ohio Gerrymandering. Cleveland.com’s Sabrina Eaton reports, “New book argues Ohio’s redistricting fights are a warning for the rest of the country.”
A journalist who covered Ohio’s redistricting wars from the Statehouse press gallery and an attorney who kept telling him someone needed to write it all down have turned that reporting into a book, arguing the state’s fight over fair district maps previewed a nationwide battle.
“Draw the Line in Ohio: How One State’s Fight for Fair Maps Explains Gerrymandering in America,” by Rory Riley Topping and Josh Rultenberg, comes out September 15 from Prometheus Books.
• Stake ‘n Shake politicizes itself. The Statehouse News Bureau’s Sarah Donaldson reports, “Steak ’n Shake is dishing out candidate endorsements in Ohio. Why?”
(W)hile corporate executives donate to political parties and candidates frequently, it’s rare for corporate companies to wade into the arena. Generally, corporations “don’t want to alienate their customers,” said Christopher Devine, associate professor of political science at the University of Dayton.
“Strategically, it just seems like a bad idea,” Devine said in an interview Monday. “No matter how much a CEO or company leadership wants to see a certain candidate win, maybe they think it’s better for their bottom line, they typically avoid that.”
But Steak ‘n Shake has recently been advertising its fries, which it began cooking in beef tallow rather than seed oils in 2025, by embracing the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement. The burger chain filmed a segment with U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. last year.
• No rules for private schools. The Hechinger Report’s Pepper Stetler reports, “Parents of students with disabilities find private school vouchers come with a catch.”
The meeting with staff members of Cincinnati Christian Schools began with a prayer. Then they told Mike Grimmer and Linda Kelly that their granddaughter could no longer attend the private school.
Annabelle Kelly had enrolled there three months earlier, in August 2025, in a program specifically for students who struggle in mainstream classrooms. Annabelle, 15, has Rett syndrome, a genetic condition accompanied by significant cognitive and developmental delays. Her grandparents, who took legal custody of Annabelle when she was 5, believed that the small, faith-based setting of CCS would be a better fit than the local public school. She received a voucher from the state through a school choice program specifically for students with disabilities, which authorized paying CCS up to $29,750 for Annabelle to attend tuition-free.
But at the meeting in November, Kelly said, the school’s director of academic support services told her and Grimmer that Annabelle’s physical and educational needs were too extensive for her to continue at CCS. If they wanted her to stay, Annabelle would need an aide to work with her one-on-one, and her grandparents would need to pay the additional cost, roughly $25,000 per year.
Disability advocates warn that as private school voucher programs spread, more parents will find themselves in similar straits. Federal protections for students with disabilities don’t apply to private schools, and neither the schools nor voucher programs like the one Annabelle qualified for are required to inform parents that they waive certain rights when they leave the public school system. When Congress passed legislation last year establishing the nation’s first federal voucher program, it did not include language that disability rights groups had lobbied for that would have required private schools receiving federal funds to follow the law known as the Individuals with Disabilities in Education Act.
• AI versus the library. Cleveland Magazine’s Abbey Weitzenkamp reports, “Willoughby Bookstore Confronts Google AI Error Claiming It Was Permanently Closed.”
Through the hand-painted door of The Viridian Bookshop in Downtown Willoughby, readers, Dungeons & Dragons enthusiasts, and anyone looking for somewhere to belong will find a home. The fiction-focused shop is built for getting lost in a story, but this summer, some customers never made it through the door.
Chanel Bush, who opened Viridian in October 2025, says the shop’s first year has come with the usual challenges. Google’s generative AI wasn’t one she saw coming.
In mid-July, a customer walked in and told Bush something strange: Google’s AI Overview stated that the shop had permanently closed. This customer was searching for bookstores in the area a few weeks prior and chose not to visit Viridian due to this misinformation. Bush searched for her own store and got the same result: her shop, at the top of the search page, labeled as closed for good. Google’s summary also listed an address a few doors down from her actual storefront.
