 New unit at men’s prison to accommodate ‘increasingly aging and infirm’ population 

The agency’s request includes $4.2 million in ongoing operating funding and $3.7 million in one-time money to open a new unit at the Idaho State Correctional Institute in Kuna. 
The new unit will include 280 beds, of which 132 would be designed to meet needs of “an increasingly aging and infirm population,” according to the agency budget request.
“IDOC does not currently have a unit designed for people with ambulatory problems but is seeing an increase in this population,” the request said. 
The bottom floor of the new facility would allow for “full ADA compliance,” and for storage of medical equipment, the request said. The site is also close to the prison’s existing medical unit. 
The budget request would fund technology, furniture, appliances, staffing, and other items to operate the facility. 
The new prison unit is expected to open April 2027. 
 New Orofino prison facility would add 112 new low-custody beds 

The budget request includes a total of about $4.5 million to open a new unit at the Idaho Correctional Institution in Orofino. The 112-bed facility would be for men in minimum custody who are eligible to seek employment in the community, the request said. 
The state lacks space for men eligible for services meant to improve their transition back to the community, such as work release or training programs, the request said. 
If the lawmakers choose not to provide funding for the staffing, furniture and other expenses to operate the new facility, eligible “minimum custody residents would continue to be housed in either county jails or out-of-state facilities beds and without the transitional release benefits” of similar facilities, the request said. 
With the opening of the new facilities, the agency is expecting to lower its costs related to contracts with county jails and out-of-state prisons to house state inmates, Derrick said. An expected increase in work-release opportunities for inmates is also expected to generate revenue, because the state collects 30% of inmates’ earnings.

name: WyoFile
title: Seminoe pumped-water storage critics cheer news that BLM will perform additional analysis
description:
The pending review appears to allow for more local and expert considerations regarding the controversial project that threatens wildlife and fisheries, concerned residents say.
The post Seminoe pumped-water storage critics cheer news that BLM will perform additional analysis appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Critics of a pumped-water storage hydroelectric project at Seminoe Reservoir are cheering news that the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission will delay its decision on whether to issue a license for the controversial proposal until another federal agency completes a closer look at potential impacts.
The Bureau of Land Management will conduct a supplemental environmental impact statement and amend its Rawlins Resource Management Plan, according to a federal filing this month. The actions trigger several more opportunities for public comment and input from local officials — an aspect that many say was severely lacking under FERC’s ongoing review.
“This feels like a small victory,” CiCi Oliver told WyoFile. 


Oliver is manager of the Ugly Bug Fly Shop and Crazy Rainbow Fly Fishing in Casper, and serves on the board of Friends of the North Platte, a group formed to advocate for myriad recreational resources that many worry would be harmed by the project. There’s been  public outcry, Oliver noted, regarding impacts to wildlife — including a biologically vital bighorn sheep herd — and fisheries, particularly the Miracle Mile blue-ribbon trout fishery along the North Platte River just below Seminoe Reservoir.
The FERC process, Oliver said, has so far failed to fully take into account those natural resource and recreational-economy concerns, while the BLM’s pending review appears to allow for more local and expert considerations.


How to comment
The Federal Energy Energy Regulatory Commission is accepting public “scoping” comments to “identify issues” that the Bureau of Land Management should consider in its pending supplemental environmental impact statement and potential amendments to its Rawlins Resource Management Plan. Comments must be received by the commission by 3 p.m. Mountain Time, Oct. 13.
Comments can be submitted via eComment. Be sure to reference project or docket number p-14787-004. New eFiling users must first create an account by clicking on “eRegister.” 
Or via U.S. mail to: Debbie-Anne A. ReeseSecretary, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission888 First Street NE, Room 1AWashington, DC 20426


“There seems to be some missing components, and I think, just in general, we’re hoping for a little bit of clarification,” Oliver said.
Utah-based rPlus Hydro proposes building a 13,400-acre-foot reservoir in the Bennett Mountains overlooking Seminoe Reservoir near the dam — one of several existing reservoirs on the North Platte River. The $4 billion facility would pump water uphill during daytime “off-peak demand” hours for electricity when wind and solar power are plentiful and wholesale electricity is cheapest, according to rPlus Hydro. Then it would release the water through hydroelectric turbines during peak demand in the evenings.



This image depicts the approximate area of Seminoe Reservoir where rPlus Hydro proposes to build a pumped-water-storage hydroelectric facility. (Patrick Harrington)

The company contends the project represents a $200 million annual savings to ratepayers. It acquired a “section 401” water quality certificate from the Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality earlier this year. 
rPlus notes the facility would take five years to build, prompting it to ask for multiple variances to long-existing seasonal restrictions designed to protect wildlife and their habitats — among several sticking points for critics, as well as hesitation from the Wyoming Game and Fish Department.
The company declined to offer a comment regarding BLM’s pending review.
Federal actions
FERC is the lead federal agency to review and potentially approve the project for its primary reliance on the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation’s hydroelectric operations. Though the agency must adhere to the National Environmental Protection Act, it takes a more high-level administrative approach compared to the BLM or other federal agencies that typically include more public and local stakeholder input, according to people familiar with the agencies who spoke with WyoFile.
Nevertheless, the BLM is obligated to perform its own assessment of the project because portions of BLM-managed lands are involved in the Bennett Mountains where rPlus Hydro proposes to build a new reservoir. Primarily, there are several sections of BLM-managed lands along a 30-mile corridor where the company proposes to add new power lines to connect the electricity to the grid.
“We are conducting the [supplemental environmental impact statement and resource management plan amendment review] specifically to evaluate impacts of granting the right-of-way on BLM land,” Wyoming BLM told WyoFile via email. “The BLM’s [resource management plan] amendment will look at potential impacts from granting the right-of-way and the development that would follow, such as impacts to visual resources and wildlife migration corridors. We will continue to consider alternatives as needed based on our analyses, interagency coordination and public input.”
The Ferris-Seminoe bighorn sheep herd pictured in December 2025. (Carl Myers)
The FERC, which published its environmental impact statement in June, has operated under a federal FAST-41 coverage schedule to expedite its process, indicating it might make its licensing decision this fall and leave the BLM to complete its work afterward. Instead, according to those close to the matter, the FERC will withhold its licensing decision until the BLM completes its more in-depth review based on a broader scope of local input.
“It puts a couple of additional comment processes in front of us,” Trout Unlimited’s Wyoming Government Relations Director Patrick Harrington told WyoFile. “I do think that those are good opportunities for the public to get engaged.”
The first is a public scoping comment period with a deadline of Oct. 13 .
How influential is the BLM’s review?
Harrington said he and others closely tracking the process are asking questions and speculating about how the BLM’s actions might influence the parameters of the project and FERC’s ultimate decision. For now, though, Trout Unlimited, Friends of the North Platte and others are taking solace in the fact that the BLM will accept “some broader critiques” of the project, he said, noting that state government agencies — including the Wyoming Game and Fish Department — have an opportunity to help the BLM craft its analysis.
“We might be able to propose some sort of new [Resource Management Plan] amendment or new alternatives,” Harrington said.
There’s an outpouring of public interest and skepticism regarding the project, said Oliver, of Friends of the North Platte, and people with concerns about the project are eager to get an audience with BLM officials in Wyoming for local input that they’re unsure the FERC took to heart.
Chief among Oliver’s concerns are the multiple variances to Wyoming-implemented seasonal restrictions on industrial activity designed to protect wildlife, as well as what she considers unanswered questions about impacts to fisheries.  
“If it fits in our landscape and it fits for Wyoming, like [rPlus Hydro says], it should fit for the existing [stipulations] that were created to protect our valuable resources,” Oliver said. 
“If an out-of-state industry can come in and change our existing rules,” Oliver added, “I think that that is a dangerous precedent to set here in Wyoming where, absolutely, we are an energy stronghold. But we are also a natural-resource stronghold, and I think that that’s what makes Wyoming so special.”

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming can still deny Trump his cronies in Congress
description:
The president has bribed voters, pledged to ‘cheat like hell’ and tried to ban mail-in ballots, opines columnist Kerry Drake. Why should that earn him GOP loyalty?
The post Wyoming can still deny Trump his cronies in Congress appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
My fellow Wyomingites, you’ve seen President Donald Trump try to buy your votes for $5,000, pledge to cheat to win in the midterms, and fortunately lose a battle in the U.S. Supreme Court to take away the votes of millions of Americans by banning mail-in ballots.
Are you finally ready to stand together and do something about it?

Opinion

Because Trump has already told us he’s not about to stop if the Nov. 3 election doesn’t go his way. If you don’t believe me, read what he wrote on Truth Social a year ago about the potential loss of Republican control in both chambers of Congress in 2026: 
“[The states] must do what the Federal Government, as represented by the President of the United States, tells them, FOR THE GOOD OF THE COUNTRY, to do.”
And why is this imperative? Because as Trump warned House Republicans in February: “You got to win the midterms, because if we don’t win the midterms, it’s just going to be, I mean they’ll find a reason to impeach me. I’ll get impeached.” 
Last week, the president sunk to new lows at a GOP midterm convention in Dallas and showed how desperate he is. Trump promised to give $5,000 to every American adult if Republicans maintain control of both the House and Senate. He called it the “Trump dividend.”
Some news organizations called it a joke and tried to claim Trump wasn’t serious, or that it technically wasn’t a bribe. Some legal scholars said it was just a campaign promise, not a violation of bribery statutes.
It’s a blatant bribe. He knows it, and we do too. We also both know that Trump doesn’t have the authority to order it on his own, and that he’d never pay up if it happened. That’s the only “joke,” and we’re all in on it.
The only question is if we care enough to end this madness. 
Norm Eisen, an ethics advisor to former President Barack Obama, stated the obvious to USA Today: Trump tied a specific payout to a specific voting action.
He called it a “cynical, desperate stunt to financially incentivize Republicans, independent voters and even traditional Democrats who may be facing financial hardship to vote for Republicans in the midterm.”
The vice chair of the Wyoming Republican Party, Bob Ferguson, told Cowboy State Daily that characterizing what Trump said as a bribe is “an outright lie.”
“The point people are missing is, if Republicans don’t win, then Democrats aren’t going to approve that dividend,” Ferguson said. 
But if that’s the case, Trump and his Republican allies in Congress could simply make the dividend a reality now. Why make it contingent on the GOP winning both chambers and doing it next year?
Campbell County Commissioner Scott Clem, a Republican and former state legislator, told the news outlet that Trump essentially offered a bribe. “I think that he knows that’s probably not going to happen, as far as retaining the House and the Senate,” Clem said. “So maybe it’s just an empty promise. Trump is Trump, but I do think it was not a very good thing to say.” 
When a progressive like myself and a conservative like Clem start agreeing, the times really are a-changing in Wyoming.
As the keynote speaker at the Republican midterm convention, Trump led a pledge to “the greatest president in the history of the United States” — himself, of course — and told his supporters to go out with family and friends to vote.
“I don’t care if I’m registered to vote or not, I’m going to try to cheat like hell like [Democrats] do,” Trump said, with his right arm raised. “So help me God.”
Vice President J.D. Vance explained that the “Trump dividend” would be paid for with money from the president’s higher tariffs. But in the current fiscal year, tariffs have only added an estimated $167 billion to U.S. revenue, while the Congressional Budget Office estimated giving every American adult $5,000 next year would cost $1.2 trillion and increase inflation.
Let that last number sink in. The national debt eclipsed $40 trillion last month, and under Trump it has increased by more than any other U.S. president: $7.8 trillion during his first term and $3.6 trillion so far in his second. And now he wants to potentially bring his total share to $12.6 trillion with the Trump bribe.
For decades, Wyoming’s all-GOP congressional delegation has claimed that Democrats caused the explosion in the national debt and demanded reduced spending. But those same politicians voted to wildly increase the national debt whenever Republicans gained White House control.
Wyoming voters know that U.S. Rep. Harriet Hageman and Secretary of State Chuck Gray — respectively the Republican nominees for the state’s U.S. Senate and U.S. House seats this year — will do anything Trump tells them to do.
Hageman and Gray have arrogantly refused to participate in Wyoming PBS debates with their opponents, taking away the opportunity for voters to compare candidates side by side. There will still be a U.S. House debate, sans Gray, but since Hageman has only one challenger, Democrat James Byrd, the U.S. Senate debate has been canceled.
Hageman and Gray said they will both take their campaigns directly to the voters.
But what if voters take their disdain for the pair’s all-encompassing loyalty to Trump and decide to make a statement of their own, denying the president his cronies in the state that is most expected to back him?
Few thought last month’s Wyoming Republican primary would result in the far-right Freedom Caucus being kicked out of power only two years after it took House control. It happened because more traditional Republicans looked at the debacle the Freedom Caucus made of its chance to govern and sent most of its members packing.
Just because Hageman and Gray have an “R” behind their names on the ballot doesn’t mean Republicans have to automatically put them in office — especially if the leader of their party openly bribes voters and announces his plan to “cheat like hell” to win.
Gray handed over sensitive Wyoming voter data to Trump and did not object when the president said it might be necessary to federalize elections. Are only Democratic voters upset about this?
Republicans in Wyoming are just as negatively impacted by Trump’s misguided war against Iran and rising gas, grocery and healthcare costs as the rest of the state. Why is it assumed that everyone will bow down to him, like our delegation does?
What’s even more concerning than Trump’s statements is his effort to do anything he can to keep more people from voting, like his lawsuit to ban states from mailing out ballots after many have already been delivered.
With its 7-2 decision Monday against Trump, the U.S. Supreme Court — even the three members he appointed — voted to preserve democracy under the U.S. Constitution and let the states run elections, not the federal government.
There’s serious concern that Trump will not allow the U.S. House to certify election results unless Republicans stay in power. U.S. Rep. Mike Johnson, R-Louisiana, is the most gutless House speaker in history, and given what Trump tried during the certification process and siege of the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, we should be more afraid today.
If Wyomingites have the courage and wisdom to rid our Capitol of most of the Freedom Caucus, anything could happen in our congressional elections. I may be a dreamer, but I hope I’m not the only one.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: 48 Nebraska judges face an up-or-down vote to stay in office after 2026
description: LINCOLN — Forty-eight Nebraska judges face an up-or-down vote this November on whether they can stay in office through 2032, including two Workers’ Compensation Court judges who serve statewide. Depending on the county where they live, Nebraska voters will see at least two judges and as many as 15 on their ballots. The most are in […]
text:
Nebraska judges, including the six judges on the Nebraska Court of Appeals, front, listen to the investiture ceremony for Nebraska Supreme Court Chief Justice Jeffrey Funke. Nov. 22, 2024. (Courtesy of Nebraska Judicial Branch)LINCOLN — Forty-eight Nebraska judges face an up-or-down vote this November on whether they can stay in office through 2032, including two Workers’ Compensation Court judges who serve statewide.
Depending on the county where they live, Nebraska voters will see at least two judges and as many as 15 on their ballots. The most are in Nebraska’s most populous county, Douglas, which is Judicial District 4. State law provides that district with the most judges.
No Supreme Court justices face retention this November. Only Court of Appeals Judge Michael W. Pirtle of Omaha, who represents part of Douglas County, faces retention for his court.
Nebraska judges, in black robes, listen to the investiture ceremony for Nebraska Supreme Court Chief Justice Jeffrey Funke. Nov. 22, 2024. (Photo courtesy of Nebraska Judicial Branch)
In addition to Pirtle, the Nov. 3 ballot will include:

Two Workers’ Compensation court judges (Judges Thomas E. Stine and Dirk V. Block).
Twenty-three district court judges (in nine of 12 judicial districts).
Two separate juvenile courts (in Douglas and Sarpy counties, but not Lancaster County).
Twenty county court judges (in 11 of 12 judicial districts).

Since 1964, judges have gone to voters for retention at the first general election at least three years after their appointment. Nebraska has nearly 150 judges in total. 
Current terms in office end Jan. 7, 2027.
The last time a Nebraska judge was not retained in office was in 2008. If allowed to stay in office, judges would serve until January 2033 and could file for retention again in 2032.
Who’s who of judges
Judges in Nebraska are arranged at different levels, consisting of county courts, district courts, separate juvenile courts (in Douglas, Lancaster and Sarpy counties), the Nebraska Court of Appeals and the Nebraska Supreme Court. There is also the six-member, statewide Workers’ Compensation Court. 
District court and county court judges sit in specific judicial districts (just two counties differ between the two court types, Otoe and Fillmore), while appellate judges sit in six districts as redistricted by the Legislature every 10 years. The chief justice and the workers’ compensation judges serve statewide.
Nebraskans who live in Judicial District 7 — Antelope, Cuming, Knox, Madison, Pierce, Stanton and Wayne — will only see the two Workers’ Compensation Court judges on their ballots.



18 first-time retention votes
This year, 18 judges face their first up-or-down vote. This includes the final 15 judges who ascended to office at former Gov. Pete Ricketts’ appointment, and the first from Gov. Jim Pillen.
Of the 48 judges, just one has been elevated to a higher position than their earlier position. That’s Sarpy County District Judge Stefanie A. Martinez, whom former Gov. Dave Heineman appointed as a county court judge in 2013. In 2017, Ricketts elevated her to the district court.
Martinez and 14 other Ricketts-appointed judges will face retention for the second time this year. Ten Heineman-appointed judges will face retention for the third time, while two Heineman appointees face retention for the fourth time. Three judges who joined a county court under former Gov. Ben Nelson in 1998, his final year in office, face their fifth retention vote.
The Nebraska State Bar Association each year polls attorneys who work before the judges. Of the 48 up for retention this year, attorneys recommended that all but one be retained in office.

Two judges did not file for retention
Two other judges this year were eligible for retention but did not file by the Aug. 3 deadline.
Douglas County District Judge Timothy P. Burns submitted his retirement this summer after 15 years of service. His last day is Oct. 30. He previously worked in the Douglas County Public Defender’s Office.
The other is Brown County District Judge Mark D. Kozisek, who was appointed in 2004. He’s a former city attorney for Ainsworth, Long Pine and Johnstown, and deputy county attorney.
Also retiring this year is Judge Vernon Daniels of the Separate Juvenile Court of Douglas County, effective Dec. 31. He’s served on the court since 2001 and was last retained in 2022.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: New TBI agents ‘embedded’ with Memphis Safe Task Force
description: The state is pouring $9 million this year into a Tennessee Bureau of Investigation task force given wide-reaching authority across the state, including working with the Memphis Safe Task Force. The legislature set up an eight-member board with the power to initiate investigations and funded 32 positions for the agency’s new group, including agents, superviso[...]
text:
The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation will embed with the Memphis Safe Task Force, which already includes members of the state National Guard, pictured above. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)The state is pouring $9 million this year into a Tennessee Bureau of Investigation task force given wide-reaching authority across the state, including working with the Memphis Safe Task Force.
The legislature set up an eight-member board with the power to initiate investigations and funded 32 positions for the agency’s new group, including agents, supervisors and intelligence analysts, 15 of whom are “embedded in existing operations” with the Memphis crimefighting initiative, according to TBI. The agency is in the process of hiring 17 more special agent criminal investigators. First-year costs include $3.8 million for salaries and $5.2 million for supplies, and in subsequent years the cost is expected to be more than $5 million.
Legislation passed by House Majority Leader William Lamberth of Portland and Republican Sen. Brent Taylor creates a board chaired by TBI Director David Rausch, which has the authority to send TBI agents into law enforcement jurisdictions across the state where crime is deemed too high or at the request of local officials. 
The task force is attached to the TBI administratively and “shall determine when criminal activity in a particular jurisdiction is so prevalent as to endanger public safety and require additional law enforcement operations,” the legislation says. 
Decisions on assignments and the rationale for deploying TBI task force agents are up to the board’s discretion. The task force is to meet quarterly or hold special meetings, when it can take up a member’s request and vote to send task force agents into a law enforcement jurisdiction. The law does not mention whether the task force would be subject to the state’s Open Meetings Act or Public Records Act.
A sheriff, police chief or district attorney general can request additional law enforcement from the task force for investigations. The board would not have to take a vote on those types of moves. 
It has the authority to dispatch agents to investigate major criminal offenses such as murder, gang activities and other crimes such as disorderly conduct, riots and drug and weapons offenses.
Task force investigators also are authorized to make investigations in any judicial district in which the Memphis Safe Task Force is working, without a request from the sheriff, police chief or district attorney.
In addition, the TBI can enter agreements with other bureaus, agencies, departments or task forces in Tennessee, in other states or with federal agencies.
Democratic state Rep. John Ray Clemmons questioned the measure when it passed with supermajority Republican support in April, saying it would allow the task force to override the judgment of local law enforcement officials. Under the legislation, the TBI may open an investigation into a local jurisdiction on its own accord, even over the objection of local district attorneys or law enforcement officials.
“This somewhat defeats the very intent of the creation of the TBI,” Clemmons said, noting the agency was designed to operate independently, following a cash-for-clemency scandal surrounding former Gov. Ray Blanton in 1980.
Giving an appointed task force authority to direct the TBI’s operations undermines the agency’s original design, he said.
Lamberth said the measure only created a group that could take requests from local law enforcement officials and district attorneys for help investigating crimes.
Yet he acknowledged that if a law enforcement agency in the state declines to investigate a potential crime, the task force could step in.
“More investigations is never a bad thing,” Lamberth said.
The TBI’s responsibilities have increased substantially over nearly 50 years, Lamberth added. District attorneys already request TBI investigations for a variety of incidents, including officer-involved shootings, often to avoid the appearance of impropriety.
Even though those types of investigations are made following local requests, Lamberth acknowledged that the task force board could determine whether potential crimes should be investigated if local officials don’t want to look into them. 
The TBI group’s involvement in Memphis also could be a sign of things to come.
Republican Rep. John Gillespie, an ardent supporter of the Memphis Safe Task Force, recently posted on Facebook that the group of federal, state and local agencies “started the process of making Tennessee a safer place. This year, we created the Tennessee Safe Initiative Task Force within the TBI to carry the mission forward, not only in Memphis, but across all of Tennessee.”
Memphis city officials didn’t request the task force, which was ordered by President Donald Trump and Gov. Bill Lee. A group made up of Memphis city officials and state lawmakers filed suit claiming deployment of the National Guard was unconstitutional, but the court ruled that they didn’t have standing to sue.
Besides Rausch, task force members are Department of Safety and Homeland Security Commissioner Jeff Long, Jackson Police Chief Thom Corley, District Attorney Russell Johnson of the 9th Judicial District in rural West Tennessee, District Attorney Mark Davidson of the 25th Judicial District in East Tennessee, Cumberland County Sheriff Casey Cox, Maury County Sheriff Buckly Rowland and Oak Ridge Police Chief Charles Smith.
Appointments were made by the governor, police chiefs association, sheriffs association, district attorneys general conference and House and Senate speakers.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Charlie Kirk’s family says lapses in event security at Utah campus left him ‘helpless’
description: Charlie Kirk’s death at Utah Valley University last year was “entirely preventable,” his family says in a notice of claim.
text:
People visit a memorial set up in honor of Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University in Orem on Tuesday, Sept. 16, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Calling Charlie Kirk’s death at Utah Valley University “entirely preventable,” his family says he wouldn’t have been shot and killed last year had the university put in place tighter security protocols. 
Attorneys representing Kirk’s family made the allegations in a notice of claim dated Sept. 9, marking the first time they have publicly blamed the university in his death. And while it’s not a lawsuit, the notice is a required step in Utah to bring a viable suit against a “governmental entity” such as a public university. 
“Through a series of stunning failures and reckless decisions, the UVU Parties created a foreseeable danger to Charlie. Those decisions ultimately rendered Mr. Kirk helpless to the rooftop shooter in an assassination that could have been avoided had the UVU Parties only taken reasonable steps to plan and oversee a safe event,” the notice reads. 
1 year after Charlie Kirk shooting, campus safety reviews are still in the works 

Attorneys for the Kirk family publicly released the letter Wednesday, a little more than a year after Kirk’s assassination at the university in Orem. Kirk, a close ally of President Donald Trump, podcaster and the founder of the student organization Turning Point USA, was answering a question just moments into the event from under a tent in a courtyard when he was shot, sending his audience running for cover. 
The conservative activist had become known for debating students in public spaces, and the university has previously said Kirk wanted to speak in a central, outdoor space where students would be walking by and could take part in the event. 
A 23-year-old Utah man, Tyler Robinson, is accused of using his grandfather’s hunting rifle to fatally shoot Kirk from a rooftop perch on the campus. A judge on Sept.1 ordered Robinson to stand trial for aggravated murder in Kirk’s death, and prosecutors, who allege Robinson targeted Kirk for his political views and endangered his audience, have said they’ll seek the death penalty if he’s convicted. Robinson has pleaded not guilty. 
Defense attorney Kathryn Nester talks to Tyler Robinson during a preliminary hearing in 4th District Court for Robinson, the Utah man accused of fatally shooting Charlie Kirk, in Provo on July 7, 2026. (Pool photo by Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune)
Kirk’s widow Erika Kirk has succeeded him as head of the organization and attended a six-day hearing in Provo alongside her late husband’s parents this summer. Donald Trump Jr. sat in the same row in a show of support. 
Attorneys for the Kirk family note that six UVU police officers staffed the event attended by some 3,000 people. They say in the notice that the university didn’t bring in any other police departments for help and didn’t use drones to secure rooftops or real-time surveillance video feeds to monitor them. 
And they allege, without providing evidence in the notice, that UVU Police Chief Jeffrey Long sought approval from then-university President Astrid Tuminez to assign six more officers for the event, but the request was denied. The eight-page letter is addressed to the office of Utah Attorney General Brown, which defends state institutions in civil matters. It also names Tuminez, the university’s police department and the police chief.
Public access to a nearby roof had been a topic of discussion between a Turning Point USA representative and the police chief before the shooting, according to the notice.
Law enforcement responds after conservative political commentator Charlie Kirk was shot and killed during an event at Utah Valley University in Orem on Wednesday, Sept. 10, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
When Turning Point received a message from a student concerned about roof access to the Sorensen Student Center near the stage location, a Turning Point representative told UVU’s police chief, Jeffrey Long, “if this is true, it would be nice to either have it controlled access or allow one of my guys to be there as well. If Possible,” the notice says. “Chief Long responded by saying, ‘I got you covered.’”
Authorities say the shot that killed Kirk was fired from a different, further rooftop of the Losee Center, but attorneys for his widow and parents say the conversation led the organization to believe UVU had a plan to address similar risks. 
“His murder was entirely preventable and, in fact, would not have happened had the State of Utah and UVU followed through on their stated security promises, which included protecting the rooftops surrounding the quad where Charlie was speaking,” the family’s attorney, Brett Parkinson, said in a prepared statement. “Those failures not only robbed Charlie Kirk of his life, but also robbed his family of their husband, father, son, and brother, with impacts that will compound for the rest of their lives.”
He was a rising political star with a vast social media footprint, the notice says, and a spate of political violence before his death illustrated the risks. Those included an attempt on President Donald Trump’s life in Pennsylvania in 2024, the letter notes, as well as the attack on former U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s husband, Paul, in 2022, and the killings of a Minnesota state lawmaker and her husband in 2025.

title: Alabama screen time commission hears recommendations on best classroom practices
description: An Alabama state commission Tuesday heard recommendations on how to best address screen usage in classrooms. The Commission on Screen-Based Instruction, created by Gov. Kay Ivey in July, heard presentations from White Board Advisors, a consulting firm based in Washington D.C., and the Screen Use Impact on Teachers subcommittee. A small survey of 61 K-12 […]
text:
An adolescent girl uses an AI application on her phone. The Commission on Screen-Based Instruction heard presentations from technology industry professionals and subcommittees on how to address screen usage in classrooms. (Getty Images)An Alabama state commission Tuesday heard recommendations on how to best address screen usage in classrooms.
The Commission on Screen-Based Instruction, created by Gov. Kay Ivey in July, heard presentations from White Board Advisors, a consulting firm based in Washington D.C., and the Screen Use Impact on Teachers subcommittee.
A small survey of 61 K-12 teachers done by the subcommittee showed that 67% of teachers are using screens in the classroom for assignments or practice and 54% of teachers are using devices for testing purposes.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Alabama has a narrative right now of we have either maintained or advanced achievement while other states have not experienced those outcomes,” said Chris Jenks, committee member and Tuscaloosa City Schools technology director. “One of the ways we know that is through our battery of assessment. Many of them, most of them, are delivered on a screen.”
The commission was created after Ivey signed HB 78, sponsored by Rep. Jeana Ross, R-Guntersville, during the 2026 regular legislative session. The bill sets screen usage limits for children up to five years old in licensed child care facilities. Ross also filed HB 584 to place screen time limits on all public K-12 students, but the bill failed to make it through the Senate before the Legislature adjourned in April.
Ben Wallerstein, chief executive officer and co-founder of Whiteboard Advisors, said during his presentation that terms associated with artificial intelligence are hazy, which could pose problems.
“If we survey parents and we ask them about what do they mean by AI (artificial intelligence), like we don’t want AI in our schools, they’re probably thinking like kids asking open-ended questions to Claude or ChatGPT,” Wallerstein said. “They’re not thinking about the application of machine learning to sift through thousands of voice recordings to differentiate between a kid who is new to speaking and learning English and is a struggling reader.”
Sen. Linda Coleman-Madison, D-Birmingham, said during the meeting that educating parents is key to the committee’s work.
“I always say, you come here like a clean piece of paper, a sponge. It’s what we allow to be soaked up and printed on that page, and so it starts at home, and parents have got to be a part of it. So somewhere in this, we’ve got to find a component, a hook, or somewhere to educate the parents on what we’re trying to do,” she said.
Alabama Department of Early Childhood Education Secretary Ami Brooks said her department has “had a lot of discussions too about making sure that the language that we use honors the parents and does not shame the parents because everyone is doing the best that they can.”
“A lot of times they’re handing them a phone and showing them a letter game, and they think that they’re helping,” Brooks said. 
Brooks also told the committee placing emphasis on everyday interactions with young children is important.
“If you have a little one, having them in the car and pointing out the, you know, the produce and those types of things-that’s what’s building the brain, not sitting passive with the screen. Just raising that awareness also about the everyday interactions that are missed when you’re handing them a screen instead of having those conversations,” she said.
The committee will deliver its final report to Ivey on Dec. 1.

ArtiCast Jackson will manufacture aerospace, defense and automotive components using high-pressure die casting equipment at the former P[...]
text:
ArtiCast Jackson, part of Michigan-based ArtiFlex Manufacturing, plans to move into Jackson, Tennessee and hire 100 employees. The die casting company will fill the vacant plant formerly operated by Pace Industries, a die casting manufacturer that closed in February. (Courtesy of ArtiCast Jackson)A Michigan-based die casting manufacturer plans to move into a vacant Madison County facility, investing $10.3 million and pledging to create 100 jobs, the company and Tennessee’s economic development arm announced Tuesday.
ArtiCast Jackson will manufacture aerospace, defense and automotive components using high-pressure die casting equipment at the former Pace Industries facility in Jackson.
The company is part of the ArtiFlex Manufacturing, an umbrella of companies that employs more than 1,000 people across design, automation, tooling and manufacturing groups located in Michigan, Ohio and Spain. 
It’s not yet clear what incentives the Tennessee Department of Economic and Community Development offered the company. Details of such incentives are typically made available to the public on the state’s FastTrack grant project database within a month of a project’s announcement.
Pace Industries, an aluminum die casting company, announced the permanent closure of its Jackson plant in February, alongside its other plants in Arkansas and Michigan. Pace Industries laid off 59 workers from the Jackson facility, according to a letter submitted to the state department of labor. Pace had previously received a $100,000 grant from the state of Tennessee in 2023 to help train new full-time workers for a $2.9 million, 49-employee expansion at its Jackson plant.
Tennessee Economic and Community Development Commissioner Stuart McWhorter called Madison County “an epicenter of economic development across Southwest Tennessee,” in a Tuesday statement.
ArtiFlex Holdings CEO and board chairman Erin Hoffmann said that the new Jackson location will position the company closer to customers in Southeastern states. 
“We can put capital investment anywhere,” Hoffmann stated in a news release. “The talented workforce in Jackson makes this the ideal location.”
“By bringing new life to an existing manufacturing facility, this project will strengthen our local economy and create quality opportunities for families across our community,” Republican state Sen. Ed Jackson said.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Why is a West Virginia principal making national news and our schools aren’t?
description: Earlier this month, the principal at Brooke High School in Wellsburg, West Virginia, was arrested for allegedly hiding cameras in female changing areas. The story has made national news, covered by such outlets as Fox, People, and the New York Post. It has even made international news, the UK’s Daily Mail writing about it under […]
text:
Inside a Kanawha County elementary classroom in West Virginia. (Photo by Lexi Browning/West Virginia Watch)Earlier this month, the principal at Brooke High School in Wellsburg, West Virginia, was arrested for allegedly hiding cameras in female changing areas. The story has made national news, covered by such outlets as Fox, People, and the New York Post. It has even made international news, the UK’s Daily Mail writing about it under the headline “Southern father-of-three school principal is charged after four secret cameras are found inside girls’ locker room.” The inclusion of the word “southern” is particularly interesting in that headline, almost as if the geographic location factors into the principal’s misdeeds (never mind that Wellsburg is north of the Mason-Dixon Line). 
It reminds me of the New York Times coverage of the Hatfield-McCoy Feud from over a hundred years ago. In reporting on the feud, the Times ran such headlines as “West Virginia’s Outlaws” and “A War of Extermination.” In one article, the Times described the feud as “a reign of terror.” In another, they wrote how the feud “fanned hatred to white heat.” In a time before TV, radio, and the internet, such descriptions were about the only picture many outsiders had of Appalachia. As historian Altina L. Waller has posited, these uncivilized, violent caricatures made it easier to justify King Coal and other extractive industries coming in to take over the land.
Is something similar happening all over again? 
On the same day the New York Post ran a story about the Brooke High School principal, Mingo county parents filed a lawsuit against state officials alleging years of underfunding that has undermined students’ right to a public education. This latter story didn’t make national news, despite the fact this underfunding has fueled the state’s current school consolidation crisis.
When a school closes in a town, property values decrease. Families move elsewhere. Depopulation ramps up even more. The students left behind are often stuck with longer commutes, overcrowded classrooms, and less extracurricular opportunities. All of that, in turn, leads to less educational achievement and more poverty, more addiction, even more depopulation. A vicious cycle.
To make matters worse, with the Hope Scholarship, public money is being funneled into private pockets — more specifically, private out-of-state pockets. With a large number of homeschooled children in the state enrolled in out-of-state virtual programs, not only are Hope funds not going to our schools, but they’re not going to any place that benefits our state.
So who does benefit? In the 1800s, it was the railroad, coal and timber industries. Robber barons living in the northeast. Now, it seems like it’s the robber barons living out west in Silicon Valley who are benefitting. Interestingly, the politicians pushing the Hope Scholarship and leading the charge to kill public education are the same ones pushing data centers. As one data company engineer put it, “We can do pretty much whatever we want to do up there [in West Virginia].” Of course, many state GOP leaders, including the governor, denounced the engineer’s comments, though they curiously haven’t pushed back on what President Donald Trump said about the topic. “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers,” Trump posted on social media, “is if they want to end up being backwards and poor.”
New century, same story.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC rural hospitals, doctors’ offices receive share of $200M in federal funding amid Medicaid cuts
description: SC Gov. Henry McMaster announced federal grant awards made to rural healthcare providers under the new Rural Health Transformation Program.
text:
Newberry Health hospital received nearly $11 million for a dozen projects Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, as part of new federal program focused on rural health. The program was created under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act as a way to help rural hospitals and healthcare organizations most heavily impacted by upcoming Medicaid funding cuts under the law. (Photo by Jessica Holdman)NEWBERRY — New MRI and CT scanners in Newberry. A mobile health van that will provide care in a dozen counties and in natural disaster situations across the state.
These are just some of the ways South Carolina plans to spend the $200 million in federal funding received this year as part of a new rural health program.
By 2043, SC hospitals could receive $2.4B less to treat Medicaid patients

Gov. Henry McMaster and other state officials traveled to Newberry Health hospital Tuesday to announce the federal grant awards made to rural healthcare providers and state agencies under the new Rural Health Transformation Program.
The program was created under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act as a way to help rural hospitals and healthcare organizations most heavily hit by upcoming Medicaid funding cuts under the law pushed through Congress by President Donald Trump’s administration. 
“We have to keep our people healthy, keep them working, and that’s what this is aimed to do,” McMaster said.
Great need
The state Medicaid agency received 712 applications for the federal funding but ultimately only had enough money to approve 227 of them.
That includes Newberry Health, which received nearly $11 million for a dozen projects.
The 90-bed hospital’s magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI machine, is two decades old and in need of replacement. And its computed tomography, or CT scanner for short, doesn’t have heart health capabilities, leaving patients to instead travel an hour to Columbia or Greenville for cardiac related scans, said CEO John Snow.
John Snow, CEO of Newberry Health, pictured Aug. 15, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)
The hospital had already planned to make the upgrades in the next couple years, but now it can use the federal dollars and spend its own money on other needs, Snow said.
“At the end of the day, it isn’t just about funding,” he said. “It’s about people and access and opportunity and making sure that high-quality healthcare remains close to home for generations to come.”
Newberry also will expand its operating rooms, upgrade its computer systems to protect against cyberthreats and add more physical security, a major priority for hospitals as healthcare staff regularly experience violence from unruly patients and family members in distress.
Lovelace Family Medicine, a private general care practice in Newberry, also will receive $1 million through the program to repave its parking lot, recruit and retain employees and update its IT.
In his 38 years in Newberry, Dr. Oscar Lovelace has seen major changes to the region’s healthcare landscape.
“I’ve seen a lot of progress but Fairfield County hospital is closed,” he said. “There’s no county hospital in Saluda. Laurens County hospital doesn’t deliver babies anymore, nor does Union County, so we’ve seen an obstetrical desert here.”
Lovelace also said technology upgrades are important, especially to primary care doctors who can spend late nights at home after hours on their computers updating patient records.
Dr. Oscar Lovelace of Lovelace Family Medicine in Newberry, pictured Tuesday, Aug. 15, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)
And AnMed in the Upstate announced that it had finally returned to normal operations Tuesday following a months-long recovery from a cybersecurity attack in which CEO William Kinley said cybercriminals accessed patients’ health information.
The state approved AnMed for $4 million in federal funding, including $1.7 million for IT improvements.
Telehealth too
Beyond hospitals and doctor’s offices, dollars are also going to telehealth organizations.
Palmetto Care Connections, a nonprofit telehealth network founded in 2010, wants to purchase its first mobile van to make house calls.
“We really believe that your zip code should not define the quality of life you live, or whether or not you have access to care,” CEO Kathy Schwarting.
The van also will be available for disaster recovery.
“If there’s a flood, if there’s a tornado, and folks don’t have access to care, we can take that mobile van and make sure they can connect to a primary or specialty care provider,” Schwarting added.
Schwarting has seen the loss of rural healthcare first hand. She previously worked at now-closed hospitals in Bamberg and Barnwell.
Kathy Schwarting, CEO of Palmetto Care Connections, pictured Tuesday, Aug. 15, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)
“It devastated our communities when that happened: lost jobs, people had to move, industries would no longer come in because you didn’t have a healthcare system,” she said. “And forget recruiting a provider because, without the support system of a hospital, they were not going to come to that community. I’ve seen it. I’ve lived it. It is devastating.”
Tight margins
South Carolina’s hospitals generally operate on margins between 0% and 4%, according to the state Hospital Association.
The margins for rural hospitals are the thinnest as they have a smaller population base over which to spread costs. They also tend to have a greater percentage of patients on Medicare and Medicaid.
In all, six rural hospitals in South Carolina have closed since 2010, according to a 2023 legislative study.
While hospitals are concentrated in South Carolina’s three major metro areas, all but five of the state’s 46 counties have at least one hospital or emergency center.
To aid the state’s rural healthcare providers, South Carolina doled out funds across eight categories: chronic disease, remote treatment and monitoring, expanding community care, facility improvements, workforce, mobile crisis response, IT and training.
Most of the money went to facility improvements, followed by IT.
The largest recipient was Self Regional Healthcare hospital system, which the state awarded nearly $31 million across eight hospitals.
SC rural hospital asks legislators to enact safety net in preparation for Medicaid cuts

The state-run Medical University of South Carolina Health system received nearly $19 million across four rural hospitals and the health system at large.
Hampton Regional Medical Center in the Lowcountry received $13 million.
The state also held back funds to study South Carolina’s greatest rural health needs, state Department of Health and Human Services Director Eunice Medina said.
That study will help the agency decide how to distribute money over the next four years of the federal program.
“We have the basic assets,” McMaster said. “But we have to tie it all together, and we have to find the weak spots to see where some innovation, where some new equipment would help.”

title: Lawmakers told data centers could be key to improving WV water issues
description: A member of the Morrisey administration told lawmakers Tuesday that data centers can improve the water quality and infrastructure in West Virginia, where brown fluid, chemical smells and more have plagued residents turning on their taps — particularly in the southern coalfields. Ongoing water issues have plagued Southern West Virginia, prompting Gov. Patrick[...]
text:
West Virginia Office of Energy Director Nicholas Preservati speaks before lawmakers at the state Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia, on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)A member of the Morrisey administration told lawmakers Tuesday that data centers can improve the water quality and infrastructure in West Virginia, where brown fluid, chemical smells and more have plagued residents turning on their taps — particularly in the southern coalfields.
Ongoing water issues have plagued Southern West Virginia, prompting Gov. Patrick Morrisey to hold a “Beautiful, Clean Water” listening tour last month in the area.
In Mingo County, residents have questioned why a proposed power plant and data center could potentially have access to new water sources while they go sometimes weeks without water. They fear that the amount of water needed for the proposed development could affect how much local water is available.
Nicholas Preservati, director of the state’s Office of Energy, appeared before the Joint Committee on Energy and Public Works on Tuesday at the State Capitol to field questions about coal operations and mining jobs. 
Del. Mark Zatezalo, R-Hancock (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Del. Mark Zatezalo, vice chair of the House Energy and Public Works Committee, asked Preservati if there’d been any consideration for the southern coalfields’ water when it came to mining.
“I’m sure you’ve been following the news with all these water problems that we’ve been having down there. So I would say that that might be something that we might want to look at,” said Zatezalo, R-Hancock.
In response, Preservati turned the conversation to data centers, saying, “I think the whole issue on water has been mischaracterized.”
“Water issues in West Virginia are not a quantity issue. Generally speaking, it’s a quality issue,” Preservati said, clarifying that he wasn’t speaking on behalf of the governor’s office. “The data centers aren’t going to be affecting the quality; they can be utilized to improve quality. So, I see the data centers and the revenue they generate to be able to increase the efficiency, to bring in revenue to southern coalfields.”
Maria Russo, policy specialist at West Virginia Rivers Coalition, said there needs to be an honest look at the cumulative impacts of data center development. She supports investment in water infrastructure across the state.
“These projects can create significant challenges and risks for water quality, water quantity and flooding as we have seen in Mason County,” she said. “We cannot look at the potential revenue from development without also accounting for the costs and compounding burdens that development will place on communities and water systems.”
Preservati’s comments at the Capitol come amid friction over data centers; residents worry about the impact on their communities while many elected officials are excited for economic development in the job-stressed state. 
Many data centers need a lot of water to function to generate electricity and cooling systems use water to keep the equipment from overheating. Some data centers can use up to 5 million gallons of drinking water a day.
Data centers’ water demand has been increasing due to growth in artificial intelligence services and cloud software. 
Across the country, communities located next to new data center developments have reported taps drying up or water contamination.
“We were glad to hear that clean water was raised in the meeting during conversations about coalfield and workforce development at interims today,” Russo said. “As West Virginia looks at opportunities for investment in Southern West Virginia, any conversation that involves development in the southern coalfields must include clean water infrastructure now.”
Preservati said in West Virginia, generally, data centers will use “a closed-door system” that won’t use a tremendous amount of water. 
Data centers in the southern coalfields, he said, could “get the tax revenue moving into the counties so that they can use tens of millions of dollars every year” to upgrade water infrastructure and prevent sewage from going into local water supplies.
“I view the data center issue and the water issue as a potential opportunity to solve one of our biggest problems, not a creator of problems, and we’d be happy to work with the Legislature on helping make that happen,” Preservati said. 
Zatezalo told West Virginia Watch that he wants to make sure water quality remains a focus in the southern coalfields.
“We have to make sure that safeguards are in place to support water resources,” he said. “Having said that, West Virginia is one of the wettest states in the country. We have plenty of water. We may not have it every place that we want it. When you get into the mountains, down in the coalfields, it’s tough. That’s why it was kind of just a cautionary question. Did he answer it? He answered it to a degree, and that’s fine for now.”
A data center in McDowell County could bring in a lot of money, he noted, though water supply in the area may not support it.
“But you know, I just wish they’d all come to Weirton because we have the Ohio River. We have 13 trillion gallons that come by Weirton every year, and we have plenty of water,” Zatezalo said. 
Russo said she hopes that communities across West Virginia benefit from a proposed 5% allocation from data center revenue that was outlined in lawmakers’ pro-data center legislation in 2025.
The revenue “could be a key part to solving West Virginia’s water infrastructure challenges,” Russo said. 
“We hope it is a transparent process that ensures communities benefit from this proposal. We need to know how those funds would be used and allocated, who would make those decisions, and how communities would have a voice,” she said. 
Public hearing scheduled involving HB 2014 rules 
The state has seen a wave of proposed data center projects, including a recent one announced by Morrisey for Mason County. A Florida-based real estate developer is spearheading a data center and natural gas plant there, and the project is still going through the state’s permitting process. The data center plans to run on a closed-loop cooling system, which generally uses less water than other systems.
Lawmakers passed their hallmark data center legislation — House Bill 2014 — with the hope of incentivizing data center development. Morrisey is all in on bringing data centers to West Virginia. 
Opponents of HB 2014 said the bill stripping communities of local control and tax revenues related to data centers. Morrisey, in turn, has said he wants to make local input a part of the data center development process.
Earlier this year, while lawmakers debated proposed rules related to the data center legislation, they declined to approve a pair of amendments seeking to protect local water supplies in West Virginia. 
An amendment by Del. Evan Hansen, D-Monongalia, would have required developers seeking to construct data centers to share specific details on where they would draw water from for operations. Developers would have been required to share how much water they thought they’d use and what impact that could have on local residents’ water supply. Hansen’s amendment was voted down 23-70.
A pair of Republican House members, Dels. Henry Dillon, R-Wayne, and Chris Anders, R-Berkeley, also tried to put guardrails on water use for data centers, introducing an amendment to limit how data center developments use groundwater and adding “guardrails” to ensure that private wells and other groundwater sources were not impacted by “thirsty data centers.” 
Anders cited constituents’ concerns about local wells running dry. 
The Dillon-Anders amendment failed 6-87.
The rules bundle for HB 2014 is still out for public comment. 
The Public Service Commission of West Virginia has scheduled a public comment Sept. 28, 9:30 a.m., in Charleston on proposed rules governing electric generating capacity requirements established under HB 2014. Members of the public who wish to participate in the hearing must notify the Public Public Service Commission by Sept. 18.

text:
Evening at camp on the Middle Fork Salmon River. (Photo courtesy of Jack Hurty)Author’s note: This is the second part of a four-part story on the looming extinction of wild Chinook salmon in Idaho’s iconic wilderness river, the Middle Fork Salmon River. The first part details the Middle Fork’s terrible salmon returns of the last decade, which if continued will result in their extinction in our lifetimes. This essential factual background will not be repeated here, so I encourage you to read part one, if you have not done so, online. This installment, and a third to follow, focus on the costs to Idaho people and communities if salmon extinction in the heart of Idaho proceeds, and, conversely, the many benefits if Idaho people and leaders don’t let it proceed.   
Business and salmon recovery. Some may incline to see these as opposed terms. But not on the Middle Fork Salmon River. 
Commercial outfitting on the Middle Fork and main Salmon Rivers is a unique business. It is state-licensed, state and federally regulated, and has its own set of necessary skills, best practices and logistics webs across water, air and land. 
Based on public lands and waters, in mountainous rural Idaho, the enterprise is seasonal, weather and conditions-dependent, visitor-dependent, with tricky profit margins and often whole-family commitment. 
On our watch: Salmon extinction on the Middle Fork Salmon River in the heart of Idaho

The business is not separable from its places or communities. Outfitting is often only one part of an economic strategy to live in Salmon, Challis and Stanley, but the challenge comes with rewards: an outdoors life, close to vast public lands and waters, in small towns, not cities. Over decades, an outfitting/guiding culture has grown around the Middle Fork Salmon River, the main Salmon River and the nearby towns.          
Idaho outfitters have supported keeping Idaho’s wild country wild for decades. Today’s Frank Church River of No Return Wilderness would be smaller and of lesser quality without the active support outfitters gave it 50 years ago. In 1979, at U.S. Sen. Frank Church’s tense, high stakes public hearing in Salmon on what wilderness to create for the Middle Fork, Salmon residents who spoke for a 2.3 million acre wilderness outnumbered residents who opposed it. 
Middle Fork guides were the difference. Earlier, when President Jimmy Carter came to Idaho in 1978, he floated the Middle Fork with outfitter Norm Guth. 
President Jimmy Carter and his family raft down the Salmon River in August 1978. (Photo courtesy of the Jimmy Carter Presidential Library)
From within this culture, I have gathered some perspectives on salmon and steelhead extinction from Middle Fork outfitters, guides who work for them, one of their customers and two local elected leaders. I mainly feature their own words. 
Together they suggest the breadth of this culture, its intimacy with the Middle Fork Salmon River, and the stakes for it as the Middle Fork’s wild salmon disappear. 
 Decades of outfitting in Idaho

Ken Helfrich co-owns Helfrich River Outfitter in Salmon. He is the third of five Helfrich generations to outfit and guide on the Middle Fork Salmon River, in his case for 50 years. 
Steve Zettel came to Idaho from Philadelphia in 1980, found work on the Middle Fork Salmon as a guide, and became an outfitter in 1993. Zettel’s Idaho Wilderness Company, in Challis, takes customers down the river, and he also has a hunting camp in Big Creek, a major Middle Fork tributary. 
Dustin Aherin is a fifth-generation Idahoan, raised in Lewiston. An adventurous young boatman and creative citizen in the 1990s, he has guided trips on the Middle Fork since 1998, and started outfitting there with his Idaho River Adventures in 2011. He resides in Salmon and Darby, Montana.
Over seven thousand people boat the Middle Fork with commercial outfitters each year. That’s about 70% of all those who take this five to eight day river journey through the largest wilderness in the 48 states. Helfrich, Zettel and Aherin are three of 27 licensed commercial outfitters on the Middle Fork Salmon River. All three have been down the river over 100 times. Helfrich’s self-estimate is an astounding 500 times. 
They know close-up that the salmon which name the river they work on are near extinction.
Dustin Aherin of Idaho River Adventures. (Photo courtesy of Dustin Aherin)
“The dire straits are obvious if you’re paying attention on the river, which we do,” says Aherin. “In my entire career,” Zettel tells me, “I’ve never seen a salmon in the mainstem Middle Fork itself.” In three weeks on the Middle Fork last year, Helfrich did not see a single salmon, redd (nest) or carcass.      
What are the consequences? Helfrich: “Uppermost for me is the value of the big biomass salmon used to leave behind with the dying fish after they spawn. The natural enzymes that salmon put back in the Middle Fork, for the aquatic life, the birds, bears, and so on. The enzymes are unique, proteins that all the aquatic life depends on. We are losing that, and I am really concerned.  
“We don’t see the life the Middle Fork had when salmon were plentiful. There’s been a big impact on trout. Bull trout feed on young salmon, but they don’t have that now so they are declining too. Years ago we’d watch black bears on the river drag salmon up into the trees to eat, and then come back to the river for more. Today the bears are pretty much gone.”
“And there are effects on vegetation, the riverbanks, the trees. They all need that salmon biomass; it’s been here millions of years. We can’t lose that. It’s hard to think we can just come in, wipe salmon out, and leave a Middle Fork without them.
“There are no hatchery fish in the Middle Fork. Its salmon have a pure genetics that produces adaptable fish that thrive in all kinds of conditions. A diverse gene pool is important. When you’re down to single pairs in most of the river, you have brothers and sisters spawning with each other, if they can even find each other. That reduces their ability to survive.” 
Dustin Aherin: “We’re at the point of no return. The lack of salmon nutrients is degrading the land and water. There aren’t enough animals. The salmon are important to me, but they’re more important to the watershed and its whole array of life.” 
Biologist Russ Thurow and two colleagues estimate that an average 48,000 Chinook returned to the Middle Fork in the 1950s. That’s close to one million tons of marine nutrition coming into the river each year. In the 1930s, it was close to two million tons. Over the last three years, the average Middle Fork salmon return is 811 fish. The 2026 return is nearly certain to be below that, about 1% of the estimated abundance 70 years ago.  
“This isn’t really a business issue for me,” says Steve Zettel. “It’s called the Salmon River, right? They should be there, in their river. They are the core of its ecology, its biology.
“What do I tell my customers? I say, welcome to the Salmon-less River.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 The salmon decline after dams, reservoirs take hold

Zettel, Aherin and Helfrich know why salmon and steelhead are going extinct in the Middle Fork. 
“It has nothing to do with this river,” Helfrich says. “The spawning capacities are still what they were when thousands of salmon returned. We started seeing the decline when the last reservoir went in downstream. It is mainly due to the number of impoundments.”
Middle Fork Salmon River outfitter Ken Helfrich. (Photo courtesy of Helfrich River Outfitter)
That number is eight. The federal government owns and operates eight dams, and 320 consecutive miles of reservoir, on the lower Snake and Columbia Rivers. Snake River salmon and steelhead must traverse this ponded gauntlet twice, going to sea and then returning. 
Salmon returns to Idaho have been dropping for 150 years, but Helfrich is correct that the final decline toward extinction has been since the last of these dams went in, in 1975. 
All three men are non-degreed students of salmon science. All hope the lower Snake will be restored to flow free by notching out the earthen sections of its four dams. 
They are not optimistic it will occur, but they know the Middle Fork Salmon will die as a salmon river if it does not occur.    
Outfitters have another concern: that their operations will again be targeted for tighter regulation, while federal agencies duck the real causes at their own dams and reservoirs. Outfitters saw that movie when salmon were listed under the Endangered Species Act in the 1990s. 
“The feds determined our use was a detriment to the salmon, and began reducing it,” says Steve Zettel. “They even installed cameras to watch our use. They’ve lightened up some since, which certainly makes sense given the lack of salmon.”
Steve Zettel of Idaho Wilderness Company. (Photo courtesy of Steve Zettel)
Dustin Aherin was president of the Middle Fork Outfitters Association for 12 years. “Our outfitters have worked hard to protect salmon during spawning, with the Redd Alert program we started in 2017. I am not interested in putting further burden on outfitters and river users that isn’t going to help prevent extinction.” 
Redd Alert volunteers tell people who are about to launch why and how to avoid salmon redds, which are flagged. Yet most of the mainstem Middle Fork no longer has redds. None have been found in the lower Middle Fork, below Indian Creek, for the last three years. (2026 returns are not yet estimated.)          
 The economic impact of outfitters, river guides

Jack Hurty is a river guide who is also policy and communications director for the Idaho Outfitters and Guides Association. One goal of his job is to restore salmon and steelhead, in the Middle Fork Salmon and across central Idaho. 
Results would include a healthier Middle Fork, more wildlife, better business for his members, healthier communities, retaining the ancient metabolic knit of salmon with the entire watershed, and assuring that knit is part of the experience outfitters can offer 7,000 people each year.         
Twenty-seven outfitters operate 28 permits on the Middle Fork Salmon River. Hurty gave me some rough estimates: “We estimate revenue from each permit averages $700,000 per year, a bit under $20 million in total. With a standard multiplier, that works out to over $30 million in positive impact, most of it felt in the small towns around the river in a three or four month period.”
“I just talked to an outfitter who had invoices from 26 local businesses. That’s how these dollars spread out. And revenue isn’t the full story. Guide wages are about 45% of outfitter costs, and guides spend a lot of that in the towns, on gear, drybags, hats, meals …”  
Then the customers. “You think about a family of four, coming to run the Middle Fork with an outfitter. There’s lodging before and after, two nights in towns at minimum. Four to six meals for four people. They buy gear at the local stores. They pay for shuttles, and flights into Indian Creek for launches. Five aviation companies and their pilots would have trouble without them.”
Hurty knows Middle Fork outfitting won’t collapse if its salmon are extinct. People will still want to run the river. “But the mid- and long term really worry me. We’re selling the experience of the Middle Fork ecosystem — the white water and river, the eagles, otters, bighorn sheep, trout, the ponderosa pine, the tributaries, the tribal and non-tribal history, the wildness. All were fueled by salmon. The Middle Fork is a world-class week-long wilderness river experience. Losing salmon and steelhead will degrade that experience, in obvious ways and ways we don’t even understand. Central Idaho’s economic and cultural future will be terribly narrowed. And we’ll lose the future upside so much has been done and spent to restore: a return to salmon abundance.”   
Plus a soul cost. “Salmon and steelhead extinction would be crushing, a terrible blow to central Idaho’s outfitter and guide culture and communities. It would mean we all had failed.” 
Steve Zettel: “You wonder who watched the last passenger pigeon die. Now here we are in the same position — watching.”
