 ‘The Middle Fork was our home. We are homesick for what our home has lost.’

Jim Norton began guiding on the Salmon River in 1993. His first Middle Fork trip was in 1997. “I joined up with Steve Zettel’s crew at Boundary Creek. The river was at eight feet, really high, really fast, a big river after a big winter. We launched late morning, had lunch over 30 miles downstream, and got to the Flying B [a private ranch] in late afternoon. We imitated baby salmon all the way down — stay in the current, using oars rather than fins to keep under control. We made 70 miles in six hours on the water, a barely controlled descent. We knew the baby salmon were zooming out to sea below us, and four years later a spike of adult salmon indeed came back. The high water sort of negated the dams, turning the Snake River back into more of a river for a couple weeks.  
“For guides, those bigger salmon returns in 2001-2 [a small spike upward that has not repeated] were the same event as the big 1997-98 flows that took those same fish to the ocean. That connected tissue of river and fish, across time and space, is our experience of the Middle Fork.”
Jim has guided on four continents, but “the Middle Fork is different. The opportunity to work on a river that flows through the largest wilderness outside Alaska, on such large scale, is special. On every trip in my first years we watched salmon, those living connections between the ocean and the mountains, leaping in front of us at Dagger Falls. It told us the world was OK.” 
Dagger Falls at sunset on the Middle Fork Salmon River. (Photo courtesy of Jack Hurty)
Dagger Falls was, and for a lucky few still is, a spectacular place to watch 2 and 3 foot salmon, bound upstream to miles of spawning grounds, leap up and through a crashing series of falls it does not seem possible they can power through. Yet they did, and in very small numbers still do. Dagger Falls is a short walk from the Boundary Creek put-in, where most Middle Fork trips begin.   
“It was a custom for guides, a pilgrimage. We’d finish rigging at Boundary for our launches next day. Then we’d jump the fence, sit out on the useless unusable fish ladder at Dagger, and watch the fish jump. We’d stay until dark. We’d cheer every leaping fish. Just awesome. The next day we’d be guides for company a, b, c, or d, but at Dagger we were one.”
“My generation of guides arrived on the scene just as what looked to us like salmon abundance was ending. But it was still such a part of the story. I was in Salmon 12 years. It took me awhile to grasp the tension: living and working in places with such salmon iconography and identity — the names, the rivers, the mountains, the town. And at the same time the absence of salmon abundance. It was palpable in the early ’90s that we’d just missed it.” 
Years later Jim found a name for this feeling: solastalgia. Wikipedia defines it as “a sense of homesickness for a place that is still home, but has become unrecognizable or distressing.” 
“There was so much cultural and economic association with salmon in the towns and on the river. But the salmon weren’t there. The whole community of guides experienced it. The Middle Fork was our home. We are homesick for what our home has lost.”
Some years ago, when Congressman Mike Simpson was assembling his inclusive vision for Columbia-Snake salmon, energy and agriculture, Norton was a panelist at a large public meeting in Salmon that was packed with guides and river people. He said something I think many there had felt, but only truly knew after he said it. “At Banner Summit, on Highway 93, you cross from the Payette River into the Salmon River and the Middle Fork’s headwaters. You pass a threshold, and you feel it. Salmon are the difference. The land and water, the relations people have with them, are so different when salmon are in the system.”  
“To think about turning the Middle Fork into the Payette,” he says now, “induces panic. Such sterilization — nutritionally, experientially, spiritually. The Payette is a fine river. But it’s wholly different without its salmon [which were lost to other dams in the 1950s-’60s]. We destroyed the Payette’s embodiment. We still have, barely, the embodiment of the Salmon River. Doing to the Middle Fork Salmon what we did to the Payette is unthinkable to me. Yet it is happening.”
 Loss of salmon season has been devastating to Idaho’s Salmon, Challis and Stanley

	    
From 1970 to 1999, Gary Power worked for the Idaho Department of Fish and Game, in Challis, Yellow Pine and Salmon, where he still lives. After 43 trips down the Middle Fork in his agency years, he got a commercial guide’s license after retiring, and made 8-10 trips each summer, working for several outfitters. 
Idaho’s general salmon season was still open his first summers with Idaho Fish and Game. “Salmon were a big food source for people here, on top of the recreation. School was out when the fish returned, so families and friends built vacations around them. I worked on the Middle Fork that last open season. People flew into Big Creek and the Middle Fork to fish. Others drove in to the top of Camas and Loon Creeks to camp, then got up at 1 a.m. to claim a good fishing hole. Tin Cup and Meyers Cove were packed with campers. It was a huge economic driver in central Idaho.”
In 1978 the general salmon season closed in the Middle Fork and the Upper Salmon, because of too few fish. “It generated all sorts of local outcry. Businesses were gutted, we had fish-ins and protests. It was devastating in Salmon, Challis and Stanley.” There has been no salmon season in the Middle Fork since — and only a few, very limited seasons in the upper Salmon.
The Boundary Creek Put-In and Eddy, where many Middle Fork Salmon trips begin. (Photo courtesy of Jack Hurty)
“In those first years I fished the Middle Fork, Loon, Camas, and Big Creeks, and more. First time you get a salmon on, it’s such a thrill. I’d take my family to see them digging their redds in the riffles, and chasing over shallows like mini-hydroplanes. It is something to be four feet from spawning salmon.” 
Power affirms the effects of lost salmon nutrients. “In 1970, when I first caught cutthroat trout in Big Creek, they were 16-18 inches. Now they are much smaller. Large numbers of deteriorating salmon carcasses used to heavily fertilize the river, to the benefit of other species. Fingerling salmon, resident fish, and all sorts of wildlife had more food. Now that’s gone.  
“These are the only watersheds on earth where salmon climb 6,000 feet or more to spawn. You can’t put a salmon from anywhere else here, and have it work. The native fish have an irreplaceable adaptation, to make this arduous migration from the ocean up to the mountains of Idaho. To lose that isn’t a reasonable option, when we can save them. 
“When obstructions in the river are removed, the effects on salmon are immediate. Look at the Klamath River after four dams were removed, and the Elwha River. For the fish, it’s like opening a new McDonald’s. They have to go check it out.  
“To lose these fish makes no sense. Everything around here that’s named after salmon — we’d have to change all the names.” 
 A Middle Fork outfitters customer’s perspective: ‘Every place on that river has a memory for me.’

Mark Williams, of Birmingham, Alabama, grew up on a farm near Nashville, camping and roaming the creeks. He is a physician, and an attorney, with two sons and two daughters. His perspective is as a customer of Middle Fork outfitters for over 40 years.   
While camping once near Stanley, by accident he met Middle Fork outfitters Dave and Sheila Mills. The next year, Mark, his father, and his brothers returned for a Rocky Mountain River Tours trip down the Middle Fork. “It was the early 1980s, spring, high water, a real adventure. I was surprised there weren’t more salmon. But I got interested. I brought more of my family out. We just loved that part of Idaho — the wildness, the adventure, the people, the joy of sharing it with family, friends and colleagues. Our guides were great people, hard-working, self-reliant. I have lifelong friends I first met as Middle Fork guides. 
“I’ve probably been down the Middle Fork 50 times now. One year, I brought over 200 physicians out. They were astonished at the beauty, the wilderness, free from their cell phones. The isolation and purity — I took great joy to watch them feel it too. Everyone regretted the last day on those trips. Over many years we introduced several hundred physicians, colleagues and other friends to this beautiful river and Wilderness, many of whom returned on family trips of their own. Every place on that river has a memory for me. I loved to watch the changes over years — deadfalls, washouts, fires, the river changes all the time.”  
He bought a home on Agency Creek, a Lemhi River tributary near Lemhi Pass — “Captain Lewis and the Corps of Discovery literally traversed our place” — and rented it to river guides when he wasn’t there. “I met people like Jim Norton, Jerry Myers, John Caccia. They really knew salmon, and had a powerful sense of stewardship. You want to be like those people.  It’s not monetary. The place is so deep in them. One of my daughters became a river guide, and so did I.
“I noticed the salmon decline. Some guides were great at explaining how the salmon were protein for all the other animals. And the decline without them, no food for the eagles and trees. People I brought would always ask, where are the salmon? They’d hear the story, and couldn’t believe it.”
What would extinction mean to him? “Oh — a profound loss and waste. An integral part of Idaho, lost forever. The Salmon River, without salmon? Salmon, Idaho, without salmon? And we just watched it happen?
His advice to Idaho’s leaders: “I know people will always love to come to Idaho just to see salmon. Salmon is a recreation hub now. Imagine if Salmon the town had salmon the fish back in the Middle Fork. What an opportunity to bring people to Idaho. I hope your representatives see the value of it for all Americans. The hundreds of people I brought to the Middle Fork — they left changed.
“And, we owe the Native Americans. The Middle Fork is a spiritual place. I’ve watched River of Return, a video of the young Shoshone-Bannock children, going down the river with Sam and Jessica Matsaw, learning about the salmon, the mussels they found, the tribal history along the river. So moving. The United States made those children a promise before they were born, to have fish to fish for. Shouldn’t we keep our promise?” 
“I have friends who still remember a super-cold trip 40 years ago. The first week in May, I brought an entire hospital leadership team from Birmingham. We came over the pass from Boise to four feet of snow. Snow everywhere. They started to wonder, why did we do this? A waitress at Redfish Lake Lodge told us a group had flipped their boat and had to hike out.  It was snowing when we put on the river, in a stiff wind. Then misery became an adventure, and it turned out fine.          
“I’m too old for it now. But what a privilege to have that time, in that country, with those Idaho people we met. It always provided peacefulness, away from the rest of the world.”
A bench above Pool Camp on the Middle Fork Salmon River. (Photo courtesy of Jack Hurty)
 A conflicting optimism/pessimism about salmon

Breann and Matt Green are life residents of Salmon, both born in Salmon’s Steele Memorial Hospital. In between raising four children, they own River of No Return Wilderness Outfitters. They operate on the wilderness stretch of the main Salmon River, into which the Middle Fork flows. Both once guided on the Middle Fork, and Matt has fished and hunted there. 
“The Middle Fork provides about half the flow for the main Salmon where we operate,” Breann says. “It is a shining gem, the most untrammeled 100-plus miles of river I know, the heart of the Frank Church Wilderness. Our business would be a lot better if salmon and steelhead were here. We’ve offered some combo trips, steelhead fishing and chukar hunting, in the spring and fall. But with fish numbers so low, it doesn’t feel right. We’d love to do that again if the numbers go up.” 
“Salmon are a keystone species,” adds Matt. “So it is catastrophic to lose them, with the chain effect on all the other species. Emotionally and culturally, it would knock us down to our knees.”
Like many in Salmon, Breann and Matt have a conflicted optimism/pessimism about salmon. The optimism is based in the resilience of the fish, the pessimism in politics and all the infrastructure built around the lower Snake dams downstream. 
Breann: “I have a lot of hope, if the fish can get here. Our town is named Salmon — it’s important to us to keep these fish and keep advocating for them.” Matt: “The impact of the reservoirs is getting worse, with how warm the water is getting. We have smallmouth bass now in the Salmon River. But you have to be optimistic, otherwise why be in our business?”  
Breann and Matt are also active in another salmon story in Lemhi County: the growing number of restored streams on ranches and private lands along the Salmon River and on tributaries like the Lemhi and Pahsimeroi Rivers. 
“When this work started in the early 1990s,” Breann recalls, “it was a little controversial here, but that’s gone now. Everyone in the valley knows and respects what’s been accomplished.” 
For several years, Breann worked for the Lemhi Regional Land Trust, a key local partner/catalyst in the restoration projects. Matt once worked for Trout Unlimited, another partner, and now, on top of his outfitting, works for Rio Applied Science and Engineering, a Boise-based company that designs stream and habitat restorations. 
“We’re restoring our watersheds and protecting ranching values,” Breann says. “We’re keeping water in the basin, rebuilding healthy braided streams with huge benefit to fish and wildlife. We’re now seeing rainbow and cutthroat trout throughout the system. We’ve created good jobs. It’s important for the whole valley.” 
“A lot of people we know have the ability to live here due to this work,” Matt adds. “It’s very positive for the community.”
The Idaho Department of Fish and Game is a key partner. Gary Power was Fish and Game’s regional supervisor in the early 1990s: “Everybody downstream was pointing fingers at the headwaters, saying salmon decline is your fault, not the dams. So we went to work on the local problems. We installed better screens, to keep the salmon and resident fish out of irrigation ditches. We restored spawning and rearing habitats. Ranchers changed grazing systems. Farmers changed from flood irrigation to sprinklers, allowing better water management for crops and fish. Historically, the Lemhi and other tributaries were de-watered; that has been corrected. A lot of good collaborative work.”
Looking downstream toward Gardell’s Hole, Middle Fork Salmon River. (Photo courtesy of Jack Hurty)
 “Resident fisheries, bull trout and cutthroat, benefited,” says Power. “But it didn’t bring the salmon back.” Breann Green: “We are building miles and miles of good salmon habitat. But we know it won’t restore the Chinook. We’ve built it, but the salmon don’t come.”  
Yet much of the work was financed with dollars dedicated to restoring salmon. “We used lots of Bonneville Power Administration and Pacific Salmon Recovery funds for the projects,” Breann adds. “Bonneville was the source for maybe a third of our funds. Now they are cutting and cutting, not renewing their funding agreement with Idaho. There is lag time, so we’ll see most of the effects in the next few years.” 
Bonneville Power is the federal agency that markets power from the federal dams. Despite its 30-year failure to recover salmon, the agency is now sharply cutting its salmon funding, including spawning habitat restoration dollars to states and tribes. The Grand Ronde Valley in eastern Oregon, the Lemhi and Pahsimeroi Valleys in Idaho, the Nez Perce, Shoshone-Bannock and Umatilla Tribes, and salmon and steelhead will be among the losers.
 Stanley’s strong connection to Middle Fork recreation, tourism

Steve Botti is the mayor of Stanley. He moved to Boise in 1988, where he worked for the U.S. Park Service at the Boise (now National) Interagency Fire Center. “In 2007, I moved to Stanley to ‘retire.’ It didn’t work out that way.” 
Stanley sits in a vast circle of salmon habitat, to north, south, east and west: the upper Salmon River, Redfish Lake and the other sockeye salmon lakes in Sawtooth Valley, the Yankee Fork Salmon River, East Fork Salmon River, and Middle Fork Salmon River. The Middle Fork’s headwaters in Marsh and Bear Valley Creeks are west of town, used in all seasons and cherished locally.
“Stanley’s economy has a strong connection to the Middle Fork,” Mayor Botti told me. “We are an outfitter and guide hub. In season, a steady stream of planes goes in and out of the Middle Fork from Stanley, and a steady stream of boats go in. Our economy is almost 100% based on recreation and tourism now. You’ll find a lot of shared values here, which is pretty essential to living, and making a living, here.” 
Stanley is 6,600 feet high; its winters are a reward for those who love snow and can handle severe conditions. 
Two years ago, I asked Mayor Botti what restoring salmon would mean to the Stanley area. “Fishing always attracts people, and is important to our economy. Fishing interest would expand dramatically if salmon could be restored. I’m a fisherman, so I understand that.      
“But deeper, we don’t see salmon as just a fish. They are a living embodiment of wildness and for their amazing migration. Most of us sense that something important is missing from our landscape and community. Let’s say all the mountain goats and elk, or the camas and shooting stars had vanished. And then, decades later, they came back. People would treasure that. 
“It would be personal for many in and around Stanley. We are keenly aware of the passing seasons, the seasonal dramas. The changes are so dramatic. People enjoy those rhythms — the sandhill cranes return in the spring, the progression of wildflowers. It’s like a movie. Salmon are minor characters in the landscape now, but people know they were once the lead actors. Having them migrating here again would reconnect our past to our present.”
The good work underway by Pacific Northwest salmon people in northeast Oregon

Two weeks ago, I asked him about the impact, locally and personally, if salmon go extinct. “Many people come to Stanley for the fishing experience, and connect to the wild lands in that way. When I dig into that experience, I find that for me, and no doubt many others, it extends far beyond catching fish. The window into the natural environment that fishing provides me is more important than catching a fish. So extinction of salmon is much deeper than just not being able to marvel at the sight of them in the river.
“For me, the loss of salmon makes the wilderness less wild in ways that I’m sure I cannot even imagine. Some of those changes are subtle, but I sense the loss even so. I recall a study years ago about how people respond to wilderness that was quite revealing. As wilderness impacts increased, those who had experienced the loss of much more natural ‘wilderness’ were displaced by those who were satisfied with a much less ‘wild’ experience. The current users mostly accepted what they found as the way it’s always been, and did not feel the loss. I suspect that is what is happening due to the immense reduction in current salmon numbers.”
In natural science, this is called the “shifting baseline syndrome.” Russ Thurow, the leading authority on Middle Fork Chinook salmon, has co-authored a paper which in part explores how the syndrome applies to Middle Fork salmon. A summary of the paper can be found at SYCU – Rethinking the possible: Applying long-term datasets to estimate historic salmon abundance in the Middle Fork Salmon River.
Mayor Botti is also a botanist, and is working on a book about Sawtooth Valley botany. “We know the nutrients salmon bring from the ocean spread far and wide through Salmon River ecosystems. If your first article is right, about 97.5% of those nutrients have already been lost in the past 60-70 years. I wonder how this ‘pre-extinction’ has already affected plant populations and species diversity. This may be an example of subtle changes we are unaware of, so we accept the flora and fauna we see now as the way it always was. We don’t have a sense of what has been lost.” 
Botti wonders if “the extinction of salmon as a profound element in the natural ecosystems of the Salmon River has already occurred.” 
I was struck by Botti’s phrase “pre-extinction.” Russ Thurow would agree that salmon “as a profound element” in Salmon River ecosystems have been severely compromised by the general absence of salmon nutrients. 
But his work, alone and with colleagues, has also shown that, even though at very low numbers, Middle Fork salmon still retain all the building blocks — genetic, behavioral, and habitat excellence, plus demonstrated resiliency — to restore themselves if we take a small part of our hydroelectric foot off their necks. 
The next step downward, which Thurow expects within 15 years unless actions are taken downstream, will be salmon numbers declining to so few that their capacity to recover will be lost. That, he says, will truly be pre-extinction, with no road back. 
Those distinctions aside, both men agree on the main point: Middle Fork salmon are in crisis, and science-based action is urgently needed now.     
 As local restoration restores ecosystems, ‘we need to connect salmon to people again’

Russ Chinske moved to Salmon from Missoula in 2002. He was a Middle Fork guide for Helfrich Outfitter and has taught Salmon’s elementary students for 23 years. Now he is in his third term on the Salmon City Council: “I decided I’d rather do something than complain.”
“Salmon are not a big priority for the City Council. We’re only 3,000 people, with a shoestring city budget. Roads, police, water, sewer — the basic needs take our time.”
But salmon are important to Mr. Chinske. “I fish less now, but I love being on the river. I agree the situation is dire. We are staring down extinction, and we need to act. I think it comes down to the dams on the lower Snake River.
“The local restoration work has been great. We now have restored habitat on the Lemhi River [which joins the main Salmon at the town]. It shows we can maintain the local ranching culture, and get the water back to high quality, and create jobs. Lots of people are engaged now. And the Middle Fork is the crown jewel of salmon habitat, as pristine as you’ll see anywhere. We are ready to have fish.
“The Middle Fork is part of our economic picture. We don’t have much stable year-round economics, and we’re pretty isolated. Agriculture has staying power. And river recreation started here right after the city was created. It is stable and sustainable, people love it, outfitters base here, there’s a strong culture. It is seasonal, but a big positive jolt to the economy. People coming off and going on the Middle Fork and main Salmon spend dollars here.”
If salmon were restored? “An economic benefit for sure, for us, for Riggins, and other towns. It would get more crowded, but … And salmon nutrients would return to the system. Salmon are a real local resource. Many people here just get by, so having fish to harvest would help people out.  
“And the sheer magic. I talk to the old-timers, hear their stories of huge abundant salmon. A great mystique — but I’ve never felt or seen it, multiple generations haven’t seen it. We need to connect salmon to people again. There is nothing bad about restoring salmon. It’s frustrating to know that long local history, the magic and benefits that used to be here, and not have it now.  
“I don’t think we have all the answers yet about how to adjust if the dams come out — for the barges getting crops to market, the energy. Until we have a ‘replace this with that’ plan, with real solutions happening, I doubt it will happen. But I’m optimistic because it’s possible. The science is clear. All the hatcheries, failure after failure. When dams come out, nature does its thing and salmon return. Look at the Elwha and Klamath dam removals.
“The state and feds are not putting huge energies into small places like Salmon. We’re only 3,000 people; we don’t have a big voice. But I see no reason we can’t have both energy and salmon. The versus, either/or stuff has to go. We can do both. We need to start thinking like that. Why not? What’s holding us back?”
 Former Republican majority leader of the US Senate calls for Snake River restoration

I had planned to end on Chinske’s excellent question. But a few days ago I heard from Mark Williams, the Alabama man interviewed above. He sent along this fine essay, written for Forbes magazine, by Bill Frist, the former Republican majority leader of the U.S. Senate: https://apple.news/Ar1T054bdSHqACMEwZrwf8w.
In August, Mr. Frist floated the Middle Fork with leaders and staff of The Nature Conservancy. Sammy Matsaw, the Shoshone-Bannock Tribal member whose Middle Fork trips with Shoshone-Bannock youth, in the film River of Return, so moved Mark Williams, is featured in Frist’s essay. 
Matsaw is Columbia Basin salmon program director for the conservancy. Five salmon the group saw in Loon Creek are also featured. Near the end of his thoughtful and feeling-full essay, Frist calls for the detailed advance planning needed to restore the lower Snake River by removing its four dams. 
U.S. Sen. Mike Crapo served with Sen. Frist, and U.S. Sen. Jim Risch likely knows him. I hope both read that their former fellow senator visited Idaho for a week on the peerless Middle Fork Salmon River — and that the powerful experience led him to a conclusion they have resisted. Mr. Frist’s float was outfitted by Solitude River Trips, so his essay is also the most recent fruit of Idaho outfitters’ continuing work to defend Idaho wild country and restore Idaho salmon.
 What’s next in the salmon series

I hope I have given readers a sense of central Idaho’s outfitter/guide culture, and of the great black hole within it which salmon extinction will leave. I thank all my interviewees for speaking with me, Jack Hurty and the Idaho Outfitters and Guides Association for invaluable contacts, and Russ Thurow for scientific guidance.
My next installment will focus on Indigenous tribes, whose treaties with our nation, should we honor them, guarantee salmon to fish for in the Middle Fork Salmon. And on Idaho young people, whose Idaho has never had abundant salmon and, unless we act quickly, never will. And on the bottomless connections between Idaho public lands and Idaho salmon. You might start to look for it in two months.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Does talking about domestic violence make you a wimp? Asking for some candidates.
description: Dr. Ralph Alvarado’s campaign pushed out a press release this week on a curious piece in the Daily Caller, the right-wing website about Alvarado’s opponent in the 6th District Congressional race, Zach Dembo. In it, author Derek VanBuskirk cited Dembo’s 2024 interview on a podcast called The Good Guy Guide, in which Dembo talked about […]
text:
Republican Ralph Alvarado, left, and Democrat Zach Dembo, right, are running in Kentucky's 6th Congressional District. (Photos provided by campaigns)Dr. Ralph Alvarado’s campaign pushed out a press release this week on a curious piece in the Daily Caller, the right-wing website about Alvarado’s opponent in the 6th District Congressional race, Zach Dembo. In it, author Derek VanBuskirk cited Dembo’s 2024 interview on a podcast called The Good Guy Guide, in which Dembo talked about performative masculinity and other issues.
“He continued, saying that ‘the biggest issue that we’re still dealing with” when it comes to problems in leadership, intimate partner violence, and sexual assaults is the “expectation of what it means to be masculine,” suggesting that when someone falls short of those expectations, they tend to overcompensate aggressively,” VanBuskirk writes.
What the author fails to mention is that the show was about domestic violence from the male perspective, and what good guys can do to stop a scourge almost entirely committed by bad ones.
How do I know this? I was sitting right there. 
I’ve written about domestic violence off and on for decades, and I was told about a new podcast being recorded by Devine Carama, who runs Lexington’s anti-gun violence organization called One Lexington. 
The show was created through the It’s Time campaign from the Fayette County Domestic and Sexual Violence Prevention Coalition, which wanted more emphasis on the root causes and prevention of domestic violence. 
As Carama has said: “Asking women to solve domestic violence is like asking Black people to solve racism.”
Carama and his frequent co-host, Sam Stockley, a British professional soccer player turned Lexington Sporting Club coach (you know how wimpy those guys are) would interview different guests about, as I wrote at the time, “love and violence and machismo and abuse and expectations and accountability and vulnerability and a bunch of other things that we assume (sometimes correctly) that men never talk about?”
Dembo also spoke about his love of butterflies as a young boy, which caused some problems at school, something the Daily Caller seems to think should disqualify him from office. 
The masculinity question is one that’s been used on other Democratic candidates, like Texas Senate aspirant James Talarico (“Low T Talarico”) and Sen. Jon Ossoff, dismissed by Trump as “PeeWee Herman.” 
Podcast co-founder Lillie Ruschell is dismayed by the hit on Dembo, but not surprised.
“The point of the podcast was to create a space where men could speak honestly about masculinity, vulnerability, accountability, and the role men have in changing a culture that too often enables violence,” she said. “To see that willingness to be vulnerable now weaponized against them is deeply disappointing.
“The goal was to create something that told survivors of domestic violence, clearly and unequivocally, that there are men in their corner,” Ruschell continued. “If we say we want men to step up, have difficult conversations, and be part of the solution, we cannot punish them when they do.”
Also, it seems like a kind of weak sauce attack (forgive me) given there are so many other issues to talk to voters about, like affordability, the Iran war, AI. But maybe it will work. 
I have no idea who’s going to win the 6th District race. All I know is domestic violence affects 10 million people in this country and kills more than 1,500 every year, and the more we talk about it – even with awkward syntax and genuine feeling – the better.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Opioid authority awards $12.3 million for prevention, treatment and recovery in Virginia
description: Virginia will steer more than $12.3 million in opioid settlement money toward state programs ranging from naloxone distribution and treatment services to youth education and recovery support on college campuses, the Virginia Opioid Abatement Authority announced recently.  The agency’s Grants Committee approved its latest round of funding for 39 projects acro[...]
text:
The Virginia Opioid Abatement Authority has awarded more than $12.3 million to support opioid prevention, treatment and recovery efforts across the commonwealth. (Photo by Getty Images)Virginia will steer more than $12.3 million in opioid settlement money toward state programs ranging from naloxone distribution and treatment services to youth education and recovery support on college campuses, the Virginia Opioid Abatement Authority announced recently. 
The agency’s Grants Committee approved its latest round of funding for 39 projects across 18 state agencies and public institutions. Seven are new projects, while 32 are continuations of previously funded efforts. 
The committee also approved carrying forward more than $3.1 million in previously awarded money, bringing the total available for the projects during the 2026-27 funding period to about $15.4 million. 
“These awards strengthen the partnerships that are helping Virginia prevent opioid misuse, expand access to treatment, and support people in recovery,” said state Sen. Todd Pillion, R-Washington, chair of the authority’s board of directors. 
“By investing in the expertise of our state agencies and public universities, we can reach more Virginians with services that save lives and help individuals and families build a healthier future.” 
The money comes from Virginia’s share of national legal settlements with opioid manufacturers, distributors and other companies. The General Assembly created the Opioid Abatement Authority in 2021 to oversee much of that money, which is restricted to efforts aimed at treating, preventing or reducing opioid-use disorder and opioid abuse. 
The authority controls 55% of Virginia’s opioid settlement funds. Another 30% goes directly to cities and counties, with the remaining 15% allocated to the state. 
Virginia’s settlement payments began in 2022 and are expected to exceed $1.1 billion before concluding in 2041. Court orders and state law restrict the money to opioid abatement and remediation efforts.
A 2021 VCU analysis and the Department of Health estimated that nearly 150,000 Virginians had opioid-use disorder that year. At least six people died from opioid overdoses each day on average.
Fentanyl and other synthetic opioids have been especially deadly. From 2020 through 2024, they were involved in roughly three out of every four fatal drug overdoses in Virginia.
The numbers have fallen sharply, however.  Virginia Department of Health data show 1,403 Virginians died from drug overdoses in 2024, down 43% from 2023.
Demand for the latest round of money exceeded what was available. The authority received 51 proposals seeking more than $21.1 million during an application period that ran from March 20 through June 8.
The Virginia Department of Health received the largest combined award, with more than $2.4 million in new funding and nearly $717,000 carried forward from the previous year. 
The money will support harm-reduction services, local opioid-use disorder coordinators, regional overdose review teams and a pilot program for pregnant women. More than $503,000 is going toward the state’s naloxone distribution infrastructure, including about $79,000 carried forward, while another $500,000 of previously awarded money will pay for naloxone purchases. 
Naloxone is a medication that can rapidly reverse an opioid overdose.
 Another $1.84 million in new funding will go to the Virginia Foundation of Healthy Youth. Most of it, about $1.47 million, will support the foundation’s “Deadly Dose” fentanyl and overdose messaging campaign. The remaining $370,000 will expand access to its Dangers of Fentanyl lesson. 
“The opioid crisis affects people in every part of the Commonwealth, and our response must reflect the different needs of those communities,” said Del. Briana Sewell, D-Prince William, vice chair of the authority’s board and acting chair of its Grants Committee.
“These investments support evidence-based approaches while helping agencies work together to expand prevention, strengthen treatment and recovery services, and make effective use of settlement dollars.” 
Seven of Virginia’s public universities also received funding, much of it aimed at prevention and recovery efforts on campus. 
Virginia Commonwealth University will get $1.6 million in new funding. Among its projects is HARBOR, a new pilot program that will pair certified peer recovery specialists with an immersive virtual reality recovery program. The authority awarded more than $267,000 for the effort. 
VCU also received renewed funding for several existing programs, including more than $582,000 for the Virginia Opioid Abatement Toolkit and about $326,000 for the Virginia Naloxone Project. Other money will support substance-abuse counselor training, student recovery services and work at the school’s Massey Cancer Center. 
Virginia Tech was awarded nearly $1.17 million in new funding, including money for two new projects. The university will receive about $115,000 for a recovery housing assessment, training and technical assistance program and more than $93,000 to expand neuroscience-based substance-use prevention education. 
Existing Virginia Tech programs receiving another round of funding include Virginia Cooperative Extension services and a campus recovery community. 
George Mason University, Radford University, the University of Mary Washington, the University of Virginia and Virginia State University also received money for recovery initiatives. 
Beyond universities, the Southwest Virginia Higher Education Center was awarded nearly $63,000 for a new simulation-based training program for first responders. 
More than $1 million in new funding will go to the Department of Education for an opioid abatement education plan and a technical assistance and grant program for Virginia recovery schools. About $74,000 left from the previous funding cycle will carry forward. 
Some of the settlement money is also headed into the criminal justice system.
 The Department of Corrections received about $840,000 in new funding for medication-assisted treatment social workers and naloxone distribution for people on probation, along with more than $223,000 carried forward from the previous funding period. 
Nearly $400,000 will go to the Virginia Indigent Defense Commission for a re-entry and recovery specialist program. The Supreme Court of Virginia was awarded about $507,000 for a statewide drug-testing contract. 
Meanwhile, the Department of Behavioral Health and Developmental Services will receive more than $210,000 for a new Recovery Workforce Conference. The agency also received another round of funding for a substance-use data analyst and the Virginia Recovery Corps. 
Because opioid settlement payments arrive over a period of years, the authority makes it awards one year at a time. 
Recipients of competitive state agency and cooperative partnership grants can seek as many as four one-year renewals, provided they remain in compliance with the authority’s requirements and continue making progress toward their project’s objectives.

title: Virginia school board settles with parents, reverses policy that blocked LGBTQ+ student club
description: King George County Schools will now allow sixth- to eighth-grade students to form non-curricular clubs, including one supporting LGBTQ+ students, after the school board settled with the families of two students who said the school did not allow them to form the LGBTQ+ club previously, according to a Monday announcement.  The school board faced litigation […]
text:
(Illustration by mustafahacalaki/Getty Images)King George County Schools will now allow sixth- to eighth-grade students to form non-curricular clubs, including one supporting LGBTQ+ students, after the school board settled with the families of two students who said the school did not allow them to form the LGBTQ+ club previously, according to a Monday announcement. 
The school board faced litigation for allegedly blocking students from creating the organization last August, after community concerns surfaced that the proposed Gay-Straight Alliance club was not “age-appropriate” and would “not be a safe space, but a dangerous place,” the lawsuit read.
ACLU of Virginia lawsuit alleges King George School Board blocked LGBTQ+ student club

The settlement reverses the board’s decision to prohibit noncurricular groups at the middle school, including the proposed GSA, and to limit such groups to the high school.
In a statement, King George Schools said it updated its student organization policy, and parents must provide written permission before their child may attend meetings or join a student club or organization.
The ACLU of Virginia and the Potomac Law Group, representing the families of the two students, said their clients suffered irreparable harm from being unable to establish and participate in the GSA, which prompted them to file a lawsuit against the district’s alleged violations of the First Amendment and the Equal Access Act protections..
The suit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia.
“It should not have taken a lawsuit for the King George County School Board to do the right thing,” ACLU-VA Staff Attorney Julia Kahn said in a statement. “The First Amendment and Equal Access Act protects all students, and school boards cannot pick and choose which clubs can form just because they don’t like what a club represents. This settlement benefits all students at King George Middle School by ensuring everyone is treated equally.”
The school division’s new student club regulation also requires a signed parental permission form as part of the application process for establishing a new non-curriculum student club or organization.
These changes, King George Public Schools said, demonstrate the school board’s commitment to family involvement, transparency, and direct communication between school leaders and parents. 
The school division said the guidelines were updated to balance its desire to offer students opportunities to “participate in student-initiated organizations” while establishing clear expectations that support student safety, positive conduct and a supportive school environment.
Across the country, advocates, including those from the Genders and Sexualities Alliance Network, are encouraging more groups to form to help LGBTQ+ youth and their allies become leaders and advocates for safer, more inclusive schools and communities.
The parents of the two students named in the suit said they are grateful their children can now participate in GSA clubs and are proud of their bravery in fighting for equal access to extracurricular activities. Still, they emphasized that students should not have had to fight for such rights in the first place.
“As parents, nothing matters more than our child’s wellbeing, safety, health, and education, and GSA clubs support all of these,” plaintiffs Teresa Catoe and John Wheeler, parents of the student identified in court documents as Z.J.W., said in a statement. 
“We are overjoyed that our child now has the opportunity to form a club that will make them excited to go to school, eager to participate, and determined to do their best. But it never should have fallen on our child’s shoulders to fight for the rights of students.”
Mary Rohmiller, a partner at Potomac Law Group, said the law is clear that schools must offer opportunities on equal terms to all students, but the King George County School Board singled out the GSA for exclusion. 
“School clubs are where students build community, discover who they are, and find the courage to thrive,” Rohmiller said. “These students were denied just that, not because of anything they did wrong, but simply because of who they are and what they believe. That kind of discrimination has no place in our schools.”
The legal team representing the students’ families said that if King George Middle School does not approve a proposal to form a GSA submitted under the new policy, they will refile the lawsuit.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Another day, another Virginia university targeted by the feds for ‘racial discrimination.’
description: In 1991, Martha Muguira became the first Latina to earn a doctorate at the College of William & Mary. The degree marked the happy ending of a local hero’s success story — and the beginning of a resource to expand educational access to other Hispanic students. After a career in community service and education, Muguira […]
text:
The Wren Building at the College of William and Mary in Williamsburg.(Photo courtesy of NBC12)In 1991, Martha Muguira became the first Latina to earn a doctorate at the College of William & Mary. The degree marked the happy ending of a local hero’s success story — and the beginning of a resource to expand educational access to other Hispanic students.
After a career in community service and education, Muguira died in 2012. Her friends and family established a privately funded fellowship to help more Latino and Hispanic students go to W&M’s graduate school of education.
“Preference is given to Hispanic or Latino women who have financial need,” the William & Mary website says.
The financial award is modest: $2,950.  
That, apparently, is still too much for President Donald Trump and his diversity-hating minions.
DOJ probes William & Mary over alleged race-based scholarship policies

The U.S. Department of Justice recently announced an investigation of the college, alleging it practiced illegal racial discrimination because of its efforts to use the Muguira fellowship and other scholarships to increase enrollment of underrepresented Black and Hispanic minorities.
A statement on William & Mary’s website says the school “ is committed to nondiscrimination and compliance with all state and federal laws,” and is cooperating with the investigation. 
Calling it criminal for campuses to reflect America’s population betrays the Civil Rights Bill of 1964, which banned racial discrimination and which Trump now uses to justify an attack on higher education.  
“It is really an insidious way of using the Civil Rights Act that grew out of (separate but equal) Jim Crow laws,” said Vania Blaiklock, a 2018 graduate of William & Mary’s law school and now a professor at Washington and Lee University School of Law.
The Williamsburg university’s current student body is 61.3% white, 11.7% Asian, 8.8% Hispanic, 6.8% multi-ethnic, 5.7% Black or African-American, 3.9% international, and 1.7% unknown, according to the website College Factual. 
The Census Bureau says Black people make up 13.5% of the U.S. population, and Hispanics make up 20.5%. 
In 2022, Hispanic teachers made up roughly 11% of the educational workforce, and Black teachers made up 9.4%, according to USAFacts.
Just 5% of lawyers are Black and only 5% are Hispanic, and the percentage of each has grown very slowly, the American Bar Association reported. 
Though they try to hide behind the word “meritocracy,” white  grievance is the hallmark of Trump and his ultra-conservative supporters’ vendetta against academia. 
William & Mary is among 45 schools across the country where the administration wants to make a merit-based argument for killing off scholarships and programs that mention race. They propose to do this  even though beneficiaries must academically qualify for admission.  
In order to destroy minority recruitment, the president and his willing accomplices first had to destroy a legal concept called disparate impact. It provided the backbone for applying the Civil Rights Act of 1964. 
Disparate impact holds that if the neutral application of a law or policy has a disparate impact on a group that can be proven, that group can claim discrimination. 
The concept grew out of a Supreme Court case where the majority of justices determined that an employer’s hiring mechanism had kept Black people out of jobs. The precedent eventually extended to other sectors where minorities were underrepresented as a result of neutral application. 
In April 2025, without seeking the public input required by federal regulation, Trump struck the first blow against disparate impact with an executive order that demonized it after 50 years of legal use.
“Disparate-impact liability all but requires individuals and businesses to consider race and engage in racial balancing to avoid potentially crippling legal liability,” the order said. “It not only undermines our national values, but also runs contrary to equal protection under the law and, therefore, violates our Constitution.” 
In December 2025, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi administered the coup de grace by formally eliminating disparate impact liability from Department of Justice regulations for implementing Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
It was a gambit to ensure that private employers, federal agencies, college admissions offices and others would never be allowed to consider race in doing business. 
This is part of Trump’s exploitation of a Supreme Court with six conservative members, including three justices the president nominated. The conservative majority has severely limited the Voting Rights Act, opining that racial discrimination does not extensively exist in the country any longer. 
Then, you read a story about a campground owner in Virginia who told a couple she would not have rented a cabin to them if she’d known one of their guests was Black. That happened in 2020 and the couple was just awarded restitution a few weeks ago.
Removing disparate impact is another way of conservatives claiming America has solved its race problems. But guess who the removal benefits? Here’s a hint: Who could never claim disparate impact in almost any neutral application of law and policy in the U.S.?
If you answered white people, take a bow. 
Trump could not change the disparate impact law, Stanford University Law School professor Richard Banks told me. So, what he chose to do was not enforce it.  
Banks has written extensively about disparate impact. He calls Trump’s “wholesale rejection” of the concept “overwrought and misguided.”
You might also call it hypocritical, in light of Trump’s demands that universities hire more conservative faculty simply because he commands it.
The quality of Trump’s cabinet appointments makes the president’s case for meritocracy “a huge irony,” added Banks. 
“You’re fighting with someone who is not playing by any rules. That’s just the world we are living in,” he said.
As if to prove Banks’ point, the Trump administration just announced rules designed to revoke the tax-exempt status of any college or university with any race-based programs.
William & Mary can mount defenses for some of the programs under investigation, Banks and Blaiklock agreed. 
For instance, a current scholarship that encourages graduates of historically Black colleges and universities (HBCUs) to apply to the W&M law school does not exclude white or Asian undergraduates from those schools. Nor does it exclude applicants from any other ethnic group, including Whites.  
The Martha Muguira Fellowship website references Muguira’s desire to give financial “assistance to Latina students seeking graduate studies in education with a concentration in leadership.” It is privately funded, but anyone can apply.  
A problem for William and Mary could be that Maguira was not some fabulously rich alumnae who founded a philanthropic foundation that raised millions, the experts said.  Her modest effort to help other Latinas get advanced degrees relies on donations made through the College of  William & Mary Foundation. This draws the college into the preference debate. 
But other ways exist to attract minority students. Banks and Blaiklock pointed to programs for students who are the first in their families to attend college or have economic needs. 
The college could also recruit at high schools with large minority populations, or reach out to minority graduates to act as intermediaries. 
For now, William & Mary, like a few other Virginia higher education institutions, must figure out how to deal with a president willing to waste millions of taxpayers’ dollars and misuse the Justice Department to disrupt America’s best universities until they run out of money and submit to his biased personal political agenda.
It is, as Blaiklock correctly pointed out, “a strategy of intimidation.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia’s federal lawmakers lock in on regulating data centers
description: Two members of Virginia’s congressional delegation have introduced bills designed to create standards for siting data centers in communities, amplify transparency about the facilities’ power and water use and protect nearby communities from international threats. “As a country we built our power infrastructure, our internet infrastructure, and the national h[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. Mark Warner and U.S. Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, both Virginia-based Democrats, have introduced legislation targeting the data center industry. (Photos by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)Two members of Virginia’s congressional delegation have introduced bills designed to create standards for siting data centers in communities, amplify transparency about the facilities’ power and water use and protect nearby communities from international threats.
“As a country we built our power infrastructure, our internet infrastructure, and the national highway system…with strong federal components or the federal government was the lead. Our data centers are looking like they could be a similar project,” U.S. Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Loudoun, said.
Subramanyam and U.S. Sen. Mark Warner D-Va. recently released a slate of legislative proposals that target the data center industry. The legislators’ bills draw on their firsthand knowledge of data centers in Virginia, which has more data centers than any state in the nation, with nearly 400 operating and over 200 planned.  
New bills, provider policies force data centers to pay up
Subramanyam’s Data Center Fair Share Act directs states to develop a tariff to levy on data centers and other large-load users, requiring the facilities to pay for energy infrastructure that must be built to serve them. 
The measure would shield residential ratepayers from shouldering the cost of energy generation, transmission and distribution lines that only serve data centers. Under the bill, if a state fails to adopt a tariff, they would lose out on federal highway funds.
In Virginia, Dominion Energy has already taken steps to separate data center-related infrastructure costs from other ratepayers, by creating the GS5 rate class. 
Power customers in that class, which mainly encapsulates data centers, are now required to meet specific contractual obligations and payment percentages for generation, distribution, and transmission costs.
Additionally, in the latest case to determine how Dominion charges customers for the buildout of high-voltage transmission lines, the State Corporation Commission ordered the company to create a tariff for data centers to cover the cost of lines that only have to be built because of data centers.
Enhancing siting standards
The Responsible Data Center Siting Act is another proposal by Subramanyam, who was first elected to serve Virginia’s 10th Congressional District in 2025 and is pursuing another term. 
His district hosts one of the densest sprawls of data centers in the world. Subramanyam’s bill directs the federal government to create comprehensive guidelines on how to site data centers in communities in a way that protects residents and the environment.
“We are placing a very large concentration of data centers in a few places, including my district. I don’t think that’s sustainable,” Subramanyam said. “We are seeing the industry and its partners prioritize short-term profit over the long term sustainability and community concerns.”
The bill directs the Secretary of Energy to work with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, Department of Defense and other appropriate agencies to establish a set of standards for where and how to place data centers in communities nationwide.
“We can’t force states and localities to make decisions about zoning and rate protections, for instance, but what we can do is set very clear guidelines that help not just the states and localities, but industry,” Subramanyam said.
Boosting transparency about power and water
Warner and Subramanyam have pitched similar bills that will require data centers to publicly disclose information about their energy and water use, emissions, backup generation and other environmental impacts.
“It would also condition valuable tax benefits on meeting strong efficiency and sustainability standards. We have to make sure big tech companies are paying for the energy used by data centers, not the residents in these communities,” Warner said in a statement.
His bill would also form the federal tax treatment of AI data centers, conditioning the federal bonus depreciation on data centers meeting various energy efficiency and environmental standards.
Subramanyam’s bill focuses on acquiring accurate projections of how much water and power a data center will need. This information can help localities better plan for the infrastructure and resources needed before they allow a data center to be built in their communities.
“The data is not always accurate and you leave a community finding out later on that they actually need to build extra energy infrastructure or have available extra water infrastructure, and then those resources get taken away from the community,” Subramanyam said.
Subramanyam has also filed a bill to develop a strategy to protect data centers and the surrounding communities from potential cyber or physical attacks from foreign adversaries.
In Virginia, state lawmakers in the General Assembly this year passed legislation to tighten restrictions on back up generators and introduce a new energy consumption tax. 
State leaders are also creating more standards for data centers’ water use in some scarcity areas and noise levels near neighborhoods.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Ideas on healthcare affordability differ among 6th District candidates
description: Candidates in Louisiana’s 6th Congressional District agree healthcare coverage affordability is a major public concern, but they have drastically different proposals for fixing the problem.
text:
Candidates for Louisiana's 6th Congressional District seat disagree on how to make health insurance more affordable and what types of rules should be applied to the government-sponsored Medicaid program. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger/States Newsroom)Candidates in Louisiana’s 6th Congressional District agree healthcare coverage affordability is a major public concern, but they have drastically different proposals for fixing the problem. 

Four major candidates are competing to be the next U.S. House member from the Baton Rouge area in the Nov. 3 election. Incumbent Cleo Fields is stepping down after the state legislature created new district boundaries last spring to make it harder for a Democrat to retain his seat. 
The two leading Democratic candidates in the race said reinstituting government subsidies for health insurance plans sold through the Obamacare exchanges would be a priority if they were elected. 

“I would reverse the cuts to the Affordable Care Act subsidies,” said Pat Forbes, a retired state employee who helped lead Louisiana’s disaster recovery efforts as the longtime head of the state Office of Community Development.
People who don’t receive health insurance through an employer, but don’t qualify for plans like Medicare or Medicaid, can purchase coverage through the government-run marketplace. 

During President Joe Biden’s term, the federal government increased subsidies to make the Obamacare plans more affordable. But those subsidies expired at the end of 2025, with President Donald Trump firmly against keeping them in place, and prices for the coverage skyrocketed.

Like Forbes, community organizer Lindsay “Rubia” Garcia said she would work to bring the subsidies back if elected. 
But she eventually wants to move to a taxpayer-funded national health insurance plan, sometimes referred to as a “Medicaid for All” strategy. Under that structure, every citizen would get access to government-sponsored health insurance, regardless of their age or economic status. 

“Healthcare is a human right in the United States,” said Garcia, a former teacher who graduated from Southern University Law Center in 2025. 
Unlike the Democratic candidates, Republican state Sen. Rick Edmonds of Baton Rouge said he would not favor restoring higher subsidies for Affordable Care Act plans. 

Instead, Edmonds said he would support giving Americans direct access to funding to cover their medical costs through expanded health savings accounts to help offset the cost of care for people with high deductible insurance plans.  

This idea, which is popular among conservatives, was pushed by outgoing U.S. Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-Baton Rouge. Trump also floated a similar plan last week when he promised to send $500 rebate checks to people enrolled in Obamacare. 
“I am a strong proponent of the open market,” Edmonds said. 
The other notable Republican candidate in the race, state Sen. Blake Miguez, R-New Iberia, did not return several phone calls and text messages over the past week asking for an interview about his healthcare priorities. 

Medicaid work requirements 

Another difference between the Democrats and Edmonds is their opinion on work requirements that take effect in January for certain low-income Medicaid recipients. 

In 2025, Trump and Congress enacted new rules that will require many Medicaid enrollees to earn at least $580 per month or complete 80 hours of volunteer work or school each month to retain their benefits.
Forbes and Garcia said they would work to repeal the work requirements, while Edmonds said he is in favor of the new restrictions. 
Forbes said the requirements mean more citizens will go without healthcare and be unable to work as a result of an illness. It will lead financially vulnerable medical providers, such as rural hospitals, to close because they will have to treat more uninsured patients who can’t cover their bills, he said. 

Garcia said working people shouldn’t make so little money that they qualify for Medicaid. If someone is working full-time, they should make enough to afford a private insurance plan, she said. 
“I’m for people working, and when they are working, earning a livable wage,” she said. 

Edmonds said the new work requirements will incentivize low-income people enrolled in the Medicaid program to get new job training. If they gain a new skill, they might be able to find employment that allows them to pick up private insurance, he said. 
“We want to push people to have a great job,” Edmonds said.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: National
title: More states embrace ‘50-50’ child custody in divorce cases
description: A growing number of states are making an equal split between parents the default child custody option in divorce cases. Louisiana and Mississippi this year joined at least five other states that have adopted the so-called 50-50 standard — four of them since 2021, as more legislators rework divorce-related laws that remained mostly unchanged for years. The […[...]
text:
A mother holds hands with her son on a swing set. At least seven states have passed laws making equally shared parenting time the legal default in child custody cases.
(Photo by Troy Bennett for Maine Morning Star)A growing number of states are making an equal split between parents the default child custody option in divorce cases.
Louisiana and Mississippi this year joined at least five other states that have adopted the so-called 50-50 standard — four of them since 2021, as more legislators rework divorce-related laws that remained mostly unchanged for years.
The 50-50 custody issue does not break down cleanly along partisan lines: The Mississippi bill was sponsored by Republicans, the Louisiana legislation by Democrats. Both states’ laws explicitly codify a custody guideline that many courts in other states follow.
Supporters say a formal 50-50 custody standard makes divorce proceedings more equitable for fathers — who historically have been awarded less custody time than mothers — and encourages them to maintain an active role in their children’s lives.
And it can reduce friction between separating parents by signaling they’re both starting the custody process on an equal playing field, said Don Hubin, board chair of the National Parents Organization, an advocacy group that has pushed for more states to adopt legal presumptions of shared parenting.
Without that presumption, Hubin said, one or both parents may feel like they have to paint each other in a bad light in order to ‘win’ more time with their children.
“It’s not just about the practice of shared parenting, but about the law signaling to parents that this is going to be the outcome unless something special is going on in your case,” he said. “It reduces the anxiety of the parents, which reduces the conflict between the parents.”
But critics say the standard might harm vulnerable women and children by making it more likely that children must spend time with a parent who isn’t safe. They fear that for women in abusive marriages, the knowledge they would have to cede 50% of their child’s time to an unsafe parent could push them to remain in a marriage just to protect their children.
Kimberly Rummage, who lives in Kentucky, calls her state’s 50-50 custody standard “absolutely diabolical.” She’s had a lengthy battle in court with her ex-husband over custody of their child.
“I think that parents should have to prove why they get that 50-50,” she said. “You should have to show what you’ve done in that child’s life, what you know about that child, how you’ve participated and supported that child.”
Some critics also argue that the 50-50 standard doesn’t account for the needs of children at different ages. Mississippi state Rep. Dana McLean, a Republican, warned her colleagues the state’s new law could harm breastfeeding infants who need to spend most of their time with their mothers during their first months of life.
Mississippi’s new law requires family courts to use equally-shared parenting time as the default in custody cases. Parents seeking more time must present evidence showing why a 50-50 split isn’t in their child’s best interest. It also changes how child support is calculated: The new formula for 50-50 custody can lower child support payments for the parent with the lower income.
Louisiana’s new law says child custody “shall” be divided equally, rather than “should,” which was the language under the previous law.
In both states, as in others that have adopted the 50-50 standard, a judge can override the rule if the court finds credible evidence for awarding more time to one parent.
But in Mississippi, several judges spoke against the bill before it passed, saying the old system — in which custody was awarded on a case-by-case basis using a specific set of factors — was the most fair.
At least five other states have similar laws, and all were approved with bipartisan support: Kentucky (2018), Arkansas (2021), West Virginia (2022), Florida (2023) and Missouri (2023).
Effects on divorce rates
Proponents of 50-50 laws say one positive side effect is that they could save some marriages. In Kentucky, the state’s divorce rate dropped 25% between 2016 and 2023, compared with an 18% decline nationwide.
But Krista Westrick-Payne, one of the researchers who studied the rates, told Stateline it’s impossible to tie Kentucky’s drop directly to the state’s 2018 50-50 custody law because too many other factors in that timeframe influenced it.
“There’s no one cause, no one single driver for these rates,” said Westrick-Payne, who is the assistant director of the National Center for Family & Marriage Research at Bowling Green State University in Kentucky.
The data shows that factors like state laws or local economic conditions tend to have a minimal effect on whether a couple divorces, she said.
“The more significant things that affect whether or not a couple decides to divorce have much more to do with their relationship and their personal situation.”
Divorce becomes next battleground as states debate family values

Westrick-Payne said she believes divorce and custody-related law should be crafted with the effects on individuals and families in mind, rather than as a way to affect widescale, population-level changes.
“When it comes to something like divorce, something that’s so personal, I think the focus needs to be more on the individuals going through it,” she said, “as opposed to some big policy to affect just whether somebody divorces or not.”
A growing effort
Hubin expects to see more states moving to codify the equal custody presumption in their laws in the coming years, as parenting norms change and more households become dual income. Fathers have taken on more caregiving responsibilities than a generation ago, he said.
“Fathers who’ve been involved with their kids, they’re not happy with being consigned to an ‘every other weekend’ visitor in their kids’ lives,” he said.
Nationally, mothers of children under 6 spend about seven and a half hours a day with their children, compared to a little over five hours for fathers, according to the latest available data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. The time gap shrinks as kids get older: Mothers spend 3.8 hours a day with their teens and fathers spend about 3 hours.
Earlier this year, a 50-50 custody bill in Oklahoma, sponsored by both Republicans and Democrats, sailed through the House but died on the Senate floor. Similar bills have been proposed in Alabama, Idaho, Indiana and North Carolina.
Stateline reporter Anna Claire Vollers can be reached at avollers@stateline.org.
