title: Montana moves to dismiss lawsuit against Yellowstone National Park bison plan
description: Montana has filed to dismiss its lawsuit against the federal government which challenged the National Park Service’s bison management plan in Yellowstone National Park.  The case, filed in Billings federal court in late 2024, argued that park officials intentionally cut the state out of management plans and ignored the agency’s own scientific consensus in or[...]
text:
Bison warming up in the sun (NPS / Jacob W. Frank)Montana has filed to dismiss its lawsuit against the federal government which challenged the National Park Service’s bison management plan in Yellowstone National Park. 
The case, filed in Billings federal court in late 2024, argued that park officials intentionally cut the state out of management plans and ignored the agency’s own scientific consensus in order to boost the number of bison in the park and avoid vaccinating them against diseases. 
At the heart of the issue is what happens when the bison inevitably roam across the man-made border of the park, often into Montana. The state argued that the park’s plan to increase the size of its herd and a decision to remove a requirement for bison to receive brucellosis vaccinations would cause harm to Montanans. 
Several conservation groups and tribal nations, including the Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes and Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes, intervened in the lawsuit, defending Yellowstone’s management plan, and offered praise for the voluntary dismissal this week. 
“The Fort Peck Tribes are encouraged to see the State of Montana dismiss its lawsuit so that the parties can move past litigation and focus on the real work ahead on the Bison Management Plan,” said Floyd G. Azure, Chairman, Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes of the Fort Peck Reservation in a statement. “We look forward to continuing to work with the National Park Service on the plan, particularly to maximize the use of the Fort Peck Tribes’ successful bison quarantine program as we continue to restore wild bison to Indian Country and fulfill treaty and trust obligations.”
Representatives from Montana Gov. Greg Gianforte did not respond to a request for comment by publication. 
In April, the National Park Service said the agency would prepare a supplemental environmental impact statement for its bison plan to include additional alternative management strategies. 
The federal government, defendants in the suit, filed a request to pause the lawsuit while that process played out, but a judge denied the request. 
With the new filing, the state and federal government jointly state that the supplemental environmental impact statement offers “potential that Montana’s claims will be addressed, if not resolved,” according to court documents. 
“Those of us who live in Montana understand that bison belong on the land,” said National Parks Conservation Association program manager Michelle Uberuaga. “Bison are woven into America’s conservation legacy and Montana’s history and cultures.”
But this doesn’t mark the end of the road for Yellowstone bison in court. 
Montana’s lawsuit was administratively consolidated with another lawsuit, filed by conservation organizations Alliance for the Wild Rockies and Council on Fish and Wildlife, which also challenged Yellowstone’s management plan, but on different grounds. 
The dismissal of Montana’s suit does not affect the conservation groups’ lawsuit, which is currently scheduled for a hearing in November. 
Part of the claims in the separate suit by the conservation groups focused on the management actions in the bison plan to reduce risk of brucellosis transmission to cattle, which is documented to come from elk, not bison, in Montana.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Enrollment declines again, but revenue up at LSU New Orleans
description: LSU New Orleans has reported another decline in its enrollment in its first semester back in the LSU System.  University officials report there are 5,533 students enrolled this fall, down from 5,670 a year ago and short of the 6,000 projected students LSU System President Wade Rousse said the campus budget was built around.  Last […]
text:
Prominent new signage fronts the University Center at LSU New Orleans, formerly known as the University of New Orleans. (Photo by Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)LSU New Orleans has reported another decline in its enrollment in its first semester back in the LSU System. 
University officials report there are 5,533 students enrolled this fall, down from 5,670 a year ago and short of the 6,000 projected students LSU System President Wade Rousse said the campus budget was built around. 
Last year, state legislators approved switching the 70-year-old school from the University of Louisiana System, which it had been a part of since 2011, back to LSU, which originally established the campus. Lawmakers believe the move will help stabilize the university, as all of LSU’s institutions have regularly boasted enrollment records in contrast to a national trend of declining student numbers. 
LSU New Orleans’ enrollment decrease spans two decades. The school had a student body of around 17,000 before Hurricane Katrina in 2005, with an immediate drop to around 6,000 after the storm.
The declining enrollment created a financial crisis that prompted lawmakers to act. 
Despite the lower student count, LSU New Orleans spokeswoman Sarah Bergez said revenue at the school has increased about $1.5 million from the prior fall. It’s being attributed to higher fees for dual-enrollment courses, which are open to qualifying high school students who want to earn college credit. 
Bergez said the university will consider mid-year budget adjustments, but she added it probably won’t be necessary based on anticipated philanthropy. 
“Enrollment loss is not newsworthy anymore. That was the problem over the last two decades, and now we’re stopping that problem as quickly as we can,” Bergez said in a statement. 
LSU System President Wade Rousse said the New Orleans campus recruited 21% more new students than it did last fall and dramatically increased its retention of students already enrolled. The anticipation is that enrollment will increase over the next year, he said.
“Make no mistake though, the financial situation of LSU New Orleans remains challenging,” Rousse said. “However, through better management, marketing that leverages the LSU brand and academic offerings tied to market demand, we believe it is on a path to success.” 
Among Rousse’s plans for boosting enrollment was offering students who applied to LSU’s main campus but were not accepted a spot at LSU New Orleans. Numbers were not made available to show how many rejected Baton Rouge campus applicants have enrolled in New Orleans 
The budget crisis at the former University of New Orleans was building for several years before finally being made public in 2023, when Kathy Johnson was hired as president to right the ship. Johnson left her position earlier this year to become provost at St. Louis University, and the search is ongoing for her replacement. 
University leaders have mitigated the crisis through layoffs, eliminating and combining academic programs, reducing the campus’ physical footprint and using state dollars to pay down outstanding debts.

Wilmington Rugby’s men’s team starts their 2026 fall season with a matchup against Northeast Philadelphia Irish Rugby Club on September 19, at Alapocus Run State Park.
WILMINGTON, Del –  Following a summer of friendlies and tournament play, the Wilmington Rugby Club’s men’s team (WRFC) will kick-off their 2026 fall season on September 19, at Alapocus Run State Park, against the men’s team from Northeast Philadelphia Irish Rugby Club. The game time has yet to be announced.
The WRFC is hoping to improve on a strong 2025 fall season in which they narrowly missed the playoffs. The team will face a strong test right out of the gate against Northeast Philadelphia Irish Rugby Club. The club’s men’s team has finished in the top two of the Eastern Pennsylvania Rugby Union (EPRU) Division III fixtures the past two seasons, according to the team’s website.
The WRFC’s match on Saturday is the first of a six game schedule they will play this fall, which includes a matchup against the Wilkes-Barre Rugby Football Club at the end of the season. The Wilkes-Barre Rugby Football Club won the EPRU Division III championship in 2025, according to its team website. That will be the final game WRFC plays in the 2026 fall season and will take place on October 31.
The WRFC is Delaware’s oldest men’s club rugby team having been around since 1972. In addition to its men’s team the organization fields a women’s team, youth teams and a team called the Old Boys for those 35 years old and older. The youth programs include a “Rookie Rugby Program” which is a non-contact, introductory style program for those ages 7-14, the Wilmington Raptors program which is a co-ed U14 team and two high school aged club teams. The Wilmington Colts are the boys high school club team and the Wilmington Vipers are the girls high school program. The Vipers inaugural season was in the spring of 2026, according to the WRFC website.
The club is always welcoming new players regardless of experience level or talent. Those interested in participating can go on the WRFC website and hit the join tab at the top of the page where they can fill out an interest form. The club also welcomes interested individuals to check out a practice or reach out with any questions. All practices during the fall season are held at the Siegel JCC in Wilmington, Delaware. The men’s team practices on Tuesdays and Thursdays and women’s team practices on Mondays and Thursdays.  
The sport of rugby is slowly gaining popularity in the United States. USA Rugby — the national governing body for rugby in the United States — says it has over 110,000 active members across its many levels, according to their website. Over 68,000 spectators flocked to M&T Bank Stadium in Baltimore to watch a match between the South Africa Springboks and New Zealand All Blacks, last week, according to the Baltimore Sun, and in 2031 the US will be a host site for the 2031 Rugby World Cup, according to an ESPN article from 2022.
To learn more about the WRFC and how to get involved with their rugby programs check out their facebook page or click here to be directed to their website.

title: FBI’s Patel dodges questions on election interference at rambunctious US Senate hearing
text:
WASHINGTON — FBI Director Kash Patel sidestepped questions about FBI agents at polling places in the midterm elections at a U.S. Senate hearing Tuesday that also featured a tense exchange between GOP Chairman Chuck Grassley of Iowa and Democratic Sen. Cory Booker of New Jersey.With the November midterm elections fast approaching and the parties jockeying for control of Congress, several Democratic senators wanted assurance from Patel, under oath, that the FBI would not send agents into polling places.“Do you pledge that you will not, in any way, interfere in the will of the American people when they go to the polls in November?” Sen. Peter Welch, a Vermont Democrat, asked.“I pledge unequivocally that I will not participate in your charade of lies,” Patel told Welch.Patel in addition faced questions during the five-hour hearing from members of the Judiciary Committee about recent changes to the agency’s hiring requirements, an ongoing probe into 2020 election ballots seized in Georgia, and how the FBI plans to handle crimes committed by AI agents. ‘We have a lackey here’A boiling point came when Booker spoke beyond his allotted time and name-called Patel a “thug” who “wouldn’t qualify” to be an FBI special agent. Booker accused Patel of not answering questions about whether the agency was improperly targeting journalists. The FBI subpoenaed multiple New York Times reporters in July after the outlet published accounts of security deficiencies on President Donald Trump’s new Qatari-donated jet now used as Air Force One. The DOJ dropped the subpoenas later that month after a federal judge pressured the agency.“My concluding remark is we don't have an FBI director. We have a lackey here who is using government, and frankly, he's not even a good lackey. He's an incompetent lackey. He's like an 18-year-old kid who wants to join a fraternity that he could never be a member of, doing keg stands and chugging with friends,” Booker said, before continuing the exchange for roughly four minutes more.“Are you ready to shut up?” Grassley, of Iowa, asked Booker with a raised voice.  Patel brushed off Grassley’s offer during the exchange to respond to Booker.“I don't have much to say. This guy called me a thug. It's kind of ironic. He's running for president of the United States. He just got his 20-second ad campaign,” Patel said. “Next.”Booker told NBC News’ “Meet the Press with Kristen Welker” in March that he’s “definitely not ruling out” a presidential run in 2028.Grassley thanked Patel for “putting up with what you had to put up with.”“And I'm sorry I couldn't control some of them more than I already did,” he said.Democratic probes promisedSen. Adam Schiff, a California Democrat, warned a Democratic-led Congress would investigate the FBI’s actions under Patel’s leadership. That includes the alleged firing of agents who worked on investigations of the Jan. 6, 2021 Capitol attack and President Donald Trump’s alleged hoarding of classified documents at Mar-a-Lago following his first term.“The FBI is being sued for wrongful termination. I will remind you, director, because you probably need reminding, that while this Congress is not going to investigate the wrongful termination of potentially hundreds of agents for working on properly predicated investigations, the next Congress will,” Schiff said.The panel’s Republicans praised Patel for his record at the agency.Patel said his agency “has made America safer than it's ever been.”“Across six America 250 events and this year's World Cup alone, we welcomed over 12 million visitors to the United States to attend these events. Not one single incident occurred at any single one of these events,” he said during his opening remarks.Bizarre exchange over FBI hiringOne topic that drew scrutiny from both sides of the aisle was a recent reported change at the FBI that lifted previous disqualifying behavior for special agent recruits, including theft from employers, prostitution and bestiality.Sen. John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, said he understands “the game” of Democrats broaching the subject of bestiality to “make you look bad,” but said he was also “trying to get to the bottom of this.”In a bizarre and unexpected exchange for a Senate hearing, Kennedy asked hypothetically, “If ‘Joe’ participated in bestiality, not as the animal, but as the human, don't you think he ought to be disqualified?” “If he voluntarily did it, sure,” Patel said.Kennedy interrupted, “Okay, how do you involuntarily do that?”Patel said some people are trafficked and forced into “degrading acts of all kind,” but later want to join the FBI.“But you're not telling us today that if a human being (voluntarily) had sex with an animal that they can still be an FBI agent?” Kennedy asked.“No,” Patel responded.“In fact, they ought to be in jail, right?” Kennedy shot back.“They all are,” Patel said.“Yea, well, okay,” Kennedy said.FBI at polling locationsOn the topic of an FBI presence at the polls on Nov. 3, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., told Patel he was "dissatisfied that you are unable to give us an unequivocal, clear, unambiguous commitment that the FBI will be kept out of election interference.”“You are involved in seven voter-related subpoenas issued to the Nevada Secretary of State's office, you were involved in seizure of election records from Fulton County, Georgia. Clearly, the FBI has been involved in possible election interference,” Blumenthal said.FBI agents seized 2020 presidential election ballots in Fulton County in January.The Trump administration served voter-related subpoenas earlier this month in Nevada.

 







FBI director Kash Patel delivers remarks on the administration's efforts to crack down on fraud during a Sept. 14, 2026, news conference at the FBI field office in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)

Welch told Patel he’s concerned about what he’s “willing to do for the president in this year's midterm elections that the president is already saying are going to be rigged if he loses.”Moments later Welch asked, “Last month, Congressman and Michigan gubernatorial candidate John James said to podcaster Benny Johnson, quote, ‘I've already had a good conversation with my friend Kash Patel, who has said already that the FBI will have a presence leading up to Election Day in Michigan, in both West Michigan and Southeast Michigan.’ Is that true?”“We have an election crimes community coordinator in all 56 field offices, so you bet we're going to have them there and manning the posts for election interference,” Patel said.The exchange continued for several minutes, growing more contentious, as Welch pressed for an answer and Patel said he would not take part in a “charade of lies.”“Then why are you being such a panderer to President Trump, who's still claiming that he won the 2020 election, and who has said the only way Democrats can win in 2026 is if they cheat. Do you believe that?” Welch replied.“I believe in the rule of law. … I want to know how your wealth increased 4,000% since you became a United States senator?” Patel shot back.“Let’s knock it off,” Sen. John Cornyn, a Texas Republican, chimed in after taking over the hearing for Grassley.AI hackingSen. Josh Hawley, who has shown skepticism of the skyrocketing growth of artificial intelligence, used part of his time to ask how the FBI will handle illegal hacking incidents by AI agents.Several incidents this summer involved AI agents hacking into other systems, including OpenAI agents that broke into tech company Hugging Face, without explicit instructions to do so.The recent explosive development of AI has dominated headlines and conversations on Capitol Hill in recent days after top tech executives warned development was moving too quickly to adhere to safety guardrails. Congress has yet to pass overarching AI regulations.“What's the role here for the bureau? How, how do you wrap your head around these kind of crimes?” asked Hawley, a Missouri Republican.“This is a great question. It's literally the new frontier, and nobody's really talking about it, so thank you. So a couple things: The president has issued his AI directive on what the government can and can't use, and that's the right first step because you don't want 77 different large language models,” Patel said.The FBI, he said, has reviewed 140 “test case models” to measure their capabilities and “make sure they are cooperating and following underlying federal statutes.”“What we need to do on a resource basis is go after the people that created these models that are going rogue,” Patel said.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana parole board schedules clemency hearings ahead of Weisheit execution
description: Jeffrey Weisheit’s bid to avoid execution is headed to the Indiana Parole Board, which has scheduled October hearings on his request to avoid the death sentence imposed for killing two children in 2010. The Indiana Parole Board received the application and issued a hearing notice Tuesday, less than two months before Weisheit’s scheduled Nov. 5 […]
text:
The Indiana Parole Board scheduled October hearings on Jeffrey Weisheit’s request to reduce his death sentence. His execution is set for Nov. 5, 2026. (Mugshot from the Indiana Department of Correction; Photo illustration by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Jeffrey Weisheit’s bid to avoid execution is headed to the Indiana Parole Board, which has scheduled October hearings on his request to avoid the death sentence imposed for killing two children in 2010.
The Indiana Parole Board received the application and issued a hearing notice Tuesday, less than two months before Weisheit’s scheduled Nov. 5 execution.
Weisheit, convicted in the 2010 murders of siblings Alyssa and Caleb Lynch, is seeking commutation — a reduction of his sentence. The board will make a recommendation to Gov. Mike Braun, who has the final say.
A prison hearing is slated for Friday, Oct. 16, at 10:30 a.m. Central, or 11:30 a.m. Eastern, at the Indiana State Prison in Michigan City. That hearing gives Weisheit an opportunity to speak directly with parole board members and answer their questions as they consider his request for a reduced sentence.
Indiana high court orders Jeffrey Weisheit executed Nov. 5

The board will hear public testimony Oct. 19 in Indiana Government Center conference rooms 1 and 2 in Indianapolis. Those supporting clemency will have an opportunity to make their case from 9 to 11 a.m., followed by testimony from those opposing the request from 1 to 3 p.m. The hearings will help inform the board’s recommendation to the governor.
In the application, signed Sept. 15, Weisheit contends that evidence relevant to his punishment was not fully presented during his court proceedings.
“Mr. Weisheit’s lifelong mental impairments including congenital dysfunctions and the effect of multiple brain traumas suffered throughout his life, beginning early in his childhood, and their mitigating effect on the crime were never adequately presented to the courts,” the petition states.
It also asserts that evidence of childhood psychological trauma was not presented and that the COVID-19 pandemic blocked investigation and presentation of such evidence in federal court.
Weisheit was sentenced to death in 2013 for killing 8-year-old Alyssa and 5-year-old Caleb, his girlfriend’s children, in a fire at their Evansville home. He was also convicted of arson.
The Indiana Supreme Court ordered his execution Aug. 28. He is scheduled to die by lethal injection before sunrise at the Michigan City prison.
Although the court upheld his death sentence during a 2018 post-conviction appeal, Chief Justice Loretta Rush dissented on that issue, concluding that ineffective legal representation warranted a new sentencing proceeding.
Braun denied clemency to Benjamin Ritchie and Roy Lee Ward before their executions in 2025. Weisheit’s would be Indiana’s fourth execution since the state ended a 15-year pause in December 2024.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Far offshore, scientists find fresh evidence of human harm to reefs
description: An isolated reef off the coast of Louisiana and Texas holds within its corals a record of Earth’s history, and scientists are reading it to understand how nutrients from the Mississippi River are affecting the reef’s health amid rising threats to corals around the globe.
text:
A scuba diver takes a core sample of coral from a reef in Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary (Photo from NOAA)
An isolated reef off the coast of Louisiana and Texas holds within its corals a record of Earth’s history, and scientists are reading it to understand how nutrients from the Mississippi River are affecting the reef’s health amid rising threats to corals around the globe.
At 80 to 125 miles off the Gulf Coast lies a little-known, impressively healthy coral reef ecosystem known as Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary. It consists of 17 distinct inter-connected reef ecosystems to form a chain over 160 square miles, or over three and a half times the size of Disney World.
Hundreds of marine species, including manta rays, sharks and sea turtles, live amongst the sanctuary’s reefs. Boulder corals, some older than the United States, remain huge and healthy despite mass die-offs of reefs elsewhere on the planet driven by disease, nutrient pollution and the rising heat of climate change.
A new study examining nitrogen levels recorded within coral skeletons shows how nutrient pollution from the Mississippi River, combined with the hot tub-like underwater heat waves are undermining the health of this otherwise hearty reef.
Concentrations of high nitrogen, when combined with extreme heat, can harm and even kill corals.
“Coral reefs are kind of like deserts. It’s kind of weird to think of it that way, but there’s not a lot of nutrients in a coral reef because it needs that clear water,” said Kristine DeLong, professor at Louisiana State University’s Department of Geography and Anthropology and co-author of the new academic study published in Science Advances.
DeLong is a paleoclimatologist, someone who studies past climates, similar to how a paleontologist examines fossils to learn more about prehistoric life such as dinosaurs.
Corals are particularly vulnerable to changes in their environment, a kind of “Goldilocks” of creatures, said DeLong, so understanding past changes in climate can help scientists try to understand how picky life-forms like coral will— or won’t— adapt as the climate rapidly warms.
A student at the PAST lab at Louisiana State University test core samples from the coral at Flower Garden Banks. (Photo by Kristine DeLong)
The research DeLong worked on at Flower Garden Banks shows that the combination of too much nitrogen from the Mississippi River undermines the health of coral, making it even more vulnerable to extreme heat and disease.
“The corals are getting stressed and as they get stressed, whenever you have disease, you’re gonna have problems,” said DeLong.
When nutrients like nitrogen enter the water, algae grows. Too much algae growth can harm corals.
“You don’t want a lot of algae in the water. The corals can’t grow because they’re photosynthesizers, and if they can’t get sunlight, they’re not gonna be able to grow,” she said.
Corals are also sensitive to heat. Water that gets too hot for too long, especially when combined with the stress from algae blocking sunlight, causes corals to bleach, become more susceptible to disease, or die.
“Flower Gardens is a healthy reef and it’s been healthy for a long time … but now it’s getting to that point where the water temperature is getting high enough that we’re starting to see disease outbreaks,” said DeLong.
“It’s not the best situation,” said Jonathan Jung, postdoctoral researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Chemistry in Germany and co-author on the study.
He worked on the chemical analysis of nitrogen in the coral samples from Flower Garden Banks, constructing a history of the changes in the Mississippi River going back to 1753 when European colonists first started to manage its channel and flow.
“What we can do now with these long and continuous records is we can contextualize what’s going on,” he said. “That’s what we’ve tried to do in this case, to show that when the temperature and nutrients kind of align, we see disease outbreaks.”
“Trees have tree rings, and you can count the rings to see how old the tree is … Corals have the same thing,” DeLong said. “They have layers in them that form every year, and so by looking at those layers we can tell what year it is.”
The researchers found that nitrogen levels in the coral skeletons increased around the same time artificial fertilizers became popular in U.S. agriculture, known as the Green Revolution,  beginning in the early 20th century.
The Flower Garden Banks’ isolated location is likely what contributes to the astounding health and size of this reef, DeLong said. But the fact that nitrogen has been recorded this far out into the Gulf of Mexico speaks to the outsized impact humans have had on the environment from agriculture, engineering and pollution along the Mississippi River, she added.
Although skeptical at first because of the distance, the numbers showed DeLong that nitrogen from the Mississippi was reaching all the way out to Flower Garden corals.
“When we plotted it up against the nitrogen load data for the Mississippi River, I was just like, OK, yeah, this is definitely Mississippi River water.”
The data also showed that in years where corals at Flower Garden Banks experienced disease outbreaks or bleaching events — 2016, 2022 and 2023 — both heat and especially high nitrogen flows from the Mississippi River were recorded both in the corals and with human technology like thermometers. The research shows the connection between nitrogen, heat and coral demise, said DeLong.
“You get corals that are already sick, and then you stress them out, and yeah, that’s the problem,” she said. “That’s what we worry about with Flower Gardens.”
By understanding the past and how humans have changed it, scientists like Jung and DeLong hope to give important environmental information to those working to preserve and protect coral reefs from becoming a thing of the past.
“We know temperatures are gonna keep going up, but can we keep the corals healthy? Because if they’re healthy they can survive bleaching and they can survive some of these disease events that come through,” said DeLong.
“There’s all sorts of interesting reefs out there that are somewhat resilient,” said Jung, referring to places like Flower Garden Banks as “hope spots” for keeping corals and reef species from becoming extinct in an era of rapid climate change.
“You hope to kind of preserve them until you can figure out what exactly makes them resilient and whether you can help coral reefs,” said Jung.

name: VTDigger
title: Prosecutors present gun, cellphone evidence they say links Burlington man to shooting of three Palestinian students
description:
The state rested its case against Jason Eaton on the trial’s second day Tuesday, clearing the way for Eaton’s defense team to present testimony they hope will bolster their argument that he was legally insane at the time of the shootings.  
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Prosecutors present gun, cellphone evidence they say links Burlington man to shootin[...]
text:
Harry Jeppe, a firearms examiner with the Vermont Forensic Laboratory, testifies in Chittenden Superior criminal court in Burlington on Tuesday, September 15, 2026. Pool photo by Paul Heintz/Boston Globe
BURLINGTON — The state rested its case against the Burlington man accused of shooting and wounding three Palestinian students, presenting law enforcement and forensic witnesses whose testimony prosecutors say tied him to the crimes. 
The move by the state comes on the second day of the trial in Chittenden Superior criminal court and appears to set the stage for the defense’s case that Jason Eaton was legally insane at the time of the shootings in November 2023 and not criminally responsible.
Among the key prosecution witnesses Tuesday was Harry Jeppe, a firearms examiner with the Vermont Forensic Laboratory. He testified about his analysis of the firearm and cartridge casings and bullets recovered at the shooting scene and during the police investigation. 
“I determined that this cartridge casing was fired from the submitted firearm,” Jeppe said at one point during his testimony, repeating a similar phrase several more times on the witness stand. 

Samuel Lizzio, a member of the New York State Police assigned to an FBI task force, testifies in Chittenden Superior criminal court in Burlington on Tuesday, September 15, 2026.  Jason Eaton faces three counts of attempted second-degree murder in the shooting of three Palestinian students visiting Burlington in November of 2023. Pool photo by Paul Heintz/Boston Globe

The jury Tuesday also heard from Samuel Lizzio, a member of the New York State Police assigned to an FBI task force. Lizzio, an expert in analyzing cellular data, testified that he used data from a cellphone belonging to Eaton and cellular networks to place him in the area at the time of the shootings. 
Bryan Smith of Powderhorn Outdoor Sports in Williston testified that, based on records, a person named Jason Eaton had bought a Ruger handgun at the store in April 2023 and had passed a federal background check. The serial number of that firearm matched the serial number on the Ruger handgun police seized from Eaton’s apartment. 
Eaton, 51, has pleaded not guilty to three counts of attempted second-degree murder, accused of firing the shots that injured three Palestinian college students as they walked on North Prospect Street in Burlington on the evening of Nov. 25, 2023. 
The students, Hisham Awartani, Kinnan Abdalhamid and Tahseen Aliahmad, each testified Monday on the trial’s opening day. They said the man who shot them had approached them without saying a word, then opened fire and fled. Two of the men were treated at the hospital. Awartani was left with his lower body paralyzed. 

READ MORE

Judge John Pacht sent the jury home a little before noon Tuesday after the state rested its case. He said that testimony set for Tuesday had gone quicker than expected. 
“Sometimes that’s the way trials go,” Pacht told the jurors.  
Eaton’s lawyers are expected to present their case starting Wednesday, putting the focus on his mental state at the time of the shootings as they raise the insanity defense. The trial is expected to run through the rest of the week.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakotan overseeing federal farm programs out to cut red tape, modernize
description: WEST FARGO, N.D. — Jared Hagert said his main message to farmers at the Big Iron farm show was: If you haven’t set up an account at login.gov, get it done. Hagert is the North Dakota farmer and former lawmaker now overseeing federal farm programs who was back in his home state Tuesday to speak […]
text:
Jared Hagert, right, deputy administrator for farm programs for the USDA’s Farm Service Agency, speaks Sept. 15, 2026, at the Big Iron farm show in West Fargo, North Dakota, with Don Wick of the Red River Farm Network. (Photo by Jeff Beach / North Dakota Monitor) WEST FARGO, N.D. — Jared Hagert said his main message to farmers at the Big Iron farm show was: If you haven’t set up an account at login.gov, get it done.
Hagert is the North Dakota farmer and former lawmaker now overseeing federal farm programs who was back in his home state Tuesday to speak at the opening day of the ag show.
A key part of his job as deputy administrator for farm programs for the Farm Service Agency is modernizing the systems for disaster aid, price supports and loan programs.
USDA calls the modernization effort One Farmer, One File, with the signup at login.gov.
Improvements in farm data reporting starting in North Dakota

Hagert said USDA plans to retire 100 outdated computer systems, but the modernization is about more than technology. The agency is trying to eliminate duplicative forms and other ways to cut red tape.
“We’re looking at all of it,” Hagert said.
The goal is to have one spot where farmers can supply information for Farm Service Agency programs but also for other USDA agencies — the Natural Resources Conservation Service and Risk Management Agency.
Chris McDonald, who farms near Leonard in Richland County, said he’s hopeful streamlining means fewer visits to USDA agency offices, where staffing has become an issue.
“It’s going to save time for everybody, not having to run from one office to the next office,” McDonald said. “They don’t have enough workers to cover everything, so it might help that way, too.”
Office staffing has come up often when Hagert visits ag producers, and some rural counties have a small workforce pool to draw from. Modernization may not lead to FSA needing less staff, he said, but should make the system more efficient for employees and farmers who can do more from their computer or their phone.
North Dakota and Grand Forks County, where Hagert farms, played a key role in what Hagert called the “tip of the spear” in the modernization effort.
Grand Forks County was a pilot county for a new system for uploading data from reporting maps, where farmers supply information about what crops have been planted in which fields and other information. North Dakota and Maryland became the first to test the system statewide before it was adopted nationwide in August, Hagert said.
Farmers should see more progress in the coming year, he said.
But for farmers who may not be ready to adjust to the new system, the county FSA offices are not going away.
“We want to meet farmers where they’re at,” he said.
Reach North Dakota Monitor deputy editor Jeff Beach at jbeach@northdakotamonitor.com

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Deportation decision for Salah Sarsour expected before end of September
description: The fate of Salah Sarsour, president of the Islamic Society of Milwaukee, is now in the hands of a federal immigration judge in Kansas City who, by Sept. 30, will decide whether Sarsour can be deported from the place where he has lived as a legal permanent resident for over 30 years. Monday concluded court […]
text:
Salah Sarsour is released from immigration detention in June, 2026 . (Photo by Yaseen Najeed)The fate of Salah Sarsour, president of the Islamic Society of Milwaukee, is now in the hands of a federal immigration judge in Kansas City who, by Sept. 30, will decide whether Sarsour can be deported from the place where he has lived as a legal permanent resident for over 30 years.
Monday concluded court testimony from experts and witnesses in Sarsour’s deportation case. Sarsour was arrested in late March by armed federal immigration agents in Milwaukee. He had never been arrested in the United States before. 
Salah Sarsour after his release from immigration detention in June. (Photo by Yaseen Najeed)
The Department of Homeland Security claimed that Sarsour lied on his green card application when he came to the United States in the late 1990s. DHS also claims that Sarsour, a Palestinian man, had been convicted in Israeli military courts of throwing Molotov cocktails at the homes of Israeli soldiers in 1988, and separately accused of illegally attempting to possess weapons and ammunition in 1995.
Attorney Patrick Taruel, representing Sarsour, disputed those accusations Monday saying DHS had broadcast them in “libelous press releases.” Taurel said Sarsour had been detained as a Palestinian teenager by Israel’s occupying army and convicted in military court for throwing stones and disorderly conduct, not for throwing Molotov cocktails. This occurred during the First Intifada, a mass Palestinian uprising against the Israeli army which lasted from 1987 to 1993.
Amahl Bishara, a professor at Tufts University, testified during one of Sarsour’s hearings in late July that stone throwing was an act of political expression against the occupation carried out by Palestinian youth. Taruel described it as “a kind of screaming into the void that they don’t approve of the occupation,” during a Monday press conference. 
Jawad Boulos, who represented Sarsour as an attorney in the West Bank, addressed the military court record from the 1990s. 
He recommended that Sarsour take a plea in the 1995 case because the Israelis were offering what Boulos felt was an unusually good deal by reducing four charges to just one of procuring weapons, and having Sarsour agree to time served. The plea deal also allowed Sarsour to avoid waiting up to two more years in detention for a trial. The lenient deal was evidence to Boulos that even the Israelis did not take their own accusations against Sarsour seriously. 
Salah Sarsour is released from immigration detention in June. (Photo by Yaseen Najeed)
Responding to DHS arguments that if Sarsour were tortured the record of his imprisonment would have shown that he suffered harm, Boulos said that the Israeli authorities sometimes did not allow him to see his client. He noted a no-contact order among the Israeli documents barring Boulos from seeing Sarsour during the first several weeks of Sarsour’s confinement. During hearings in July, Sari Bashi, an Israeli lawyer and human rights investigator, described the West Bank, where Sarsour grew up, as a place under “belligerent occupation” where confessions are coerced through torture, and the local Israeli commander acts as the executive, lawmaker, judge, and executor of law.  
Dr. Jackie Bashkoff, a forensic psychologist, testified in July that after evaluating Sarsour, she determined that he suffers from Post Traumatic Stress Disorder stemming from his experiences of being tortured.
Prosecutors said Monday that Sarsour’s defense team “completely glossed over” that Sarsour never “complained about mistreatment” by the Israelis. “That silence says everything,” said attorney Scott Jebson, representing the Department of Homeland Security. He added that Sarsour never mentioned having gone to the hospital due to torture, and that Israeli court records don’t mention that he claimed he was abused by the Israeli interrogators. 
In earlier hearings, prosecutors also attempted to cast doubt on Sarsour’s PTSD diagnosis. Jebson said that Dr. Bashkoff used “buzz words” to describe Sarsour as having a “startle response.” Prosecutors also suggested in earlier hearings that symptoms of his type 2 diabetes could be confused for PTSD. “I can go through every witness they called” and discredit or undermine their testimony, Jebson told the judge on Monday.
Milwaukee residents protest Israel’s war in Gaza. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
Besides Sarsour’s detention by Israeli authorities, DHS is also accusing him of attempting to register to vote despite not being a U.S. citizen in the lead-up to the 2004 elections. Prosecutors have pointed to a voter registration card with Sarsour’s name on it. 
Sarsour never attempted to cast a ballot, and his defense team suggested that the registration card could be linked to documented problems with a voter registration drive involving about 3,000 special registration deputies in Milwaukee. The Legislative Audit Bureau issued a letter in 2005 highlighting problems with the deputies. “Some special registration deputies are municipal officials, but many work for interest groups or political parties,” the report read. “Problems have been identified with registrations completed by some special registration deputies, including inaccurate, illegible, and falsified registration forms.”
Taurel said Sarsour had no recollection of signing the card and that when he learned about it in 2009, he took steps to remove it. Taurel also said that even if Sarsour signed the card it wouldn’t matter because he never actually voted, and thus would not have received a benefit by claiming to be a U.S. citizen under the law. 
Mark Robel, an FBI polygraph examiner, testified in July that he examined Sarsour asking him whether he ever knowingly voted as a non-citizen during the 2004 election and whether he ever registered to vote. Robel said Sarsour passed the polygraph with no deception detected. “If he had tried to register to vote in any election, he would not have passed that test,” Robel told prosecutors when they questioned the polygraph’s accuracy.
A check of MyVote Wisconsin shows that Sarsour is not currently registered to vote.
Taurel said the Trump administration has targeted Sarsour because of his outspoken advocacy for Palestinian rights. “We are here because of Salah’s speech,” he said. “I’m not speculating about this,” Taurel said. “The reason they arrested him, the reason we’re here, is his speech.”
Community members call for the release of Salah Sarsour. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
In June, Sarsour was released from an Indiana immigration detention center, where he was held for more than 80 days. He was ordered released by a Trump-appointed federal judge, who ruled that Sarsour had a “substantial” claim that his arrest was First Amendment retaliation. 
Sarsour is both the president of Wisconsin’s largest mosque and a board member of American Muslims for Palestine, which has been labeled by the conservative Heritage Foundation as part of a support network for Hamas. 
In June 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued a memorandum stating that Sarsour was eligible for deportation because “his actions undermine U.S. foreign policy.”  In February of this year, the Justice Department announced that it would target groups like American Muslims for Palestine. The following month in March, Sarsour’s profile on a pro-Israel doxxing website called the Canary Mission was updated. Four days later he was arrested by federal immigration agents. 
Taurel said that while he believes that Sarsour has a strong case against being deported, immigration judges are under extraordinary pressure from the Trump administration and  the neutrality of the immigration court system “has been severely undermined.” 
The judge in Sarsour’s immigration case, Jayme Salinardi, is expected to make a ruling on whether he can be deported by the end of the month. The Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reports that Salinardi has a record of denying asylum claims 90% of the time — far above the national average of 59%. A Democratic appointee, he previously worked as an attorney for ICE.
Salah Sarsour speaks to supporters after his released from immigration detention. (Photo by Yaseen Najeed)
On Sept. 30, the court will hold a status conference on the case. If the judge decides that Sarsour can be deported, then his attorneys will push for relief. Taurel said that “we fear the worst,” if he is sent back to Israel-occupied territory. 
Taurel said that Sarsour is not backing down, adding that Sarsour will appear with Taruel on a podcast in the coming weeks, and is expected to travel to Washington D.C. to speak with elected officials. “Salah refuses to be cowed by this,” he said on Monday. “He is a brave, courageous advocate for Palestine. He won’t be silenced. He is not required to be muzzled in any way.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Trump aims to shore up support for Whatley in NC with Wednesday visit
description: North Carolina’s open Senate seat could be key to majority control of the upper chamber.
text:
North Carolina Republican Senate hopeful Michael Whatley (R) speaks alongside U.S. President Donald Trump at the Rocky Mount Event Center on Dec. 19, 2025 in Rocky Mount. (Photo by Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images)President Donald Trump is visiting North Carolina on Wednesday to campaign with Republican U.S. Senate nominee Michael Whatley.
It’s a sign the party is concerned about its prospects in the purple state. 
Whatley, the former chair of the Republican National Committee and the North Carolina Republican Party, continues to trail Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper in recent polls and fundraising. 
Whatley said on social media that he’s “thrilled” to welcome Trump to his home of Gastonia. 
“President Trump needs an ally in the Senate and North Carolina needs a fighter,” Whatley posted. “That’s why we will win on November 3!”
North Carolina’s open Senate seat, soon to be vacated by retiring GOP U.S. Sen. Thom Tillis, could be key to majority control of the upper chamber. Cook Political Report rates the race as “lean Democrat.”
At the moment, Republicans hold 53 seats, while Democrats have 45. Two independent senators caucus with the Democrats.
‘Garbage and lies’: Senate candidate Michael Whatley lashes out at media as campaign flounders

In addition to the Tar Heel State, Republicans are looking to defend competitive open seats in Iowa and Texas — states that haven’t historically needed much GOP attention — and back their incumbents in Alaska, Maine, and Ohio. They’re also eyeing pick-up opportunities in Michigan, New Hampshire, and Georgia. 
North Carolina has some of the country’s most expensive media markets in Charlotte and the Raleigh-Durham area. Both parties may need to spend significantly more than expected, which may leave them needing to triage their resources. 
“The Republicans can still hold the majority in the Senate even if they lose North Carolina,” UNC Charlotte political science professor Eric Heberlig told NC Newsline. “That’s part of their calculations as well: Where do they think they have the best chance of mitigating any losses?”
A presidential visit shows the importance of the Senate contest on the national scene, according to Heberlig. 
With Trump’s approval rating hovering around 35% in North Carolina, his appearance in Gastonia is unlikely to win Whatley many swing voters. But Heberlig says that’s not the main goal. 
The aim, he says, is to mobilize the GOP’s base, especially low-propensity voters who may not be familiar with Whatley and may not turn out to vote in the midterm.
“If you’re the Republican, what you need to do is hold those Republican voters who have voted for President Trump, who have voted for Thom Tillis and Ted Budd. You just need to get them to pull that ‘R’ lever again,” Heberlig told NC Newsline. 
Trump’s visit could also help boost GOP turnout in a scandal-ridden western North Carolina congressional district.
GOP U.S. Rep. Chuck Edwards abruptly dropped his reelection bid in the state’s 11th Congressional District last month, leaving party leaders scrambling to find a replacement. Earlier this month, the U.S. House voted to censure Edwards for inappropriate conduct. 
The NCGOP selected state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom to replace Edwards on the ballot. She’ll face Democrat Jamie Ager, a fourth-generation farmer from a political family, in November. Cook Political Report rates the seat as “lean Republican.”
Former Gov. Roy Cooper centered his general election kickoff event in Raleigh on March 4, 2026 on policies he said would make food and grocery prices more affordable. (Photo: Brandon Kingdollar/NC Newsline)
While Democratic candidates have performed well recently in North Carolina for state-level positions, it isn’t always the same case for federal contests.
The Tar Heel State last elected a Democratic U.S. senator in 2008, when Barack Obama became the first Democratic presidential candidate to win North Carolina in 32 years. No Democratic presidential or senatorial candidates have won North Carolina since.
On the other hand, Cooper is the best-known U.S. Senate candidate Democrats have fielded in decades. He’s won numerous statewide elections as a two-term governor and four-term attorney general. His 16-year tenure in that office was the longest in North Carolina history. 
“Having a candidate such as Roy Cooper, who’s won statewide multiple times, helps a lot there because it’s somebody that voters have already voted for, has name recognition, has a positive image, so that gives you a good foundation to build on,” Heberlig said.
Ahead of the rally, North Carolina Democratic Party chair Anderson Clayton said the event indicates the GOP is worried. 
The party also gave Whatley the spotlight last week with a speaking slot at its midterm convention in Dallas. 
“It just goes to show you right now how scared Republicans are in this state,” Clayton said. “They’re treating every single county like it matters, and so are we in North Carolina.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Democrat Rob Sand calls for prioritizing public safety as property tax growth slows
description: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand said Tuesday he would work to ensure resources are protected for Iowa law enforcement and other public safety officials if he is elected in 2026. Sand was joined by law enforcement officials, prosecutors, and other public safety workers at a campaign event at the Des Moines Firefighters Local Four union […]
text:
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand was joined by local law enforcement officers and Iowans working in the court system for a campaign event Sept. 15, 2026 in Des Moines. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand said Tuesday he would work to ensure resources are protected for Iowa law enforcement and other public safety officials if he is elected in 2026.
Sand was joined by law enforcement officials, prosecutors, and other public safety workers at a campaign event at the Des Moines Firefighters Local Four union hall, who spoke about the reasons why they supported the Democrat for Iowa governor in 2026. Sand said as Iowa communities work through the implementation of Senate File 2472, a property tax law signed by Gov. Kim Reynolds in May, the top funding priority “has got to be public safety, firefighters, first responders, police officers, sheriff’s departments.”
“These are the folks that are making sure that when you call 911 there’s somebody who can get there, and get there quickly,” Sand said. “And so that should be that should be the first group of people that we’re listening to, and the first group of people where, even if we’re only a short time into our experience in this new law, if we’re hearing from them something consistently, that’s the first place where we should be willing to listen to that and make changes based on what we’re hearing.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Democratic candidate’s comments come as Iowa local governments like Des Moines are preparing to make reductions to account for budget gaps due to the new property tax law.
The event came a day after Sand’s campaign announced a slate of endorsements from 60 Iowans involved in public safety work, including former Attorney General Tom Miller — for whom Sand worked as an assistant attorney general before becoming state auditor — Iowa Professional Firefighters Association President Ryan Hanghian, as well as several county attorneys and county sheriffs.
Former Marshalltown Police Chief Mike Tupper said he met with Sand when the auditor came to Marshalltown at least once a year to speak with members of the community — conversations where Tupper said he “learned firsthand that Rob supports public safety.”
“Public safety is a high priority for him, and he worked it, he lived it,” Tupper said. “He was in the trenches with with law enforcement. He understands law enforcement, and he wants to make sure that we have the safest state in the country. He’s very intentional about building relationships with law enforcement and focusing on public safety, and we’ve all saw his work in the state auditor’s office.”
Des Moines Local 4 Firefighter President Joe Van Haalen thanked Sand for supporting firefighters as they advocated to pass House File 969, a law expanding disability and death benefits for firefighters, emergency medical services responders and law enforcement officers from the current 14 cancers covered to all types of cancer.
“Throughout our work to pass our cancer legislation, Rob was there to offer encouragement and advice, and quite simply, he cared about what we were doing and pushed us forward,” Van Haalen said. “Today, Rob is here to talk about something that affects every Iowan, regardless of where they live or how they vote — keeping our communities safe and making sure that people we depend on in an emergency have the resources, support, and leadership that they need.”
Sand said the cancer coverage law should have been a “20-minute conversation,” and was an example of an issue he would work to move forward if elected governor.
“If you want people to do public service work, they’re willing to sacrifice … the way people do when they run into a burning building, when they move into a situation where they know someone’s got a gun and they’re angry, the least that we can be doing is making sure that the exposure that they have to risk is something that we recognize, respect, and cover,” Sand said. “Because the bottom line is they’re still going to be taking risks. They’re risking life and limb on our behalf. The easiest thing for us to do is to say that if it’s some long- term chemical exposure because of the work that you do, that’s a no brainer. That obviously we should be covering that. So at the end of the day, a lot of this just comes down to having a conversation and listening to people.”
Sand also said he wanted to bring the attitude of public safety and law enforcement work to the governor’s office if elected.
“That attitude that I’m talking about is the one where … you might have a ‘D’ or an ‘R’ after your name on the ballot, but you don’t ask people when they call 911 whether or not they’re a Democrat or a Republican,” Sand said. “You go and you help them out, and it doesn’t matter,  because you’re there to serve the public. And I want that attitude that you find in law enforcement, that you find in public safety, that you find from firefighters across the state, that you find from first responders across the state — I want that attitude to be found in the Capitol building in Des Moines. I am sick and tired of a politics that feels like it’s two private clubs beating up on each other, when fundamentally it is supposed to be about public service, and working together for the good of all and the good of anyone.”
In a Monday news release, Sac County Attorney Ben Smith, a Republican, said he supported Sand for governor because “he has the experience and judgment to keep our communities safe.”
“As a conservative Republican, I won’t agree with Rob on every issue,” Smith said in a statement. “On law enforcement, though, I don’t have to guess where he stands. He’ll fight for the men and women who run toward danger so the rest of us don’t have to, putting public safety ahead of politics.”
Sand is running against Republican Zach Lahn in the general election. Lahn’s campaign announced Tuesday an endorsement from the National Rifle Association Political Victory Fund. In a news release, Dan Capodilupo, a spokesperson for Lahn’s campaign, criticized Sand as a candidate who “likes Gun Control.” Sand hunts using firearms and has regularly said he supports the 2nd Amendment.
“Zach Lahn is a rock solid Second Amendment defender and that’s why the NRA endorsed him today,” Capodilupo said.

title: Federal judge ends North Carolina mental health settlement after 14 years
description: A federal judge on Monday ended nearly 14 years of court oversight of North Carolina’s program to help people with serious mental illness move from institutional settings into community housing.  U.S. District Judge James C. Dever III approved a request from North Carolina and the U.S. Justice Department to end the 2012 settlement. The program, […]
text:
People rally for mental health care funding at the Pennsylvania Capitol in 2022. Federal Medicaid cuts could threaten already-struggling psychiatric units at hospitals across the country. (Photo by Amanda Berg for Pennsylvania Capital-Star)A federal judge on Monday ended nearly 14 years of court oversight of North Carolina’s program to help people with serious mental illness move from institutional settings into community housing. 
U.S. District Judge James C. Dever III approved a request from North Carolina and the U.S. Justice Department to end the 2012 settlement. The program, known as Transitions to Community Living, was created as part of the agreement.
In their filing, both sides agreed North Carolina had substantially complied with the deal and that court oversight should end early.
The settlement followed a federal investigation into North Carolina’s practice of institutionalizing people with serious mental illness in adult care homes. It required the state to provide housing, mental health services and employment assistance to help people who were able to live in the community to do so.
The agreement was supposed to end in July 2020. The state and Justice Department modified the agreement six times, extending the deadline and removing requirements the state had completed. The latest extension set a July 1, 2027, deadline.
The state says more than 4,150 people now have stable housing through the program and more than 6,700 have been diverted from adult care homes.
Advocates for people with disabilities say they’ll be watching closely to make sure the state maintains its efforts. 
“North Carolina cannot afford to lose the progress it has made under this settlement,” Virginia Knowlton Marcus, CEO of Disability Rights North Carolina, told NC Newsline. 
Marcus said the group appreciates the state’s renewed commitment to community living but will continue monitoring the state’s progress.
But the state still has work to do. That’s according to the court-appointed independent reviewer tasked with monitoring North Carolina’s compliance.
In a report filed in January, reviewer Martha B. Knisley said the state continued to struggle to provide supported housing, mental health services and employment. She said the state did not meet any new major requirements during the 2025 fiscal year.
Knisley was particularly critical of the state’s progress in moving people from adult care homes into supported housing. The settlement called for 2,000 people with serious mental illness living in adult care homes to receive supported housing in communities. As of January, the state was providing those slots to 1,022 people, up 22 from the previous year. 
Knisley described the states’ progress in 2025 as “negligible.” She also found the state was not meeting some requirements for mental health services and supported employment.
For this Mama Bear, home is a right worth fighting for

The state, however, had surpassed several of the settlement’s broader goals. By June 2025, it had provided housing services to 3,998 people, above the 3,000 target. It also exceeded targets for Assertive Community Treatment and supported employment.
North Carolina and the Justice Department acknowledged the remaining gaps, but said they did not outweigh the state’s overall progress, according to the joint filing.
NCDHHS said the state will continue the work through its broader efforts to provide community-based housing and services.
“For almost 15 years, our mission has been to provide the right services at the right time so people with disabilities can live, work and receive treatment in the communities of their choice,” NCDHHS Secretary Dev Sangvai said in a statement.

title: Hagley Car Show Spotlights American-Made Classics
description: 30th annual show celebrates nation’s 250th anniversary with rare vehicles from independent automakers WILMINGTON, Del. — Hundreds of classic vehicles will roll into Hagley Museum and Library on Sunday, Sept. 20, as the Hagley Car Show celebrates its 30th anniversary and America’s 250th birthday. text:
30th annual show celebrates nation’s 250th anniversary with rare vehicles from independent automakers
WILMINGTON, Del. — Hundreds of classic vehicles will roll into Hagley Museum and Library on Sunday, Sept. 20, as the Hagley Car Show celebrates its 30th anniversary and America’s 250th birthday.
The rain-or-shine show will run from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. in the fields surrounding the first du Pont family home. Thousands of automobile enthusiasts are expected to attend.
This year’s theme, “American Independent Automakers,” will spotlight companies that competed outside Detroit’s “Big Three” of Ford, General Motors and Chrysler. Featured manufacturers will include AMC, Packard, Studebaker and Hudson.
Classic cars of all makes and models, dating from the early 20th century through 2001, will fill the main show field.
Rare vehicles highlight American innovation
Among the lesser-known automobiles scheduled to appear is a 1940 Graham Hollywood Supercharged Sedan.
Graham-Paige was founded in 1927 after three brothers purchased the Paige-Detroit Motor Car Co. for $4 million and invested an additional $4 million in the business. The company introduced innovations including shatterproof windshields and its distinctive “shark-nose” body design before automobile production ended in 1940.
The featured field will also include a rare 1963 Kellison J-3 Roadster. Its aerodynamic fiberglass body reflects the aviation background of company founder Jim Kellison, a former Air Force mechanic who drew inspiration from fighter jets and Italian sports cars.
The vehicles represent a period when smaller manufacturers tested new designs and technologies while competing against the nation’s dominant automakers.
30 years of automotive history
Hagley launched the car show in 1996 as “100 Years of Cars,” commemorating the Duryea brothers’ first production run of gasoline-powered vehicles in 1896.
Three decades later, the annual event has grown into a gathering for collectors, families and automobile enthusiasts from across the region.
Visitors can walk among rows of vintage vehicles while listening to music from different motoring eras. A parade featuring some of the show’s most distinctive vehicles will begin at 11:30 a.m.
Food trucks will offer meals and refreshments throughout the day.
Admission is sold by the carload and must be purchased in advance. Passes will not be available at the gate. General admission is $30 per vehicle, while Hagley members pay $25.
To Go Box:

What: Hagley Car Show
When: Sunday, Sept. 20, from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.
Vehicle parade: 11:30 a.m.
Where: Hagley Museum and Library, 200 Hagley Creek Road, Wilmington
Admission: $30 per carload for the general public; $25 per carload for Hagley members
Tickets: Advance purchase is required at hagley.org/carshow, the Hagley Visitor Center or the Museum Store through Saturday, Sept. 19. No tickets will be sold at the gate.
Arrival: Visitors must enter through Hagley’s main entrance off Route 141 and arrive no later than 1 p.m.
Weather: The show will be held rain or shine.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Republican AG nominee proposes criminal charges against men for unwanted pregnancies
description: Republican attorney general nominee Alan Gordon said he’s confident in his legal analysis of the 19-page plan he unveiled Tuesday in his campaign’s first press conference at the Rhode Island State House. “I ran it through three AIs,” he told the only reporter who showed up. His idea: to criminally charge men whose consensual sex […]
text:
Alan Gordon, the Republican nominee running for Rhode Island attorney general, stands next to a statue of 19th century antislavery activist and women’s suffragist Elizabeth Buffum Chace on the second floor of the State House on Sept. 15, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Republican attorney general nominee Alan Gordon said he’s confident in his legal analysis of the 19-page plan he unveiled Tuesday in his campaign’s first press conference at the Rhode Island State House.
“I ran it through three AIs,” he told the only reporter who showed up.
His idea: to criminally charge men whose consensual sex results in an unwanted pregnancy. 
“Where a man has accidentally, recklessly, or even deliberately caused such profound changes to a woman’s body, he’s going to have to answer for that,” Gordon, 56, said while standing near a statue of 19th century antislavery activist and women’s suffragist Elizabeth Buffum Chace.
Gordon argues that an unwanted pregnancy amounts to unlawful bodily harm whatever the outcome — whether birth, miscarriage, or abortion. So his plan would let prosecutors pursue felony charges under existing Rhode Island assault and battery statutes.
First-time offenders would be eligible for diversion rather than traditional incarceration under Gordon’s proposal. He envisions a residential program where participants would receive vocational, educational and personal-development training.
Rhode Island’s felony assault law covers conduct that causes serious bodily injury, while the criminal-negligence statute cited by Gordon applies when a person causes serious bodily injury through criminal negligence. But neither law specifically identifies pregnancy as bodily harm.
AG candidates show mostly subtle differences in first public forum

Gordon was unopposed in the Sept. 9 Republican primary that saw contested races for governor and the 2nd Congressional District. Gordon received 20,288 votes, according to unofficial results from the Rhode Island Board of Elections. 
Approximately 23,000 ballots were cast in the GOP’s gubernatorial contest between Aaron Guckian and Elaine Pelino. Just over 15,000 votes were cast in the Republican race to represent Rhode Island’s 2nd Congressional District where Vic Mellor defeated Dr. Stephen Skoly.
Kim Ahern received 46,025 votes in the four-way Democratic AG race that drew 126,718 ballots.
Gordon came to the State House with his cousin and campaign manager Anne Armstrong, who said she sent the campaign’s proposal to a former Roger Williams University School of Law professor for vetting. The professor did not immediately respond when Rhode Island Current reached out with a request for comment.
However, Steven Brown, executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union of Rhode Island, offered a blunt assessment, calling Gordon’s idea “too ridiculous to warrant any comment.” 
Jocelyn Foye, director and co-founder of the Womxn Project, said the proposal was simply “a publicity stunt.”
“It would be nice to see him work on real issues that affect people’s day-to-day lives,” Foye said in a phone interview. “People are genuinely getting rounded up for reasons that aren’t legal.” 
Gordon said his proposal latches on to his Democratic opponent’s idea to create a “reproductive justice unit” in the attorney general’s office. 
Ahern’s team wants to focus on protecting reproductive rights through litigation, public education, a legal helpline and coordination with advocacy groups. 
“I have to be honest about having sort of stolen their idea of a reproductive justice unit,” Gordon said. “She’s got a good idea, and I’m not going to oppose it just because I’m her political opponent.”
Gordon had hoped Ahern would stop by the State House to debate him on the finer points of his policy proposal. Ahern’s campaign confirmed an invite was received, and described her Republican opponent as “staunchly anti-choice and opposed to abortion under any circumstances.”
“Kim believes defending reproductive justice means protecting a woman’s right to choose whether, how, and when to start a family, not prohibiting access to critical care,” spokesperson Josh Block said in an emailed statement.
Gordon acknowledged he personally opposes abortion, but would enforce “the law of the land” if elected.
Gordon referred to himself as a “longshot RI GOP AG candidate” in a Sept. 10 press release ahead of Tuesday’s press event. A canon lawyer is trained in the legal system governing the Catholic Church. He previously ran for attorney general as an independent in 2018 and is seeking the office this year as a Republican. 
Gordon’s campaign website states he received an accelerated Honors LL.B. law degree from the University of Buckingham in England in 2012, “graduating at the top of his class in Criminology and Criminal Justice.” He received a self-designed Bachelor of Arts degree from The Pennsylvania State University in 1992, with a concentration focused on the legal and public policy issues surrounding cannabis reform.
The GOP’s nominee “has never taken the oath required for admission to the Rhode Island Bar,” according to his campaign biography.
His Democratic opponent, Ahern, who most recently chaired the state’s Cannabis Control Commission, served nine years as a special assistant attorney general under three attorneys general: Peter Neronha, Peter Kilmartin and Patrick Lynch. She later served as deputy counsel to former Gov. Gina Raimondo and deputy chief of staff to Gov. Dan McKee
Early voting begins Oct. 14 ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Board appoints Nonya Thrasher as superintendent of Hazlehurst public schools
description: Hazlehurst school board President Paul Rhodes, board Secretary Oscar Tanner and Superintendent Nonya Thrasher are pictured at a meeting on Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026.
text:
Nonya Thrasher, who has led Hazlehurst City School District as interim leader since June, is now the permanent superintendent. 
Hazlehurst City School District Superintendent Nonya Thrasher Credit: Courtesy: Nonya Thrasher
The school board voted 3-2 Tuesday to appoint Thrasher and offer her a one-year, $130,000 contract. Darryl Hilliard Jr., Gloria Sandifer and school board President Paul Rhodes supported Thrasher’s appointment. Corey Murray and Oscar Tanner III voted no. 
Rhodes said there was no reason why the board offered Thrasher a one-year contract instead of a longer one.
Thrasher had served as the district’s director of accountability, compliance and accreditation since July 2023. Before working in Hazlehurst, she was superintendent of Claiborne County School District during the COVID-19 pandemic. 
With Hazlehurst, Thrasher inherits a district in crisis. The Mississippi Department of Education may take over the district by December if it does not clear outstanding accreditation violations. In March, the state Board of Education rejected the district’s corrective action plan to address those violations. 
For nearly a decade, the state Education Department has downgraded the district’s accreditation to probation. The agency previously took over the district from 2008 through 2014.
Before Thrasher took over as the interim leader, district facilities needed maintenance, its dysfunctional special education department failed students, and poor administrative oversight allowed for poor recordkeeping. 
The district has received a “C” rating on the state accountability system the past two years. Both its high and middle schools earned “D” accountability ratings in the 2024-25 school year.
As Hazlehurst schools’ accountability chief and later, interim superintendent, Thrasher reduced the number of accreditation violations from 11 to two since January.
Her predecessor, Cloyd Garth, left the district on June 5. The school board would not confirm if Garth resigned or was fired. He had failed to act on state education department reports that detailed problems in the district’s special education department. The district’s graduation rate for disabled students dropped to 17% last year, the lowest in the state.
Thrasher hired a new special education director over the summer and told Mississippi Today on Tuesday that clearing remaining violations is a top priority. Hazlehurst schools still face another threat: consolidation with the Copiah County School District. Lawmakers have been meeting to discuss school district consolidation ahead of the 2027 session. Consolidation bills introduced last session failed. 
Thrasher plans to meet with lawmakers next month.“We want to avoid consolidation if at all possible,” she said.
Rep. Greg Holloway, D-Hazlehurst, looks over a document during a meeting of the House Select Committee on Consolidation at the Capitol in Jackson on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Democratic Rep. Greg Holloway of Hazlehurst, the Copiah County board of supervisors and other local leaders have expressed support for Thrasher. Hazlehurst residents also rallied for Thrasher in recent weeks. District alumni, parents and community members posted messages of support on Facebook and circulated posters and flyers listing her qualifications.
Rhodes said Tuesday community members have recently approached him in Walmart to voice their support for her.
Thrasher said she is heartened by the support as a Hazlehurst resident.
“I’m ready to get the job done,” she said. “I have been overjoyed, overwhelmed and overloved by the community, but I have always worked in this community long before sitting in this seat. Whatever we need to do to move this community forward, I have always been in the forefront to make that happen.”
Rhodes feels optimistic, too. He said he believes Thrasher will help the district better serve students and improve academic standards.
“I believe we reached that point to where we can now move forward, straighten things up and educate our kids,” Rhodes said, “which is the reason why we’re here.”
