name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: MacDonald resigns from NH Supreme Court amid judicial misconduct allegations
description: Chief Justice Gordon MacDonald resigned from his position on the New Hampshire Supreme Court Tuesday, the governor’s office announced, amid allegations of judicial misconduct and an unexplained medical leave. In October, New Hampshire Public Radio reported that Dianne Martin, a MacDonald ally, had received nearly $50,000 by completing an unusual personnel ma[...]
text:
Supreme Court Chief Justice Gordon MacDonald (left) presents to Executive Councilors Joseph Kenney and John Stephen on July 24, 2025. (Photo by Ethan DeWitt/New Hampshire Bulletin)Chief Justice Gordon MacDonald resigned from his position on the New Hampshire Supreme Court Tuesday, the governor’s office announced, amid allegations of judicial misconduct and an unexplained medical leave.
In October, New Hampshire Public Radio reported that Dianne Martin, a MacDonald ally, had received nearly $50,000 by completing an unusual personnel maneuver. Martin had been MacDonald’s chief of staff in his previous role as New Hampshire’s attorney general. As Supreme Court chief justice a few years later, MacDonald and his colleagues recruited Martin to lead the court’s administrative office. Before she accepted the role, however, Martin was laid off from state government for about 48 hours before being immediately rehired into her new role. The highly unusual move, which was orchestrated by MacDonald, according to NHPR’s reporting, allowed her to collect almost $50,000 for unused vacation, sick time, and other benefits. State policy typically prohibits employees from receiving any accrued benefits when transitioning between roles.
Also on Tuesday, the New Hampshire State Judicial Conduct Committee, which had been investigating the issue since November, reported that MacDonald admitted to violating three provisions of the Judicial Code of Conduct. According to the Judicial Conduct Committee, MacDonald “failed to avoid favoritism with respect to the removal of Dianne Martin,” “failed to act in a manner that promotes public confidence in the impartiality of the judiciary,” and “failed to avoid the appearance of impropriety.” The committee ruled that formal disciplinary measures were appropriate but because MacDonald resigned, “no additional disciplinary action is available.”
In his resignation letter, MacDonald wrote: “I believe this is in the best interests of the New Hampshire Judicial Branch. I accept responsibility and accountability for my conduct.” He wrote in a separate statement that he takes “full responsibility for my shortcomings,” and that “to maintain the integrity of the judicial branch and to avoid the protracted and disruptive spectacle a public hearing would cause to the judicial branch and its dedicated employees, I have agreed to resign my position.”
Meanwhile, MacDonald has been on medical leave since July. Neither MacDonald nor the judicial branch provided an explanation for the leave.
MacDonald, 64, was appointed to the court by former Gov. Chris Sununu in 2021. He was also the state attorney general from 2017 to 2021. He’s a Dartmouth College and Cornell University alum.
His resignation opens a seat on the bench for Ayotte to nominate his successor. Unless she loses November’s general election before she can announce and have her nominee confirmed, this will be her third pick for the Supreme Court. In March, Ayotte appointed Daniel Will to the court and in 2025, she appointed Bryan Gould.

name: WyoFile
title: Laramie trans woman arguing self defense wants a look at witness’s past behavior. State calls request a ‘fishing expedition.’
description:
Man who pushed Ríhanna Kelver to the ground before she drew a gun on him has a checkered past in Colorado, according to news reports. His disciplinary records are relevant to her self-defense claims, attorney says. 
The post Laramie trans woman arguing self defense wants a look at witness’s past behavior. State calls request a ‘fishing expedition.’ appeare[...]
text:
After a transgender woman drew a gun on a man in what she called an act of self-defense, information came to light about the man’s past in Colorado, including that he once allegedly belonged to Patriot Front, a white supremacist group. 
To support her defense against charges resulting from the altercation, the woman’s attorney wants to look deeper into the man’s past. The state is trying to quash that effort.
Ríhanna Kelver, a vocal trans rights activist, is facing felony charges for aggravated assault and possession of a deadly weapon following the incident in downtown Laramie. Her case has drawn national attention, with media and other observers asking why a trans woman faces criminal charges for her actions in a state with a stand your ground law.
Kelver’s attorney, Andrew Holcomb, attempted to have those charges dismissed on self-defense claims. But Albany County District Judge Misha Westby ruled that she wasn’t immune from prosecution. While Kelver can still raise a self-defense argument at trial, the burden of proof will be higher.
In court filings, Holcomb has noted that Scott Durham, the man who pushed Kelver to the ground before she drew a gun on him, was allegedly “previously the subject of disciplinary proceedings at the University of Colorado Boulder,” which culminated in his departure from the school. 
Holcomb’s filings cite articles from the Laramie Reporter and CU Independent, which reported that Durham was once a member of Patriot Front and has a history of posting online content targeting minorities. A Colorado police report included in the court record also recounts a student calling police because he was “in fear” of Durham, who was “an active known racist throughout the campus.”
Last month, Holcomb filed a request in Albany County District Court to subpoena University of Colorado Boulder. The proposed subpoena asks the university to provide any disciplinary records concerning Durham, including records of his social media activity. Holcomb asked that those records be handed over to the court for an “in camera inspection” — a process in which a judge privately inspects records to decide if they can be released. 
Holcomb stated that these records are relevant to issues he expects will come up at trial, such as the “credibility of the complaining witness,” “potential bias or motive” and “prior conduct” relevant to Kelver’s asserted defenses. 
While the Wyoming Rules of Evidence usually bar evidence that attacks the character of a witness, “a criminal defendant is allowed to introduce evidence of a pertinent character trait possessed by the alleged victim for the purpose of establishing that the alleged victim was the initial aggressor, an essential component of a self-defense claim that arises within a public space,” Holcomb wrote. 
Last week, Albany County Attorney Kurt Britzius, who is representing the state of Wyoming, asked the court to quash the request, writing that the state has “a legitimate interest in protecting witnesses from undue harassment and from Defendant prying into a witness’ educational/disciplinary file merely for a fishing expedition.” 
Britzius also argued that the records aren’t relevant to Kelver’s case. “The State does not believe it is contested that, at the time of the incident, neither Defendant nor Mr. Durham knew each other,” he wrote. “It was only after the fact that these individuals learned of each other’s identity. Thus, nothing in Mr. Durham’s past, including the requested disciplinary records, is relevant in the current case.” 
The September 2025 incident in downtown Laramie started with a verbal exchange between Kelver and Durham, although accounts differ as to what exactly was said. 
According to Kelver, Durham allegedly taunted her as she sat in front of the Crowbar & Grill before a late-night shift, yelling that “the [Crowbar] should be closing you bunch of fags.” Kelver asked him, “What the fuck did you say?” Kelver also recounted that Durham allegedly told her: “I’ll fuck you up, faggot,” and “I’ll fucking kill you, you fucking faggot.” Meanwhile, Durham told police that he had yelled “‘fuck the Crowbar’ because he likes the Buckhorn Bar better,” without using any slurs, according to a Laramie police affidavit.
Court filings and video recount what happened next. Kelver walked toward Durham and the two individuals he was with, meeting them in the crosswalk at the intersection of 2nd Street and Ivinson Avenue. As she approached them, Kelver had her right hand on her hip where she wore a satchel that carried her gun. When she neared, Durham pushed Kelver, causing her to fall. When she hit the pavement, she pulled the pistol out of her bag, racked the slide and pointed it at Durham. Kelver lowered the firearm and stood when Durham was past her. 
Westby will decide whether to grant Holcomb’s request to probe Durham’s past.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Inola smelting ban will appear on spring referendum ballot, moratorium will remain in effect
description: Inola residents will decide the fate of a massive aluminum smelter in a town-wide vote next spring. Until then, city officials have paused heavy industrial development — including the aluminum smelting facility, which would be the largest in the country. Inola’s town council voted unanimously in favor of extending the moratorium through April 7, 2027. […]
text:
A crowd at Inola High School cheers after their local town council votes unanimously to pass a heavy industry moratorium until next April. At that time there will be a vote of the people to ultimately decide the fate of a massive smelter project in their community. (Photo by Graycen Wheeler/KOSU)Inola residents will decide the fate of a massive aluminum smelter in a town-wide vote next spring. Until then, city officials have paused heavy industrial development — including the aluminum smelting facility, which would be the largest in the country.
Inola’s town council voted unanimously in favor of extending the moratorium through April 7, 2027. They originally enacted the pause on development in late June, and it expired at the end of August.
The five-member council also voted unanimously to put an initiative petition that would ban primary aluminum smelting within town limits on the April 7 ballot.
“I’m going to stand with my community,” said Mayor Darlene Shear. “I am against the smelter plant… I don’t feel that I’ve been given the information that I need to know in my heart that everything is safe.”
The smelter issue has become a lightning rod, garnering strong opposition from local residents who fear its impact on the community and support from President Donald Trump for its potential national security benefits.
Dozens signed up to share their thoughts on the smelter before the town council considered its agenda items. Many asked for the council to extend the moratorium and send the smelter ban measure to a vote of the people.
Chris Thomas was among them. They’re from nearby Verdigris and currently attend Rogers State University in Claremore.
“Word around the school is if this smelter goes in we’re going to get our diplomas and we’re going to head out,” Thomas said. “Most of us, we don’t have kids, we don’t have property. And we’re just graduating. So if we’re going to build a life somewhere, we want it to be somewhere that’s not toxic.”
Angela Jungbluth also spoke to the council ahead of their votes, asking for them to extend the moratorium and advance the initiative petition to a vote.
“We poured our entire lives into this little farm that we have,” Jungbluth said. “We hope to pass it down to our kids. And the smelter threatens that completely, the peaceful agrarian lifestyle that we had hoped for.”
At the June meeting where the moratorium was originally implemented, federal and state officials attended to voice support for the smelter. None offered public comment at Monday’s meeting.
When the council voted to extend the moratorium, the crowd of nearly 300 erupted into a standing ovation. Thomas said it had reinstated their faith in the governing system. Jungbluth agreed.
“I think I was the loudest one screaming up there in positivity,” Jungbluth said. “It was the best outcome I could have ever hoped for.”
Hurdles remain for initiative petition
The citizen-led initiative petition to ban smelting garnered 201 valid signatures. But the deputy town clerk said that wasn’t sufficient, resulting in a lawsuit.
According to state law, the number of signatures on a municipal initiative petition must be at least a quarter of the votes cast in the municipality’s most recent town-wide election. For Inola, that was the April 2023 town council race, in which 288 ballots were cast.
But the town argued the law isn’t based on ballots, it’s based on votes. And in the single race for three town trustee positions, Inolans cast 944 total votes. Using that number, the initiative petition would require 236 signatures.
Earlier this month, a Rogers County judge determined the initiative petition had enough signatures and ordered the town council to proceed with considering it.
Representatives from Century Aluminum, Oklahoma Primary Aluminum and the Tulsa-Rogers County Port Authority intervened in the matter, asking the court to prevent the Inola town council from considering the petition until the court could hear their input next month.
The judge denied that request, clearing the way for the Inola town council to consider the initiative petition Monday night. Their options were to adopt the ordinance immediately or put it to a town-wide vote in spring of 2027, as they ultimately opted to do.
Legal challenges of the moratorium are also possible.
Oklahoma Primary Aluminum, the company behind the smelter, threatened legal action ahead of the first moratorium vote in June, as did Tulsa Ports’ lawyer.
“Given the tens of millions of dollars already invested in the property and Project, Oklahoma Primary Aluminum would have an obligation to its stakeholders to pursue available legal remedies to recover those investment losses,” Oklahoma Primary Aluminum Executive Director Ziad Fares wrote. “Such litigation would impose substantial expense on Inola.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri schools to get first look at ‘A’ through ‘F’ grades as public release is delayed
description: Missouri education officials on Tuesday pushed back the release of “A” through “F” grades for public schools until at least mid-November, giving districts a chance to review the ratings first after administrators raised concerns about the system. “We want to make sure that there’s not a premature release, and that all of a sudden schools […]
text:
Four Missouri school superintendents share their concerns about an "A" through "F" rating system during the State Board of Education meeting Tuesday, asking for more time to review scores and methodology. (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri)Missouri education officials on Tuesday pushed back the release of “A” through “F” grades for public schools until at least mid-November, giving districts a chance to review the ratings first after administrators raised concerns about the system.
“We want to make sure that there’s not a premature release, and that all of a sudden schools and districts are labeled with something that maybe does not line up with what we all consider accurate for our districts,” Joplin Schools Superintendent Kerry Sachetta told the State Board of Education Tuesday. “To publicly assign grades before schools have an opportunity to understand the metrics is problematic.”
During its regular monthly meeting, the board approved a framework for the grade cards while acknowledging that more work remains before the ratings are made public.
“By us approving it today, it does not mean that it is cast in stone,” said Kerry Casey, a board member from Chesterfield. “It allows (the department) to move forward.”
The vote allows the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education to create technical documentation and run a simulation. Those results will be shared with superintendents and used to gather another round of feedback before the system goes public. If any problems are identified, the board will have a chance to make changes.
“A lot of people have been putting a lot of time and effort into this,” said interim Education Commissioner Stacey Preis. “And we just are really trying hard to do it right.”
Attendance during Tuesday’s State Board of Education meeting in Jefferson City was unusually high, with many leaving after discussions on “A” through “F” report cards. (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent)
Last month, leaders with the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education told the board the public could see initial reports by the end of September or October in an attempt to meet a timeline requested by Gov. Mike Kehoe. But Tuesday morning, Deputy Commissioner of Learning Services Lisa Sireno said mid-November would be the earliest the department could publish a report.
Between the two meetings, the department held public feedback sessions, which uncovered concerns with parts of the proposed system, including an arbitrary cap on reading scores that education officials planned to use as a measure of literacy. The last of those forums was Friday. That day, the department sent more information to the board, setting up for Tuesday’s discussion.
“Fundamental questions about this process have come up during this debate. This is not ready for prime time,” said board member Vince Schoemehl, of St. Louis. “I don’t think the program has been put together properly.”
Schoemehl was the only member to vote against the framework, saying he had concerns with the underlying premise.
His comments garnered applause from the approximately 100 educators in attendance.
Prior to the board’s discussion, four superintendents urged members to delay public reports until schools have a chance to review the ratings and methodology — a request the board largely accommodated.
They also reiterated two requests the department had already fulfilled: a promise not to shorten standardized testing windows to speed up reports and a delay of the literacy metric until problems could be resolved.
“We think that piloting is not about avoiding accountability, but it’s about the integrity of what we’re trying to launch,” said Pattonville R-III Superintendent Matt Goodman. “We feel like if we do launch an untested model that issues mathematically flawed grades, we’re going to destroy trust across the state.”
The group also asked for the department not to shorten the window of time for districts to appeal and correct data annually.
“We believe moving forward, the best path for us to optimize, for us to achieve the best ‘A’ through ‘F’ framework to serve students has got to be a partnership,” said Adam Friga, superintendent of Oran R-III School District. “It has got to be a partnership between the state board, the department and school districts. We cannot work in silos.”
Superintendents’ concerns were largely separate from the framework up for a vote Tuesday, Sireno said, allowing for ongoing collaboration.
“We may not always agree on the details of every single report, but I think if we come together in that spirit of what’s best for children, we can get it right,” she said.
Preis told the board she “feels good about where the framework is right now,” but “there are some things that we would still like to work through with our colleagues.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Yellowstone’s Mollie’s Pack is mostly back in the park, but not before spurring threats, bounties
description: A historic wolf pack whose bloodlines and territory trace to the 1995-96 reintroduction of wolves has mostly returned to its traditional Yellowstone National Park turf, increasing the odds that its naive-to-humans members will survive a Wyoming hunting season that starts today. Named after former U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Director Mollie Beattie, who di[...]
text:
Wolf 1090F, pictured, is the former alpha female of the Mollie’s Pack and among the oldest known wolves in Yellowstone National Park history. (Photo courtesy of Sylvia Borgonovo)A historic wolf pack whose bloodlines and territory trace to the 1995-96 reintroduction of wolves has mostly returned to its traditional Yellowstone National Park turf, increasing the odds that its naive-to-humans members will survive a Wyoming hunting season that starts today.
Trump gives feds 90 days to consider removing endangered species protections for wolves 


Named after former U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Director Mollie Beattie, who died of cancer during the reintroduction, Mollie’s Pack made waves early this summer when the pack shifted its primary territory to the Absaroka Range northwest of Cody outside of the park. The move drew threats from hunters vowing to go after the pack and, in a tit-for-tat, an offer of a $10,000 bounty intended to identify and doxx anyone who legally kills the animals.
Since July, however, when WyoFile first reported the pack’s move, the dynamic has flipped, and the pack has predominantly remained inside park boundaries, where hunting isn’t allowed.
“They’ve mostly been back in the park, and that includes the pups,” Yellowstone Wolf Project Leader Dan Stahler told WyoFile. “The last couple months, they’re back in their home core territory.”
That territory stretches roughly from Yellowstone Lake, up through Pelican Valley and north all the way into Lamar Valley.
 Wyoming Game and Fish Commission rejects requests to adjust the hunting seasons to protect wolf pack

Stahler declined Thursday to discuss the precise makeup of the pack, though he noted that there are “some surviving pups” as of a couple weeks ago. In July, Mollie’s Pack consisted of five adults, three of which were equipped with tracking collars, and five pups.
Members of the Mollie’s Pack, Yellowstone’s last original wolf pack from the 1995-96 reintroduction, has mostly returned to the home range delineated in this National Park Service map. (Map courtesy of Yellowstone National Park)
One of its remaining members, 12-year-old Wolf 1090F, is among the oldest wolves on record for both Yellowstone and Wyoming. (The record-setter, Wolf 840M, survived to age 13 living in the western Teton Range foothills, where wolves are hunted.)
“We’re not missing the reality of this,” Wyoming Game and Fish Department Deputy Director Jeff Davis told WyoFile last week. “This would be a big damn thing. She is dangerously close to being the oldest wolf ever recorded in Wyoming.”
Because of the vulnerability of the Mollie’s Pack generally and Wolf 1090F specifically, state wildlife managers have faced repeated calls to close down the portion of Wyoming’s tightly managed hunt, specifically hunt area one, where the pack denned and localized earlier in the summer. Up to four wolves can be killed in the zone, which is being managed collectively with hunt area two, located just to the south.
The Wyoming Game and Fish Commission rejected requests to adjust the hunting seasons to give the pack relief from hunting when the panel approved the wolf hunting regulations in July. Talking with WyoFile on Wednesday, Game and Fish Interim Director Eric Wiltanger stood behind that decision.
“We manage our populations not based around one animal,” Wiltanger said.
Game and Fish staff has been inundated with requests to do otherwise.
“I got 1,100 emails in five minutes last week,” Wiltanger said, recounting a barrage of form letters that all hit his inbox at the same time.
There is some precedent for Wyoming adapting its hunting seasons to protect wildlife that’s become famous. In 2018, when state wildlife managers were setting seasons for their first grizzly bear hunt in four decades (a hunting season that never happened, because of a judge’s decision), the state imposed an expansive no-hunting buffer area to protect the roadside grizzly bears of Grand Teton National Park, especially the celebrity matriarch Grizzly 399.
Eight years later, wildlife managers went in a different direction, declining to adopt special management aimed at protecting the well-known Mollie’s Pack, which has been the subject of an IMAX documentary. They’ve also faced pressure to not bend to wolf advocates’ requests. MeatEater founder Steve Rinella, perhaps the most famous hunter alive, said on his podcast that the Mollie’s Pack naturally returning to Yellowstone “might be the best thing,” but he also implored wildlife managers to not give in to wolf advocates’ requests to adjust the hunt.
“The national forest and the state cannot capitulate,” Rinella said. “You cannot capitulate to the mob and say, ‘OK, we’re going to extend park jurisdictions way out into the national forest.’”
Rinella also had a message for hunters who may target the Mollie’s Pack: “I don’t hate you,” he said.
Facebook-posting hunters have threatened to go after the pack and specifically 12-year-old Wolf 1090F when the season begins today. A Nevada man who operates a Facebook page made bombastic threats to “shoot her at the back end so it will take 6 hours for the [wolf] to bleed to death.” And a Big Piney resident fond of AI imagery has tried to divert attention to his own Mollie’s Pack declarations, posting repeatedly about his own supposed hunting plans.
Those who seek to protect the Mollie’s Pack from hunting have also engaged in the social media theater, which has been amplified by the Wyoming news outlet Cowboy State Daily and other publications.
Disease outbreak cuts Wyoming, Yellowstone wolf numbers to lowest level since reintroduction era

Jonas Black, a Texas dog handler and social media influencer who became engaged in Wyoming wildlife controversies in the aftermath of the Cody Roberts felony animal cruelty wolf capture case, offered a $10,000 “bounty” payment to anyone who identified a Wyoming hunter who legally kills a Mollie’s Pack wolf. Black later withdrew the reward offer. (Wyoming has a statute protecting the identity of legal wolf hunters that’s been interpreted very broadly.)
“What this has turned into is a fiasco of passionate people on one side and passionate people on the other side, trying to out passion each other,” Game and Fish Large Carnivore Supervisor Dan Thompson said.
Amid the drama, Thompson and his fellow wildlife managers have been preparing for what’s shaping up to be a high-profile wolf hunting season opener. Where wolves are managed as trophy game in the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem, the season runs from tosday until the end of December.
Game and Fish officials have declined to discuss the location of Mollie’s Pack or any wolf pack with the hunting season fast approaching. But they’re cautioning wolf hunters who don’t want to kill one of the famous wolves and risk being doxxed, that just because Mollie’s Pack has mostly been in Yellowstone doesn’t mean that its members will stay there.
“We’re reluctant to say anything,” Thompson said. “These are unprecedented moves, so it’s hard to predict what may or may not happen.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas will bolster services for kids with disabilities after public outcry over long waitlist
description: Arkansas will provide additional support to children with disabilities who have been waiting for services, Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders said Tuesday, in response to growing demands from families for a special legislative session to address the issue.  Sanders announced that the Department of Human Services will provide supportive living services to families o[...]
text:
Susan Roberts uses a device hanging from their ceiling to help lift her 16-year-old son, TJ, into his bed on July 29, 2026. The device is covered by a Medicaid waiver for people with disabilities that need supportive living services. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas will provide additional support to children with disabilities who have been waiting for services, Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders said Tuesday, in response to growing demands from families for a special legislative session to address the issue. 
Sanders announced that the Department of Human Services will provide supportive living services to families on the waiting list for the Community and Employment Services Medicaid waiver. The department will also work on “additional long-term solutions for these families,” the Republican governor said in a news release.
More than 2,400 Arkansas families are waiting for health insurance coverage that will help them meet their children’s complex medical and non-medical needs.
“This will go a long way toward addressing the number one concern we hear from families about the CES waitlist,” Sanders said. “As we work to get this change in place, DHS is also convening relevant stakeholders and policymakers to create additional long-term solutions for these families.”
The move comes after families have taken to social media to highlight the waitlist and obstacles in receiving needed services, with posts that have been shared thousands of times.
The parents include Paige McCammon, who posted a Facebook video of her son Turner’s seizures on Sunday as part of the ongoing effort to bring Arkansas leaders’ attention to children with disabilities. Turner has severe epilepsy and a neurodegenerative condition.
“It has become easier to catch a seizure on video than it is not to, and that is a terrifying thing to be able to say about your 2-year-old,” McCammon wrote Saturday in another post.
Waitlist, policy changes stir worries among families of Arkansans with disabilities

Disabled Arkansans on the waitlist receive health insurance via the Provider-Led Arkansas Shared Savings Entity program, also known as PASSE, a managed-care Medicaid program the state implemented in 2018. As of Sept. 1, the four participating insurance companies cover 46,779 Arkansans, including those on the waiver, Department of Human Services spokesperson Gavin Lesnick said.
Families on the waitlist can receive most of the services available to people on the waiver, but one of the few exceptions and the one most requested is supportive living services, or affordable in-home care for people with disabilities.
The PASSEs should start providing supportive living services to families on the waitlist by January at the latest, and the state will incorporate the change into its request for the federal government to renew the waiver next year, according to the news release.
The changes will cost $17 million, and Sanders will meet with lawmakers to discuss short-term and long-term funding, the release states.
McCammon expressed her gratitude in a Tuesday Facebook post.
“We still have work to do,” she wrote. “But Arkansas, look at what happened when enough people decided this mattered and refused to be quiet about it.”
 Online advocacy

Some Arkansans, including Brintlee Cherry, included their numbers on the waitlist in their Facebook posts asking Sanders for help. Cherry’s daughter Eden is the 1,900th person waiting for services, and their insurance policy denied a request for a special needs stroller to keep Eden from running off in public, Cherry wrote on Facebook Sept. 3.
“Caregivers are physically and emotionally exhausted. People are crying out, and it feels like no one is listening,” said Cherry, who posted photos of the bruises she gets from trying to keep Eden with her. “But the squeaky wheel is about to get oiled. We are our children’s voices.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Shelby Brazeal’s teenage son is the 1,935th person on the waitlist, she posted Sept. 4, and he needs waiver services so he can live independently after high school and so at least one parent won’t have to stop working and care for him full-time.
“This isn’t about politics,” Brazeal wrote. “Just the greater good for those who cannot advocate or fully care for themselves.”
An online petition to gather support for a special session had 2,960 signatures as of Tuesday.
The effort ramped up in late August and early September after McCammon said Sanders called her and her husband in response to their advocacy. At the time, Turner was receiving care at Arkansas Children’s Hospital, and the Capitol was visible from his room.
Sanders told the McCammons that they and other families would likely have to wait until the Legislature’s regular session in January for officials to address the waitlist, but “she is looking into what can be done in the meantime,” McCammon wrote on Facebook Aug. 26.
A maximum of 8,233 Arkansans can receive supportive services from the waiver, and many families spend years on the waitlist. TJ Roberts, a 16-year-old from Bella Vista, was on the waitlist for 11 years and has been on the waiver since 2021. One of the supportive living services he’s received is a ceiling track in his family’s house that lifts him in and out of his wheelchair.
Susan Roberts, TJ’s mother, told the Advocate that she spreads awareness of the waiver program and encourages eligible families to apply because it isn’t widely known when it’s not receiving media attention.
“If it doesn’t directly impact you, you don’t tend to pay attention to it, but [now] I really think it’s putting us in a place where we have to talk about it,” said Little Rock Democratic state Rep. Denise Ennett, whose 18-year-old son is on the waiver.
Several Arkansas families plan to hold a news conference at the Capitol at 4 p.m. Wednesday to call further attention to the waitlist and their children’s needs. McCammon said Tuesday that the rally will go on as planned after Sanders announced impending new services for people on the waitlist.



Quotation







We still have work to do, but Arkansas, look at what happened when enough people decided this mattered and refused to be quiet about it.


– Paige McCammon, mother of a 2-year-old with complex disabilities


 Past efforts to help

In 2021, then-Gov. Asa Hutchinson directed $37.6 million toward disability support services in an effort to clear the waitlist, which had more than 3,000 people on it. All of those people received services by 2025, including Ennett’s son, who had been on the waitlist for eight years.
Besides Ennett, lawmakers expressing support for the families on the waitlist include Republican Rep. Rick Beck, who represents the McCammons in Morrilton, and Little Rock Democratic Rep. Ashley Hudson, who has also called for a special session.
“We should use a responsible portion of the surplus to fund additional waiver slots, and we should develop a long-term plan to make sure we don’t continue creating long waitlists for these vital services,” Hudson wrote on Facebook.
Arkansas ended the 2026 fiscal year June 30 with a $655 million budget surplus, nearly $300 million more than the previous year. The state has about $4 billion in reserves.
Before Hutchinson took executive action in 2021, the Legislature passed Act 1033 of 2019 directing the Department of Human Services to clear the waitlist, said Democratic Rep. Denise Garner, who was serving her first term in 2019.
Garner, who is now running for Fayetteville’s open state Senate seat, suggested in a Facebook post that Arkansas could fund some non-medical support services, such as respite and assistive technology, while people wait for full coverage.
“The goal shouldn’t only be to make the waiting list smaller,” Garner wrote. “The goal should be to make the waiting unnecessary.”
Garner also noted that services for children with complex medical needs require multiple solutions: state funding, a federal funding match, qualified healthcare professionals and a robust workforce in addition to open waiver slots.
The current workforce largely consists of parents like McCammon, who said she often misses work to care for Turner, and Roberts, who left a full-time job to care for TJ after he was born with cerebral palsy. The PASSE covering TJ’s healthcare pays Roberts $11 per hour, a recent decrease from $14 per hour.
Libertarian Colt Shelby, who is challenging Sanders in the governor’s race, has also called for the state to direct funding to clear the waitlist.
“If we’re not taking care of our most vulnerable children, we are failing as a state,” Shelby posted on Facebook.
State Sen. Fred Love, Sanders’ Democratic challenger, has promised to make children’s healthcare more accessible. As of Tuesday morning, Love had not responded to a request for comment about the waitlist and Sanders’ announcement.

title: Term-limited in role, Kentucky’s Comer to not seek another term as House Oversight chair
description: Kentucky U.S. Rep. James Comer will not seek another term as the chairman of the House Oversight Committee.  Comer, a Republican who represents the state’s 1st Congressional District, first became chairman of the committee in 2023. The committee gave him a second term starting in 2025.  Austin Hacker, a spokesperson for Comer, said that chairs […]
text:
U.S. Rep. James Comer and his wife TJ wave to the crowd during the Fancy Farm Picnic on Saturday, Aug 2, 2025. (Austin Anthony for the Kentucky Lantern)Kentucky U.S. Rep. James Comer will not seek another term as the chairman of the House Oversight Committee. 
Comer, a Republican who represents the state’s 1st Congressional District, first became chairman of the committee in 2023. The committee gave him a second term starting in 2025. 
Austin Hacker, a spokesperson for Comer, said that chairs are subject to term limits. The congressman “supports term limits and will not seek a waiver to continue serving as Chairman next Congress,” he added. 
Comer was first elected to the House in 2016. He is currently seeking reelection to his seat this November, but he is a rumored candidate for the Kentucky governor’s race next year. At the Fancy Farm Picnic in August, Republicans publicly rallied behind Comer and encouraged him to run for the office. Comer later said at the Kentucky Farm Bureau Ham Breakfast he’d likely make an announcement after the November election. 
Two high-profile Kentucky Democrats — Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and former state Rep. Rocky Adkins — have already launched their gubernatorial campaigns. 
Under Comer’s leadership, the House Oversight Committee has made national headlines for its fiery debates. In 2024, U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, asked if a committee member could discuss someone’s “bleach blond bad built butch body” after former U.S. Rep. Majorie Taylor Greene, R-Georgia, accused Crockett of wearing “fake eyelashes.” The committee has also led queries into Democrats, like Hunter Biden, the son of former President Joe Biden, and his laptop usage. Earlier this year, the committee held former President Bill Clinton and former U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton in contempt for refusing to testify as part of the committee’s investigation into convicted sex offender and financer Jeffery Epstein. 
Meanwhile, Democratic U.S. Rep. Morgan McGarvey, who represents Kentucky’s 3rd Congressional District, said in a Monday letter  to fellow members who have served less than five years in Congress that he is running for Democratic Caucus Leadership Representative. McGarvey was elected to the House in 2022. 
The position can “amplify the voices and priorities of newer Members directly to leadership,” said Caroline Rinker, a spokesperson for McGarvey. 
“He’s currently co-chair of the Future Forum Caucus, which is a generational caucus comprised of 53 young Members of Congress who focus on issues important to younger Americans,” she added.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Dem NM governor nominee Haaland raises another $3.4M in recent filings
description: Former U.S. Interior Secretary and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Deb Haaland’s latest campaign filings show she has raised roughly $3.4 million over the last several months, nearly four times as much as her Republican opponent Gregg Hull.
text:
New Mexico Democratic gubernatorial candidate Deb Haaland raised roughly $3.4 million between June 28, 2026, and Sept. 7, 2026, according to recent campaign filings, compared with approximately $934,000 that her Republican opponent Gregg Hull raised. (Joshua Bowling/Source NM)Former U.S. Interior Secretary and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Deb Haaland’s latest campaign filings show she has raised roughly $3.4 million over the last several months, nearly four times as much as her Republican opponent Gregg Hull. 
Still, Hull, a former Rio Rancho mayor, has seen increased donations in recent weeks, including after a poll late last month suggested the race is closer than expected. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Haaland’s campaign contributions, reported in a voluminous Monday filing to the New Mexico Secretary of State’s Office, show she has maintained her fundraising advantage with 50 days remaining until the Nov. 3 election.  The most recent reporting period captured activity between June 28 and Sept. 7. 
The Democrat, a former U.S. congresswoman who has a national profile after becoming the nation’s first-ever Indigenous cabinet secretary during Joe Biden’s presidency, hailed the filings in a statement Monday evening as proof of her grassroots support. 
“I know firsthand how hard people work to earn every paycheck, and I am deeply grateful for everyone who shares my vision for New Mexico,” she said.
In total, Haaland has raised more than $17.3 million from 446,000 individual contributions and spent nearly $13.8 million on her campaign. Over the last three months, she spent roughly $2.3 million, according to her filings. 
Hull reported a little over $930,000 in the most recent period, which represents roughly half of the approximately $1.9 million he’s raised over the course of his campaign. 
Still, Hull has seen an increase in donations in recent weeks, along with a large spike in financial contributions on Aug. 30, which is when the Albuquerque Journal released a poll of likely voters, 43% of whom said they planned to vote for the Republican compared to 49% for Haaland. 
The survey, which showed 8% of voters undecided, struck observers as a closer-than-expected race, including Brian Sanderoff, the president of Albuquerque-based Research & Polling Inc., which conducted the poll. 
Sanderoff told the Journal that the poll shows the race is “narrower than many people expected, including me,” but that Hull still had an “uphill battle” to defeat Haaland. 
The day the poll was published, Hull received roughly $51,500 from 146 donors. That marked his single-largest fundraising day in the most-recent reporting period.
Since the poll was released, Hull has raised nearly $2,100 a day. In the period before the poll, between June 28 and Aug. 30 he raised nearly $1,200 a day, according to a Source NM review. 
Hull did not respond to Source NM’s request for comment Tuesday, but he previously defended his fundraising shortfall compared with Haaland as reflective of his campaign strategy, which he said is focused on in-state campaigning and courting New Mexico-based donors. 
In the most recent filings, 1,862 of 1,925 donors to his campaign — roughly 97% — listed New Mexico addresses. 
Of roughly 75,000 donors who gave to Haaland this reporting period, a little more than 13,000 are from New Mexico, according to her filings.

description: Republican Paul LePage and Democrat Matt Dunlap, who are vying to represent Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, will debate at least twice in October.  LePage announced on Monday that he accepted invitations to debate on WMTW on Oct. 1 and on WABI on Oct. 15, after Dunlap agreed to those forums last week. WMTW’s main coverage […]
text:
Republican Paul LePage speaks at an Aug. 6 press conference at Maine Military Supply in Holden, where the NRA’s political arm announced its endorsement of the former governor in the race to replace Democratic U.S. Rep. Jared Golden. (Photo by Andrew Clark/ Maine Morning Star)Republican Paul LePage and Democrat Matt Dunlap, who are vying to represent Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, will debate at least twice in October. 
LePage announced on Monday that he accepted invitations to debate on WMTW on Oct. 1 and on WABI on Oct. 15, after Dunlap agreed to those forums last week. WMTW’s main coverage area is southern Maine, while WABI covers the central and eastern parts of the state. 
Dunlap, the state auditor, has called for four debates overall, but it remains unclear if others will be held. He and LePage, the two-term former governor of Maine, are competing to replace Democratic U.S. Rep. Jared Golden, who is not seeking reelection. 
Maine’s 2nd District, which covers most of the northern half of the state, is a top target for Republicans to flip in the 2026 midterm elections. Voters there have re-elected Golden, a moderate Democrat who frequently breaks with his party, while also voting for President Donald Trump in the last three presidential elections.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Assistant principal at New Haven’s Hillhouse High charged with sexual assault of student
description: Asst Principal Daniel Bonet turned himself in after police issued a warrant alleging he sexually assaulted an underage student during school hours.
text:
A Hillhouse High School assistant principal turned himself in for arrest on Monday night after police issued a warrant alleging that he sexually assaulted an underage student on two occasions during school hours.
The school district had placed the assistant principal, Daniel Bonet, on administrative leave on Tuesday, May 26, as he faced investigations from both the New Haven Police Department and the state Department of Children and Families.
According to a statement from the NHPD on Tuesday, the police department received a call about the allegations four days prior, on Friday, May 22, which preceded Memorial Day Weekend.
Bonet, 49, is now facing charges of two counts of sexual assault in the second degree and two counts of sexual assault in the fourth degree. His bond has been set at $250,000.
According to the NHPD’s statement, the student “disclosed two separate allegations of sexual assault which occurred on consecutive days in Bonet’s office after he arranged to be alone with her while school was in session.”
Detective Mariah Miller of the Special Victim Unit “was able to corroborate the victim’s account with video surveillance from the school which corroborated her accounts” as well as “statements with witnesses and staff members,” according to the statement.
Bonet did not respond to a request for comment in time for the publication of this story.
His lawyer, Don Cretella, wrote in an email to the Independent, “I was in court today, representing Mr. Bonet at his arraignment. Unfortunately, the court did not lower his bond and it remained as set at the police department at 250,000 Mr. Bonet is attempting to make bail.”
“I just received a copy of the warrant and have not had a chance to thoroughly review it,” Cretella wrote. “Once I do, Mr. Bonet and I will begin his defense.”
“At this point, we have no indication” of allegations that Bonet assaulted other students, said NHPD spokesperson Officer Christian Bruckhart — “not to say that there are no other victims, but at this point we only know of one.”
Hillhouse Principal Antoine Billy sent a letter to families affiliated with the high school on Tuesday announcing that a warrant for Bonet’s arrest had been issued.
NHPS spokesperson Justin Harmon wrote in a statement that, “We are working with our school social workers and specialized staff to support our students and staff. JHHS [James Hillhouse High School] and NHPS are committed to maintaining a healthy and supportive school community. Support is available for any students and staff who need it.”
“Nothing is more important than the safety of our students,” Harmon wrote. “Hillhouse families with questions or concerns have been invited to reach out to the school.”
Harmon said that Bonet continues to be on paid administrative leave. “We always put people on paid administrative leave when an allegation is made,” Harmon said. “What will happen next is currently being worked out.”
Mayor Justin Elicker said in a statement on Tuesday that “the allegations of sexual assault and the arrest of this school administrator are extremely disturbing and rightfully shock the conscience of every student, parent and educator at the Hillhouse High School community. Our schools must always be safe and supportive places where our students can learn, grow and thrive.”
“This individual will be held accountable for their actions to the fullest extent of the law,” Elicker wrote, “and New Haven Public Schools will be there to support this student and the larger school community during this difficult time.”
This is not the first time Bonet has been placed on leave while helming a New Haven public school. In January 2019, he was placed on temporary leave from his role as principal of John C. Daniels School due to allegations of staff harassment and non-compliance with DCF reporting mandates, allegations he denied. When Bonet was cleared to return to work, he was transferred to the assistant principal role at Hillhouse in August 2019.
The RAINN National Sexual Assault hotline provides resources for teens and families about how to recognize grooming and child sexual assault, and about how to support loved ones and community members through those experiences. The hotline is available 24/7 for survivors and loved ones who want to speak to a trained listener. Call (800) 656-HOPE or text HOPE to 64673.
This story was first published Sept. 15, 2026 by New Haven Independent.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: In New Hampshire’s 1st District, DiLorenzo and Shaheen face off in a consequential race
description: After winning their respective primary elections last week, Republican Anthony DiLorenzo and Democrat Stefany Shaheen will face off in November’s general election to see who will represent New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District. Both candidates call Portsmouth home and both present themselves as centrist options within their parties. DiLorenzo is a car d[...]
text:
Left: Anthony DiLorenzo speaks to supporters in the Music Hall Lounge in Portsmouth after winning the Republican nomination for New Hampshire's 1st Congressional District in the Sept. 8, 2026, primary. Right: Stefany Shaheen speaks to supports at an election results watch party in Portsmouth on Sept. 8, 2026. (Photos by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)After winning their respective primary elections last week, Republican Anthony DiLorenzo and Democrat Stefany Shaheen will face off in November’s general election to see who will represent New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District.
Both candidates call Portsmouth home and both present themselves as centrist options within their parties.
DiLorenzo is a car dealer with over a dozen locations who self-funded much of his campaign and earned the endorsement of President Donald Trump. He tried to paint himself as a pragmatic businessman from humble beginnings who can use his business acumen and previous successes to solve problems in Congress.
Voters hold signs of support for Maura Sullivan at primary watch party at To Share Brewery in Manchester after the Sept. 8 primary. Hours later, they learned that Stefany Shaheen had beaten their preferred candidate in the primary. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)
“My opponents talk about what they are going to do,” DiLorenzo said to a crowd of supporters in Portsmouth immediately after The Associated Press called his victory. “I want to talk about what I’ve done: building businesses, creating jobs, and giving back to my community — something I’ve done for over 35 years.”
Shaheen, the daughter of U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, served on the Portsmouth City Council and worked as a consultant for a Manchester biotech firm. Like many Democrats this cycle, she’s sought to center Trump, who has historically low approval ratings and has lost New Hampshire in three consecutive presidential elections. At an election watch party a couple blocks away from DiLorenzo’s, Shaheen echoed that messaging in a speech to supporters as election results were trickling in in her favor.
“This race has always, from day one, been about tackling the challenges that matter most to New Hampshire families,” Shaheen said. “It has meant the need and the focus to tackle and take on Donald Trump and his disastrous corruption, his endless war, his attacks on small business with these disastrous tariffs, the skyrocketing costs families are facing in New Hampshire and across the country.”
However, she suggested that messaging must go further.
“But let’s just be clear: It’s not enough to stop Trump’s damage,” Shaheen continued. “We have to do better than that. We have to give a reason for people to feel motivated and inspired and ready to show up between now and November, and that’s what we will do.”
The district covers the eastern half of the state, including Manchester, the Seacoast, and much of the Lakes Region. Since 2018, Chris Pappas has held the seat, but the Manchester Democrat is now his party’s nominee for New Hampshire’s open U.S. Senate seat. 
DiLorenzo beat out a slew of other conservatives including Hollie Noveletsky, who owns Novel Iron Works in Greenland and was once chair of the New Hampshire Republican Party, and State Rep. Brian Cole, who represents Manchester in the State House. DiLorenzo won with 51.7% of votes (per the AP as of Tuesday when 99% of votes had been counted) compared to Noveletsky’s 26.2% and Cole’s 14.1%. Two other candidates, Melissa Bailey and Lindsey Anderson, took less than 5% each.
DiLorenzo has dismissed questions about his lack of legislative experience: “I have exceptional experience, all sorts of different ranges of experience.”
Stefany Shaheen hugs her daughter at an election results watch party in Portsmouth soon before The Associated Press called the primary election for her. In the early hours of the next day, Sept. 9, 2026, she was declared the winner of the Democratic primary for New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
He also said he doesn’t plan on changing his campaign messaging much for the general election. During the primary, DiLorenzo weathered attacks from fellow Republicans that he wasn’t sufficiently conservative on issues such as abortion, where he opposes federal legislation on the issue, and immigration, where he’s suggested openness to pathways for citizenship.
Throughout the primary, though, the Republican candidates struggled to differentiate themselves.
“How do you break out from that field, right?” Noveletsky said in an interview. “When we’re all Republicans and we’re all really philosophically similar.”
In order to earn her spot on the general election ballot, Shaheen fought off another centrist, Marine Corps veteran Maura Sullivan, and a host of progressives led by Hampton Select Board member Carleigh Beriont. She walked away with 36.9% of the vote, narrowly edging Sullivan, who won 34.8% of the vote. Beriont took 22.5%.
GOP congressional candidate Hollie Noveletsky (foreground left) peeks over the shoulders of supporters at a TV displaying partial election results at a watch party at Novel Iron Works in Greenland on Sept. 8, 2026. Soon after, her opponent Anthony DiLorenzo was declared the victor. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Shaheen promised to fight for a single-payer Medicare for All system like many of her primary opponents. She also opposes the Trump administration’s tariff policies and, as the mother of a diabetic daughter, wants to make insulin prices a priority.
If elected, DiLorenzo would be the first Republican to represent New Hampshire in Congress in over a decade. Before Pappas first won the district in 2018, the seat had flipped between Republicans and Democrats in five consecutive elections. Political observers are now wondering whether the district soured on Republicans or if Pappas was a uniquely strong candidate. This election could provide insight into that question, but it will also have ramifications nationwide as the two parties battle for control of the House of Representatives.
“We all know the map to a Democratic Congress runs through New Hampshire,” Shaheen said. “And it runs through the 1st District, running through communities like Rochester and Merrimack and Derry.”
Shaheen is trying to extend the tenure of her politically powerful family. Her mother, Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, announced her retirement last year after 18 years in Congress. Before that, she was governor of New Hampshire for six years. If elected, the younger Shaheen will be sworn in at the same time her mother leaves office. The candidate is also the daughter of Billy Shaheen, an attorney and Democratic Party operative who was involved in helping Jimmy Carter win New Hampshire’s 1976 primary election and the White House. Since that 1976 election, he’s been a player in New Hampshire Democratic politics. With that, Stefany Shaheen has faced accusations of nepotism throughout her bid for Congress.
DiLorenzo is likely to highlight that dynamic over the next several weeks.
“Growing up in a working-class family, we often sat around the kitchen table talking about things, and I often dreamed about being successful,” DiLorenzo said. “And I never, ever imagined that I’d be up on stage talking about running for Congress. It’s a great country, America.”
Anthony DiLorenzo celebrates his primary victory as confetti flies over him in the Music Hall Lounge in Portsmouth after the Sept. 8, 2026, election for New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Bishop William Barber, NC faith leaders call for ‘conspicuous courage’ to combat voter confusion
description: One month before early in-person voting begins in North Carolina, civil rights leader and Repairers of the Breach President Bishop William Barber said voters should not fall victim to the confusion surrounding voting in the midterms. The Trump administration asked the U.S. Supreme Court to approve the president’s executive order restricting mail-in voting ah[...]
text:
Bishop William Barber, president of Repairers of the Breach and founder of the Moral Monday movement (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)One month before early in-person voting begins in North Carolina, civil rights leader and Repairers of the Breach President Bishop William Barber said voters should not fall victim to the confusion surrounding voting in the midterms.
The Trump administration asked the U.S. Supreme Court to approve the president’s executive order restricting mail-in voting ahead of the midterm elections, directing the postal service to refuse to deliver mail ballots to certain voters. Late Monday, the high court kept in place a lower court’s order blocking President Donald Trump’s plan to place new restrictions on mail ballots ahead of the Nov. 3 elections.
Voting rights advocates remain concerned that Homeland Security and ICE may dissuade some individuals from showing up at the polls.
Trump has called voting by mail a “hoax,” and he and Republican supporters claim more restrictions on it are needed to prevent election fraud in November. However, Trump himself regularly votes by mail, and study after study has found that mail-in voting fraud is extremely rare.


Upcoming election dates:
Oct. 9: Voter registration deadline.
Oct. 15: In-person early voting begins; same-day registration available. Vote Early in Person.
Oct. 20: Absentee ballot request deadline
Oct. 31: In-person early voting ends (3 p.m.).
Nov. 3: Election Day.
Source: NC State Board of Elections


Barber, founder of the Moral Monday movement, told reporters at a Monday press conference at Raleigh’s Martin Street Baptist Church this was all about creating confusion.
Trump won North Carolina in 2024 by 183,000 votes, but Barber said 1.2 million poor and low wage workers stayed on the sidelines and did not vote. If just 15% of the voters who didn’t cast a ballot two years ago were mobilized to vote in the midterms, the entire outcome could shift, said Barber.
Barber said extremists trying to cling to power are trying to sow confusion into the election process, even as North Carolina absentee ballots are being mailed out, in hopes that some potential voters will become discouraged and decide not to vote.
“What they’re doing is creating confusion where there has been no confusion. That’s what’s going on,” said Barber. “It’s not good for North Carolina. It’s not good for democracy. And lastly, they’re creating confusion that’s so bad that they’re hurting their own people.”
Barber said the only way to push back against the confusion surrounding the mail-in voting rules and other changes is to vote early and, if possible, in person.
More absentee ballots in NC in danger of being tossed under new directives

Barber and faith leaders announced in early August plans to mobilize 1,000 marches to the polls. Their goal is to engage with 5 million low-wage voters and at least 1 million Black men, particularly in the South. As of Monday, they had 320 marches organized in 23 states.
Rev. Dr. Hanna R. Broome said the country is facing a moral crisis when people in power try to make it harder for eligible voters to participate.
“You are telling somebody their voice is too much trouble to count,” said Broome. “And here’s what people behind these attacks are counting on – that no one will call it what it is. This is evil.”
Broome said the best way to combat that strategy  is to make a plan to vote, and volunteer to lead a local march to the polls.
Rev. Dr. Hanna R. Broome. (Photo: Repairers of the Breach video stream)
“Anyone  – your church, your organization, fraternity, sorority, lodge, barbershop, hair salon, or family reunion – can march or caravan to the polls,” said Broome.
Barber said the hope is that five people can organize 50, and that 10 people might have the power to encourage 100 more to vote. He calls such visible demonstrations “conspicuous courage” that will inspire infrequent or anxious voters to cast a ballot this fall.
Even though early voting hours and Sunday voting hours may shift in some counties this fall, he said voters must remain determined and vote en masse.
“What we’re not going to do is retreat,” said Barber. “Don’t you get weary. Know what side you’re on. You’re on the side of democracy.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Trump administration helps announce Hitachi Energy plans for $528M transformer factory in Copiah County
description: Gov. Tate Reeves says he believes Mississippi's SNAP payment error rate will fall below 8% before the end of September. Reeves also says workforce development should be part of efforts to reduce dependence on federal assistance.
text:
Hitachi Energy is investing $528 million to build a new transformer factory in Copiah County, with plans to create 654 jobs. 
Gov. Tate Reeves announced the development on Tuesday morning from the G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial in Houston, alongside President Donald Trump administration leaders. 
Federal leaders emphasized that the Zurich-based company’s investment is a part of Trump’s “energy dominance” agenda and goal to bring back American manufacturing.
“This is bigger than just one factory announcement,” said U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, chairman of the National Energy Dominance Council.  “This is about America’s determination to build the infrastructure to win the intelligence race, to power the next generation of American manufacturing and to bring prosperity and affordability to American citizens.”
Reeves said: “This administration is doing the work to bring back jobs to America because in Mississippi just like in America this what we do. We make stuff. We build stuff.”
The plant would be Hitachi Energy’s largest investment in America and is part of the company’s total $1.5-billion investment across the U.S. to increase production of transformers and other grid infrastructure to meet energy demand. The company is a subsidiary of multi-billion dollar Japanese firm Hitachi, Ltd.
Trump has said that he wants the U.S. to be the leader in energy production and exports. 
According to the company, the transformers produced in Mississippi will bring additional capacity to help growing demand for electricity. Consulting company Mckinsey has estimated that the U.S. demand for power will increase by 3.5% annually through 2040. 
“America needs more affordable, reliable and secure electricity generation, and this new investment by Hitachi will help make that happen,” said Secretary of Energy Chris Wright. “The Trump Administration welcomes today’s announcement of a Hitachi transformer manufacturing facility that will provide jobs to local Mississippi communities while also helping improve electricity reliability and affordability for millions of Americans.”
Hitachi Energy has been in Mississippi for 70 years, but this investment would double the size of its existing operation. The company will build the new factory on a 45-acre site at the Copiah County Industrial Park in Gallman. Construction is expected to begin later this year with production to start in 2029.
Reeves called it a historic day for the U.S., Japan and Mississippi, emphasizing Mississippi’s existing relationship with other Japanese companies such as Toyota and Nissan. 
“Hitachi could’ve picked any state in the country. They chose Copiah County. They chose Mississippi,” Reeves wrote on social media.

title: State Land Office says New Mexico’s renewable energy brings in revenue, offsets environmental harm
description: Renewable energy projects leased on state land are expected to bring in billions of dollars for New Mexico in the years to come, State Land Office officials told legislators Monday. The 55 active green energy projects, such as solar and wind farms, brought in $8 million in revenue this year, a 1,287% increase from 2019, […]
text:
New Mexico State Land Office officials shared projected revenue from renewable energy sources such as solar with legislators during the Sept. 14, 2026, meeting of the interim Revenue Stabilization and Tax Police committee meeting.  (Photo by Anna Padilla for Source New Mexico)Renewable energy projects leased on state land are expected to bring in billions of dollars for New Mexico in the years to come, State Land Office officials told legislators Monday.
The 55 active green energy projects, such as solar and wind farms, brought in $8 million in revenue this year, a 1,287% increase from 2019, they said. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Around 12% of all land in New Mexico is managed by the State Land Office, which offers bonds for leases of the land for various projects: energy, commercial development and agriculture. The office generated $16 billion in eight years.
Though the renewable energy revenue may seem small now compared to the $3.1 billion that went into the state permanent fund last year from oil and gas revenues, the projected revenue on just existing leased projects, not including pending or future leases, will bring in $2.5 billion by 2040, State Land Office Deputy Commissioner Sunalei Stewart told lawmakers on the interim Revenue Stabilization and Tax Policy Committee during their meeting at the state Capitol.
Moreover, Stewart said, those renewables will offset air pollution equivalent to the carbon emissions of 380 million barrels of oil.
Stewart said the long projection time stems from renewable energy projects having a different life span when compared to oil and gas projects. While oil and gas leases generate massive revenues in the short term and decline over a long period, renewable energy leases are “the inverse,” Steward said, due to the “initial phase” of building renewable energy: securing the capital, acquiring the lease for the plant site and building the infrastructure. 
The long-term nature of building renewable energy infrastructure left some lawmakers concerned about the possibility of energy developers failing during the long lifespan of solar and wind farms, which would leave the state with the decommission costs. 
“I think you’re putting us at risk,” Sen. George Muñoz (R-Gallup) said.
Steward noted that the State Land Office’s lease agreements include decommissioning costs.
The state is also planning to expand the geothermal energy sector. In May, the State Land Office published a new rule that would allow for larger projects to be developed on state lands. Last year, Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham touted the state as a potential leader for geothermal energy, following a report about its potential here.
“New Mexico is primed to attract additional renewable energy business,” Steward told state lawmakers. “We’re beginning to see the state investment council do more renewable energy investments because they’re seeing the value in it.”

name: Delaware
title: Officer’s quick response removes loaded handgun from Glasgow High
description:
The Delaware State Police arrested a 17-year-old Glasgow High School student, from Newark, Delaware, on firearm and related charges after a loaded handgun was discovered in his backpack Monday afternoon. […]
The post State Police Arrest Glasgow High School Student After Loaded Gun Found in Backpack appeared first on Delaware State Police - State of Delaware.
text:
Photo caption: Delaware State Police released this photograph of the loaded handgun investigators said was recovered from a 17-year-old Glasgow High School student’s backpack.
The incident demonstrates the value of having trained law enforcement officers inside schools, where an immediate response can prevent a dangerous situation from escalating.
NEWARK, Del. — A Delaware State Police school resource officer deserves credit for helping bring a potentially dangerous situation at Glasgow High School under control Monday and removing a loaded handgun from the building.
The officer was already inside the school when a hallway fight was reported at about 1 p.m. Sept. 14. Working with school staff, the officer separated the students and began investigating what had happened.
That investigation led to the backpack of a 17-year-old student from Newark. Police said the student had removed the backpack before the fight and that the officer learned it allegedly contained marijuana.
A search uncovered a loaded handgun and a small quantity of marijuana, according to Delaware State Police.
The student was taken into custody and transported to an area hospital for treatment of injuries sustained during the fight. Police described the injuries as not life-threatening and said no other injuries were reported.
After being discharged, the student was taken to Delaware State Police Troop 2 and charged with possession of a firearm by a person under 21, possession of ammunition by a person under 21, possession of a firearm in a safe school zone, possession of a firearm during the commission of a felony and possession of marijuana by a person under 18.
Four of the five charges are felonies.
The student, whose name was withheld because he is a juvenile, was arraigned by Justice of the Peace Court and committed to the Delaware Department of Services for Children, Youth and Their Families in lieu of an $87,000 cash bond.
Officer’s presence made a difference
It is impossible to know what might have happened if the backpack had not been searched or if the loaded handgun had remained inside the school. What is clear is that the school resource officer was in the building, responded immediately and had the training and legal authority to investigate.
The result was not merely an arrest. It was the removal of a loaded firearm from a school before the situation became more dangerous.
The incident offers a practical reminder of why trained officers belong in schools. Their presence provides an immediate response to violence, allows suspicious behavior to be investigated and creates a visible warning that weapons and criminal activity can be detected.
Deterrence does not mean every student will follow the law or that no weapon will ever enter a school. It means increasing the likelihood that violations will be discovered and addressed quickly. At Glasgow High, that system worked.
Research on the overall effects of school resource officer programs remains mixed, and properly trained officers must avoid becoming involved in routine disciplinary matters that belong with educators. But federal research also recognizes that school officers can support safety through law enforcement, problem-solving, community relationships and crisis response.
The National Institute of Justice has found that school resource officers often perform several overlapping roles in maintaining a safe learning environment. Justice Department-supported research has also documented cases in which officers intervened before planned school violence could be carried out.
Those broader debates should not obscure what happened Monday. A fight drew an immediate response. An officer followed the evidence. A loaded handgun was found. Students and staff were protected from the risk posed by a firearm inside their school.
That is public safety at its most direct, and it is why the officer’s work should be recognized.
To Go Box

What happened: Delaware State Police said a school resource officer recovered a loaded handgun and marijuana from a 17-year-old student’s backpack.
Where: Glasgow High School, 1901 S. College Ave., Newark.
When: About 1 p.m. Monday, Sept. 14.
Student’s status: The student was committed to the Department of Services for Children, Youth and Their Families on an $87,000 cash bond.
Learn more: Read the Delaware State Police report and review the National Institute of Justice’s research on school resource officers.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi Republicans warn of the red menace, even as Comrade Trump breaks out the Marx-Engels playbook
description: President Donald Trump speaks at the Republican convention Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026, in Dallas.
text:
A national trend of Republican candidates warning that Democrats are a bunch of Bolsheviks trying to turn the U.S. into the USSR has trickled down to Mississippi, with some of our GOP politicians warning of the red menace in the midterms.  
But Mississippi McCarthyites seeking reelection to Congress or other offices might want to look inward, to the current administration they appear to support without question. As they seek to root out socialists and communists on the Mississippi midterm ballot, Comrade President Donald J. Trump appears to have broken out the Marx-Engels playbook. He’s been pushing to seize the means of production, redistribute wealth and institute what appears to be socialist-leaning market and price controls.

“If you elect a Democrat, you’re going to elect a socialist party,” Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Ezell told Mississippi Today recently. “Anybody that votes for a Democrat, that’s what we’re going to get.”
But if Ezell’s Democratic opponent, state Rep. Jeffrey Hulum, is a fellow traveler, he must be one heck of an embedded sleeper agent. Retired Army Sgt. Maj. Hulum, a 22-year combat veteran, has shown no overt socialist or communist leanings in his nearly five years in the Legislature nor in his congressional race platform.  
That’s exactly what commie sleeper agents do. Better keep an eye on him.
But despite their vocal fears of the creep of socialism and communism into American government, Ezell and his fellow Republicans in Mississippi’s congressional delegation have been noticeably quiet about what critics and analysts have called “Trump socialism,” or “state capitalism.”
A Wall Street Journal column recently opined that Trump is “imitating the Chinese Community Party by extending political control ever deeper into the economy.” The libertarian think tank the Cato Institute has noted the “irony” of the Trump administration denouncing the left for socialism while it seizes federal equity stakes in private businesses and implements centralized planning. 
The Trump administration has taken federal government equity stakes in more than two dozen companies. It has converted federal grants into stock and taken “golden shares” of private companies. The federal government has created quite a venture investment portfolio, seeking control production in industries including nuclear power, semiconductors, steel, minerals and quantum computing.
The pretense for federal government control of private companies has been national security and to — kid you not — promote innovation.
Anyone who believes socialism or communism promotes product innovation should go out and buy a Lada automobile.
The real corker is the potential U.S.-Venezuelan oil “deal.” The term deal here means the U.S. taking another country’s oil production at gunpoint, ousting one dictator and installing another and cooking up a deal in secret without approval from the elected legislatures of either country for the U.S. government to seize more control of the global oil market.
But don’t worry, Trump is full of proposals to redistribute wealth to the workers, although his promised checks have a way of not ever showing up in the bank accounts of the proletariat.
Back home in Mississippi, our Republican politicians appear unperturbed and unimpressed by this. Instead, they are trying to create a new Red Scare for Mississippi voters to shun those commie Democrats in the midterms and next year’s statewide elections.

“This November 3rd, we must rally and defeat the Marxist Communists, Democratic Socialists and Red-Green alliance …” wrote Republican Agriculture Commissioner and gubernatorial candidate Andy Gipson. “Standing with President Trump, we will never let the enemies of freedom win!”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Blaze engulfs vacant commercial building in Jackson; no injuries reported
authors: Aaron Lampley, Simeon Gates and Sophia Paffenroth
description: The Jackson Fire Department was dispatched to 1030 Mill Street at about 5:30 a.m., Tuesday, September 15, 2026 in Jackson, Miss.
text:
An early morning blaze engulfed the old Midtown Center located on Mill Street in downtown Jackson Tuesday, causing extensive damage but no injuries, fire officials said..
The Jackson Fire Department was dispatched to 1030 Mill Street at about 5:30 a.m. Crews arrived to heavy smoke and flames.
Division Fire Chief of Investigations Charles Felton confirmed the building was vacant and there were no injuries.
“At this time, I do not have any information as to how long it’s been vacant. We do know it’s been vacant for some time. But the definite time frame we do not have,” Felton said.
The cause of the fire is under investigation.
The fire broke out near a residential neighborhood and not far from the Midtown Head Start Center on East Fortification Street.
Luckily, the childcare facility was not in operation, said Nita Norphlet-Thompson, the executive director of the Mississippi Head Start Association. The building is under construction, according to Norphlet-Thompson.
“Currently, that center is under renovation and probably won’t be open until the 1st of the year,” Norphlet-Thompson told Mississippi Today.  
Capitol Police closed off nearby streets near the fire zone, as water from firetrucks slickened streets.
